- Root: ف-ر-ع (F-R-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Branching off from a trunk; subsidiary offshoots (furūʿ) stemming from a principal root (aṣl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Jurisprudential derivative rulings that ramify from a foundational legal axiom.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical branching; metaphorical for legal sub-questions (masāʾil) derived from a core doctrine.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Protasis-Apodosis Structure (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The phrase "إن أبطلنا" sets a hypothetical condition, with the apodosis "فعليه فروع أربعة" governing the ensuing enumeration; subordinate "وجهان" clauses are parenthetical disjunctives requiring precise coordination.
chapters.translation:
I say: If we invalidate the purchase [of a Muslim slave by an infidel], then upon it are four subsidiary branches.

The first branch concerns pledging (rahn) and hiring (ijārah) [of the slave by the infidel purchaser]. There are two views: one holds it valid, since neither involves ownership (milk); the second holds it prohibited, because seizing [the slave] for benefit and detention constitutes degradation (idhlāl). If we affirm the validity of hiring, then is the infidel compelled to hire him out to a Muslim? There are two views: one says it is obligatory upon him, as in the case of purchase; the second says no, for when a Muslim works for a wage, there is no degradation therein—it is as though he works for himself. The more appropriate (al-awlā) view is the permissibility of pledging and hiring, just as in deposit (īdāʿ) and lending (iʿārah). As for hiring that falls upon the dhimmah (i.e., a contractual obligation of service), there is no disagreement regarding its validity.

The second branch: If a Muslim purchases a Muslim slave for an infidel, it is not valid. But if an infidel purchases [a slave] for a Muslim—if he explicitly attributes the purchase to the Muslim, it is valid; if he conceals the intent, then there are two views, built upon whether the contractual liability (ʿuhdah) attaches to the agent (wakīl).

The third branch: If a Muslim purchases a Muslim slave from an infidel with a garment, and the infidel then discovers a defect in the garment, then regarding his returning it so that the slave reverts to him, there are two views: one says no, because he is seeking to acquire ownership through his own choice (ikhtiyār); the second permits it, for the choice lies in the return—whereas the reversion of the counter-value (ʿiwaḍ) to him occurs by necessity and compulsion. Likewise, if the Muslim discovers a defect in the slave, then regarding his returning him [to the infidel], there are two views, because he is prevented from transferring ownership (tamlīk) just as the infidel is prevented from it. Then, if we prevent the return, the compensation for defect (arsh) becomes fixed, and that constitutes a preventing excuse (ʿudhr māniʿ).

The fourth branch: If the slave were an infidel and then embraced Islam before taking possession (qabḍ), does the contract dissolve (yanfasikh) as it dissolves upon death, or is an option (khiyār) established as it is established upon flight (ibāq)? There are two views, and likening it to flight is more appropriate. This applies if he purchased him from a Muslim. But if he purchased him from an infidel, then regarding dissolution there are two subordinate views (wajhān murattabān), and the more appropriate is that it does not dissolve—because however the matter turns, [the slave] reverts to an infidel [if the contract is voided], so the presumption of continuity (istisḥāb) is more fitting. If we rule that the contract remains, then does the infidel take possession of him, after which he is sold on his behalf, or does the judge appoint a deputy to take possession on his behalf, lest the slave be degraded by the infidel's grasp? There are two views. And if we build upon the view of validity [of the original purchase], then he is sold on his behalf after his possession, or after the judge's possession on his behalf, in either manner. Likewise, whenever a slave embraces Islam during the continuance of ownership [by an infidel], if he dies before the sale, he is sold on behalf of his heir, and the demand for his manumission (iʿtāq) is cut off from him. And everything that removes ownership (izālat al-milk) [cuts off this demand], but it is not cut off by marriage (tazwīj), pledging (rahn), or hiring (ijārah). Does it cut off by kitābah (manumission contract)?—even though it does not remove ownership immediately, due to its leading to removal and the imposition of interdiction (ḥajr) in the present—there are two views, and the more appropriate is to suffice with it. And if [the infidel] is content with mere separation between them [i.e., the slave and his family], that does not suffice—except in the case of the umm walad (slave-mother of his child), for her sale is impossible and her manumission is a loss; so she is made to earn for his sake in the hands of another. It was said that she is manumitted upon him, but that is remote.

---

### The Third Pillar: The Object of Contract (al-Maʿqūd ʿAlayh), namely the Sold Item (al-Mabīʿ)

It has five conditions: that it be pure (ṭāhir), beneficial (muntafaʿ bih), owned by the contracting party or by the one on whose behalf the contract is made, capable of delivery (maqdūr ʿalā taslīmih), and known to the two contracting parties.

### The First Condition: Purity (al-Ṭahārah)

It is not permissible to sell dung (sirqīn) or any other impure substances (aʿyān najisah), contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah. The relied-upon position of the school (muʿtamad al-madhhab) is the consensus (ijmāʿ) on the nullity of selling wine (khamr), carrion (jīfah), and filth (ʿadharah). The benefit of filth is fertilizing the earth; the benefit of carrion is feeding it to birds of prey; the benefit of wine is its transformation into vinegar—just as a newborn infant becomes beneficial in adulthood. Thus, there is no cause for the nullity of their sale except impurity (najāsah).

### Branch

As for impure animal fat (wadak) into which impurity has fallen: if we rule that its washing is possible, then its sale is permissible; otherwise, it is built upon the permissibility of burning it for illumination (istiṣbāḥ), concerning which there are two positions. The basis for prohibition is the spread of its impure smoke, with the impossibility of guarding against it. And by impurity is explained, according to al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—the prohibition of selling dogs and swine. The report (khabar) has also come regarding this. Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik said: its sale is valid; but the swine is not sold, by agreement. And whatever is generated from a dog and a swine, or from one of them and a pure animal, has their ruling in the nullity of sale.

### The Second Condition: That It Be Beneficial

For by this is realized financial value (māliyyah). That which has no benefit is of three categories:

The first: benefit is dropped due to its insignificance (qillah), like a single grain of wheat—that which has no perceptible benefit in itself except by attaching something else to it. Its sale is null, and whoever destroys it owes nothing, for it has no value. Al-Qaffāl said: upon him is its equivalent (mithl) if it belongs to the class of fungibles (dhawāt al-amthāl); others disagreed with him.

The second: its benefit is dropped due to its baseness (khissah), like the crawling creatures of the earth—beetles and scorpions. As for the cat, the elephant, and the bee, they have benefit, so their sale is permissible. The lion, the leopard, and beasts of prey that are not hunted have no benefit; but regarding them, and regarding the donkey whose legs are broken, there is a view that is not objectionable: that their sale is valid for their skins—unlike the skin of carrion, which is not sold due to its impurity, not due to lack of benefit. Regarding the sale of the leech (ʿalaq)—which has the benefit of sucking blood—and of poison that is only useful for killing, there is hesitation. The more appropriate is validity. The basis for prohibition is that such benefit is not regarded, for one might benefit from a single grain placed in a bird-trap, and such is not counted.

It is permissible to sell human milk, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, for it is pure and beneficial, and it is not a human being [in legal status]. It is permissible to sell water on the seashore and to sell a rock on the mountains, due to the existence of benefit—though one may dispense with them due to their abundance. Likewise the sale of earth. It was said that water cannot be owned, but that is remote.

The third: that whose benefit is dropped by sacred law (sharʿan), like musical instruments (maʿāzif) and whatever is for a prohibited purpose and is not fit for anything else. For that prohibited benefit, legally, is like what is non-existent perceptually. However, if it is broken fragments (ruḍāḍah)—with the kasrah of the ḍād, after supposing the breaking—that are valuable (mutamawwal), then regarding the validity of its sale in reliance upon that [value], there are three views. The most apparent (al-aẓhar) is that if it is of gold, silver, wood, or something precious, it is valid—because it is an intended object, so the purpose of craftsmanship (ṣināʿah) predominates. But if it is of [ordinary] wood, then no—because the intent is tied to the craftsmanship, so the sale cannot be relied upon for anything else. Regarding the sale of the qunyah (a bird kept for companionship) and the ram sought for butting, there is discussion that we shall mention.

chapters.title_en: The Third Condition: That the Object Be Owned by the Contractor
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الشرط الثالث أن يكون مملوكا للعاقد

فبيع الفضولي مال الغير عندنا باطل وقال أبو حنيفة يقف على إجازته وهو
قول قديم لم يعرفه العراقيون ونص الشافعي رضي الله عنه على قولين فيمن غصب
أموالا واتجر فيها وتصرف في أثمانها أحدهما بطلان البياعات وتتبعها بالنقض
وهو قياس المذهب والثاني أن المالك بالخيار فان شاء أجاز واخذ الأثمان
وتعليله بالمصلحة والحاجة لعسر تتبع التصرفات المتعاقبة

### | فرع

لو قال اشتريت لزيد وهو ليس بوكيل لم يقع عن زيد وهل يقع عنه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لان الفاسد إضافته فتخصص بالإفساد ويبقى قوله اشتريت
والثاني لا وهو الأولى لان الكلام يعتبر جملة وهو لم يشتر شيئا لنفسه
أصلا
فان قيل لو باع مالا على ظن انه ملك الغير فإذا هو ملكه هل يصح قلنا نقل
العراقيون قولين فيما إذا باع مال أبيه على ظن انه حي فإذا هو ميت فالقياس
صحته والظن الخطأ لا أثر له ووجه المنع أن مقتضى لفظه من حيث قرينة الحال
تعليق البيع على الموت وان أتى بصيغة التنجيز فلا يكون بعبارته معربا عن
تنجيز الملك في الحال وهو لا يعتقد لنفسه ملكا

### | الشرط الرابع أن يكون مقدورا على تسليمه حسا وشرعا

ومستنده النهي عن بيع الغرر والعجز الحسي في الضال والآبق والمغصوب

### | فروع

ثلاثة الأول بيع السمك في الحوض الواسع المسدودة المنافذ والطير المفلت
في دار فيحاء الذي يقدر عليه ولكن بعد عسر وتعب فيه وجهان أحدهما لا لان
مثل هذا التعب لا يحتمل في غرض البيع فلا نظر إلى القدرة بعد تحمله والثاني
وهو الأولى الصحة لأنه مقدور عليه ومستند هذا الشرط النهي عن بيع الغرر
وهذا موثوق به بالا  لا غرر فيه
الثاني بيع حمام البرج نهارا وعادته أن تأوي إلى البرج ليلا فيه وجهان
أحدهما الجواز كالعبد الغائب ثقة بعوده الطبيعي والثاني المنع لان الغرر
ظاهر في عوده بخلاف العبد وهو الأولى إذ الاشتغال بأسباب التسليم من طلب
العبد ممكن وها هنا لا طريق إلى الانتظار على غرر الثالث المغصوب الذي يقدر
المشتري على استرداده دون البائع فيه خلاف لتعارض القدرة والعجز من
الجانبين والأولى الصحة إذا المقصود التسليم وهو ممكن في نفسه
نعم لو كان المشتري جاهلا فله الخيار إذا البيع لا يكلفه تعب الانتزاع
وان كان عالما فله الخيار أن عجز وإلا فلا أما المعجوز عن تسليمه شرعا فهو
المرهون فبيعه باطل وفي بيع الدار المكراة خلاف سيأتي وفي بيع العبد الجاني
جناية تعلق الارش برقبته قولان أحدهما المنع كالرهن وأولى فانه أقوى من
وثيقة الرهن ولذلك يقدم الأرش إذا جنى العبد المرهون
والثاني الصحة وهو الأولى لأنه لم يحجر على نفسه وجناية العبد لا تحجر
عليه في ملكه وتصرفه لكن يثبت متعلقا في رقبته إن رغب السيد عن
فدائه ليكون عصمة لحقه بقدر الضرورة أما إذا استوجب العبد القطع بالسرقة
أو بالقتل بالردة فيصح بيعه إذ لا ارش وفي القتل الموجب للقصاص خلاف مرتب
على أن موجب العمد ماذا وعلى كل حال فهذا أولى بجواز البيع لان الدية غير
متعينة للوجوب

### | التفريع

أن حكمنا بفساد البيع ففي الإعتاق خلاف كما في الرهن وان حكمنا بالصحة
فلو كان معسرا بالفداء فالظاهر المنع وفيه وجه منقاس انه يصح ولكن يثبت
الخيار للمجني عليه وان كان موسرا مهما امتنع الفداء بسبب من الأسباب أما
السيد ففي ثبوت الخيار له وجهان ووجه الإثبات انه لم يصرح بالتزام الفداء
فلا يلزمه وله دفع الطلبة عن نفسه بالفسخ
وهذا بعيد عند علمه بجناية العبد فانه بالتزام التسليم إلى المشتري التزم
الفداء فليؤاخذ بهما ولكن لو كان جاهلا فيظهر إثبات الخيار له

### | فرع

إذا باع نصفا من نصل أو سيف أو آنية  ينقصها التبعيض فهو باطل لان البيع
لا يلزم بنقيض غير المبيع والشرع قد يمنع منه إذا كان فيه إسراف فيتقاعد
البيع عن إيجاب التسليم ولو باع ذراعا من كرباس لا تنقص بالقطع قيمته فيه
وجهان ذهب صاحب التلخيص إلى المنع لأنه غير ممكن إلا بتغيير عين المبيع
والبيع لا يلزمه ولعل التصحيح أولى

### | الشرط الخامس أن يكون معلوما للمتعاقدين

والعلم يتعلق بعين المبيع وقدره ووصفه مرتبة من مراتب العلم العلم بالعين
وهو شرط فلو باع عبدا من عبيده أو ثوبا من ثيابه أو شاة من قطيعه لا على
التعيين بطل لما فيه من الغرر الذي يسهل اجتنابه ولان العقد لم يجد موردا
يتأثر به في الحال فأشبه النكاح
وقال أبو حنيفة لو قال بعت عبدا من العبيد الثلاثة ولك خيار التعيين صح
ولم يصحح في الثياب ولا فيما فوق الثلاثة ولا دون شرط الخيار
وفساد هذه التحكمات بين
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-ل-ك (m-l-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ownership, possession, dominion over a thing; the state of having lawful authority over property.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ownership (milk) as a legal capacity entitling one to exclusive disposal (tasarruf); contrasted with mere physical custody.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of lawful dominion; metaphorical (majāz) usage would be figurative claims of control.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Dependency (Taʿlīq al-Sharṭ) — the validity of an act is suspended upon the fulfillment of its stipulated condition, affecting the syntactic-semantic force of the contract.
chapters.translation:
I say: The sale by an unauthorized person (al-fuḍūlī) of another's property is, in our school, void. Abū Ḥanīfah held that it is suspended pending the owner's ratification — a position that the Iraqis did not recognize. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly stated two opinions regarding one who seizes goods by usurpation (ghaṣb), trades with them, and disposes of their proceeds: The first is the nullity of all such sales, which are to be pursued and rescinded — this being the analogical corollary of the school (qiyās al-madhhab). The second is that the owner has the option: if he wishes, he may ratify and take the proceeds. This latter is justified by consideration of public interest (maṣlaḥah) and necessity, given the difficulty of pursuing a succession of successive transactions.

### | Sub-Branch

If one says, "I purchased for Zayd," while not being his agent, the purchase does not fall to Zayd. As to whether it falls to the speaker himself, there are two views: The first is yes, because the defective element is the attribution (al-iḍāfah), which is thereby nullified, leaving intact his statement "I purchased." The second is no — and this is the preferable view — because speech is considered as a whole, and he did not purchase anything for himself at all.

If it is objected: Suppose one sold property under the mistaken belief that it belonged to another, and it turned out to be his own — is the sale valid? We reply: The Iraqis transmitted two opinions regarding one who sold his father's property believing him to be alive, when in fact he was dead. The analogical ruling is validity, for a mistaken assumption has no effect. The ground for prohibition is that the import of his utterance, in light of the contextual indication (qarīnat al-ḥāl), suspends the sale upon death — even though he uttered the formula of immediacy (ṣīghat al-tanjīz). Thus his expression does not signify the immediate transfer of ownership at that moment, since he does not believe himself to own it.

### | The Fourth Condition: That the Object Be Deliverable, Both Physically and Legally

Its basis is the prohibition of selling uncertain goods (gharar), and physical incapacity in the case of a stray animal, an escaped slave, or usurped property.

### | Sub-Branches

Three. First: The sale of fish in a wide pond whose outlets are sealed, or of a bird let loose in an open courtyard — where one can obtain it, but only with difficulty and exertion. There are two views: The first is invalidity, because such exertion is not tolerable within the purpose of sale; no consideration is given to capacity once such burden is involved. The second — and this is the preferable view — is validity, because it is within one's power. The basis of this condition is the prohibition of selling gharar, and this is reliable, for there is no gharar in it.

Second: The sale of a dovecote pigeon by day, when its habit is to return to the dovecote by night. There are two views: The first is permissibility, like an absent slave whose natural return is trusted. The second is prohibition, because the uncertainty regarding its return is manifest, unlike the slave — and this is the preferable view, for pursuing the means of delivery, such as seeking the slave, is possible, whereas here there is no way to await its return without uncertainty.

Third: Usurped property which the buyer can recover but the seller cannot. There is disagreement here due to the conflict of capacity and incapacity from both sides. The preferable view is validity, for the purpose is delivery, which is possible in itself. However, if the buyer was ignorant, he has the option (khiyār), for the sale does not oblige him to bear the burden of forcible recovery. If he was aware, he has the option only if he proves unable; otherwise not.

As for what is legally incapable of delivery, it is the pledged item (al-marhūn); its sale is void. Regarding the sale of a rented house, there is disagreement to come. Regarding the sale of a slave who has committed an offense (jināyah) entailing compensation (arsh) attached to his neck, there are two opinions: The first is prohibition, like the pledge — indeed more so, for it is stronger than a pledge security, which is why the arsh takes precedence when a pledged slave commits an offense. The second is validity — and this is the preferable view — because the owner has not placed a restriction upon himself, and the slave's offense does not restrict him in his ownership and disposal. Rather, the arsh attaches to the slave's neck if the master declines to ransom him, serving as a safeguard for the claimant's right to the extent of necessity.

But if the slave has incurred amputation for theft, or execution for apostasy, his sale is valid, for there is no arsh involved. As for homicide warranting retaliation (qiṣāṣ), there is disagreement dependent upon whether the intentional act entails what — and in any case, this is more apt for permissibility of sale, for the blood-wit (diyah) is not definitively established as obligatory.

### | Ramification

If we rule the sale void, then regarding manumission there is disagreement as in the case of the pledge. If we rule it valid, then if the seller is insolvent for the ransom, the apparent ruling is prohibition; there is an analogized view that it is valid, but the victim acquires the option. If he is solvent, then whenever he refuses the ransom for any reason — as for the seller, there are two views on whether he has the option. The ground for affirming it is that he did not explicitly commit to the ransom, so it is not binding upon him, and he may repel the claim against himself by rescission. This is remote when he knew of the slave's offense, for by committing to deliver the slave to the buyer, he committed to the ransom, and he should be held to both. But if he was ignorant, affirming the option for him is manifest.

### | Sub-Branch

If one sells half of a blade, a sword, or a vessel whose division diminishes its value, the sale is void, for the sale does not oblige the delivery of what is other than the sold item, and the Law may prohibit it when it involves wastefulness (isrāf); thus the sale falls short of effecting delivery. If one sells a cubit of cloth (karbās) whose value is not diminished by cutting, there are two views. The author of al-Talkhīṣ held prohibition, because it is impossible except by altering the very substance of the sold item, and the sale does not oblige that. Perhaps validity is preferable.

### | The Fifth Condition: That the Object Be Known to the Two Contracting Parties

Knowledge pertains to the essence of the sold item, its quantity, and its description — each being a rank of knowledge. Knowledge of the essence is a condition. Thus, if one sells a slave from among his slaves, a garment from among his garments, or a sheep from his flock, without specification, the sale is void — due to the gharar therein, which is easily avoided, and because the contract finds no specific object upon which it takes effect at once, resembling marriage (nikāḥ).

Abū Ḥanīfah held that if one says, "I sold one of the three slaves, with you having the option of specification," it is valid — but he did not deem it valid for garments, nor for more than three, nor without the condition of the option. The corruption of these arbitrary distinctions is manifest.

chapters.title_en: Three Subsidiary Branches and the Third Rank: Knowledge of Quantity
chapters.arabic_text: ### | فروع ثلاثة أحدهما لو قال بعت صاعا من هذه الصبرة وهي معلومة الصيعان صح قطعا وان كانت مجهولة فوجهان يبتنيان على العلتين إن عللنا بان مورد العقد لم يتأثر به في الحال بطل هذا العقد فان الإبهام موجود ههنا وفي صورة العلم بعدد الصيعان ينزل على الإشاعة حتى لو تلف نصف الصبرة انفسخ العقد بتلفه في ذلك القدر والباقي يخرج على قولي تفريق الصفقة وهذا اختيار القفال وهو الأصح وان عللنا بان الإبهام منع لأجل الغرر فلا غرر ها هنا لتساوي أجزاء الصبرة بخلاف العبيد وبخلاف ما إذا باع ذراعا من ارض لا على التعيين فان الغرض يختلف فيه باختلاف الجوانب ويلزم عليه التصحيح إذا باع قدر صاع من جملة الصبرة وقد فرقت صيعانها وبه استشهد القفال ويبعد تصحيحه واستشهد بأنه لو قال بعت منك هذه الصبرة إلا صاعا وهي مجهولة الصيعان بطل فأي فرق بين استثناء المعلوم من المجهول واستثناء المجهول من المعلوم والإبهام يعمهما وفي الفرق غموض الثاني إذا اشترى قطعة من الأرض محفوفة بملك البائع فان صرح بإثبات الممر ثبت حق الاجتياز من كل جانب إلا إذا كان أحد جوانبها متاخما للشارع أو ملك المشترى فالعرف خصص المرور به وان خصص بجانب من الجوانب لا على التعيين فسد للإيهام وتفاوت الأغراض وان صرح بنفي الممر ففي صحة البيع ولا منفعة للمبيع دون الممر وجهان أظهرهما الصحة إذا التوصل إلى الانتفاع بشراء الممر واستعارته واجارته ممكن وان سكت عن ذكر الممر فطريقان أحدهما انه يقتضي الممر من كل جانب اعتمادا على العرف والثاني انه يخرج على الوجهين كما إذا نفى الممر لأنه ساكت عنه الثالث لو عين جانبا من الأرض وباع عشرة اذرع ولكن لم يذرع حتى يتبين مقطع الملكين في العيان ففيه وجهان أظهرهما الصحة للتعيين وانتفاء الغرر ووجود العيان ولو باع الصوف على ظهر الحيوان ولم يعين المقطع فسد لان العادة تتفاوت في مقادير الجز بخلاف الكراث فان العادة في جزه تتقارب ولو قبض على كتلة وعين المجز صح وفيه احتمال لأنه يتعين به عين المبيع خلاف الأرض والشجر فان الجز والقطع لا يغيرهما ### | المرتبة الثالثة العلم بالقدر أما إذا كان في الذمة فلا بد من التقدير سواء كان نقدا أو عرضا فلو قال بعت بما باع به فلان فرسه أو ثوبه أو بزنة هذه الصنجة لا يصح لأنه غرر مجتنب يسهل دفعه ولا بد من تعريف جنسه وإذا تعارضت النقود لا بد من التعريف فإن غلب واحد كفى الإطلاق وان غلب في العروض جنس واحد ففي الاكتفاء بالإطلاق اعتبار بالنقد أو اشتراط الوصف نظرا إلى أن الأصل في العروض التفاوت وجهان ### | فروع ثلاثة الأول إذا قال بعت منك هذه الصبرة بعشرة دراهم وهي معاينة غير معلومة الصيعان صح وكذلك إذا باع بصرة معاينة من الدراهم لان العيان هو المنتهي عرفا في العقود ولو قال بعتك الصبرة كل صاع بدرهم صح وان كانت مجهولة الصيعان ولم يكن مبلغ جملة الثمن معلوما لأنه إذا رأى جنس المبيع وعرف قدر ثمن كل صاع فقد انتفى الغرر وسلك طريق معرفة الربح والخسران الثاني إذا قال بعتك هذه الصبرة بعشرة على أن أزيدك صاعا فان أراد به التبرع بالزيادة فهو شرط هبة في بيع فيفسد وان أراد إدخاله في المقابلة بالثمن فان كانت معلومة الصيعان صح وان كانت الصبرة عشرة أصيع فمعناه صاع وعشر بدرهم وان كانت مجهولة لم يصح لأنه لا يدري اشترى بدرهم صاعا وعشرا أو صاعا وتسعا أو ما يتردد فيه فيكون الثمن مجهول الجملة والتفصيل فان قيل فإذا تردد اللفظ بين الاحتمالات فكيف يصح العقد بمجرد إرادة صورة الصحة قلنا يلتفت هذا على الأصح في انعقاد البيع بالكناية الثالث إذا باع سمنا في بستوقة تتفاوت أجزاؤها في الغلظ والدقة او صبرة على ارض فيها حفر متفاوتة فهذا يبطل فائدة العيان في تخمين المقدار لا في معرفة الصفقة ففيه ثلاث طرق قال الشيخ أبو علي في مجموعه وجهان في أن البيع يصح لان معرفة المقدار بعد العيان لو كانت شرطا لما صح البيع بصبرة من الدراهم مرتبة غير موزونة وهذا غريب لم يذكره في شرحه الثانية أن العقد باطل قطع به بعض المحققين لان غرره كغرر الجهل بالصفة وقد تعذر تخريجه على بيع الغائب لان الرؤية حاصلة فمتى يثبت الخيار أو كيف يلزم دون الخيار وهذا هو المشهور الثالثة وهو المنقاس تخريجه على بيع الغائب فانه لا يتقاصر عما إذا قال بعتك الثوب الذي في كمي فان فيه قولين فكذلك ها هنا وهذا وجه التخريج اختاره الشيخ أبو محمد ثم قياسه أن يقال معرفة المقدار بالوزن أو برؤية الدكة وقت ثبوت الخيار كما أن معرفة الصفة بالرؤية وقته في بيع الغائب ### | ### | التفريع أن أبطلنا العقد فلو نظر إلى صبرة ولم يدر أن تحتها دكة فعقد اعتمادا على اعتقاده فظهرت دكة فهل يتبين بطلان العقد أم يقتصر على الخيار وجهان اختار الشيخ أبو محمد الأبطال لان معرفة القدر تحقيقا أو تخمينا شرط وقد تبين فقد الشرط والثاني انه يصح اعتمادا على الاعتقاد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ز-ز (j-z-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cutting, shearing, clipping (esp. wool from an animal); the act of severing at the surface.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes extraction of a benefit from a substrate, implying a defined locus of severance; in sale, it marks the boundary of the transferred object.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical shearing; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to legal determination of a cut-off point in a transaction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Dependency (Taʿlīq al-Sharṭ) — The validity of a ruling hinges on the stated cause (ʿillah); when the cause is absent, the ruling is inverted, as seen in the dual-basis analysis of the indeterminate sale.
chapters.translation:
I say: Three subsidiary branches [follow].

**First Branch:** If a man says, “I sold you a ṣāʿ from this heap,” and the heap’s measure of ṣāʿs is known, the sale is valid unequivocally. But if it is unknown, there are two views, built upon the two causes [for invalidating indeterminate sales]. If we ground [the prohibition] on the fact that the object of the contract is not affected by it at the present moment, then this contract is void—for indeterminacy (ibhām) exists here. Yet in the case where the number of ṣāʿs is known, [the sale] is construed as a fractional share (ishāʿah); thus, if half the heap perishes, the contract is dissolved to that extent, and the remainder follows the two opinions on splitting a single bargain (tafrīq al-ṣafqah). This is the choice of al-Qaffāl and is the more correct [view].

But if we ground [the prohibition] on the claim that indeterminacy is barred due to hazard (gharar), then there is no hazard here, for the parts of the heap are uniform—unlike slaves, and unlike the case where one sells a cubit of land without specification, for the purpose varies with the sides. It follows necessarily that the sale is validated when he sells the measure of a ṣāʿ from the whole heap, even if its ṣāʿs have been differentiated. Al-Qaffāl adduced evidence for this, though its validation is remote. He argued: if a man said, “I sold you this heap except a ṣāʿ,” while its ṣāʿs are unknown, it would be void. So what difference is there between excepting the known from the unknown and excepting the unknown from the known? Indeterminacy encompasses both, and in the distinction there is subtlety.

**Second Branch:** If one buys a plot of land surrounded by the seller’s property, then if he explicitly stipulates the establishment of a passage, the right of passage is affirmed from every side—unless one side adjoins the public road or the buyer’s own property, for custom (ʿurf) then restricts the passage to that side. But if he specifies a side without determination, the sale is void due to ambiguity and the divergence of purposes. If he explicitly negates the passage, there are two views on the validity of the sale, given that the sold object has no utility without a passage. The more apparent of the two is validity, since access to benefit is possible by purchasing, borrowing, or renting a passage. If he remains silent about the passage, there are two paths: one, that it entails a passage from every side, relying on custom; the second, that it follows the two views as when he negates the passage, because he is silent about it.

**Third Branch:** If one specifies a side of the land and sells ten cubits, but does not measure it until the boundary between the two properties becomes evident by direct sight (ʿiyān), there are two views. The more apparent is validity, due to specification, the absence of hazard, and the presence of direct sight. But if one sells the wool on an animal’s back without specifying the shearing point, the sale is void, for customary practice varies in the amounts of shearing—unlike leeks, for the custom in cutting them is uniform. If one grasps a clump and specifies the sheared portion, it is valid, though there is a possibility [of invalidity], because the very object of sale is thereby determined—unlike land and trees, for shearing and cutting do not alter them.

**The Third Rank: Knowledge of Quantity**

As for [a sale] against one’s liability (dhimmah), quantification is indispensable, whether it be specie or commodity. Thus, if one says, “I sold [it] for what so-and-so sold his horse for,” or “his garment,” or “for the weight of this scale,” it is not valid—for it is hazard (gharar) to be avoided, easily obviated. Its genus must be defined. When currencies conflict, definition is required; if one [currency] predominates, the unqualified expression suffices. If in commodities one genus predominates, there are two views: whether the unqualified expression suffices, by analogy to currency, or whether description is required, considering that the norm in commodities is variation.

**Three Subsidiary Branches:**

**First:** If one says, “I sold you this heap for ten dirhams,” while it is seen but its ṣāʿs are unknown, the sale is valid. Likewise, if one sells a seen pile of dirhams [for a lump sum], for direct sight is the customary terminus in contracts. And if one says, “I sold you the heap, each ṣāʿ for a dirham,” it is valid even if the ṣāʿs are unknown and the total price is not known—for when he sees the genus of the sold object and knows the price of each ṣāʿ, hazard is removed, and he has a path to knowing profit and loss.

**Second:** If one says, “I sold you this heap for ten, on condition that I add a ṣāʿ to you,” then if he intends the addition as a gift, it is a stipulation of a donation in a sale, and the sale is corrupted. But if he intends to include it in the exchange for the price, then if the heap’s ṣāʿs are known, it is valid—if the heap is ten ṣāʿs, its meaning is “a ṣāʿ and a tenth for a dirham.” If it is unknown, it is not valid, for he does not know whether he bought, for a dirham, a ṣāʿ and a tenth, or a ṣāʿ and a ninth, or something fluctuating—so the price is unknown in total and in detail. If it is said, “When the wording wavers between possibilities, how can the contract be valid merely by intending the form of validity?” We reply: this turns upon the more correct view regarding the formation of a sale by indirect expression (kināyah).

**Third:** If one sells butter in a vessel whose parts vary in thickness and thinness, or a heap on ground with uneven hollows, this nullifies the benefit of direct sight in estimating the quantity—though not in knowing the bargain. Here there are three paths. Shaykh Abū ʿAlī stated in his Compendium two views on whether the sale is valid, for if knowing the quantity after sight were a condition, then a sale of a pile of dirhams, stacked but unweighed, would not be valid. This is odd, and he did not mention it in his Commentary. The second [path]: the contract is void, as some verifiers decisively held, for its hazard is like the hazard of ignorance of a quality; and it cannot be derived from the sale of an absent thing (bayʿ al-ghāʾib), for sight has occurred—so when would the option (khiyār) be established, or how would it bind without an option? This is the well-known [view]. The third [path], which is the analogically derived one, is to derive it from the sale of an absent thing—for it is no less than if he said, “I sold you the garment in my sleeve,” which has two opinions. So too here. This is the mode of derivation chosen by Shaykh Abū Muḥammad. Then its analogy requires that knowledge of quantity be achieved by weighing or by seeing the platform (dukkah) at the time the option is established, just as knowledge of quality is achieved by sight at that time in the sale of an absent thing.

**Subsidiary Derivation (Tafrīʿ):**

If we declare the contract void, then [consider]: a man looked at a heap and did not realize that beneath it was a platform; he contracted relying on his belief, and the platform then appeared. Is the contract revealed to be void, or is it limited to an option? There are two views. Shaykh Abū Muḥammad chose invalidation, for knowledge of quantity—whether by exact measure or by estimation—is a condition, and the condition’s absence has become manifest. The second [view]: it is valid, relying on his belief.

chapters.title_en: The Third Rank: Knowledge of Attributes by Way of Vision (al-Ruʾyah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | المرتبة الثالثة العلم بالصفات بطريق الرؤية

وفي  اشتراطه في الشراء قولان وفي الهبة قولان مرتبان وأولى بالا يشترط
لأنه ليس من عقود المغايبات ليبعد عن الغرر
وذهب المزني إلى الإبطال لان الغرر المجتنب الذي يسهل إزالته يبطل العقد
لنهيه عن بيع الغرر
ولا خلاف أن الشم والذوق في المشموم والمذوق غير مشروط لان الرؤية اعظم
طريق يعرف به جميع الأشياء فالصفات المرئية تدل على جميع المقاصد الخفية
غالبا واضطرب الأصحاب في مسألتين
إحداهما البائع إذا باع ما لم يره منهم من قال فيه قولان مرتبان وأولى
بالبطلان لان الخيار بعيد عن البائع قاله المراوزة وقيل أولى بالصحة لأن
المشترى محصل والبائع معرض والمتملك بالاحتياط أجدر قاله العراقيون واصح
المذهب البطلان في الشراء والبيع جميعا
ثم أن صححنا بيع الغائب ففي ثبوت الخيار له عند الرؤية وجهان أصحهما
الثبوت كالمشتري وقيل لا يثبت لان جانبه بعيد عن الخيار
ولذلك إذا ظن المبيع معيبا فإذا هو سليم لا خيار له وان استضر به
وهذا يبطل بخيار المجلس والشرط فانهما يشتركان فيه وهذا من جنسه
الثانية في شراء الأعمى طريقان ينشآن على أن التوكيل بالرؤية والفسخ هل
يجوز وفيه وجهان أحدهما المنع لأنه رأي مجرد فصار كما إذا أسلم على عشر
نسوة ووكل بالاختيار والثاني الجواز كالتوكيل بالرؤية والشراء
فان جوزنا بالتوكيل خرج شراؤه على القولين وإلا قطعنا بالبطلان إذ لا
سبيل إلى الإلزام ولا إلى خيار لا منتهى له
وفي قبضه بالهبة والدين خلاف مرتب على شرائه وأولى بالصحة لأنه فعل يبعد
عن الغرر ولو عمى بعد شراء الغائب فقلنا لا توكيل في الرؤية انفسخ العقد
لاستحالة التقييد
وصحح الشافعي رضي الله عنه سلم الأعمى فقال المزني لم يرد به إلا كمه
لأنه لا يعرف الصفات
ومن الأصحاب من خالفه لأنه يتخيل فرقا بين صفات الرداءة والجودة

### | التفريع

أن فرعنا على قول اشتراط الرؤية فعليه ثلاث مسائل
المسألة الأولى أن استقصاء الأوصاف على وجه يفيد الإحاطة بالمقاصد هل
يقوم مقام الرؤية فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لحصول ثمرتها وهي المعرفة
والثاني لا إذ الرؤية تطلع على دقائق لا تحيط العبارة بها
الثانية رؤية بعض المبيع تقوم مقام رؤية الكل إذا كان المرئي يدل على
الباقي كظاهر صبرة الحبوب والمائعات هذا إذا كان متصلا
فان رأى منه أنموذجا ولم يدخل في البيع فهو كاستقصاء وصف المبيع والأصح
وهو اختيار الشيخ أبي محمد انه لا يقوم مقام الوصف في السلم لان اللفظ
والوصف هو المرجع عند الأشكال في السلم
وان ادخل في البيع صح على اختيار القفال وهو الأصح وفيه وجه
وان كان المرئي لا يماثل الباقي نظر فان كان صلاح الشيء في إبقائه مستورا
كحب الرمان ولب الجوز واللوز وأمثاله كفى رؤية الظاهر للحاجة وما ليس كذلك
يخرج على بيع الغائب

### | فروع أربعة

الأول القشرة العليا من الجوز الرطب منهم من جعله مانعا للاستغناء عنه
ومنهم من ألحقه بالسفلى ففيه مصلحة إبقاء الرطوبة والظاهر أن النشرة العليا
من الباقي تكفي رؤيتها لان الرطوبة فيها مقصودة
والثاني الفأرة من المسك كالمسح من النوري والجلد من اللحم
فلا يكفي النظر إليه إذ لا يتعلق به كثير صلاح والمسك نفيس فلا يحتمل ذلك
فيه اعتيادا
وقال صاحب التقريب إذا لم تكن الفأرة مفتوحة يحتمل إلحاقها بقشرة الجوز
ثم
إذا أدخلت الفأرة في البيع خرج على نجاسة الفأرة والصحيح أنها طاهرة
تشبيها بالبيضة فان الطبية تلقي بطبعها في كل سنة واحدة والمسك كان احب
الطيب إلى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فلا يليق بالشرع تنجيس طرفه وقيل
انه نجس لأنه جزء مبان من حي
الثالث الديباج المنقش لا يدل أحد وجهيه على الآخر والأصح أن الكرباس يدل
أحد وجهيه على الآخر وفيه وجه اعتبارا لأحد الوجهين بأحد النصفين
المسألة الثالثة الرؤية السابقة كالمقارنة إذا كان الشيء مما لا يتغير
غالبا خلافا لأبي القاسم الانماطي لان المقصود المعرفة

### | فرعان

أحدهما إذا اقدم على العقد على ظن انه لم يتغير على الغالب فكان قد تغير
على الندور فيتبين بطلان العقد لتبين انتفاء المعرفة أم يكتفي بالخيار
لبناء العقد على ظن فيه خلاف
الثاني إذا قال المشتري تغير ولي الخيار وأنكره البائع قال صاحب
التقريب القول قول البائع إذ الأصل عدم التغيير وقال الخضري بل الأصل عدم
لزوم الثمن والأول اصح
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-أ-ي (r-ʾ-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Visual perception; ocular sight; also opinion and deliberation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The most complete epistemic avenue for apprehending existents; in legal context, the direct sensory ground for contractual consent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical sight; metaphorical (majāz) for intellectual discernment—here anchored to the literal.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis Ellipsis (ḥadhf al-sharṭ) — legal rulings are framed as apodoses with implicit conditions, requiring the translator to preserve the conditional logic of the juristic discourse.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third rank concerns knowledge of attributes by way of vision (al-ruʾyah). Regarding its stipulation in purchase, there are two positions; and in gift, two positions, arranged hierarchically. The more preponderant view is that it is not stipulated, for this is not among contracts of unseen things (ʿuqūd al-mughāyabāt) that would be remote from hazard (gharar). Al-Muzanī, however, held the view of nullification, for the hazard that is avoided—that which is easily removable—nullifies the contract, due to his (peace be upon him) prohibition of the sale of hazard. There is no disagreement that smell and taste are not stipulated in the case of what is smelled and tasted, for vision is the greatest avenue by which all things are known; visible attributes generally indicate all hidden purposes. The companions (al-aṣḥāb) differed on two questions:

The first: when a seller sells what he has not seen—among them are those who said there are two positions, arranged, with the preponderance toward nullification, because the option (khiyār) is remote from the seller; this was stated by the Marāwizah. And it was said: the preponderance is toward validity, because the buyer obtains his object while the seller is merely divesting, and the one who acquires ownership is more deserving of caution; this was stated by the ʿIrāqiyyūn. The sounder view of the school is nullification in both purchase and sale alike.

Then, if we validate the sale of the absent thing, there are two aspects regarding the establishment of the option for him upon seeing it—the sounder of which is its establishment, like the buyer. And it was said: it does not establish, for his side is remote from the option. For this reason, if he supposes the sold item defective and it turns out sound, he has no option even if he is harmed thereby. But this is refuted by the option of the session (khiyār al-majlis) and the stipulated option, for both parties share in these—and this is of that genus.

The second: regarding the purchase of the blind man, there are two paths branching from whether deputization (tawkīl) for vision and rescission is permissible. On this there are two aspects: one is prohibition, because it is a bare opinion, becoming like one who embraces Islam upon ten women and deputizes for the choice; the second is permissibility, like deputization for vision and purchase. If we permit deputization, his purchase proceeds on the two positions; otherwise we decisively rule nullification, since there is no path to binding him nor to an option without end.

Regarding his taking possession by gift and debt, there is a disagreement arranged upon his purchase—and the preponderance is toward validity, because it is an act remote from hazard. If he becomes blind after purchasing the absent thing, and we say there is no deputization in vision, the contract is dissolved due to the impossibility of restriction.

Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) validated the blind man's salam (advance sale), but al-Muzanī said he intended thereby only his being blind, because he does not know the attributes. Some companions opposed him, for he imagined a distinction between attributes of defect and those of quality.

### | Subdivision (al-Tafrīʿ)

If we branch upon the position stipulating vision, then three questions follow:

The first question: Does exhaustive description of attributes—in a manner that yields comprehension of the purposes—stand in place of vision? On this there are two aspects: one is yes, because its fruit is attained, namely knowledge; the second is no, for vision discloses subtleties that expression cannot encompass.

The second: The vision of part of the sold item stands in place of vision of the whole when the seen part indicates the remainder—like the apparent surface of a heap of grain and liquids. This applies when it is contiguous. If he saw a sample from it that was not included in the sale, it is like exhaustively describing the sold item. The sounder view—and it is the choice of Abū Muḥammad—is that it does not stand in place of description in salam, for the word and description are the reference at points of ambiguity in salam. But if the sample was included in the sale, it is valid upon the choice of al-Qaffāl—and this is the sounder—though there is another aspect. If the seen part does not resemble the remainder, then consider: if the thing's soundness lies in its being kept concealed—like pomegranate seeds, walnut and almond kernels, and the like—then seeing the exterior suffices due to necessity. What is not so proceeds upon the sale of the absent thing.

### | Four Branches

The first: The upper shell of the fresh walnut—among them are those who made it a barrier to dispensing with it, and among them are those who annexed it to the lower shell, for in it lies the benefit of preserving moisture. The apparent view is that seeing the upper shell of the remainder suffices, for the moisture in it is intended.

The second: The musk pod (al-fārah) is like the leather from the fur, and the skin from the meat—so looking at it does not suffice, for no great benefit attaches to it, and musk is precious and does not tolerate that customarily. The author of al-Taqrīb said: if the pod is not opened, it is plausible to annex it to the walnut shell. Then, if the pod is included in the sale, it branches upon the impurity of the pod. The correct view is that it is pure, by analogy to the egg—for the musk deer naturally casts it every year—and musk was the most beloved perfume to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), so it befits not the Sacred Law to declare its extremity impure. And it was said: it is impure, because it is a part severed from a living being.

The third: Embroidered brocade—one of its faces does not indicate the other. The sounder view is that coarse cloth (karbās) has one face indicating the other, though there is an aspect considering one of the two faces by analogy to one of the two halves.

The third question: Prior vision is like concurrent vision when the thing does not generally change—contrary to Abū al-Qāsim al-Anmāṭī—for the purpose is knowledge.

### | Two Branches

The first: If one proceeds upon the contract with the presumption that it has not changed in the usual course, and it had in fact changed rarely, does the contract become null because the absence of knowledge is revealed, or is the option sufficient, since the contract was built upon presumption? There is a disagreement on this.

The second: If the buyer says, "It has changed, and I have the option," while the seller denies it, the author of al-Taqrīb said: the seller's word is accepted, for the default is absence of change. Al-Khaḍarī said: rather, the default is that the price is not binding. The first is the sounder.

### | التفريع على صحة بيع الغائب أربع مسائل

الأولى إذا اشترى منديلا نصفه في صندوق لم يره قطع المزني بالإبطال فيما
نقله نصا ومن الأصحاب من تكلف له وجها وهو أن إثبات الخيار في النصف تخصيصا
محال والتعميم إثبات في المرئي فيؤدي إلى تناقض الحكم ومنهم من جعل هذا بيع
غائب وهو الاقيس فان موجب الخيار في البعض تسليط على رد كل المبيع كالعيب
بأحد العبدين فالتعميم غير ممتنع
الثانية بيع اللبن في الضرع باطل فانه انضم إلى عدم الرؤية العجز عن
تمييز المعقود عليه عن غيره إذا اللبن في العروق ينصب إلى الضرع وقت الحلب
فيختلط به وكذلك لو رأى منه أنموذجا وغلط الفوراني إذ ذكر في الأنموذج
وجهين نعم لو قبض على قدر من الضرع واحكم شده فوجهان منهم من حسم الباب لان
الاطلاع على عدم الاختلاط غير ممكن والشد قد يكون سبب حركة الطبيعة وانصباب
اللبن
وكذلك إذا باع اللحم في الجلد قبل السلخ فهو باطل لأنه أن باع دون الجلد
فلا يمكن تسليمه إلا بتغيير الجلد
وبشقه ثقبه غالبا وان باع مع الجلد قطع الشيخ أبو علي بالبطلان ووجهه
اتصال المقصود بما ليس بمقصود على وجه لا يمكن تحصيل المقصود إلا بتغيير
وتصرف في الجلد بالسلخ والصحيح تخريجه على القولين
أما بيع الروس والاكارع المسموطة مع النظر إلى الظاهر فجائز على القولين
فان الجلد في حكم جزء يؤكل منه
الثالثة إذا صححنا بيع الغائب فقد اتفق الاكثرون على انه لو قال بعت منك
ما في كمي ولم يذكر الجنس لا يجوز وهو ظاهر مذهب أبي حنيفة
وفيه وجه منقاس انه يجوز بحصول التعيين بالإشارة ثم للأصحاب طريقان قالت
المراوزة لا يشترط شيء سوى ذكر الجنس كقوله بعت العبد الذي في البيت
فلو استقصى  الأوصاف فهل يسقط الخيار لقيام الوصف مقام الرؤية فعلى الخلاف
السابق
قال العراقيون يشترط ذكر النوع مع الجنس قطعا وهو أن يقول عبدي التركي
وهل يشترط استقصاء الأوصاف حتى ينعقد بيع الغائب على خيار الرؤية فعلى
وجهين والطريقتان متباعدتان
الرابعة يثبت الخيار في بيع الغائب بالرؤية وله الفسخ قبل الرؤية وفي
الإجازة قبلها وجهان أظهرهما أنها لا تصح لان الرضا قبل حقيقة المعرفة ولو
تصور لحصل بقوله اشتريت فليس في قوله أجزت زيادة عليه

### | فرع

لو رأى ثوبين ثم سرق أحدهما من البيت وهو لا يدري أن المسروق أيهما
فاشترى الثوب الباقي فقد اشترى معينا مرئيا وقد وقعت المسألة في الفتاوى
فقلت أن تساوى صفة الثوبين وقدرهما وقيمتهما كنصفي كرباس واحد صح العقد
وان اختلف شيء من ذلك خرج على قولي بيع الغائب لأنه ليس يدري أن المشترى
خمسة اذرع مثلا أم عشرة ورؤيته السابقة لم تفد العلم بقدر المبيع ووصفه في
حالة البيع فلا اثر لها
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في فساد البيع بجهة الربا - صلى
الله عليه وسلم -
المبيع إذا كان ربويا اشترط في عقده وراء ما ذكرناه من الشرائط السابقة
في الباب الأول ثلاث شرائط
التماثل بمعيار الشرع والحلول ونعني به منع الأجل والسلم ووجوب التقابض
في مجلس العقد
هذا إذا بيع الربوي بجنسه فإن بيع بربوي آخر يشاركه في العلة التي هي
قرينة الجنسية يسقط اشتراط التماثل وبقي اشتراط التقابض والحلول
وأنكر أبو حنيفة رحمه الله شرط التقابض إلا في عقد الصرف
وان بيع بما لا يدخل في الربويات سقطت هذه الشرائط كلها
ومعتمد الباب ما روى الشافعي رضي الله عنه بإسناده عن مسلم بن يسار ورجل
آخر عن عبادة بن الصامت عن النبي عليه السلام انه قال لا تبيعوا الذهب
بالذهب والورق بالورق والبر بالبر والتمر بالتمر والشعير بالشعير والملح
بالملح إلا سواء بسواء عينا بعين يدا بيد فإذا اختلف الجنسان فبيعوا كيف
شئتم يدا بيد
أوجب عند التجانس ثلاثة أمور وعند اختلاف  الجنس أوجب التقابض ونفي السلم
بقوله يدا بيد
والربا في النقدين عندنا معلل بكونهما جوهري الأثمان فيتعدى إلى الحلي
وكل ما يتخذ منهما ولا يتعدى إلى غيرهما وكذلك عند مالك وقال أبو حنيفة
معلل بالوزن والجنسية
وعلة الربا في الأشياء الأربعة عندنا الطعم والجنس
وقال أبو حنيفة العلة مركبة من الكيل والجنسية ومذهب ابن المسيب أن العلة
هي الطعم في الجنس والتقدير وهو قول قديم للشافعي رضي الله عنه
والجنسية عندنا محل العلة فهي بمجردها لا تحرم النساء بل يجوز إسلام
الثوب
في جنسه خلافا لأبي حنيفة ويجري الربا عندنا في دار الحرب خلافا له
وإذا اشترى الشيء بأقل مما باعه نقدا صح العقدان عندنا
وقال مالك بطل العقدان لأنه ذريعة إلى الربا
وقال أبو حنيفة بطل العقد الثاني
وأدلة هذه المسائل مستقصاة في الخلاف
والنظر الآن إنما يطول في الربا الفضل فان التقابض وتحريم النسيئة فرعان
له يجريان في كل عينين جمعتهما قرينة الجنسية من النقدية أو الطعم والكلام
يتعلق بأطراف

- Root: غ-ي-ب (gh-y-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Absence, concealment from perception; that which is hidden from sight.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The unseen (al-ghayb) as that which lies beyond sensory apprehension, entailing juridical uncertainty in transactions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical absence from view; metaphorical (majāz) — absence of full specification (taʿyīn) even if partially seen.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The protasis (law/ idhā) governs the apodosis, requiring precise parsing of hypothetical juridical cases where the condition determines the ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: The ramifications upon the validity of selling an unseen object comprise four questions.

**The First:** If one purchases a cloth, half of which lies within a chest that he has not seen, al-Muzanī decisively ruled its nullity, as he transmitted this as an explicit text (naṣṣ). Among our companions (al-aṣḥāb) there are those who labored to devise a juridical basis (wajh) for this, namely: that affirming the option (al-khiyār) with respect to the half would be a specification (takhṣīṣ) that is impossible, while generalizing it would affirm [the option] over what was seen, leading to a contradiction in the ruling. And among them are those who deemed this a sale of an unseen object (bayʿ al-ghāʾib) — and this is the more analogically sound (al-aqyas) — for the entailment of the option over a part is an empowerment to return the entire sold object, just as [the option arises] due to a defect in one of two slaves. Thus, generalization is not precluded.

**The Second:** The sale of milk within the udder is void, for to the absence of sight is joined the incapacity to distinguish the object of contract from what is other than it, since the milk in the veins flows down into the udder at the time of milking and becomes intermixed with it. Likewise, [it is void] even if he saw a sample of it. Al-Fūrānī erred when he mentioned two juridical bases (wajhān) regarding the sample. Indeed, if he grasped a portion of the udder and bound it tightly, then there are two bases: among them are those who sealed off the matter entirely, for ascertaining the absence of intermixing is impossible, and the binding may itself be a cause for the movement of nature and the flowing down of the milk.

Likewise, if one sells the meat within the skin before flaying, it is void — because if he sells it without the skin, its delivery is impossible except by altering the skin, through splitting and perforating it in most cases; and if he sells it with the skin, Shaykh Abū ʿAlī decisively ruled its nullity, its basis being the connection of the intended object to what is not intended in a manner whereby the intended object cannot be obtained except by alteration and disposal of the skin through flaying. The sound [view] is to derive it (takhrij) upon the two bases [of the sale of the unseen].

As for the sale of heads and trotters that have been skinned (al-maslūkhah), with consideration of the apparent [condition], it is permissible upon the two bases, for the skin is, in effect, a part that is eaten from it.

**The Third:** If we affirm the validity of selling the unseen object, then the majority have agreed that if he said, “I have sold you what is in my sleeve,” without mentioning the genus (al-jins), it is not permissible — and this is the apparent position of Abū Ḥanīfah. There is an analogically derived basis (wajh maqīs) that it is permissible, due to the attainment of specification (al-taʿyīn) by indication (al-ishārah). Then, for the companions there are two paths: The Marāwizah said that nothing is required beyond the mention of the genus, such as his saying, “I sold the slave who is in the house.” If he then exhaustively detailed the attributes (al-ṣifāt), does the option fall away because the description stands in the place of sight? This follows the earlier disagreement.

The Iraqis said: The mention of the type (al-nawʿ) is required along with the genus, definitively — namely, that he say, “My Turkish slave.” And is the exhaustive detailing of attributes required, such that the sale of the unseen object is concluded upon the option of sight? This follows two bases. And the two paths are far apart.

**The Fourth:** The option in the sale of the unseen object is established by sight, and he has the right to rescind (al-faskh) before sight. Regarding ratification (al-ijāzah) before sight, there are two bases; the more manifest (aẓharuhumā) is that it is not valid, for consent before true knowledge [is impossible] — and had it been conceivable, it would have been attained by his saying, “I purchased,” so there is nothing in his saying, “I ratified,” that adds to it.

### | Branch

If he saw two garments, then one of them was stolen from the house while he did not know which of the two was stolen, and he then purchased the remaining garment — he has purchased something specified and seen. This question has occurred in the legal opinions (al-fatāwā), and I said: If the description, measure, and value of the two garments are equal, like two halves of a single bolt of cloth, the contract is valid. But if any of that differs, it is derived upon the two bases of selling the unseen object — because he does not know whether what he purchased is, for example, five cubits or ten, and his prior sight did not yield knowledge of the measure and description of the sold object at the time of the sale, so it has no effect.

---

**The Second Chapter — On the Corruption of Sale by Virtue of Usury (Ribā)**

When the sold object is of a usurious category (ribawī), three conditions are required in its contract, beyond the conditions previously mentioned in the first chapter:

1. Equality (al-tamāthul) by the legal standard (miʿyār al-sharʿ);
2. Immediacy (al-ḥulūl) — by which I mean the prohibition of deferment (al-ajal) and salam;
3. The obligation of mutual taking possession (al-taqābuḍ) in the session of the contract.

This [applies] when the usurious item is sold for its own genus. If it is sold for another usurious item that shares with it the effective cause (al-ʿillah) — which is the indicator of generic kinship (qarīnat al-jinsiyyah) — then the condition of equality falls away, while the conditions of mutual taking possession and immediacy remain.

Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — denied the condition of mutual taking possession except in the contract of currency exchange (al-ṣarf).

And if it is sold for what does not enter into the usurious categories, all these conditions fall away entirely.

The foundation of this chapter is what al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — narrated with his chain from Muslim ibn Yasār and another man, from ʿUbādah ibn al-Ṣāmit, from the Prophet — peace be upon him — that he said: {«Do not sell gold for gold, nor silver for silver, nor wheat for wheat, nor dates for dates, nor barley for barley, nor salt for salt, except equal for equal, hand to hand. But if the two genera differ, then sell as you wish, hand to hand.»} Thus, He made three things obligatory upon homogeneity, and upon difference of genus He made obligatory mutual taking possession and negated deferment by His saying, “hand to hand.”

Usury in the two monetary metals (al-naqdayn), in our view, is caused by their being the substances of prices (jawharā al-athmān), and it extends to ornaments (al-ḥulī) and to everything made from them, but does not extend to anything other than them. This is likewise the position of Mālik. Abū Ḥanīfah said: It is caused by weight (al-wazn) and generic kinship.

The cause of usury in the four [remaining] things, in our view, is edibility (al-ṭuʿm) and generic kinship. Abū Ḥanīfah said: The cause is composite, of measure (al-kayl) and generic kinship. The position of Ibn al-Musayyib is that the cause is edibility within the genus, along with [legal] quantification (al-taqdīr) — and this is an old position (qawl qadīm) of al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him.

Generic kinship, in our view, is the locus of the cause (maḥall al-ʿillah); by itself it does not render exchange unlawful, for it is permissible to sell a garment for its own genus — contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah. And usury runs, in our view, in the Abode of War (dār al-ḥarb) — contrary to him.

And if one purchases a thing for less than what he sold it for in cash, both contracts are valid in our view. Mālik said: Both contracts are void, because it is a means (dharīʿah) to usury. Abū Ḥanīfah said: The second contract is void.

The evidences for these questions are exhaustively treated in the book on Disputed Questions (al-Khilāf).

Our present inquiry, however, extends only to usury of surplus (ribā al-faḍl), for mutual taking possession and the prohibition of deferment (al-nasīʾah) are two branches of it, running in every two substances united by the indicator of generic kinship — whether of monetary character or of edibility. And the discourse pertains to its extremities.

### | الطرف الأول فيما يجري الربا فيه بعلة الطعم

وهو كل ما ظهر منه قصد الطعم وان ظهر منه قصد آخر ويدخل فيه الفواكه
والأدوية ومنه الطين الأرضي وكذا الطين الذي يؤكل سفها على الصحيح وكذا
الزعفران وان قصد منه الصبغ وكذا الماء فانه مطعوم
وفي دهن البنفسج ودهن الكتان وودك السمك خلاف وقطع العراقيون بأن الربا
لا يجري فيها لأنها لا تؤكل في حالها على عموم ولا على الندور بل دهن
الكتان للاستصباح وودك السمك لطلي السفن
أما دهن البنفسج قال العراقيون القول المنصوص فيه انه يجري فيه الربا لأن
الناس لا يتناولونه ضنة به وفيه قول قديم مخرج
ومن أصحابنا من أجرى الربا في الكل نظرا إلى الأصل الذي منه الاستخراج
وإعراضا عن الحال

### | الطرف الثاني في الخلاص من ربا الفضل

والمطعوم ينقسم فالذي يعتاد تقديره تحصل المماثلة فيه بمعيار الشرع
والعبرة فيه بعصر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فلا يوزن مكيل في عصره ولا
يكال  موزون فإن فعل فلا أثر له في الصحة
وان وجد شيء لا يعرف له معيار في عصره فخمسة أوجه
أحدهما الوزن لأنه احصر
الثاني الكيل لأنه أعم
الثالث التخيير للتعادل
الرابع يرجع إلى عادة أهل العصر وهو الأفقه
الرابع يرجع إلى معيار اصله أن كان مستخرجا من أصل
ويجوز الكيل بقصعة لا يعتاد الكيل بها كما يجوز التعديل بالوضع في كفتي
الميزان وللقفال في الكيل بالقصعة تردد
أما إذا باع صبرة بصيرة جزافا فهو باطل وإن خرجتا متماثلتين خلافا لزفر
أما غير المقدر كالبطيخ والسفرجل والقثاء والبيض والجوز مما له كمال في
حالة جفافه فلا يباع بعضه بالبعض في حالة الرطوبة أصلا وإن لم يكن له حالة
جفاف فوجهان أحدهما جواز البيع بالوزن متساويا والثاني أنه لا يجوز إذ ليس
للشرع فيه معيار ولا للعادة
ثم إن جفف نادرا ففي بيع بعضه بالبعض وزنا وجهان مرتبان على حالة الرطوبة
وأولى بالجواز ووجه المنع أن الجفاف نادر فيه غير مقصود فيلحق بحالة
الرطوبة كأنه لم يوجد الجفاف والجواز أقيس

### | الطرف الثالث في الحالة التي تعتبر المماثلة فيها

وقد سئل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن بيع الرطب بالتمر فقال أينقص
الرطب إذا جف فقال السائل نعم فقال فلا إذا منع وعلل بتوقع النقصان بالنسبة
إلى حالة الجفاف فدل على أن المطلوب التماثل بالإضافة إلى تلك الحالة فلا
يباع الرطب
بالرطب والعنب بالعنب وان تماثلا لان تفاوت النقصان عند الجفاف لا ينضبط
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يجوز بيع الرطب بالرطب والتمر بالتمر جميعا
وما تختلف حاله من المطعومات ثلاثة الفواكه والحبوب والمعروضات على النار
أما الفواكه فكل ما يجفف للادخار يحرم بيعه في حالة الرطوبة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط ع م (ṭ-ʿ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes tasting, eating, and that which is consumed as nourishment; ṭuʿm is the substance ingested, whether wholesome or not.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juridical-theological usage, maṭʿūm (foodstuff) is the technical trigger (ʿillah) for riba transactions, extending beyond mere nutrition to anything intended for consumption.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is actual ingestion; metaphorical (majāz) extension covers items like clay eaten frivolously, where the intent of consumption is aberrant yet real.
- Root: ك ي ل (k-y-l) and و ز ن (w-z-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Kayl is measurement by volume (a standard container); wazn is measurement by weight (balance scales). Both are the two canonical modes of equivalence in exchange.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The Sharīʿah fixes these as objective criteria for tamāthul (equivalence), overriding local custom or subjective estimation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal use refers to physical measuring instruments; metaphorical use extends to any standard of equivalence, including the jurist's analogical reasoning (qiyās).
- Root: ج ف ف (j-f-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Drying, desiccation; the state of a thing when its moisture has departed, rendering it stable and storable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In riba law, the dried state (yubūsah) is the benchmark for equivalence because it represents the intrinsic, non-perishable substance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal drying of fruits; metaphorical application to the "dried" or settled state of any commodity as the juridical reference point.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Apodosis (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb al-maḥdhūf) — In the Prophetic hadith "If it decreases when dried?" the response "Then no" omits the full apodosis, relying on context to supply the prohibition, a structure Ghazali parses to extract the legal ratio.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first aspect concerns that in which riba runs by virtue of the cause of being a foodstuff (ʿillat al-ṭuʿm). It is everything in which the intent of consumption (qaṣd al-ṭuʿm) is manifest, even if another intent is also manifest. Included therein are fruits and medicines, and likewise the earthy clay (al-ṭīn al-arḍī) — and similarly the clay that is eaten frivolously (safahan), according to the sounder view. Likewise saffron (zaʿfarān), even if the intent in it is dyeing. And likewise water, for it is a foodstuff (maṭʿūm).

Concerning violet oil (duhn al-banafsaj), linseed oil (duhn al-kattān), and fish grease (wadak al-samak), there is a divergence of opinion. The Iraqis (al-ʿIrāqiyyūn) decisively held that riba does not run in these, because they are not eaten in their present state — neither generally nor rarely. Rather, linseed oil is for illumination (istisbāḥ) and fish grease is for caulking ships (ṭaly al-sufun). As for violet oil, the Iraqis said: the textually transmitted ruling (al-qawl al-manṣūṣ) is that riba does run in it, because people do not consume it only out of preciousness (ḍinnatan bihī). There is also an old, derived opinion (qawl qadīm mukharraj). Among our companions (aṣḥābinā) is one who ran riba in all of these, looking to the origin (al-aṣl) from which they are extracted and disregarding the present state (al-ḥāl).

The second aspect concerns escape from excess riba (ribā al-faḍl). The foodstuff divides into two categories. That which is customarily measured by volume (takdīr) achieves equivalence (tamāthul) by the Sharīʿah's standard (miʿyār al-sharʿ). The criterion is the era of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him: thus, a thing that was weighed in his era is not weighed [now], nor is a thing that was measured by volume in his era measured by volume [now]. If one does so, it has no effect on validity (ṣiḥḥah). If a thing is found for which no standard is known from his era, there are five views: first, weight (wazn), because it is more precise (aḥṣar); second, volume (kayl), because it is more general (aʿamm); third, choice (takhyīr) for equivalence; fourth, recourse to the custom of the people of the era (ʿādat ahl al-ʿaṣr) — and this is the most jurisprudentially sound (afqah); fifth, recourse to the standard of its origin (aṣl), if it is extracted from an origin.

It is permissible to measure by volume with a bowl (qaṣʿah) not customarily used for such measurement, just as it is permissible to achieve equalization by placing [items] in the two pans of the balance. Al-Qaffāl had hesitation (taraddud) regarding measuring by volume with a bowl. As for selling a heap (ṣubrah) for a heap by guesswork (jizāfan), it is invalid (bāṭil), even if the two turn out to be equal — contrary to Zufar.

As for that which is not customarily measured — such as watermelon, quince, cucumber, eggs, and walnuts, which have a state of completeness (kamāl) in their dried condition — it is absolutely impermissible to sell some of it for some of it in the moist state (rūṭūbah). If it has no dried state, there are two views: one, that selling it by weight equally is permissible; the second, that it is impermissible, since neither the Sharīʿah nor custom has a standard for it. Then, if it is dried rarely (nādiran), there are two views on selling some of it for some by weight, ranked upon the moist-state ruling — and it is more deserving of permissibility. The view of prohibition holds that drying is rare in it and unintended, so it is annexed to the moist state, as if drying had not occurred. Permissibility is more analogically sound (aqyas).

The third aspect concerns the state in which equivalence is considered. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about selling fresh dates (ruṭab) for dried dates (tamr). He said: "Does the fresh date decrease when it dries?" The questioner said: "Yes." He said: "Then no" — thus he prohibited it, and he reasoned by the expectation of decrease relative to the dried state. This indicates that what is sought is equivalence relative to that state. Therefore, fresh dates are not sold for fresh dates, nor grapes for grapes, even if they are equal [at present], because the disparity in decrease upon drying cannot be precisely controlled (lā yanḍabiṭ). Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: selling fresh dates for fresh dates and dried dates for dried dates is permissible in all cases.

What differs in state among foodstuffs is of three kinds: fruits (fawākih), grains (ḥubūb), and things exposed to fire (maʿrūḍāt ʿalā al-nār). As for fruits, everything that is dried for storage (iddikhār) is prohibited to sell in the moist state.

chapters.title_en: Four Subsidiary Branches Concerning the Exchange of Commodities with Their Own Kind
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع أربعة

أحدها الرطب الذي لا يتهمر فيه وجهان أحدهما منع البيع لأن له حالة جفاف
على الجملة والرطوبة توجب تفاوتا والثاني الجواز لأنا فهمنا رعاية المماثلة
في أكمل الأحوال وفي أشرف الأشياء والشرف في الطعم وكمال الحال في الرطوبة
فيما يفسد بالجفاف وعلى هذا  لا يجوز بيع رطبه بالتمر
هذا مدلول كلام الأصحاب وينقدح جوازه كما جاز بالرطب
الثاني المشمش والخوخ وما يجفف على ندور فيه ثلاثة أوجه أحدها المنع لأن
له حالة جفاف والثاني الجواز لأن الرطوبة أكمل أحواله والثالث المنع رطبا
ويابسا إذا لم يتقرر له حالة كمال وللعنب في الكمال حالتان الزبيب والخل
الثالث يباع الزيتون بالزيتون واللبن باللبن وهي أحوال كمالها فإن الزيت
والسمن وما إليه مصيرهما ليس من جنسهما
الرابع يحرم بيع التمر بعد نزع النوى لأنه يفسد كماله وادخاره وللعراقيين
فيه وجه واللحم يباع البعض بالبعض في حالة التعدد بعد نزع العظم ومع العظم
لا لأن الإصلاح في نزعه
وقيل إنه يجوز بيع اللحم في حالة الرطوبة باللحم لأن التقدير فيه كالنادر
وقيل إن نزع العظم غير واجب وهو بعيد
وأما المشمش والخوخ منهم من ألحقهما بالتمر ومنهم من ألحقهما باللحم
في وجوب نزع النوى أو منعه
أما الحبوب فلا خلاص عن الربا فيها بالمماثلة إلا في حالة كمالها وهو أن
يكون حبا فكمال البر في حالة كونه برا إلا أن تكون مقلية أو مبلولة أو كشكا
مهرسا فان كل ذلك يفسد الادخار والأرز لا يبطل ادخاره بتنحية قشرته
وفي الجاورش تردد فان خرج عن كونه حبا فلا خلاص فيها بالمماثلة كالدقيق
والسويق والكعك والخبز وسائر أجزاء البر
وللشافعي نصوص قديمة في أجزاء البر مضطربة ولكن قرار المذهب ما ذكرناه
نعم السمسم وماله دهن من الحبوب يجوز بيع الدهن بالدهن منه متماثلا لأنه
أيضا حالة كمال
أما اللبن فكماله أن يكون لبنا ويباع الزبد بالزبد أيضا كما في دهن
السمسم بدهن السمسم وكذا المخيض بالمخيض إلا أن يكون فيه ماء
ويباع اللبن بالرائب المنعقد وان كان خاثرا إلا أن يكون معروضا على النار
وأجزاء اللبن كالمصل والأقط والجبن لا يباع بعضها ببعض ولا بالمخيض ولا
باللبن لمفارقة حالة الكمال وأجزاء اللبن كالدقيق والخبز مع البر
أما المعروضات على النار فهي مفارقة لحالة الكمال ومنه اللحم المشوي
والمطبوخ والدبس
أما السكر والفانيذ والقند واللبأ وهو لبن عرض على النار أدنى عرض والعسل
المصفى بالنار في كل ذلك خلاف لضعف أثر النار والعسل المصفى بالشمس حاله
حال كمال وفاقا
والصحيح جواز بيع العسل بالعسل وان عرض على النار لان ذلك للتمييز فهو
كبيع السمن بالسمن فانه جائز وان كان لا يجوز بيع السمن بالزبد لان اثر
النار عند ذلك يظهر التفاوت
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ط-ب (raṭaba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Freshness, moisture, succulence; the state of being freshly plucked as opposed to desiccated.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The natural perfection (kamāl) of a fruit resides in its fresh state; desiccation marks departure from that perfection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes physical moisture; metaphorical extension applies to the "freshness" of a condition as its optimal mode.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Alternation (al-Taqsīm al-Sharṭī) — the enumeration of mutually exclusive juridical possibilities (wajh) governed by the particle "أحدها" (one of them), requiring each branch to be parsed as a complete nominal sentence.
chapters.translation:
I say: There are four subsidiary branches.

The first concerns fresh dates (ruṭab) whose desiccation is not hastened. There are two views. One is the prohibition of sale, because such dates have a state of dryness in general, and moisture entails disparity. The second is permissibility, for we have understood that the observance of equivalence is intended in the most complete states and in the most noble of things. Nobility resides in taste, and completeness of state resides in moisture — in that which is corrupted by desiccation. Upon this basis, it is not permissible to sell its fresh dates for dried dates (tamr). This is the purport of the companions' doctrine. Yet a permissibility may be discerned, just as it is permitted in the case of fresh dates [sold for fresh dates].

The second concerns apricots (mishmish) and peaches (khawkh) and whatever is dried only rarely. There are three views. One is prohibition, because they possess a state of dryness. The second is permissibility, because moisture is their most complete state. The third is prohibition — both fresh and dried — since no state of perfection is established for them. As for grapes, they have two states of perfection: raisins and vinegar.

The third: olives are sold for olives, and milk for milk, these being their states of perfection. For oil and clarified butter (samn) and the like — their final transformation is not of their own genus.

The fourth: it is unlawful to sell dates after the removal of their pits, because this corrupts their perfection and their storability. The Iraqis have a view concerning this. Meat may be sold part for part when it is in a state of multiplicity after the removal of the bone; but not with the bone, because the corrective act lies in its removal. It has been said that it is permissible to sell meat in its moist state for meat, because estimation therein is as if rare. And it has been said that the removal of the bone is not obligatory — but this is remote.

As for apricots and peaches, some have annexed them to dates, and some have annexed them to meat, regarding the obligation of removing the pit or its prohibition.

As for grains, there is no escape from usury (ribā) therein except through equivalence, and that only in their state of perfection — namely, that it be grain. Thus the perfection of wheat is in its being wheat, unless it be roasted, or moistened, or crushed into bulgur (kashk). For all of that corrupts storability. As for rice, its storability is not nullified by the removal of its husk. Concerning the husked grain (jāwarsh), there is hesitation. For if it departs from being grain, there is no escape from usury through equivalence — like flour, parched grain (sawīq), cake (kaʿk), bread, and all other parts of wheat.

Al-Shāfiʿī has ancient texts (nuṣūṣ qadīmah) concerning the parts of wheat that are inconsistent, but the settled doctrine of the school is what we have mentioned. Yes — sesame and whatever grain possesses oil: it is permissible to sell its oil for its oil in equal measure, because that too is a state of perfection.

As for milk, its perfection is that it be milk. Butter is sold for butter just as sesame oil is sold for sesame oil. Likewise, buttermilk (makhīḍ) is sold for buttermilk, unless it contains water. Milk is sold for curdled milk (rāʾib) that has coagulated, even if it be thick (khāthir), unless it has been exposed to fire. The parts of milk — such as whey (maṣl), dried curd (aqṭ), and cheese (jubn) — are not sold part for part, nor for buttermilk, nor for milk, because they depart from the state of perfection. The parts of milk are like flour and bread with respect to wheat.

As for things exposed to fire, they depart from the state of perfection — and from this category is roasted meat, cooked meat, and molasses (dibs).

As for sugar (sukkar), crystallized sugar (fānīdh), lump sugar (qand), and colostrum (libāʾ) — which is milk exposed to fire with the slightest exposure — and honey clarified by fire: in all of these there is disagreement, owing to the weakness of fire's effect. Honey clarified by the sun retains its state of perfection, by agreement.

The correct view is the permissibility of selling honey for honey even if exposed to fire, because that is for the purpose of purification. It is thus like selling clarified butter for clarified butter, which is permissible. However, it is not permissible to sell clarified butter for butter, because the effect of fire therein manifests disparity.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth and Fifth Branches: Unity and Difference of Genus, and the Rule of "Mudd ʿAjwah"
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الطرف الرابع في اتحاد الجنس واختلافه

والنظر في اللحوم والألبان والأدقة والأدهان والخلول والحلاوات
أما اللحوم ففيها قولان أصحهما وهو اختيار المزني أنها أجناس
لاختلاف الحيوانات وكيف يجانس لحم العصفور لحم الإبل والثاني أنها جنس
لأنها اندرجت تحت اسم واحد لا يتميز بعضها إلا بالإضافة كأنواع التمر
والعنب
وعلى هذا في البري مع البحري وجهان لأنا قد لا ندرج الحوت تحت اسم اللحم
في التمييز
وان قلنا إنها أجناس فأنواع الغنم من الضأن والمعز جنس واحد وكذا أنواع
الحمام من الدبسي والفواخت والبحريات جنس واحد إن أطلقناه أحللنا الكل
بتسميتها حوتا وان لم ندرجها تحت اسم الحوت فهي أجناس
فان قيل الكرش والكبد والطحال والرئة والأمعاء وما يختص باسم واحد خاص ما
حكمها
إن قلنا إن اللحوم أجناس فهذه مع اختلاف الأسامي أولى وان قلنا أنها جنس
فهذا ينبني على اليمين فكل ما يحنث الحالف على تناول اللحم بتناوله فهو جنس
اللحم وكل ما لا يحنث به ففيه وجهان لان اليمين يبنى على الاسم لا على
حقيقة الجنسية والمذهب أن الحالف على اللحم لا يحنث بشيء من ذلك ويحنث
بالروس والأكارع ولا يحنث بالشحم والإلية ويحنث بسمين اللحم
وألحق المراوزة القلب باللحم وألحقه العراقيون بالكبد
فان قيل هل يجوز بيع اللحم بالحيوان
قلنا لا إذ ورد النهي فيه وذلك في بيع لحم الغنم بالغنم
أما البقر وغير الغنم يبنى على اتحاد الجنس إن قلنا اللحوم جنس حرم وان
قلنا أجناس فقولان أقيسهما الصحة إذ فهمنا تقدير اللحم بالحيوان إذا قوبل
بجنسه إذ لو استرسلنا على العموم انجر إلى منع  بيع اللحم بالحمار وبالعبد
ونحن قد نخصص العموم بقرينة معنوية تفهم من اللفظ كتخصيصنا اللمس بغير
المحارم وحرمان الميراث بمن ليس مستحقا للقتل حتى لا يحرم المقتص والجلاد
أما الأدقة فهي أجناس مختلفة
والمذهب أن الألبان كاللحوم لأنها أجزاؤها انحصرت منها والأدهان مختلفة
وقيل يخرج على قولي اللحوم
أما الدهن والكسب فجنسان كالسمن والمخيض والخلول كالأدهان
وفي خل العنب وعصيره وجهان أظهرهما اختلاف الجنس وان كان ذلك بغير الصفة
لان تغيير الصفة قد يجعل غير الربوي ربويا والظاهر أن السكر والفانيذ جنسي
لان اصلهما القصب والتفاوت يسير

### | الطرف الخامس في قاعدة مد عجوة

وضبط القاعدة أن الصفقة مهما اشتملت على مال الربا من الجانبين واختلف
الجنس من الجانبين أو من أحدهما فالبيع باطل ولأجله يبطل بيع الهروي
بالهروي وبالنقرة وبالنيسابوري وكذلك بيع المعجونات والمخلوطات بعضها ببعض
وكذلك الشهد فانه عسل وشمع وكذا الجبن ففيه ماء وملح وكذا خل الزبيب ففيه
ماء وبيع مد ودرهم بمدين أو درهمين أو مد ودرهم باطل
والأصل فيه ما روى فضالة بن عبيد أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أتي
بقلادة فيها ذهب وخرز
تباع بالذهب فأمر بنزع الذهب وقال الذهب بالذهب وزنا بوزن
ولان ما في أحد الجانبين إذا وزع على ما في الجانب الثاني باعتبار القيمة
أفضى إلى المفاضلة أو الجهل بالمماثلة
وهذا المعنى يجري في اختلاف النوع فنص الشافعي على انه لو راطل مائة
دينار عتق ومائة دينار رديء بمائتي دينار وسط بطل العقد
وهذا مشكل مع تحقق المماثلة في الوزن بين العوضين ولكن التوزيع باعتبار
القيمة يفضي إلى المفاضلة
وكان إمام الحرمين يخالف المذهب في مسألة المراطلة ويبطل التعليل
بالتوزيع ويعلل بالجهل بالمماثلة وذلك يجري عند اختلاف الجنس
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ن-س (j-n-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Genus, kind, category; a class of things sharing a common essence or attribute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, genus (jins) denotes a universal category under which species (anwāʿ) fall; its unity or plurality determines ribawī exchange rulings.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to real ontological kind; metaphorical (majāz) usage applies when mere linguistic naming (ism) groups disparate items, as in "meat" (laḥm) for diverse animals.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Disjunctive Parsing (al-sharṭ wa al-taqsīm) — The text alternates between protasis (in qīla...) and apodosis (qulnā...), requiring precise tracking of hypothetical legal scenarios and their rulings.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now for the fourth branch, concerning the unity and difference of genus — and the examination pertains to meats, milks, flours, oils, vinegars, and sweet things.

As for meats, there are two positions. The sounder of the two — and it is the choice of al-Muzanī — is that they constitute multiple genera (ajnās), due to the difference of the animals [from which they derive]. For how could the meat of a sparrow be homogeneous with the meat of a camel? The second position is that they constitute a single genus, because they fall under one single name, and some are not distinguished from others except by attribution (bi-al-iḍāfah), like the varieties of dates and grapes.

Upon this [second view], there are two aspects (wajhān) regarding the wild versus the aquatic, for we may not include the fish (ḥūt) under the name "meat" in the matter of differentiation.

And if we say they are multiple genera, then the varieties of sheep — the ẓaʾn and the maʿz — are a single genus. Likewise, the varieties of pigeons — the dubsī, the fawākhit, and the aquatic ones — are a single genus if we apply [the name "meat"] broadly; then we deem all permissible by calling them "fish." But if we do not include them under the name "fish," then they are multiple genera.

If it is said: What of the tripe (kirsh), the liver (kabid), the spleen (ṭiḥāl), the lung (riʾah), the intestines (amʿāʾ), and whatever is distinguished by its own particular name — what is their ruling?

If we say meats are multiple genera, then these are even more so [multiple], given the difference of their names. But if we say they are a single genus, then this builds upon the [matter of] oath (yamīn). Thus, everything by the consumption of which one who swears [not to eat] meat would be guilty of oath-breaking is of the genus of meat; and everything by which he would not be guilty — there are two aspects [concerning it]. For the oath is built upon the name, not upon the reality of genus-ness.
