And the [adopted] school (madhhab) is that one who swears [to abstain from] meat does not break his oath by any of these [organs], but does break it by heads and trotters (akāriʿ), does not break it by fat (shaḥm) and the fatty tail (aliyyah), and does break it by the fatty part of the meat (samīn al-laḥm).

The Marwazīs annexed the heart (qalb) to meat, while the Iraqis annexed it to the liver.

If it is said: Is it permissible to sell meat for a live animal? We say: No, for the prohibition has come down concerning this — namely, in the sale of sheep-meat for sheep.

As for cattle and other than sheep, it builds upon the unity of genus: if we say meats are a single genus, it is forbidden; if we say they are multiple genera, then there are two positions, the more analogically sound (aqyasuhumā) of which is validity. For we understand the estimation of the meat by the animal when it is compared with its own genus. For if we were to proceed upon the general [prohibition] unrestrictedly, it would lead to forbidding the sale of meat for a donkey and for a slave. Yet we may specify the general [text] by a meaningful indication (qarīnah maʿnawiyyah) understood from the utterance — just as we specify "touching" (al-lams) to exclude mahārim, and the deprivation of inheritance to exclude one who is not deserving of being killed, so that the retaliator (muqaṣṣ) and the flogger (jallād) are not deprived.

As for flours (adqiqah), they are multiple, differing genera.

And the [adopted] school is that milks (albān) are like meats, because they are parts thereof, derived from them. And oils (adhān) are different [genera]; and it was said [they] are derived according to the two positions on meats.

As for the oil-press cake (duhn) and the seed-cake (kusp), they are two genera — like butter (samn) and buttermilk (makhīḍ). And vinegars (khulūl) are like oils.

Regarding vinegar of grapes and its juice [must], there are two aspects, the more manifest of which is difference of genus — even though that [difference] is not by [change of] attribute. For the change of attribute may render what is not ribawī into ribawī. And the manifest [view] is that sugar (sukkar) and candy (fānīdh) are a single genus, because their origin is sugarcane, and the disparity is slight.

---

I say: Now for the fifth branch, concerning the rule of "Mudd ʿAjwah."

The control of the rule is that whenever a transaction (ṣafqah) comprises ribawī wealth from both sides, and the genus differs from both sides or from one of them, the sale is void. For this reason, the sale of Harawī [silver] for Harawī, for nugget (naqrah), and for Naysābūrī [silver] is void. Likewise, the sale of confections (maʿjūnāt) and mixtures (makhlūṭāt), some for others. Likewise, honeycomb (shahd), for it is honey and wax; and likewise cheese (jubn), for it contains water and salt; and likewise raisin-vinegar, for it contains water. And the sale of a mudd and a dirham for two mudds, or two dirhams, or a mudd and a dirham, is void.

The basis of this is what Fuḍālah ibn ʿUbayd narrated: that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) was brought a necklace containing gold and beads, sold for gold; so he ordered the gold to be removed, and said: {«الذهب بالذهب وزنا بوزن»} — "Gold for gold, weight for weight."

And [the rationale is] that what is in one of the two sides, when distributed (wuzziʿa) upon what is in the second side by consideration of value, leads to disparity (mufāḍalah) or to ignorance of equivalence (al-jahl bi-al-mumāthalah).

And this meaning runs in the difference of type (nawʿ). Thus al-Shāfiʿī explicitly stated that if one were to weigh (rāṭala) one hundred excellent dīnārs and one hundred inferior dīnārs against two hundred medium dīnārs, the contract is void. This is problematic given that equivalence in weight between the two countervalues is realized — but the distribution by consideration of value leads to disparity.

And Imām al-Ḥaramayn [al-Juwaynī] used to oppose the school (madhhab) in the matter of weighing (murāṭalah), and would invalidate the rationale of distribution, instead rationalizing by ignorance of equivalence — and that runs when the genus differs.

chapters.title_en: Three Subsidiary Branches and the Prohibition of the Contract by the Lawgiver's Command
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع ثلاثة

الأول إذا باع خمسة دراهم مكسرة وخمسة صحاحا بعشرة مكسرة أو صحيحة فيه
وجهان ذكرهما الأصحاب أحدهما البطلان كما في مسألة
المراطلة لأن القيمة تختلف بالصحة والتكسر والثاني الصحة إذ الغالب جريان
المسامحة باشتمال الدراهم على مكسرات فصفة الصحة في  محل المسامحة فهو خارج
عن القصد بخلاف العتق والرداءة في الذهب بل هذا كاشتمال الصاع على تميزات
رديئة لو ميزت لنقص قيمتها بالإضافة إلي غيرها ولا خلاف أن ذلك غير منظور
إليه
الثاني إذا باع الحنطة بالشعير وفي أحدهما حبات من جنس الآخر إن كان
مقدارا يقصد اختلاطه أو تحصيله فهو مانع وإلا فلا
وكذلك إن بيع الحنطة بالحنطة وفيهما تراب إن كان يظهر أثره في المكيال
فباطل لأنه يتفاوت القدر وتجهل المماثلة ويرعى في الحبات من جنس الآخر ظهور
قصد المالية لا النقصان في المكيال
الثالث بيع الشاة اللبون بالشاة اللبون باطل لان اللبن مقصود مع الشاة
وفي بيع دار فيها جمة ماء بمثلها وجهان إذا قلنا الماء ربوي لان الماء لا
يقصد عينه مع الدار واللبن مقصود مع الشاة
وسوى أبو الطيب بن سلمة بين اللبون وبين مسألة الدار في المنع
فان قيل ما الفرق بين التمر والشهد وفي التمر نوى كما أن في الشهد شمعا
قلنا النوى من صلاح التمر وليس الشمع من صلاح العسل فلم يعد جزءا منه
فان قيل إذا جوزتم بيع اللبن باللبن ولم تقدروه سمنا ومخيضا فلم منعتم
بيع السمن باللبن وهلا قلتم لا يقدر السمن في اللبن كما لم يقدر إذا قوبل
اللبن باللبن قلنا لان الجنسية معلومة بين اللبنين فلا يحتاج إلى تقدير ولا
تمييز بين السمن والمخيض فيه حتى نحكم باجتماع الجنسين وإذا قوبل السمن
باللبن لم يمكن إطلاق القول بالجنسية ولا باختلاف الجنس لأن فيه من جنسه
فغلب جانب التحريم
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثالث في فساد العقد من جهة نهي الشارع
عنه - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
وعندنا أن مطلق النهي عن العقد يدل على فساد العقد إلا إذا ظهر تعلق
النهي بأمر غير العقد اتفق مجاورته للعقد
كقوله تبارك وتعالى {فاسعوا إلى ذكر الله وذروا البيع} فحكم بصحة البيع
في وقت النداء إذ علم قطعا أن النهي عن البيع لا لأمر راجع إلى عينه فانه
غير محذور  والمحذور ترك الجمعة وقد حصل البيع وهو غير متعلق بمقاصد البيع
فلم يتأثر به
فإذن المناهي قسمان

### | القسم الأول ما لم يدل على الفساد وهي خمسة

### | الأول نهيه صلى الله عليه وسلم عن النجش

قال الشافعي ليس ذلك من أخلاق ذوي الدين
والنجش هو الرفع والناجش من يطلب سلعة بين يدي الراغب فيها بأكثر من
قيمتها وهو لا يريدها ليرغب فيها المستام
فهذه خديعة محرمة ولكن العقد صحيح من العاقدين والإثم يلحق غيرهما ثم لا
خيار إن لم تجر مواطأة من البائع وان جرى فوجهان
أحدهما لا كما لا يثبت بالغبن في كل بيع
والثاني نعم لأنه غبن استند إلى تلبيس فضاهى غبن المصراة وصورة تلقي
الركبان

### | الثاني قوله عليه السلام لا يبيعن أحدكم على بيع أخيه ولا يسومن على سوم أخيه

فإذا كان المتعاقدان في مجلس العقد فطلب طالب السلعة بأكثر من الثمن
ليرغب البائع في فسخ العقد فهذا هو البيع على بيع الغير وهو محرم لأنه
إضرار بالغير ولكنه منعقد لأن نفس البيع غير مقصودة بالنهي فإنه لا خلل فيه
وكذلك إذا رغب المشتري في الفسخ لغرض سلعة أجود منها بمثل ثمنها أو مثلها
بدون ذلك الثمن
والسوم على السوم أن يطلب السلعة بزيادة على ما استقر الأمر عليه بين
المتساومين قبل البيع
وإنما يحرم على من بلغه الخبر فان تحريمه خفي قد لا يعرفه كل واحد بخلاف
النجش فان تحريم الخداع جلي في الشرع
ثم قالت المراوزة الخطبة على الخطبة أيضا محرمة كالسوم ولكن سكوت الولي
ثم كالإجابة على أحد القولين كما ذكرناه في النكاح والسكوت في البيع لا
يحرم السوم
وقال العراقيون لا فرق بل التعويل على فهم الرضا بالقرينة في المسألتين
فيحرم ذلك بعد فهم الرضا بالإجابة فيهما وهذا أفقه

### | الثالث نهى صلى الله عليه وسلم عن أن يبيع حاضر لباد

وهو أن يأتي البدوي البلدة ومعه قوت يبغي التسارع إلى بيعه رخيصا فيقول
له البلدي اتركه عندي لأغالي في بيعته
فهذا الصنيع محرم لما  فيه من الإضرار بالغير والبيع إذا جرى مع المغالاة
منعقد وهذا إذا كانت السلعة مما تعم الحاجة إليها فان كانت سلعة مما لا
تعم الحاجة إليها وكثرت الأقوات واستغني عنه ففي التحريم وجهان يعول في
أحدهما على عموم ظاهر النهي وحسم باب الضرر وفي الثاني على معنى الضرر
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-س-ر (kasara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To break, shatter, fragment; a broken piece (kisr) as opposed to whole
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes deficiency in physical integrity affecting value; in transactional contexts, a qualitative variance from the sound type
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical breakage; metaphorical (majāz) for diminution of worth or status
- Root: ل-ب-ن (labana)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Milk; a milk-yielding ewe (shāh labūn) — the animal whose milk is present and flowing
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Milk as a distinct substance with its own genus (jins) in ribā transactions; its presence in an animal creates a composite object of sale
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the dairy fluid; metaphorical extension to the animal's productive capacity as an intended attribute
- Root: ن-ه-ي (nahā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To forbid, prohibit; prohibition (nahy) as a directive of abstention
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In uṣūl al-fiqh, a prohibition attached to an act; its import for validity (ṣiḥḥah) vs. corruption (fasād) depends on whether the prohibited attribute is intrinsic to the act's essence
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal command to desist; metaphorical when the prohibition targets an extrinsic circumstance adjacent to the act
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ʿāmil (Ellipsis of the Governing Operator) — In conditional clauses like "if it is said," the governing verb is understood; also, the rule of ʿaṭf (coordination) where parallel branches (furūʿ) are syntactically balanced by wa (and) to preserve logical equivalence.
chapters.translation:
I say: Three subsidiary branches [follow].

**The First Branch:** If one sells five broken dirhams and five sound dirhams for ten broken or ten sound dirhams, there are two aspects (wajhān) mentioned by the companions [of al-Shāfiʿī]. One of them is nullity (buṭlān), as in the case of murāṭalah (weight-for-weight exchange of unequal metals), because the value differs with soundness and breakage. The second is validity (ṣiḥḥah), since the prevailing custom is that tolerance (musāmaḥah) runs with the inclusion of broken pieces among dirhams; thus the attribute of soundness lies in a locus of tolerance, and it falls outside the intent [of the parties] — unlike the defect (ʿatq) and inferiority (radhā'ah) in gold. Rather, this is like the inclusion in a ṣāʿ (measure) of inferior grains which, if separated, would diminish its value relative to others; and there is no disagreement that such is not regarded.

**The Second Branch:** If one sells wheat for barley, and in one of the two there are grains of the other kind — if the amount is such that its admixture or its extraction is intended, it is a preventive impediment (māniʿ); otherwise, it is not. Likewise, if wheat is sold for wheat and in both there is dust — if its effect appears in the measuring vessel, it is void (bāṭil), because the quantity varies and equality (mumāthalah) becomes unknown. In the grains of the other kind, regard is given to the appearance of intent toward monetary value, not the deficiency in the measuring vessel.

**The Third Branch:** The sale of a milk-yielding ewe for a milk-yielding ewe is void, because the milk is intended along with the ewe. In the sale of a house containing a spring of water for its like, there are two aspects when we say water is ribawī (subject to usury rules): for water's essence is not intended with the house, whereas milk is intended with the ewe. Abū al-Ṭayyib ibn Salmah equated the milk-yielding case with the house case in prohibition.

If it is said: What is the difference between dates and honey, when dates contain pits just as honey contains wax? We say: The pit is part of the date's soundness (ṣalāḥ), but the wax is not part of the honey's soundness, so it is not reckoned as a component of it.

If it is said: When you permit the sale of milk for milk without estimating it as butter (samn) or buttermilk (makhīḍ), why do you forbid the sale of butter for milk? Why not say: Butter is not estimated in milk, just as it is not estimated when milk is compared with milk? We say: Because the genus-identity (jinsiyyah) between the two milks is known, so no estimation is needed, nor any distinction between butter and buttermilk therein, such that we could rule on the conjunction of the two genera. But when butter is compared with milk, one cannot absolutely affirm genus-identity nor genus-difference, because in it there is something of its genus; thus the side of prohibition prevails.

— Peace be upon him — **The Third Chapter: On the Corruption of the Contract by Virtue of the Lawgiver's Prohibition of It** — Peace be upon him —

In our view, an absolute prohibition (muṭlaq al-nahy) of a contract indicates the corruption (fasād) of the contract, except when it becomes apparent that the prohibition attaches to a matter other than the contract that happens to be adjacent to it. Like His saying, Blessed and Exalted: {«فَاسْعَوْا إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَذَرُوا الْبَيْعَ»} ("Hasten to the remembrance of God and leave off selling") — for He ruled the sale valid at the time of the call, since it is known with certainty that the prohibition of selling is not for a matter reverting to its essence, for it is not objectionable in itself; the objectionable thing is abandoning the Friday prayer, and the sale has occurred while not being connected to the purposes of selling, so it is unaffected by it.

Thus, the prohibitions are of two divisions:

### | The First Division: What Does Not Indicate Corruption — Five [Types]

**The First:** His prohibition, peace be upon him, of najash (inflating price). Al-Shāfiʿī said: That is not among the morals of the religious. Najash is the raising [of price]; the nājish is one who seeks a commodity in the presence of one desiring it at more than its value, while not intending to buy it, so as to make the bargainer desire it. This is a deception (khidāʿah) that is forbidden, but the contract is valid between the two contractors, and the sin attaches to other than them. Then, there is no option [of rescission] if no collusion (muwāṭa'ah) from the seller occurred; if it did occur, there are two aspects: One — no, just as no option is established by ghabn (disparity in price) in every sale. The second — yes, because it is a disparity based on deceit (talbīs), thus resembling the ghabn of the musarrāh (milk-retained ewe) and the case of intercepting caravans (talqqī al-rukbān).

**The Second:** His saying, peace be upon him: "Let none of you sell over the sale of his brother, nor bid over his bidding." So if the two contractors are in the session of contract, and a seeker demands the commodity at more than the price to make the seller desire to rescind the contract — this is selling over the sale of another, and it is forbidden because it is harm to another, but it is concluded (munʿaqid), because the very sale is not intended by the prohibition, for there is no defect in it. Likewise, if the buyer desires rescission for the purpose of obtaining a better commodity at its like price, or its like at less than that price. Bidding over bidding (sawm ʿalā sawm) is seeking the commodity at an increase over what was settled between the two bargainers before the sale. It is only forbidden for one whom the news has reached, for its prohibition is obscure and may not be known to everyone — unlike najash, for the prohibition of deception is manifest in the Law.

Then the Marwazīs said: Seeking a betrothal (khiṭbah) over a betrothal is also forbidden, like bidding; but the silence of the guardian is then like acceptance (ijābah) on one of the two opinions, as we mentioned in marriage. Silence in sale does not forbid bidding. The Iraqīs said: There is no difference; rather, reliance is on understanding consent (riḍā) by contextual indication (qarīnah) in both matters, so it is forbidden after understanding consent by acceptance in both. This is more jurisprudentially sound.

**The Third:** His prohibition, peace be upon him, of a townsman selling for a Bedouin (ḥāḍir li-bādin). This is: a Bedouin comes to the town with provisions, seeking to hasten their sale cheaply, and the townsman says to him: Leave it with me so I may sell it at an inflated price. This act is forbidden for the harm it contains toward others; but the sale, when it occurs with inflation, is concluded. This applies when the commodity is one of general need. If it is a commodity not of general need, and provisions are abundant and there is no need of it, then there are two aspects on prohibition: in one, reliance is on the general import of the apparent prohibition and the closing of the door of harm; in the second, on the meaning of harm.

chapters.title_en: The Fourth and Fifth Prohibited Sales, and the Second Category of Prohibitions Implying Invalidity
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الرابع قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا تتلقوا الركبان بالبيع فمن تلقي فصاحب السلعة بالخيار بعد أن يقدم السوق

وصورته أن يستقبل الركبان ويكذب في سعر البلد ويشتري بأقل من ثمن المثل
فهو تغرير محرم ولكن الشراء منعقد
ثم إن كذب وظهر الغبن ثبت الخيار وإن صدق فوجهان يعول في أحدهما على عموم
النهي وفي الآخر على معنى الضرر
فجامع هذه المناهي يرجع إلى عقد لا خلل فيه ويتضمن إضرارا ولأجله نهى
عليه السلام عن الاحتكار وهو ادخار الأقوات للغلاء ونهى عن التسعير لان
تصرف الإمام في الأسعار يحرك الرغبات ويفضي إلى القحط وقال العلماء يكره
بيع السلاح من قطاع الطريق وبيع العصير من الخمار لأنه إعانة على المعصية
والإضرار

### | الخامس نهى عن التفريق بين الوالدة وولدها في البيع

والظاهر أن الوالد في معنى الوالدة ولا يتعدى إلى غيرهما من الأقارب وفي
الجدة احتمال
ثم يختص بما قبل التمييز فلا يجري فيما بعد البلوغ وفيما بين السنين
وجهان
وفي فساد هذا البيع قولان أحدهما لا لأن النهي راجع للأضرار فيحرم ولا
يفسد البيع إذ لا خلل في نفسه والثاني أنه لا ينعقد لان التسليم تفريق وهو
محرم والممنوع شرعا كالممتنع حسا فيلحق بالعجز عن التسليم
ويقرب من هذا بيع السلاح من أهل الحرب قال الأصحاب هو باطل لأنهم لا
يعدون إلا لقتالنا فالتسليم إليهم إعانة محرمة وفيه وجه آخر أنه محرم
وينعقد كالبيع من قطاع الطريق وهو منقاس ولكنه غير مشهور

### | القسم الثاني من المناهي ما حمل على الفساد

وذلك إما لتطرق خلل إلى الأركان والشرائط التي سبقت في الباب
الأول أو لأنه لم يبق للنهي متعلق سوى العقد منفصلا عنه فحمل  على الفساد
وهي ثمانية

### | الأول نهيه عن بيع حبل الحبلة وله تأويلان

أحدهما أن يبيع بثمن إلى اجل وهو وضع نتاج الناقة فإنه اجل مجهول يطرق
جهلا إلى الثمن
والثاني بيع نتاج النتاج قبل الوجود على عادة العرب وهو بيع ما ليس
بمملوك ولا مقدور ولا معلوم

### | الثاني نهيه عن بيع الملاقيح والمضامين

والملقاح هو ما في بطن الأم
والمضامين ما هو في أصلاب الفحول فهي غير مقدورة ولا معلومة

### | الثالث نهيه عن بيع الملامسة وله تأويلان

أحدهما أن يقول مهما لمست ثوبي فهو مبيع منك وهو باطل لانه تعليق أو عدول
عن الصيغة الشرعية وقيل معناه أن يجعل اللمس بالليل في الظلمة قاطعا للخيار
ويرجع ذلك إلى تعليق اللزوم وهو غير نافذ
ونهى عن بيع المنابذة وهو في معنى الملامسة فالنبذ كاللمس
وقيل معناه أن تتنابذ السلع وتكون معاطاة ولا ينعقد بها البيع عندنا

### | الرابع نهى عن بيع الحصاة

وهو أن يجعل رمي الحصاة بيعا أو يقول بعت منك من السلع ما تقع عليه حصاتك
إذا رميت أو بعت من الأرض إلى حيث تنتهي حصاتك فالكل فاسد لما سبق من
المعاني

### | الخامس نهيه عن بيعتين في بيعة ذكر الشافعي رضي الله عنه تأولين

أحدهما أن تقول بعتك بألفين نسيئة أو بألف نقدا أيهما شئت أخذت به فاخذ
بأحدهما فهو فاسد لانه إبهام وتعليق
والآخر أن تقول بعتك عبدي على أن تبيعني فرسك وهو فاسد لانه شرط لا يلزم
ويتفاوت بعدمه مقصود العقد وقد نهى مطلقا عن بيع وشرط وكذلك نهى عن بيع
وسلف ومعناه أن يشترط فيه قرضا

### | السادس نهى عن ثمن الكلب والخمر

وهو معلل بالنجاسة فيتعدى إلى كل نجس عندنا
وصحح أبو حنيفة رحمه الله شراء الخمر للمسلم بوكالة الذمي إذا باشره
الذمي وهو وكيل

### | السابع نهى عن بيع ما لم يقبض

وعن بيع الطعام حتى يجري فيه الصاعان وعن بيع الكالئ بالكالئ وسيأتي
تفصيله ونهى عن بيع الغرر
وعن بيع اللحم بالحيوان وقد ذكرناه وقد نهى  عن ثمن عسب الفحل وذلك لانه
غير مقدور على التسليم

### | الثامن نهى عن بيع وشرط
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-ق-ي (la-qā-ya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To meet, encounter, confront face-to-face; al-talāqī implies deliberate interception.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Used for meeting with intent to transact, often involving deception in market context.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meeting vs. metaphorical interception for trade advantage; here literal.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — the phrase "فصاحب السلعة بالخيار" is a result clause following a conditional, parsed as jumla sharṭiyya with the answer in the nominative predicate.
chapters.translation:
**The Fourth [Prohibition]:** His saying, peace be upon him: «Do not intercept the camel-riders [coming to market] for trade; whoever intercepts them, the owner of the goods has the option [to rescind] after he arrives at the market.»

Its form is that one meets the caravan [before they reach town], lies about the price in the city, and buys [their goods] for less than the fair market value. This is a prohibited deception (taghrīr), yet the purchase is validly concluded (munʿaqid). Then, if he lied and the loss [to the seller] became evident, the option [of rescission] is established. If he spoke truthfully, there are two views: one relies on the general import of the prohibition, the other on the meaning of harm (ḍarar).

The common thread of these prohibitions reverts to a contract that has no intrinsic defect, yet entails harm to others; for this reason, peace be upon him, prohibited hoarding (iḥtikār)—which is storing staple foods to await price inflation—and prohibited price-fixing (tasʿīr), because the ruler's intervention in prices stirs desires and leads to scarcity. The scholars said: it is disliked (makrūh) to sell weapons to highway robbers and to sell grape juice to a wine-maker, because it is assistance upon sin and harm.

**The Fifth [Prohibition]:** He prohibited separating a mother from her child in a sale.

The apparent [position] is that the father is included in the meaning of the mother, and it does not extend to other relatives. Regarding the grandmother, there is a probability [of inclusion]. Then, it is specific to [the child] before the age of discernment (tamyīz); it does not apply after puberty. Concerning [separation] between the two ages, there are two views.

Regarding the corruption (fasād) of this sale, there are two positions: one says it is not corrupt, because the prohibition reverts to harm—it is forbidden but does not invalidate the sale, since there is no defect in itself. The second says it is not concluded, because delivery [of the child] entails separation, which is prohibited; and what is legally prevented is like what is physically impossible, so it falls under incapacity to deliver.

Close to this is selling weapons to people of war (ahl al-ḥarb). The companions [of al-Shāfiʿī] said: it is void (bāṭil), because they only use them to fight us, so delivering [weapons] to them is a prohibited assistance. There is another view that it is forbidden yet validly concluded, like the sale to highway robbers—this is analogically derived but not the well-known [position].

**The Second Category of Prohibitions:** What is construed as implying invalidity (fasād).

This is either because a defect enters the pillars (arkān) and conditions (shurūṭ) previously discussed in the first chapter, or because the prohibition has no object other than the contract itself, apart from it, so it is construed as invalidating. These are eight:

**The First:** His prohibition of selling "the pregnancy of a pregnancy" (ḥabl al-ḥabala). It has two interpretations: one is selling with a price deferred to a term, namely the time of the she-camel's delivery—for that is an unknown term introducing ignorance (jahāla) into the price. The second is selling the offspring of the offspring before its existence, as was the Arab custom—selling what is neither owned, nor within power, nor known.

**The Second:** His prohibition of selling al-malāqīḥ and al-maḍāmīn. Al-malqūḥ is what is in the mother's womb; al-maḍāmīn is what is in the loins of the stallions. These are neither within power nor known.

**The Third:** His prohibition of selling by touch (mulāmasa). It has two interpretations: one is that he says, "Whatever garment you touch, it is sold to you"—this is void because it is a conditional suspension or a deviation from the prescribed formula (ṣīgha). It is also said its meaning is that he makes touching at night in darkness a termination of the option [of inspection], which reverts to suspending the bindingness (luzūm)—and this is not effective. He also prohibited selling by throwing (munābadha), which is analogous to mulāmasa, for throwing is like touching. It is said its meaning is that they throw their goods to each other as a mutual exchange (muʿāṭāh), and by our [school's] view, no sale is concluded thereby.

**The Fourth:** His prohibition of selling by pebble (ḥaṣāh). This is making the throwing of a pebble itself a sale, or saying, "I sell you whatever of my goods your pebble lands upon when you throw," or "I sell you land from here to where your pebble reaches." All of this is corrupt (fāsid) for the meanings previously mentioned.

**The Fifth:** His prohibition of "two sales in one sale" (bayʿatān fī bayʿa). Al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, mentioned two interpretations: one is that you say, "I sell you [this] for two thousand on credit, or for one thousand in cash—whichever you choose, I take it," and he takes one of them—this is corrupt because it involves ambiguity (ibhām) and suspension (taʿlīq). The other is that you say, "I sell you my slave on condition that you sell me your horse"—this is corrupt because it is a condition that is not binding, and by its absence the purpose of the contract is vitiated. He also prohibited absolutely "a sale with a condition" (bayʿ wa-sharṭ), and likewise prohibited "a sale with a loan" (bayʿ wa-salaf), meaning that a loan is stipulated therein.

**The Sixth:** His prohibition of the price of a dog and wine. This is reasoned by impurity (najāsa), so it extends to every impure thing in our [school's] view. Abū Ḥanīfa, may God have mercy on him, validated the purchase of wine for a Muslim through the agency of a dhimmī, when the dhimmī as agent executes it directly.

**The Seventh:** His prohibition of selling what has not been received (qabḍ), and of selling food until two measures (ṣāʿān) have passed through it, and of selling debt for debt (kalīʾ bi-kalīʾ)—its detail will follow. He also prohibited selling with uncertainty (gharar), and selling meat for a living animal—which we have mentioned. He also prohibited the price of a stallion's stud fee (ʿasb al-faḥl), because it is not within power to deliver.

**The Eighth:** His prohibition of a sale with a condition (bayʿ wa-sharṭ).

chapters.title_en: The Intermediate Compendium in Jurisprudence — Section 145: Conditions in Sales and Their Exceptions
chapters.arabic_text:
فاقتضى مطلقه امتناع كل شرط في البيع والمفهوم من تعليله انه إذا انضم
شرط إلى البيع بقيت معه علقة بعد العقد يتصور بسببها منازعة ويفوت بفواتها
مقصود العاقد وينعكس على أصل العقد فيحسم الباب ولم يكن محذور هذا النهي
منفصلا عن العقد فيدل على فساده أو فساد الشرط لا محالة
ويستثنى من هذا الأصل حال الإطلاق ستة شروط الأول أن يشترط ما يوافق
العقد كقوله بعت بشرط أن تنتفع به وتتصرف كما تريد لا يبقى علقة
وكذلك إذا قال ألا يأكل إلا الهريسة ولا تلبس إلا الخز وما لا غرض فيه
لانه ليس فيه علقة يتعلق بها نزاع يتغير به غرض فهو هذيان ساقط وهذا
استثناء عن صورة اللفظ ولكنه منطبق على المعنى المفهوم الثاني شرط الخيار
ثلاثة أيام فما دونه بشرط أن يكون معلوما وان لا يكون زائدا
وسببه الحاجة لكثرة الغبينة وعرف ذلك بنص الأحاديث الثالث شرط المهلة في
الثمن إلى ميقات معلوم عرف ذلك بالنص ويتأيد ذلك بالحاجة العامة الرابع شرط
الوثيقة في الثمن بالرهن أو الكفيل أو الشهادة عرف ذلك بالنص ويعلل بعموم
الحاجة لكي يعرف الكفيل بتعيينه والمرهون بتعيينه
أن الغرض يتفاوت به ولا يشترط تعيين الشهود إذ لا يتفاوت الغرض وهل يشترط
تعيين من يعدل الرهن على يده فيه وجهان
ولو عين الشهود فهل يتعين فيه وجهان أحدهما يتعين كالكفيل والثاني لا
كتعيين الميزان إذا لا أرب فيه
فان قلنا لا يتعين فلا يفسد به العقد بل هو لاغ لا يتأثر العقد به
ولو شرط أن يكون المبيع رهنا بالثمن
قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه البيع مفسوخ قال الأصحاب ذلك يبنى على قولنا
البداية في التسليم بالبائع او فان قلنا البداية بالبائع أو يجب التسليم
عليهما فيتخيران بالمشتري أو يتساويان ليكون الشرط مغيرا مقتضى العقد
وتعليله أن التسليم إذا وجب عليه بمقتضى العقد فاشترط أن يكون البيع رهنا
في  يده على الثمن فقد غير مقتضى العقد في إيجاب التسليم
فيفسد
وان قلنا البداية بالمشتري فوجهان أحدهما الصحة إذ لا مانع والثاني
البطلان لان يد البائع يد ضمان وليس يد المرتهن يد ضمان بل يد أمانة فهما
ضدان فلا يجمع بين حكميهما في حال واحدة والأول أظهر
ثم هذه الشروط إذا صححت فلو امتنع المشتري عن الوفاء بالكفيل والرهن
والإشهاد ثبت له الخيار في البيع ولو أجاب فامتنع البائع من قبول الرهن
مثلا فيجبر أم يخير بين القبول وبطلان الخيار فيه تردد ذكره صاحب التقريب
ويثبت الخيار مهما تلف المرهون قبل التسليم وكذلك إذا خرج العين المعين
للرهن معيبا وهو لم يطلع عليه ولو تلف بعد القبض في المرهون فلا خيار
ولو اطلع بعد فواته في يده على عيب ففي ثبوت الخيار في اصل البيع وجهان
أحدهما لا لانه لم يتمكن من الرد
والثاني نعم إذ بان أن ما سبق لم يكن وفاء بالملتزم
فان قيل فهذه الشروط لو فسدت بجهالة أو غيرها أو ذكر شرطا ليس في هذه
الأقسام المستثناة وحكم بفسادها فهل يفسد العقد وتبقى علته وذلك في الأجل
والخيار وغيره
وفي شرط الوثيقة قولان ووجه الفرق أنها أمور مستقلة منفصلة ففسادها لا
يوجب فساد العقد بل يلغو
والاقيس الأول لانه عليه الصلاة والسلام نهى عن بيع وشرط والمقصود بالنهي
البيع فليفسد العقد بمطلق النهي ولان ما يستقل بنفسه إذا ضم إلى العقد تأثر
به فاشبه الخيار والأجل
وحكى صاحب التقريب والشيخ أبو علي نصا غريبا أن البيع لا يفسد بالشرائط
الفاسدة بل يلغو الشرط كما في النكاح وحكاه أبو ثور أيضا عن الشافعي وهو
بعيدة
الخامس مما استثني عن النهي شرط العتق في المبيع لما روى أن بريرة قالت
لها
عائشة رضي الله عنها لو باعك أولياؤك لصببت لهم ثمنك صبا فقال السادة لا
نفعل ذلك إلا بشرط أن تعتقك ويكون الولاء لنا فذكرت عائشة رضي الله عنها
ذلك لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال عليه  الصلاة والسلام اشتري واشترطي
لهم الولاء ثم قام خطيبا فقال ما بال أقوام يشترطون شروطا ليست في كتاب
الله عز وجل في خطبة طويلة فأذن في ذلك ولا يأذن في باطل وأنكر هذا التكليف
عليهم مع الإذن في الإجابة
وخرج بعض الأصحاب قولا أن شرط العتق كسائر الشروط الفاسدة وهو القياس وهو
مذهب أبي حنيفة ولكنه لا وجه له بتأييد القول الغريب به وهو أن العقد صحيح
والشرط فاسد
وتأويل الحديث انه إذن في العقد والشرط أما العقد فصحيح واما الشرط فغير
لازم ولكن كان يثق بعائشة أنها تفي بالشرط تكرما وهذا أولى كي لا يكون
مناقضا للقياس والتأويل بالقياس غير ممنوع
ونص الشافعي رحمه الله على ما ذكرناه وهو موافقة الحديث في تصحيح الشرط
والعقد
أما المصير إلى فساد العقد فلا يعقل له وجه مع الحديث بحال ولو قال به
قائلون
والتفريع به على النص في صحة الشرط فعلى هذا لو شرط الولاء للبائع فوجهان
أحدهما يصح وله الولاء لقصة بريرة رحمها الله وانه عليه الصلاة والسلام لا
يأمر بفساد
والثاني المنع فانه في غاية البعد عن القياس واحتمال تقدير مساهلة من
الشارع في هذه المشارطة أهون من تشويش قاعدة القياس
وهذا أيضا يشوش التعلق بالنص في اصل الشرط فليقبل النص جملة وتفصيلا
فان قيل العتق المستحق بعد صحة الشرط لمن هو
قلنا اختلف أصحابنا فيه فمنهم من قال هو حق الله تعالى
كأنه التزم العتق بشرطه فاشبه النذر ومنهم من قال هو حق البائع لانه ثبت
بشرطه
ويبتنى عليه ثلاثة أمور
أحدهما أنه هل تثبت له المطالبة
فان قلنا حقه فنعم وان قلنا حق الله تعالى فوجهان
أصحهما انه يملك الطلب إذ ثبت بشرطه وتعلق به غرضه وان كان لله تعالى فيه
حق الثاني انه هل يسقط اللزوم بعفوه
وان قلنا حق الله تعالى فلا وان قلنا حقه فوجهان إذ رب الحق لا يقبل
الإسقاط إفرادا كالأجل ويطرد هذا في عفو مستحق الكفيل والرهن
وعلى الاحتمالين لا يجري  إعتاق المشتري إياه عن الكفارة لتعلق استحقاق
الغير به
الثالث إذا امتنع المشتري من الإعتاق ذكر صاحب التقريب قولين
أحدهما ثبوت الخيار للبائع كما في الامتناع من الكفيل والرهن
والثاني انه يجبر على العتق كما يجبر المولى على الطلاق
وهذا يلتفت على انه حق الله تعالى فلا وجه لإسقاطه بفسخ البائع ولا
بإجازته ورضاه بعدم العتق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش ر ط (sharṭa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A mark, sign, or stipulation; that which is conditioned or made a prerequisite.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A stipulated condition that binds an act to a requisite, often entailing a legal consequence (ḥukm) upon fulfillment or breach.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is a physical mark; metaphorical usage denotes a contractual stipulation that alters or qualifies an obligation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Dependency (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is governed by the protasis, mirroring how a contractual condition (sharṭ) is syntactically and legally subordinate to the main contract (ʿaqd), yet can invalidate it if it introduces a conflicting element.
chapters.translation:
I say: The unqualified prohibition (of stipulations in sales) necessitated the impermissibility of every condition in a sale. What is understood from its rationale (taʿlīl) is that when a condition is annexed to a sale, a lingering connection (ʿulqa) remains after the contract, through which a dispute (munāzaʿa) is conceivable, and by whose loss the contracting party's purpose is defeated. This reflects back upon the root of the contract, thus sealing the door (against such conditions). The harm of this prohibition was not separable from the contract itself, thereby indicating, without doubt, the corruption (fasād) of the contract or the corruption of the condition.

From this general principle, six conditions are excepted in the case of absolute (unrestricted) sales. The first: that one stipulates what accords with the contract, such as his saying, "I sold on the condition that you benefit from it and dispose of it as you wish" — for no lingering connection remains. Likewise, if he says, "that you eat nothing but harīsah" or "wear nothing but silk (khazz)," and whatever involves no purpose (gharaḍ) — for there is no connection therein to which a dispute might attach, altering thereby the purpose; it is mere idle talk (hadhayān), null and void. This is an exception to the literal wording, but it conforms to the understood meaning.

The second: the condition of the option (khiyār) for three days or less, provided it be known (maʿlūm) and not excessive. Its cause is necessity due to the prevalence of being cheated (ghabīnah), and this was established by the text of the hadiths.

The third: the condition of deferment (muhlah) in the price to a known term (mīqāt maʿlūm), established by the textual evidence (naṣṣ) and reinforced by general necessity.

The fourth: the condition of a security (wathīqah) for the price, whether by pledge (rahn), surety (kafīl), or witnesses (shuhūd), established by the text and reasoned by the generality of need. The surety must be specified by name, and the pledged item specified by identity, for the purpose varies with them. It is not required to specify the witnesses, since the purpose does not vary. As for specifying the one who holds the pledge in trust (ʿadl), there are two views (wajhān).

If the witnesses are specified, are they thereby fixed? Two views: one, they are fixed like the surety; the second, they are not, like specifying the scales (mīzān), since no benefit is sought therein. If we say they are not fixed, the contract is not corrupted thereby; rather, it is void (lāghw), and the contract is unaffected by it.

If one stipulates that the sold item be a pledge (rahn) for the price, al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — said: The sale is annulled (mafsūkh). The companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: This builds upon our position regarding who initiates delivery (al-bidāyah fī al-taslīm) — whether it is the seller or the buyer. If we say the seller initiates, or that delivery is obligatory upon both, such that they choose — whether by the buyer or equally — then the condition becomes a modifier of the contract's requirement (muqtaḍā al-ʿaqd). Its rationale: when delivery is obligatory upon him by the contract's requirement, stipulating that the sale be a pledge in his hand for the price has altered the contract's requirement regarding the obligation of delivery, so it is corrupted.

If we say the buyer initiates, then two views: one, validity (ṣiḥḥah), since there is no impediment; the second, nullity (buṭlān), because the seller's hand is a hand of guarantee (yad ḍamān), whereas the pledge-holder's hand is not a hand of guarantee but a hand of trust (yad amānah). They are opposites, so their two rulings cannot be combined in a single state. The first is more apparent (aẓhar).

Then, when these conditions are validated, if the buyer refuses to fulfill the surety, pledge, or witnessing, the seller acquires the option (khiyār) in the sale. If he complies but the seller refuses to accept the pledge, for instance, is he compelled (yujbar), or is he given the choice between acceptance and the lapse of the option? There is hesitation (taraddud) mentioned by the author of al-Taqrīb. The option is established whenever the pledged item perishes before delivery. Likewise, if the specifically designated item for pledge emerges defective and he was unaware of it. If it perishes after taking possession (qabḍ) of the pledge, there is no option. If he discovers a defect after its loss in his hand, there are two views on whether the option in the original sale is established: one, no, because he was unable to return it; the second, yes, for it became clear that what preceded was not fulfillment of the obligation undertaken.

If it is said: These conditions, if corrupted by ignorance (jahālah) or otherwise, or if a condition is mentioned not among these excepted categories and its corruption is ruled, does the contract become corrupted while its rationale remains — and this applies to the term (ajal), the option, and others? Regarding the condition of security, there are two positions (qawlān). The point of distinction: these are independent, separable matters, so their corruption does not necessitate the corruption of the contract; rather, they are void. The more analogically sound (al-qiyāsī) is the first — that the contract is corrupted — because the Prophet, peace be upon him, prohibited "a sale with a condition," and the object of the prohibition is the sale, so the contract should be corrupted by the absolute prohibition. Also, because what is independent in itself, when annexed to a contract, is affected by it, resembling the option and the term.

The author of al-Taqrīb and Shaykh Abū ʿAlī reported a strange text (naṣṣ gharīb) that the sale is not corrupted by corrupt conditions; rather, the condition is void, as in marriage (nikāḥ). Abū Thawr also reported this from al-Shāfiʿī, but it is far-fetched (baʿīdah).

The fifth of what is excepted from the prohibition: the condition of manumission (ʿitq) in the sold item, based on the report that Barīrah — may Allah be pleased with her — said to ʿĀʾishah: "If your masters were to sell you, I would pour out their price for them profusely." The masters said: "We will not do so except on the condition that she be freed and the clientage (walāʾ) be ours." ʿĀʾishah mentioned this to the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, and he said: "Buy her and stipulate the clientage for them." Then he stood as a preacher and said: "What is the matter with people who stipulate conditions not in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?" — in a lengthy sermon. So he permitted that, and he does not permit falsehood, and he denounced this imposition upon them while permitting compliance.

Some companions derived a position that the condition of manumission is like other corrupt conditions — and this is the analogical view (qiyās), and it is the school of Abū Ḥanīfah. But it has no basis, given the support of the strange position — namely, that the contract is valid and the condition is corrupt. The interpretation (taʾwīl) of the hadith is that it was permission for the contract and the condition. As for the contract, it is valid; as for the condition, it is not binding, but he trusted that ʿĀʾishah would fulfill the condition out of generosity. This is more appropriate, so as not to contradict the analogy, and interpretation by analogy is not forbidden.

Al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah have mercy on him — explicitly stated what we have mentioned, which is conformity with the hadith in validating both the condition and the contract. As for resorting to the corruption of the contract, no basis for it can be conceived with the hadith in any way, even if some might say so.

The branching (tafrīʿ) upon the text regarding the validity of the condition: on this basis, if one stipulates the clientage for the seller, there are two views. One: it is valid, and he has the clientage, due to the story of Barīrah — may Allah have mercy on her — and because he, peace be upon him, does not command corruption. The second: prohibition, for it is extremely remote from analogy, and the possibility of presuming a concession (musāhalah) from the Lawgiver in this particular stipulation is lighter than disturbing the foundation of analogical reasoning. This also disturbs the reliance on the text regarding the original condition, so let the text be accepted in its entirety and in its details.

If it is said: The manumission that becomes due after the validity of the condition — to whom does it belong? I say: Our companions differed on it. Some said it is a right of Allah, the Exalted — as if he undertook the manumission by its condition, resembling a vow (nadhr). Others said it is a right of the seller, because it was established by his condition. Three matters build upon this:

First: whether he has the right to demand it (muṭālabah). If we say it is his right, then yes. If we say it is a right of Allah, then two views; the more correct (aṣaḥḥuhumā) is that he possesses the right of demand, since it was established by his condition and his purpose is attached to it, even if Allah has a right therein.

Second: whether its binding force (luzūm) is dropped by his pardon (ʿafw). If we say it is a right of Allah, then no. If we say it is his right, then two views, for the possessor of a right may not accept its waiver individually, like the term (ajal). This applies consistently to the pardon of the one entitled to the surety and the pledge. On both probabilities, the buyer's manumission of the slave as expiation (kaffārah) is not valid, due to the attachment of another's entitlement to him.

Third: If the buyer refuses to manumit, the author of al-Taqrīb mentioned two positions: one, the seller has the option, as in the refusal of the surety and pledge; the second, he is compelled to manumit, just as a master is compelled to divorce (ṭalāq). This hinges on whether it is a right of Allah, in which case there is no basis for dropping it by the seller's rescission (faskh) or by his permission and satisfaction with the non-manumission.

chapters.title_en: Section 146 — On Defective Conditions and the Division of the Transaction (Tafrīq al-Ṣafqah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرع

لو مات العبد قبل اتفاق العتق فقد تصدى تفويت حق البائع من العتق إلى غير
بدل أو إيجاب بدل بعد زوال ملكه وسلامة الثمن له
فاختلف الأصحاب منهم من قال يفسخ العقد فيسترد الثمن ويضمن المشتري
القيمة حذارا عن ارتكاب محال
ومنهم من قال الانفساخ بعد القبض من غير سبب أيضا محال فيغرم المشتري قدر
التفاوت بين قيمته مع الشرط وقيمته دون الشرط
والثالث أن الغرم لا بد منه ولكن يغرم مثل نسبة هذا التفاوت من الثمن لا
من القيمة بعينها وهذا أعدل الوجوه
السادس إذا شرط في البيع وصفا ناجزا ليس يتوقف على إنشاء أمر بعده وذلك
ينقسم إلى ما يرجع إلى عين والى ما هو وصف محض
أما الوصف المحض فيصح شرطه كقوله بعت العبد على انه كاتب أو خباز ثم أن
اخلف ثبت له الخيار
أما ما يرجع إلى العين كقوله بعت الجارية على أنها حبلى وكذا البهيمة
ففيه قولان أحدهما البطلان لانه يرجع إلى شرط إدراج الحمل في البيع فكأنه
قال بعت الجارية وحملها بدينار فيلتفت على تفريق الصفقة ووجه الأول أن
الحمل كالوصف في الحيوان
أما إذا شرط في الشاة أن تكون لبونا منهم من قال هو كوصف الحرفة والكتابة
فانه ليس بشرط وجود اللبن في الحال فاللبن يتحصل بصفة غريزية ناجزة واللبن
من ثمرتها
ومنهم من قال هو كالحمل فيخرج على القولين
ولو شرط حشو في الجبة فهو من قبيل الحمل وأولى بالصحة لان الحشو يعلم
وجوده والحمل يتردد فيه
ولسنا نشترط رؤية حشو الجبة على قول منع بيع الغائب لان الجبة قد تقصد
على هذا الوجه
وكذلك لا نشترط أن يرى من الدار كل ضبة وسلسلة على باب لانه صار وصفا
وتبعا
أما إذا قال بعتك هذه الصبرة على أنها ثلاثون صاعا فالشرط صحيح فان خرج
كذلك فلا كلام
وان زاد لم يصح في الزائد وفي الباقي يخرج على قولي تفريق الصفقة
وان نقص ففي صحته في ذلك القدر خلاف يلتفت على ما إذا قال بعت منك هذه
النعجة فإذا هي رمكة
ففي قول يعول على الإشارة وفي آخر يعول على العبارة وانما صححنا الشرط
ولم نفسد العقد في الأصل لان كثرة الصيعان في حكم الوصف للصبرة

### | فروع ثلاثة

أحدها إذا قال بعتك ولم يذكر الثمن فسد والمبيع مضمون في يد المشتري أن
قبضه وان لم يذكر الثمن لان البيع يقتضي بمطلقه طلب عوض
وان قال بعتك بلا ثمن فهل ينعقد هبة ذكر القاضي قولين أحدهما نعم لانه
أفاد معناه وهو التمليك مجانا والثاني لا لان اللفظ متهافت فان البيع يقتضي
ثمنا
فان قلنا لم ينعقد ففي الضمان على المشترى إذا قبض وجهان أحدهما يجب ككل
شراء فاسد والثاني لا لان علة الضمان انه لم ينزل عنه إلا ببدل فليرد إليه
او بدله وها هنا نزل عنه مجانا
الثاني إذا استثنى حمل الحيوان عن البيع ففيه وجهان
أحدهما الصحة كما لو كان الولد حرا فان بيع ألام صحيح على الظاهر
والثاني لا لان المبيع معرض لغرر بسبب غير المبيع
الثالث إذا قال اشتريت منك هذا الزرع بدينار على أن تحصده لي
من أصحابنا من قال يفسد لانه شرط فعلا في عقد فكأنه يبغي منه فعلا مع
المبيع
ومنهم من قال لا بل معناه اشتريت منك هذا الزرع واستأجرتك على حصاده
بدينار فالدينار ثمن واجرة فهو جمع بين الإجارة والبيع فيخرج على قولي
تفريق الصفقة في الجمع بين مختلفات الأحكام
فان جوزنا الجمع بين البيع والإجارة على الجملة فهذا يلتفت على اصل آخر
وهو أن أحد شقي عقد الإجارة على العمل في الزرع جرى قبل ملك الزرع
والاستئجار على العمل في ملك الغير غير جائز فيخرج على وجهين فيما إذا قال
لعبده كاتبتك وبعتك ثوبي هذا بألف فقال العبد قبلت واشتريت لانه جرى إيجاب
البيع قبل أن صار العبد أهلا للبيع منه ولكن تأخر القبول عنه والمسألة
محتملة
هذا تمام القول في الشرائط الفاسدة وما فسد منها وافسد العقد قبل اللزوم
فان الملك وان لم ينقل ها هنا ألا أن المقابلة بالعقد حاصلة فلا ينقلب
صحيحا بالحذف في مدة الخيار ولا في مجلس العقد خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله
وكذلك الجهالة المفسدة إذا رفعت في المجلس لم ينتفع
أما الشرط الصحيح إذا الحق بالعقد في المجلس كالخيار والأجل أو زيادة
الثمن والمثمن ففيه وجهان أحدهما المنع كما بعد اللزوم والثاني انه يصح لان
المجلس كأنه حريم العقد وأوله وهذا يفسده قولنا أن حذف الجهالة في المجلس
لا يغني فيعلل هذا التفريع على قولنا الملك غير منتقل
فقبل العوض والزيادة والنقصان وهذا أيضا مشكل على قياس مذهب الشافعي رحمه
الله في المنع من إلحاق الزوائد والشروط
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الرابع في فساد العقد لانضمام فاسد إليه
وهو المعروف بتفريق الصفقة وذلك له ثلاث مراتب - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿ-t-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be free" or "to become emancipated" — the release from bondage, whether physical or metaphorical.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, it denotes the removal of the impediment of slavery (riqq), a definitive act of manumission that severs the master's proprietary right.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the context of freeing a slave; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the "freeing" of a right or obligation from encumbrance.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Conditional Suspension) — The syntactic structure of conditional clauses (sharṭ) governs whether a stipulation is operative at the moment of utterance or deferred, affecting the validity of the contract's binding force.
chapters.translation:
I say: A subsidiary branch — If the slave dies before the agreement on manumission [is concluded], then the seller's right to manumission has been frustrated without compensation, or the imposition of compensation after the seller's ownership has ceased while the price remains secure for him. The companions (al-aṣḥāb) differed on this. Among them was one who said: The contract is rescinded (yufsakh), so the price is reclaimed, and the buyer must guarantee the value (al-qīmah), as a precaution against committing an impossibility (muḥāl). Another said: Rescission after delivery (al-qabḍ) without a cause is also impossible, so the buyer must pay the amount of the disparity between its value with the condition and its value without the condition. The third view is that liability (al-ghurm) is unavoidable, but he pays the equivalent of the proportion of that disparity from the price, not from the value itself — and this is the most equitable of the positions.

The sixth [topic]: If a condition is stipulated in a sale for an immediate (nājiz) attribute that does not depend on the origination of a subsequent matter, it divides into what pertains to the essence (ʿayn) and what is a pure attribute (waṣf maḥḍ). As for the pure attribute, its stipulation is valid, such as his saying: "I sold the slave on the condition that he is a scribe (kātib) or a baker (khabbāz)." Then if he proves contrary, the option (khiyār) is established for him. As for what pertains to the essence, such as his saying: "I sold the slave-girl on the condition that she is pregnant (ḥublā)," and likewise the beast — there are two opinions (qawlān). One is nullification (al-buṭlān), because it reverts to stipulating the inclusion of the fetus in the sale, as if he said: "I sold the slave-girl and her fetus for a dīnār," which turns upon the division of the transaction (tafrīq al-ṣafqah). The basis of the first [valid] view is that the fetus is like an attribute in the case of animals.

As for when he stipulates in the sheep that it is lactating (labūn), some said it is like the attribute of craft or literacy, for it is not a stipulation of the existence of milk at the present moment — rather, the milk is produced by an innate, immediate disposition, and the milk is among its fruits. Others said it is like the fetus, so it is adjudicated upon the two opinions.

If he stipulates stuffing (ḥashw) in the jubba (outer garment), it is of the category of the fetus, but more deserving of validity, because the stuffing's existence is known, whereas the fetus is uncertain. We do not require the seeing of the jubba's stuffing, according to the view that prohibits selling the unseen (ghāʾib), for the jubba may be intended precisely on this basis. Likewise, we do not require that one see every clasp and chain on the door of the house, for it has become an attribute and a subordinate (tabaʿan).

As for when he says: "I sold you this pile (ṣubrah) on the condition that it is thirty ṣāʿs," the condition is valid. If it turns out accordingly, there is no dispute. If it exceeds, it is not valid regarding the excess, and regarding the remainder it is adjudicated upon the two opinions of division of the transaction. If it falls short, then regarding its validity for that amount there is a disagreement that turns upon the case where he says: "I sold you this ewe, and behold it is black (ramkāʾ)." One opinion relies on the indication (al-ishārah), and another relies on the explicit statement (al-ʿibārah). We only validated the condition and did not corrupt the contract in principle because the abundance of ṣāʿs is in the ruling of an attribute for the pile.

Three subsidiary branches — The first: If he says "I sold you" without mentioning the price, the sale is corrupt (fāsid), and the sold item is guaranteed (maḍmūn) in the buyer's hand if he has taken delivery, even if the price was not mentioned, because the sale by its absolute import demands a countervalue (ʿiwaḍ). If he says "I sold you without a price," does it conclude as a gift (hibah)? Al-Qāḍī mentioned two opinions: One, yes, because it conveys its meaning, namely gratuitous transfer of ownership (tamlīk mujjānan). The second, no, because the utterance is self-contradictory (mutahāfit), for the sale demands a price. If we say it does not conclude, then regarding liability upon the buyer if he takes delivery, there are two aspects (wajhān): One, it is obligatory as in every corrupt purchase. The second, no, because the cause of liability is that [the seller] did not relinquish it except for a substitute, so it must be returned to him or its substitute — and here he relinquished it gratuitously.

The second: If he excludes the fetus of an animal from the sale, there are two aspects. One is validity, just as if the offspring were free, for the sale of the mother is valid on the apparent view. The second is no, because the sold item is exposed to uncertainty (gharar) due to something other than the sold item.

The third: If he says "I bought from you this crop for a dīnār on the condition that you harvest it for me," some of our companions said it is corrupt, because it is a stipulation of an act in a contract, as if he seeks from him an act alongside the sold item. Others said no — rather, its meaning is: "I bought from you this crop and hired you to harvest it for a dīnār," so the dīnār is both price and wage. Thus it combines hire (ijārah) and sale, and it is adjudicated upon the two opinions of division of the transaction in combining matters of differing rulings. If we permit the combination of sale and hire in general, then this turns upon another principle — namely, that one half of the hire contract on the labor in the crop occurred before ownership of the crop, and hiring for labor on the property of another is not permissible. So it is adjudicated upon two aspects in the case where he says to his slave: "I have made a kitābah with you and sold you this garment of mine for a thousand," and the slave says: "I accept and I buy" — because the offer of sale occurred before the slave became eligible to purchase from him, but the acceptance was deferred. The matter is plausible.

This completes the discourse on corrupt conditions (al-shurūṭ al-fāsidah), and what among them is corrupt and corrupts the contract before binding (luzūm). For even if ownership is not transferred here, the mutual exchange by the contract is nonetheless realized, so it does not become valid by deletion during the option period, nor in the session of the contract — contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him. Likewise, the corrupting ignorance (al-jahālah al-mufsidah), if removed in the session, does not avail.

As for the valid condition, if it is appended to the contract in the session — like the option, the term, or an increase in price or the priced item — there are two aspects: One is prohibition, as after binding. The second is that it is valid, because the session is like the precinct (ḥarīm) of the contract and its beginning. This is vitiated by our statement that the deletion of ignorance in the session does not avail, so this subdivision is reasoned upon our view that ownership is not transferred before the countervalue, nor the increase or decrease. This too is problematic on the analogy of the school of al-Shāfiʿī, may God have mercy on him, regarding the prohibition of appending increases and conditions.

— Peace be upon him — The Fourth Chapter: On the corruption of the contract due to the attachment of a corrupt element to it, which is known as the division of the transaction (tafrīq al-ṣafqah). It has three ranks — Peace be upon him —

chapters.title_en: The First Rank: The Initial Contract and the Second Rank: Severance in Continuance
chapters.arabic_text:
### | المرتبة الأولى

أن يجري في الابتداء كما لو باع ملكه وملك الغير في صفقة واحدة فسد في
ملك الغير وفي ملكه قولان
أحدهما الصحة لان الصحيح لم يتأثر بالفاسد فلا يفسد بمساوقته
والثاني الفساد لعلتين
أصحهما أن الصحيح تأثر به إذ صار ما يخصه من الثمن مجهولا وجميع المستحق
ثمنا ينبغي أن يعلم وحصة ملكه من الجميع لم يعرف مبلغه فصار كما إذا قال
بعت منك عبدي هذا بما يخصه من الألف لو وزع عليه وعلى قيمة عبد فلان
والثانية أن الصيغة المتحدة إذا فسدت في بعض مسمياتها لم تقبل التبعيض
وهذه العلة توجب الفساد بحكم التفريق في النكاح أيضا
وان عللنا بجهالة العوض لم يجز في الرهن والهبة إذ لا عوض فيهما ولا في
النكاح فان الجهل  فيه بالعوض لا يفسد ولا فيما تتناسب أجزاؤه كعبد مشترك
انفرد أحدهما ببيعه فانه يعلم أن النصف مشترى بالنصف والثلث بالثلث وكذا في
سائر الأجزاء المتناسبة
وان فرعنا على الصحة ثبت الخيار للمشتري فإن فسخ فذاك وان أجاز فبقسطه من
الثمن
وفيه قول آخر انه يخبر بكل الثمن حذارا من أن يكون مبلغ الثمن المستحق
غير معلوم وكأن هذه زيادة فاسدة لم تقبل العوض كالعيب وهو بعيد
والصحيح أن البائع لا خيار له وان أجيز بقسط من الثمن لانه سلم له كل بدل
ملكه هذا إذا باع مملوكا ومعصوبا فان ضم إلى المملوك حرا فالخلاف مرتب
والفساد أولى إذ تقدير قيمة الحر أبعد فإن ضم إليه خمرا أو خنزيرا أو كلبا
فمر به على الحر والفساد أولى إذ لا بد من تقدير صفة خلقته لمعرفة القيمة
ثم إن صححنا فقد قيل يقدر الخنزير نعجة والخمر خلا ليمكن تقويمه وهو بعيد
بل الأصح أن تقدر قيمته على حاله عند من له قيمة عنده
أما إذا ضم إلى الصحيح غائب مجهول لا مطمع في معرفة قيمته فيتعين إبطال
العقد إلا على القول الضعيف في أن الإجازة تجري بكل الثمن فأما إن أجزنا
بقسطه لم نعرف مبلغه بحال
فان قيل قطعتم بالبطلان فيما إذا قال بعتك عبدي بما يخصه من الألف لو وزع
على قيمته وقيمة عبد آخر عينه وترددتم في هذه المسألة فما الفرق
قلنا إن كان المتعاقدان عالمين بحقيقة الحال عند العقد بطل العقد إذ لا
فرق هكذا قاله الشيخ أبو محمد وانما الخلاف عند الجهل إذ قد ظنا أن مبلغ
الثمن معلوم حالة العقد وللظن تأثير في أمثاله كما سبق في نظائره في فصول
علم المبيع ولا وجه إلا ما ذكره الشيخ أبو محمد رحمه الله

### | المرتبة الثانية التفريق في الدوام

وذلك بأن يتلف أحد العبدين قبل القبض على وجه ينفسخ فيه ففي الانفساخ في
الباقي قولان مرتبان على العلتين
والصحيح انه لا ينفسخ لان الجهل محذور في الابتداء والعقد  الآن قد استقر
وعلى هذا يأخذ الباقي بقسطه
وقول التكميل ها هنا في نهاية الضعف لأن العقد قد سبق مقتضيا للتوزيع

### | التفريع

إن جوزنا تفريق الصفقة في الدوام فلو اشترى عبدين ووجد بأحدهما أو بهما
عيبا وأراد إفراد واحد بالرد وهو المعيب فله ذلك
ولو أراد ردهما جاز أيضا وان كان المعيب واحدا لانه لم يسلم له كل
المشترى
وفيه وجه انه لا يردهما إلا إذا كانا معيبين
ولا خلاف في أنه لو أراد رد نصف عبد لم يجز لان التبعيض عيب في حق البائع
وان

### | فرع

نا على القول الآخر فليس له إفراد أحد العبدين بالرد أن رضي البائع
فوجهان
أقيسهما المنع لان استحالة تفريق الصفقة الواحدة لا تختلف بالتراضي
والثاني الجواز وكأن هذا القائل يعلل بتضرر البائع برجوع بعض المبيع إليه
ولو كان الثاني تالفا فهل يمهل عذره في إفراد القائم فيه وجهان فان
منعناه فلو ضم قيمة التالف إليه فهل يتمكن منه فيه خلاف مرتب على ما إذا
أراد ضم ارش العيب الحادث إلى المبيع ورده بالعيب القديم
وها هنا أولى بالمنع لان النقصان في حكم تابع والعبد مستقل بنفسه فلا
يجعل تابعا للقائم

### | فرع

لو حكمنا برد قيمة التالف ضما الى القائم فتنازعا في مقداره فالقول قول
المشتري لانه الغارم والاصل براءة ذمته
ولو تلف أحد العبدين قبل القبض وقلنا يرد البائع ما يخصه دون الباقي
فتنازعا ففيه قولان أحدهما أن القول قول البائع لانه الغارم برد بعض الثمن
والثاني بل القول قول المشتري لانه الذي يسلم بعض الثمن للباقي والمنازع
يرجع إلى مزيد فيه يدعيه البائع وينكره المشتري
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ق-د (ʿAqd)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Binding and tightening; a knot that secures two ends firmly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contractual covenant (ʿaqd) whose validity (ṣiḥḥah) or corruption (fasād) hinges on the integrity of its object and consideration.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical tying; metaphorical for legal obligation binding parties.
- Root: ف-س-د (Fasād)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Corruption, ruin, departure from soundness (ṣalāḥ).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal invalidity arising from a defect in the contract's essence, not mere prohibition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for decay; metaphorical for juristic nullity.
- Root: خ-ي-ر (Khiyār)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Choice, selection between alternatives.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The option granted to a contracting party to affirm or rescind.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for preference; metaphorical for legal discretion.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Dependency (Taʿlīq al-Sharṭ) — The ruling follows the stated cause (ʿillah); when two causes are cited, the stronger governs the branch rulings.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first rank is that severance occurs at the inception [of the contract], as when a man sells his own property along with another's property in a single transaction. Then the contract is corrupted with respect to the other's property, but concerning his own property there are two opinions.

One of them is validity, because the sound [portion] is not affected by the corrupt [portion], so it is not nullified by mere concurrence with it.

The second is corruption, on account of two causes. The more authoritative of them is that the sound [portion] is indeed affected by it, since the share of the price allocated to it has become unknown. For the entire sum owed as a price ought to be known, and the portion pertaining to his own property out of the whole has not been ascertained in its amount. Thus it becomes as if he had said: "I sell you this slave of mine for whatever share of the thousand [dirhams] falls to him, were it apportioned between his value and the value of so-and-so's slave." The second cause is that a single formula (ṣīghah), when it is corrupted in some of its referents, does not admit of division. This cause entails corruption by virtue of severance in marriage (nikāḥ) as well.

But if we ground [the ruling] on the ignorance of the consideration (jahālat al-ʿiwaḍ), then it does not apply to pledge (rahn) or gift (hibah), since there is no consideration in them, nor to marriage, for ignorance of the consideration therein does not corrupt it. Nor does it apply to what has proportionate parts, such as a jointly owned slave when one co-owner alone sells him; for it is known that the half is purchased by the half and the third by the third, and likewise for all other proportionate parts.

If we branch upon validity, then the buyer has the option (khiyār). If he rescinds, that is his right; and if he ratifies, then [he takes the property] for its share of the price.

There is another opinion that he is obligated to pay the entire price, as a precaution lest the amount of the price owed be unknown. This is as if a corrupt increase had been added that does not accept a countervalue, like a defect — and this is remote.

The correct view is that the seller has no option, even if ratification occurs for a share of the price, because he has received the full substitute for his own property. This applies when he sold a possessed [slave] along with a free person. If he appended a free man to the owned slave, then the disagreement is ordered [according to the same two causes], and corruption is more apt, since estimating the value of a free man is more remote. If he appended wine, a pig, or a dog, then pass it over the case of the free man, and corruption is even more apt, for one must estimate the attributes of its created nature to ascertain its value.

Then, if we declare it valid, it has been said that the pig is estimated as a sheep and the wine as vinegar, so that valuation becomes possible — but this is remote. Rather, the more correct view is that its value is estimated in its actual state, according to those who hold a value for it.

As for when he appends to the sound [property] an absent, unknown item whose value cannot be hoped to be known, then nullification of the contract is determined — except on the weak opinion that ratification proceeds with the entire price. For if we ratify for its share, we would never know its amount.

If it is said: "You have ruled definitively for nullity in the case where he said, 'I sell you my slave for whatever share of the thousand falls to him, were it apportioned between his value and the value of another slave he specified,' yet you have hesitated in this very question — what is the difference?"

I say: If the two contracting parties knew the true state of affairs at the time of the contract, then the contract is nullified, for there is no difference. Thus said Shaykh Abū Muḥammad. The disagreement arises only in cases of ignorance, for they supposed that the amount of the price was known at the time of the contract, and supposition (ẓann) has effect in such matters, as has preceded in its analogues in the chapters on the knowledge of the object of sale. There is no position except what Shaykh Abū Muḥammad — may God have mercy on him — mentioned.

### | The Second Rank: Severance in Continuance

This occurs when one of the two slaves perishes before delivery in a manner that entails rescission. Concerning whether the contract is rescinded with respect to the remaining one, there are two opinions, ordered upon the two causes [mentioned above].

The correct view is that it is not rescinded, because ignorance is a hazard at the inception, whereas the contract has now become settled. On this basis, the buyer takes the remaining [slave] for his share [of the price].

The opinion of completion (takmīl) here is at the extreme of weakness, because the contract has already proceeded, necessitating apportionment.

### | The Ramification

If we permit severance of the transaction in continuance, then if a man buys two slaves and finds in one of them — or in both — a defect, and wishes to single out one for return, namely the defective one, he may do so.

If he wishes to return both, that is also permissible, even if only one is defective, because not all of what he purchased has been delivered to him sound.

There is a position that he may not return both unless both are defective.

There is no disagreement that if he wished to return half of a slave, it is not permissible, because division is a defect with respect to the seller.

### | Branch

If we branch upon the other opinion, then he may not single out one of the two slaves for return unless the seller consents. There are two positions:

The more analogical of them is prohibition, because the impossibility of severing a single transaction does not differ with mutual consent.

The second is permissibility — as if this proponent grounds [the ruling] on the seller's harm from the return of part of the sold property to him.

If the second [slave] had perished, is the excuse of the buyer excused in singling out the surviving one? There are two positions. If we prohibit it, then if he appends the value of the perished one to the surviving one, can he accomplish it? There is a disagreement ordered upon the case where he wishes to append the compensation (arsh) for a newly occurring defect to the sold item and return it for an old defect.

Here prohibition is more apt, because the deficiency is in the status of a dependent, whereas the slave is independent in himself; he is not made dependent upon the surviving one.

### | Branch

If we rule for returning the value of the perished one appended to the surviving one, and they dispute over its amount, then the statement is that of the buyer, because he is the guarantor (ghārim), and the principle is the exoneration of his liability.

If one of the two slaves perishes before delivery, and we say that the seller returns what pertains to it without the remaining one, and they dispute, then there are two opinions. One of them is that the statement is that of the seller, because he is the guarantor in returning part of the price. The second is rather that the statement is that of the buyer, because he is the one surrendering part of the price for the remaining one, and the disputant reverts to an increase that the seller claims while the buyer denies.

chapters.title_en: The Third Rank: Combining Two Contracts Differing in Rescission and Dissolution
chapters.arabic_text:
### | المرتبة الثالثة أن يجمع بين عقدين مختلفي الحكم في الفسخ والانفساخ

كالإجارة والبيع أو النكاح والبيع أو الصرف والسلم الذي ينفسخ بالتفرق
قبل
القبض مع غيره مما لا ينفسخ به أو السلم في جنس واحد إلى آجال أو في
أجناس إلى اجل واحد فيه قولان مرتبان على المرتبة الثانية وأولى بالصحة إذ
آحاد هذه العقود صحيحة فلا  مانع في الجمع في الحكم
ووجه الفساد أن انفساخ العقد في البعض لو جرى لانفسخ الباقي وذلك مترقب
فان العقود المتفرقة لا تنتظم أحوالها في المآل فجعل المتوقع كالواقع وهذا
بعيد جدا
فان قيل إذا كان سبب الفساد تفرقا واقعا في صفقة متحدة فبم يعرف اتحاد
الصفقة وتعددها
قلنا إن اتحد البائع والمشتري والعوض اتحدت الصفقة وتتعدد بتعدد البائع
قطعا وكذا بتعدد العوض فإذا قال اشتريت عبدك بدينار واستأجرت جاريتك بدرهم
كانت الصفقة متعددة
فإذا قال اشتريت العبد واستأجرت الجارية بدينار فعند ذلك تتحد وفي التعدد
بتعدد المشتري مع اتحاد البائع وصيغة العقد والعوض قولان أحدهما القياس على
البائع والثاني الفرق فان المشتري كالقائل الثاني على الإيجاب السابق
فالنظر إلى من منه الإيجاب أما إذا اتحد الوكيل وتعدد الموكل أو على العكس
فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها النظر إلى الوكيل فانه العاقد
والثاني إلى الموكل فانه من يقع العقد له
والثالث أن النظر في الشراء إلى الوكيل لانه الذي يتعلق به العقد ظاهرا
وفي البيع إلى الموكل لانه سفير لا يتعلق به حكم

### | التفريع

إن قلنا يتعدد بتعدد المشتري فلو قال لرجلين بعت منكما فقبل أحدهما دون
الآخر ففيه وجهان أحدهما الصحة للتعدد
والثاني المنع لان الجواب غير منطبق على الخطاب وقد التبس جوابهما جميعا
وهذا بعيد إذ نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه على انه لو خالع زوجتيه فقبلت
إحداهما صح مع أن فيه معنى التعليق والمعلق بصفتين لا يحصل بإحداهما
ولا خلاف أنه لو قال لواحد بعت منك هذين الصاعين بدرهم فقال اشتريت
أحدهما بنصف درهم لا يصح وإن فرعنا فعلى جواز تفريق الصفقة للخلل في القبول
وعدم مطابقته للخطاب
وقطع الشيخ أبو علي بأنه لو قال لعبده زوجت منك أمتي فقبل إحداهما صح
النكاح وفرق بينه وبين البيع ولا ينقدح فيه فرق من حيث انتظام الجواب
والخطاب ولكن النكاح أبعد عن قبول الفساد بانضمام فاسد إليه فان غايته أن
يكون ضم الفاسد إليه كشرط فاسد والنكاح لا يفسد به ولعله  رأى تعدد الصفقة
بتعدد الزوجة فان منصبها منصب العاقد لا منصب المبيع
إلا أن هذا التعليل تخدشه مسألة وهي انه لو اصدق امرأتيه عبدا ثم بان
الفساد في نكاح إحداهما قال الشيخ أبو علي للزوج الخيار على التي صح نكاحها
في نصف العبد حتى ينفسخ ويسلم مهر المثل حتى لا يتبعض عليه العبد قال وعرضت
هذا على القفال فارتضاه
ولا تنفك هذه المسألة عن احتمال فإن المرأتين كالمشتريين للعبد فلا يبعد
تعدد الصفقة بهما وسنذكر انفراد أحد المشتريين بالرد إن شاء الله تعالى
ولا خلاف أن أحد المشتريين لو وفى نصيبه من الثمن وقلنا الصفقة متعددة
تسلم إليه حصته من المبيع
وان قلنا الصفقة متحدة فهما كالمشتري الواحد
وفيه إذا سلم بعض الثمن خلاف والظاهر انه لا يسلم إليه شيء من المبيع وان
كان ينقسم كالحنطة مثلا ما لم يسلم تمام الثمن
وفيه وجه أنه يسلم بقدره لأن الثمن متوزع على المبيع لا كالدين في حق
المرهون
فأما إذا كان لا ينقسم فلا خلاف في أنا لا نكلفه المهايأة في قدر ما سلم
ثمنه لأن حق الجنس ضعيف لا يحتمل التسليم والاسترداد ولذلك يبطل بالإعارة

### | القسم الثاني في بيان لزوم العقد وجوازه

وهو أهم ما يذكر بعد بيان صحته وفساده والأصل في البيع اللزوم والجواز
بأسباب خاصة فنعقد فيها ثلاثة أبواب
الباب الأول في خيار المجلس
الباب الثاني في خيار الشرط
في خيار النقيصة
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في خيار المجلس وفيه فصلان - صلى
الله عليه وسلم -
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ق-د (ʿAqada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Binding and tightening; a contract as a firm knot (ʿaqd) between parties.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A covenant (ʿahd) with legal effect; in jurisprudence, the conjunction of offer (ījāb) and acceptance (qabūl) producing obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical tying; metaphorical (majāz) for legal commitment—here used technically.
- Root: ف-س-خ (Fasakha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To undo, unravel, or annul; reversal of a binding state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Dissolution of a contract (infisākh) by legal cause, distinct from revocation (iqālah) which is mutual.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for untying a knot; metaphorical for terminating legal effect.
- Root: ص-ف-ق (Ṣafaqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Striking of hands in a sale; a single transaction (ṣafqah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The unified exchange act; unity of bargain determines legal indivisibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for hand-clap sealing a deal; metaphorical for the transactional unit.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taṭābuq al-Khiṭāb wa al-Jawāb (Correspondence of address and response) — For a valid acceptance, the response must syntactically and semantically mirror the offer; mismatch voids the reply.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third rank is that one combines two contracts whose rulings differ regarding rescission (fasādh) and dissolution (infisākh) — such as hire (ijārah) and sale (bayʿ), or marriage (nikāḥ) and sale, or currency exchange (ṣarf) and salam sale (salaf) which dissolves by separation (tafarruq) before receipt (qabḍ), combined with another contract that does not dissolve thereby — or salam in a single genus (jins) with deferred terms (ājāl), or in multiple genera with a single term. Concerning these, there are two opinions (qawlān), arranged upon the second rank, and [the validity] is more apt (awlā bi-al-ṣiḥḥah), since each individual contract among these is sound; thus there is no impediment to combining them in ruling.

The ground for corruption (fasād) is that if dissolution of one part of the contract were to occur, the remainder would dissolve as well — and this is anticipated (mutaraqqab). For separate contracts do not have their conditions harmonized in the final outcome (maʾāl); thus one treats the anticipated as the actual (al-mutawaqqaʿ ka-al-wāqiʿ) — and this is far-fetched (baʿīd jiddan).

If it is said: "When the cause of corruption is a separation (tafarruq) occurring within a single transaction (ṣafqah wāḥidah), how is the unity of the transaction and its multiplicity known?"

I say: If the seller and buyer and the counter-value (ʿiwaḍ) are unified, the transaction is unified; and it becomes multiple by the multiplicity of the seller — definitively (qaṭʿan) — and likewise by the multiplicity of the counter-value. Thus if one says: "I bought your slave for a dinar and hired your slave-girl for a dirham," the transaction is multiple.

But if he says: "I bought the slave and hired the slave-girl for a dinar," then it is unified. Regarding multiplicity by the multiplicity of the buyer, with unity of the seller, the contract formula (ṣīghah), and the counter-value, there are two opinions: one is analogy (qiyās) upon the seller; the second is differentiation (farq) — for the buyer is like the second speaker responding to the preceding offer (ījāb), so consideration is given to the one from whom the offer emanates.

As for when the agent (wakīl) is unified but the principals (muwakkilūn) are multiple — or the reverse — there are three aspects (awjuh):
One: consideration is given to the agent, for he is the contracting party (al-ʿāqid).
Second: to the principal, for the contract is concluded on his behalf.
Third: in purchase, consideration is to the agent, for the contract attaches to him outwardly (ẓāhir); in sale, to the principal, for the agent is merely an intermediary (safīr) to whom no ruling attaches.

### | Subdivision (Tafrīʿ)

If we say it becomes multiple by the multiplicity of the buyer — then if he said to two men: "I sold to both of you," and one of them accepted without the other, there are two aspects: one is validity (ṣiḥḥah) due to multiplicity; the second is prohibition (manʿ), because the response does not correspond to the address (khiṭāb), and their joint response is ambiguous (multabis). This [second view] is far-fetched, for Imam al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — explicitly ruled that if a man divorced (khālaʿa) his two wives and one of them accepted, it is valid, even though it contains the meaning of suspension (taʿlīq), and what is suspended upon two conditions is not effected by one of them.

There is no disagreement that if he said to one man: "I sold you these two ṣāʿs for a dirham," and he replied: "I bought one of them for half a dirham," it is not valid — even if we branch [on the permissibility of splitting], for the defect lies in the acceptance and its non-correspondence to the address.

Shaykh Abū ʿAlī definitively ruled that if he said to his slave: "I have married you to my slave-girl," and she accepted, the marriage is valid. He distinguished between this and sale, though no distinction is apparent regarding the coherence of response and address — but marriage is more remote from accepting corruption by the annexation of a corrupt element to it. For at most, annexing a corrupt element to it is like a corrupt condition (sharṭ fāsid), and marriage is not invalidated thereby. Perhaps he held the transaction to be multiple by the multiplicity of the wife, for her station is that of a contracting party, not that of the sold object (mabīʿ).

Yet this reasoning is undermined by a case: if he gave two wives a slave as dower (ṣadāq), and then corruption became apparent in the marriage of one of them — Shaykh Abū ʿAlī said: the husband has the option (khiyār) regarding the wife whose marriage is sound, over half the slave, so that it dissolves and he pays the equivalent dower (mahr al-mithl), so that the slave is not divided against him. He said: "I presented this to al-Qaffāl, and he approved it."

This case is not free from possibility, for the two wives are like two buyers of the slave; thus the multiplicity of the transaction by them is not improbable. We shall mention the sole buyer's right of return (radd) alone, God willing.

There is no disagreement that if one of two buyers paid his share of the price, and we hold the transaction to be multiple, his portion of the sold item is delivered to him.

But if we hold the transaction to be unified, they are like a single buyer. In this case, if part of the price is paid, there is disagreement; the apparent view is that nothing of the sold item is delivered to him — even if it is divisible, like wheat, for example — until the full price is paid. Another view holds that an amount proportional to it is delivered, because the price is apportioned over the sold item, not like a debt (dayn) against a pledged item (marhūn).

As for when it is not divisible, there is no disagreement that we do not compel him to time-sharing (muhāyāʾah) for the portion whose price he has paid, for the right of the genus (jins) is weak and cannot bear delivery and retrieval — and for this reason it is voided by lending (iʿārah).

### | Section Two: Clarifying the Bindingness (Luzūm) and Permissibility (Jawāz) of Contracts

This is the most important matter to mention after clarifying their validity and corruption. The principle in sale is bindingness, and permissibility arises through specific causes. Thus we devote three chapters to it:

Chapter One: The Option of the Session (Khiyār al-Majlis)
Chapter Two: The Option of Stipulation (Khiyār al-Sharṭ)
Chapter Three: The Option of Defect (Khiyār al-Naqīṣah)

— May God bless him and grant him peace — Chapter One: On the Option of the Session, containing two sections — May God bless him and grant him peace —
