chapters.arabic_text:
### | المانع الثالث هلاك المعقود عليه

حسيا بالتلف أو حكما بالعتق والاستيلاد فإذا اطلع بعد الفوات فلا رد إذ
لا مردود وتعين الحق في الأرش وهو جزء من الثمن كما سبق وهل يبرأ عن ذلك
الجزء من الثمن بمجرد الاطلاع أم يتوقف على طلبه فيه تردد
وميل القاضي إلى انه لا يتوقف على الطلب بخلاف ما لو قدر على الرد فان
الفسخ لا يحصل دون طلبه ومن الأصحاب من قال كما بقي له طريق الرضا بالمعيب
بكل الثمن مع البقاء يبقى له ذلك بعد الفوات فلا بد من الطلب
فان قيل لو كان قد استوفى الثمن وطلب المشتري الأرش فهل يتعين حقه في عين
الثمن أم يجوز للبائع الإبدال
قلنا فيه تردد للأصحاب إذ يحتمل أن يقال المعيب في مقابلة كل الثمن إن
رضي به وإلا فهو في مقابلة بعضه فيخرج ذلك البعض عن المقابلة وتعين
لاستحقاقه وهو ظاهر كلام الأصحاب وكأن المقابلة تغيرت ولكن جوز ذلك مهما
استند إلى سبب في اصل العقد وان كان لا يجوز ذلك بالتراضي عند إلحاق زيادة
بالثمن بعد اللزوم
ويحتمل أن يقال هذه غرامة وكأن البائع جعل معيبا لملك المشتري إذ العقد
الواحد لا يقتضي مقابلتين في حالتين ويشهد له  أن مشتري الجارية بعبد معيب
يعلم عيبه يستحل وطأها ولو كان جزء منه لغرض العود إلى بائع الجارية لو
اطلع على عيب العبد لا ورث توقعه شبهة وهذه المباحثة من دقيق الفقه فلتفهم

### | فرع

لو تلف أحد العوضين في بيع العبد بالجارية فمن وجد عيبا بالقائم رده ورجع
إلى قيمة المعوض الفائت اعتمادا في الرد على قيام المردود
ولو اشترى عبدين فتلف أحدهما وقلنا يمتنع إفراد أحد العبدين بالرد لتفريق
الصفقة رجع بالأرش والقيمة المعرفة لنسبة الارش حيث يرجع إلى الارش قيمة
يوم العقد أو قيمة يوم القبض فيه ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها يوم العقد فانه يوم الاستحقاق
والثاني يوم القبض لانه يوم الضمان
والثالث اقل القيمتين نظرا لجانب المشتري

### | المانع الرابع زوال الملك عن البيع

يمنعه من الرد في الحال فلو عاد إليه بان باع فرد إليه بالعيب فله الرد
على الأول لان العائد هو الملك الأول
وان عاد إليه ببيع مستأنف فإن رد على الأخير حتى إذا رد عليه على الأول
جاز وان ابتدأ بالأول ورد عليه فوجهان وكذلك لو عاد إليه بهبة فوجهان
مرتبان وأولى بالجواز إذ في البيع قدر على الرد على الثاني حتى يرد على
الأول بعد العود إليه بالرد
ومنشأ الوجهين أن الزائل العائد كالذي لم يزل أو كالذي لم يعد ويجري ذلك
في رجوع شطر الصداق بالطلاق وفي رجوع البائع إلى السلعة بعد إفلاس المشتري
بالثمن فمن قائل رد ما اشترى كما اشترى ومن قائل ليس هذا الملك الذي ينقصه
ما استفاد منه بل استفاده بالهبة وإنما ذلك الملك قد زال ولم يعد فصار كما
إذا فات ثم إذا منعناه من الرد ثبت له الارش وان كان ذلك في ملك الغير
وامتنع الرد في الحال ولكن قلنا لو عاد لقدر على الرد ففي جواز المطالبة
بالارش في الحال لوقوع الحيلولة وجهان يقربان من القولين في شهود الأموال
إذا رجعوا لان الحيلولة واقعة في المسألتين وتوقع الوصول إلى أصل الحق مرجو
فيهما والأصح جواز طلب  البدل في الحال

### | فرعان

أحدهما لو رضي المشتري الثاني بالعيب فالأصح أن للأول المطالبة
بالارش فان تبرع غيره عليه لا يلزمه التبرع على غيره
الثاني إذا كان عوض المردود خارجا عن الملك وعائدا فالأصح أن ذلك لا يضر
وجها واحدا لان عود ذلك يجري قهرا فيرجع إلى عينه ولأنه لو تلف لرجع إلى
قيمته جبرا له والآن هو بعينه قائم فهو أولى بأن يكون جائزا

### | المانع الخامس العيب الحادث

يمنع من الرد بالعيب القديم لان جانب البائع أيضا يصان عن الضرر الحادث
كما صين جانب المشتري عن القديم فمسلك التدارك أن يضم المشتري أرش العيب
الحادث إليه ويرد أو يغرم البائع أرش العيب القديم حتى لا يرد فإن اتفقا
على أحد المسلكين فذاك وان تنازعا في التعيين فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أن البائع متبوع لان الأصل ألا يلحقه درك أصلا إلا إذا لم يتضرر
والثاني المشتري متبوع لان الأصل إن تمام الثمن لا يلزمه إلا بمبيع سليم
والثالث أن من يدعو إلى ارش العيب القديم أولى لأن استرداده يستند إلى
اصل العقد أما ملك الارش عن العيب الحادث فجديد لا مدخل له في العقد
فان قيل لو زال العيب الحادث بعد اخذ الارش عن القديم هل يعود حقه في
الرد
قلنا فيه وجهان أحدهما بلى إذ الارش مأخوذة للحيلولة الناجزة
والثاني لا لوقوع الرضا بالعيب فان لم يقبض بعد ولكن قضى القاضي بالارش
فوجهان مرتبان وأولى بأن يعود الحق
أما إذا لم يطلع حتى زال العيب الحادث فالمذهب جواز الرد بالعيب القديم
هذا إذا لم يكن للعيب الحادث أمد ينتظر زواله
فإن كان له أمد كعدة الوطء بالشبهة إذا طرأت على الجارية فانه عيب
فلو اطلع على العيب ولم يرد في الحال منتظرا زواله ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه يبطل حقه إذ قدر على طلب الارش
والثاني لا لكونه معذورا في الانتظار
chapters.anchors:
- Root: هـ-ل-ك (halaka)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Physical perishing, annihilation, or ruin of a thing's substance
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal contexts, denotes the cessation of the thing's legal identity—whether by physical extinction or by a juridical construct that removes it from the sphere of return (e.g., manumission)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal sense (ḥaqīqah) for physical destruction, and metaphorically (majāz) for legal extinction such as ʿitq (emancipation) which renders the object non-returnable
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Ellipsis (al-Sharṭ wa-l-Jawāb bi-Ḥadhf) — The protasis "if he becomes aware after the loss" implies an elided apodosis governing the legal consequence, requiring the reader to supply the operative ruling from context
chapters.translation:
I say: The third impediment [to exercising the option of defect] is the destruction of the object of the contract—whether physically, by perishing, or legally, by manumission or by the master's begetting a child upon a slave-girl (istīlād). When the buyer becomes aware [of the defect] after the object has been lost, there is no return (radd), for there is nothing to be returned. His right becomes fixed exclusively in the compensation for the defect (arsh), which is a portion of the price, as previously established. Concerning whether he is discharged from that portion of the price merely upon becoming aware [of the defect], or whether it is contingent upon his demanding it—there is a divergence of opinion (taraddud).

The judge [Abū Ṭayyib al-Ṭabarī] inclined toward the view that it is not contingent upon his demand, unlike the case where he is able to return [the object], for rescission (faskh) is not effected without his demand. Among our companions (aṣḥāb) there are those who said: Just as he retains the avenue of acquiescing to the defective [article] for the full price while it remains [in his possession], so too he retains that [avenue] after its loss; hence, his demand is required [for the arsh to be fixed].

If it is said: If the seller had already received the full price, and the buyer demands the arsh—is his right fixed specifically in the very price (ʿayn al-thaman), or is the seller permitted to substitute [other property]?

I say: There is a divergence among the companions here. For it may be said that the defective [article] stands in exchange for the entire price if he is satisfied with it; otherwise, it stands in exchange for a portion thereof. That portion then exits from the exchange and becomes fixed as his entitlement—and this is the apparent purport of the companions' statements. It is as though the exchange-relationship (muqābalah) has been altered; yet this alteration is permitted whenever it traces back to a cause rooted in the original contract, even though such alteration would not be permissible by mutual consent when an addition to the price is appended after the contract has become binding (luzūm).

And it may be said: This is a compensatory indemnity (gharāmah), as though the seller had rendered the defective [article] a liability upon the buyer's ownership. For a single contract cannot entail two distinct exchange-relationships in two different states. This is corroborated by the fact that one who purchases a slave-girl with a defective slave, knowing the defect [in the slave], may lawfully have intercourse with her. Had a portion [of the price] been reserved for the purpose of reverting to the seller of the slave-girl upon discovering the slave's defect, he would not have anticipated [such intercourse] without the taint of uncertainty (shubhah). This inquiry belongs to the subtle points of jurisprudence (daqīq al-fiqh)—so comprehend it well.

### | Subsidiary Issue

If one of the two exchanged objects perishes in a sale of a slave for a slave-girl, then whoever finds a defect in the surviving object may return it and revert to the value of the lost counter-value, relying for the validity of the return upon the continued existence of the returned object.

If one purchases two slaves and one of them perishes, and we hold that isolating one of the two slaves for return is impermissible due to the division of the transaction (tafrīq al-ṣafqah), he reverts to the arsh. The value by which the proportion of the arsh is determined—where he reverts to the arsh—is it the value on the day of contract or the value on the day of delivery? There are three opinions:

One: The day of contract, for that is the day of entitlement (istiḥqāq).
Second: The day of delivery, for that is the day of liability (ḍamān).
Third: The lesser of the two values, out of consideration for the buyer's interest.

### | The Fourth Impediment: The Transfer of Ownership from the Sale

It prevents him from returning [the object] at the present moment. If ownership reverts to him—for instance, the buyer sold it and then it was returned to him due to a defect—he may return it to the first seller, for what has reverted is the original ownership itself.

But if it reverts to him through a fresh, independent sale, then he may return it to the latter [seller]; and when he has returned it to him, he may then return it to the first [seller]. If he begins with the first and returns it to him, there are two aspects (wajhān). Likewise, if it reverts to him by gift (hibah), there are two aspects, arranged in order [of strength], with the permissibility being more likely [in the gift case]. For in the sale, he was able to return to the second [seller] so that he could then return to the first after ownership had reverted to him through that return.

The origin of the two aspects is whether the ownership that departed and then returned is like that which never departed, or like that which never returned. This principle applies also to the return of a portion of the dower (ṣadāq) upon divorce, and to the seller's reversion to the commodity after the buyer's bankruptcy with respect to the price. Thus, some say: "He returns what he purchased as he purchased it." Others say: "This is not the same ownership that is diminished by what he derived from it; rather, he acquired it through the gift. That original ownership has departed and not returned, so it is as though it had perished."

Then, when we prevent him from returning, the arsh is established for him—even if [the object] is in the possession of a third party. And although return is prevented at present, we said: If it were to revert, he would be able to return. Concerning the permissibility of demanding the arsh at present, given that the obstruction (ḥaylūlah) exists—there are two aspects, closely paralleling the two opinions regarding witnesses of wealth (shuhūd al-amwāl) when they retract [their testimony]. For the obstruction is present in both cases, and the hope of attaining the original right is deferred in both. The more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is the permissibility of demanding the substitute at present.

### | Two Subsidiary Issues

First: If the second buyer acquiesces to the defect, the more correct view is that the first [buyer] may still demand the arsh. For if another voluntarily forgoes [his right] on his behalf, that does not oblige him to forgo on behalf of another.

Second: If the counter-value of the returned object has left the ownership [of the one holding it] and then reverted, the more correct view—unanimously—is that this causes no harm. For the reversion of that occurs by compulsion (qahran), so it reverts to its very identity (ʿayn). And because, had it perished, he would have reverted to its value by way of compulsory compensation; now that it remains in its very identity, it is even more fitting that it be permissible.

### | The Fifth Impediment: A Supervening Defect

It prevents return on account of the pre-existing defect, for the seller's side is also protected against supervening harm just as the buyer's side is protected against the pre-existing harm. The path of rectification (maslak al-tadāruk) is that the buyer either adds the arsh of the supervening defect to [the object] and returns it, or the seller pays the arsh of the pre-existing defect so that he does not return it. If they agree upon one of the two paths, that is [valid]. If they dispute over which is to be specified, there are three aspects:

One: The seller is to be followed, for the original principle is that no recourse (darak) attaches to him at all—except when he suffers no harm [thereby].
Second: The buyer is to be followed, for the original principle is that the full price is not incumbent upon him except for a sound commodity.
Third: The one who calls for the arsh of the pre-existing defect is more deserving, for his recovery traces back to the original contract. As for the entitlement to the arsh for the supervening defect, it is novel and has no entry into the contract.

If it is said: If the supervening defect disappears after he has taken the arsh for the pre-existing defect, does his right of return revert?

I say: There are two aspects. One: Yes, for the arsh was taken for an immediate obstruction (ḥaylūlah nājizah). Second: No, for acquiescence to the defect has occurred. If he has not yet received [the arsh], but the judge has decreed it, then there are two aspects, arranged in order [of strength], with the reversion of the right being more likely.

As for the case where he does not become aware [of the defect] until the supervening defect has disappeared—the established doctrine (al-madhhab) is the permissibility of return on account of the pre-existing defect. This applies when the supervening defect has no fixed term awaiting its disappearance.

But if it has a fixed term—such as the waiting period (ʿiddah) following intercourse under a defective contract (waṭʾ bi-l-shubhah) when it supervenes upon a slave-girl, for that is a defect—then if he becomes aware of the [pre-existing] defect and does not return at once, waiting for its disappearance, there are two aspects:

One: His right is nullified, for he was able to demand the arsh.
Second: It is not nullified, for he is excused in waiting.

chapters.title_en: Three Subsidiary Branches — On Defects, Augmentations, and the Return of the Sold Object
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع ثلاثة

أحدها لو أنعل الدابة ثم اطلع على العيب فلينزع النعل وليرده إن كان لا
يتعيب بالنزع وليس يلزم  البائع قبول النعل وان كان يعيبه فله الرد وعلى
البائع
قبول النعل فانه تابعا ولو قال المشتري لا اسمح بالنعل وأطلب الارش لم
يكن له ذلك فإنه كالمحتقر في مؤنة الرد
نعم تردد الأصحاب في أن ذلك إعراض عن النعل أو تمليك حتى لو سقط فهو
للبائع أو المشتري وهو محتمل أما إذا صبغ الثوب وزادت قيمته فله الرد
بالعيب القديم إن لم يطلب قيمة الصبغ وليس للبائع الامتناع
وان طلب قيمة الصبغ فهل يجب على البائع ذلك مع رد الثمن وجهان والفرق إن
النعل تابع والصبغ مقصود ولا يسمح به
فإن قلنا لا نكلفه قيمته فهو كعيب حادث فتعود الأوجه الثلاثة في أن تمليك
أرش عيب حادث أولى أم غرم أرش العيب القديم
ولم يذهب أحد إلى أن المشتري يبقى شريكا بالصبغ لأن المشتري يتضرر بذلك
بخلاف الغاصب إذا صبغ فإنا نبقيه شريكا ولا نلتفت إلى تضرره لعدوانه
أما إذ اشترى رجلان عبدين ففي انفراد أحدهما برد نصيبه قولان
ووجه المنع تفريق الصفقة إن قلنا إنها تتحد مع تعدد المشتري أو عيب
التبعيض على البائع إذا عاد إليه النصف وإذا عللنا بهذا جوزنا الرد فيما لا
ينقصه التبعيض
والمقصود أنا لو منعناه من الأفراد فاشترى نصيب شريكه واخذ برد الكل
دافعا عنه ضرر التبعيض ويطالب بقيمة النصف فهل يجبر البائع عليه فيه وجهان
كما في الصبغ
الثاني اشترى حليا وزنه ألف درهم بألف حدث به عيب انكسار واطلع على عيب
قديم فلو ضم إليه أرش العيب الحادث لاسترد ألفا ورد ما يزيد عليه وهو عين
الربا
ولو كلف البائع أرش العيب القديم لصار الألف بعد حط الارش في مقابلة
الألف فهو ربا فقال ابن سريج هذا عقد تعذر إمضاؤه فينفسخ ويسترد الثمن ولا
ترد الحلي بل يغرم قيمته غير معيب بالعيب الحادث بالذهب إن كان الحلي من
الفضة
أو بالفضة إن كان من الذهب فرارا من ربا الفضل
وهذا يستمد مما نفرد من أن الارش يتعين في الثمن ويتعين  المقابلة بأخذه
وقال صاحب التقريب بل يغرم البائع أرش العيب القديم فإن ذلك الأرش غرم في
مقابلة العيب وكأن البائع هو المعيب وهذا إشارة إلى أنه لا يتعين في الثمن
وقال العراقيون بل يغرم المشتري أرش العيب الحادث ويرد ولا مقابلة إلا
بين الثمن والحلي وهما متوازيان وهذه غرامة عيب حدث في يد المشتري مضمونا
وهذا أيضا بعيد لان الارش كالبدل عن ذلك الجزء من المعقود عليه الذي فات
بالعيب حتى يرد الفسخ عليه فتتناوله المقابلة فتحصلنا على احتمالين في
حقيقة كل واحد من الأرشين وأنه غرم مبتدأ أم هو من مقابلة المعقود عليه
والمشهور ما أشار إليه ابن سريج فيهما جميعا
الثالث إذا قور البطيخ وكسر الجوز والرمان والبيض واطلع على عيب باطن فإن
زاد في الكسر على حاجة المعرفة فعيب حادث وإن اقتصر فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه عيب حادث وهو ظاهر النص
والثاني أنه يرد من غير أرش إذ يستحيل أن يبطل رده بطريق الاطلاع
والاطلاع سبب الرد
والثالث وهو الأعدل أن استقلاله بالرد لا يبطل ولكن يضم أرش الكسر حتى لا
يتضرر البائع أيضا
أما إذا لم يبق له بعد الكسر قيمة كالبيضة المذرة قال الشافعي رضي الله
عنه يسترد كمال الثمن
فقال الأصحاب معناه انه يسترد أرش النقصان ولكن أرش النقصان كمال الثمن
إذا لم يبق له قيمة وفائدته أن القشرة تبقى مختصة بالمشتري فتبقى الطريق
عنهما
والوجه أن يقال تبين أن العقد باطل إذ ورد على غير متمول وهو تأويل كلام
الشافعي رضي الله عنه والقشرة مختصة بالبائع فإن فرض له قيمة قبل الكسر
للنقش ولعب الصبيان فقد بطلت المالية الآن
فإن قلنا إن طريق الاطلاع من عهدة البائع حتى لا يجب به أرش فها هنا أيضا
ينقدح معه استرداد تمام الثمن ويجعل كأنه لم يشتر إلا ما بقي بعد الإطلاع
وإن جعل ذلك من ضمان المشتري فلا ينقدح معه استرداد تمام الثمن
هذا تمام القول في لزوم العقد وجوازه واختتام القسم بثلاثة فصول

- Root: ن-ع-ل (na-ʿa-la)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To shoe a beast; the horseshoe (naʿl) as an attached, non-essential addition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Augmentation (ziyādah) attached to the substance of the sold object; its legal status depends on whether it is incidental (tābiʿ) or independent (maqṣūd).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical attachment; metaphorical — legal subordination (tabaʿiyyah) in the contract.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The protasis (law) governs the apodosis (fa-), requiring precise parsing of hypothetical legal cases.
chapters.translation:
I say: Three subsidiary branches [follow].

**The First Branch:** If a man shoes the beast [of burden] and then discovers a defect [in it], let him remove the shoe and return [the beast], if it is not damaged by the removal. The seller is not obliged to accept the shoe [as part of the return]. But if [the beast] is damaged by the removal, then he has the right of return, and the seller is obliged to accept the shoe, for it is a subordinate [attachment]. And if the buyer says, "I will not part with the shoe, and I demand the compensation for the defect (ar sh)," he has no such right, for he is like one who disdains [to bear] the expense of the return.

Indeed, the companions (al-aṣḥāb) wavered on whether this constitutes an abandonment (iʿrāḍ) of the shoe or a transfer of ownership (tamlīk), such that if it falls [and is lost], it belongs to the seller or to the buyer — and this is a matter of probability. As for when he dyes the garment and its value increases, he has the right of return due to the ancient defect, if he does not demand the value of the dye; and the seller has no right to refuse. But if he demands the value of the dye, is the seller obliged to pay it along with the return of the price? There are two views (wajhān). The distinction is that the shoe is subordinate, while the dye is an intended [augmentation], and one does not part with it freely.

If we say that we do not burden him with its value, then it is like a newly-arisen defect (ʿayb ḥādith), and the three views return concerning whether the transfer of the compensation for a newly-arisen defect is more appropriate, or the payment of the compensation for the ancient defect. And no one has held that the buyer remains a partner in the dye, because the buyer is harmed by that — unlike the usurper (ghāṣib) who dyes [a garment], for we keep him as a partner and do not heed his harm, due to his transgression.

**As for when two men purchase two slaves:** Concerning the exclusivity of one of them in returning his share, there are two opinions (qawlān). The ground for prohibition is the splitting of the bargain (tafrīq al-ṣafqah), if we say that it is unified despite the multiplicity of buyers; or [it is] the defect of partition (ʿayb al-tabʿīḍ) upon the seller, when the half returns to him. And if we ground [the ruling] on this [latter], we permit the return in whatever is not diminished by partition.

And the point is: if we prevent him from [returning] his share alone, and he purchases the share of his partner and undertakes the return of the whole, warding off from himself the harm of partition, and demands the value of the half — is the seller compelled to [accept] that? There are two views, as in the case of the dye.

**The Second Branch:** He purchased jewelry weighing one thousand dirhams for one thousand [dirhams]. A defect of breakage occurred to it, and he discovered an ancient defect. If he were to add to it the compensation for the newly-arisen defect, he would recover one thousand and return what exceeds it — and that is the very essence of usury (ribā). And if he were to burden the seller with the compensation for the ancient defect, then the thousand, after deducting the compensation, would stand in exchange for the thousand — and that is usury. Thus Ibn Surayj said: This is a contract whose execution (imḍāʾ) has become impossible; therefore it is dissolved (yanfasikh), and the price is recovered, and the jewelry is not returned; rather, its value, free of the newly-arisen defect, is paid in gold if the jewelry is of silver, or in silver if it is of gold — fleeing from the usury of excess (ribā al-faḍl).

This derives from what we have isolated [as a principle]: that the compensation (ar sh) is determined in the price, and the exchange is determined by taking it. And the author of al-Taqrīb said: Rather, the seller pays the compensation for the ancient defect, for that compensation is a payment in exchange for the defect, and it is as though the seller is the defective one. This indicates that it is not determined in the price. And the Iraqis said: Rather, the buyer pays the compensation for the newly-arisen defect and returns [the jewelry], and there is no exchange except between the price and the jewelry, and they are equivalent — and this is a payment for a defect that occurred in the buyer's hand while it was under his liability (maḍmūn). This too is remote, because the compensation is like a substitute for that part of the object of sale which has perished through the defect, such that the dissolution (faskh) reverts upon it, and the exchange encompasses it. Thus we arrive at two probabilities concerning the reality of each of the two compensations — whether it is an initiating payment (ghurm mubtadaʾ) or [a payment] from the exchange of the object of sale. And the well-known [view] is what Ibn Surayj indicated concerning both of them.

**The Third Branch:** If he splits open the watermelon, cracks the walnut, the pomegranate, and the egg, and discovers an internal defect — if the cracking exceeds the need of inspection, then it is a newly-arisen defect. But if he confines [the cracking to the need], then there are three views:

One: It is a newly-arisen defect, and this is the apparent [import] of the text (naṣṣ).

Second: He returns [the object] without compensation, for it is impossible that his right of return be nullified by the very means of inspection, and inspection is the cause of the return.

Third — and this is the most equitable: His independent right of return is not nullified, but he adds the compensation for the cracking, so that the seller is not harmed either.

As for when no value remains after the cracking — like the egg that is spilled — al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, said: He recovers the full price. The companions said: Its meaning is that he recovers the compensation for the deficiency, but the compensation for the deficiency is the full price when no value remains. And its benefit is that the shell remains exclusively the buyer's, and thus the path [of return] is blocked for both of them.

And the [correct] view is that it becomes evident that the contract is void (bāṭil), since it was concluded upon a non-valuable thing (ghayr mutamawwal) — and this is the interpretation of al-Shāfiʿī's statement, may God be pleased with him — and the shell is exclusively the seller's. For if a value is supposed for it before the cracking, due to engraving or children's play, then the monetary value has now been nullified.

If we say that the path of inspection is from the seller's warranty (ʿuhdah), such that no compensation is thereby obligated, then here too the recovery of the full price emerges with it, and it is as though he purchased nothing but what remained after the inspection. But if that is made from the buyer's liability (ḍamān), then the recovery of the full price does not emerge with it.

This completes the discourse on the bindingness (luzūm) of the contract and its permissibility (jawāz), and the section concludes with three chapters.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل  الأول في حقيقة الرد والفسخ

وهو عندنا رفع العقد من وقته ولذلك لم يمتنع الرد بالعيب بالزوائد
المنفصلة ولا بوطء الثيب
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله هو رفع للعقد من أصله ولأجله خالف في وطء الثيب
والزوائد المنفصلة
أما الفسخ قبل القبض ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه رفع من أصله لأن العقد بعد ضعيف لم يتكامل وعلى هذا نقول
الزوائد الحاصلة قبل القبض تنقلب بالفسخ إلى البائع
والثاني انه رفع من وقته كما بعد القبض وعلى هذا فالزوائد تبقى للمشتري
فإن قلنا تنقلب بالفسخ إلى البائع فله حبس الزوائد للثمن إذا قلنا له حبس
المبيع لانه يتوقع التعلق به
وان قلنا تسلم للمشتري فليس له فيه حق الحبس
فان قيل وما وجه رجوع الزوائد إلى ملك البائع وقد حدثت في ملك المشتري
كما بعد القبض
قلنا لأجله قال فريق لا يرجع إليه والقائل الآخر يتعلق بما روي انه عليه
السلام سئل عن غلة المبيع تسلم للمشتري بعد الفسخ وبعد القبض فقال الخراج
بالضمان أي هو على خطر الضمان
بالقبض فالغنم بالغرم ومفهومه أنه لا يسلم قبل القبض له
والقائل الأول يتبع القياس ويقول ذلك علة لمنع الرجوع ذكره لقطع استبعاد
السائل وقبل القبض لا يرجع لعلة أخرى وهو أنه حدث من ملكه والحكم قد يعلل
بعلتين

### | الفصل الثاني في حقيقة الإقالة وفيه قولان

الجديد أنه فسخ لان اللفظ ينبئ عنه ولأنه جائز قبل القبض وفي المسلم فيه
والبيع لا يجوز
والقديم أنه بيع جديد وليس له وجه وان تكلفنا له تقريرا في كتاب البسيط
في المذهب

### | فرع

لو كان المبيع تالفا ففي جواز الإقالة على الجديد وجهان
أحدهما المنع كالرد بالعيب فانه يمتنع بعد الفوات والثاني الجواز فإن
العقد معتمد الفسخ وهو قائم والرد يعتمد المردود وهو هالك
فإن كان الهالك أحد العبدين ففي جواز الإقالة وجهان مرتبان وأولى بالجواز
إذ القائم يستتبع الهالك وإن كانا قائمين فأراد إفراد أحدها بالفسخ فليلتفت
على تفريق الصفقة
والمذهب جوازه لا سيما في الدوام

### | الفصل الثالث في النزاع في الرد بالعيب

فإذا قال المشتري هذا العيب قديم وقال البائع بل هو حادث فالقول قول
البائع لان الأصل السلامة ولزوم العقد
فلو حلف ثم جرى الفسخ بعده بتحالف فأخذ يطالب المشتري بأرشه وزعم أني
أثبت حدوثه بيميني لم نمكنه لان يمينه صلحت للدفع عنه فلا يصلح لشغل ذمة
المشتري بل للمشتري أن يحلف الآن على أنه ليس بحادث
ثم قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه يحلف أني بعته وما به عيب فقال المزني بل
يزيد ويقول بعته وأقبضته وما به عيب فقال الأصحاب أراد الشافعي رضي الله
عنه ما إذا لم يدع المشتري إلا عيبا قبل العبد فيكفيه يمين على مطابقة ضد
الدعوى
قال ابن أبي ليلي كيف يحلف على البت ما به عيب فلعله كان ولم يعرفه
فليحلف على نفي العلم
قال الأصحاب بل يحلف على البت كما قال الشافعي رحمه الله كما يشهد على
الملك والإعسار ونفي وارث سوى الحاضر وكل ذلك على النفي يعرف بطول الخبرة
بل أمر اليمين أسهل ولذلك ثبت الحلف على اعتماد حظ أبيه فلا يشهد به
فإذا لم يعرف عيبا جاز له أن يطلق اليمين لأجل الحاجة

### | فرع

لو توافقا على وجود بياضين بالعبد أحدهما قديم والآخر حادث وقد زال
أحدهما وتنازعا في أن الزائل هو القديم أو الحادث فدعواهما على التعارض
والقول قول البائع لأن الأصل هو اللزوم

### | القسم الثالث من كتاب البيع في حكمه قبل القبض وبعده

والنظر في القبض يتعلق بثمرته وحكمه ثم بصورته وكيفيته ثم بصفته في
الوجوب والإجبار عليه

### | النظر الأول في ثمرته وحكمه وله حكمان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ف-ع (rafʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Lifting, raising, removing a thing from its place or status
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Elevation or removal of a legal effect; in contract law, the abrogation of a binding obligation
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical lifting; metaphorical (majāz) — annulment of a legal construct
- Root: ف-س-خ (faskh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To undo, dissolve, or tear apart a binding
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Termination of a contract's efficacy, distinct from ṭalāq (divorce) in its retroactive or prospective operation
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — tearing a seam; metaphorical — dissolution of a legal nexus
- Root: ق-ب-ض (qabḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taking hold, seizing, receiving possession
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Physical or legal acquisition of control over an object of sale
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — manual grasp; metaphorical — legal possession conferring liability (ḍamān)
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The phrase "fa-in qīla" (if it is said) introduces a protasis requiring an apodosis, governing the dialectical structure of objection and response.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first chapter concerns the reality of rescission (radd) and annulment (faskh).

In our school, it is the lifting of the contract from its time [of occurrence], and for this reason, rescission due to a defect is not prevented by detached increments [accruing to the sold item] nor by intercourse with a deflowered [slave-girl]. Abu Hanifah — may God have mercy on him — held that it is a lifting of the contract from its very origin, and for that reason he differed regarding intercourse with a deflowered [slave-girl] and detached increments.

As for annulment before delivery (qabḍ), there are two positions. One: it is a lifting from the origin, because the contract at that stage is weak and has not attained completion; upon this view, we say that increments arising before delivery revert to the seller by virtue of the annulment. The second: it is a lifting from its time, just as after delivery; upon this view, the increments remain for the purchaser.

If we say they revert to the seller by the annulment, then he has the right to detain the increments for the price, when we grant him the right to detain the sold object itself, because he anticipates attachment to it. But if we say they are delivered to the purchaser, then the seller has no right of detention over them.

If it is said: What is the basis for the return of increments to the seller's ownership, given that they arose within the purchaser's ownership, just as after delivery? We reply: For this reason, one faction said they do not revert, while the other faction adheres to what is narrated — that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was asked about the yield of a sold object: is it delivered to the purchaser after annulment and after delivery? He said: {«الخراج بالضمان»} — "The yield is in exchange for liability," meaning it is subject to the risk of liability through delivery; thus, profit is paired with loss. Its implication is that it is not delivered to him before delivery. The first faction follows analogical reasoning (qiyās) and says that [the Prophetic statement] is a cause (ʿillah) for preventing reversion, mentioned to cut off the questioner's astonishment; and before delivery, it does not revert due to another cause — namely, that it arose from his [the purchaser's] ownership. A ruling may be justified by two causes.

The second chapter concerns the reality of rescission by mutual consent (iqālah), and there are two opinions. The new [opinion] (al-jadīd) is that it is an annulment (faskh), because the verbal expression indicates it, and because it is permissible before delivery and in the case of salam (advance payment for deferred delivery), whereas sale is not [permissible in such a state]. The old [opinion] (al-qadīm) is that it is a new sale — though this has no sound basis, even if we have labored to provide a justification for it in the book al-Basīṭ on the school.

A subsidiary point: If the sold object is destroyed, then regarding the permissibility of iqālah upon the new opinion, there are two positions. One: prohibition, like rescission due to a defect, which is prevented after the object's loss. The second: permissibility, for the contract relies on annulment, and the contract subsists, whereas rescission relies on the returned object, which is perished. If the perished item is one of two slaves, then there are two ranked positions on the permissibility of iqālah, and it is more apt to be permissible, since the extant one draws the perished one along. If both are extant and he wishes to single out one for annulment, then one must attend to the splitting of the bargain (tafrīq al-ṣafqah). The school's position is its permissibility, especially in ongoing transactions.

The third chapter concerns the dispute over rescission due to a defect. If the purchaser says, "This defect is pre-existing," and the seller says, "Rather, it is newly arisen," then the seller's word is accepted, because the default is soundness and the contract's binding force. If he [the seller] swears, and then annulment occurs afterward through mutual imprecation (taḥāluf), and he then seeks to claim the price reduction (arsh) from the purchaser, claiming, "I established its newness by my oath," we do not enable him to do so, for his oath sufficed to repel [the claim] from him, so it does not suffice to burden the purchaser's liability. Rather, the purchaser may now swear that it is not newly arisen.

Then al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — said: He swears, "I sold it to him and it had no defect." Al-Muzanī said: Rather, he adds and says, "I sold it to him and delivered it to him, and it had no defect." The companions [of al-Shāfiʿī] said: Al-Shāfiʿī intended the case where the purchaser claims only a defect that preceded the slave; thus, an oath matching the contrary of the claim suffices for him. Ibn Abī Laylā said: How can he swear categorically that it had no defect, for perhaps it existed and he did not know it? Let him swear to the negation of knowledge. The companions said: Rather, he swears categorically, as al-Shāfiʿī — may God have mercy on him — said, just as one testifies to ownership, insolvency, and the negation of any heir other than the present one — all of which are negations known through prolonged experience. Indeed, the matter of oath is easier, and therefore an oath is established regarding reliance on his father's share, which is not testified to. Thus, when he does not know of a defect, it is permissible for him to utter the oath absolutely, due to necessity.

A subsidiary point: If they agree that there are two white spots on the slave, one pre-existing and the other newly arisen, and one of them has disappeared, and they dispute whether the disappeared one is the pre-existing or the newly arisen, then their claims are mutually contradictory, and the seller's word is accepted, because the default is the contract's binding force.

The third division of the Book of Sale concerns its ruling before and after delivery. The consideration of delivery pertains to its fruit and ruling, then to its form and modality, then to its attribute regarding obligation and compulsion upon it.

The first consideration concerns its fruit and ruling, and it has two rulings.
