### | الحكم الرابع للوكالة الجواز

فهو جائز من الجانبين وينعزل الوكيل بثلاثة أسباب
الأول عزول الموكل إياه بمشهد منه وإن كان في غيبته فينعزل مهما بلغه
الخبر وقيل بلوغ الخبر قولان
المنصوص أنه ينعزل لأنه لا يفتقر إلى رضاه فلا يفتقر إلى حضوره وعلمه
والثاني لا لأنه لا يوثق بتصرفه لتصور عزله دون معرفته فصار كالقاضي
وفي القاضي وجه أنه ينعزل في الغيبة وهو بعيد فإن عزل القاضي بغير سبب لا
يجوز وعزل الوكيل جائز ولا خلاف في أن الموكل لو باع ما وكل في بيعه أو
أعتق انعزل الوكيل ضمنا فإن قلنا ينفذ عزله في الغيبة فليشهد الموكل عليه
فإنه لا يسمع مجرد قوله بعد تصرف الوكيل
السبب الثاني عزل الوكيل نفسه وتعديه في مال الوكالة ليس ردا للوكالة بل
يبقى وكيلا على الأصح وإن صار ضامنا بإنكاره الوكالة هل يجعل إنشاء للرد
فيه ثلاثة أوجه والأصح هو الثالث وهو أنه إن قال ذلك عن نسيان
أو لغرض في إخفاء الوكالة فلا يكون عزلا وإن أنكر مع العلم فهو رد
للوكالة من جهته
الثالث أن يخرج الموكل بالجنون أو الموت عن أهلية التوكيل أو الوكيل عن
أهلية التوكيل أو الوكيل عن أهلية الامتثال بالجنون والموت والأصح أنه لا
ينعزل بالإغماء وينعزل بالجنون وإن قل وقيل لا ينعزل بهما وقيل ينعزل بهما
جميعا
فلو وكل عبده ثم أعتقه أو باعه أو كاتبه ففي انعزاله ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها لا لعموم الإذن وبقاء الأهلية
والثاني نعم لأن أمره محمول على الاستخدام وقد بطل محلية الاستخدام في
حقه
والثالث أنه ينظر إلى لفظه فإن قال وكلتك بقي بعد زوال سلطنته وإن قال بع
واشتر بصيغة الأمر فهو محمول على الاستخدام
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثالث  في تنازع الوكيل والموكل - صلى الله
عليه وسلم -
وتنازعهما في ثلاثة مواضع

### | الأول التنازع في أصل الوكالة أو صفتها

كقول الوكيل وكلتني فقال ما وكلتك أو قال وكلتني ببيع الكل فقال بل
بالبعض أو قال أذنت لي في البيع بالنسيئة فقال بل بالنقد أو قال أذنت في
الشراء بعشرين فقال بل بالعشرة فالقول في جميع ذلك قول الموكل لأن الأصل
عدمه
فرعان
أحدهما إذا باع الوكيل بالنسيئة وأنكر البائع الإذن في الأجل فإن كان
المبيع قائما استرد والقول قوله ولو أنكر المشتري كونه وكيلا لم يقبل قول
الموكل عليه بل يحلفه على أنه لا يعلم كونه وكيلا من جهته فإذا حلف فللموكل
مطالبة الوكيل بقيمة السلعة ثم إذا انقضى الأجل فللوكيل أن يطالب المشتري
بالثمن ويأخذه بما غرمه فإن زاد على ما غرمه فالزيادة لا يدعيها لنفسه ولا
البائع ولا المشتري فماذا يصنع به وفي مثله خلاف مشهور
فإن كذب الوكيل نفسه أيضا وقال صدق الموكل لم يكن له أن يطالب إلا بأقل
الأمرين من الثمن أو القيمة ليجبر حق نفسه مما غرم
الثاني إذا اشترى جارية عشرين فقال الموكل ما أذنت إلا في عشرة فالقول
قوله فإن كان اشترى بعين ماله فهو باطل وإن اشترى في الذمة واعترف البائع
بالوكالة فكمثل فإن أنكر الوكالة لم يقبل قوله على البائع ويغرم الوكيل
للموكل ماله مهما حلف على أنه لم يأذن وتبقى الجارية في يد الوكيل فيتلطف
الحاكم بالموكل ويقول له لا يضرك أن تقول للوكيل بعتك الجارية بعشرين حتى
تسلم لك العشرون فإن قال ذلك حصل الغرض
فإن قال إن كنت قد أذنت لك فلو بعتك ففي هذه الصيغة وجهان أصحهما وهو
ظاهر كلام المزني الصحة لأن هذا من مقتضى الشرع وإن لم يصرح
وإن أبى الموكل ذلك قال المزني يبيع الوكيل الجارية ويأخذ ما غرم من
ثمنها
وقال الإصطخري وجهان
أحدهما ما قاله المزني والثاني أنه يملك ظاهرا وباطنا بناء على ما إذا
ادعى على غيره أنك اشتريت داري  فأنكر وحلف فيستحب للمشتري أن يقول إن كنت
اشتريته فقد فسخت فإن لم يقل فالبائع على قول يبيع الدار ويأخذ ثمنها وعلى
قول يملكه ويكون إنكاره كإفلاسه فهو أحق بعين ماله
قال أبو إسحاق لا يملك الجارية قولا واحدا وهو الصحيح بخلاف مسالة
الدار فإن تعذر الثمن ثبت الرجوع إلى المبيع وهاهنا لا معاملة بين الوكيل
والموكل فعلى هذا الوجه أن يقال قد ظفر بغير جنس حقه فيأخذه بحقه ويقطع
بهذا القول هاهنا لأن من له الحق لا يدعيه لنفسه بخلاف ما إذا ظفر بغير جنس
حقه من مال من يدعي المال لنفسه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-و-ز (j-w-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pass through, be permissible, traverse a threshold; denotes what is legally allowable and effective.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Permissibility (jawāz) as opposed to obligation; in agency, it signifies contractual validity without binding necessity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal permissibility of the contract itself; metaphorical extension to the agent's discretionary authority.
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿ-z-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To separate, remove, set aside; core sense of dismissal from a position.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Termination of delegated authority; a unilateral act not requiring consent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal removal of the agent's standing; metaphorical in cases of implied dismissal (e.g., principal's own sale).
- Root: و-ك-ل (w-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To entrust, delegate, rely upon; the root of agency (wakālah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Delegation of authority where the agent acts on behalf of the principal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal entrustment of a task; metaphorical in cases of disputed scope.
- Root: خ-ص-م (kh-ṣ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To dispute, litigate, contend; the basis of legal conflict.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Disputation over rights, requiring judicial resolution.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal verbal contention; metaphorical in cases of conflicting claims.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the parsing of "if...then" rulings and the scope of exceptions (e.g., "unless he acted from forgetfulness"), which determine legal outcomes in disputed agency cases.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth ruling on agency is its permissibility (jawāz). It is permissible from both sides, and the agent is dismissed by three causes.

The first cause: The principal's dismissal of him, witnessed by the agent — even if [the dismissal occurs] in his absence, he is dismissed once the news reaches him. It was said [that dismissal requires] the news reaching him; there are two positions. The textually stipulated [position] is that he is dismissed, because [dismissal] does not require his consent, so it does not require his presence or knowledge. The second [position] is that he is not dismissed, because his transactions cannot be trusted [as valid] given the possibility of his dismissal without his knowledge — thus he becomes like a judge. Regarding the judge, there is a view that he is dismissed in absence, but this is far-fetched, for dismissing a judge without cause is not permissible, whereas dismissing an agent is permissible. There is no disagreement that if the principal sold what he had delegated to the agent to sell, or manumitted [a slave he had delegated to sell], the agent is dismissed implicitly. If we say his dismissal takes effect in absence, then let the principal bear witness against him, for his mere statement will not be heard after the agent's transaction.

The second cause: The agent's dismissal of himself. His transgression (taʿaddī) regarding the wealth of the agency is not a revocation of the agency; rather, he remains an agent on the soundest view, though he becomes a guarantor. Regarding his denial of the agency — is it considered an initiation of revocation? There are three aspects. The soundest is the third: if he said that from forgetfulness or for a purpose of concealing the agency, it is not a dismissal; but if he denied with knowledge, it is a revocation from his side.

The third cause: That the principal exits, through insanity or death, from the capacity for delegation — or the agent exits from the capacity for compliance through insanity and death. The soundest view is that he is not dismissed by fainting, but is dismissed by insanity, even if brief. It was said he is not dismissed by either; and it was said he is dismissed by both together.

Thus, if a man delegated his slave, then manumitted him, sold him, or made a kitābah contract with him, there are three aspects regarding his dismissal: One — no, due to the generality of the permission and the persistence of capacity. The second — yes, because his command is construed as [intended for] employment (istikhdām), and the locus of employment has ceased regarding him. The third — one looks to his wording: if he said "I have delegated you," he remains [agent] after the removal of his authority; but if he said "Sell and buy" in the imperative form, it is construed as employment.

— Peace be upon him — The Third Chapter: On the Dispute Between the Agent and the Principal — Peace be upon him —

Their dispute occurs in three places.

### | The First: Dispute Over the Origin of the Agency or Its Attribute

Such as the agent saying, "You delegated me," and [the principal] saying, "I did not delegate you"; or [the agent] saying, "You delegated me to sell the whole," and [the principal] saying, "Rather, [I delegated you to sell] part"; or [the agent] saying, "You permitted me to sell on credit," and [the principal] saying, "Rather, for cash"; or [the agent] saying, "You permitted the purchase for twenty," and [the principal] saying, "Rather, for ten." In all of this, the statement is the principal's, because the default is non-existence [of the delegation].

Two subsidiary branches:

The first: If the agent sold on credit and the seller [i.e., the principal] denied permission for the term, then if the sold object is still extant, he reclaims it, and his statement is accepted. But if the buyer denied that [the agent] was an agent, the principal's statement is not accepted against him; rather, [the buyer] is made to swear that he does not know him to be an agent from [the principal's] side. When he swears, the principal may demand from the agent the value of the commodity. Then, when the term expires, the agent may demand from the buyer the price and take from him what he has paid. If it exceeds what he paid, the excess is not claimed by himself, nor by the seller, nor by the buyer — so what is done with it? Regarding this, there is a well-known disagreement.

If the agent also contradicts himself and says, "The principal is truthful," he may not demand except the lesser of the two — the price or the value — to compensate his own right for what he paid.

The second: If he purchased a slave-girl for twenty, and the principal said, "I only permitted you [to purchase] for ten," then the statement is his. If he purchased with the specific wealth of the principal, it is void. But if he purchased on credit (fī al-dhimmah) and the seller acknowledged the agency, then it is as [the previous case]. If [the seller] denied the agency, his statement is not accepted against the seller, and the agent must pay the principal his wealth, whenever [the principal] swears that he did not permit [it]. The slave-girl remains in the agent's hand. The judge then deals gently with the principal and says to him: "It will not harm you to say to the agent, 'I have sold you the slave-girl for twenty,' so that the twenty are delivered to you." If he says that, the purpose is achieved.

If he says, "If I had permitted you, then I would sell [her] to you" — regarding this formulation there are two aspects. The sounder of them, which is the apparent [import] of al-Muzanī's statement, is validity, because this is required by the Law (sharʿ), even if not explicitly stated.

If the principal refuses that, al-Muzanī said: The agent sells the slave-girl and takes what he paid of her price. Al-Iṣṭakhrī said there are two aspects: One is what al-Muzanī said. The second is that he owns [her] both outwardly and inwardly, based on the case where one claims against another, "You purchased my house," and he denies and swears — then it is recommended for the purchaser to say, "If I had purchased it, I have rescinded." If he does not say it, then the seller, on one view, sells the house and takes its price; and on another view, he owns it, and his denial is like his insolvency — so he is more entitled to his specific wealth.

Abū Isḥāq said: He does not own the slave-girl, as a single position — and this is the correct one, unlike the case of the house. For if the price is unattainable, recourse to the sold object is established; but here there is no transaction between the agent and the principal. Thus, on this view, it is said: He has seized something not of the same genus as his right, so he takes it for his right. And this position is decisive here, because the one who has the right does not claim it for himself — unlike the case where one seizes something not of the same genus as his right from the wealth of one who claims the wealth for himself.
