chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ز-ع (n-z-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pull, snatch, or contest; mutual contention over a single object.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Disputation (tanāzuʿ) implying each party claims an exclusive right, entailing judicial resolution.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in physical seizure; metaphorical in legal claims (daʿwā) over title.
- Root: خ-ص-م (kh-ṣ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To dispute, litigate; a litigant (khaṣm) before a judge.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Formal legal contention requiring evidence (bayyinah) and oath (yamīn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for verbal quarrel; technical for procedural adversary in court.
- Root: و-ل-د (w-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To beget, give birth; istīlād — a master impregnating his slave-girl.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal status of umm walad (mother of a child) affecting manumission and sale.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for biological generation; metaphorical for legal filiation and its consequences.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The phrase "if he has not impregnated her" governs the apodosis, restricting the seller's right of return; also, the rule of "oath of denial" (yamīn al-nafy) as a response to a claim, parsed as a verbal predicate requiring a direct object (the negated act).
chapters.translation:
I say: A subsidiary branch inserted into this book — When two men dispute over a slave-girl, one saying, "She is my wife, you married her to me," and the other saying, "I sold her to you," the consideration falls into four matters.

The first: In adjudicating the dispute. The Companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: These are two separate litigations, for each one claims a contract, so each must prove it; and each is faced with a contract claimed against him, so his word (with oath) is accepted. Thus, an oath is administered to each one — to deny what is claimed against him and to affirm what he claims — whenever the oath is referred back to him (upon the other's refusal).

The reviser (ṣāḥib al-Taqrīb) objected, saying: The one who claims that the other sold — he seeks the price, so he may demand an oath denying the purchase. But as for the one who claims marriage against the other, and the other has said "I sold" — he has thereby denied his own ownership of the slave-girl; if he were to confess (to the marriage), his confession would not be accepted (since he had already negated his ownership). So what benefit is there in administering an oath to him? Then he said: Now this builds upon whether the oath of refusal (yamīn al-radd) is like evidence (bayyinah); its benefit would be the consequence of refusal (nukūl). And his objection stands on its proper footing.

The second consideration: If the husband swears to deny the purchase, he is not pursued for the price, and the seller has the right to reclaim the slave-girl. Among them (the jurists) are those who said: It becomes as though the buyer had failed to pay the price due to insolvency (iflās), so the seller is given leeway and his right is established in the slave-girl, even if her value exceeds the price. And among them are those who said: No — rather, his path is that he has seized something not of the same genus as his right (ghayr jins ḥaqqihi), so he takes from her an amount equivalent to the price.

All this applies if he had not impregnated her. But if impregnation (istīlād) has occurred, reclamation is barred by virtue of the seller's own statement, and the child is free by virtue of his statement as well — so the seller has no recourse.

The third consideration: Whether the husband is permitted to have intercourse with her. If he is truthful, it is lawful for him inwardly (bāṭinan). In the outward ruling (ẓāhir), there are two views. One: Yes, it is lawful, because the operative factor is their two statements, and she is lawful by virtue of both the seller's and the husband's statements. The second: She is unlawful, due to the disagreement over the legal basis (al-jihah). For if one said, "I owe you a thousand from a loan," and the other said, "Rather, from the price of goods sold," there is disagreement over whether he can demand it — so disagreement over the basis in the case of sexual intercourse (al-buḍʿ) is even more apt.

And among them is one who analogized this to a man purchasing his own wife with a condition of option (khiyār). Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: He shall not have intercourse with her during the option period, for he does not know whether he is having intercourse with his wife or his slave-girl — even though, however it is, it is lawful. And the way to resolve the difficulty of the text is to derive it upon the rulings of ownership. If we say ownership belongs to the seller, then he may do so, for he knows he is having intercourse with his wife. If we say it belongs to the buyer, then he may not, because he would be having intercourse with his slave-girl under a weak ownership (milk ḍaʿīf), which prevents intercourse due to the seller's remaining option. And if we say it is suspended (mawqūf), he shall not have intercourse — and this is what al-Shāfiʿī intended, because he does not know whether he is having intercourse with his wife, which would be lawful, or with his slave-girl under weak ownership, which would not be lawful for him.

The fourth consideration: The maintenance (nafaqah) of the child after impregnation falls upon the impregnator (al-mustawlid), because the child is free by virtue of the seller's statement, so his maintenance is upon his father. And the maintenance of the impregnated slave-girl falls upon the impregnator if we say she is lawful for him. But if we say she is not lawful for him, there are two views. One: It falls upon the seller, since his statement is accepted regarding the removal of his ownership over her, but not regarding what is upon others — namely, the dropping of maintenance. The second: She eats from her own earnings; if she has none, then from the public treasury (bayt al-māl), because she is poor.

— Peace be upon him — The third chapter: On the retraction of an acknowledgment (iqrār) by what nullifies it. And it is of two divisions — Peace be upon him —

The first: That he follows it with something that nullifies it entirely.

وفيه مسائل سبع
الأولى إذا قال لفلان على ألف من ثمن خمر أو خنزير أو من ضمان شرط فيه
الخيار لنفسه أو سبب فاسد أسنده إليه ويعتاد التعامل بمثله على الفساد ففيه
قولان
أحدهما أنه يلزمه الألف والإضافة الفاسدة رفع بعد إثبات فهو كقوله على
ألف ألا ألفا
والثاني ولعله الأولى أنه لا يلزمه لأنه لم يقر بملزوم شئ وكلامه منظوم
في نفسه فصار كما إذا قال أنت طالق أن شاء الله فإنه لما أنتظم لم يكترث
باندفاع الطلاق
وقطع الاكثرون بأنه لو قال لفلان على ألف أن شاء الله لا يلزمه شئ لأنه
للشك في الإقرار وللتعليق في الإقرار وحكي صاحب التقريب عن بعض الأصحاب طرد
القولين
ولا خلاف في أنه إذا قال له على ألف إذا جاء رأس الشهر وقصد به التعليق
أنه
يخرج عن القولين بخلاف ما إذا قال إذا جاء رأس الشهر فله على ألف فإنه لا
يلزمه قولا واحد لأنه قدم كلمة التعليق إلا أن يفسر ذلك بأجل أو وصية
فيحتمل ولكن لا يلزمه دون تفسيره
ولو قال لك على ألف ان شئت قال الأصحاب لا يلزمه لأنه تعليق بالمشيئة قال
الإمام ليخرج على القولين إن قدم صيغة الالتزام وإن أخر فيقطع بأنه لا
يلزمه
الثانية إذا قال على ألف لا يلزمني يلزمه الألف لأنه متناقض ولو قال ألف
قضيته فطريقان
منهم من قطع باللزوم لتناقضه
ومنهم من خرج على القولين إذ ذلك مما يطلق في العادة
الثالثة إذا قال علي ألف مؤجل طريقان
منهم من قطع بالقبول للصحة والاعتياد جميعا
ومنهم من خرج على القولين لأنه لو ذكر الأجل منفصلا لم يقبل وجعل مانعا
للزوم فكذلك إذا ذكره متصلا
وكذا إذا قال علي ألف من ثمن عبد أن سلم سلمت لأنه إضافة صحيحة معتادة
ولو قال علي ألف مؤجل من جهة تحمل العقل فيقطع بصحته لأن الأصل فيه الأجل
والحلول فيه دخيل ومنهم من خرج على القولين
الرابعة إذا قال له علي ألف ثم جاء بألف وقال هذه وديعة عندي فقال المقر
له ما أقررت به ألف أخر هو دين فالذي قطع به المراوزة قبوله وعليه يدل نص
الشافعي رضي الله عنه على أنه لو قال علي شئ ثم فسر بالوديعة قبل لأن
الوديعة عليه ردها وقد يتعدى فيها فيضمن
نعم لو قال تلف في يدي فلا يقبل قوله في سقوط الضمان لأن قوله علي مستشعر
به وقال العراقيون في اتحاد الألف قولان
وإن قال له على ألف في ذمتي فقولان مرتبان وأولى بأن لا يفسر بالوديعة
ولو قال له علي ألف دينا في ذمتي فأولي بأن يتعدد وها هنا يظهر خيال
التعدد ويبعد تفسيره بالوديعة فإن قلنا إن التفسير بالوديعة  منفصلا مقبول
فمتصلا أولى وإن قلنا لا يقبل فيخرج المتصل على قولي الإضافة إلي الجهات
الفاسدة
ولو قال له علي ألف درهم عارية في طريقة العراق أنه يلزمه لأن إعارة
الدراهم يصح فتكون مضمونة وإن قلنا لا يصح فهي عارية فاسدة مضمونه وفي
طريقة المراوزة أن عارية الدراهم إذا لم تصح فهي باطلة لأنها غير قابلة
للانتفاع أصلا فلا ضمان فعلى هذا يخرج على قولي الإضافة إلي الجهة الفاسدة
الخامسة لو قال هذه الدار لك عارية أو هبة قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه له
أن يخرج المقر له منها مهما شاء لأن قوله لك وإن كان ظاهره للملك فإذا تعقب
بالعارية نزل عليه
وكذا لو قال لك هبة ثم قال أردت هبة لم أقبضها فموجب النص القبول وقال
صاحب التقريب ينبغي أن يخرج الكل على قولي ثمن الخمر والخنزير لأنه
رفع لما تقدم من لام التمليك وهو فاسد لأن اللام ظاهر في التمليك ومحتمل
لوجوه في الإضافة إذا ذكر متصلا به
السادسة إذا قال رهنت فأقبضت أو وهبت وأقبضت ثم قال كنت أقبضت فلانا
وظننت أن القبض حاصل به نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه على قبول دعواه في تحلف
الخصم ولا خلاف أنه لو قال كذبت من غير تأويل لم تقبل دعواه
ولو قال أقررت أشهادا على الصك على العارية ثم لم يتفق ففي قبول الدعوى
للتحليف وجهان أولاهما القبول لأنه محتمل فلا خلاف أن العربي إذا أقر
بالعجمية ثم قال لقنت ولم أفهم أنه تقبل دعواه
السابعة إذا قال هذه الدار لزيد بل لعمرو سلم إلي زيد فهل يغرم لعمرو فيه
قولان
المنصوص ها هنا أنه لا يغرم لأن الدار قائمة ومنازعة صاحب اليد فيها ممكن
ولم يصدر منه إلا مجرد قول
والثاني وهو القياس أنه يضمن بالحيلولة كما لو أبق المغصوب من يده
وهذا الخلاف جار في شهود المال إذا رجعوا وعين المال باقية أو إمكان
المطالبة بقيمته قائم فإنهم هل يغرمون
ثم من الأصحاب من أطلق القولين  ومنهم من خصص بما إذا لم يسلم إلى زيد
بنفسه بل أخرج القاضي من يده فإن سلمه ففعله غصب بموجب قوله موجب للضمان
أما إذا قال غصبت الدار من زيد وملكها لعمرو وسلم إلى زيد لم يلزمه شيء
لعمرو لأنه يحتمل أن يكون مرتهنا أو مستأجرا وغصبت فبرىء بالرد عليه فلا
يغرم للثاني وقيل بتخريج ذلك على القولين منه
أما إذا قدم الإقرار بالملك فقال هي لفلان وأنا غصبتها من فلان فالأكثرون
سووا بين الصورتين حتى يسلم إلى من غضب منه ولا يغرم للمالك
ومنهم من رأى تخريج هذا على القولين ظاهرا وزعم أنه يسلم إلى الأول وهل
يغرم للثاني قولان

- Root: ق-ر-ر (q-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To affirm, establish, or settle; acknowledgment (iqrār) as a binding declaration of a prior right.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iqrār is an epistemic act of confirming a liability (dayn) or obligation (ḥaqq) upon oneself, distinct from testimony (shahādah) which concerns others.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in legal stipulation; metaphorical (majāz) when qualified by conditions (sharṭ) or suspended clauses, shifting its binding force.
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, ensure, or be liable; damān as compensatory responsibility for loss or misappropriation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Liability arising from unlawful possession (yaḍ) or transgression (taʿaddī), tied to the notion of kafālah (suretyship) in contractual ethics.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Concrete in financial restitution; abstract when used for moral or procedural accountability.
- Root: ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hang, suspend, or attach; taʿlīq as conditional suspension of an effect upon a future contingency.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, suspension of a ruling (ḥukm) on a condition (sharṭ) reflects divine and human volition (mashīʾah), as in oaths and vows.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in physical attachment; metaphorical in legal causality, where the condition is the efficient cause (sabab).
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīm wa-Taʾkhīr (Fronting and Postponement) — The syntactic position of a conditional clause (sharṭ) or qualifier (ṣifah) relative to the main assertion (jukm) determines whether it restricts or nullifies the prior acknowledgment; fronting (taqdīm) of the condition voids the iqrār, while postponement (taʾkhīr) may be interpreted as a valid qualification.
chapters.translation:
Within this section are seven subsidiary questions.

**The First:** If a man says, "So-and-so has against me a thousand [dirhams] from the price of wine or swine, or from a guarantee (ḍamān) in which the option (khiyār) was stipulated for himself, or from a corrupt cause (sabab fāsid) which he attributes to himself, and it is customary for people to transact in like manner upon corruption — then there are two opinions (qawlān) concerning it.

One of them is that the thousand is incumbent upon him, and the corrupt attribution (al-iḍāfah al-fāsidah) is deemed raised after having been established (rafʿ baʿd ithbāt); thus it is as if he said, "He has against me a thousand, nay, a thousand."

The second — and perhaps it is the more correct (al-awlā) — is that it is not incumbent upon him, because he has not acknowledged (lam yuqirr) anything entailed (malzūm), and his speech is coherent in itself (manẓūm fī nafsihi); so it becomes like his saying, "You are divorced, if God wills (anta ṭāliq in shāʾ Allāh)" — for when it was coherent, he did not care about the repulsion of the divorce (indifāʿ al-ṭalāq).

The majority (al-aktharūn) decisively ruled that if he said, "So-and-so has against me a thousand, if God wills," nothing is incumbent upon him, because of the doubt (shakk) in the acknowledgment and the suspension (taʿlīq) in it. And the author of *al-Taqrīb* related from some of the companions (al-aṣḥāb) the extension of the two opinions [to this case].

There is no disagreement that if he said, "He has against me a thousand when the head of the month comes," intending thereby suspension (taʿlīq), it falls outside the two opinions — unlike his saying, "When the head of the month comes, he has against me a thousand," for then it is not incumbent upon him by unanimous opinion (qawlan wāḥidan), because he fronted the conditional clause (kalimat al-taʿlīq) — unless he interprets that as a term (ajal) or a bequest (waṣiyyah), in which case it is possible, but it is not incumbent upon him without such interpretation.

And if he said, "You have against me a thousand, if you wish," the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said it is not incumbent upon him, because it is suspension upon volition (mashīʾah). Imām [al-Ghazālī] said: It should be extended to the two opinions if he fronted the formula of commitment (ṣīghat al-iltizām); but if he postponed it, then it is decisively ruled that it is not incumbent upon him.

**The Second:** If he said, "I have against me a thousand — it does not bind me (lā yalzamunī)," the thousand is incumbent upon him, because it is self-contradictory (mutanāqiḍ). And if he said, "A thousand which I have paid (qaḍaytuhu)," then there are two paths (ṭarīqān):

Among them is one who decisively ruled for liability (luzūm) due to its contradiction.
And among them is one who extended it to the two opinions, since such [an expression] is commonly uttered in customary usage (al-ʿādah).

**The Third:** If he said, "I have against me a thousand, deferred (muʾajjal)," there are two paths:

Among them is one who decisively ruled for acceptance (al-qabūl) due to both validity (al-ṣiḥḥah) and customary usage (al-iʿtiyād) together.
And among them is one who extended it to the two opinions, because if he had mentioned the term (al-ajal) separately, it would not be accepted and would be made an impediment to liability; so likewise when he mentions it connectedly (muttaṣilan).

And likewise if he said, "I have against me a thousand from the price of a slave, if he is delivered safely, I am delivered (in sallimtu sallimtu)" — because it is a valid and customary attribution (iḍāfah ṣaḥīḥah muʿtādah).

But if he said, "I have against me a thousand, deferred, by way of undertaking a blood-wit (taḥammul al-ʿaql)," then it is decisively ruled valid, because the origin in it is deferment (al-ajal), and immediacy (al-ḥulūl) therein is extraneous (dakhīl). And among them is one who extended it to the two opinions.

**The Fourth:** If he said, "He has against me a thousand," then he brought a thousand and said, "This is a deposit (wadīʿah) with me," and the acknowledged party (al-muqarr lahu) said, "What I acknowledged is another thousand which is a debt" — then what the Marwazīs (al-Marāwizah) decisively ruled is its acceptance, and upon it the text (naṣṣ) of al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) indicates: that if he said, "I have against me something (shayʾ)," then interpreted it as a deposit, it is accepted, because the deposit is incumbent upon him to return, and he may transgress (yataʿaddā) therein and thus become liable (yaḍman).

Yes, if he said, "It perished in my hand (tālifa fī yadī)," then his statement is not accepted regarding the dropping of liability (sukūṭ al-ḍamān), because his saying "against me" (ʿalayya) is suggestive of it (mustashʿir). And the Iraqis (al-ʿIrāqiyyūn) held two opinions concerning the identity of the thousand (ittiḥād al-alf).

And if he said, "He has against me a thousand in my liability (fī dhimmatī)," then there are two opinions, arranged (murattabān), and it is more fitting that it not be interpreted as a deposit. And if he said, "He has against me a thousand, a debt in my liability," then it is more fitting that it be multiple (yataʿaddad), and here the notion of multiplicity (khayāl al-taʿaddud) appears, and its interpretation as a deposit is remote.

If we say that the interpretation as a deposit, when separate (munfaṣilan), is accepted, then when connected (muttaṣilan) it is more fitting [for acceptance]. And if we say it is not accepted, then the connected [case] is extended to the two opinions concerning attribution to corrupt causes (al-iḍāfah ilā al-jihāt al-fāsidah).

And if he said, "He has against me a thousand dirhams, a loan for use (ʿāriyah)," then in the Iraqi path (ṭarīqat al-ʿIrāq), it is incumbent upon him, because lending dirhams is valid, and thus they are guaranteed (maḍmūnah). And if we say it is not valid, then it is a corrupt loan for use (ʿāriyah fāsidah), which is guaranteed. And in the Marwazī path (ṭarīqat al-Marāwizah), if lending dirhams is not valid, then it is void (bāṭilah), because they are not susceptible to benefit at all, so there is no liability. Upon this, it is extended to the two opinions concerning attribution to a corrupt cause.

**The Fifth:** If he said, "This house is yours, as a loan for use (ʿāriyah) or a gift (hibah)," al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: He has the right to expel the acknowledged party from it whenever he wishes, because his saying "yours" (laka), although its apparent sense is ownership (al-milk), when it is followed by "loan for use," it is interpreted accordingly (yunazzal ʿalayhi).

And likewise, if he said, "Yours, as a gift," then said, "I meant a gift which I did not deliver (lam aqbiḍhā)," then the import of the text (mūjib al-naṣṣ) is acceptance. And the author of *al-Taqrīb* said: It is fitting that all of this be extended to the two opinions concerning the price of wine and swine, because it is a raising of what preceded from the lām of ownership (lām al-tamlīk), and it is corrupt, because the lām is apparent in ownership and susceptible to various aspects in attribution when mentioned connectedly with it.

**The Sixth:** If he said, "I pledged (rahanntu) and delivered possession (aqbaḍtu)," or "I gifted and delivered possession," then said, "I had delivered possession to so-and-so, and I thought that delivery was effected by him," al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) ruled upon the acceptance of his claim (daʿwāhu) in the oath of the opponent (taḥlīf al-khaṣm). And there is no disagreement that if he said, "You have lied (kadhabta)" without interpretation (taʾwīl), his claim is not accepted.

And if he said, "I acknowledged, making witnesses upon the document (al-ṣikk) for the loan for use, then it did not occur (lam yattaﬁq)," then concerning the acceptance of the claim for the purpose of administering the oath, there are two faces (wajhān). The more appropriate of them is acceptance, because it is plausible (muḥtamal). Thus there is no disagreement that if an Arab acknowledges in a non-Arab tongue (al-ʿajamiyyah), then says, "I was prompted (luqqintu) and did not understand," his claim is accepted.

**The Seventh:** If he said, "This house is Zayd's — nay, ʿAmr's," and he delivered it to Zayd, is he liable (yaghram) to ʿAmr? Therein are two opinions:

The textually ruled one (al-manṣūṣ) here is that he is not liable, because the house remains extant (qāʾimah), and the dispute of the possessor (ṣāḥib al-yad) therein is possible, and nothing issued from him except mere speech (mujarrad qawl).

The second — and it is the analogical one (al-qiyās) — is that he is liable for the obstruction (al-ḥaylūlah), just as if the usurped object (al-maghṣūb) had escaped from his hand.

And this disagreement applies to the witnesses of wealth (shuhūd al-māl) when they retract (rajaʿū), and the very object of wealth (ʿayn al-māl) remains, or the possibility of claiming its value (qīmah) stands — are they liable or not?

Then among the companions (al-aṣḥāb) is one who absolved the two opinions, and among them is one who specified [the non-liability] for the case where he did not deliver to Zayd himself, but rather the judge (al-qāḍī) removed it from his hand. For if he delivered it himself, then his act is usurpation (ghaṣb) by virtue of his own statement, which necessitates liability.

As for if he said, "I usurped the house from Zayd, and its ownership (milkuhā) belongs to ʿAmr," and he delivered it to Zayd, then nothing is incumbent upon him toward ʿAmr, because it is plausible that [Zayd] was a pledgee (murtahinan) or a lessee (mustaʾjiran), and "I usurped" — so he is absolved by returning it to him, and thus he is not liable to the second. And it was said: this is extended to the two opinions from him.

As for if he fronted the acknowledgment of ownership, saying, "It is so-and-so's, and I usurped it from so-and-so," then the majority (al-aktharūn) equated the two cases, so that he delivers to the one from whom he usurped and is not liable to the owner.

And among them is one who saw the extension of this to the two opinions as apparent (ẓāhir), and he claimed that he delivers to the first, and whether he is liable to the second — therein are two opinions.

chapters.title_en: Section 192 — The Second Division: On What Nullifies Part of an Acknowledgment
chapters.arabic_text:
### | القسم الثاني فيما يرفع بعض الإقرار

وفيه ثلاث مسائل
الأولى جواز الاستثناء الأقل والأكثر مهما بقي من المقر به شيء
فلو قال علي عشرة إلا تسعة قبل فما يلزمه إلا درهم ولو قال عشرة إلا عشرة
بطل الاستثناء ولزمه العشرة
ولو قال علي عشرة إلا تسعة إلا ثمانية إلا سبعة إلا ستة هكذا إلى أن
انتهى إلى الواحد يلزمه خمسة لأن الاستثناء من الإثبات نفي ومن النفي إثبات
فإذا جمع صيغ الإثبات على اليد اليمنى والصيغ التي بعدها على اليسرى
اجتمع على اليسرى خمسة وعشرون وعلى اليمن ثلاثون فإذا أسقطت المنفي عن
المثبت بقي خمسة
الثانية الاستثناء من غير الجنس صحيح عندنا وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لا
يصح إلا في استثناء المكيل من الموزون أو الموزون من المكيل
وصورته أن يقول علي ألف درهم إلا ثوبا فمعناه إلا قيمة ثوب ولكن
معناه أن يفسر قيمة الثوب بما ينقص عن الألف فلو فسره بما استغرق فوجهان
أحدهما بطلان التفسير إلى أن يفسر بما ينقص عن الألف
والثاني بطلان أصل الاستثناء
الثالثة الاستثناء عن العين كقوله هذه الدار لفلان والبيت الفلاني منها
لي أو هذه الدار لفلان إلا الباب أو هذا الخاتم إلا الفص أو هؤلاء العبيد
إلا واحدا
فالمذهب صحة الاستثناء وفيه وجه أن الاستثناء إنما ورد في اللسان  عن
الأعداد فلذلك يقبل وإلا فالأصل أن رفع الإقرار السابق باطل
فرع لو قال هؤلاء العبيد لفلان إلا واحدا وقلنا صح طولب بتعيينه وقبل
قوله
فلو ماتوا إلا واحدا فقال هذا هو المستثنى فالصحيح قبوله كما لو عين أولا
ثم مات الآخر
وفيه وجه أنه لا يقبل لأنه يوجب إعدام أثر الإقرار بخلاف ما لو قال غصبت
هؤلاء العبيد إلا واحدا فإنه يقبل تعين الواحد الباقي لأن أثر الإقرار يبقى
في مطالبته بقيمة الموت
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الرابع في الإقرار بالنسب وهو قسمان - صلى
الله عليه وسلم -

### | أحدهما أن يقر على نفسه ويستلحق شخصا

فقوله مقبول بشرط أن يسلم عن تكذيب الحس بأن يكون المستلحق أكبر سنا منه
أو مثله وعن تكذيب الشرع بأن يكون المستلحق مشهور النسب لغيره وعن تكذيب
المقر له بأن يكون بالغا فيكذبه
فلا يثبت النسب في هذه الصور الثلاثة وإنما يثبت في مجهول يولد مثله
لمثله وهو أن يقر إن كان بالغا أو هو صغير أو مجنون أو ميت حتى لا يتصور
تكذيبه فإن إقراره ليس بشرط فلو استلحق صغيرا فمات الصغير ورثه ولو مات
المستلحق ورثه الصغير بل لو مات الصغير أولا وله ميراث ثم استلحقه قبل قوله
عندنا ولم يترك بسبب التهمة خلافا لأبي حنيفة
نعم لو مات بالغا فاستلحقه ذكر العراقيون وجهين ومال القاضي إلى أنه لا
يقبل إذا خيره إلى موته مع مصادفته حالة يتصور تصديق المقر له فيه يوهم
كذبه وهذا لا يليق بمذهب الشافعي رضي الله عنه فإنه لا يرد الأقارير بالتهم
نعم لو استلحق صغيرا فبلغ وأنكر فيه وجهان
أحدهما لا مبالاة بإنكاره إذ حكمنا بثبوت النسب والتوريث من الجانبين
والثاني يقبل وإنما كان ذلك حكما بشرط سلامة العاقبة كتصحيح الأقارير
والتصرفات في مرض الموت
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ث ن ي (th-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Dual, second, repetition; division into two parts
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sequential ordering in legal rulings (aḥkām) and the bifurcation of juridical categories
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of "second division" (al-qism al-thānī) as structural partition, not metaphorical
- Root: ر ف ع (r-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To raise, remove, annul; elevation of a burden
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal nullification (rafʿ) of an operative effect — here, partial abrogation of an iqrār
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in legal parlance; metaphorical only when applied to ranks or degrees
- Root: ا س ت ث ن ا (s-t-th-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exception, exclusion; derived from th-n-y (making something second, setting apart)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory (uṣūl), istithnāʾ is a qualifier (mustathnā) that restricts the scope of the acknowledgment
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in arithmetic and legal contexts; metaphorical when used for rhetorical exclusion
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Naqīḍ (Conjoining of Negation and Affirmation) — In serial exceptions, each exception operates on the immediately preceding clause, alternating between affirmation and negation, requiring careful parsing of the syntactic chain.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division concerns that which nullifies part of an acknowledgment (iqrār). It comprises three questions.

**The First Question:** The permissibility of the exception (istithnāʾ), whether lesser or greater, so long as something of the acknowledged amount remains. Thus, if one says: "Upon me is ten, except nine," it is accepted, and nothing is incumbent upon him save one dirham. But if he says: "Upon me is ten, except ten," the exception is void, and the ten is incumbent upon him.

And if he says: "Upon me is ten, except nine, except eight, except seven, except six," continuing thus until he reaches one, then five is incumbent upon him. For the exception from an affirmation is a negation, and from a negation is an affirmation. So when one gathers the affirmative formulations on the right hand and the formulations that follow them on the left hand, there accumulates on the left twenty-five and on the right thirty. Then when one subtracts the negated from the affirmed, five remains.

**The Second Question:** The exception of something from a different genus (ghayr al-jins) is valid in our school. Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — held that it is not valid except in the exception of a measured quantity (makīl) from a weighed quantity (mawzūn), or a weighed quantity from a measured quantity. Its form is that one says: "Upon me is a thousand dirhams, except a garment." Its meaning is: "except the value of a garment." But its meaning requires that he specify the value of the garment as something less than the thousand. If he specifies it as something that exhausts the whole, then there are two aspects (wajhān): one, that the specification is void until he specifies it as less than the thousand; the second, that the exception itself is void in its origin.

**The Third Question:** The exception from a specific entity (al-ʿayn), such as one's saying: "This house is for so-and-so, and such-and-such a room within it is mine," or "This house is for so-and-so, except the door," or "This ring is for so-and-so, except the gemstone," or "These slaves are for so-and-so, except one." The established school (al-madhhab) holds the validity of the exception. There is an aspect (wajh) that the exception occurred in the tongue only with respect to numbers, and therefore it is accepted; otherwise, the principle is that nullifying a prior acknowledgment is void.

**A Branch (farʿ):** If he says: "These slaves are for so-and-so, except one," and we hold the exception valid, he is required to specify the one excepted, and his statement is accepted. If they all die except one, and he says: "This is the one excepted," the correct view is its acceptance, just as if he had specified it at the outset and then the others died. There is an aspect that it is not accepted, because it entails the annihilation of the effect of the acknowledgment — unlike the case where he says: "I usurped these slaves, except one," for then the specification of the one remaining is accepted, because the effect of the acknowledgment remains in the claim against him for the value of the deceased.

**The Fourth Chapter: On Acknowledgment of Lineage (al-nasab)** — and it is of two divisions.

**The First Division:** That one acknowledges concerning himself and claims a person as his offspring (istilḥāq). His statement is accepted on the condition that it be free from the falsification of the senses — namely, that the claimed person be older than him or his equal in age; free from the falsification of the Sacred Law — namely, that the claimed person be of well-known lineage to another; and free from the falsification of the one acknowledged for — namely, that he be a major who denies him. Thus lineage is not established in these three cases. It is established only in the case of an unknown person of whom one like him is born to one like him — namely, that he acknowledges while the claimant is a minor, or insane, or deceased, such that his denial is inconceivable; for his acknowledgment is not a condition. So if he claims a minor and the minor dies, he inherits from him; and if the claimant dies, the minor inherits from him. Indeed, even if the minor dies first, leaving an inheritance, and then he claims him, his statement is accepted in our school, and he does not forfeit it due to suspicion (tuhmah), contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah.

Yes, if the claimed person died as a major and he then claimed him, the Iraqis mentioned two aspects (wajhān). The judge (al-Qāḍī) inclined to the view that it is not accepted — for he had the choice until his death, and its coincidence with a state in which the acknowledgment of the one acknowledged for is conceivable suggests his falsehood. But this does not befit the school of al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — for he does not reject acknowledgments on account of suspicions. Yes, if he claims a minor and the minor reaches majority and denies, there are two aspects: one, that no heed is paid to his denial, since we have ruled the establishment of lineage and inheritance from both sides; the second, that it is accepted — for that ruling was conditional upon a sound outcome, like the validation of acknowledgments and dispositions during mortal illness.

### | فرعان

أحدهما له أمتان ولكل واحدة منهما ولد ولا زوج لهما فقال أحد هذين
الابنين ولدي فقد ثبت نسب واحد مبهما فيطالب بالتعيين فإذا عين تعين وعتق
وصارت الأم مستولدة إن  كان قد قال هذا ولدي منها قد علقت به في ملكي وإن
أطلق وقال ولدي منها فقد ذكرنا فيه وجهين فإن مات قبل التعيين فتعيين
الورثة كتعيين المورث وإن عجزنا عرضنا على القائف وتعيين القائف كتعينه في
النسب والاستيلاد وسائر الأحكام فإن عجزنا عن القائف أقرعنا بينهما فمن
خرجت قرعته عتق ولم يثبت نسبه ولا ميراثه إذ لا عمل للقرعة إلا في العتق
وبينهما عتق مبهم
وهل يقرع بين الأمتين وجهان
أحدهما لا إذ أمية الولد والعتق به تبع بسبب الولد ولا نسب
والثاني نعم لأن لهما نسبا وإحداهما عتيقة بحكم ذلك فيقرع لأجل العتق وهل
يقف نصيب ابن من الميراث وجهان
أحدهما بلى إذ أحدهما نسيب
والثاني لا لأنه نسب ميئوس عن ظهوره والموالاة به فلا يؤثر في التوريث
الفرع الثاني أمة لها ثلاثة أولاد فقال السيد أحد هؤلاء ولدي استولدتها
به في ملكي فهو إقرار بأمية الولد ويطالب بالتعيين فإن عين الأصغر عتق وثبت
نسبه وإن عين الأوسط ثبت نسبه وعتق الأصغر أيضا وثبت نسبه لأنه ولد على
فراشه إلا إذا ادعى الاستبراء وقلنا الولد ينتفي بمجرد دعوى الاستبراء في
المستولدة وعند ذلك يحكم بعتق الأصغر لأنه ولد المستولدة ولاكن ولكن إذا
عتقت الستولدة بموت السيد وفيه وجه أنه لا يعتق لاحتمال استولدها بالأوسط
وهي مرهونة ولنا لا ينفذ الاستيلاد فبيعت وولدت الأصغر في يد المشتري ثم
اشتراهما المستولد وقلنا يقود الاستيلاد ولكن لا يتعدى إلى ولد ولدت في ملك
الغير والقائل الأول إن اعترف بهذا التفريع فيأتي دفع مطلق الإقرار بهذا
التقدير البعيد
هذا إذا عين قبل الموت فإن مات فوارثة أو القائف يقومون مقامه فإن عجزنا
عنهم أقرع بين الأولاد الثلاثة فإن خرج على الأصغر تعين للعتق وإن خرج على
الأوسط عتق مع الأصغر إلا على تقدير الخروج على مسألة الرد
قال المزني معترضا على نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه كيف يدخل الصغير القرعة
وهو حر بكل حال وما ذكره المزني خطأ لأنه يدخل في القرعة  ليخرج عليه فيقتصر
العتق علي أو يخرج على غيره فيعتق هو مع غيره
ثم قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه لا تأثير للقرعة في النسب والميراث مصروف
إلى الوارث المتيقن وراثته
قال المزني وينبغي أن يوقف ميراث ابن وهو ظاهر القياس ولكن الشافعي رضي
الله عنه لم ير الموقف بعد اليأس عن ظهور هذا النسب

### | القسم الثاني أن يقر بالنسب على مورثه

ومن له ولاية استغراق الميراث فله إلحاق النسب بمورثه سواء انفرد أو
كانوا جميعا
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لو خلف ابنا واحدا فأقر بأخ آخر لم يثبت إلا
إذا كانا ابنين وهو ضعيف فإنه إذا لم تعتبر صفات الشهود بل قبل قبول
الأقارير فلا معنى للعدد
ثم قال الأصحاب يعتبر إقرار الزوج والمولى المعتق إذا كان من جملة الورثة
ولا مبالاة بإقرار التقريب المحجور بسبب من الأسباب وإن كان هو أقرب إلى
النسب لأنه مأخوذ من استحقاق الإرث وفي الزوج والمولى المعتق وجه أنه لا
يعتبر قولهما
والبنت الواحدة إذا أقرت وأقر معها إمام المسلمين ففي ثبوت النسب بقول
الإمام وجهان
أحدهما نعم كالمولى المعتق
والثاني لا لأنه غير مستحق وإنما المستحق وجهة الإسلام فلا يتصور صدر
الإقرار منه
أما إذا خلف ابنين فأقر أحدهما وأنكر الآخر فالنسب لا يثبت قطعا ونص
الشافعي رضي الله عنه على أن الميراث لا يثبت لأنه فرع النسب وعليه إشكالات
قررناها في مسائل الخلاف ولأجله خرج ابن سريج وجها أنه يرث وذكر صاحب
التقريب طريقين
أحدهما أن الميراث يثبت باطنا وهل يثبت ظاهرا وجهان
والثاني أنه لا يثبت ظاهرا وهل يثبت باطنا وجهان

### | التفريع

إن قلنا يثبت الميراث على المقر فإذا كانت التركة ستمائة فيأخذ المقر له
من المقر كم وجهان
أحدهما مائة وخمسين وهو نصف ما في يده لأنه أعترف له بالمساواة في كل شيء
والثاني مائة وهو ثلث ما في يده فإنه مظلوم بالمائة الأخرى من المنكر
وقال صاحب التقريب هذا إذا كان المقر مجبرا في القسمة فلو كان القسمة
بالتراضي فقد تعدى بتسليم نصيبه إلى المكذوب فيغرم له والقياس ما قاله

  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Genealogical connection establishing legal identity and inheritance rights

  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Procedural device for resolving competing claims when evidence fails
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (drawing lots); used metaphorically for judicial determination
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿ-t-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Freedom, liberation from slavery; nobility
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal emancipation of a slave, a status change with juridical effects
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (manumission); metaphorical in "free-born" (ḥurr)

chapters.translation:
### | Two Subsidiary Branches

**First Branch:** A man has two slave-women (ummatān), each having a child, and neither woman has a husband. One of these two sons said: "This is my father." Thus, lineage to one of them is established ambiguously (mubhaman), and he is required to specify. When he specifies, the designation becomes fixed, [the designated man] is emancipated, and the woman becomes an umm walad (mother of a master's child) — if he had said: "This is my son from her; I conceived him with her while she was in my ownership." But if he spoke absolutely and said: "This is my son from her," we have already mentioned two positions (wajhān) regarding this.

If he dies before specification, then the specification by the heirs is like the specification by the testator. If we are unable [to determine], we present [the case] to the qā'if (lineage assessor), and the qā'if's determination is like his own determination regarding lineage, umm walad status, and all other rulings. If we are unable [to find] a qā'if, we cast lots (aqraʿnā) between the two. Whichever one the lot falls upon is emancipated, but neither his lineage nor his inheritance is established — for the lot has no effect except in emancipation. Between them there is an ambiguous emancipation (ʿitq mubham).

Are lots cast between the two slave-women? Two positions:
- One: No — for the child's status as umm walad and the emancipation [of the mother] are subsidiary to the child, and there is no lineage [for the mother herself].
- The second: Yes — for they have lineage [of their own], and one of them becomes free by virtue of that [ruling]; thus lots are cast for the sake of emancipation.

Is the share of the son from the inheritance suspended (mawqūf)? Two positions:
- One: Yes — for one of them is a relative.
- The second: No — for it is a lineage whose emergence is despaired of, and clientage (muwālāh) through it [is impossible]; thus it has no effect on inheritance.

**Second Branch:** A slave-woman has three children. The master said: "One of these is my son; I made her an umm walad by him while she was in my ownership." This is an acknowledgment of the child's umm walad status, and he is required to specify. If he specifies the youngest, he is emancipated and his lineage is established. If he specifies the middle one, his lineage is established, and the youngest is also emancipated and his lineage established — because he was born on his bed (firāsh), unless he claims istibrā' (period of abstention) and we hold that the child is disowned by the mere claim of istibrā' regarding an umm walad. In that case, it is ruled that the youngest is emancipated because he is the child of the umm walad. But if the umm walad is emancipated by the master's death, there is a position that he is not emancipated — due to the possibility that he made her an umm walad by the middle one while she was mortgaged (marhūnah), and we hold that istīlād (making an umm walad) does not take effect [on a mortgaged slave], so she was sold and gave birth to the youngest in the hands of the purchaser. Then the one who made her an umm walad purchased both, and we hold that istīlād takes effect but does not extend to a child born in the ownership of another. The proponent of the first position, if he acknowledges this sub-branching, then the absolute rejection of the acknowledgment is repelled by this remote supposition.

This [applies] if he specified before death. If he dies, then the heirs or the qā'if stand in his place. If we are unable [to determine] through them, we cast lots among the three children. If the lot falls upon the youngest, he is designated for emancipation. If it falls upon the middle one, he is emancipated along with the youngest — except upon the supposition of the lot falling in the matter of the objection (mas'alat al-radd).

Al-Muzanī said, objecting to the text of al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him): "How does the young one enter the lot, when he is free in all circumstances?" What al-Muzanī mentioned is an error — for he enters the lot so that if it falls upon him, emancipation is restricted to him; or if it falls upon another, he is emancipated along with that other.

Then al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The lot has no effect on lineage, and inheritance is diverted to the heir whose inheritance is certain."

Al-Muzanī said: "The inheritance of the son ought to be suspended." This is the apparent analogical reasoning (ẓāhir al-qiyās). But al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) did not deem suspension [valid] after despair of this lineage's emergence.

### | The Second Category: Acknowledgment of Lineage Upon One's Testator

Whoever holds the authority of comprehensive inheritance (wilāyat istighrāq al-mīrāth) may affiliate lineage to his testator — whether he is alone or they are all [jointly].

Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "If [the deceased] leaves a single son who acknowledges another brother, it is not established unless there are two sons." This is weak — for when the qualities of witnesses are not considered, and acknowledgments are accepted, then number has no meaning.

Then the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: The acknowledgment of the husband and the manumitting patron (al-mawlā al-muʿtiq) is considered if they are among the heirs. No regard is given to the acknowledgment of a close relative (al-qarīb) who is barred (maḥjūb) by any cause, even if he is closer to the lineage — because it is derived from entitlement to inheritance. Regarding the husband and the manumitting patron, there is a position that their statement is not considered.

If a single daughter acknowledges, and with her the Imām of the Muslims acknowledges, then regarding the establishment of lineage by the Imām's statement there are two positions:
- One: Yes — like the manumitting patron.
- The second: No — for he is not an entitled heir; rather, the entitled party is the treasury of Islam (bayt al-māl), so the issuance of acknowledgment from him is inconceivable.

As for when [the deceased] leaves two sons, one acknowledges and the other denies — lineage is not established definitively. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly stated that inheritance is not established, because it is subsidiary to lineage. Upon this there are difficulties which we have set forth in the disputed questions (masā'il al-khilāf). For this reason, Ibn Surayj derived a position that he does inherit. The author of al-Taqrīb mentioned two paths:
- One: Inheritance is established inwardly (bāṭinan); is it established outwardly (ẓāhiran)? Two positions.
- The second: It is not established outwardly; is it established inwardly? Two positions.

### | The Sub-Branching

If we say inheritance is established upon the acknowledger (al-muqirr), then when the estate is six hundred, how much does the acknowledged one (al-muqarr lahu) take from the acknowledger? Two positions:
- One: One hundred and fifty — which is half of what is in his hand, because he acknowledged equality with him in everything.
- The second: One hundred — which is one-third of what is in his hand, for he is wronged regarding the other hundred by the denier.

The author of al-Taqrīb said: "This [applies] when the acknowledger is compelled in the division. But if the division was by mutual consent, then he has transgressed by delivering his share to the one who is denied, so he is liable for it." The analogical reasoning is what he stated.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع سبعة

الأول لو أقر أحد الابنين بزوجية امرأة لأبيه وأنكر الآخر فالظاهر أنه لا
يثبت الميراث كما في النسب وفيه وجه أنه يثبت لأن المقصود بالإقرار ها هنا
الإرث دون الزوجية
الثاني أقر أحد الابنين وأنكر الآخر ومات المنكر نظر فإن كان خلف ابنا
وهو مقر ففيه وجهان
أحدهما يثبت الميراث لأن الاستغراق لهم وقد توافقوا
والثاني لا لأنه فرع فليس له تكذيب أصله وهو يلتفت على أن الوارث هل
يلتحق بمن نفاه المورث باللعان
وإن لم يخلفا إلا الأخ المقر فوجهان مرتبان وأولى بالثبوت ولو أنه مات
قبل التكذيب فلا خلاف في أن الميراث يثبت بتوافق الباقين لأن التكذيب لم
يصدر منه بعد
الثالث خلف ابنين صغيرا وكبيرا فأقر الكبير بأخ ثالث وجهان أحدهما أنه لا
يثبت لا نسب ولا ميراث إذ الحق لهما
والثاني نعم يثبت ويستدام بشرط أن لا ينكر الصبي إذا بلغ
الرابع إذا خلف ابنا واحدا فقال لمجهول أنت ابن أبي فقال وأنت لست ابنا
له وأنا ابن له فوجهان
أحدها أن المقر يحجب لأن المجهول وارث بقوله وهو منكر قوله
والثاني أنهما يشتركان ولا يبالى بتكذيبه
وفيه وجه ثالث أن المكذب لا يستحق شيئا لأنه أخرجه عن أهلية الإقرار
بتكذيبه
الخامس اقر لاثنين بالأخوة فتكاذبا بينهما فوجهان
أحدهما أنهم يشتركون ولا يؤثر تكاذبهما نظرا إلى قول الأصل
والثاني أنهما لا يرثان إذ لم يتوافق على إرث كل واحد منهما الجميع
السادس إذا أقر الأخ بابن لأخيه قال الأصحاب يثبت النسب دون الميراث إذ
لو ثبت الميراث لحرم الأخ عن الميراث وخرج عن أهلية
الإقرار وصار دورا
ومنهم من قال يثبت النسب والميراث جميعا ومنهم من قال لا يثبت النسب أيضا
مع الميراث
السابع إذا أقر أحد الابنين بألف وأنكر الآخر والتركة ألفان فيؤخذ من
نصيب المقر خمسمائة أو ألف فيه قولان
أحدهما ألف مؤاخذة له بموجب قوله في أنه لا ينفك  جزء من التركة بما بقي
من الدين شيء والثاني يكتفى بحصته والتوجيه مذكور في الخلاف
= كتاب العارية = والنظر في
أركانها وأحكامها وفصل الخصومة فيها فإما الأركان فأربعة

### | الأول المعير

ولا يعتبر فيه إلا كونه مالكا للمنفعة غير محجور عليه في التبرع فأن
العارية تبرع بالمنافع فيصح من المستأجر
وللمستعير أن يستوفي المنافع بوكيله بنفسه وهل له ان يعير فيه وجهان
أظهرهما المنع لأن الإذن مخصوص به فهو كالضيف

### | الثاني المستعير

ولا يعتبر فيه إلا أن يكون أهلا للتبرع عليه

### | الثالث المعار

ويعتبر فيه شرطان
أحدهما أن يكون منتفعا به مع بقائه فلا معنى لإعاره الأطعمة وفي
إعارة الدراهم والدنانير وإجارتهما لمنفعة التزيين ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها نعم لأن غرض التزيين من المقاصد والثاني لا لأنه غرض بعيد والثالث
يصح الإعارة لأنه مبرة ولا يصح الإجارة لأنه معاوضة فيستدعي منفعة متقومة
فإن أبطلناها ففي طريقة العراق أنها مضمونة لأنها إعارة فاسدة وفي طريق
المراوزة أنها غير مضمونه لأنها غير قابلة للإعارة فهي باطلة الشرط الثاني
أن يكون الانتفاع مستباحا فلا يجوز إعارة الجواري للاستمتاع ولا للاستخدام
إذا كان المستعير غير محرم وكانت الجارية في محل الشهوة فإن جرى
فهو صحيح ولكنه محظور
وكذا تكره استعارة أحد الأبوين للخدمة وكذا إعارة العبد المسلم من الكافر
وتحرم إعارة الصيد من المحرم

### | الرابع صيغة الإعارة

ولابد فيه من الإيجاب وهو قوله أعرت أو خذ أو ما يفيد معناه ويكفي القبول
بالفعل ولا يشترط اللفظ كاستباحة الضيفان فلو قال أعرتك حماري لتعيرني فرسك
فهو أجاره فاسدة غير مضمونة ولو قال اغسل هذا الثوب فهو استعارة لبدنه لأجل
العمل فإن كان الغاسل ممن يعمل بالأجرة فالظاهر أنه يستحق الأجرة كما يستحق
الحمامي والحلاق والتعويل فيه على القرائن ولهذا ذكر القاضي في المعاطاة في
البيع وجهين لأجل القرائن أما أحكامها فثلاثة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ق-ر (a-q-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To affirm, acknowledge, or confess; establishing a claim by one's own admission (iqrār) as a binding legal declaration.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, iqrār is a self-imposed evidentiary act (iʿtirāf) that creates obligations, distinct from testimonial proof (bayyinah) which binds others.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in legal stipulation; metaphorical (majāz) when used for tacit acquiescence (sukūt) — here, strictly literal as an explicit utterance.
- Root: و-ر-ث (w-r-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Inheritance; the transfer of proprietary rights from a deceased (muwarriṯ) to heirs (warathah) by divine allotment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām, mīrāth signifies the divinely ordained distribution of estates, a fixed share (farīḍah) that cannot be altered by human stipulation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for property succession; metaphorical for spiritual or epistemic inheritance — here, purely literal.
- Root: ع-ا-ر (ʿ-ā-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ʿĀriyah — a loan of a usufruct (manfaʿah) without compensation; derived from ʿār (a transient defect), indicating the temporary nature of the transfer.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A gratuitous conveyance of benefit (ibāḥat al-manfaʿah) retaining ownership of the substance (raqabah) with the lender (muʿīr).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the legal contract; metaphorical in the phrase "ʿārat al-ṣaḥīfah" (the page was borrowed) for any temporary use.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Taqdīr (Ellipsis) — In "لو أقر... وأنكر الآخر" (if one confessed... and the other denied), the protasis (sharṭ) governs a hypothetical scenario requiring juristic estimation (taqdīr) of the unstated legal effect, a hallmark of periodic legal reasoning.
chapters.translation:
I say — Section 194: Seven Subsidiary Branches.

**The First Branch:** If one of the two sons acknowledges the marital bond (zawjiyyah) of a woman to his father, and the other son denies it, then the apparent ruling (al-ẓāhir) is that inheritance (mīrāth) is not established, just as in the case of lineage (nasab). Yet there is a face (wajh) that it is established, because the intended purpose of the acknowledgment here is inheritance, not the marital bond itself.

**The Second Branch:** One of the two sons acknowledges, the other denies, and then the denying one dies. We consider: if the denier left behind a son who is himself an acknowledger, then there are two faces:
- The first: inheritance is established, because the entire estate is absorbed by them (the acknowledgers), and they have mutually agreed.
- The second: it is not established, because he (the grandson) is a branch (farʿ), and it is not his place to give the lie to his root (aṣl). This hinges on whether an heir can be affiliated to one whom the deceased (muwarriṯ) repudiated through the oath of imprecation (liʿān).
If they (the two sons) left behind only the acknowledging brother, then there are two faces, ordered in priority, and the establishment (of inheritance) is more apt. And if he (the acknowledging brother) died before the repudiation (takdhīb), then there is no disagreement that inheritance is established by the agreement of the remaining ones, because the repudiation had not yet issued from him.

**The Third Branch:** He left behind two sons — one minor and one major. The major one acknowledges a third brother. Two faces:
- The first: it is not established — neither lineage nor inheritance — because the right belongs to both of them (jointly).
- The second: yes, it is established and continues, on the condition that the minor does not deny it upon reaching majority (bulūgh).

**The Fourth Branch:** If he left behind a single son, and he (that son) said to an unknown person (majhūl): "You are my father's son," and the unknown person replied: "You are not his son, and I am his son," then two faces:
- The first: the acknowledger is excluded (yuḥjab), because the unknown person is an heir by his own statement, while the acknowledger denies his statement.
- The second: they both share (in the estate), and no heed is paid to his denial.
There is a third face: the one who denies (the other's claim) deserves nothing, because he has removed himself from the capacity for valid acknowledgment (ahliyyat al-iqrār) by his own denial.

**The Fifth Branch:** He acknowledged two persons as brothers, and the two mutually denied each other. Two faces:
- The first: they share, and their mutual denial has no effect, with consideration given to the statement of the original (the deceased).
- The second: they do not inherit, since there was no mutual agreement on the inheritance of the entirety for each one of them.

**The Sixth Branch:** If a brother acknowledges a son for his (deceased) brother, the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: lineage is established without inheritance — for if inheritance were established, the brother would be excluded from inheritance, and he would exit the capacity for acknowledgment, resulting in a circularity (dawr). Among them are those who said: both lineage and inheritance are established together. And among them are those who said: lineage is not established either, along with inheritance.

**The Seventh Branch:** If one of the two sons acknowledges a debt of one thousand, and the other denies it, and the estate is two thousand — then is taken from the acknowledging one's share five hundred or one thousand? Two sayings (qawlān):
- The first: one thousand, holding him to the import of his statement, in that no part of the estate is free from the remainder of the debt.
- The second: his share suffices. The justification (tawjīh) is mentioned in the Book of Disputes (al-Khilāf).

= The Book of ʿĀriyah (Gratuitous Loan) = And the consideration is in its pillars (arkān), its rulings (aḥkām), and the adjudication of disputes therein. As for its pillars, they are four:

**The First Pillar: The Lender (al-Muʿīr)**
Nothing is considered in him except that he be a possessor of the usufruct (mālikan lil-manfaʿah), not barred (maḥjūr) from gratuitous donation (tabarruʿ). For ʿāriyah is a gratuitous grant of usufructs, so it is valid from a lessee (mustaʾjir). And the borrower (mustaʿīr) may exact the usufruct by his own agent or himself. Does he have the right to lend it (to a third party)? Two faces — the more apparent of them is prohibition, because the permission is specific to him, like the guest (ḍayf).

**The Second Pillar: The Borrower (al-Mustaʿīr)**
Nothing is considered in him except that he be qualified for gratuitous donation upon him (i.e., legally competent to receive a gift).

**The Third Pillar: The Loaned Object (al-Muʿār)**
Two conditions are considered in it:
- The first: that it be utilizable while remaining intact (baqāʾ). Thus, there is no meaning in lending foods. Regarding the lending of dirhams and dīnārs, and their lease (ijārah) for the purpose of adornment (tazyīn), there are three faces:
  - The first: yes (valid), because the purpose of adornment is among the recognized objectives (maqāṣid).
  - The second: no, because it is a remote purpose.
  - The third: the loan (ʿāriyah) is valid because it is a gratuitous act (mabirrah), but the lease is not valid because it is a compensatory contract (muʿāwaḍah) requiring a valued usufruct (manfaʿah mutaqawwimah). If we nullify it (the loan), then in the path of the Iraqis (ṭarīqat al-ʿIrāq), it is guaranteed (maḍmūnah) because it is a corrupt loan (ʿāriyah fāsidah). In the path of the Marwazis (ṭarīqat al-Marāwizah), it is not guaranteed because it is not susceptible to loan, so it is void (bāṭilah).
- The second condition: that the usufruct be permissible (mustabāḥ). Thus, it is not permissible to lend slave-girls (jawārī) for sexual enjoyment (istimtāʿ), nor for service, if the borrower is not a maḥram and the slave-girl is in a place of desire (maḥall al-shahwah). If it occurs, it is valid (ṣaḥīḥ) but prohibited (maḥẓūr). Likewise, it is disliked (makrūh) to borrow one of the parents for service. Likewise, lending a Muslim slave to a disbeliever (kāfir). And it is prohibited to lend a hunting animal (ṣayd) to a person in iḥrām.

**The Fourth Pillar: The Formula of the Loan (Ṣīghat al-ʿĀriyah)**
It requires an offer (ījāb), which is his saying: "I lend you" (aʿartuka), or "Take" (khudh), or whatever conveys its meaning. Acceptance (qabūl) by act suffices, and utterance (lafẓ) is not stipulated — like the permissibility of guests (isti bāḥat al-ḍuyūf). If he said: "I lend you my donkey on condition that you lend me your horse," it is a corrupt lease (ijārah fāsidah) that is not guaranteed. If he said: "Wash this garment," it is a loan of his body (badan) for the sake of the work. If the washer is one who works for wages, the apparent ruling is that he deserves the wage, just as the bath-attendant (ḥammāmī) and the barber (ḥallāq) deserve it. Reliance therein is on contextual indicators (qarāʾin). For this reason, the Judge (al-Qāḍī) mentioned two faces in muʿāṭāh (exchange by mutual delivery) in sales, on account of contextual indicators. As for its rulings (aḥkām), they are three:

chapters.title_en: Section 195 — The First Issue: Liability (Ḍamān) for the ʿĀriyah (Loan for Use)

### | الأول الضمان

قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم العارية مضمونة مؤداة وقال أبو حنيفة
رحمة الله أنها غير مضمونة ولا خلاف أنها مضمونة الرد على المستعير
ثم في كيفية الضمان ثلاثة أقوال أحدها أنه يضمن بأقصى قيمته من يوم القبض
الى يوم التلف كضمان المغصوب وعلى هذا يحدث وكذا المستعار في يده مضمونا
والثاني أنه يعتبر قيمته يوم القبض
والثالث هو الأصح أنه يعتبر قيمته يوم التلف إذ في اعتبار يوم القبض ما
يوجب ضمان الأجزاء المستحقة بالاستعمال وضمانها غير واجب لأنها تلفت بالإذن
وفيه وجه بعيد
والمستعير من المستأجر هل يضمن فيه وجهان
أحدهما لا ابتناء يده على يد غير مضمونة
والثاني نعم نظرا إليه في نفسه
والمستعير من الغاصب يستقر عليه الضمان إذا تلف العين في يده ولو طولب
بالأجرة ولم يكن استوفي المنفعة بل تلفت تحت يده يرجع به على المعير لأن
يده في المنفعة ليس يد ضمان وإن كان استوفاه ففي الرجوع قولان
أحدهما نعم للغرور فأنه لم يرض بضمان المنافع
والثاني لا تغليبا للإتلاف على الغرور
وحد المستعير كل طالب أخذ المال لغرض نفسه من غير استحقاق فعلى هذا لو
جمحت دابة فأركبها ر أيضا ليروضها له وارسل وكيلا في شغل له واركبه دابته
وفتلفت لا ضمان له لأنه ليس آخذا لغرض نفسه ولو وجد من اعيا في الطريق
فأركبه بطريق القربة ففيه نظر من حيث أن الراكب منتفع ولكن الأظهر أن لا
ضمان لأن المالك هو المطالب لركوبه ليقترب به الى الله تبارك وتعالى
ولو أركب المالك مع نفسه رديفا فتلفت الدابة تحتهما قال الأصحاب على
الرديف نصف الضمان الأولى أن لا يجب لأن الدابة في الملك ما دام هو راكبا
والرديف ضيف كالضيف الداخل في الدار
ولو أودعه ثوبا وقال إن شئت فالبسه عند الحاجة فهو قبل اللبس وديعة وبعده
عارية مضمونة

### | الحكم الثاني التسلط على الانتفاع

وهو بقدر التسليط لأن منتفع بالأذن فإن تعين جهة المنفعة فلا كلام
وإن تعددت كما إذا أعار أرضا فإن عين زراعة الحنطة مثلا فله أن يزرع ما
ضرره مثل ضرر الحنطة ودونه ولا يزرع ما ضرره فوقه وإن أطلق فالظاهر فساده
إذ  يتردد بين الغراس والبناء والزراعة فهو غرر ظاهر وفيه وجه أنه يصح
ويتسلط على الكل ولو قال أنتفع كيف شئت فوجهان من حيث أنه
فوض الى مشيئته ولو عين الزراعة فالظاهر الجواز وإن لم يعين المزروع لأن
الأمر فيه قريب ولو عين الغراس فله أن يبني
وكذلك بالعكس لتساويهما وقيل لا لأن ضرر الغراس في باطن الأرض وضرر
البناء في ظاهر الأرض فهما مختلفان في الجنس
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, to be answerable for, to incur liability for loss or damage; the core sense is "inclusion" or "embrace" of responsibility.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Liability (ḍamān) as a juristic construct tied to the obligation to compensate (taʿwīḍ) for what is destroyed or consumed, whether by usurpation (ghaṣb) or by contractual permission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for financial liability; metaphorically (majāz) for moral accountability. Here it is strictly literal in the financial sense.
- Root: ع-و-ر (ʿ-w-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The ʿāriyah (loan for use) derives from the root meaning "to come and go" or "to alternate," indicating something that passes from hand to hand without permanent transfer of ownership.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A gratuitous transfer of usufruct (manfaʿah) with the obligation to return the substance (ʿayn) itself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The term is literal for the contract itself; the "guarantee" attached to it is a legal stipulation, not a natural consequence.
- Root: ق-ب-ض (q-b-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taking possession, seizing, holding in one's control.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In liability contexts, the moment of taking possession (qabḍ) is the operative point for determining the commencement of responsibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical taking; legally constructive for the transfer of risk.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional particles (in, law) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal outcomes precisely, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first issue is liability (ḍamān).

The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: {«العارية مضمونة مؤداة»} — "The loan for use is guaranteed and must be returned." Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it is not guaranteed. There is no disagreement, however, that the return of the borrowed object to the borrower is guaranteed.

Then, concerning the manner of liability, there are three positions. One of them is that he is liable for its highest value from the day of taking possession (qabḍ) until the day of its destruction, like the liability for a usurped object (al-maghṣūb). Upon this view, the borrowed object remains in his hand as a guaranteed thing. The second is that its value is considered as of the day of taking possession. The third — and this is the most correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) — is that its value is considered as of the day of destruction. For in considering the day of taking possession, there is something that necessitates liability for the parts consumed by use, yet liability for them is not obligatory, because they were destroyed with permission. There is a remote opinion (wajh baʿīd) on this.

As for the one who borrows from a borrower (al-mustaʿīr min al-mustaʾjir), is he liable? There are two opinions (wajhān). One of them is no, because his hand is built upon a hand that is not a hand of liability. The second is yes, looking to him in himself.

As for the one who borrows from a usurper (al-ghāṣib), liability is settled upon him if the object itself is destroyed in his hand. And if he is demanded for the rent (ujrah) and had not yet enjoyed the usufruct, but rather it was destroyed under his hand, he may seek recourse against the lender (al-muʿīr), because his hand over the usufruct is not a hand of liability. But if he had enjoyed it, then there are two opinions (qawlān) concerning recourse. One of them is yes, due to deception (ghurūr), for he did not consent to liability for the usufructs. The second is no, giving preponderance to destruction (itlāf) over deception.

The definition of a borrower (mustaʿīr) is: every seeker who takes property for his own purpose without entitlement. Upon this basis, if a horse bolted and a man mounted it to calm it for its owner, or if the owner sent an agent on his own business and mounted him on his beast, and it was destroyed, there is no liability upon him, because he is not one taking for his own purpose. And if he found a man exhausted on the road and mounted him by way of piety (qurbah), there is a consideration (naẓar) therein, from the angle that the rider is benefiting. But the more apparent (al-aẓhar) is that there is no liability, because the owner is the one who sought the riding so that he might draw near thereby to Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

And if the owner mounted a second rider behind himself (radīf) and the beast was destroyed beneath both of them, the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: upon the second rider is half the liability. The first (al-ūlā) is that it should not be obligatory, because the beast remains in the ownership of the owner as long as he is riding it, and the second rider is a guest, like a guest entering a house.

And if someone deposited a garment with him and said, "If you wish, wear it when needed," then before wearing it, it is a deposit (wadīʿah), and after wearing it, it is a guaranteed loan (ʿāriyah maḍmūnah).

The second ruling: The authority over the usufruct (al-tasalluṭ ʿalā al-intifāʿ).

This is according to the extent of the authorization (taslīṭ), because the user benefits by permission. If the mode of benefit is specified, then there is no discussion. But if it is multiple — as when one lends land — then if he specified, for example, the cultivation of wheat, he may cultivate what causes harm equal to the harm of wheat or less, and he may not cultivate what causes harm greater than it. If he left it absolutely unrestricted (muṭlaq), then the apparent (al-ẓāhir) view is its invalidity (fasād), since it oscillates between planting trees (ghirās), building (bināʾ), and cultivation (zirāʿah), and this is manifest uncertainty (gharar ẓāhir). There is an opinion (wajh) that it is valid, and he has authority over all of it. And if he said, "Benefit however you wish," there are two opinions, from the angle that he delegated it to his will. And if he specified cultivation, then the apparent view is permissibility, even if he did not specify the crop, because the matter therein is close in degree. And if he specified planting trees, he may build as well, and likewise the reverse, because the two are equal. And it was said: no, because the harm of planting trees is in the interior of the earth, while the harm of building is on the exterior of the earth, so they differ in kind.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الحكم الثالث الجواز

وللمعير الرجوع مهما شاء إلا إذا أعار لدفن ميت فيمتنع نبش القبر سواء
كان الميت جديدا أو عتيقا إلى أن يندرس أثر المدفون فعند ذلك يفعل ما يريد
وقبل الاندراس لو كان له فيه أشجار فله السقي بشرط أن لا يظهر الميت
وكذلك لو أعار جدارا ليضع الجار عليه جذعه فلا يستفيد بالرجوع قبل الانهدام
شيئا إذ لا أجرة له حتى يطالب به
وفي هدمه بأرش النقض تصرف في خاص ملك الجار في الجانب الثاني من الجذع
فأما إذا أعار أرضا للبناء والغراس مطلقا فله الرجوع وليس له لنقض ملك
المستعير مجانا لأنه محترم وضعه من غير عدوان ولكن يتخير المالك بين الثلاث
خصال بين أن يبقى بأجرة أو يتملك البناء بقيمته أو ينقض ويبذل أرشه والخيرة
في التعيين للمالك ترجيحا لجانبه فإنه معير ولا حق للمستعير إلا أن لا يضيع
ماليته
ثم إذا رجع والبناء بعد لم يرفع جاز للمالك الدخول ولا يتصرف في البناء
ولا
يجوز للمستعير الدخول وتنزها
وهل يجوز مرمة الجدران فيه خلاف وجه الجواز أن حقه مضمون عن التلف وفي
المنع من العمارة تضييع ويجوز للمعير بيع الأرض وعليها بناء المستعير قبل
التملك
وهل يجوز للمستعير بيع البناء فيه وجهان
وجه المنع أنه معرض للهدم أن أراد المعير هذا إذا كانت الإعارة مطلقة أو
مقيدة بالتأبيد فلو قال أعرت سنة فإذا مضت قلعت البناء مجانا فله ذلك
اتباعا للشرط ولو اقتصر على قوله أعرت سنة لم يجز له النقض بعده مجانا فكان
يحتمل أن يحمل على  طلب الأجرة بعده كما يحتمل الهدم والأصل حرمة ملكه
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله فائدة التأقيت جواز القلع مجانا أما إذا أعار
للزراعة ورجع قبل الإدراك فالمذهب أنه يجب ابقاؤه الى الإدراك وليس له قلع
الزرع ولكن له أخذ الأجرة لأن هذا اقرب الطرق بخلاف الغراس في الإجارة
المؤقتة فإنه وإن صبر بقية المدة افتقر إلى القلع بعدها
وفيه وجه للعراقيين أنه لا يستحق الأجرة إلى الإدراك ووجه لصاحب التقريب
أنه يقلع الزرع كالغراس أو لا يقلع الغراس كالزرع وهو من تخريجه وتصرفه
فرعان
أحدهما لو بادر المستعير وقلع الغراس هل يلزمه تسوية الحفر فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم ليرد ما أخذ كما أخذ
والثاني لا لأن المأذون في الغرس مأذون في القلع وقد حصل من المأذون فيه
فصار كما لو تلفت الدابة المستعارة أو تعبت بالركوب
الثاني إذا حمل السيل ونواة لأنسان إلى ملك غيره فأنبتت شجرة فهل لمالك
الأرض قلعها مجانا فيه وجهان لتعارض الحرمة في الجانبين والأولى ترجيح مالك
الأرض وتسليطه على القلع

### | وأما فصل الخصومة

فلها ثلاث صور
الأولى إذا قال راكب الدابة لمالكها أغرتنيها فقال المالك بل أجرتكها قال
الشافعي رضي الله عنه القول قول الراكب ولو قال ذلك زارع الأرض لماكلها قال
القول قول المالك نص عليه في المزارعة فأختلف الأصحاب على طريقين أحدهما
قولان لتقابل الاصلين إذ يمكن أن يقال الأصل وجوب الضمان في المنفعة وعدم
ما يسقطها أو الأصل عند طريان الأذن عدم الضمان
ومنهم من قرر التعيين وفرق بأن العارية في الدواب ليس ببعيد وفي الأرض
بعيد وهذا الترجيح في مظنة تعارض الاصلين لا بأس به
التفريع الأول
إن قلنا القول قول الماك فيحلف على نفي الإعارة ولا يتعرض لإثبات الإجازة
والمسمى فإنه مدع فيهما ثم إذا حلف أخذ أقل الأمرين من المسمى أو أجرة
المثل
وقال القاضي والعراقيون إنه يتعرض للإجارة فيحلف أنه ما أعار ولكنه أجر
لينتظم الكلام لا ليثبت الإجارة وذكر العراقيون قولا آخر أن فائدته إثبات
المسمى إظهارا  لفائدته وهو بعيد
أما إذا نكل المالك قال العراقيون لا يرد على الراكب لأنه لا يدعي لنفسه
حقا فيبني عليه القضاء بالنكول قال القاضي ترد وفائدته دفع الغريم وهو أقرب
من القضاء بالنكول
فإن قيل فلو تنازعا قبل مضي مده تتقدم المنفعة فيها قلنا القول قول
الراكب في نفي ما يدعى عليه من الإجارة للمستقبل الصورة الثانيه أن يقول
المالك بل غصبتنيها
قال المزني القول قول الركب إذ الأصل عدم الغضب إحسانا للظن بالناس ثم
خالفا أكثر الأصحاب وقالوا الأصل عدم الأذن وبقاء حق المالك في المنفعة
وقيل المذهبان قولان للشافعي والأولى القول المخالف للمزني
الثالثة
أن يقول الراكب أكريتنيها وغرضه إسقاط الضمان عند التلف واستحقاق الإمساك
فقال المالك أعرتكبها فالقول قول المالك فإنه يدعي عليه إجارة والأصل عدمها
ثم يستفيد بالحلف استحقاق القيمة عند التلف وجواز الرجوع عند القيام
= كتاب الغصب =
الغصب عدوان محض لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم من غضي شبرا من أرض طوقه الله
من سبع أرضين يوم القيامة
وهو سبب للضمان لقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام على اليد ما أخذت حتى ترد
والنظر في الكتاب يحصره بابان
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في الضمان - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
والنظر في ثلاثة أركان الموجب والموجب فيه والواجب

### | الركن الأول الموجب للضمان

- Root: ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, reversion, withdrawal from a prior state or commitment
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Revocation of a permissive grant (ibāḥah) — the lender's retained right over his property
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of physical return; metaphorical (majāz) in contractual revocation
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — "مهما شاء" governs the temporal scope of the right, with the apodosis implied by the preceding ruling
chapters.translation:
I say: The lender (al-muʿīr) may revoke the loan whenever he wishes — except when he has lent [land] for the burial of a corpse, in which case exhumation of the grave is prohibited, whether the deceased is recently buried or long since interred, until the trace of the buried one has completely vanished. At that point, he may do as he pleases. Before such obliteration, if he has trees therein, he may water them on the condition that the corpse does not become exposed.

Likewise, if one lends a wall for a neighbor to place his beam upon it, the lender gains nothing by revoking before the wall collapses — for he has no claim to rent that he might demand. And in demolishing it with compensation for the damage (arsh al-naqḍ), he would be disposing of what is specifically the neighbor's property right in the second side of the beam.

As for when he lends land for building or planting absolutely (muṭlaqan), he may revoke, but he may not demolish the borrower's property (milk al-mustaʿīr) without compensation, for the borrower's placement was inviolable (muḥtaram), being done without aggression. Rather, the owner is given a choice among three options: either to leave the structure in place for rent, or to take ownership of the building at its value, or to demolish it while paying compensation for the damage. The selection among these three is reserved to the owner, favoring his side, for he is the lender; the borrower has no right except that the monetary value (māliyyah) of his property not be squandered.

Then, if the lender revokes while the building has not yet been removed, the owner may enter [the land] but may not dispose of the building; and the borrower may not enter — out of propriety (tanazzuhan).

As for whether the borrower may repair the walls, there is a difference of opinion. The basis for permissibility is that his right is guaranteed against destruction, and preventing maintenance would constitute waste (taḍyīʿ). The lender may sell the land with the borrower's building upon it before taking ownership [of the building].

As for whether the borrower may sell the building, there are two positions (wajhān). The basis for prohibition is that it is subject to demolition should the lender so wish. This applies when the loan is absolute or restricted to perpetuity (taʾbīd). But if he said, "I lend it for a year, and when it passes, you shall uproot the building without compensation," then he has that right, in accordance with the stipulation. If he merely said, "I lend it for a year," he may not demolish it afterward without compensation — for the expression could plausibly be construed as seeking rent after the term, just as it could plausibly mean demolition; and the default principle is the inviolability of the borrower's property.

Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) held that the benefit of fixing a term is the permissibility of uprooting without compensation.

As for when he lends for cultivation and revokes before the crop reaches maturity, the established doctrine (al-madhhab) is that the crop must be left until maturity, and he may not uproot it — but he may take rent, for this is the nearest means [to justice]. This differs from the case of planting (ghirās) in a fixed-term lease, where even if the planter waits out the remainder of the term, he is still required to uproot afterward.

There is a position of the Iraqis that he does not deserve rent until maturity, and a position of the author of al-Taqrīb that he uproots the crop like the planting — or alternatively, that he does not uproot the planting just as he does not uproot the crop. This latter is from his own derivation (takhrij) and independent reasoning.

Two subsidiary questions (farʿān):

First: If the borrower hastens and uproots the planting himself, is he obligated to level the holes? There are two positions. One: yes, so that he returns what he took in the manner he took it. The second: no — for one authorized to plant is authorized to uproot, and what was done fell within the scope of authorization, just as if the borrowed beast perished or became fatigued from riding.

Second: If a flood carries a date-pit belonging to someone into another's property, and it grows into a tree, may the landowner uproot it without compensation? There are two positions, due to the conflict of inviolability on both sides. The preferable view is to favor the landowner and grant him authority to uproot.

### | On the Chapter of Dispute Resolution (Faṣl al-Khuṣūmah)

This has three forms:

**First form:** If the rider of a beast says to its owner, "You lent it to me," and the owner says, "Rather, I leased it to you," al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) held that the rider's word is accepted. But if the cultivator of land says this to its owner, the owner's word is accepted — as he explicitly stated in the chapter on sharecropping (al-muzāraʿah). The companions (al-aṣḥāb) then differed along two paths. One path: there are two rulings (qawlān), due to the conflict of two default principles — for it may be said that the default is the obligation of liability (ḍamān) for the usufruct and the absence of anything that negates it; or it may be said that the default, when permission (idhn) has intervened, is the absence of liability.

Among them are those who settled the distinction and differentiated by noting that loaning beasts is not far-fetched, whereas loaning land is far-fetched. This preference, in a context where the two default principles conflict, is unobjectionable.

**First ramification:** If we say the owner's word is accepted, he takes an oath denying the loan (iʿārah) — and he does not address himself to affirming the lease or its named rent (al-musammā), for he is the claimant with respect to both. Then, when he has sworn, he takes the lesser of the two amounts: the named rent or the equivalent rent (ujrat al-mithl).

Al-Qāḍī and the Iraqis held that he does address the lease, swearing: "I did not lend it, but rather I leased it" — to make his statement coherent, not to establish the lease. The Iraqis also mentioned another position that its benefit is to establish the named rent, manifesting its utility — but this is far-fetched.

As for when the owner refuses to take the oath (nukūl), the Iraqis said it is not returned to the rider, for he claims no right for himself upon which judgment by refusal could be based. Al-Qāḍī said it is returned, and its benefit is to repel the claimant — and this is closer [to the principles] than judgment by refusal.

If it is said: "What if they dispute before the term has elapsed — the usufruct being prospective therein?" We say: the rider's word is accepted in denying what is claimed against him, namely the lease for the future.

**Second form:** The owner says, "Rather, you usurped it from me." Al-Muzanī held that the rider's word is accepted, for the default is the absence of usurpation (ghaṣb), thinking well of people. But most of the companions dissented, saying: the default is the absence of permission and the persistence of the owner's right over the usufruct. It was said that the two doctrines are two rulings of al-Shāfiʿī. The preferable view is the one contrary to al-Muzanī.

**Third form:** The rider says, "You leased it to me" — his purpose being to negate liability upon destruction and to establish his right to retain possession. The owner says, "I lent it to you." The owner's word is accepted, for the rider claims a lease against him, and the default is its absence. By his oath, the owner gains the right to claim value upon destruction and the permissibility of revocation while the beast is still extant.

= The Book of Usurpation (Kitāb al-Ghaṣb) =

Usurpation is pure aggression (ʿudwān muḥaḍ), for the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: {«من غصب شبرا من أرض طوقه الله من سبع أرضين يوم القيامة»} — "Whoever usurps a span of land, Allah will collar him with seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."

It is a cause of liability, for the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: {«على اليد ما أخذت حتى ترد»} — "The hand is liable for what it has taken until it returns it."

The inquiry of this book is encompassed in two chapters:

### | Chapter One: On Liability (al-Ḍamān)

The inquiry concerns three pillars: the cause of liability (al-mūjib), the subject upon whom it falls (al-mūjab ʿalayh), and the object obligated (al-wājib).

### | First Pillar: The Cause of Liability
