chapters.arabic_text:
### | أما الصفة

فلو آتى بغير جنسه لم يجز قبوله لأنه أعتياض
وإن أتي باردا منه جاز قبوله ولم يجب
وإن أتى بأجود وجب قبوله وقيل لا يجب لأنه فيه منة وهو بعيد
ولو أتي بنوع أخر كما لو أسلم في الزبيب الأبيض فأتى بالأسود ففي جواز
القبول وجهان منشؤه أن أختلاف النوع كاختلاف الوصف أو كاختلاف الجنس
وترددوا في أن التفاوت بين السقية من الحنطة وما يسقى من السماء تفاوت
صفة أو تفاوت نوع وكذلك في الرطب  مع التمر
وترددوا في أن التفاوت بين الهندي والتركي من العبيد اختلاف جنس أو
اختلاف نوع
فرع
لو أسلم في لحم السمك لم يلزمه قبول الرأس والذنب وكذا لحم الطير ولو
أسلم في السمك والطير لزمه القبول
أما الزمان
فلا يطالب الا بعد المحل ولكنه لو جاء به قبل المحل فإن كان له في
التعجيل غرض فإن كان له بالدين رهن أو ضمان أو المكاتب عجل النجوم يجبر على
القبول
وإن لم يكن غرض سوى البراءه نظر فإن كان للممتنع غرض بأن كان في وقت نهب
وعارة أو كانت دابة يحذر من علفها فلا يجبر
وإن لم يكن غرض في الامتناع فقولان
أحدهما يجبر لأن الأجل حق من عليه الدين وقد أسقطه
والثاني لا لأن فيه منة
فإن قيل لو صرح من عليه الدين بإسقاط الأجل هل يسقط حتى تتوجه عليه
المطالبة
قلنا فيه وجهان
أحدهما لا لأن الأجل وصف تابع كالصحة في الدراهم لا يسقط بمجردها مع بقاء
الأصل
والثاني نعم لأن الدين عليه والأجل هو له

### | فرعان

أحدهما لو خاف المسلم إلية الانقطاع لدى المحل فهل يكون هذا عذرا في
التعجيل فيه وجهان
الثاني لو سلم في غير مكان العقد وكان فيه مئونة فهذا عذر من جانب
المستحق فلا يجبر
أما إذا أتى بالحق بعد حلوله فلا شك في الإجبار إن كان للمؤدي غرض
وإن لم يكن غرض فطريقان ولا أثر ها هنا لعذر المستحق
منهم من قال فيه قولان كما قبل المحل لأنه حقه فله التأخير إلى حيث يشاء
ومنهم من قطع بالإجبار لغرض البراءة فليأخذ أم ليبرىء
أما مكان التسليم يتعين فيه مكان العقد إما بالتعيين أو بالإطلاق فلو ظفر
به في غيره وكان في نقله مؤنة لم يطالب به وإن لم يكن مؤنة فله المطالبة
وكذا في سائر الديون إلا في الغاصب فإن في مطالبته مع لزوم المؤنة وجهان
تغليظا عليه من حيث منعناه من المطالبة بالمثل لما فيه من المؤونة فلا بد
من القيمة  لوقوع الحيلولة بعد ثبوت الاستحقاق وتوجه المطالبة هذا تمام
القول في السلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع و ض (ʿ-w-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exchange, substitution, compensation; the act of giving one thing in place of another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In contractual theology, ʿiwaḍ denotes a counter-value that must be equivalent in kind to the original obligation; deviation entails injustice (ẓulm) in exchange.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in monetary transactions; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to moral recompense.
- Root: م ن ن (m-n-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A favor or benefaction that humiliates the recipient; to bestow with reproach.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, minnah is the imposition of a gratuitous burden that alters the contractual equilibrium; rejected as a basis for obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in social exchange; metaphorical in divine grace (minnah) where no humiliation attaches.
- Root: ج ب ر (j-b-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To compel, force, or coerce; to set a bone (jabara) — restoring to proper state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ijbār in jurisprudence is the court's coercive power to enforce contractual performance against a recalcitrant party.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical compulsion; metaphorical for legal enforcement.
- Root: ح ل ل (ḥ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To become permissible, to arrive at maturity; the dissolution of a knot.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥulūl marks the temporal point at which a deferred obligation (dayn) becomes due and demandable.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for time-based maturity; metaphorical for the resolution of legal impediments.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The particle "law" (if) introduces hypothetical legal scenarios whose apodosis is governed by the protasis; "fa" in "fa-lam yajuz" marks the consequential ruling, requiring careful parsing of nested conditions (e.g., "wa-in atā... fa-fī jawāz al-qabūl wajhān").
chapters.translation:
### | As for the Attribute (of the Delivered Commodity)

If he delivers something of a different genus (ghayr jinsihi), it is not permissible to accept it, because that would constitute an exchange (iʿtiyāḍ) [of the contract terms].

And if he delivers it cold (bārid) [i.e., of inferior quality within the same genus], acceptance is permissible but not obligatory.

And if he delivers a superior quality (ajwad), acceptance is obligatory. It was also said: it is not obligatory, because therein lies a favor (minnah) [imposed upon the recipient] — but this view is remote (baʿīd).

And if he delivers a different species (nawʿ ākhar) — as when one contracts salam in white raisins (zabīb abyaḍ) and he delivers black ones — then regarding the permissibility of acceptance there are two views (wajhān). Their origin is whether the difference of species is like the difference of attribute (ikhtilāf al-waṣf) or like the difference of genus (ikhtilāf al-jins).

And they deliberated whether the disparity between irrigated wheat (saqīyah) and rain-fed wheat (mā yusqā min al-samāʾ) is a disparity of attribute or a disparity of species — and likewise regarding fresh dates (ruṭab) versus dried dates (tamr).

And they deliberated whether the disparity between the Indian and the Turkish [slaves] among captives (ʿabīd) is a difference of genus or a difference of species.

### Branch

If one contracts salam in fish meat (laḥm al-samak), he is not obliged to accept the head and the tail [as part of the delivery]. Likewise for bird meat (laḥm al-ṭayr). But if he contracts salam in [whole] fish or [whole] birds, acceptance is obligatory.

### As for the Time (al-zamān)

He cannot demand [delivery] except after the term (maḥall) has arrived. However, if he brings it before the term — then if he (the debtor) has an interest in expediting (gharaḍ fī al-taʿjīl): if the debt is secured by a pledge (rahn) or a guarantor (ḍamān), or [the debtor] is a mukātab [slave under manumission contract] who expedites his installments (nujūm), he is compelled (yujbar) to accept.

But if he has no interest other than discharge (barāʾah), then consider: if the one refusing (al-mumtaniʿ) has an interest [in refusing] — such as a time of plunder (nahb) or lending (ʿārah), or an animal whose fodder he fears [to provide] — then he is not compelled.

And if there is no interest in refusing, then there are two opinions (qawlān):
One: he is compelled, because the term is a right of the debtor, and he has waived it.
The second: he is not [compelled], because therein lies a favor (minnah).

If it is said: If the debtor explicitly declares the waiver of the term (isqāṭ al-ajal), does the term lapse such that the demand becomes incumbent upon him? We say: therein are two views (wajhān):
One: no — because the term is a subordinate attribute (waṣf tābiʿ), like soundness (ṣiḥḥah) in dirhams, which does not lapse by its mere [waiver] while the principal (aṣl) remains.
The second: yes — because the debt is upon him, and the term is for his benefit.

### | Two Branches

First: If the Muslim [creditor] fears cessation (inqiṭāʿ) [of supply] at the term, is this an excuse (ʿudhr) for expediting [demand]? Therein are two views.

Second: If he delivers in a place other than the place of contract (makān al-ʿaqd), and therein is transport cost (maʾūnah), this is an excuse on the side of the one entitled (al-mustaḥiqq), so he is not compelled [to accept].

As for when he brings the right (al-ḥaqq) after the term has matured — there is no doubt about compulsion (ijbār) if the payer has an interest [in paying]. And if he has no interest, then there are two paths (ṭarīqān), and no effect here for the excuse of the one entitled:
Some said: therein are two opinions, as before the term, because it is his right, so he may delay to whenever he wishes.
And some decisively affirmed compulsion, for the purpose of discharge (barāʾah) — so let him take it, or let him grant discharge.

### As for the Place of Delivery (makān al-taslīm)

The place of contract is specified — either by explicit stipulation (taʿyīn) or by absolute [default] (iṭlāq). So if he finds him elsewhere, and transporting it entails cost (maʾūnah), he cannot be demanded [to accept it there]. But if there is no cost, he may demand it. Likewise for all other debts — except in the case of the usurper (ghāṣib), for regarding demanding him [to accept] while transport cost is incumbent, there are two views, as a severity (taghlīẓ) upon him: because we have prevented him from demanding the equivalent (mithl) due to the cost therein, so the value (qīmah) is necessarily [required], due to the occurrence of obstruction (ḥaylūlah) after the establishment of entitlement (istiḥqāq) and the direction of the demand. This completes the discourse on salam.

chapters.title_en: Section 210 — On Qarḍ (Loan): Its Reality, Pillar, Condition, and Ruling
chapters.arabic_text:
### | القسم الثاني من الكتاب النظر في القرض والنظر في حقيقته وركنه وشرطه وحكمه

أما الحقيقية
فهي مكرمة جوزتها الشريعة لحاجة الفقراء ليس على حقائق المعاوضات ولذلك
لا يجوز شرط الأجل فيه لأن المقرض متبرع والمتبرع بالخيار في تبرعه بالرجوع
والأجل يمنع الرجوع ولو لزم الأجل لكان معاوضة ولو جب التقابض في المجلس
فإنه مقابلة دراهم بمثلها
وقال مالك رحمه الله يثبت الأجل
ولذلك لو رجع عن الإقراض في الحال قبل تصرف المستقرض وطالب به جاز
وقال مالك رحمه الله لا يجوز وطرد ذلك في العواري وكأن القرض
عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه إذن في الإتلاف بشرط الضمان فهو قريب منه إن لم
يكن عينه أما ركنه
فالمقرض والمقرض والصيغة
أما الصيغة فقوله أقرضتك أو أخذه بمثله وهل يشترط القبول وجهان أحدهما لا
لأنه أن في الإتلاف بعوض
والثاني نعم لأنه يملكه المستقرض بالقبض أو التصرف فليس إتلافا محضا
وأما المقرض فليس يشترط فيه الا أهلية التمليك والتبرع فإنه تبرع ولذلك
لا يجوز في مال الطفل الا لضرورة وكذا المكاتب على ما سيأتي في الرهن
أما المقرض فكل ما يجوز السلم فيه ويتسلط قرضه الا الجواري ففيه قولان
منصوصان
القياس الجواز كما في العبيد
ووجه المنع أن المستقرض يتسلط على الوطء ويتسلط على الاسترداد فيبقى الطء
في صورة إباحة
ولا خلاف في أنه لو كانت الجاريه محرما للمستقرض جاز إقراضها وقد نقل عن
الصحابة النهي عن إقراض الجواري فاستحسن الشافعي رضي الله عنه ذلك
وقال الأصحاب بناء القولين على أن المستقرض يملك بالقبض أم بالتصرف
فإن قلنا يملك بالقبض فلا يجوز الإقراض لأنه يؤدي الى استباحة الوطء
وإن قلنا بالتصرف فعم
ومنهم من عكس الترتيب وقال إن قلنا يملك بالتصرف فلا لأنه يقع في يده من
غير ملك ففيه خطر الوطء ولا خطر إذا ملكناه فليطأها فإن قيل وما لا يجوز
السلم فيه ولا يجوز بيع بعضه ببعض هل  يجوز إقراضه
قلنا أطلق الأصحاب منعه
وذكر الشيخ أبو على وجها في جواره وهل هو مبني على أن المقرض يرد المثل
في ذوات القيم فإن قلنا يرد القيمة أو القيمة جاز إقراض كل مال متقدم
أما شرطه
فهو أن لا يجر منفعة لنهي رسول صلى الله عليه وسلم عن قرض جر منفعة
فإن شرط زيادة أو منفعة فسد حتى لا يفيد الملك وصحة التصرف فيه
وللشرط صور
أحدها إن شرط الكفيل والرهن والشهادة في القرض يجوز لأنه أحكام له لا
زيادة عليه
ولو شرط رهنا في دين آخر فهو منفعة وكذا إذا شرط في المكسرة رد الصحيح أو
أن يشتري منه شيئا
الثانية أن يشترط في الصحيح رد المكسور فهذا غير مفسد لأنه وعد بمسامحة
ثم لا يلزم
وكذلك إذا شرط الأجل لا يلزم ولا يفسد الا إذا كان في زمان نهب وغارة فهو
مفسد لأن فيه غرضا
الثالثة أن يقول أقرضتك هذا بشرط أن أقرضك غيره صح ولم يلزم الشرط لأنه
وعد وكذا إذا قال وهبت بشرط أن أهب
بخلاف ما إذا قال بعتك بشرط أن أهبك شيئا فيفسد البيع لأن العوض يكون
مبذولا في مقابلة المبيع والمتوقع هبته فيتطرق إليه خلل وجهل
هذا في الربويات أما في غير الربويات ففي شرط الزيادة وجهان
أحدهما التسوية لعموم النهي
والثاني الجواز لأن الزيادة تلزم بالعقد والمقابلة وقد وجدت ولكن يمتنع
ذلك
في الربويات وهذا فاسد لأن صيغة المعارضة لم تشترط فإن شرط فهو بيع فاسد
وليس بقرض والقرض بمطلقه ليس له حكم البيع ولذلك عند ترك الزيادة في
الربويات لم يشترط التقابض
فإن قيل نقل أنه عليه السلام أستسلف بعيرا ببعيرين
قلنا كان ذلك في عقد السلم
أما حكمه
فهو التمليك ولكن بالقبض أو بالتصرف فيه قولان مفهومان من معاني كلام
الشافعي رضي الله عنه
أقيسهما أنه بالقبض لأنه لا يتقاعد عن الهبة مع أنه للعوض فيه مدخل ولأنه
يملك التصرف بعد القبض فيدل على تقدم الملك
والثاني أنه يملك  بالتصرف فيتبين تقدم الملك عليه لأنه تفويت بالأذن بشرط
الضمان وليس بتمليك وعقد والتفويت يحصل بإزالة العين أو الملك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ر-ض (q-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cut, sever, or clip a portion; a loan (qarḍ) is that which is cut off from one's property and given to another for return of its like.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A beneficent transfer (tamlīk) of fungible wealth with a binding obligation to return an equivalent (mithl), distinct from commutative contracts (muʿāwaḍāt) in its gratuitous essence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "cutting"; metaphorically extended to the loan contract as a severance of property from the owner's dominion for another's benefit — a ḥaqīqah ʿurfiyyah (customary literal usage).
- Root: س-ل-ف (s-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To send forward, advance; salaf (loan/advance) implies precedence of payment over delivery.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Salaf in juristic usage denotes a sale with deferred delivery (salam), where the price is advanced — distinct from qarḍ's gratuitous nature.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "preceding"; technical shift to salam contract, showing terminological transfer (naql) from physical to contractual priority.
- Root: ع-و-ض (ʿ-w-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Compensation, substitute, exchange; ʿiwaḍ is what stands in place of another thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In muʿāwaḍāt, each party's consideration is the object of exchange; in qarḍ, the return of mithl is not a true ʿiwaḍ but a restitution (radd) of what was consumed.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "substitution"; in qarḍ, the returned mithl is majāz for ʿiwaḍ since no exchange intent (qasd al-muʿāwaḍah) exists.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ʿāmil (Ellipsis of the Governing Operator) — In conditional clauses like "if he stipulates a guarantor," the governing verb is implicit, and the stipulation (sharṭ) functions as a nominalized clause (maṣdar muʾawwal), affecting the validity of the contract's ʿaqd al-ījāb.
chapters.translation:
I say — This is the second division of the book: the examination of the loan (qarḍ), comprising an examination of its reality (ḥaqīqah), its pillar (rukn), its condition (sharṭ), and its ruling (ḥukm).

As for its reality: It is a gracious act (mukramah) that the Sacred Law permitted for the need of the poor, not upon the basis of commutative contracts (ḥaqāʾiq al-muʿāwaḍāt). For this reason, stipulating a term (ajal) therein is not permissible, because the lender is a benefactor (mutabarriʿ), and the benefactor retains the option in his benefaction to revoke it; and the term prevents revocation. Were the term binding, it would be a commutative exchange; and were exchange-binding (taqābuḍ) required in the session (majlis), it would be a mutual exchange of dirhams for their like. Mālik — may Allah have mercy on him — said: The term is established. And for this reason, if he revokes the loan before the borrower's disposition and demands its return, it is permissible. Mālik — may Allah have mercy on him — said: It is not permissible. He extended this consistently to loans of usufruct (aʿāriyyah). It is as though the loan, according to al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — is a permission for destruction (idhn fī al-itlāf) conditional upon liability (ḍamān); thus it is proximate to that [i.e., ʿāriyah], if not identical to it.

As for its pillar: It consists of the lender (muqriḍ), the borrower (muqtariḍ), and the formula (ṣīghah).

As for the formula: It is his saying, "I lend you" (aqraḍtuka), or his taking [the property] with the obligation of its like. Is acceptance (qabūl) stipulated? There are two positions (wajhān): One — no, because it is a permission for destruction in exchange for compensation. The second — yes, because the borrower owns it by virtue of taking possession (qabḍ) or disposition (taṣarruf), so it is not pure destruction.

As for the lender: Nothing is stipulated in him except the capacity for granting ownership (ahliyyat al-tamlīk) and benefaction (tabarruʿ), for it is a benefaction. Therefore, it is not permissible regarding the property of a minor (ṭifl) except for necessity; likewise the mukātab (slave under manumission contract), as will come in the chapter on pledge (rahn).

As for the borrower: [He may borrow] everything in which salam is valid, and its loan is permissible — except for slave-girls (jawārī), concerning which there are two transmitted positions (qawlān mansūṣān): The analogical position (qiyās) is permissibility, as with male slaves (ʿabīd). The basis of prohibition is that the borrower gains authority over sexual intercourse (waṭʾ) and authority over restitution, so intercourse remains in the form of permissibility [without true ownership]. There is no disagreement that if the slave-girl were a prohibited relative (maḥram) to the borrower, lending her is permissible. It has been transmitted from the Companions a prohibition against lending slave-girls, and al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — deemed this commendable (istaḥsana). The Companions (aṣḥāb) built the two positions upon whether the borrower owns by taking possession or by disposition: If we say he owns by taking possession, then lending is impermissible, because it leads to the licitization of intercourse; if we say by disposition, then it is permissible. Among them is one who reversed the ordering and said: If we say he owns by disposition, then it is impermissible, because it falls into his hand without ownership, so there is danger of intercourse; and there is no danger if we grant him ownership — so let him have intercourse with her.

If it is said: What is not valid in salam, and the sale of some of it for some of it is not permissible — is its loan permissible? We say: The Companions (aṣḥāb) stated its prohibition absolutely. Shaykh Abū ʿAlī mentioned a position (wajh) on its permissibility. Is this built upon whether the lender returns the like (mithl) in items of value (dhawāt al-qiyam)? For if we say he returns the value (qīmah), then lending every type of wealth is permissible.

As for its condition: It is that it not draw a benefit [to the lender], due to the Prophet's — may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him — prohibition of a loan that draws a benefit (qarḍ jarra manfaʿah). If he stipulates an increase (ziyādah) or a benefit, the contract is corrupted (fasada), such that it does not effect ownership nor the validity of disposition therein.

The stipulation has several forms:

The first: If he stipulates a guarantor (kafīl), a pledge (rahn), or witnesses (shahādah) in the loan, it is permissible, because these are rulings (aḥkām) for it, not an increase upon it. But if he stipulates a pledge for another debt, that is a benefit. Likewise, if he stipulates in [lending] broken coins (maksūrah) the return of sound ones, or that the borrower purchase something from him [— this is a benefit].

The second: That he stipulates in [lending] sound coins the return of broken ones. This is not corrupting, because it is a promise of indulgence (musāmaḥah); then it is not binding. Likewise, if he stipulates a term, it is not binding and does not corrupt — except when it is in a time of plunder and raid (nahb wa-ghārah), for then it is corrupting, because therein lies a purpose (gharaḍ).

The third: That he says, "I lend you this on the condition that you lend me something else" — this is valid, and the condition is not binding, because it is a promise (waʿd). Likewise, if he says, "I gift you on the condition that you gift me" — [valid]. This differs from his saying, "I sell you on the condition that you gift me something," for that corrupts the sale, because the consideration (ʿiwaḍ) would be given in exchange for the sold item, and the anticipated gift would be subject to defect (khalal) and ignorance (jahl).

This [prohibition of stipulating increase] applies to ribawī items (amwāl ribawiyyah). As for non-ribawī items, there are two positions on stipulating an increase: One — equalizing [with ribawī items] due to the generality of the prohibition. The second — permissibility, because the increase is binding by the contract, and mutual exchange (muqābalah) has occurred; but this is precluded in ribawī items. And this [stipulation in ribawī items] is corrupt, because the formula of exchange (ṣīghat al-muʿāwaḍah) was not stipulated; if it were stipulated, it would be a corrupt sale (bayʿ fāsid), not a loan. And the loan in its absolute sense does not have the ruling of sale; therefore, when the increase is omitted in ribawī items, exchange-in-session (taqābuḍ) is not stipulated.

If it is said: It is transmitted that he — upon him be peace — borrowed a camel (baʿīr) for two camels. We say: That was in the contract of salam.

As for its ruling: It is granting of ownership (tamlīk), but [whether it occurs] by taking possession or by disposition — there are two positions, both understood from the meanings of al-Shāfiʿī's — may Allah be pleased with him — statements. The more analogically sound of the two (aqyasuhumā) is that it is by taking possession, because it does not fall short of gift (hibah), even though compensation has an entry therein; and because he owns disposition after possession, which indicates the precedence of ownership. The second: That he owns by disposition, so the precedence of ownership upon it becomes evident, because it is a destruction (tafwīt) by permission, conditional upon liability, and it is not a granting of ownership nor a contract; and destruction is effected by the removal of the substance (ʿayn) or of ownership.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | التفريع

إن قلنا يملك بالقبض فله أن يرده بعينه إذله أن يرد بدله فهو أولى ولو
رجع المقرض في عينه جاز له لأنه أقرب من بدله وله أخذ بدله
وذكر الشيخ أبو محمد وجها أن النظر فيه الى جانب المستقرض وإرادته فإن لم
يرد عينه فله ذلك
وأن قلنا يملك بالتصرف فلا خلاف في أنه يملك بكل تصرف مزيل للملك كالبيع
والإعتاق وما يستباح بالإباحة كالاعاره والاستخدام فلا يملك به
واما الإجارة والرهن والبيع بشرط الخيار ففيه طرق
قال الشيخ أبو محمد كل ما يقطع رجوع الواهب والبائع في عين متاع المفلس
يملك نه هاهنا
وقال آخرون كل تصرف لا ينعقد بدون الملك فيخرج الرهن عنه فإنه يجوز في
المستعار بخلاف الإجارة
وقال آخرون كل تصرف لازم يتعلق بالرقبة فيدخل فيه الرهن ويخرج منه
الإجارة والبيع الجائز
وقال آخرون لا يملك الا بتصرف مزيل للملك أصلا
فإن قيل المستقرض ماذا يؤدي قلنا المثل في المثليات
وفي ذوات القيم وجهان
أشبههما بالحديث رد المثل لما روي انه عليه السلام أستقرض بكرا ورد بازلا
وقال عليه السلام خيركم أحسنكم قضاء ولأنه لو
وجب القيمة لافتقر الى الإعلام
والثاني وهو القياس وجوب القيمة والله أعلم وأحكم
= كتاب الرهن وفيه أربعة أبواب=
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في أركان عقد الرهن ومصححاته وأركانه
أربعة الراهن والمرهون والمرهون به وصيغة العقد - صلى الله عليه وسلم -

### | الركن الأول في المرهون

وفيه ثلاثة شرائط الشرط الأول أن يكون عينا
فلو رهن دينا لم يصح لأنه يلزم بالقبض والقبض لا يصادف غير ما يتناوله
العقد ولا مستحقا بالعقد ولذلك لا يصح هبة الدين فإنه لا يلزم إلا بالقبض
بخلاف بيع الدين فإنه يصح على رأي
وكذلك لو باع درهما بدرهم ثم عين في المجلس صح لأن البيع سبب استحقاق قبل
القبض فيتعين بالقبض بخلاف الهبة والرهن

### | فرع
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-د-د (r-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To return, restore, or send back; the act of restitution of a thing to its owner or original state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, it denotes the restoration of a specific object (ʿayn) as opposed to its equivalent (badal), emphasizing the priority of specific restitution in contractual rescission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of physical return; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to returning a right or obligation, as in "returning the equivalent" (radd al-mithl).
- Root: ق-ب-ض (q-b-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Taking possession, seizing, or grasping with the hand; legal possession that transfers liability or ownership.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act of physical or legal reception that validates contracts like loan (qarḍ), gift (hibah), and pledge (rahn); it is the operative condition for bindingness (luzūm).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for manual seizure; metaphorical for constructive possession (taṣarruf) that establishes legal control without physical touch.
- Root: ت-ص-ر-ف (t-ṣ-r-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To manage, dispose, or act upon something; the exercise of authority over property.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Any legal act (ʿaqd) that alters the status of ownership, whether transferring (naql), terminating (izālah), or restricting (taqyīd) it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for any disposition; metaphorical when restricted to acts that sever ownership (muzīl li'l-milk) versus those that merely permit usufruct (ibāḥah).
- Root: ر-ه-ن (r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pledge or pawn; a thing held as security for a debt, enduring and binding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contract of surety where a corporeal asset (ʿayn) is detained as collateral for a claim, requiring delivery (qabḍ) for validity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the physical detention of collateral; metaphorical for any binding commitment that "holds" a right in place.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-Sharṭ wa'l-Istithnāʾ) — The phrase "If we say..." (in qulnā) introduces a protasis governing the apodosis, with the particle "in" marking a hypothetical condition that determines the legal outcome; the exceptive "illā" (in "no disposition without ownership") restricts the scope of the predicate, requiring precise parsing of what is excluded versus included.
chapters.translation:
### | Subsidiary Rulings

If we hold that he acquires ownership by taking possession (qabḍ), then he may return the specific object (ʿayn) itself, for if he may return its equivalent (badal), then returning the specific object is more appropriate. And if the lender (muqriḍ) seeks the return of the specific object, it is permissible for him, because it is closer than its equivalent, and he may also take its equivalent.

Shaykh Abū Muḥammad mentioned a view that the consideration is given to the borrower's (mustaqriḍ) side and his intention: if he does not return the specific object, he has that right [to return the equivalent instead].

But if we hold that he acquires ownership only by disposition (taṣarruf), then there is no disagreement that he acquires ownership through any disposition that removes ownership (muzīl li'l-milk), such as sale (bayʿ) and manumission (iʿtāq). As for what is rendered permissible through permission (ibāḥah), such as lending (iʿārah) and using the object for service (istikhdām), he does not acquire ownership thereby.

As for lease (ijārah), pledge (rahn), and sale with a condition of option (bayʿ bi-sharṭ al-khiyār), there are multiple paths (ṭuruq) of scholarly opinion.

Shaykh Abū Muḥammad said: Everything that cuts off the return of the donor (wāhib) or seller (bāyiʿ) regarding the specific object of the bankrupt's (muflis) goods, he acquires ownership of it here [in the loan].

Others said: Every disposition that cannot be concluded without ownership [is effective], and thus pledge (rahn) is excluded from this, for it is permissible in the borrowed object (mustaʿār), unlike lease (ijārah).

Others said: Every binding (lāzim) disposition that attaches to the corpus (raqabah) [is effective], so pledge (rahn) enters therein, and lease (ijārah) and non-binding sale (al-bayʿ al-jāʾiz) are excluded.

Others said: He acquires ownership only through a disposition that removes ownership absolutely (aṣlan).

If it is asked: What does the borrower (mustaqriḍ) pay [upon return]? We say: The equivalent (mithl) in fungible goods (mithliyyāt). Regarding non-fungible goods (dhawāt al-qiyam), there are two views.

The more similar to the ḥadīth is the return of the equivalent, for it is narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) borrowed a young camel (bakr) and returned a mature camel (bāzil), and he said (peace be upon him): {«خَيْرُكُمْ أَحْسَنُكُمْ قَضَاءً»} — "The best of you are those who are best in repayment." And also because if value (qīmah) were obligatory, it would require notification (iʿlām) [of the value].

The second view — which is the analogical one (qiyās) — is the obligation of value (qīmah). And God knows best and is most wise.

= The Book of Pledge (Rahn), containing four chapters =

### | Chapter One: On the Pillars (Arkān) of the Pledge Contract and Its Validators

Its pillars are four: the pledgor (rāhin), the pledged object (marhūn), the debt secured thereby (marhūn bihi), and the contractual formula (ṣīghah).

### | The First Pillar: On the Pledged Object (Marhūn)

It contains three conditions. The first condition: that it be a corporeal asset (ʿayn).

Thus, if one pledges a debt (dayn), it is not valid, because it requires possession (qabḍ), and possession cannot encounter anything other than what the contract addresses, nor anything not acquired by the contract. For this reason, the gift (hibah) of a debt is not valid, for it is not binding except through possession — unlike the sale of a debt, which is valid according to one view.

Similarly, if one sells a dirham for a dirham and then specifies (ʿayyana) it in the session (majlis), it is valid, because sale is a cause of entitlement (istiḥqāq) before possession, so it becomes specified through possession — unlike gift (hibah) and pledge (rahn).

### | Subsidiary Branch

chapters.arabic_text:
الإفراز  ليس بشرط بل يصح رهن المشاع خلافا لأبي حنيفة ثم تجري المهايأة
بين الراهن والمالك
نعم لو رهن نصيبه من بيت معين من جملة دار مشتركة ففيه وجهان
ومنشأ المنع أنه ربما يقتسم الشريك فيقع الجميع في حصته فلا يبقى للرهن
مقر
فلو صححنا فوقع ذلك احتمل أن يقال هو تلف واحتمل أن يقال الراهن ضامن
والتفويت منسوب إليه
الشرط الثاني أن يكون المرهون قابلا للبيع عند حلول الحق
فلا يجوز رهن الموقوف وأم الولد وكل ما لا يجوز بيعه
وبيان هذا الشرط برسم ثمان مسائل
المسألة الأولى رهن سواد العراق من عبادان إلى الموصل طولا ومن القادسية
إلى حلوان عرضا فإن اعتقاد الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن عمر رضي الله عنه أخذها
من الغانمين وحبسها على المسلمين والخراج عليهم أجرة فيها
وقال ابن سريج بل باعها من أهل العراق فهو ملك
وأما أشجارها وأبنيتها فيجوز رهنها وفاقا فإنها مستحدثة
المسألة الثانية رهن المبيع في زمان الخيار جائز إن كان الخيار للمشتري
وحده ولزم البيع هكذا ذكره الشافعي رضي الله عنه
وفيه وجه أنه لا ينعقد بل لا بد من تقديم الإلزام
ووجه أخر أنه يلزم البيع ولا ينعقد الرهن وقد ذكرناه في كتاب البيع
المسألة الثالثة قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه رهن الأم دون ولدها جائز إذا
لاتفرق فيه
اختلف الأصحاب منهم من قال معناه أنها تباع عند الحاجة مع الولد
ومنهم من قال لا بل أراد به أنه لا تفرقه في نفس الرهن وإلا فتباع دون
الولد فإن الرهن لم يرد على الولد ولكن يقع ذلك قهريا لا اختياريا فلا
يمتنع التفريق التفريع
إن قلنا تباع مفردا فلا كلام
وإن قلنا تباع مع الولد فيتعلق حق المرتهن بما يخص من الثمن وفي تقديره
وجهان
أحدهما أنه تقوم الأم مفردا فإذا هي تساوي مائة فتقدر مع الولد فإذا هي
تساوي مائة وعشرون فالولد سدس الجملة فيختص المالك بسدس جملة الثمن ولا
يتعلق الرهن به
والثاني أن الولد أيضا يقدر  مفردا كما قدرت الأم مفردة فيقال الولد دون
الأم كم يساوي وفي هذا تقل قيمته لأنه يكون ضائعا فإذا قالوا خمسين مثلا
وقيمة الأم مائة فالولد ثلث
وهذا الخلاف جار في أرض بيضاء رهنت ثم أنبتت غراسا لأن الغراس غير مرهون
وذكر صاحب التقريب أن الأم أيضا تقوم مع الولد فيقال أم لها ولد
كم قيمتها فينقص إذ يكون قلبها إلى ولدها لأنها رهنت مع وجود الولد
نعم لو حدث الولد بعد الرهن كان نظيرا لمسألة الغراس
المسألة الرابعة رهن ما يتسارع إليه الفساد بالدين الحال أو بدين مؤجل
يحل قبل توقع الفساد جائز فيباع عند الإشراف على الفساد في الدين
وإن كان يفسد قبل الحلول وشرط بيعه عند الإشراف وجعل ثمنه رهنا صح أيضا
وإن شرط أن لا يباع بطل وإن أطلق ففيه قولان أحدهما أنه يصح مطلقة مشعر
بالإذن في البيع وتحول الوثيق إلى الثمن
والثاني الفساد لأنه ليس مفهوما بمطلق الرهن
فإن قيل لو طرأ دواما ما يعرضه للفساد
قلنا لم يفسد الرهن ولكن يباع عند الإشراف على الفساد ويجعل بدله رهنا
فإن قيل لو تطابق المتعاقدان على نقل الوثيقة من عين المرهون إلى غيره
فينبغي أن يجوز كما لو شرط ذلك فيما يشرف على الهلاك في ابتداء العقد
قلنا فيه وجهان ووجه المنع أن ما يحتمل في الدوام إذا طرأ بالضرورة لا
يحتمل ابتداء ولذلك لا يجوز رهن الدين وإن تعلق في الدوام بالقيمة في ذمة
المتلف
المسألة الخامسة رهن العبد المرتد صحيح بناء على الصحيح في جواز بيعه
ثم إن قتل في يد المرتهن وكان الرهن مشروطا في بيع فثبوت الفسخ للمرتهن
في البيع يبتنى على أن من اشترى عبدا مرتدا وقتل في يده هل يكون من ضمان
البائع
المسألة السادسة رهن العبد الجاني يبتنى على صحة بيعه فإن منعناه فهو
ممنوع وإلا فوجهان
ووجه المنع أنه يمنع الوثيقة ولذلك يمتنع رهن المرهون وإن قدر الراهن على
بيعه إذا قضى الدين وهاهنا يقدر على بيع  شرط الفداء بعده وقد يتعوق فيفسخ
بيعه فلا تحصل معه الوثيقة ولذلك يقدم أرش الجناية في دوام الرهن على الرهن
فرع لو حفر العبد بئرا فرهن فتردى فيها إنسان فتعلق الضمان برقبته ففي
تبيين فساد الرهن وجهان مستندهما إسناد التعلق إلى أول السبب فيكون
كالمقارن
ولو قتل قتلا موجبا للقصاص وقلنا موجب العمد القود المحض فرهن ثم عفى
على مال ففي إسناد انتقال التعلق وجهان
وهاهنا الاستناد أولى لأن القتل سبب تام دون حفر البئر
المسألة السابعة إذا علق عتق العبد بصفة ثم رهنه فإن قلنا لو وجدت الصفة
في حالة الرهن نفذ إما لقوة العتق أو لأن العبرة بحالة التعليق خرج ذلك على
رهن ما يتسارع إليه الفساد
فإن قلنا لا ينفذ فهو بالرهن مدافع حكم التعليق فالأصح جوازه
كما لو دفعه بالبيع
وفيه وجه آخر أنه يفسد لضعف الرهن بخلاف البيع
أما المدبر فقد قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه ولو دبره ثم رهنه كان الرهن
مفسوخا وهذا مشكل لأن بيع المدبر جائز عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه وليس يندفع
التدبر أيضا بالرهن فإنه إذا مات يقضى ديونه ويعتق المدبر وإن لم يكن في
ماله وفاء فالمدبر لا يعتق وإن لم يرهن فذهب أكثر الأصحاب لذلك إلى صحة
الرهن
ووجه النص أن يقال لعله يموت وله مال فلا يمكن تنجيز العتق قبل أداء دينه
وتأخيره إلى الأداء دفع للعتق فالرهن لا يقوى عليه
ويتأيد بالوجه المذكور في إبطال رهن العبد المعلق عتقه بصفة
المسألة الثامنة إذا رهن الثمار على الأشجار نظر إن كان بعد بدو الصلاح
والدين حال جاز ذلك ثم يقطف في أوانه ويباع بعضه ويجعل مؤنة على القطاف
ويجفف إن أمكن وإلا التحق بما يتسارع إليه الفساد
وإن كان قبل بدو الصلاح فللفساد ثلاث مثارات
أحدها تسارع الفساد بعد التجفيف وقد سبق
والثاني امتناع بيعه إلا بشرط القطع فإن أذن في البيع بشرط القطع جاز وإن
صرح بمنع البيع بشرط القطع فسد وإن أطلق فالظاهر أنه يصح  وبشرط القطع في
بيعه ويباع
وذكر صاحب التقريب قولين في موجب الإطلاق ووجهه أنه لم يرض بنقصان
المالية فعلى هذا يفسد الرهن وله التفات على إطلاق الرهن فما يتسارع إليه
الفساد أنه هل يكون كالمصرح بتجويز بيعه
المثار الثالث للفساد توقع الآفة والجوائح ويظهر ذلك إذا قدر الدين مؤجلا
وفي المنع بهذا السبب قولان أحدهما يمنع كما يمنع البيع
والثاني لا لأن المحذور ثم ضياع الثمن عند الاجتياح وهاهنا لا يفوت أصل
الحق
فرع إذا تلاحقت الثمار بعد الرهن ففي انفساخ الرهن قولان كما في التلاحق
في الثمار المبيعة قبل القبض
والأصح أنه لو كان قبل القبض ينفسخ
وفيه وجه مستخرج من الخلاف في العصير إذا صار خمرا قبل القبض وهو بعيد
لأن ذلك يتوقع مصيره خلا بخلاف التلاحق فإنه لا يزول
ولو رهن زرعا يتزايد وشرط قطعه في الحال جاز
وإن شرط التبقية فحكمه حكم الثمار التي تتلاحق غالبا والرهن باطل فيهما
كما في البيع الشرط الثالث أن لا يمتنع إثبات يد المرتهن عليه وقبضه له
فإن القبض ركن في الرهن وفيه مسألتان
إحداهما رهن المصحف والعبد المسلم من الكافر فهو مرتب على البيع وأولى
بالصحة لأن إثبات اليد أهون من إثبات الملك
وكذا رهن السلاح من الحربي مرتب على بيعه منه ورهنه من الذمي جائز وفاقا
كبيعه
الثانية رهن الجواري صحيح على المذهب الظاهر
وذكر الشيخ أبو علي قولا أن رهن الجارية الحسناء باطل إلا أن تكون محرما
للمرتهن فالوجه القطع بالصحة
ثم إن كان محرما أو عدل على يد عدل أو كان المرتهن يوثق بديانته أو كان
معه جماعة من أهله ترعه الحشمة عنها لم يكره التسليم وإلا فيكره إثبات يده
عليها
وعلى الجملة فهو قريب من رهن المصحف من الكافر
فإن قيل فهل يشترط أن يكون المرهون ملك الراهن
قلنا لا فإن الشافعي رضي الله عنه نص على أنه لو رهن المستعار بإذن
المعير صح الرهن
وغمض حقيقة هذا العقد على الأصحاب واستخرجوا من تردد الشافعي  رضي الله
عنه في بعض الأحكام قولين في أن هذا عارية أم ضمان
فمن قال إنه عارية أشكل عليه لزومه
ومن قال ضمان أشكل عليه تعلق الضمان برقبة المال
ثم بنوا الأحكام على قولين وهذا البناء غير مرتض عندنا بل نعلل كل حكم
بما يليق به من غير بناء
وحقيقة هذا العقد لا يتمحض بل هو فيما يدور بين المرتهن والراهن رهن محض
وفيما بين المعير والمستعير عارية وفيما بين المعير والمرتهن حكم الضمان
يزدحم عليه مشابه العارية والضمان ويتبين ذلك بالنظر في ثلاثة أحكام
الأول اللزوم في حق المعير
ولا يلزم قبل قبض المرتهن بحال وإذا قبض المرتهن فالصحيح أنه يلزم في حق
المعير لأنه أثبت بعاريته شيئا من حقه أن لا يعير وتلزم فهو كما لو أعار
الأرض لدفن الأموات إذ لزم لأن فيه هتك حرمة الميت كذلك في رجوعه إبطال
وثيقة المرتهن بعين ماله وقد أذن في إثباته
وقال القاضي له الرجوع إذا فرعنا على قولنا إنه عارية وهذا ضعيف لأنه لا
يبقى للرهن معنى
وقد حكى العراقيون عن ابن سريج أنا إذا قلنا إنه عارية فلا يصح هذا العقد
إذ لا يبقى له فائدة وهو فاسد لأنه خلاف نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه
وقال صاحب التقريب إن كان الدين حالا رجع وإن كان مؤجلا فوجهان يقربان
مما إذا أعار أرضا للبناء إلى مدة وفيه كلام
فإن قيل فهل يقدر على إجبار الراهن على فك الرهن وإن لم يقدر على فسخ
الرهن
قلنا إن كان الدين حالا فلا خلاف في أنه يملك إجباره وقبل حلول للأجل
قولان
أحدهما أنه يملك لأنه عارية في حق المستعير
والثاني لا يملك لأن فيه أداء الدين قبل لزومه وهو متعلق بالمرتهن
فإن قيل فهل يباع هذا في حق المرتهن فقط
قلنا إن كان للراهن مالا فلا يباع بحال لأن مطلق الرهن لا يسلط عليه إلا
إذا جدد به إذنا
وإن صار معسرا ففيه خلاف إذ أطلق الأصحاب أن إذا قلنا إنه  عارية فلا يباع
إلا بإذن مجدد وهذا أيضا يضعف القول بصحة الرهن فإنه أخص فوائده فليجعل
الإذن حاصل بالرهن ولازما بحكم الحال وهو الذي يقتضيه فقه المسألة ولا يترك
الفقه بقول القائل إن هذا لا نظير له فإن سببه أن يقال إن مثل هذه الواقعة
غير متصور
وينبني على ما تقدم خلاف لا محالة في أن عتقه هل ينفذ
الحكم الثاني أن العبد لو تلف في يد المرتهن فهو غير ضامن تمحيصا للرهن
في حقه والمستعير هل يضمن
قالوا ينبغي على أنه عارية أو ضمان
فإن قلنا ضمان لا يضمن وهو ضعيف بل هو مستعير محض في حق المعير فينبغي أن
يضمن
ولكن نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه وقال ولو أذن له فرهنه فجنى فأشبه
الأمرين أنه لا يضمن بخلاف المستعير وفرع على أن المستعير يضمن ما فات
بجناية العبد بناء على أحد الرأيين في ان المستعير يضمن ضمان المغصوب
وهاهنا لم يضمنه فعن هذا اضطر الأصحاب إلى ذكر قول في أنه ليس بعارية وإنما
هو ضمان
فرع لو بيع العبد في الدين بإذن مجدد أو بأصل الرهن يرجع المعير على
المستعير بقيمته أو بالثمن فيه خلاف
قال القاضي إذا قلنا (إنه) عارية يرجع بالقيمة وهو بعيد فإن ما زاد على
القيمة مستفاد في مقابلة ملكه فكيف يسلم للمستعير
الحكم الثالث أنه هل يشترط في هذه الإعارة معرفة قدر الدين وجنسه وحلوله
وتأجيله فيه خلاف
يحتمل أن لا يشترط ذلك ويجعل عارية في هذا الحكم ويحتمل أن يشترط لأن
الأغراض تتفاوت به وينتهي إلى اللزوم وبنى الأصحاب ذلك على أنه عارية أو
ضمان
فرع إذا عين المعير شيئا من ذلك
إن قلنا إنه لا يشترط فلا يجوز مخالفته إذا عين إلا في النقصان كما إذا
أذن في الرهن بألف فرهن بخمسمائة فإنه زاد خيرا
ولو قال أعرني لأرهن بألف فأعاره هل يتقيد بما ذكره المستعير تنزيلا
للإسعاف على تفصيل الالتماس فيه وجهان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ر-ز (faraza)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, division, setting apart; "ifrāz" denotes the physical segregation of a portion from a whole.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal contexts, the demarcation of a specific share from joint property; not a constitutive element of the contract itself.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical partition; here used metaphorically as a legal formality, not a substantive pillar.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The phrase "ليس بشرط" (is not a condition) employs negation of a predicate to establish a ruling of permissibility, with the exception clause "خلافًا" marking juristic opposition.
chapters.translation:
I say: Segregation (ifrāz) is not a condition [of valid pledge], rather it is permissible to pledge an undivided share (al-mushāʿ), contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah. Then division by mutual allotment (al-muhāyāʾah) is executed between the pledgor and the co-owner.

Yes — if he pledges his share of a specific house within a jointly-owned dwelling, there are two positions [on its validity].

The source of prohibition [in one view] is that the partner might partition [the property], and the entirety falls within the pledgor's allotment, leaving no locus for the pledge.

If we uphold validity and this occurs, it may be said: this is destruction (talaf) [of the pledged item], and it may be said: the pledgor is liable (ḍāmin), for the vitiation is attributed to him.

The second condition: the pledged item must be saleable at the maturity of the debt.

Thus, it is impermissible to pledge an endowment (al-mawqūf), an umm walad, and everything whose sale is impermissible.

The exposition of this condition is by way of eight sub-questions.

The first sub-question: Pledging the Sawād of Iraq — from ʿAbbādān to al-Mawṣil in length, and from al-Qādisiyyah to Ḥulwān in breadth. For the belief of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, is that ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, took it from the warriors (al-ghānimīn) and sequestered it (ḥabasahā) for the Muslims, with the land-tax (al-kharāj) upon them as its rent.

Ibn Surayj said: Rather, he sold it to the people of Iraq, so it is their property.

As for its trees and buildings, pledging them is permissible by agreement, for they are newly originated (mustaḥdathah).

The second sub-question: Pledging the sold item during the period of option (khiyār) is permissible if the option belongs to the buyer alone, and the sale becomes binding. Thus stated al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him.

There is a position that it does not contract, rather the binding [of the sale] must precede.

Another position: the sale becomes binding but the pledge does not contract — and we have mentioned this in the Book of Sales.

The third sub-question: Al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, said: Pledging the mother without her child is permissible when there is no separation [involved] therein.

The companions differed: among them are those who said its meaning is that she is sold at need together with the child; and among them are those who said: No — rather he meant that there is no separation in the pledge itself; otherwise she is sold without the child, for the pledge did not extend to the child. But this occurs coercively (qahran), not voluntarily, so separation is not thereby prohibited.

Derivation (tafrīʿ): If we say she is sold alone, there is no discussion.

If we say she is sold with the child, then the pledgee's right attaches to what corresponds to her from the price. In estimating this, there are two positions:

One: the mother is valued alone — if she equals one hundred, then she is valued with the child — if she equals one hundred twenty, then the child is one-sixth of the total. Thus the owner is entitled to one-sixth of the total price, and the pledge does not attach to it.

The second: the child is also valued alone, just as the mother was valued alone. It is said: the child without the mother — how much is it worth? Here its value diminishes because it would be neglected. If they say fifty, for example, and the mother's value is one hundred, then the child is one-third.

This disagreement applies to a bare plot of land (arḍ bayḍāʾ) pledged, then producing plantings (ghirās), because the plantings are not pledged.

The author of al-Taqrīb mentioned that the mother is also valued with the child — it is said: a mother having a child — how much is her value? It diminishes because her heart inclines to her child, since she was pledged while the child existed.

Yes — if the child is born after the pledge, it is analogous to the case of the plantings.

The fourth sub-question: Pledging what rapidly corrupts (mā yatasāraʿu ilayhi al-fasād) for an immediate debt, or for a deferred debt that matures before corruption is anticipated, is permissible. It is then sold when corruption impends, [proceeds going] toward the debt.

If it corrupts before maturity, and it is stipulated that it be sold when corruption impends and its price be made a pledge, this is also valid.

If it is stipulated that it not be sold, the pledge is void.

If left unrestricted (muṭlaq), there are two positions: one, that it is valid in its unrestricted form, implying authorization to sell and the transfer of the security (al-wathīqah) to the price.

The second: it is void, because [sale] is not implied by the mere pledge.

If it is said: What if a perpetual [cause of] corruption supervenes upon it?

We say: the pledge is not voided, rather it is sold when corruption impends and its substitute is made a pledge.

If it is said: What if the two contracting parties agree to transfer the security from the pledged corpus to something else — should this not be permissible, just as if it were stipulated at the inception of the contract regarding something on the verge of destruction?

We say: there are two positions. The position of prohibition [argues]: what is tolerated in perpetuity when it supervenes by necessity is not tolerated at inception. For this reason, pledging a debt (al-dayn) is impermissible, even though in perpetuity [the right] attaches to value in the obligor's liability (al-dhimmah).

The fifth sub-question: Pledging an apostate slave (al-ʿabd al-murtadd) is valid, based on the sounder view that his sale is permissible.

Then, if he is killed in the pledgee's possession, and the pledge was stipulated in a sale, then the establishment of rescission (al-faskh) for the pledgee in the sale is built upon [the question]: if one purchases an apostate slave and he is killed in his possession, is this from the seller's liability (ḍamān al-bāʿiʿ) or not?

The sixth sub-question: Pledging a slave who has committed an offense (al-ʿabd al-jānī) is built upon the validity of his sale. If we prohibit his sale, then [the pledge] is prohibited; otherwise, there are two positions.

The position of prohibition [argues]: it impedes the security. For this reason, pledging an already-pledged item (al-marhūn) is prohibited, even if the pledgor could sell it upon paying the debt. Here, he can sell [the offending slave] with the condition of subsequent redemption (sharṭ al-fidāʾ), but this may be impeded, and his sale may be rescinded — thus the security is not achieved. For this reason, the compensation for the offense (arsh al-jināyah) takes precedence over the pledge during the continuance of the pledge.

Branch: If a slave digs a well, then is pledged, and a person falls into it, whereby liability attaches to his neck (raqabah) — regarding the clarification of the pledge's invalidity, there are two positions, whose basis is whether the attachment is attributed to the first cause, making it like a concurrent [attachment].

If he commits a killing warranting retaliation (qiṣāṣ), and we hold that the requisite for intentional [homicide] is pure retaliation, then he is pledged, then [the victim's heir] pardons for a monetary compensation — regarding the attribution of the transfer of attachment, there are two positions.

Here, attribution to the [original] cause is more appropriate, because killing is a complete cause, unlike digging the well.

The seventh sub-question: If a slave's emancipation is suspended upon a condition (ṣifah), then he is pledged — if we say that upon the condition's occurrence during the pledge, [the emancipation] takes effect — either due to the strength of emancipation, or because the consideration is the state of suspension — then this is subsumed under pledging what rapidly corrupts.

If we say it does not take effect, then [the pledge] repels the effect of the suspension — so the sounder view is its permissibility, just as if he were sold.

There is another position: it is void, due to the weakness of the pledge, unlike sale.

As for the mudabbar (slave whose emancipation is suspended upon the master's death): al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, said: If he makes him mudabbar, then pledges him, the pledge is rescinded (mafsūkh). This is problematic, because selling the mudabbar is permissible according to al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, and the tadbīr is not repelled by the pledge either — for if he dies, his debts are paid and the mudabbar is emancipated; if his estate has no sufficient funds, the mudabbar is not emancipated, even without the pledge. Therefore, most companions inclined to the validity of the pledge.

The basis of the [literal] text [of al-Shāfiʿī] is to say: Perhaps he dies with wealth, and emancipation cannot be executed before the payment of his debt; deferring it until payment constitutes a repulsion of emancipation — and the pledge is not strong enough to overcome this.

This is reinforced by the position mentioned regarding the invalidation of pledging a slave whose emancipation is suspended upon a condition.

The eighth sub-question: If fruits are pledged upon the trees — consider: if [the pledge occurs] after the appearance of ripeness (budūw al-ṣalāḥ) and the debt is immediate, this is permissible. Then [the fruits] are picked at their proper time, some are sold, and the cost of picking is made an expense; they are dried if possible — otherwise, they are subsumed under what rapidly corrupts.

If [the pledge occurs] before the appearance of ripeness, there are three grounds for invalidity:

One: rapid corruption after drying — this has preceded.

The second: the impermissibility of selling them except with the condition of cutting. If he authorizes sale with the condition of cutting, it is permissible. If he explicitly prohibits sale with the condition of cutting, it is void. If left unrestricted, the apparent [view] is that it is valid, with the condition of cutting in its sale, and it is sold.

The author of al-Taqrīb mentioned two positions regarding the import of the unrestricted form. Its basis: he did not consent to the diminution of monetary value. On this [second] view, the pledge is void. And there is an examination of the unrestricted pledge of what rapidly corrupts: whether it is like explicit authorization of its sale.

The third ground for invalidity: the anticipation of blight (āfah) and calamities (jawāʾiḥ). This appears when the debt is deferred. Regarding prohibition on this ground, there are two positions: one, it is prohibited, just as sale is prohibited; the second, it is not, because the harm there is the loss of the price upon devastation, whereas here the principal right is not lost.

Branch: If the fruits become overripe (talāḥaqat) after the pledge, regarding the dissolution of the pledge there are two positions, as with overripeness in fruits sold before delivery.

The sounder [view]: if [overripeness occurs] before delivery, the [sale] is dissolved.

There is a position extracted from the disagreement regarding grape juice (al-ʿaṣīr) when it becomes wine before delivery — but this is remote, because that [transformation] anticipates becoming vinegar, unlike overripeness, which does not revert.

If he pledges a growing crop (zarʿ) and stipulates its cutting immediately, it is permissible.

If he stipulates its retention, its ruling is the ruling of fruits that typically overripen — and the pledge is void in both cases, as in sale.

The third condition: that the pledgee's possession (yad) of the pledged item and his taking delivery (qabḍ) thereof not be prohibited. For delivery is a pillar (rukn) in the pledge. There are two sub-questions herein:

One: Pledging the muṣḥaf (Quranic codex) and a Muslim slave to a disbeliever — this is dependent upon [the ruling of] sale, and more deserving of validity, because establishing possession is lighter than establishing ownership.

Likewise, pledging weapons to a harbī (warring disbeliever) is dependent upon selling to him; pledging to a dhimmī is permissible by agreement, like selling to him.

The second: Pledging slave-girls (jawārī) is valid on the apparent [school] doctrine.

Abū ʿAlī mentioned a position that pledging a beautiful slave-girl is void, unless she is an unmarriageable kin (maḥram) to the pledgee — then the definitive [view] is validity.

Then: if he is a maḥram, or she is [held] with a trustworthy person, or the pledgee is relied upon for his religiosity, or there is with him a group of his family whose presence restrains him by modesty (ḥishmah) — then delivery is not disliked. Otherwise, establishing his possession over her is disliked.

In sum, it is close to pledging the muṣḥaf to a disbeliever.

If it is said: Is it required that the pledged item be the pledgor's property?

We say: No. For al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, explicitly ruled that if one pledges a borrowed item (al-mustaʿār) with the lender's (al-muʿīr) permission, the pledge is valid.

The true nature of this contract was obscure to the companions, and they extracted — from al-Shāfiʿī's, may God be pleased with him, hesitation in some rulings — two positions: whether this is a loan for use (ʿāriyah) or a guarantee (ḍamān).

Whoever said it is ʿāriyah found its bindingness (luzūm) problematic. Whoever said it is ḍamān found the attachment of liability to the corpus of the property problematic.

Then they built the rulings upon the two positions. But this building is not approved by us; rather, we explain each ruling by what befits it, without such building.

The true nature of this contract is not purely one thing. Rather, it is a pure pledge (rahn maḥḍ) between the pledgee and the pledgor; between the lender and the borrower it is ʿāriyah; and between the lender and the pledgee it has the ruling of liability (ḥukm al-ḍamān). The semblances of ʿāriyah and ḍamān converge upon it. This becomes clear by examining three rulings:

The first: bindingness (luzūm) with respect to the lender.

It is not binding before the pledgee's delivery in any case. When the pledgee takes delivery, the sound [view] is that it becomes binding with respect to the lender — because by his lending he established something of his right not to lend, and it becomes binding. It is like lending land for the burial of the dead, which is binding because it involves violating the sanctity of the deceased. Likewise, his revocation would nullify the pledgee's security through the lender's own property, having authorized its establishment.

Al-Qāḍī said: He may revoke if we proceed on our position that it is ʿāriyah. But this is weak, because no meaning would remain for the pledge.

The Iraqis have related from Ibn Surayj: if we say it is ʿāriyah, then this contract is not valid, since no benefit remains in it. But this is corrupt, because it contradicts the explicit text of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him.

The author of al-Taqrīb said: If the debt is immediate, he may revoke; if deferred, there are two positions — close to the case of lending land for building for a specified period. There is discussion therein.

If it is said: Can he compel the pledgor to release the pledge (fakk al-rahn), even if he cannot rescind the pledge?

We say: If the debt is immediate, there is no disagreement that he may compel him. Before maturity, there are two positions:

One: he may compel, because it is ʿāriyah with respect to the borrower.

The second: he may not, because it involves paying the debt before its obligation, and [the right] is attached to the pledgee.

If it is said: Is this [pledged item] sold with respect to the pledgee only?

We say: If the pledgor has wealth, it is not sold in any case, because the absolute pledge does not authorize sale over it unless new authorization is given.

If he becomes insolvent, there is disagreement therein. For the companions stated absolutely that if we say it is ʿāriyah, it is not sold except with renewed authorization. This also weakens the position of the pledge's validity — for its most specific benefit would be lost. Let the authorization be deemed obtained through the pledge itself, and binding by virtue of the circumstance. This is what the fiqh of the matter requires; and fiqh is not abandoned for the saying of one who claims "this has no parallel" — for its cause is to say that such an occurrence is inconceivable.

Upon what preceded, there is necessarily a disagreement as to whether his emancipation takes effect.

The second ruling: If the slave perishes in the pledgee's possession, he is not liable — in purification (tamḥīṣ) of the pledge with respect to him. But is the borrower (al-mustaʿīr) liable?

They said: it is built upon whether it is ʿāriyah or ḍamān.

If we say it is ḍamān, he is not liable — but this is weak. Rather, he is a pure borrower (mustaʿīr maḥḍ) with respect to the lender, so he should be liable.

But al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, explicitly ruled — and he said: "If he authorized him to pledge it, and then it committed an offense (jannā), it resembles both matters — that he is not liable," unlike the borrower. And he branched upon [the view] that the borrower is liable for what is lost through the slave's offense, based on one of the two views that the borrower is liable with the liability of a usurper (ḍamān al-maghṣūb). Here, he did not hold him liable. From this, the companions were compelled to mention a position that it is not ʿāriyah but rather ḍamān.

Branch: If the slave is sold for the debt — by renewed authorization or by the original pledge — the lender has recourse against the borrower for its value or for the price. There is disagreement therein.

Al-Qāḍī said: If we say it is ʿāriyah, he has recourse for the value. But this is remote — for what exceeds the value is acquired in exchange for his ownership, so how could it be surrendered to the borrower?

The third ruling: Is knowledge of the amount of the debt, its type, its immediacy, and its deferment required in this lending? There is disagreement therein.

It is possible that this is not required, and it is treated as ʿāriyah in this ruling. And it is possible that it is required, because purposes vary with it, and it culminates in bindingness. The companions built this upon whether it is ʿāriyah or ḍamān.

Branch: If the lender specifies something of that [i.e., the debt's parameters]:

If we say it is not required, then when he specifies, it is impermissible to contravene him — except toward diminution, as when he authorizes pledging for one thousand and he pledges for five hundred, for he has added good.

If he says: "Lend me [the item] so that I may pledge it for one thousand," and he lends him — is he restricted to what the borrower mentioned, by way of applying the accommodation (al-isʿāf) to the detail of the request? There are two positions.

chapters.title_en: The Second Pillar: That Which Is Pledged for the Debt (Al-Rahn bihi)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الركن الثاني المرهون به

وله ثلاث شرائط (وهو)  أن يكون دينا ثابتا لازما
الأول أن يكون دينا فلا يجوز الرهن بعين معصوبة ولا مستعارة
وإن جوزنا كفالة الأعيان على الرأي فالرهن وثيقة دين في عين والضمان
توثيق دين بضم ذمة إلى ذمة فلا يفارق الرهن الضمان إلا في ضمان العهدة فإنه
جائز
والصحيح أن الرهن به غير جائز لأنه جوز للمصلحة ترغيبا في معاملة من لا
يعرف حاله ولا ضرر على الضامن وفي الرهن ضرر لا ينظر له آخر
وفيه وجه أنه يجوز كالضمان لأنه إذا رضي به فقد أضر بنفسه
الشرط الثاني أن يكون الدين ثابتا فلو قال رهنت منك هذا بألف تقرضنيه
فقال ارتهنت ثم أقرض لم ينعقد الرهن بل يجب إعادته
وكذلك إذا قال بألف تبيع به هذا الثوب مثلا فثبوت الدين حالة الرهن لا بد
منه
وقيل إنه لو جرى الإقراض والبيع في مجلس الرهن صح وهو فاسد
فرع لو مزجا شقي البيع بشقي الرهن كما إذا قال بعت منك العبد بألف
وارتهنت منك هذا الثوب به فقال اشتريت ورهنت
قال الأصحاب هذا صحيح بخلاف ما إذا قال لعبده كاتبتك على ألف
وبعت منك هذا الثوب بدينار فقال قبلت الكتابة واشتريت فإنه فيه وجهين
لتقدم شق البيع على تمام الكتابة
والفرق أن الرهن من مصالح البيع ولذلك جاز شرطه فيه مع امتناع شرط عقد في
عقد فمزجه به أكد فيحتمل للمصلحة
وذكر القاضي وجها مخرجا في الرهن من الكتابة والفرق واضح
هذا إذا وقع الختم بأحد شقي الرهن والبداية بأحد شقي البيع فإن وقع الختم
بأحد شقي البيع فلا يصح لتقدم تمام الرهن على صحة البيع وثبوت الدين
الشرط الثالث لزوم الدين والديون منقسمة فما لا مصير له إلى اللزوم فلا
رهن به كنجوم الكتابة فإن للعبد أن يعجز نفسه مهما شاء
وما وضعه على اللزوم والجواز فيه طارئ يجوز الرهن به كالثمن في مدة
الخيار وهو تفريع على قول زوال الملك واستحقاق الثمن
وما وضع على الجواز ولكن قد يصير إلى اللزوم كالرهن  بالجعل في الجعالة
قبل العمل فيه وجهان
ولعل سبب المنع التخريج على الشرط الثاني وهو أن سبب ثبوت الدين هو العمل
المأذون فيه دون مجرد الإذن فكأن سبب الثبوت لم يجز بخلاف البيع في زمان
الخيار فإنه سبب تام على الجملة في الاستحقاق
فإن قيل وهل يشترط للدين أن لا يكون به رهن
قلنا لا بل يجوز أن يزاد في المرهون وإن اتحد الدين لأن الدين غير مشغول
بالرهن فزيادة الوثيقة فيه معقولة وهل تجوز الزيادة في الدين مع اتحاد
المرهون فيه قولان
أحدهما وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله المنع لأن رهن المرهون باطل وإليه
يرجع حاصلة
والثاني وهو اختيار المزني الصحة لأن الحق لا يعدوهما ولا مقابلة بين
المرهون والدين إلا من جهة الوثيقة وإنما لا يجوز رهنه من غير المرتهن لحقه
وإن رضي فمن ضرورة أن يجعل فسخا لأن الجمع بين حقيهما غير ممكن
فرع لو جنى العبد المرهون جناية فقال المرتهن أنا أفديه ليكون مرهونا
عندي بالفداء وأصل الدين
فإن جوزنا الزيادة في الدين فلا كلام
وإن منعنا فقولان مفهومان من معاني كلام الشافعي رضي الله عنه في أن
المشرف على الزوال كالزائل أم لا
فإن قلنا كالزائل فهو جائز فكأنه ابتداء رهن بالدينين جميعا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ر-ه-ن (R-H-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Retention, constancy, and binding; a pledge (rahn) is what is held as security against a debt.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contractual detention of a tangible asset as a guarantor of a financial obligation, entailing both trust and liability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in the sense of perpetual holding; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to abstract securities like a guarantor's liability.
- Root: ض-م-ن (Ḍ-M-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Inclusion and undertaking; ḍamān is the joining of one liability to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A surety obligation that attaches a second obligation to the primary one without detaining property.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the act of inclusion; metaphorical for the transfer of responsibility.
- Root: ث-ب-ت (Th-B-T)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Firmness, establishment, and permanence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The settled and verified status of a debt as an actual, non-contingent obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical stability; metaphorical for legal certainty.
- Root: ل-ز-م (L-Z-M)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Adherence and necessity; what is inseparable.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The binding character of an obligation that cannot be unilaterally dissolved.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical clinging; metaphorical for legal irrevocability.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — Governing the logical parsing of stipulations (shurūṭ) and their exceptions, ensuring precise legal distinctions between necessary and contingent conditions.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second pillar is that which is pledged for the debt (al-marhūn bihi), and it has three conditions.

The first condition is that it must be a debt (dayn). Thus, it is not permissible to pledge for a specific corporeal object (ʿayn) that is wrongfully seized (maʿṣūbah) nor for a borrowed object (mustaʿārah). Even if we permit the suretyship of corporeal objects (kafālat al-aʿyān) according to one opinion, the pledge (rahn) is a security for a debt against a corporeal object, whereas the guarantee (ḍamān) is a securing of a debt by joining one liability (dhimmah) to another. Thus, the pledge does not differ from the guarantee except in the case of the guarantee of title (ḍamān al-ʿuhdah), for that is permissible.

The sound position is that pledging for it is not permissible, because the guarantee was permitted for the sake of public benefit (maṣlaḥah), as an encouragement to transact with one whose condition is unknown, and there is no harm upon the guarantor. But in the pledge there is harm with no one looking after its ultimate consequence. There is another face (wajh) that it is permissible like the guarantee, because when he consents to it, he has harmed himself.

The second condition is that the debt must be established (thābit). Thus, if one says: "I pledge this to you for a thousand [dirhams] which you will lend me," and he replies: "I accept the pledge," then he lends [the money], the pledge does not contract; rather, it must be renewed. Likewise, if he says: "for a thousand [dirhams] for which you will sell this garment, for example," the establishment of the debt at the time of the pledge is indispensable.

It has been said that if the lending and the sale occur within the session of the pledge, it is valid — but this is corrupt (fāsid).

A branch (farʿ): If they combine the two halves of a sale with the two halves of a pledge — as when he says: "I have sold you the slave for a thousand, and I have pledged this garment to you for it," and he replies: "I have purchased and accepted the pledge" — the companions (al-aṣḥāb) say this is valid, unlike the case where he says to his slave: "I have made a kitābāh (manumission contract) with you for a thousand, and I have sold you this garment for a dinar," and he replies: "I accept the kitābāh and I have purchased." For that, there are two faces (wajhān), due to the precedence of the half of the sale over the completion of the kitābāh.

The difference is that the pledge is among the benefits (maṣāliḥ) of the sale; therefore, it is permissible to stipulate it within the sale, even though stipulating one contract within another is prohibited. Thus, mixing it [with the sale] is more emphatic, and it is therefore probable [to permit it] for the sake of benefit. Al-Qāḍī mentioned a derived face (wajh mukharraj) regarding the pledge from the kitābāh, but the difference is clear.

This [ruling] applies when the conclusion (al-khatm) occurs with one half of the pledge and the beginning (al-bidāyah) with one half of the sale. But if the conclusion occurs with one half of the sale, it is not valid, due to the precedence of the completion of the pledge over the validity of the sale and the establishment of the debt.

The third condition is the irrevocability (luzūm) of the debt. Debts are divided [into categories]: whatever has no course toward irrevocability cannot be pledged for, such as the installments of the kitābāh (nujūm al-kitābah), for the slave may incapacitate himself whenever he wishes. Whatever is founded upon irrevocability, with permissibility being merely incidental to it, may be pledged for, such as the price (thaman) during the period of the option (khiyār) — this being a derivation upon the opinion that ownership is voided and the price is earned. Whatever is founded upon permissibility but may become irrevocable — such as pledging for the reward (juʿl) in a reward-contract (jiʿālah) before the work — there are two faces (wajhān) regarding it.

Perhaps the cause of prohibition is the derivation upon the second condition, namely that the cause of the establishment of the debt is the authorized work itself, not the mere authorization. Thus, it is as if the cause of establishment has not yet occurred, unlike the sale during the period of the option, for it is a complete cause, in sum, for entitlement.

If it is said: "Is it required that the debt not already have a pledge against it?" We say: No. Rather, it is permissible to increase [the value of] what is pledged (al-marhūn) even if the debt is one, because the debt is not occupied by the pledge; thus, increasing the security upon it is intelligible. As for increasing the debt while the pledged object remains one, there are two opinions (qawlān):

One of them — and it is the school of Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him — is prohibition, because pledging an already-pledged object is void, and to this his conclusion returns.

The second — and it is the choice of al-Muzanī — is validity, because the right does not exceed the two of them [i.e., the debtor and the creditor], and there is no correspondence between the pledged object and the debt except by way of security. It is only impermissible to pledge it to someone other than the original pledgee due to his right; and if he consents, then it is necessary to render it a rescission (faskh), because combining both of their rights is impossible.

A branch (farʿ): If the pledged slave commits an offense (jināyah), and the pledgee says: "I will ransom him (afdīhi) so that he remains pledged to me for the ransom and the original debt" — if we permit the increase in the debt, then there is no discussion. But if we prohibit it, then there are two opinions (qawlān) understood from the meanings of the words of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, regarding whether that which is on the verge of perishing is like that which has perished, or not.

If we say it is like that which has perished, then it is permissible, as if he initiated a pledge for both debts together.

chapters.title_en: The Third Pillar: The Formula (Ṣīghah), Its Conditions, and Its Requisite Effect
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الركن الثالث الصيغة وشرطها وموجبها

ونريد بالصيغة الإيجاب والقبول ولا بد منهما
وفيه مسائل خمسة
الأولى كل شرط يوافق وضع الرهن كقوله بشرط أن يباع في حقك أو يقبض أو
(غرض) لا يتعلق بالعقد كقوله بشرط أن لا يأكل إلا الشعير ولا يلبس إلا
الحرير فهو لغو لا يضر اقترانه بالصيغة
وكل شرط يناقض مقتضاه كقوله بشرط أن لا أقبض ولا يتقدم به على الغرماء
فهو مفسد للرهن
وكل شرط لا يناقض ولكن لا يقتضيه لمطلق العقد ويرتبط به غرض كقوله بشرط
أن تكون المنافع أو النتاج أو الثمار الحاصلة من المرهون لك ففي فساد الرهن
قولان
ووجه التصحيح أن الشرط ليس يتعرض لمقاصد المرهون بالتغير بل يزيد مالا
يقتضيه فيلغى
ولا خلاف في أنه لو باع بشرط أن يرهن بالثمن ما يسلم للبائع منافعه
فالبيع فاسد لأن الطمع يتعلق بالزوائد ويصير كالجزء من العوض فيرجع الفساد
إلى
ركن العقد وأما الرهن فليس بمعاوضة
الثانية إذا قال رهنت الأشجار بشرط أن تكون الثمار رهنا إذا حدد ففي صحة
الشرط قولان
ووجه الصحة أن الرهن عندنا لا يسري لضعفه فإذا قوي بالشرط سرى
الثالثة إذا قال أقرضتك هذا الألف بشرط أن ترهن به وبالألف القديم الذي
لي عليك شيئا فالقرض فاسد لأنه جر منفعة ولكن إذا أخذ ووفى بالشرط ورهن
بالألفين لم يصح بالألف الذي فسد قرضه لأنه ما ملكه بعد ولم يتلف إلا إذا
أتلفه فيكون ذلك دينا
وإذا لم يصح به فهل يصح بالألف القديم فيه قولا تفريق الصفقة
فإن صححنا فلا يوزع بل يجعل الكل مرهونا به بخلاف البيع فإن وضع الرهن
على أن كال جزء مرهون بجميع الدين
هذا إذا علم أن الرهن غير واجب عليه لفساد الشرط فإن ظن وجوبه لأجل الشرط
قال القاضي لا يصح كما لو أدى ألفا على ظن أنه عليه فلم يكن فإنه يسترد لأن
الرهن تبرع وهو يظن الآن وجوبه
وقطع الشيخ أبو محمد وغيره بالصحة لأن الأداء لا يتصور إلا بوجوب سابق
ولا وجوب والرهن يتصور من غير وجوب
ومساق كلام القاضي يلزمه أن يقول لو شرط بيعا في بيع فباع وفى بالشرط على
ظن الوجوب يفسد بيعه
والشيخ أبو محمد يصحح البيع ولا ينظر إلى اعتقاده
الرابعة إذا قال رهنتك هذه الخريطة بما فيها وما فيها غير مرئي خرج على
بيع الغائب فإن أبطل خرج في الخريطة على تفريق الصفقة فإن كانت الخريطة لا
يقصد رهنه في مثل هذا الدين فوجهان
أحدهما الصحة لظاهر اللفظ
والثاني المنع لفهم المقصود
ولو قال رهنت الخريطة ولم يتعرض لما فيها وكانت الخريطة لا تقصد فهل تجعل
عبارة عما في الخريطة مجازا بقرينة الحال يخرج على هذين الوجهين
الخامسة هل يندرج الأس والمغرس تحت  اسم الشجرة والجدار في الرهن
فيه خلاف مرتب على البيع وأولى بأن لا يندرج لضعف الرهن
وفي الثمار غير المؤبرة وجهان بخلاف ضعف الرهن
وكذا في الجنين خلاف وأولى بأن يدرج من الثمار لأن الثمار قد تفرد
بالاستثناء والتصرفات
واللبن في الضرع منهم من ألحقه بالجنين ومنهم من قطع بأنه لا يندرج لتحقق
وجوده فهو كالثمار المؤبرة
والأوراق من التوت كالثمار المؤبرة ومن غيره يندرج
وفي الصوف على ظهر الحيوان ثلاثة أوجه من حيث إنه يضاهي الثمار المؤبرة
من وجه والأغصان من وجه وفي الثالث يفرق بين ما استجز وبين القصير الذي لا
يعتاد جزه
وأغصان الخلاف كالصوف المستجز وأغصان سائر الأشجار يندرج
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ص-ي-غ (ṣ-y-gh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes the casting, forging, or fashioning of a form; hence the verbal formula of a contract as its constitutive mold.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In contractual theology, the ṣīghah is the articulated expression that actualizes the legal intent (ījāb wa qabūl), paralleling the divine creative command in its efficacy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the uttered words of offer and acceptance; metaphorically (majāz) for any legally constitutive act.
- Root: ش-ر-ط (sh-r-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A mark, sign, or condition; that which is stipulated as a binding prerequisite.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A stipulation that qualifies the contractual obligation, either harmonizing with its essence or corrupting it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the contractual condition; metaphorical for the inherent requisite of an act.
- Root: ر-ه-ن (r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hold something in pledge or pawn; permanence and retention.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A collateral security that remains with the creditor until the debt is discharged; its weakness (ḍuʿf) is a recurring technical motif.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the pledged object; metaphorical for the binding of a right to an asset.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-Sharṭ (Conditional Suspension) — The syntactic structure of stipulations determines whether they are operative (muʾaththir), void (lāghw), or corrupting (mufsid), based on their concord or discord with the governing verb's semantic requirement.
chapters.translation:
I say: By the formula (ṣīghah) I mean the offer (ījāb) and the acceptance (qabūl), and both are indispensable. There are five questions pertaining to this.

**The First Question:** Every condition that accords with the nature of the pledge (waḍʿ al-rahn) — such as his saying, "On the condition that it be sold on your behalf," or "that it be taken into possession" — or a condition that involves no purpose connected to the contract — such as his saying, "On the condition that he eats nothing but barley," or "wears nothing but silk" — such a condition is void (laghw) and its conjunction with the formula does no harm.

Every condition that contradicts the very requisite of the contract (muqtaḍāh) — such as his saying, "On the condition that I do not take possession," or "that I do not take precedence over the creditors" — such a condition corrupts the pledge (mufsid lil-rahn).

Every condition that neither contradicts the requisite nor is entailed by the absolute contract, yet a purpose is attached to it — such as his saying, "On the condition that the usufructs, the offspring, or the fruits accruing from the pledged property be yours" — there are two opinions (qawlān) concerning the corruption of the pledge.

The basis of validating (taṣḥīḥ) is that the condition does not alter the purposes of the pledged property itself, but rather adds something not entailed by the contract; hence it is annulled (yulghā).

There is no disagreement that if one sells on the condition that the buyer pledge the price with something whose usufructs are surrendered to the seller, the sale is corrupt — because the covetousness attaches to the increments, making them as though part of the countervalue, so the corruption reverts to the very pillar of the contract. As for the pledge, it is not an exchange transaction (muʿāwaḍah).

**The Second Question:** If he says, "I pledge the trees on the condition that the fruits be pledged as well, when they appear," there are two opinions on the validity of the condition.

The basis of validity is that, in our school, the pledge does not extend (lā yasrī) due to its weakness; so when it is strengthened by the condition, it extends.

**The Third Question:** If he says, "I lend you this thousand on the condition that you pledge something to me for it and for the old thousand you owe me," the loan is corrupt because it draws a benefit (jarra manfaʿah). However, if he takes the loan and fulfills the condition, pledging for both thousands, it is not valid with respect to the thousand whose loan was corrupted — because he has not yet owned it, and it is not destroyed unless he destroys it, in which case it becomes a debt.

If it is not valid with respect to that thousand, is it valid with respect to the old thousand? There are two opinions based on the doctrine of severance of the transaction (tafrīq al-ṣafqah).

If we validate it, it is not apportioned; rather, the whole is made pledged for the entire debt — unlike the case of sale, where the pledge is structured such that each part is pledged for the whole debt.

This ruling applies when he knows that the pledge is not obligatory upon him due to the corruption of the condition. But if he supposes it obligatory because of the condition, Judge (al-Qāḍī) said it is not valid — just as one who pays a thousand supposing it to be owed, and it turns out not to be owed, may reclaim it — because the pledge is a voluntary donation (tabarruʿ), and he now supposes it obligatory.

Shaykh Abū Muḥammad and others decisively ruled its validity, because payment cannot be conceived except with a prior obligation, and there is none; whereas the pledge can be conceived without any obligation.

The drift of the Judge's reasoning would compel him to say: if one stipulates a sale within a sale, then sells and fulfills the condition, supposing it obligatory, his sale is corrupted. But Shaykh Abū Muḥammad validates the sale and does not look to his belief.

**The Fourth Question:** If he says, "I pledge to you this pouch with whatever is in it," and what is inside is not visible — this is derived from the sale of the absent object (bayʿ al-ghāʾib). If one invalidates that, then regarding the pouch itself, it is derived from the doctrine of severance of the transaction. If the pouch is not intended for pledge in a debt of this magnitude, there are two aspects (wajhān):

One: validity, due to the apparent wording.
The second: prohibition, due to understanding the intended purpose.

If he says, "I pledge the pouch," without mentioning its contents, and the pouch is not itself intended, then is it made an expression for what is inside the pouch metaphorically (majāzan), by virtue of the contextual indication (qarīnat al-ḥāl)? This is derived from these same two aspects.

**The Fifth Question:** Does the term "tree" (shajarah) and "wall" (jidār) in a pledge include the roots (asl) and the planting site (maghris)?

There is a disagreement on this, arranged upon the doctrine of sale — and it is even more apt not to be included, due to the weakness of the pledge.

Regarding un-pollinated fruits (thimār ghayr muʾabbirah), there are two aspects, contrary to the weakness of the pledge.

Likewise, concerning the fetus (janīn) there is a disagreement — and it is more apt to be included than fruits, because fruits may be singled out for exclusion and independent dispositions.

As for milk in the udder, some have likened it to the fetus; others decisively ruled it is not included, because its existence is verified — so it is like pollinated fruits.

Leaves of the mulberry tree are like pollinated fruits; leaves of other trees are included.

Regarding wool on the back of an animal, there are three aspects (awjuh): since it resembles pollinated fruits in one respect, and branches in another; in the third aspect, a distinction is made between wool that is customarily shorn and the short wool not customarily shorn.

The branches of the disputed tree (aghṣān al-khilāf) are like the customarily shorn wool; the branches of all other trees are included.
