chapters.arabic_text:
### | الركن الرابع العاقد

ويعتبر فيه ما يعتبر في البيع وزيادة أمر وهو أن يكون من أهل التبرع
بالمرهون لأن الرهن تبرع فلا يجوز لولي الطفل وللمكاتب والمأذون في التجارة
على كل حال بل لا بد من تفصيل
أما ولي الطفل فالنظر في رهنه وارتهانه
أما ارتهانه فيجوز عند العجز عن استيفاء الدين ولا يجوز مع القدرة ويجوز
عند تأجيل الدين ويتأجل دينه بالبيع بالنسيئة وله ذلك إذا ظهرت فيه الغبطة
ولكن بشرط الارتهان حتى قال العراقيون لو باع ما يساوي مائة بمائة نقدا
وعشرين نسيئة لم يجز الإ بشرط الارتهان بالعشرين
وهو سرف بل الوجه جوازه دون الرهن إذا كان يثق بذمة من عليه الدين فلا
يزيد ذلك على إيضاعه مال اليتيم للتجارة وهو جائز لأجل الزيادة بخلاف
الإقراض فإنه يحرم فيه الزيادة فلا يجوز إلا في زمان نهب وغارة
أما رهن ماله فلا يجوز إلا بغبطة ظاهرة كما إذا بيع منه ما يساوي ألفين
بألف وأخذ منه رهن يساوي ألفا لأن أقصى ما في الباب أن يتلف المرهون
أمانة فيكون قد حصل على ألفين في مقابلة ألفين
فإن زاد قيمة المرهون وجملة الثمن على المشتري لم يجز لانه حجر ناجز في
ألفين من غير حصول على ألفين
قال الشيخ أبو محمد لو رهن عقارا وكان في  الشراء غبطة جاز إذ لا يخاف فوت
العقار والمنفعة له
وبيع عقار الطفل لا يجوز إلا لحاجة حتى نفك الحجر عنه
ويجوز الرهن أيضا لحاجة فاقة كما إذا افتقر الصبي إلى طعام وله عقار
يتوقع من ريعه ما يفي بثمن الطعام فله أن يشتري ويرهن
وحكم المكاتب حكم ولي الطفل وحكم المأذون مرتب على المكاتب وأولى بالمنع
لأن الرهن قد لا يتناوله اسم التجارة ولذلك لا يقدر على إجارة نفسه
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في القبض والطوارئ قبله وفيه قسمان
- صلى الله عليه وسلم -
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ل-ي (w-l-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity, guardianship, and authority over another’s affairs; the walī is one who assumes charge (wilāyah) over a minor or incapacitated person.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, wilāyah denotes a delegated custodianship entailing discretionary power over another’s property, constrained by the ward’s benefit (maṣlaḥah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is physical adjacency; metaphorical extension (majāz) applies to legal authority, where the guardian “stands near” the ward’s interests.
- Root: ر-ه-ن (r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To bind, detain, or hold something as security; the marhūn is the pledged object held in collateral.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contractual detention (ḥabs) of property as a guarantee for a debt, entailing trust (amānah) in the pledgee’s custody.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical restraint; metaphorical: legal encumbrance of an asset, not its transfer of ownership.
- Root: غ-ب-ط (gh-b-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To desire a state of well-being without envy; ghubṭah here denotes a manifest advantage or beneficial bargain.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic discourse, ghubṭah is the evident benefit justifying a guardian’s transaction on behalf of a minor.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: commendable aspiration; metaphorical: the objective criterion of commercial prudence in fiduciary acts.
- Root: ك-ت-ب (k-t-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To write, inscribe; mukātab is the slave who has contracted manumission for a stipulated payment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The mukātab holds a binding covenant (kitābah) with his master, granting him limited proprietary autonomy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: writing; metaphorical: the written deed of emancipation that partially liberates the slave’s legal capacity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa’l-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (e.g., “if he trusts the debtor’s liability”) and exceptions (“except with the condition of pledging”) to delineate permissibility boundaries, requiring precise parsing of the protasis and apodosis to capture the juristic nuance.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth pillar is the contracting party (al-ʿāqid). In him, the same conditions are considered as in sale, with one additional matter: he must be one who is qualified to make a gratuitous disposition (ahl al-tabarruʿ) with the pledged property. For pledging (al-rahn) is a gratuitous act, and thus it is not permissible for the guardian of a minor, nor for the mukātab (slave under contract of manumission), nor for the one authorized to trade (al-maʾdhūn) — in all cases without qualification. Rather, a detailed distinction is necessary.

As for the guardian of a minor, consideration is given to his pledging (rahn) on the minor’s behalf and his accepting a pledge (irtihān) for the minor’s debt. As for his accepting a pledge, it is permissible when the minor is unable to recover the debt, and it is not permissible when he is able [to recover it without security]. It is permissible when the debt is deferred, and the minor’s debt becomes deferred by selling on credit (al-bayʿ bi’l-nasīʾah). He may do this if a manifest advantage (ghubṭah) appears therein, but on the condition of taking a pledge. Thus the Iraqis said: If he sells what is worth one hundred for one hundred in cash, or for one hundred and twenty on credit, it is not permissible except with the condition of taking a pledge for the twenty. But this is excessive (saraf); rather, the correct view (al-wajh) is that it is permissible without the pledge, if he trusts the liability of the one who owes the debt. For this does not exceed entrusting the orphan’s wealth to trade (īḍāʿuhu), which is permissible for the sake of increase. This is unlike lending (al-iqrāḍ), where increase is prohibited; thus it is not permissible except in a time of plunder and raid.

As for the guardian’s pledging the minor’s property, it is not permissible except with a manifest advantage (ghubṭah ẓāhirah), as when he sells from it what is worth two thousand for one thousand, and takes a pledge worth one thousand. For the utmost that could occur in this matter is that the pledged object is lost while being a trust (amānah), in which case he would have obtained two thousand in exchange for two thousand. But if the value of the pledged object together with the total price exceeds [what is due to] the buyer, it is not permissible, because it is an immediate restraint (ḥajr nājiz) upon two thousand without obtaining two thousand.

Shaykh Abū Muḥammad said: If he pledges real estate (ʿaqār) and there is advantage in the purchase, it is permissible, since there is no fear of the real estate being lost, and the usufruct remains for him. The sale of a minor’s real estate is not permissible except for necessity, until the restraint (ḥajr) is lifted from him. Pledging is also permissible for the necessity of dire need (ḥājat fāqah), as when a minor becomes destitute of food and possesses real estate whose yield is expected to cover the price of the food; then he may buy and pledge.

The ruling for the mukātab is the same as the ruling for the guardian of a minor. And the ruling for the one authorized to trade (al-maʾdhūn) is ordered upon the mukātab, and he is even more deserving of prohibition, because pledging may not fall under the name of trade (tijārah); for this reason, he is not able to hire himself out.

— Peace be upon him — The Second Chapter: On Taking Possession (al-qabḍ) and the Contingencies Preceding It. It contains two sections.
— Peace be upon him —

chapters.arabic_text:
### | القسم الأول في القبض

وهو ركن في الرهن لا يلزم إلا به خلافا لمالك رحمه الله فإنه قال يلزم
بنفسه وطرد ذلك في الهبة والإعارة وكل تبرع
ثم يشترط لصحة القبض من التكليف والأهلية ما يشترط للعقد واليد مستحقة
للمرتهن
ولو أناب فيه نائبا جاز ولا يجوز أن ينيب الراهن ولا عبده القن ولا
مستولدته لآن يدهم يد الراهن ويجوز أن ينيب مكاتبه
وفي عبده المأذون له في التجارة ثلاثه أوجه يفرق في الثالث بين أن تركبه
الديون فتنقطع سلطته السيد عما في يده ويضاهي المكاتب وبين أن لا تركبه
الديون
والنظر الآن في صوره القبض وهو التخليه في العقار والنقل في المنقول
وفي الاكتفاء في المنقول في التخليه خلاف كما في البيع وقطع القاضي
بالفرق لأن البيع يوجب استحقاق القبض فيكفي التمكين فيه وهاهنا لا استحقاق
بل القبض سبب الاستحقاق فلا وقع لمجرد التمكين
أما إذا رهن المودع من المودع الوديعة فقد نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه
لا يلزم بمجرد قوله رهنت بل لابد من إذن جديد في القبض ونص في الهبة على
خلافه
فقال الأصحاب قولان بالنقل والتخريج ومن قرر النصين فرق بالضعف والقوة
وتوجيه القولين من قال يكتفي به جعل قوله رهنت بقرينة الحال رضا بالقبض
ومن لم يكتف به نظر إلى مجرد الصيغة وهي لا تدل على القبض
ولذلك لا يجوز للمرتهن أخذ المرهون إذا لم يكن في يده  إلا بإذن جديد ثم
سواء قلنا لا يفتقر إلى إذن جديد أو قلنا يفتقر فإذا فلا بد من مضي مدة
يتصور تحقيق صورة القبض فيها حتى يلزم
فهل يشترط الرجوع إلى بينة ومشاهدة المرهون فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه لا بد منه ليتحقق التمكن يكون كالقبض لنفسه وهو نص الشافعي رضي
الله عنه إذ قال ولو كان في المسجد والوديعة في بيته لم يكن قبضا حتى يصير
إلى منزله
والثاني أنه لا يشترط الرجوع إذ لا فائدة للرجوع
والثالث أنه إن استيقن وجوده أو غلب على ظنه فلا فائدة في الرجوع وإلا
فيرجع ليتيقن وجوده
فإن قلنا يشترط الرجوع ففي اشتراط نقله من مكان إلى مكان وجهان واشتراط
النقل هو الغاية فلا ذاهب إلى أنه يجب رده على الراهن واسترداده بعد ذلك
وروى العراقيون عن حرملة أنا إذا لم يشترط إذنا جديدا فلا يشترط أيضا
مضي الزمان وهو محتمل لكنه بعيد من المذهب
ثم إن شرطنا شيئا سوى مضي الزمان فهل تجوز الاستنابة فيه فعلى وجهين
ووجه المنع أنه إنما يصير قابضا بالضم إلى ما سبق من النقل فلا يقبل
التعدد
والأصح أن البيع من المودع مسلط على التصرف وناقل للضمان دون إذن جديد
بخلاف الرهن فإنه محصل للملك وهو في يده
وفيه وجه أنه كالرهن
والأصح أن الرهن من الغاصب كالرهن من المودع
وفيه وجه أنه لا بد من إذن جديد قطعا إذ لم يسبق هاهنا إذن حتى ينصرف
الآن إلى جهة الرهن
فإن قيل فهل يبرأ الغاصب عن ضمان الغصب بالرهن
قلنا عندنا لا يبرأ خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله لأن يد الغاصب لم تنقطع
فلا ينقطع حكمه بخلاف ما إذا أودع عند الغاصب فإن الطاهر
ينقطع لأنه عاد إلى المالك حكما إذ يده يد المودع ويد المرتهن لنفسه
ولو آجره فوجهان لأنه مردد بين أن نجعل للآجر لما فيه من تقرير أجرته أو
للمستأجر للانتفاع
وفي الوكالة بالبيع وجهان مرتبان على الإجارة وأولى بأن لا يبرأ لأنه
كالمستأجر فيه إلا أن غرض المالك هاهنا في اليد أظهر
ولو رهن من المستعير ففي براءته عن ضمان العارية وجهان مبنيان على أنه هل
يضمن ضمان المغصوب
ولو أبرأ الغاصب صريحا عن الضمان مع بقاء اليد ففي البراءة وجهان من حيث
إنه إبراء عما لم يتم سبب وجوبه إذ تمام الوجوب بالتلف
ثم إذا قلنا لا يبرأ الغاصب فله أن يرد على الراهن ويسترد ويجبر الراهن
على الأخذ والرد بعد لزوم الرهن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ب-ض (q-b-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To grasp, seize, take hold of something with the hand; contraction or retention of a thing in one's control.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, the actual physical or constructive acquisition of a thing that completes a transactional cause (sabab) into binding effect (luzūm), particularly in pledges (rah n).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — manual seizure; metaphorical (majāz) — legal possession through authorization or constructive delivery (takhliyah), where the hand (yad) stands as a metonym for custodial authority.
- Root: ر-ه-ن (r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pledge, pawn, or hold a thing as security against a debt; permanence and retention.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contractual security (wathīqah) that binds the creditor's claim to a specific asset, effective only upon possession.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the pledged object itself; metaphorical — the legal nexus of liability and entitlement created by the contract.
- Root: ي-د (y-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The hand; by extension, power, control, or custodial authority over an object.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The juridical "hand" (yad) as the basis of presumptive ownership and liability (ḍamān), distinguishing trustee-custody (yad amānah) from tortious-custody (yad ḍamān).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the physical limb; metaphorical — legal control, whether direct or through a deputy (nā'ib), where the deputy's hand is attributed to the principal.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Exceptive Construction (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnā') — The text repeatedly employs conditional clauses (law, in) with apodoses (fa-jawāb) to delineate juristic branches, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the author's dialectical structure.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first division concerns taking possession (al-qabḍ). It is a pillar (rukn) of the pledge (al-rahn); the pledge is not binding except through it, contrary to Mālik — may Allah have mercy on him — for he held that it is binding by itself, and he extended this consistently to gifts (al-hibah), loans for use (al-iʿārah), and every gratuitous transfer (tabarruʿ).

Then, for the validity of taking possession, the same conditions of legal capacity (al-taklīf) and eligibility (al-ahliyyah) are required as are required for the contract itself. The hand (al-yad) is vested in the pledgee (al-murtahin).

If he appoints a deputy (nā'ib) for it, it is permissible. It is not permissible for the pledgor (al-rāhin) to appoint a deputy, nor his chattel slave (ʿabduhu al-qinn), nor his umm walad (mustawladatahu), because their hand is the hand of the pledgor. But it is permissible for him to appoint his mukātab (slave under contract of manumission) as deputy.

Regarding his slave who is permitted to engage in trade (al-ma'dhūn lahu fī al-tijārah), there are three views (awjuh). In the third, a distinction is drawn between whether debts have mounted upon him — in which case the master's authority over what is in his hand is severed, and he resembles the mukātab — and whether debts have not mounted upon him.

Now the inquiry concerns the forms of taking possession: it is constructive delivery (al-takhliyah) in real property (al-ʿiqār) and physical transfer (al-naql) in movables (al-manqūl). Regarding sufficiency of constructive delivery in movables, there is a difference of opinion, as in sale (al-bayʿ). The Judge (al-Qāḍī) decisively affirmed a distinction, because sale entails an entitlement to possession, so mere enabling (al-tamkīn) suffices therein; but here there is no entitlement — rather, possession is the cause of entitlement — so mere enabling has no effect.

As for when a depositor (al-mūdiʿ) pledges the deposit (al-wadīʿah) with the depositary (al-mūdaʿ), al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — explicitly ruled that it is not binding by his mere saying "I have pledged it"; rather, a fresh authorization (idhn jadīd) for taking possession is indispensable. But he explicitly ruled the contrary in the case of gift (al-hibah).

The Companions (al-aṣḥāb) thus stated two positions, one based on transmission (naql) and one on derivation (takhrij). Whoever reconciled the two explicit rulings distinguished by weakness versus strength. As for the justification of the two positions: he who deemed the mere statement sufficient treated his saying "I have pledged it," in light of the contextual indication (qarīnat al-ḥāl), as consent to possession. He who did not deem it sufficient looked only to the bare formula (al-ṣīghah), which does not indicate possession.

For this reason, the pledgee is not permitted to take the pledged object, if it is not already in his hand, except with fresh authorization. Then, whether we say it does not require fresh authorization or we say it does, in either case a period of time must elapse within which the actual form of possession could be realized, so that it becomes binding.

Does it then require returning to inspect the pledged object with evidence and visual confirmation (al-rujūʿ ilā bayyinah wa mushāhadah)? There are three views:

One: It is indispensable, so that actual enablement is verified, making it like taking possession for oneself. This is the explicit ruling of al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — for he said: "Even if he were in the mosque and the deposit were in his house, it would not be possession until he returns to his dwelling."

The second: Returning is not required, for there is no benefit in returning.

The third: If he is certain of its existence or it is overwhelmingly probable, then there is no benefit in returning; otherwise, he returns to ascertain its existence.

If we say returning is required, then regarding the requirement of moving it from one place to another, there are two aspects (wajhān). Requiring the transfer is the extreme position; thus no one holds that he must return it to the pledgor and then reclaim it afterward.

The Iraqis narrated from Harmalah that if we do not require fresh authorization, we likewise do not require the passage of time. This is possible, but it is remote from the school (al-madhhab).

Then, if we stipulate something beyond the passage of time, is deputization permissible therein? There are two aspects. The aspect of prohibition is that he only becomes a possessor by conjoining the prior transfer, which does not admit of multiplicity.

The more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that the sale by the depositary is an empowerment over disposition and a transfer of liability (al-ḍamān) without fresh authorization, unlike the pledge, for the pledge consolidates ownership while the thing is in his hand.

There is an aspect that it is like the pledge.

The more correct view is that the pledge from a usurper (al-ghāṣib) is like the pledge from the depositary. There is an aspect that fresh authorization is categorically indispensable, since no prior authorization exists here to be redirected toward the pledge.

If it is said: Does the usurper become discharged from the liability of usurpation (ḍamān al-ghaṣb) by the pledge? We say: In our school, he is not discharged, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah — may Allah have mercy on him — because the usurper's hand is not severed, so its legal effect is not severed. This differs from the case where one deposits with the usurper, for the depositor's liability is severed because the thing returns to the owner constructively (ḥukman), since the depositary's hand is the hand of the depositor, whereas the pledgee's hand is for himself.

If he leases it (ājarah), there are two aspects, because it is ambiguous between making it for the lessor, given the establishment of his rent, or for the lessee, for the purpose of usufruct.

Regarding agency for sale (al-wakālah bil-bayʿ), there are two aspects, ranked upon the lease, and more apt for non-discharge, because he is like the lessee therein, except that the owner's purpose in the hand is more manifest here.

If he pledges with the borrower for use (al-mustaʿīr), then regarding his discharge from the liability of the loan for use (ḍamān al-ʿāriyah), there are two aspects, built upon whether he is liable with the liability of the usurped thing.

If the usurper is explicitly released (ibrā') from liability while the hand remains, then regarding the discharge there are two aspects, from the consideration that it is a release from something whose cause of obligation is not yet complete, since the completion of obligation occurs upon destruction (al-talaf).

Then, if we say the usurper is not discharged, he may return the object to the pledgor and reclaim it, and the pledgor is compelled to accept and return it after the pledge has become binding.

### | القسم الثاني من الباب الكلام في الطوارئ قبل القبض

والنظر في تصرفات الراهن وأحوال العاقد وأحوال المعقود عليه
أما التصرفات فكل ما يزيل الملك فهو رجوع عن الرهن لأنه جائز وهو ضده وما
لا يزيل الملك كالتزويج ليس برجوع إذ لا مضادة والإجارة رجوع عن الرهن إن
قلنا يمنع البيع وإلا فالظاهر أنه ليس برجوع كالتزويج
والتدبير بحكم نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه رجوع إذ جعله مانعا من الرهن
كما سبق
وعلى تخريج الربيع ليس برجوع وهو القياس
أما أحوال العاقدين فموت الراهن نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه سبب للفسخ
ونص في موت المرتهن على أنه يسلم إلى الورثة فقيل قولان بالنقل والتخريج
ووجه التردد متشابهته للجعالة والوكالة وهي تنفسخ بالموت وللبيع الجائز
فإن مصيره إلي اللزوم وهو لا ينفسخ
ومن قرر النصين فرقة من حقوق الغرماء والورثة يتعلق بالمرهون عند موت
الراهن فإن مصيره إلى اللزوم وهو لا ينفسخ
ومن قرر فرق من حقوق الغرماء والورثة يتعلق بالمرهون عند موت الراهن
وعماد الرهن من جانب المرتهن الدين واستحقاقه لا يتأثر موته
وفي جنون العاقدين خلاف مرتب على الموت وفي السفه خلاف مرتب على الجنون
وأولى بأن لا ينفسخ فإن عدم العقل دون عدم الروح
أما الأحوال المعقود عليه ففي انفساخ الرهن بإنقلاب العصير خمرا وجهان
وفي جناية العبد وإباقه وجهان مرتبان وأولى بأن لا ينفسخ وهو قريب من
الخلاف في الجنون
وأنقلاب العصير خمرا أولى بالفسخ لأنه ينافي المالية ولذلك يزول الرهن
بعد القبض به  ولكن إذا عاد خلا عاد وثيقة الرهن بسبب اختصاص اليد كما عاد
ملك المالك بسبب الاختصاص بالعين
ويمكن أن يقال كان الرهن موقوفا كما نقول في وقف النكاح على انقضاء العدة
في ردة المنكوحة ومصير العصير خمرا في البيع قبل القبض كهو في الرهن بعد
القبض
التفريع إذا قلنا لا ينفسخ به قبل القبض بل إذا عاد خلا عاد الرهن كما
بعد القبض فلو أقبض وهو خمرا فالقبض فاسد فلو صار خلا أمسكه لنفسك لم يكف
ولو قال أقبضه لنفسك فيكون هو القابض والمقبض وفي مثله خلاف في البيع هكذا
قاله الأصحاب
قال صاحب التقريب أبو القاسم بن قاسم القفال الشاشي ينبغي أن يكون هذا
كإذن المودع بعد الرهن منه إذ لا فرق بينهما
فإن قيل وهل يجوز السعي في التخليل
قلنا التخليل حرام عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه لحديث أبي طلحة ثم الخمر إن
لم يكن محترما وهو ما أعتصر لأجل الخمريه فإن خلل بالقاء ملح
فهو تجس لعلتين إحداهما تحريم الخليل
والأخرى ثبوت حكم النجاسة للمتحلل وذلك لا يزول إلا بالماء تعبدا بخلاف
أجراء الدن فإن فيه ضرورة
فإن خلل بالنقل من ظل إلى شمس فوجهان بناء على العلتين وإن لم يجر إلا
مجرد قصد الإمساك ليتخلل فالظاهر أنه طاهر وفيه وجه فإن أعتصره للخمريه
فصار خلا من غير قصد فهو طاهر إذ لا قصد ولا فعل وإن كانت الخمرة محترمه
وفي التي أعتصرت للخل فهو طاهر في جميع الصور إلا إذا القي فيه ملح فإن نقل
من الظل إلى الشمس فالظاهر طهارته
فإن قيل فالعناقيد إذا استحالت بواطنها وأشتدت ما حكمها
قلنا بواطئها نجسة وفي جواز بيعها وجهان يجريان في البيضة المذرة
ووجه التصحيح الاعتماد في الحال على طهارة الظاهر وفائدته المنتظرة عند
التخلل والتفرخ
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثالث في حكم الرهون بعد القبض في حق
المرتهن والراهن
فهذا يبني على فهم حقيقة الرهن وحقيقته إثبات الوثيقة لدين المرتهن في
العين حتى يثبت عليه اليد  ويختص به فيقدم على الغرباء عند الزحمة وبأمن
فوات الدين بالإفلاس
فيتضمن الرهن تجديد سلطنة للمرتهن لم تكن وقطع سلطنة للراهن كانت فالنظر
يتعلق بما انقطع من الراهن وما تجدد للمرتهن وبيان محل الوثيقة وغايتها
التى عندها ينقطع فهي أربعة أطراف

### | الطرف الأول فيما حجر على المالك فيه

وهو كل ما يفوت وثيقة المرتهن أو بعضها أو ينقصها وتصرف الراهن من ثلاثة
أوجه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ط-ر-أ (ṭ-r-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Sudden occurrence, befalling unexpectedly; that which arrives anew (ṭāriʾ) upon an established state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Contingent events that supervene upon a contract, altering its original presumption (al-aṣl) — distinct from essential (dhātī) conditions.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is temporal arrival; here used metaphorically (majāz) for juridical events that "arrive" upon the transaction.
- Root: ر-ه-ن (r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pledge, hold as security; permanence and detention of a thing against a debt.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A collateral bond (wathīqah) entailing restricted disposal (ḥajr) over the pledged object.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: detention; juridical: the right of exclusive priority (ikhtiṣāṣ) established by possession.
- Root: ف-س-خ (f-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To dissolve, annul, undo a binding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Rescission ab initio versus termination (inḥilāl) — a distinction central to whether a contract is revocable (jāʾiz) or binding (lāzim).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: tearing apart; juridical metaphor: dissolution of legal effect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Exceptive Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The phrase "إن قلنا... وإلا فـ" establishes a protasis-apodosis structure where the ruling branches on a prior doctrinal position, requiring precise parsing of the implied disjunction.

---

### The Second Division of the Chapter: Discourse on Contingencies Prior to Seizure

The investigation concerns the dispositions of the pledgor (al-rāhin), the states of the two contracting parties, and the states of the object pledged (al-maʿqūd ʿalayh).

As for the dispositions: everything that removes ownership (milk) constitutes a revocation (rujūʿ) of the pledge, because it is permissible (jāʾiz) and is its opposite. What does not remove ownership — such as marriage (tazwīj) — is not a revocation, since there is no opposition. Leasing (ijārah) is a revocation of the pledge if we hold that it prevents sale; otherwise, the apparent position is that it is not a revocation, like marriage.

Manumission by tadbīr (taqbīl al-tadbīr) — according to the explicit text (naṣṣ) of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him — is a revocation, since he made it a preventive of the pledge, as previously established. On the derivation (takhrīj) of al-Rabīʿ, it is not a revocation, and that is the analogical position (qiyās).

As for the states of the two contracting parties: the death of the pledgor — al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, explicitly ruled that it is a cause for rescission (faskh). He also explicitly ruled regarding the death of the pledgee that [the pledge] is surrendered to the heirs. It was then said: there are two opinions (qawlān), by transmission (naql) and by derivation (takhrīj). The basis of the hesitation is its resemblance to juʿālah (reward-based agency) and wikālah (agency), both of which are rescinded by death, and to a permissive sale (bayʿ jāʾiz), whose final end is bindingness (luzūm) and which is not rescinded.

Whoever establishes the two texts [as consistent] distinguishes: the rights of creditors (ghuraamāʾ) and heirs become attached to the pledged object upon the death of the pledgor, for its final end is bindingness, and it is not rescinded. Whoever establishes the distinction [based on] the rights of creditors and heirs attaching to the pledge upon the pledgor's death — the pillar (ʿimād) of the pledge on the pledgee's side is the debt, and his entitlement (istiḥqāq) is not affected by his death.

Regarding the insanity (junūn) of the two contracting parties, there is a dispute (khilāf) ranked upon the [dispute over] death. Regarding squandering (safah), there is a dispute ranked upon insanity — and it is more fitting that [the pledge] not be rescinded, for the loss of intellect is [lesser] than the loss of the spirit.

As for the states of the object pledged: concerning the rescission of the pledge by the transformation of grape juice (ʿaṣīr) into wine (khamr), there are two aspects (wajhān). Concerning the felony (jināyah) of the slave and his flight (ibāq), there are two aspects ranked [upon the former] — and it is more fitting that it not be rescinded, and this is close to the dispute over insanity.

The transformation of grape juice into wine is more fitting for rescission, because it negates monetary value (māliyyah); for this reason, the pledge is removed by it after seizure. But if it reverts to vinegar (khall), the pledge-security reverts due to the special attachment of the hand (ikhtiṣāṣ al-yad), just as the owner's ownership reverts due to the special attachment to the substance (al-ʿayn).

It may be said: the pledge was suspended (mawqūf), just as we say regarding the suspension of marriage upon the expiry of the waiting period (ʿiddah) in the case of the apostasy (riddah) of the married woman. And the transformation of grape juice into wine in a sale prior to seizure is like its [transformation] in a pledge after seizure.

**Derivation (tafrīʿ):** If we say it is not rescinded by it prior to seizure — rather, if it reverts to vinegar, the pledge reverts, just as after seizure — then if he handed it over (aqbaḍa) while it was wine, the seizure is invalid (fāsid). If it then became vinegar, and he said, "Retain it for yourself," this would not suffice. If he said, "Seize it for yourself," then he would be both the seizer and the one authorizing seizure — and in a similar case there is a dispute in sale; thus said the companions (al-aṣḥāb).

The author of al-Taqrīb, Abū al-Qāsim ibn Qāsim al-Qaffāl al-Shāshī, said: This should be like the permission of the depositary (maʾdhūn) after the pledge from him, for there is no difference between the two.

If it is said: Is it permissible to strive for the vinegar-making (takhallul)?

We say: Vinegar-making is unlawful (ḥarām) according to al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, due to the ḥadīth of Abū Ṭalḥah. Then, the wine — if it is not inviolable (ghayr muḥtaram), namely what was pressed for the purpose of wine-making — if it is turned to vinegar by casting salt, this is a transgression (tajassus) for two causes: one is the unlawfulness of the vinegar [so produced], and the other is the establishment of the ruling of impurity (najāsah) for what has dissolved, which is not removed except by water, as a matter of devotional determination (taʿabbudan) — unlike the distillation of date-wine (dinn), for therein is necessity (ḍarūrah).

If it is turned to vinegar by transfer from shade to sun, there are two aspects built upon the two causes. If nothing occurred except the mere intention of retention (qaṣd al-imsāk) so that it might turn to vinegar, the apparent position is that it is pure (ṭāhir), and there is an aspect [to the contrary]. If he pressed it for wine-making and it became vinegar without intention, it is pure, for there is neither intention nor act. And if the wine is inviolable (muḥtaramah) — namely that which was pressed for vinegar — it is pure in all cases, except if salt is cast into it. If it is transferred from shade to sun, the apparent position is its purity.

If it is said: What of grape clusters (ʿanāqīd) whose interiors have transformed and hardened — what is their ruling?

We say: Their interiors are impure, and regarding the permissibility of their sale there are two aspects that run parallel to those in the case of a rotten egg (al-bayḍah al-mudhirah). The basis of the sounder position (taṣḥīḥ) is reliance, in the present state, upon the purity of the exterior, and its expected benefit at the time of vinegar-making and hatching.

---

### The Third Chapter: On the Ruling of Pledges After Seizure, with Respect to the Pledgee and the Pledgor

This is built upon understanding the reality (ḥaqīqah) of the pledge. Its reality is the establishment of a security-bond (wathīqah) for the pledgee's debt upon the substance (al-ʿayn), such that the hand is established over it, and he is exclusively entitled (yakhtaṣṣu) to it, so that he is given precedence over outsiders (ghurabāʾ) at the time of crowding (zahmah), and the loss of the debt through bankruptcy (iflās) is guarded against.

Thus the pledge entails the renewal of a dominion (sulṭānah) for the pledgee that did not exist, and the severance of a dominion of the pledgor that did exist. The inquiry concerns what is severed from the pledgor and what is renewed for the pledgee, and the clarification of the locus (maḥall) of the security-bond and its limit (ghāyah) at which it is severed. These are four aspects (aṭrāf).

---

### The First Aspect: On What the Owner Is Restricted From (al-ḥajr ʿalā al-mālik)

It is everything that defeats the pledgee's security-bond, or part of it, or diminishes it. The pledgor's disposition is from three angles:

### | الأول التصرف القولي

فكل ما ينقل الملك الى غيره كالبيع والهبة او ينقص الملك كالتزويج
والاجارة إذ يقلل الرغبة في الحال أو يزحم المرتهن كالرهن من غيره ه فهو
ممنوع ولا منع من إجارة تنقضي مدتها قبل حلول الدين
أما ما يسقط الملك كالإعتاق فيه ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها انه لا ينفذ فانه يفوت الوثيقة من العين كالبيع
والثاني ينفذ ويغرم فانه يسري الى ملك الشريك وحق المرتهن لايزيد عليه
والثالث أنه أن كان موسرا نفذ وغرم وإلا فلا فانه إذا لم يمكن تغريمه يبق
العتق في المرتهن تفويتا محضا
أما إذا رهن نصف العبد فالصحيح آن أعتاقه في النصف المستبقى إذا نفذ سرى
الى المرهون مهما كان موسرا ألانه في معنى صورة السراية إلى ملك الغير
لوجوده محلا فارغا في الابتداء بل أولى منه
التفريع إن قلنا ينفذ ويغرم ففي وقت نفوذ العتق طريقان
أحدهما أنه ينفذ في الحال لأنه صادف ملكه
والثاني أنه يخرج على الأقوال في ملك الشريك فعلى قول متنجز وعلى آخر
يتوقف على بذل البدل وعلى الثالث على بذل البدل يتبين حصوله من وقت الانشاء
وإن وإن قلنا لا ينفذ العتق ففي نفوذه عند فك الرهن وجهان
أحدهما بلى إذ صادف ملكه وأندفع لمانع وألان فقد أرتفع
والثاني لا لأنه ليس بمعلق ولم يتنجر فلا يعود بعد اندفاعه
ولا خلاف في أنه لو بيع في حق المرتهن وعاد إليه يوما من الدهر لا ينفذ
أما تعليق العتق في المرهون إن أتصل بالصفة قبل فك الرهن فحكمه حكم العتق
وإن وجد الصفة بعده فالأصح  النفوذ
وفيه وجه أنه لا ينعقد التعليق في حاله لا يملك التنجير فيها وهو ملتف
تعليق الطلقة الثالثة في حق العبد

### | الوجه الثاني لتصرفه الوطء

وهو ممنوع لأنه يعرض الملك لنقصان الولادة
وفي الصغيرة والآيسة وجه والأصح حسم الباب فإن أقدم فلا حدو لا مهر
والولد حر نسيب له
وفي الاستيلاد خلاف مرتب على العتق وأولى بالحصول لأنه من جملة الأفعال
فإن حكمنا به وجب عليه قيمتها يوم الاحبال فيجعلها رهنا بدلها
وإن قلنا لا يحصل فإن بيعت وفي بطنها الولد الحر صح وفيه وجه أنه يبطل
ويجعل ذلك كاستثناء الحمل وإن أنفك الرهن فالأصح هاهنا عود الاستيلاد وإن
ماتت من طلق هذا الاستيلاد فعليه القيمة لأنه المتلف بوطئه وكذلك إذا وطئ
أمه بالشبهة الغير فماتت في الطلق
وفيه وجه آخر ذكره الفوراني أنه لا يجب إذ يبعد إحالة الهلاك على الوطء
مع تخلل أسباب حبلية
ولو ماتت زوجته من الطلق فلا ضمان قطعا لأنه تولد من مستحق وفي الحرة
الموطوءة بالشبهة وجهان
ووجه الفرق أن الحوالة عليها ممكن فإنها صاحبة الحق واليد لها في نفسها
بخلاف الأمة وكذلك في الزنا فإن كان مع استكراه فلا يمكن الحوالة عليها
لأنا لا نعرف كون الولد منه والشرع منع النسب
فإن أقر بإنه من إحباله ففي كلام الأصحاب ما يدل على أنه لا يجب أيضا فإن
السبب ضعيف وكأنه في الأمة حصل مثل إثبات اليد عليها باستعمال رحمها في
تربية الولد فكان كالهلاكه تحت اليد
التفريع إذا أوجبنا القيمة ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه باعتبار أقصى القيم من يوم الاحبال الى يوم الموت وكأن الاحبال
غصب وأستيلاد
والثاني باعتبار يوم الموت
والثالث باعتبار يوم الاحبال
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ق-ل (naqala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To transfer, convey, or move something from one locus to another; in juristic usage, transference of ownership.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Transfer of a legal attribute (ḥukm) from one subject to another; implies a relational change in entitlement.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in physical movement; metaphorical (majāz) in legal transference of rights.
- Root: ر-ه-ن (rahana)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pledge or hold as security; permanence and retention of a thing as collateral.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The pledge (rahn) creates a lien (ḥaqq) that restricts the owner's full disposal (taṣarruf) over the corpus (ʿayn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical detention; metaphorical for the legal restraint upon the owner's disposition.
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿataqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be free, to be released from bondage; root denotes liberation from constraint.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Manumission (iʿtāq) extinguishes the proprietary right (milk) over the slave entirely, unlike transfer or diminution.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for emancipation; in legal discourse, it signifies complete removal of ownership, not mere release.
- Root: و-ط-ء (waṭi'a)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To tread upon; in juristic context, sexual intercourse.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): An act (fiʿl) that may generate offspring, thereby affecting the pledged value of the slave-woman.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical contact; metaphorical extension to the legal consequences of paternity and compensation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Construction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The protasis (sharṭ) governs the apodosis (jawāb) such that the ruling is suspended upon the occurrence of the condition; when the condition is impossible at the time of utterance, the suspension is void, as in the case of taʿlīq of manumission during the pledge.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first category is the verbal disposition (al-taṣarruf al-qawlī).

Everything that transfers ownership to another — such as sale (bayʿ) or gift (hibah) — or that diminishes ownership — such as marriage (tazwīj) or lease (ijārah), since it reduces the desire [for the pledged property] in the present, or that crowds the pledgee's right — such as pledging [the same property] to another — is prohibited [to the pledgor]. However, there is no prohibition against a lease whose term expires before the debt falls due.

As for that which extinguishes ownership entirely, such as manumission (iʿtāq), there are three opinions (aqwāl):

One: It does not take effect, for it defeats the security (wathīqah) over the corpus, just like sale.

The second: It takes effect, and he must pay compensation (yaghram), for it permeates (yasrī) into the partner's share [in cases of joint ownership], and the pledgee's right is no greater than that.

The third: If he is solvent (mūsir), it takes effect and he pays compensation; otherwise it does not. For if compensation cannot be exacted from him, the manumission remains [operative] against the pledgee's interest as a pure defeat of the security (tafwīt maḥḍ).

As for the case where he pledges half of a slave: The correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that if he manumits his share in the remaining half, and it takes effect, it permeates into the pledged portion whenever he is solvent — because this falls under the same meaning as permeation into the property of another (milk al-ghayr), since it finds a vacant locus (maḥall khālī) at the outset; indeed, it is even more apt [than that case].

Branch (tafrīʿ): If we adopt the view that it takes effect and he pays compensation, then regarding the time of the manumission's effectiveness there are two paths (ṭarīqān):

One: It takes effect immediately, because it encountered his own property (milk).

The second: It is derived from the opinions concerning the partner's share. On one opinion, it is operative immediately (mutanajjiz); on another, it is suspended upon the payment of the substitute (badal); on the third, upon payment of the substitute it becomes evident that it occurred from the time of the origination (inshāʾ).

And if we adopt the view that the manumission does not take effect [during the pledge], then regarding its effectiveness upon the release of the pledge (fakk al-rahn) there are two aspects (wajhān):

One: Yes, it takes effect — for it encountered his property, and it was repelled by an obstacle (māniʿ), and now that obstacle has been removed.

The second: No — for it was not suspended (muʿallaq) and did not become operative immediately, so it does not return after being repelled.

There is no disagreement that if [the slave] were sold for the pledgee's right and later returned to him at any time whatsoever, the manumission would not take effect.

As for suspending manumission (taʿlīq al-ʿitq) upon a pledged slave: If the condition (ṣifah) occurs before the release of the pledge, its ruling is the ruling of manumission [as discussed]. If the condition occurs after [release], the most correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that it takes effect. There is also an aspect that the suspension is not validly contracted (lā yanʿaqid) during a state in which he does not possess the power to render it immediate (tanjīz) — and this is analogous to suspending the third divorce (ṭalqah thālithah) in the case of a slave [who lacks the capacity to divorce].

The second aspect of his disposition is intercourse (al-waṭʾ).

It is prohibited, because it exposes the property to diminution through offspring (wilādah). Regarding [intercourse with] a minor (ṣaghīrah) or a woman past childbearing age (āʾisah), there is an aspect [of permissibility], but the most correct view is to close the door entirely (ḥasm al-bāb). If he does commit it, then there is no prescribed punishment (ḥadd) and no dower (mahr), and the child is free and of legitimate lineage (nasab) to him.

Regarding istīlād (seeking motherhood, i.e., begetting a child upon a slave-woman): There is a disagreement built upon the opinions on manumission, and it is even more apt to be established, because it is among the class of acts (afʿāl). If we rule that it is established, then he must pay her value on the day of impregnation (yawm al-iḥbāl), and it is made a pledge in place of her.

If we rule that it is not established, then if she is sold while carrying in her womb a free child, the sale is valid. There is an aspect that it is void, treating that as an exception of the pregnancy (istithnāʾ al-ḥaml). If the pledge is released, the most correct view here is the return of istīlād. If she dies from the labor (ṭalaq) of this istīlād, then he must pay her value, because he is the one who destroyed her (mutlif) through his intercourse. Likewise, if he had intercourse with her mother [i.e., a slave-woman belonging to another] under a mistaken claim of right (shubhah) and she died in labor.

There is another aspect mentioned by al-Fūrānī that no compensation is due, for it is far-fetched to attribute the destruction to the intercourse when causes of pregnancy (asbāb ḥamliyyah) intervened.

If his wife dies from labor, there is no liability (ḍamān) categorically, because it arose from a rightful cause (mustaḥaqq). As for a free woman with whom intercourse occurred under shubhah, there are two aspects. The basis for the distinction is that attribution of the destruction to her is possible, for she is the possessor of the right and has authority over herself, unlike the slave-woman. Likewise in the case of fornication (zinā) — if it involved coercion (istikrāh), attribution to her is not possible, for we do not know that the child is from him, and the Law (sharʿ) precludes lineage (nasab). If he acknowledges (aqarra) that the child is from his impregnation, then in the statements of the jurists (aṣḥāb) there is an indication that no compensation is due either — for the cause is weak, and it is as though in the case of the slave-woman, there occurred something like establishing a hand (yad) over her by employing her womb in the rearing of the child, making it as if she perished under his hand.

Branch: If we impose the value, there are three aspects:

One: It is assessed by the highest value (aqṣā al-qiyam) from the day of impregnation to the day of death — as though the impregnation were a usurpation (ghaṣb) combined with istīlād.

The second: It is assessed by the value on the day of death.

The third: It is assessed by the value on the day of impregnation.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الوجه الثالث الانتفاع

وهو جائز عندنا للراهن في الدار المرهونه بالسكون وفي العبد
المحترف بالاستكساب وفي الفحل بإنزائه على الإناث إن لم ينقص من قيمته
وكذا الإنزاء على الأنثى إن لم ينقص الإحبال من قيمتها
أما الغراس في الأرض فممنوع لأنه يقلل الرغبة في الأرض إذا بيعت  دون
الغراس
وذكر الربيع في الدين المؤجل وجها أنه لا يمنع من الغراس فربما تفي الأرض
بجميع الدين أو توفى الزيادة من موضع آخر فإن لم يكن قلع عند البيع أما في
الحال فلا منع وهو منقاس
التفريع إن قلنا يمنع فلو غرس قلع ولو حمل السيل النوى فأنبت لا يقلع في
الحال ولكن عند البيع يقلع إن لم يتعلق حق الغرماء به بالحجر عليه بالفلس
فإن تعلق لم يقلع وكذلك على مذهب الربيع إذا جوز الغراس بل يباع الكل ويوزع
الثمن وفي كيفية التوزيع كلام سبق في التفريق بين الولد والأم في الرهن
فرع ليس للراهن المسافرة بالعبد المرهون أصلا لأنه حيلولة عظيمة واليد
مستحقة للمرتهن فلا تزال إلا لضرورة والضرورة في الانتفاع لا في السفر
وكذلك لا يسافر زوج الأمة بها ويسافر بها سيدها تقديما لحقه وترغيبا له
في تزويجها ويسافر الزوج بزوجته الحرة لأن مقصود النكاح أغلب وهو صاحبه وهي
صاحبة الحق والحظ في النكاح
وكذلك لو أمكن استسكاب العبد في يد المرتهن لم ينتزع من يده فإن لم يحسن
إلا الخدمة انتزع من يده نهارا ورد ليلا وللمرتهن أن يكلفه الإشهاد عند
الانتزاع في كل يوم وهل له أن يكلف الراهن ذلك وهو مشهور العدالة فيه وجهان
فإن قيل ما منعتموه من التصرفات لو أذن فيه المرتهن
قلنا لايمتنع منه بإذنه فالحق لا يعدوهما ثم ما من ضرورته فسخ الرهن
كالإعتاق والهبة يرفع الرهن ولا قيمة عليه إذا أعتق بإذنه وله أن يرجع عن
الإذن قبل وقوع التصرف فإذا أذن في الهبة فله الرجوع قبل القبض إذ به يتم
المأذون فيه
وفي الرجوع عن الإذن في البيع في مدة الخيار وجهان فإن قيل هل يتعلق حقه
بالثمن إذا أذن في البيع في مدة الخيار قلنا إن كان بعد حلول الدين وأذن
لأجل قضاء حقه فلا شك وإن كان قبله
فإن أطلق لم يكن الثمن عندنا رهنا خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمة الله عليه
فإن قال بشرط أن  يجعل الثمن رهنا ففي ذلك قولان مأخذه جواز نقل الوثيقة
إلى عين أخرى
وإن قال بشرط أن يعجل حقي من الثمن فالشرط فاسد وكذا الإذن لأنه ما رضي
بالبيع إلا بعوض وهو التعجيل ولم يسلم العوض بخلاف ما إذا قال للوكيل بع
ولك من الثمن عشرة أجرة فإنه لم يفسد الإذن وفسد الشرط لأنه لم يقابل العوض
بالإذن بل قابله بالعمل فعند الفساد يرجع إلى أجرة المثل
فإن قيل فمن مات وعليه دين فتعلقت الديون بتركته فما قولكم في تصرف
الورثة فيها بالبيع
قلنا فيه طريقان
منهم من خرج على قولي العبد الجاني لأنه ثبت شرعا لا اختيارا بخلاف الرهن
ومنهم من قطع بالمنع نظرا للميت ومبادرة إلى تبرئة ذمته
ثم اختلفوا في أن قول المنع هل يطرد في الدين إذا لم يستغرق
ومن لم يطرد علل بأن أكثر التركات لا تخلو عن دين ما فيبعد الحجر بسبب
درهم في مال كثير
فإن قيل فلو ظهر دين برد عوض بالعيب وتوجهت المطالبة بالثمن بعد أن باع
الورثة التركة
قلنا إن فرعنا على المنع من البيع ففي تتبعه بالنقض وجهان من حيث إن
الدين متراخ وسببه متقدم وكذلك لو كان حفر بئرا فتردى فيه بعد موته إنسان
وهاهنا أولى بأن لا يسند إذ الحفر ليس سببا للهلاك بمجرده
فإن قلنا لا يتبع بالنقض فإن وفوا بالدين فذاك وإلا فالأصح أنه الآن
يفسخ إذ لا دين عليهم حتى يطالبوا
وفيه وجه أن ما مضى وتعلق به حق المشتري لا يفسخ فكأنهم قد فوتوا التركة
فعليهم الضمان

### | الطرف الثاني في بيان جانب المرتهن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ف-ع (n-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is benefit, utility, or advantage; al-nafʿ is the opposite of ḍarar (harm).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, it denotes lawful appropriation of a thing's utility without consuming its substance (ʿayn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its literal (ḥaqīqah) sense of deriving benefit; metaphorical extension (majāz) would be "benefit" as in reward (thawāb), which is not intended in this juristic context.
- Root: ر-ه-ن (r-h-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hold a thing as a pledge or security; al-rahīn is the pledged object.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, rahn establishes a possessory right (yad) for the creditor over the pledged asset as collateral for a debt.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "to bind" or "to detain"; here it is the technical legal contract of pledge.
- Root: ق-ل-ع (q-l-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To uproot, pluck out, or remove forcibly from a fixed position.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic discourse, it refers to the physical removal of an object (e.g., a tree) from land, often in disputes over improvements to pledged property.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal action of extraction; metaphorically used for annulment of a contract, but here strictly physical.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Sentence Structure (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The frequent use of "in" (if) clauses with apodosis (jawāb) governs the legal hypotheticals; the protasis states the condition, the apodosis the ruling, requiring precise parsing to distinguish permissive from prohibitive outcomes.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third aspect is usufruct (al-intifāʿ).

It is permissible in our school for the pledgor (al-rāhin) to dwell in the pledged house, and for the skilled slave to earn a living through his craft, and for the stud camel to be put to the females, provided that this does not diminish its value. Likewise, it is permissible to put the male to the female [for breeding] if the impregnation does not diminish her value.

As for planting trees (al-ghirās) in the pledged land, it is prohibited, because it reduces the desirability of the land when it is sold without the trees.

Al-Rabīʿ mentioned, regarding a deferred debt, a position (wajh) that planting is not prohibited, for perhaps the land will suffice for the entire debt, or the increase will be made up from another source — if it is not uprooted at the time of sale. As for the present moment, there is no prohibition; and this is analogically derived (munqās).

The ramification: If we say it is prohibited, then if he planted, it is uprooted. And if a flood carried seeds and they sprouted, it is not uprooted at present, but at the time of sale it is uprooted — unless the right of the creditors has attached to it by the court's interdiction over him due to bankruptcy (al-ḥajr ʿalayhi bi al-flas). If it has attached, it is not uprooted. Likewise, on the school of al-Rabīʿ, when planting is permitted, rather the whole is sold and the price is apportioned. Regarding the manner of apportionment, there is a discussion that preceded in the section on distinguishing between the offspring and the mother in the pledge.

A subsidiary point: The pledgor has absolutely no right to travel with the pledged slave, because this is a grave obstruction (ḥaylūlah ʿaẓīmah), and the hand (al-yad) is due to the pledgee (al-murtahin); it is not removed except for necessity. And necessity applies to usufruct, not to travel.

Likewise, the husband of a female slave may not travel with her, but her master may travel with her, giving precedence to his right and encouraging him to marry her off. And a free husband may travel with his free wife, because the purpose of marriage is predominant, and he is its master, while she is the possessor of the right and the share in the marriage.

Similarly, if the slave can earn a living in the hand of the pledgee, he is not taken from his hand. But if he is only skilled at service, he is taken from his hand by day and returned by night. The pledgee may require him to have witnesses (al-ishhād) at the time of taking [the slave] each day. And is he entitled to require the pledgor to do so when he is of well-known probity? There are two positions (wajhān).

If it is said: "What you have prohibited of dispositions — if the pledgee permits it?" We say: It is not prohibited with his permission, for the right does not extend beyond the two of them. Then, whatever necessitates the dissolution of the pledge (faskh al-rahn) — such as manumission (al-iʿtāq) and gift (al-hibah) — removes the pledge, and no value is owed upon him if he manumits with his permission. And he may revoke the permission before the disposition occurs. So if he permitted a gift, he may revoke before delivery (al-qabḍ), for by delivery the permitted act is completed.

Regarding revoking permission for sale during the option period (muddat al-khiyār), there are two positions.

If it is said: "Does his right attach to the price when he permits the sale during the option period?" We say: If it was after the debt had fallen due, and he permitted it for the purpose of satisfying his right, then there is no doubt. But if it was before [the debt fell due], and he gave an absolute permission, then in our school the price is not a pledge — contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him.

If he said: "On the condition that the price be made a pledge," then there are two opinions (qawlān) on this, whose basis is the permissibility of transferring the security (al-wathīqah) to another specific object (ʿayn).

If he said: "On the condition that you hasten my right from the price," then the condition is void (fāsid), and likewise the permission [is void], because he did not consent to the sale except for a consideration, namely the hastening, and the consideration was not delivered. This differs from the case where he says to an agent: "Sell, and you have ten from the price as a fee" — for here the permission is not voided, but the condition is voided, because he did not offset the consideration against the permission, but rather against the work. So upon the voidness, one reverts to the equivalent fee (ujrat al-mithl).

If it is said: "If a man dies owing a debt, and debts attach to his estate (tarikah), what is your opinion regarding the heirs' disposition of it by sale?" We say: There are two paths (ṭarīqān) on this.

Some derive it from the two opinions on the offending slave (al-ʿabd al-jānī), because it is established by divine law (sharʿan), not by choice — unlike the pledge. And some definitively rule its prohibition, out of consideration for the deceased and hastening to clear his liability (dimmah).

Then they differed as to whether the ruling of prohibition applies to the debt when it does not encompass [the entire estate]. And those who did not apply it reasoned that most estates are not free of some debt, so it would be far-fetched to impose interdiction (al-ḥajr) due to a single dirham in a large property.

If it is said: "If a debt appears by way of returning the price due to a defect (radd bi al-ʿayb), and the claim for the price arises after the heirs have sold the estate?" We say: If we base this on the prohibition of sale, then there are two positions on pursuing them with rescission (al-naqḍ), on the grounds that the debt is subsequent (mutarākhin) while its cause is prior. Likewise, if a man dug a well and after his death a person fell into it — and here it is even more apt not to attribute [the harm to him], since digging is not by itself a cause of destruction.

If we say it is not pursued by rescission: then if they pay the debt, that is fine; otherwise, the more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that it is now rescinded, for there is no debt upon them until they are claimed against. And there is a position that what has passed, to which the buyer's right has attached, is not rescinded — as if they had already dissipated the estate, so they are liable for compensation (al-ḍamān).

### | The Second Pole: Elucidating the Side of the Pledgee (al-Murtahin)

chapters.title_en: Section 220 — The Rights and Obligations of the Pledgee (al-Murtahin) and the Custodian (al-ʿAdl)
chapters.arabic_text:
وقد تحدد له استحقاق اليد في الحال واستحقاق البيع في تأني الحال
ولأجل استحقاق اليد وجب على الراهن التعهد والمؤنة لبقائه في يده ولا يجب
على المرتهن الضمان بحكم هذه اليد ولا يملك الانتفاع والاستمتاع
فهذه خمسة أمور في جانبه لا بد من معرفتها الأول استحقاق اليد في الحال
وهو ثابت بمطلق الرهن عند اللزوم بالقبض ولذلك يرد ليلا إليه  عند
الانتفاع نهارا ولا تزال يده إلا خوفا من فوات منفعة مقصودة فتقدم المنفعة
المقصودة على اليد التابعة للحق لأنها لا تطلب إلا لحفظ محل الحق
ولو شرط التعديل على يد ثالث جاز ويكون العدل نائبا عن المرتهن لأنه
مستحق اليد ولذلك لا يجوز شرط التعديل على يد المالك لأن يده لا تصلح
للنيابة عن غيره وهو مستقل بالملك
وللراهن أيضا حظ في يد العدل فإنه ربما لا يثق بيد المرتهن فلهذا لا يجوز
للعدل أن يسلم إلى أحدهما دون إذن صاحبه ولا أن يسلم إلى ثالث دون إذنهما
فإن فعل ضمن ثم إن سلم إلى المرتهن ضمن للراهن والقرار على المرتهن مهما
تلف في يده
وإن سلم إلى الراهن ضمن للمرتهن القيمة لتكون عنده رهنا فإذا قضي الدين
ردت إليه القيمة وله أن يكلف الراهن القضاء لفك ملكه كما في المعير لأجل
الرهن
فرع لو تغير حال العدل بفسقه أو جنايته على العبد قصدا أو بزيادة فسق على
ما عهد من قبل فلكل واحد طلب إزالة يده إلى عدل آخر
الأمر الثاني استحقاق البيع
وهو ثابت عند حلول الدين إن لم يوف الراهن الدين من موضع آخر ولكن لا
يستقل به المرتهن ولا العدل الذي في يده دون إذن الراهن أو إذن القاضي ولو
باع العدل بإذن أحدهما لم يصح بل لا بد من إذنهما وفيه فروع أربعة
الأول أنه لو رجع أحدهما عن الإذن امتنع العدل عن البيع فرجوع الراهن عزل
فإنه الموكل وإذن المرتهن شرط وليس بتوكيل ولذلك لو عاد المرتهن وأذن بعد
رجوعه جاز ولم يجب تجديد التوكيل من الراهن
ومساق هذا الكلام من الأصحاب مشعر بأنه لو عزل الراهن ثم عاد ووكل افتقر
المرتهن إلى تجديد الإذن وعليه يلزم لو قيل به أن لا يعتد بإذنه للعدل قبل
توكيل الراهن فليؤخر عنه
ويلزم عليه الحكم ببطلان رضا المرأة للوكيل بالنكاح قبل توكيل الولي وكل
ذلك محتمل
ووجه المساهلة إقامة دوام الإذن مقام الابتداء تعلقا بعمومه  وأنه إن لم
يكن يعمل في الحال أولى بالاحتمال فليقدر مضافا إلى وقت التوكيل وإذا
احتملت الوكالة التأقيت والتعليق كان الإذن أولى بالاحتمال
الثاني لو إذن الراهن للعدل عند الرهن بالبيع عند حلول الأجل لم يفتقر
إلى مراجعته ثانيا عند الحلول
وفيه وجه أنه لا بد منه إذ قد يسمح بالإذن في غير وقت البيع ثم يرى أن
يوفي الدين من موضع آخر في وقت الحلول
الثالث أنه لو ضاع الثمن في يد العدل فهو أمانة فلو سلمه إلى أحدهما دون
إذن الثاني فهو ضامن
ولو أذن له الراهن في التسليم إلى المرتهن فسلم وأنكر المرتهن فهو ضامن
لعجزه عن الإثبات فإن صدقه الراهن ونسبه إلى التقصير في ترك الإشهاد ففي
الضمان وجهان
ولو كان قد شرط الإشهاد فلا شك أنه يضمن ولو ادعى موت الشهود وصدق لم
يضمن وإن كذب فوجهان
الرابع إذا باع العدل بالغبن بطل بيعه وإن باع بثمن المثل وهو في الحال
يطلب بزيادة لم يصح وإن طلب في المجلس أيضا انفسخ العقد لأنه في حكم
الابتداء
فإن أبى الراغب من قبول البيع بعد إظهاره فالأصح أنا نتبين أن الانفساخ
لم يكن إذ بان أن الزيادة لم يكن لها حقيقة
وفيه وجه أنه لا بد من تجديد العقد فإن الفسخ قد وقع
ثم في تجديد البيع من الأول والبيع من الراغب الثاني عند إطلاق الإذن
وجهان
أحدهما أنه لا يجوز إلا بإذن مجدد إذا الوكالة الأولى انفسخت بالامتثال
بالبيع الأول
والثاني الجواز وتنزيل البيع على ما يفيد ويتقرر وإخراج الأول عن كونه
امتثالا
الأمر الثالث تعهد المرهون ومؤنته على الراهن
وليس يمنع منه حتى من الفصد والحجامة والختان ويمنع عن قطع سلعة يخاف
منها سراية ويجب عليه كراء الإصطبل للدابة مع العلف
وقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه إذا رهنه ثمرة الشجرة فعلى الراهن سقيها
وإصلاحها وجذاذها وتشميسها كما يكون عليه نفقة العبد وقد قال صلى الله عليه
وسلم وعلى من يحلبه ويركبه نفقته له غنمه وعليه  غرمه
فإن امتنع أجبره القاضي لحق المرتهن هذا مذهب العراقيين وقالت المراوزة
لا يلزمه الإنفاق على الحيوان إلا لحق الله تعالى فلم يرهن منه إلا على ذلك
فإن امتنع بيع جزء من المرهون وجعل نفقة له فإن خيف استيعاب المرهون
بالنفقة ألحق بما يتسارع إليه الفساد وبيع بما لا يحتاج إلى نفقة
وكذلك يحذر من بيع البعض لأنه تشقيص فينفق عليه من منفعته وكسبه وإلا
فيباع ولعل الأول أصح 0 ويتأيد بالمكري فإنه يجب عليه عمارة الدار من
عنده وفاء بتقدير ما التزم
الأمر الرابع المرهون أمانة في يد المرتهن
لا يسقط بتلفه شيء من الدين خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله فلو تصرف فيه بما
لا يجوز ضمن ضمان المغصوب
فروع أربعة
أحدها لو رهن عنده أرضا وأذن له في الغراس بعد شهر فهو قبل الغراس أمانة
وبعده عارية مضمونة والرهن مستمر فإن غرس قبل الشهر قلع مجانا وإن غرس بعد
الشهر لم يقلع إلا ببدل
الثاني إذا كان الدين مؤجلا بشهر فقال رهنت منك بشرط أن يكون مبيعا منك
بالدين عند حلول الأجل فالرهن فاسد والشرط فاسد ولكنه في الشهر الأول أمانة
لأنه مقبوض على حكم الرهن وفي الثاني مضمون لأنه مقبوض على حكم شراء فاسد
وللفاسد حكم الصحيح في الضمان
ومنهم من استثنى ما إذا عرف فساد البيع فأمسكه عن جهة الرهن
التفريع لو غرس بعد مضي الشهر على ظن صحة البيع لم يقلع غرسه مجانا لأنه
مأذون فيه في ضمن البيع ولو علم الفساد قلع مجانا لأنه حرم عليه ذلك فلا
حرمة لقلعة
الثالث إذا ادعى المرتهن رد الرهن أو تلفه فالقول قوله عند المراوزة كما
في المودع وطردوا ذلك في المستأجر وأيدي الأمانات كلها
وقال العراقيون ذلك من خصائص الائتمان لأنه مصدق بقوله إذا ائتمنه
وألحقوا الوكيل بغير أجرة بالمودع وذكروا في الوكيل بأجرة وجهين
الرابع قال المراوزة المرتهن من الغاصب والمستأجر منه على جهل حكمهما حكم
المودع على جهل حتى إنهم يطالبون بالضمان والقرار على  الغاصب
والعراقيون سووا بين الكل وذكروا في مطالبتهم وجهين وعند المطالبة ذكروا
في قرار الضمان وجهين
الأمر الخامس تصرفات المرتهن
وهو ممنوع من جميعها قولا وفعلا وليس له الانتفاع أيضا ولو وطئ مع العلم
بالتحريم فحكمه الوطء بالشبهة حكم الزنا وإن جهل وكان حديث العهد بالإسلام
فحكمه حكم الوطء بالشبهة ومنهم من قطع بسقوط الحد وتردد في المهر والنسب
وحرية الولد لضعف هذه الشبهة وهو بعيد
ثم قال القاضي من لا يعرف هذا القدر فكأنه لا معرفة له فإذا اكتفينا بهذا
في إثبات الأحكام فينبغي أن نقول المجنون إذا زنا فحكمه حكم الوطء بالشبهة
وإن إذن الراهن وعلم التحريم فهو زان
وقيل إن مذهب عطاء إباحة الوطء بالإذن فيصير شبهة ويلتحق بالوطء بالشبهة
فأما إذا ظن الإباحة فهذه الشبهة أقوى
وفي المهر وجهان أحدهما السقوط لإذنه
والثاني الوجوب كما للمفوضة إذ لا يؤثر الإذن في إسقاط عوض الأبضاع
وفي قيمة الولد طريقان أحدهما أنه كالمهر لأنه نتيجة الوطء
والثاني القطع بالوجوب لأنه لم يأذن في الاستيلاد وهذا ينقضه أن المرتهن
لو إذن للراهن نفد استيلاده قطعا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ل-ي (w-l-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity, guardianship, and rightful authority over a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal competence (wilāyah) entailing both right and duty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in reference to physical custody; metaphorical for legal authority.
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, to be liable, to compensate.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Liability arising from unlawful possession (ḍamān al-ghaṣb).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for financial liability; metaphorical for moral responsibility.
- Root: أ-ذ-ن (ʾ-dh-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Permission, declaration of allowance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Conditional authorization (idhn) distinct from agency (tawkīl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for explicit consent; metaphorical for implied tolerance.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — Governing the legal validity of stipulations (shurūṭ) and their exceptions in contractual language.
chapters.translation:
I say: There is established for him (the pledgee) the entitlement to possession (istiḥqāq al-yad) in the present moment, and the entitlement to sale (istiḥqāq al-bayʿ) at the deferral of the moment. And by virtue of the entitlement to possession, it is incumbent upon the pledgor (al-rāhin) to undertake maintenance and expenses (al-taʿahhud wa al-mūnah) for the preservation of the pledge in his (the pledgee's) hand, and it is not incumbent upon the pledgee (al-murtahin) to bear liability (al-ḍamān) by virtue of this possession, nor does he own the right of usufruct (al-intifāʿ) or enjoyment (al-istimtāʿ).

These, then, are five matters on his side that must be known.

**The First Matter: The Entitlement to Possession in the Present Moment**
This is established by the absolute pledge (muṭlaq al-rahn) upon its binding (luzūm) through delivery (al-qabḍ). For this reason, it (the pledge) is returned to him at night, even as he (the pledgor) uses it by day. And his (the pledgee's) hand is not removed except out of fear of the loss of an intended benefit (manfaʿah maqṣūdah); thus the intended benefit is given precedence over the hand that is subordinate to the right (al-ḥaqq), because the latter is sought only for the preservation of the locus of the right (maḥall al-ḥaqq).

If it is stipulated that the pledge be placed in the hand of a third party (al-ʿadl), this is permissible, and the custodian (al-ʿadl) stands as deputy (nāʾib) for the pledgee, because he (the pledgee) is the one entitled to possession. For this reason, it is not permissible to stipulate placement in the hand of the owner (al-mālik), because his hand is not suitable for deputizing on behalf of another, as he is independent in ownership (mustaqill bi al-milk).

The pledgor also has a share in the hand of the custodian, for he may not trust the hand of the pledgee. Hence, it is not permissible for the custodian to deliver (the pledge) to either of them without the permission of the other, nor to deliver it to a third party without the permission of both. If he does so, he becomes liable (ḍāmin). Then, if he delivers it to the pledgee, he is liable to the pledgor, and the final liability (al-qarār) rests upon the pledgee whenever it (the pledge) perishes in his hand.

And if he delivers it to the pledgor, he is liable to the pledgee for the value (al-qīmah), so that it may be held by him as a pledge. When the debt is discharged, the value is returned to him (the pledgor). And he (the pledgee) has the right to compel the pledgor to discharge (the debt) to free his property, just as in the case of the borrowed item (al-muʿār) given for the sake of the pledge.

**A Branch (Farʿ):** If the custodian's condition changes — through his corruption (fisq), or his deliberate assault (jināyah) upon the slave, or an increase in corruption beyond what was previously known of him — then each of the two parties has the right to demand the removal of his hand and (the transfer) to another custodian.

**The Second Matter: The Entitlement to Sale**
This is established upon the maturity of the debt (ḥulūl al-dayn) if the pledgor does not discharge the debt from another source. However, neither the pledgee nor the custodian in whose hand it lies may act independently in this matter without the permission of the pledgor or the permission of the judge (al-qāḍī). If the custodian sells with the permission of one of them alone, it is not valid; rather, the permission of both is required. There are four branches concerning this:

**The First Branch:** If one of them retracts his permission, the custodian is prevented from selling. The retraction of the pledgor constitutes a dismissal (ʿazl), for he is the principal (al-muwakkil). The permission of the pledgee, however, is a condition (sharṭ) and not an agency (tawkīl). For this reason, if the pledgee returns and grants permission after his retraction, it is permissible, and there is no need to renew the agency from the pledgor.

The drift of this discourse from our companions (al-aṣḥāb) suggests that if the pledgor dismissed (the custodian) and then returned and appointed him as agent (wakkal), the pledgee would need to renew his permission. Upon this, it would follow — if one were to adopt it — that his (the pledgee's) permission to the custodian before the pledgor's appointment of agency would not be counted, so let it be deferred until after it.

And upon this would follow the ruling of the invalidity of a woman's consent (riḍā) given to an agent for marriage (al-wakīl bi al-nikāḥ) before the appointment of agency by the guardian (al-walī). All of this is plausible (muḥtamal).

The basis of the lenient view (al-musāhalah) is the establishment of the continuity of permission (dawām al-idhn) in place of its initiation, relying upon its generality (ʿumūm), and that if it was not operative at the present moment, it is more fitting for probability (iḥtimāl), so let it be reckoned as attached to the time of the appointment of agency. And since agency (al-wakālah) admits of temporal limitation (al-tawqīt) and conditionality (al-taʿlīq), permission is even more fitting for such probability.

**The Second Branch:** If the pledgor gave permission to the custodian at the time of the pledge to sell upon the maturity of the term, he does not need to be consulted a second time at maturity. There is a view that this is necessary, for he (the pledgor) might have been lenient with permission at a time other than the time of sale, and then at maturity he might see fit to discharge the debt from another source.

**The Third Branch:** If the price (al-thaman) is lost in the hand of the custodian, it is a trust (amānah). If he delivers it to one of them without the permission of the other, he is liable. If the pledgor permitted him to deliver it to the pledgee, and he delivered it, and the pledgee denied (receipt), then he (the custodian) is liable, due to his inability to prove (the delivery). If the pledgor affirms his (the custodian's) truthfulness but attributes negligence to him for failing to secure witnesses (al-ishhād), then there are two views concerning liability. If he had stipulated the securing of witnesses, there is no doubt that he is liable. And if he claims the death of the witnesses and is affirmed (by the pledgor), he is not liable; but if he is contradicted, there are two views.

**The Fourth Branch:** If the custodian sells with gross undervaluation (al-ghabn), his sale is void. If he sells at the fair market price (thaman al-mithl) while at that very moment he is being offered an increase, the sale is not valid. If the increase is offered during the same session (al-majlis), the contract is rescinded (infasakha), because it is in the status of a new initiation (ibtidāʾ). If the prospective buyer (al-rāghib) refuses to accept the sale after having shown (interest), the more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that we determine that the rescission did not occur, for it became clear that the increase had no reality. There is a view that a renewal of the contract is necessary, for the rescission had indeed occurred.

Then, concerning the renewal of the sale from the first (buyer) or the sale to the second prospective buyer when the permission was absolute (muṭlaq), there are two views: One is that it is not permissible except with renewed permission, for the first agency was rescinded by compliance (imtithāl) through the first sale. The second is that it is permissible, treating the sale as effective upon what is beneficial and settled, and excluding the first from being an act of compliance.

**The Third Matter: The Maintenance of the Pledge and Its Expenses Fall upon the Pledgor**
He is not prevented from (the pledge) even in matters of bloodletting (al-faṣd), cupping (al-ḥijāmah), and circumcision (al-khitān). But he is prevented from cutting off a growth (salʿah) from which the spread (of harm) is feared. And he must pay the rent of the stable (kirāʾ al-iṣṭabl) for the animal, along with its fodder (al-ʿalaf).

Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: If he pledges the fruit of a tree, then upon the pledgor is its watering (saqy), its cultivation (iṣlāḥ), its harvesting (jidhādh), and its drying (tashmīs), just as the maintenance of the slave falls upon him. And the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«وَعَلَى مَنْ يَحْلُبُهُ وَيَرْكَبُهُ نَفَقَتُهُ، لَهُ غُنْمُهُ وَعَلَيْهِ غُرْمُهُ»} ("And upon the one who milks it and rides it is its maintenance; for him is its benefit, and upon him is its loss.") If he (the pledgor) refuses, the judge compels him, for the right of the pledgee. This is the doctrine of the Iraqis (al-ʿIrāqiyyūn). The Marāwizah (al-Marāwizah) said: Expenditure upon the animal is not incumbent upon him except for the right of Allah (may He be exalted), so he (the pledgor) did not pledge it except upon that basis. If he refuses, a portion of the pledge is sold and its proceeds are made his maintenance. If it is feared that the pledge will be entirely consumed by maintenance, it is joined to that which rapidly deteriorates (mā yatasāraʿu ilayhi al-fasād) and is sold, (being replaced by) what does not require maintenance. Likewise, one is wary of selling a part, because it constitutes division (tashqīṣ); so expenditure is made upon it from its usufruct and its earnings; otherwise, it is sold. Perhaps the first view is more correct. It is supported by the case of the lessor (al-mukrī), for he must repair the house from his own means, in fulfillment of what he has undertaken by estimation.

**The Fourth Matter: The Pledge Is a Trust (Amānah) in the Hand of the Pledgee**
Nothing of the debt is discharged by its perishing, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him). If he (the pledgee) disposes of it in a manner not permissible, he becomes liable with the liability of the usurped item (ḍamān al-maghṣūb).

**Four Branches:**

**The First:** If he pledges land with him and permits him to plant (al-ghirās) after a month, then before the planting it is a trust, and after it, it is a borrowed item with liability (ʿāriyah maḍmūnah), while the pledge continues. If he plants before the month, it is uprooted without compensation; if he plants after the month, it is not uprooted except with compensation (badal).

**The Second:** If the debt is deferred by a month, and he says: "I have pledged this to you on the condition that it be sold to you for the debt upon the maturity of the term," then the pledge is corrupt (fāsid) and the condition is corrupt. However, in the first month it is a trust, because it is received upon the basis of the pledge; and in the second it is with liability, because it is received upon the basis of a corrupt sale (shirāʾ fāsid). And the corrupt has the ruling of the valid in matters of liability. Among them (the scholars) is one who excepts the case where he knew of the corruption of the sale and retained it (the property) not on the basis of the pledge.

**A Sub-Branch (Tafrīʿ):** If he plants after the passage of the month, believing the sale to be valid, his planting is not uprooted without compensation, because it was permitted within the sale. If he knew of the corruption, it is uprooted without compensation, because it was forbidden to him, and thus there is no inviolability (ḥurmah) for its uprooting.

**The Third:** If the pledgee claims the return of the pledge or its perishing, his word is accepted according to the Marāwizah, just as in the case of the depositary (al-mūdaʿ). They extended this to the lessee (al-mustaʾjir) and all hands of trust (aydī al-amānāt). The Iraqis said this is among the specificities of entrustment (al-ʾitimān), for he is believed in his statement when he is entrusted. They attached the agent without fee (al-wakīl bi ghayr ujrah) to the depositary, and mentioned two views concerning the agent with a fee.

**The Fourth:** The Marāwizah said: The pledgee from a usurper (al-ghāṣib), and the lessee from him, when ignorant of their status, have the status of the depositary in ignorance, such that they are pursued for liability, while the final liability rests upon the usurper. The Iraqis equated all of them and mentioned two views concerning pursuing them (for liability). And upon pursuit, they mentioned two views concerning the final liability (qarār al-ḍamān).

**The Fifth Matter: The Dispositions of the Pledgee**
He is prohibited from all of them, in word and deed, and he has no right of usufruct either. If he commits sexual intercourse (waṭʾ) with knowledge of its prohibition, his ruling is the ruling of intercourse by ambiguity (waṭʾ al-shubhah), not the ruling of fornication (zinā). If he was ignorant, being new to Islam (ḥadīth al-ʿahd bi al-Islām), his ruling is the ruling of intercourse by ambiguity. Among them is one who decisively ruled the dropping of the ḥadd (punishment) and hesitated concerning the dowry (al-mahr), the lineage (al-nasab), and the freedom of the child (ḥurriyyat al-walad), due to the weakness of this ambiguity — and this is far-fetched (baʿīd).

Then al-Qāḍī said: One who does not know this much is as if he has no knowledge. If we suffice with this in establishing rulings, then we should say: If a madman (majnūn) commits fornication, his ruling is the ruling of intercourse by ambiguity. And if the pledgor gives permission and he (the pledgee) knows of the prohibition, then he is a fornicator (zānin). It was said that the doctrine of ʿAṭāʾ is the permissibility of intercourse with permission, such that it becomes an ambiguity and is annexed to intercourse by ambiguity. As for when he assumes permissibility (al-ibāḥah), this ambiguity is stronger.

Concerning the dowry, there are two views: One is its dropping, due to his (the pledgor's) permission. The second is its obligation, as in the case of the woman with unfixed dowry (al-mufawwaḍah), for permission has no effect in dropping the compensation for sexual organs (aʿwāḍ al-abḍāʿ). Concerning the value of the child, there are two paths: One is that it is like the dowry, because it is the result of the intercourse. The second is the decisive ruling of its obligation, because he (the pledgor) did not permit procreation (al-istīlād). This is refuted by the fact that if the pledgee permitted the pledgor (to have intercourse with the slave-woman), his procreation would be effective decisively.
