### | فروع أربعة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, be liable, or undertake responsibility for loss or compensation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Liability (ḍamān) as a jurisprudential obligation to compensate for damage or destruction of property.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of "inclusion" (iḍmām) — the hand that holds property is "included" under the owner's guarantee; metaphorical extension to legal responsibility.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (Shart) — "If... then..." (law/fa) constructions governing legal outcomes; the protasis (condition) determines the apodosis (ruling).
chapters.translation:
I say: The consideration here concerns the lessee (mustaʾjir) and the hired worker (ajīr).

As for the lessee, his hand is a hand of trust (yad amānah) during the period of usufruct. Even if the rented house collapses, or the garment rented for wearing is destroyed, or the beast rented for riding perishes — without transgression (ʿudwān) — there is no liability (ḍamān). This is because the delivery of the usufruct is obligatory upon the lessor, and it cannot be achieved except by establishing the lessee's hand [over the object]. Thus, it is as if he holds it for the lessor's own purpose.

However, if he transgresses by striking the beast without need, or by some other cause, and it perishes, then he is liable with the liability of transgression (ḍamān al-ʿudwān).

As for when the period expires: Al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — said: "If he detains it after the period and it perishes, he is liable."

The companions (aṣḥāb) differed [on this]. Among them were those who definitively held that his hand remains a hand of trust after the period, just as during the period; that he is not obligated for the expense of returning it; and that if it perishes, there is no liability. They interpreted al-Shāfiʿī's statement as applying to the case where he detains it after being demanded [to return it].

Among them were those who said: His hand after the period is like the hand of the borrower (mustaʿīr) — thus he bears the expense of return and liability.

As for before the period of usufruct: If the beast is handed over to him and he ties it in the stable, and it dies, there is no liability before the lapse of the usufruct period.

But if the stable collapses upon it, the companions said: Liability is obligatory, for had he ridden it on the road, he would have been safe from this calamity.

As for the hired worker (ajīr) upon the beast for training (riyāḍah), upon the garment for tailoring, and upon the dough for baking — he is liable (ḍāmin) if the property perishes due to his negligence (taqṣīr) in the work.

If he was not negligent and it perished by a calamity, then consider: If [the property] was in the owner's house, in his presence, and the thing was in the owner's hand — then no liability.

If it was in the hired worker's hand and his shop, then there are three opinions (aqwāl):

The most sound (aṣaḥḥ) is that there is no liability.

Al-Rabīʿ said: Al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — held the conviction that there is no liability upon the hired worker, and that the judge would rule according to his own knowledge [of this], but he would not openly declare it, out of fear of corrupt judges and corrupt employers.

This is supported by the fact that if a shepherd's sheep perish under his hand by death from a heavenly calamity, he is not liable by consensus (ijmāʿ); the agent in a qirad partnership (ʿāmil al-qirāḍ) is not liable by consensus; and the lessee is not liable by consensus.

The second [opinion] is that he is liable.

This is supported by reports (āthār) from the Companions, and in it lies benefit for the people — safeguarding wealth from corrupt hired workers. Also, because the work became obligatory upon him, and he is only a borrower of the garment for his own purpose, so that he may fulfill his work through it — unlike the lessee.

The third [opinion] is that the common hired worker (ajīr mushtarak) — who is able to accomplish the work himself or through others — is liable; while the exclusive worker (munfarid muʿayyan) — whose person is specified for the work — is not liable. But this distinction is weak.

Then follow four subsidiary branches (furūʿ).

chapters.title_en: Section 259 — On Compensation for Services Rendered Without Explicit Contractual Wording, and Related Subsidiary Issues
chapters.arabic_text: الأول إذا غسل ثوب غيره أو حلق رأسه أو دلكه من غير جريان لفظ في الإجارة فظاهر نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه لا يستحق شيئا وهو قياس مذهبه لأن الأجرة تجب بعقد ومجرد القرينة عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه لا تقوم مقام العقد ولأجله لم تكن المعاطاة بيعا أو تجب بالإتلاف والغسال والدلال والحلاق هم الذين أتلفوا منافع أنفسهم ولم يجر منه إلا سكوت أو إذن ولو أتلف ملك غيره بإذنه لم يضمن فكيف إذا أتلف المالك منفعة نفسه واختار المزني أنه يضمن له إذا كان مثله يعمل بأجرة ويكون بالإذن مستوفيا للمنفعة وفعله لا يدل على المسامحة فيبقى مضمونا كما أن من دخل الحمام جعل مستوفيا للمنفعة ضامنا ومن أصحابنا من قال إن كان الالتماس من صاحب الثوب ضمن وإن كان من الغسال لم يستحق فإن قيل وما يستحقه الحمامي عوض ماذا قلنا من أصحابنا من قال هو ثمن الماء وإلا فهو متبرع بالسطل والإزار إعارة له ومتبرع بحفظ الثياب وهو ضعيف لأن الماء تابع في مقصود الاستحمام ولو كان مقصودا لكان يضمن بالمثل إن كان متقوما بل ما يستحقه أجره منفعة السطل والإزار والحمام وحفظ الثياب فهو في حق الثوب كأجير مشترك حتى يخرج ضمانه على القولين والداخل لا يضمن السطل والإزار ضمان المستعير بل هو كالمستأجر الفرع الثاني إذا قصر الثوب فتلف بعد القصارة إن كان يغسل في يد المالك وداره فيستحق الأجرة ولا ضمان وإن كان في يد الغسال ففي الضمان القولان وفي الأجرة قولان مأخذهما أن القصارة عين أو أثر وفائدته أن القصار هل له حق الحبس كما للصباغ فإن قلنا له حق الحبس فقد تلف قبل التسليم فلا أجرة له وإن قلنا أثر ولا حبس فقد صار بمجرد الفراغ مسلما فله الأجرة والصحيح أنه لا أجرة له ولا ضمان وفي طريقة العراق أنا إن ضمناه فله الأجرة وإن جعلناه أمينا فلا أجرة له وقدمناه من البناء أظهر الفرع الثالث إذا استأجر دابة ليحملها عشرة آصع فأخذ الدابة وحملها أحد عشر صاعا وتلف تحت يده ضمن كلها لأنه غاصب ولو أسلم أحد عشر صاعا إلى المكري وليس عليه فظن أنه عشرة فحملها فتلفت الدابة بآفة أخرى فلا ضمان عليه وإنما عليه أجرة المثل للزيادة وإن تلفت بثقل الحمل فالأظهر أن الغار يطالب بالضمان وإن كان مباشرة الحمل من مالك الدابة وفي قدر الضمان قولان أحدهما النصف لأنه تلف بمضمون وغير مضمون فهو كالجراحات والثاني يوزع على قدر الحمل فيلزمه جزء من أحد عشر جزءا من الضمان بخلاف الجراحات فإن آثارها لا ينضبط ومثل هذا الخلاف جار في الجلاد إذ زاد على الحد واحدة أنه يوزع على العدد أو ينصف ولو استأجر رجلان ظهرا فارتدفهما ثالث بغير إذنهما وهلكت الدابة ففيما على الرديف ثلاثة أوجه أحدها النصف إذ هلك بمضمون وغير مضمون والثاني أنهم يوزنون ويقسط الضمان على وزنه بحصته والثالث أن عليه الثلث فإن وزن الرجال بعيد الفرع الرابع سلم ثوبا إلى خياط فخاطه قباء فقال المالك ما أذنت لك إلا في خياطته قميصا وتنازعا قال ابن أبي ليلى القول قول الخياط لأن الإذن في أصله متفق عليه وهو أمين فالقول قوله في التفصيل وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله القول قول المالك لأنه الآذن فيرجع إله ف تفصيل إذنه قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه وقول أبي حنيفة رحمه الله أولى ثم ذكر قولا ثالثا وهو أنهما يتحالفان إذ المالك يدعي عليه خيانة وهو ينكرها والخياط يدعي على المالك إذنا في خياطة القباء وهو ينكره فمن الأصحاب من قال للشافعي رضي الله عنه ثلاثة أقوال إذ لا يرجح فاسد على فاسد فدل على أنه رأى مذهبهما رأيا ومنهم من قال مذهبه التحالف وذاك حكاية عن مذهب الغير وهو الأصح التفريع إن قلنا يحلف الأجير فحلف سقط عنه الأرش وهل يستحق الأجرة وجهان أحدهما وهو قول أبي إسحاق المروزي لا لأن يمينه نافية فلا تصلح للإثبات والثاني أنه يستحق لأنا نحلفه على أنه أذن له في خياطته قباء لا قميصا فليستفد بيمينه استحقاق الأجرة فإن قلنا يستحق فأجرة المثل أو المسمى فيه وجهان أحدهما المسمى تصديقا له كما قال فإن كان من إشكال فهو من ضعف هذا القول ولزومه عليه والثاني أجرة المثل إذ ربما يكثر المسمى ويبعد إثباته بيمين النفي فإن قلنا لا يستحق فيدعي على المالك الأجرة فإن حلف سقط وإن نكل فهل تجدد اليمين عليه قال القاضي حسين رحمه الله لا إذ لا فائدة في التكرير فكأن يمينه السابقة كانت موقوفة على النكول لتصير حجة والثاني أنه يكرر اليمين إذ لا عهد بتقديم اليمين على النكول في الإثبات وإن فرعنا على أن القول قول المالك فيحلف له أنه أذن له في القميص لا في القباء وتسقط عنه الأجرة ويستحق الضمان لأنه إذا انتفى الإذن فالأصل الضمان وفي قدر الضمان قولان أحدهما التفاوت بين المقطوع وغير المقطوع والثاني التفاوت بين المقطوع قميصا وقباء لأن هذا القدر مأذون فيه وهذا يلتفت على أن الوكيل إذا ضمن في البيع هل يحط عنه ما يتغابن الناس به فإنه كالمأذون فيه لو تم البيع ثم مهما لم يأخذ الأجير الأجرة فله نزع الخيط إذا كان ملكا له وإن فرعنا على التخالف فإذا تحالفا سقطت الأجرة وهل يسقط الضمان قولان أحدهما لا إذ فائدة التحالف رفع العقد والرجوع إلى ما قبله والثاني وهو الأصح أنه يسقط لأنه حلف على نفي العدوان أعني الخياطة ولو نكل لكان لا يلزمه إلا الضمان فليكن ليمينه فائدة - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثالث في الطوارئ الموجبة للفسخ - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وهو ثلاثة أقسام الأول ما ينقص المنفعة من العيوب فهي سبب للخيار قبل القبض وبعد القبض لأنه وإن قبض الدار والدابة فالمنافع غير مقبوضة بعد نعم أقيم قبض محل المنافع مقام قبض المبيع في التسليط على الإجارة وفي لزوم تسليم البضع إن كانت المنفعة صداقا وحصول العتق إن كانت المنفعة نجوم كتابة وذلك لأجل الضرورة ولا ضرورة في نفي خيار العيب والعيب كل ما يؤثر في المنفعة تأثيرا يظهر به تفاوت الأجرة ما لا يظهر به تفاوت قيمة الرقبة فإن مورد العقد المنفعة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-س-ل (gh-s-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Washing, cleansing; the washerman (al-ghassāl) as one whose profession is washing garments
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The action of removing impurity or filth; in juristic context, a service (manfaʿah) that is a recognized compensable act
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical washing; metaphorical (majāz) extension to "purification" of legal liability
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, to be liable, to compensate; the state of being responsible for loss or damage
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal liability arising from transgression (taʿaddī) or from valid possession (yaḍ) of another's property
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of "inclusion" or "containment"; juristic technical sense of "guarantee/liability" as a transferable obligation
- Root: أ-ج-ر (ʾ-j-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Reward, recompense, hire; the wage paid for a service or benefit
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The countervalue (ʿiwaḍ) in a contract of hire (ijārah); distinct from gratuitous benefit (taṭawwuʿ)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for "wage"; metaphorical for "divine reward" — here restricted to the contractual sense
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs conditional particles (in, law) and exceptions (illā) to delineate juristic outcomes, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the legal conditional logic.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first [subsidiary issue]: If a person washes another's garment, or shaves his head, or massages him, without any verbal formulation (lafẓ) occurring in a contract of hire (ijārah) — then the apparent text (naṣṣ) of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, is that he deserves nothing. And this is the analogical consequence (qiyās) of his school, because the wage (ujrah) is obligated only by a contract, and a mere indication (qarīnah) — in the view of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him — does not stand in the place of a contract. For this reason, mutual exchange by hand (muʿāṭāh) is not [valid as] a sale. Or [alternatively, one might say] it is obligated by destruction (itlāf) — yet the washerman, the bath-attendant, and the barber are the very ones who have destroyed the benefits (manāfiʿ) of their own selves, and nothing issued from [the owner] except silence or permission. And if one who destroys another's property with his permission is not liable, then how [could liability attach] when the owner destroys the benefit of his own self?

Al-Muzanī chose the view that he is liable [to pay] if one like him works for wages, and that by the permission he becomes a recipient of the benefit (mustawfī), and his act does not indicate gratuitousness (musāmaḥah) — so it remains guaranteed, just as one who enters the bathhouse is deemed a recipient of the benefit and thus liable.

Among our companions there is one who said: If the request (iltimās) came from the owner of the garment, he is liable [to pay]; but if it came from the washerman, he deserves nothing.

If it is said: "And what does the bath-attendant deserve as compensation for what?" — We say: Among our companions there is one who said it is the price of the water; otherwise he is a volunteer (mutabarriʿ) regarding the bucket and the wrapper (izār), [the wrapper being] a loan (iʿārah) to him, and a volunteer regarding the guarding of the garments. But this is weak, because the water is subordinate (tābiʿ) to the intended purpose of bathing; and if it were intended, he would be liable for its equivalent (mithl) if it were a valued commodity (mutaqawwim). Rather, what he deserves is the wage for the benefit of the bucket, the wrapper, the bathhouse, and the guarding of the garments. Thus, with respect to the garment, he is like a common hireling (ajīr mushtarak), such that his liability is resolved according to the two opinions [on the hireling's liability].

And the entrant [into the bathhouse] is not liable for the bucket and wrapper with the liability of a borrower (mustaʿīr); rather, he is like a hirer (mustaʾjir).

The second subsidiary issue: If a garment is fulled (quṣṣira) and then perishes after the fulling (qiṣārah): If it was washed in the hands of the owner and in his house, then he deserves the wage and there is no liability. But if it was in the hands of the fuller (ghassāl), then regarding liability there are the two opinions; and regarding the wage there are two opinions, whose basis (maʾkhadh) is whether fulling is a [material] entity (ʿayn) or an [mere] effect (athar).

The benefit of this [distinction] is: Does the fuller have a right of retention (ḥaqq al-ḥabs) like the dyer? If we say he has a right of retention, then [the garment] perished before delivery (taslīm), so he has no wage. But if we say it is an effect and there is no retention, then by mere completion it has become delivered, so he has the wage. The correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that he has neither wage nor liability.

In the Iraqi method (ṭarīqat al-ʿIrāq): If we hold him liable, he has the wage; but if we deem him a trustee (amīn), he has no wage. And what we have presented from the building [analogy] is the more apparent (aẓhar).

The third subsidiary issue: If a person hires a beast to carry ten ṣāʿs [of grain], then takes the beast and loads upon it eleven ṣāʿs, and it perishes under his hand — he is liable for all of it, because he is a usurper (ghāṣib). But if he delivered eleven ṣāʿs to the lessor (mukrī), and the latter was not aware, thinking it was ten, and loaded it, and the beast perished by some other calamity (āfah) — then there is no liability upon him; rather, he owes only the wage of the equivalent (ujrat al-mithl) for the increase. But if it perished due to the weight of the load, then the more apparent (aẓhar) view is that the deceiver (ghārr) is pursued for liability, even though the direct loading was done by the owner of the beast.

Regarding the extent of liability, there are two opinions: One is half, because it perished by something guaranteed and something not guaranteed, like the case of wounds (jirāḥāt). The second is that it is apportioned according to the weight of the load, so that he bears a portion of eleven parts of the liability — unlike wounds, for their effects cannot be precisely determined.

And a similar disagreement applies in the case of the flogger (jallād) who exceeds the fixed number of lashes by one: is it apportioned by number, or halved?

And if two men hire a mount and a third rides behind them (irtadafa) without their permission, and the beast dies — then regarding what is upon the one riding behind (radīf), there are three aspects (awjuh): One is half, since it perished by something guaranteed and something not guaranteed. The second is that they are weighed, and the liability is apportioned according to his weight in proportion to his share. The third is that upon him is one-third, for weighing the men is far-fetched.

The fourth subsidiary issue: A person delivered a garment to a tailor, and he sewed it as a cloak (qabāʾ). The owner said: "I did not permit you except to sew it as a shirt (qamīṣ)," and they disputed. Ibn Abī Laylā said: The statement is that of the tailor, because permission regarding its essence is agreed upon, and he is a trustee (amīn), so his statement prevails regarding the detail. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: The statement is that of the owner, because he is the one who grants permission, so the detailing of his permission reverts to him. Al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, said: The statement of Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, is more appropriate (awlā).

Then he mentioned a third opinion: that they both take oaths (taḥāluf), for the owner claims treachery (khiyānah) against him, which he denies; and the tailor claims against the owner permission for sewing the cloak, which he denies. Among the companions there are those who say al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, had three opinions — for he did not prefer one corrupt [view] over another corrupt [view], which indicates that he regarded their two schools as [merely] an opinion. And among them are those who say his school is mutual oath-taking, and that [the other] is a narration of another's school — and this is the more correct (aṣaḥḥ).

The ramification: If we say the hireling takes the oath, and he does so, the diminution in value (arsh) is dropped from him. But does he deserve the wage? There are two aspects: One — which is the statement of Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī — is no, because his oath is negating (nāfiyah), so it is not suited for affirmation (ithbāt). The second is that he deserves it, for we administer the oath to him [only] that [the owner] permitted him to sew it as a cloak, not a shirt — so let him derive through his oath the entitlement to the wage.

If we say he deserves it: is it the wage of the equivalent (ujrat al-mithl) or the stipulated wage (al-musammā)? There are two aspects: One is the stipulated wage, in affirmation of his claim — for if there is a problem [in this], it is from the weakness of this opinion and its consequence upon him. The second is the wage of the equivalent, for perhaps the stipulated [wage] is excessive, and proving it by a negating oath is far-fetched.

If we say he does not deserve it, then he claims the wage against the owner: if he [the owner] takes the oath, it is dropped; but if he refuses (nakala), is the oath renewed against him? Al-Qāḍī Ḥusayn, may God have mercy on him, said: No, for there is no benefit in repetition, as if his previous oath was suspended upon the refusal so that it might become a proof. The second [view] is that the oath is repeated, for there is no precedent of presenting the oath before the refusal in matters of affirmation.

And if we branch upon [the view] that the statement is that of the owner — then he takes an oath that he permitted him [to sew] the shirt, not the cloak; the wage is dropped from him; and he deserves the liability (ḍamān), because when permission is negated, the principle is liability. Regarding the extent of liability, there are two opinions: One is the difference between the cut [cloth] and the uncut; the second is the difference between the cut-as-shirt and the cut-as-cloak, because this amount was permitted. And this depends upon [the question of] whether the agent (wakīl), when liable in a sale, has deducted from him what people ordinarily overlook (taghābun) — for it is as if permitted, had the sale been completed.

Then, whenever the hireling does not take the wage, he has the right to remove the thread (khayṭ) if it is his property.

And if we branch upon mutual oath-taking: when they both take oaths, the wage is dropped. But is the liability dropped? There are two opinions: One is no, for the benefit of mutual oath-taking is the nullification of the contract and reversion to what preceded it. The second — and it is the more correct (aṣaḥḥ) — is that it is dropped, because he took an oath negating the transgression (ʿudwān), namely the sewing [of the cloak]; and had he refused, nothing would have been incumbent upon him except the liability — so let his oath have a benefit.

— Peace be upon him — The third chapter: On the contingencies (ṭawāriʾ) that necessitate rescission (faskh) — Peace be upon him — and it comprises three divisions:

The first: What diminishes the benefit (manfaʿah) among defects (ʿuyūb). These are a ground for the option (khiyār) before taking possession (qabḍ) and after taking possession — because even if one has taken possession of the house or the beast, the benefits have not yet been taken possession of. Yes, the taking possession of the locus of benefits (maḥall al-manāfiʿ) has been made to stand in the place of taking possession of the sold item (mabīʿ) regarding: the empowerment over the hire (taslīṭ ʿalā al-ijārah); the obligation of delivering the vulva (taslīm al-baḍʿ) if the benefit is a dower (ṣadāq); and the occurrence of emancipation (itq) if the benefit is the installments of a kitābah (nujūm kitābah). This is due to necessity (ḍarūrah) — and there is no necessity in negating the option for defect. And a defect is everything that affects the benefit with an effect by which the disparity in the wage becomes apparent, even if no disparity in the value of the slave-body (raqabah) becomes apparent thereby — for the object of the contract is the benefit.

chapters.title_en: Four Subsidiary Branches and Total Loss of Utility
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع أربعة

أحدها أن عذر المستأجر في نفسه لا يسلط على الفسخ كما إذا  استأجر دابة
لسفر فمرض أو حماما فتعذر عليه الوقود أو حانوتا فاحترف بحرفة أخرى فإنه لا
خلل في المعقود عليه
وقال أبو حنيفة يثبت الفسخ بهذه المعاذير
الثاني لو استرم الجدار فهو عيب
فلو بادر المكري إلى الإصلاح لم يثبت الفسخ وإنما الخيار إذا امتنع عن
العمارة أو افتقر إلى تعطيل مدة فإن رضي المكتري دون الإصلاح فالصحيح أنه
يلزمه تمام الأجرة
الثالث إذا أكرى أرضا للزراعة ففسد الزرع يحائحة من برد أو صاعقة لم يثبت
بالفسخ ولا ينقص شئ من الأجرة لأن الأرض لم تتعيب وإنما النازلة نزلت بملكه
وإن أفسدت الجائحة الأرض وأبطلت فيها قوة الإنبات ثم فسد الزرع بعده
فيفسخ العقد فيما بقي من الزمان
والظاهر أنه يسترد أجرة ما سبق إذ كان موقوفا على الآجر فإن أول الزراعة
غير مقصود ولم يسلم له الآجر
وإن أفسد الأرض بعد إفساد الزرع فالظاهر أنه لا يسترد شيئا لأنه لو بقيت
صلاحية الأرض وقوتها لم يكن للمستأجر فيها فائدة بعد فوات زرعه
الرابع مهما أثبتنا له الخيار فإن رضي فالصحيح أنه مأخوذ بتمام الأجرة
وإن فسخ فالصحيح أنه لا ينفسخ فيما مضى وتوزع الأجرة المسماة
على قدر أجرة المثل في المدتين لا على المدة

### | القسم الثاني فوات المنفعة الكلية

فموت الدابة المعينة والعبد المعين للعمل يوجب انفساخ الإجارة إن وقع عقب
العقد
وإن مضت مدة انفسخ بالإضافة إلى الباقي
وبالإضافة إلى الماضي يخرج على نظيره في تفريق الصفقة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ذ-ر (ʿ-dh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Excuse, impediment arising from the agent's own condition, not from the object of contract
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A legal concession (rukhṣah) due to unforeseen hardship, distinct from defect in the contracted thing (maʿqūd ʿalayh)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — a genuine excuse; metaphorical — pretext without substantive ground
- Root: ج-و-ح (j-w-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Calamity that devastates property or crops (āfah)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine affliction striking the lessee's own domain (milk), not the leased object
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical destruction; metaphorical — nullification of benefit
- Root: ف-س-خ (f-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Annulment, dissolution of a contract
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Rescission ab initio versus termination pro futuro
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — unbinding a knot; metaphorical — legal rescission
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — "If he consents... then" (fa-in raḍiya... fa-) establishes legal consequence contingent upon choice, with the apodosis governing the entire protasis.
chapters.translation:
### Four Subsidiary Branches

**First:** An excuse pertaining to the lessee's own person does not authorize rescission. For example, if he hires a mount for a journey and then falls ill, or hires a bathhouse and then finds fuel unavailable to him, or hires a shop and then takes up a different trade — in all these cases there is no defect in the contracted object. Abū Ḥanīfah held that rescission is established by such excuses.

**Second:** If the wall leans (i.e., becomes liable to collapse), this constitutes a defect. If the lessor hastens to repair it, rescission is not established. The option (khiyār) arises only when he refuses to repair, or when repair requires a period of closure. If the lessee consents to accept the premises without repair, the correct ruling (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that he remains liable for the full rent.

**Third:** If one leases land for cultivation, and the crop is ruined by a calamity (jāʾiḥah) of cold or lightning, rescission is not established, nor is any portion of the rent abated — because the land itself has not become defective; rather, the calamity befell what is within the lessee's own ownership. But if the calamity damaged the land itself, destroying its power of germination, and the crop then perished thereafter, the contract is rescinded with respect to the remaining period of the term. The apparent position (al-ẓāhir) is that he recovers the rent for the elapsed period, since that rent was suspended upon the benefit (al-ujrah), and the beginning of cultivation was not the intended purpose, nor was the benefit delivered to him. If the land was damaged after the crop had already been ruined, the apparent position is that he recovers nothing — because even if the land's suitability and power had remained, the lessee would have had no benefit in it after the loss of his crop.

**Fourth:** Whenever we establish the option for him, if he consents, the correct ruling is that he is held to the full rent. If he rescinds, the correct ruling is that the contract does not dissolve with respect to the past period; rather, the named rent is apportioned according to the rate of equivalent rent (ujrat al-mithl) for the two periods — not according to the mere duration of time.

### Section Two: Total Loss of Utility

The death of a specific animal, or of a specific slave designated for work, necessitates the dissolution of the lease (ijārah) if it occurs immediately after the contract. If a period of the term has already elapsed, the contract dissolves with respect to the remaining portion. With respect to the elapsed portion, the ruling follows the parallel case of splitting a single sale (tafrīq al-ṣafqah).

chapters.title_en: Section 261 — Branches on Termination of Lease Due to Loss of the Object or Impediment to Benefit
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع

الأول إذا انهدمت الدار نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن الإجارة تنفسخ وإذا
انقطع شرب الأرض المستأجرة للزراعة نص أن يثبت الخيار
فقال الأصحاب فيه قولان بالنقل والتخريج
أحدهما الانفساخ إذ فاتت المنفعة المقصودة
والثاني ثبوت الخيار إذ الأرض على الجملة تبقى منتفعا بها بوجه ما ومنهم
من قرر النصين وفرق بأن الدار لم تبق دارا بعد الانهدام والأرض بقيت أرضا
فإن قلنا له الخيار فأجاز فهل يجيز بكل الأجرة أم يحط قسط لأجل الشرب فيه
وجهان
وهذا أيضا يضاهي  التردد في أن اللبن مقصود مع الحضانة أو هو تابع
ولو كان عود الماء متوقعا فلم يفسخ ثم بعد ذلك أراد الفسخ إذا لم يعد فله
ذلك وهو كالمرأة إذا أخرت الفسخ بعد ثبوت إعسار الزوج ومضي مدة الإيلاء
الثاني إذا مات الصبي الذى استؤجر على إرضاعه أو العبد الذى استؤجر على
تعليمه أو تلف الثوب الذى استؤجر على خياطته ففي الانفساخ وجهان ذكرناهما
أحدهما أنه لا ينفسخ لأنه كالمستوفي فأشبه موت العاقدين فإنه لا يوجب
الفسخ عندنا
والثاني نعم بل هو كموت الأجير لأن الغرض يختلف به
وقد نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه على أنه لو أصدقها خياطة ثوب فتلف الثوب
رجعت إلى مهر المثل وهو حكم بالانفساخ
وفيه وجه ثالث وهو الأعدل وهو أنهما إن لم يتشاحا في الإبدال استمر العقد
وإلا ثبت الفسخ
الثالث إذا غصبت الدار المستأجرة حتى مضت مدة الإجارة قال المراوزة ينفسخ
العقد
وذكر العراقيون قولين أحدهما أنه ينفسخ والثاني للمستأجر الخيار
فإن أجاز طالب الغاصب بالأجرة كالبيع إذا أتلفه أجنبي قبل القبض
وهذا بخلاف المنكوحة إذا وطئت بشبهة فإن البدل لا يصرف إلى
الزوج لأن النكاح لا يوجب حقا في المال بخلاف منفعة الإجارة هذا إذا مضت
المدة
وأما في ابتداء الغصب فكما جرى يثبت الخيار للمكتري لأنه تأخر حقه بعد
التعيين
ولو ادعى الغاصب ملك الرقبة لنفسه فاللمكري حق المخاصمة
قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه وليس للمكتري حق المخاصمة لأنه لو أقر ما كنت
أقبل إقراره
وذكر المراوزة وجها منقاسا أنه يخاصم لطلب المنفعة وإن كان لا يقبل
إقراره في الرقبة
فلو أقر المكري بالدار للغاصب فإن قلنا يصح بيعه نفذ إقراره
وإن قلنا لا يصح بيعه ففي إقراره من الخلاف ما في إقرار الراهن
فإن قبلنا إقراره ففي سقوط استحقاق المستأجر من المنفعة ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها يسقط تابعا للرقبة
والثاني لا لأنه التزم حقه في المنفعة فلا يقدر على إبطاله
والثالث إن كانت الدار في يد المكتري لا تزايل يده إلى  مضي المدة وإن
كانت في يد المقر له فلا تنزع من يده أيضا
الرابع إذا هرب الجمال بجماله فقد تعذرت المنفعة
فإن ورد العقد على العين فله الفسخ وإذا مضت المدة انفسخ
وإن ورد على الذمة فللقاضي أن يستأجر عليه استقراضا إلى أن يرجع وإن كان
له مال باع فيه
وإن ترك جماله استوفيت منفعتها والقاضي ينفق عليها
فإن انفق المكتري بنفسه ففي رجوعه عند العجز عن القاضي خلاف ذكرناه في
المساقاة
وحيث قضينا بالانفساخ في موت الدابة والعبد والغصب أردنا به ما إذا وردت
الإجارة على العين
فإن وردت على الذمة فلا تنفسخ ولكن يطالب بالتوفية من عين أخرى
الخامس إذا حبس المكتري الدابة التى استأجرها استقرت عليه الأجرة وإن لم
يستعملها مهما مضت المدة في حبسه سواء كانت الإجارة وردت على عين الدابة أو
على الذمة وسلمت الدابة
فأما المكري إذا حبس ولم يسلم انفسخت الإجارة إن كان قد عين مدة وإن لم
تكن المدة معينة فوجهان
أحدهما نعم ينفسخ كما تستقر به الأجرة في حبس المكتري
والثاني لا ينفسخ بل يقال تأخر حقه فله الخيار إن شاء لأن الوقت غير
متعين
السادس التلف الموجب للانفساخ أو للخيار موجب حكمه وإن صدر من المكتري
ولكنه ضامن
وهو كما لو جبت المرأة زوجها ضمنت وثبت لها فسخ النكاح

### | القسم الثالث ما يمنع من استيفاء المنفعة شرعا

فهو أيضا موجب للانفساخ كما لو استأجر على قلع سن فسكن الألم أو قطع يد
فسلمت اليد أو ليقطع يد من عليه القصاص فعفا انفسخت الإجارة في الكل لأن
الفوات شرعا كالفوات حسا إلا عند من يرى الإبدال في مثل هذه الأمور وتيسر
الإبدال
chapters.anchors:
- Root: هدم (hadama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To demolish, pull down, causing structural collapse; the essence of a building (dār) is its walls and roof.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Physical annihilation of the 'ayn (substance) that is the locus of the leased benefit (manfaʿah); contrasts with mere defect.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — literal destruction of the structure; majāz would be figurative ruin (e.g., of reputation), not intended here.
- Root: شرب (shirb)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Watering right, irrigation share for cultivated land; the vital supply enabling agricultural yield.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intended benefit (manfaʿah maqṣūdah) in a lease for farming; its loss negates the purpose of the contract.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the water itself; here used metonymically for the benefit of irrigation, not the water as a corporeal thing.
- Root: غصب (ghaṣb)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Usurpation, taking property by force or wrongfully; entails liability (ḍamān) for the usurper.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Wrongful seizure that suspends the owner's/lessee's access; jurisprudentially triggers either termination or option (khiyār).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical seizure; extended to any wrongful deprivation of benefit.
- Root: حبس (ḥabs)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Detention, imprisonment, withholding; keeping something from its rightful user.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In lease law — the lessor's failure to deliver (taslīm) or the lessee's retention after delivery; affects rent liability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal confinement; here applied to legal detention of the leased object.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Disjunctive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-taqsīm) — The text uses "إذا" (idhā) for factual conditionals and "فإن" (fa-in) for hypothetical alternatives, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to track the branching legal rulings (wujūh).
chapters.translation:
### | Branches

**First:** If the house collapses, al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) explicitly ruled that the lease is dissolved (tansakhu). And if the irrigation water of land leased for agriculture is cut off, he explicitly ruled that an option (khiyār) is established. The companions (al-aṣḥāb) then stated two opinions, one transmitted and one derived:
- First: dissolution, because the intended benefit has been lost.
- Second: establishment of the option, because the land, in general, remains utilizable in some manner.
Among them is one who reconciled the two explicit rulings and distinguished: the house, after collapse, no longer remains a house, whereas the land remains land.

If we say he has the option and he ratifies the lease, does he ratify it for the full rent, or is a portion deducted for the [loss of] irrigation? There are two views. This also resembles the hesitation over whether the wet-nurse's milk is an intended purpose alongside custody or merely subordinate to it.

If the return of the water was expected, and he did not rescind, then afterward he wishes to rescind when it does not return — he has that right. This is like the woman who delays the dissolution [of marriage] after the husband's insolvency (iʿsār) is established and the period of īlā' (vow of abstinence) has elapsed.

**Second:** If the infant hired for wet-nursing dies, or the slave hired for teaching dies, or the garment hired for tailoring is destroyed — regarding dissolution there are two views we have mentioned:
- First: it does not dissolve, because [the benefit] is like one already received (kā-l-mustawfā), thus resembling the death of the two contracting parties, which does not necessitate dissolution in our school.
- Second: rather, it does dissolve, because it is like the death of the hired worker (ajīr), since the purpose varies with it.
Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) explicitly ruled: if a man gives as dower (ṣadāq) the tailoring of a garment, and the garment is destroyed, she returns to the equivalent dower (mahr al-mithl) — and this is a ruling of dissolution.
There is a third view, which is the most balanced: if the two parties do not dispute over substitution (ibdāl), the contract continues; otherwise, dissolution is established.

**Third:** If the leased house is usurped (ghuṣibat) until the entire lease term elapses, the Marwazīs said: the contract dissolves. The Iraqis mentioned two opinions: one that it dissolves, and the second that the lessee has the option. If he ratifies, he claims the rent from the usurper — like a sale when a third party destroys the object before delivery. This differs from the case of a married woman who is intercourse with under a mistaken claim (shubhah): the compensation is not directed to the husband, because marriage does not establish a right over property, unlike the benefit in a lease. This applies when the term has elapsed.

As for at the inception of the usurpation, as previously discussed, the option is established for the lessee because his right is delayed after being specified. If the usurper claims ownership of the corpus (raqabah) for himself, the lessor has the right of litigation. Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: the lessee has no right of litigation, because if [the lessee] were to admit [the usurper's claim], I would not accept his admission. The Marwazīs mentioned a derived view (wajh munqās): he may litigate to claim the benefit, even if his admission regarding the corpus is not accepted.

If the lessor admits that the house belongs to the usurper: if we hold that his sale is valid, his admission is effective; if we hold that his sale is not valid, then his admission is subject to the same dispute as the admission of a pledgor (rāhin). If we accept his admission, then regarding the fall of the lessee's entitlement to the benefit there are three views:
- First: it falls, as subordinate to the corpus.
- Second: it does not fall, because he [the lessor] had obligated himself for the benefit and cannot annul it.
- Third: if the house is in the lessee's possession, it is not removed from his hand until the term elapses; and if it is in the possession of the one in whose favor admission was made, it is likewise not seized from his hand.

**Fourth:** If the camel-driver (jammāl) flees with his camel, the benefit has become impossible. If the contract was upon the specific 'ayn (the camel), he has the option to rescind, and when the term elapses it dissolves. If the contract was upon the dhimmah (liability), the judge may hire another on his behalf by way of borrowing (istiqrāḍ) until he returns; and if he has property, it is sold for that purpose. If he abandons his camel, its benefit is utilized and the judge spends upon it. If the lessee himself spends [on the camel], then regarding his recourse when the judge is unable [to cover it], there is the dispute we mentioned in the chapter on musāqāh (sharecropping).

Wherever we rule dissolution due to the death of the animal, the slave, or usurpation, we mean when the lease was upon the specific 'ayn. If it was upon the dhimmah, it does not dissolve; rather, he is pursued for fulfillment from another specific 'ayn.

**Fifth:** If the lessee detains (ḥabasa) the animal he leased, the rent is firmly established against him even if he does not use it, as long as the term elapses during his detention — whether the lease was upon the specific animal or upon the dhimmah, provided the animal was delivered. As for the lessor: if he detains and does not deliver, the lease dissolves if a term was specified. If the term was not specified, there are two views:
- First: yes, it dissolves, just as the rent becomes firmly established upon the lessee's detention.
- Second: it does not dissolve; rather, it is said his right is delayed, so he has the option if he wishes, because the time is not specified.

**Sixth:** The destruction that necessitates dissolution or the option necessitates its ruling even if it originates from the lessee's act — but he is liable (ḍāmin). This is like the case of a woman who kills her husband: she is liable, yet the dissolution of the marriage is established for her.

### | Third Category: What Prevents the Extraction of Benefit by Sacred Law (Sharʿan)

This too necessitates dissolution — as when one hires [a surgeon] to extract a tooth and the pain subsides, or to cut off a hand and the hand is saved, or to amputate the hand of one upon whom qiṣāṣ (retaliation) is due and the victim pardons — the lease dissolves in all these cases, because legal loss (al-fawāt sharʿan) is like physical loss (al-fawāt ḥissan), except for those who hold substitution (ibdāl) in such matters when substitution is readily available.

chapters.title_en: Four Subsidiary Branches and the Book of Reward (Juʿālah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع أربعة

الأول إذا أجر الوقف المرتب على البطون ومات ففي انفساخ الإجارة وجهان
أحدهما لا لأنه عاقد والإجارة لا تنفسخ بموت العاقد فعلى هذا البطن
الثاني يرجع في تركته بأجرة المدة الباقية
والثاني وهو الأظهر أنه ينفسخ إذ بان أن بإجارته تناول ما لا حق فيه
وفي إلزام  إجارته على من بعده من البطون ضرر ظاهر بخلاف الوارث
فإنه يلزمه تسليم الدار المكراة لأنه يأخذ الملك من المورث ولم يملك إلا
دارا لا منفعة لها
الثاني إذا آجر الصبي أو ماله على وفق الغبطة مدة تزيد على مدة الصبى فهو
باطل في القدر الفاضل وفي القدر الباقي ينبني على تفريق الصفقة وإن كان
متقاصرا عن سن بلوغه صحت الإجارة
فإن بلغ قبل السن بالاحتلام ففي انفساخ الإجارة وجهان
الأظهر أنه لا ينفسخ لأنه وليه وقد نظر له والأجرة قد سلمت له
والثاني أنه ينفسخ إذ بان أنه تناول يعقدة ما خرج عن محل ولايته
الثالث إذا آجر عبدا ثم أعتقه قبل مضي المدة صح العتق كما لو زوج جارية
ثم أعتقها إذ لا يناقض الإجارة العتق
والمذهب المقطوع به أنه لا تنفسخ الإجارة
وفيه وجه ذكره صاحب التقريب أنه ينفسخ كموت البطن الأول
نعم اختلفوا فيما للعبد فمنهم من قال له الخيار وهو أيضا بعيد في المذهب
بل الصحيح استمرار الإجارة على اللزوم
وفي رجوع العبد بأجرة مثله على السيد وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأنه فوته بعد الحرية والمنفعة حدثت على ملك العبد
والثاني لا وكأنه كالمستوفى في حالة الرق
فإن قلنا لا يرجع بالأجرة ففي نفقته وجهان
أحدهما على السيد وكأنه استبقى حبسه مع العتق
والثاني على بيت المال فإن الملك قد زال وهو فقير في نفسه
الرابع إذا باع الدار المستأجرة من أجنبي قبل مضي مدة الإجارة ففيه قولان
أظهرهما الصحة وكأن المنافع مستثناة
ولو استثنى المنافع لنفسه مدة فهو على هذا الخلاف ويشهد لجواز الاستثناء
حديث ورد فيه وإن كان القياس يقتضي البطلان
ولو انفسخت الإجارة بعذر في بقية المدة فالمنفعة الباقية للمشتري أو
للبائع فيه وجهان
أحدهما للمشتري فإنه يحدث على ملكه بعد انفساخ الإجارة
والثاني لا لأنه كان للمستأجر فيعود بفسخه إلى العاقد للإجارة لا غير أما
إذا باعها من المستأجر فالظاهر الصحة وتستوفى المنفعة في بقية المدة بحكم
الإجارة
وفيه وجه آخر أنه  تنفسخ الإجارة كما لو اشترى زوجته فإن ملك العين أقوى
في إفادة المنفعة من الإجارة فيدفع الأضعف
أما إذا أجر المستأجر الدار المستأجرة من المالك صح على الظاهر
وعلى قولنا ملك العين والإجارة لا يجتمعان لا يصح أصلا
= كتاب الجعالة=
وهي معاملة صحيحة لقوله سبحانه وتعالى {ولمن جاء به حمل بعير وأنا به
زعيم}
ولما روي أن قوما من أصحابه صلى الله عليه وسلم نزلوا بحي من أحياء العرب
فلدغ سيدهم فالتمسوا منهم رقية فأبوا إلا بجعل فجعلوا لهم قطيعا من الشاة
ومضى إليهم واحد وقرأ أم القرآن وتفل فيه بلعابه فبرئ فسلم القطيع فقالوا
لا نأخذ حتى نسأل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فحكي ذلك له فضحك وقال
ما أدراك أنها رقية خذوها واضربوا لي فيها بسهم
ويتأيد ذلك بالحاجة إذ قد تمس الحاجة إلى ذلك في رد عبد آبق أو ضالة وما
لا يدرى من الذى تعذر عليه

### | والنظر في أحكامها وأركانها أما الأركان فأربعة

الركن الأول الصيغة وهي قول المستعمل من رد عبدي الآبق أو ضالتي أو عمل
العمل الذى يريده مما يجوز فعله ويستباح فله دينار أو ما يريد صح العقد ولم
يشترط القبول لفظا بل اكل من سمعه اشترك في حكمه فمن قام بالعمل استحق
ولو لم يصدر منه لفظ فرد إنسان عبده الآبق أو عمل له عملا لم يستحق شيئا
لأنه متبرع
ولو قال رد عبدي ولم يقطع له أجرة فرد ففي استحقاقه ما ذكرناه في استعمال
القصار والدلاك والمزين
وكذا إذا نادى ولكن رد العبد من لم يسمع نداءه فلا يستحق شيئا لأن النداء
يتناول من سمع وهو قصد التبرع به
وكذا الفضولي إذا كذب وقال قال فلان من رد عبدي فله دينار فرده إنسان لا
يستحق لا على المالك ولا على الفضولي
ولو قال من رد عبد فلان فله دينار وجب على الفضولي لأنه ضمنه بقوله

### | الركن الثاني العاقد

ولا يشترط في الجاعل إلا أهلية الاستئجار ولا في المجعول له إلا  أهلية
العمل ولا يشترط التعيين إذ يخالف اشتراط تعيين الشخص مصلحة العقد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف ر ع (f-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Branching off from a trunk; subsidiary offshoot (farʿ) as opposed to root (aṣl)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A derivative ruling that follows from an established principle
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — a branch of a tree; metaphorical — a legal sub-case derived from a primary case
- Root: ج ع ل (j-ʿ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Making, appointing, or stipulating a reward for a service
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A contractual reward (juʿālah) where one party undertakes to pay a specified compensation for a specified result
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — placing/setting; metaphorical — the act of offering a prize or wage for a task
- Root: ف س خ (f-s-kh)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Annulment, dissolution, cancellation
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Termination of a contract due to a legal impediment or discovered defect
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — erasing/unstitching; metaphorical — rescinding a binding agreement
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Dual Predication (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — the protasis (e.g., "if he dies") governs the apodosis, which may carry two divergent legal verdicts (wajhān) depending on the underlying ratio legis.
chapters.translation:
I say: [This section comprises] four subsidiary branches.

**The First Branch:** If the administrator of an endowment (waqf) that is arranged in successive layers (al-buṭūn) leases it out, and then dies, there are two positions (wajhān) concerning whether the lease is annulled. One of them is that it is not annulled, because he is the contracting party, and a lease is not annulled by the death of the contracting party. On this basis, the second layer (al-baṭn al-thānī) recovers from his estate the rent for the remaining period. The second position — and it is the more manifest (al-aẓhar) — is that it is annulled, for it has become evident that through his leasing he disposed of something in which he had no right. And imposing his lease upon the subsequent layers would entail manifest harm — unlike the case of the heir, for the heir is bound to hand over the leased house because he takes ownership from the testator, and he has not inherited anything but a house devoid of usufruct.

**The Second Branch:** If a guardian leases out a minor, or his property, in accordance with the minor's best interest (ʿalā waqf al-ghibṭah) for a period exceeding the duration of the minor's minority, then [the lease] is void with respect to the excess portion. As for the remaining portion, [its validity] turns on the principle of splitting a single transaction (tafrīq al-ṣafqah). If [the minor] is close to the age of majority, the lease is valid. If he reaches majority before that age through nocturnal emission (al-iḥtilām), then there are two positions concerning the annulment of the lease. The more manifest is that it is not annulled, because [the guardian] is his legal guardian, has acted in his interest, and the rent has already been delivered to him. The second is that it is annulled, for it has become evident that he executed a contract concerning what lay outside the domain of his guardianship.

**The Third Branch:** If a man leases out a slave, then emancipates him before the expiry of the term, the emancipation is valid — just as if he married off a slave-girl and then emancipated her, for emancipation does not contradict the lease. The definitive position of the school (al-madhhab al-maqṭūʿ bihī) is that the lease is not annulled. There is, however, a position mentioned by the author of al-Taqrīb that it is annulled, like the death of the first layer [in the endowment case]. Indeed, they differed concerning what the slave is entitled to. Some said he has the option (al-khiyār), but this too is remote in the school. Rather, the correct view is that the lease continues in its binding force (al-luzūm). Concerning whether the slave may recover from the master the equivalent rent (ujrat al-mithl), there are two positions. One is that yes, he may, because [the master] caused him to forfeit it after [his] freedom, and the usufruct arose while the slave was in possession of it. The second is that no, he may not, as though [the usufruct] were already consumed during the state of slavery. If we say he does not recover the rent, then concerning his maintenance (nafaqah) there are two positions. One is that it falls upon the master, as though he had retained his detention along with the emancipation. The second is that it falls upon the public treasury (bayt al-māl), for ownership has ceased and he is poor in himself.

**The Fourth Branch:** If the owner sells the leased house to a third party before the expiry of the lease term, there are two positions (qawlān). The more manifest of them is its validity, as though the usufructs were excepted [from the sale]. If he explicitly excepts the usufructs for himself for the term, it falls under this same disagreement. A hadith supports the permissibility of such an exception, even though analogical reasoning (al-qiyās) would dictate its nullity. If the lease is annulled due to an excuse (ʿudhr) for the remainder of the term, then whether the remaining usufruct belongs to the purchaser or to the seller involves two positions. One is that it belongs to the purchaser, for it arises within his ownership after the annulment of the lease. The second is that it does not, because it belonged to the lessee, and its annulment returns it only to the original contracting party of the lease, and no other. As for the case where he sells it to the lessee himself, the manifest view is its validity, and the usufruct is enjoyed for the remainder of the term by virtue of the lease. There is another position that the lease is annulled — just as if a man purchased his own wife [while married], for ownership of the substance (milk al-ʿayn) is stronger in conferring usufruct than a lease, so the weaker is repelled. As for the case where the lessee subleases the rented house from the owner, it is valid on the manifest view. On our position that ownership of the substance and lease cannot coexist, it is not valid at all.

**The Book of Reward (Juʿālah)**

It is a valid transaction, by virtue of His saying, the Exalted: {«وَلِمَن جَاءَ بِهِ حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ وَأَنَا بِهِ زَعِيمٌ»} ("And for whoever brings it, a camel-load [of grain], and I am its guarantor"). And by virtue of what has been related that a group of his Companions, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, alighted upon one of the Arab tribes, and their chieftain was stung [by a scorpion]. They sought a ruqyah (incantation) from them, but they refused unless given a reward (juʿl). So they stipulated for them a flock of sheep. One of them went forth, recited the Mother of the Qur'an, and spat upon him with his saliva, and he was cured. They handed over the flock, but [the Companions] said: "We will not take it until we ask the Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him." This was related to him, and he laughed and said: "What made you know that it is a ruqyah? Take it, and give me a share in it." This is further supported by necessity, for need may arise for this in recovering a runaway slave or a lost item, where it is unknown who will be able to accomplish it.

**The consideration is in its rulings and its pillars. As for the pillars, they are four.**

**The First Pillar: The Formula (al-ṣīghah).** It is the utterance of the employer (al-mustaʿmil): "Whoever returns my runaway slave, or my lost item, or performs the work he desires — of what is permissible to do and lawful to benefit from — shall have a dinar," or whatever he specifies. The contract is valid, and acceptance (al-qabūl) is not required verbally. Rather, everyone who hears it shares in its ruling; whoever performs the work becomes entitled [to the reward]. If no utterance issues from him — e.g., a man returns his runaway slave or performs work for him — he is entitled to nothing, because he is a volunteer (mutabarriʿ). If he says: "Return my slave" without stipulating a wage, and he returns him, then concerning his entitlement [to the equivalent wage], [the ruling] is what we mentioned in the case of employing a washer, a masseur, and a barber. Likewise, if he makes a public announcement, but the one who returns the slave did not hear the announcement, he is entitled to nothing, because the announcement addresses only those who hear it, and [the non-hearer] intended volunteering. Likewise, an unauthorized intermediary (al-fuḍūlī) who lies and says: "So-and-so said: 'Whoever returns my slave shall have a dinar,'" and someone returns him — he is entitled to nothing, neither from the owner nor from the intermediary. If he says: "Whoever returns the slave of so-and-so shall have a dinar," it is binding upon the intermediary, because he has guaranteed it by his utterance.

**The Second Pillar: The Contracting Party (al-ʿāqid).** For the offeror of the reward (al-jāʿil), only the capacity to hire (ahliyyat al-istīʾjār) is required. For the one to whom the reward is offered (al-majʿūl lahū), only the capacity to perform the work is required. Specific designation (al-taʿyīn) is not required, for requiring the designation of a specific person would contradict the very purpose of the contract.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الركن الثالث العمل

وهو كل ما يجوز الاستئجار عليه ولكن لا يشترط كونه معلوما فإن رد الآبق
لا ينضبط العمل فيه وكان ينقدح أن يشترط كون العمل مجهولا ولا يتقدر
كالمضاربة ولكن قطع العراقيون بأنه لو قال من بني حائطي أو خاط ثوبي فله
كذا أن ذلك لا يجوز
وكذا إذا قال أول من يحج عني فله دينار استحق الدينار هذا رواه المزني عن
الشافعي رضي الله عنه في المنثور ثم قال المزني ينبغي أن يستحق أجرة المثل
لأنه إجارة فلا يصح بغير تعيين
وهذا يدل على أن المزني اعتقد اختصاص الجعالة بالمجهول الذى لا يستأجر
عليه
وقد نسب العراقيون المزني إلى الغلط فيه وقالوا هذه جعالة

### | الركن الرابع الجعل

وشرطه أن يكون مالا معلوما فلو شرط مجهولا فسد واستحق العامل
أجرة المثل كما في المضاربة الفاسدة

### | فروع ثلاثة

أحدها لو قال من رد عبدي من البصرة فله دينار وهو ببغداد فرده من نصف
الطريق استحق نصف الدينار
ومن الثلث الثلث لأنه قدر المسافة
وإن رد من مكان أبعد لم يستحق للزيادة شيئا لأنه لم يشترط عليه شيئا
الثاني إذا قال من رد عبدي فله دينار فاشترك في رده اثنان اشتركا في
الجعل
وإن عين شخصا وقال إن رددت فلك دينار فشاركه غيره وقال قصدت معاونه
العامل استحق العامل الدينار وإن قال قصدت المساهمة فللعامل نصف الدينار
ولا شئ للمعين فإنه لم يشرط له شئ
الثالث إذا قال لأحدهما إن رددت عبدي فلله دينار وقال لآخر إن رددت فلك
دينار فاشتركا فلكل واحد نصف ما شرط له وإن شرط لأحدهما دينارا وللآخر ثوبا
مجهولا فاشتركا استحق من شرط له الدينار نصفه وللآخر نصف أجرة المثل

### | أما أحكامها فأربعة

الأول أنه جائز من الجانبين كالمضاربة إذ لا يليق بها اللزوم ثم إن فسخه
المالك قبل العمل انفسخ
وإن كان بعد الشروع في العمل وقبل الفراغ انفسخ ولزمه أجرة المثل
وإن كان بعد الفراغ من العمل فلا معنى للفسخ
الثاني جواز الزيادة والنقصان
فلو قال من رد عبدي فله عشرة ثم قال من رد عبدي فله دينار فمن رده استحق
الدينار وكذا على العكس والاعتبار بالأخير
فإن لم يسمع العامل النداء الناقص الأخير فينقدح أن يقال يرجع إلى أجرة
المثل
الثالث أن العامل لا يستحق شيئا إلا بالفراغ من العمل فلو رد العبد إلى
باب داره فهرب أو مات قبل التسليم لم يستحق شيئا لأن المقصود قد فات وهو
الرد
الرابع لو تنازعا في أصل شرط الجعل فأنكره المالك أو في عين عبد فأنكر
المالك الشرط فيه وقال إنه شرط في عبد غيره أو أنكر المالك سعيه في الرد
وقال رجع العبد بنفسه فالقول في ذلك كله قول المالك فإن العامل مدع فليثبت
وإن اختلفا في مقدار المشروط تحالفا ورجع إلى أجرة المثل كما في الإجارة
= كتاب إحياء الموات = وفيه ثلاثة أبواب
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في تملك الأراضي - صلى الله عليه
وسلم - وفيه فصلان
الأول فيما يملك من الأراضي بالإحياء وهي الموات
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم
من أحيا أرضا ميتة فهي له
والموات هى الأرض المنفكة عن الاختصاصات
والاختصاصات ستة أنواع

### | النوع الأول العمارة

فكل أرض معمورة فهي محياة فلا تتملك بالإحياء سواء كان ذلك من دار
الإسلام أو دار الحرب
وإن اندرست العمارة وبقي أثرها فإن كان من عمارة الإسلام فلا تملك لأنه
موروث عمن ملكه فينتظر صاحبه أو يحفظ لبيت المال ويتصرف الإمام فيه
كما يتصرف في مال ضائع لا يتعين مالكه
وإن كان من عمارات الجاهلية وعلم وجه دخولها في يد المسلمين إما بطريق
الاغتنام أو الفئ استصحب ذلك الحكم ولم تتملك بالإحياء وإن وقع اليأس عن
معرفته فقولان
أحدهما يتملك إذ لا حرمة لعمارة الكفار فصار كركازهم
والثاني لا لأنه دخل في يد أهل الإسلام فالأصل سبق ملك عليه وأما الركاز
فحكمه حكم لقطة معرضة للضياع
هذا حكم دار الإسلام أما دار  الحرب فمعمورها كسائر أموالهم يملك
بالاغتنام
وأما مواتها فما لا يدفعون المسلمين عنها فهو كموات دار الإسلام يتملك
بالإحياء ويفارقها في أمر وهو أن الكافر لو أحياها ملكها
ولو أحيا موات دار الإسلام لم يملكها عندنا خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله
لأن لأهل الإسلام اختصاصا بحكم الإضافة إلى الدار
أما ما يدفعون المسلمين عنه فلو أحياها مسلم وقدر على الإقامة ملكه وإن
استولى عليها بعض الغانمين وقصدوا الاختصاص بها فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها انه يفيدهم الاختصاص بالاستيلاء ما يفيد التحجر كما سيأتي
والثاني أنه يفيدهم الملك في الحال لأن مال الكفار يملك بالاستيلاء
والثالث أنه لا يفيد الملك لأنه ليس ملك الكفار وإنما هو موات ولا اختصاص
لأنه لا يحجر وإنما هو مجرد يد فهو كمجرد الاستيلاء على موات دار الإسلام

- Root: ع-م-ل (ʿamila)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exertion of effort in a task; the act itself as a locus of compensation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, ʿamal is the deliberate act (fiʿl) that may be commissioned; its knowability (maʿlūmiyyah) is a condition in hire (ijārah) but not in reward (juʿl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical exertion; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to mental or unspecified tasks.
- Root: ج-ع-ل (jaʿala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To make, appoint, or stipulate a thing; the reward (juʿl) is that which is placed as compensation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A stipulated recompense (ʿiwaḍ) for a specified or unspecified service; distinct from ujrah (hire) in that it need not be predetermined in scope.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the act of setting; metaphorical for the contractual reward, emphasizing its conditional nature.
- Root: أ-ج-ر (ajara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Recompense, wage, or hire; the countervalue for a service.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ujrat al-mithl (equivalent wage) is the equitable standard when a contract is vitiated (fāsid) or unspecified.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for monetary hire; metaphorical for divine reward, but here strictly juristic.
- Root: ح-ي-ي (ḥayiya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To live; iḥyāʾ (revival) of land means rendering it productive.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iḥyāʾ al-mawāt is the legal act of bringing dead land into beneficial use, conferring ownership.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for cultivation; metaphorical for legal appropriation through development.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazāʾ) — The protasis (e.g., "whoever returns") governs the apodosis ("has a reward"), requiring precise parsing of stipulations and their legal consequences.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third pillar is the work (al-ʿamal). It is everything upon which hiring is permissible, but it is not required to be known (maʿlūm). For returning a runaway slave (al-ābiq) is a work that cannot be precisely delimited. It might occur to one that the work should be stipulated as unknown (majhūl) and unquantified, like in muḍārabah (silent partnership). However, the Iraqis decisively ruled that if one says, "Whoever builds my wall or sews my garment, for him is such-and-such," this is not permissible. Likewise, if one says, "Whoever performs the pilgrimage on my behalf, for him is a dīnār," he is entitled to the dīnār. This was narrated by al-Muzanī from al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) in al-Manthūr. Then al-Muzanī said: He should be entitled to the equivalent wage (ujrat al-mithl), because it is a hire (ijārah) and thus invalid without specification. This indicates that al-Muzanī held that juʿl (reward) is confined to the unknown (majhūl) that cannot be hired upon. The Iraqis attributed error to al-Muzanī in this, saying: This is a juʿl (reward contract).

The fourth pillar is the reward (al-jaʿl). Its condition is that it be known wealth (māl maʿlūm). If one stipulates it as unknown, the contract is vitiated (fasada), and the worker is entitled to the equivalent wage, as in the case of vitiated muḍārabah.

Three branches: First, if one says, "Whoever returns my slave from Basra, for him is a dīnār," while the slave is in Baghdad, and he returns him from halfway, he is entitled to half the dīnār; from one-third, one-third, because it is apportioned by distance. If he returns him from a farther place, he is not entitled to anything extra, because nothing was stipulated upon him. Second, if one says, "Whoever returns my slave, for him is a dīnār," and two persons jointly return him, they share the reward. If he designates a specific person and says, "If you return him, for you is a dīnār," and another joins him, and the designated one says, "I intended assistance (muʿāwanah)," the worker is entitled to the dīnār. If he says, "I intended co-participation (musāhamah)," then the worker has half the dīnār, and nothing for the designated one, for nothing was stipulated for him. Third, if he says to one of them, "If you return my slave, for you is a dīnār," and to another, "If you return him, for you is a dīnār," and they jointly return him, each has half of what was stipulated for him. If he stipulates for one a dīnār and for another an unknown garment, and they jointly return him, the one for whom the dīnār was stipulated takes half of it, and the other takes half the equivalent wage.

As for its rulings, they are four: First, it is permissible (jāʾiz) from both sides, like muḍārabah, for bindingness (luzūm) does not befit it. If the owner rescinds before the work begins, it is rescinded. If it is after commencement and before completion, it is rescinded, and he is liable for the equivalent wage. If it is after completion, rescission has no meaning. Second, the permissibility of increase and decrease. If one says, "Whoever returns my slave, for him is ten," then says, "Whoever returns my slave, for him is a dīnār," whoever returns him is entitled to the dīnār; likewise in reverse, and consideration is given to the last statement. If the worker did not hear the final decreasing call, it may be said that one reverts to the equivalent wage. Third, the worker is not entitled to anything except upon completion of the work. If he returns the slave to the door of his house, and the slave flees or dies before delivery, he is entitled to nothing, because the objective—the return—has been lost. Fourth, if they dispute over the very stipulation of the reward, and the owner denies it, or over the identity of the slave, and the owner denies the stipulation regarding him, saying, "It was stipulated regarding another slave," or the owner denies his effort in the return, saying, "The slave returned on his own," then in all this, the owner's word is accepted, for the worker is the claimant (muddaʿī) and must provide proof. If they differ over the amount stipulated, they both take an oath (taḥāluf), and one reverts to the equivalent wage, as in hire (ijārah).

= The Book of Reviving Dead Lands (Iḥyāʾ al-Mawāt) = It contains three chapters. The first chapter concerns the ownership of lands—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and contains two sections. The first concerns what is owned of lands through revival (iḥyāʾ), namely, dead lands (al-mawāt). He (peace be upon him) said: {«Whoever revives a dead land, it is his»}. Dead land is land that is free from all special claims (ikhtiṣāṣāt). The special claims are of six types.

The first type: Cultivation (al-ʿimārah). Every cultivated land is revived (muḥyāh), so it cannot be owned through revival, whether it is in the Abode of Islam (dār al-Islām) or the Abode of War (dār al-ḥarb). If the cultivation is effaced but its trace remains, then if it was from the cultivation of Islam, it cannot be owned, because it is inherited from one who owned it; so its owner is awaited, or it is preserved for the public treasury (bayt al-māl), and the Imām disposes of it as he disposes of lost property whose owner is unknown. If it was from the cultivation of the pre-Islamic era (al-Jāhiliyyah), and the manner of its entry into Muslim hands is known—either by way of spoils (ghanīmah) or fayʾ—that ruling is maintained, and it cannot be owned through revival. If knowledge of it is despaired of, there are two opinions: One, it can be owned, for there is no sanctity for the cultivation of unbelievers, so it becomes like their buried treasure (rikāz). The second, it cannot, because it entered the hands of the people of Islam, so the presumption is that prior ownership attached to it. As for rikāz, its ruling is that of lost property exposed to loss. This is the ruling for the Abode of Islam. As for the Abode of War, its cultivated land is like their other wealth, owned by spoils. As for its dead land, what they do not defend against Muslims is like the dead land of the Abode of Islam, owned through revival. It differs in one matter: if an unbeliever revives it, he owns it. If one revives dead land of the Abode of Islam, he does not own it in our school, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him), because the people of Islam have a special claim by virtue of their attachment to the Abode. As for what they do defend against Muslims, if a Muslim revives it and is able to settle there, he owns it. If some of the warriors (ghānimūn) seize it and intend to claim it specially, there are three aspects: One, that seizure confers upon them the special claim (ikhtiṣāṣ) that taḥajjur (marking off) confers, as will come. The second, that it confers ownership immediately, because the wealth of unbelievers is owned by seizure. The third, that it does not confer ownership, because it is not the wealth of unbelievers; rather, it is dead land, and there is no special claim, for they did not mark it off; it is merely a hand (yad), so it is like mere seizure of dead land in the Abode of Islam.

chapters.title_en: The Second Type of Special Right: The Protected Perimeter (Ḥarīm) of a Constructed Property
chapters.arabic_text:
### | النوع الثاني من الاختصاص أن يكون حريم عمارة

فيختص به صاحب العمارة ولا يملك بالإحياء
فإن قيل وما حد الحريم
قلنا أما البلدة التى قررنا الكفار عليها بالمصالحة فلما حواليها من
الموات التى يدفعون المسلمين عنها لا تحيا وفاء بالصلح فإنها حريم البلدة
وأما القرية المعمورة في الإسلام فما يتصل بها من مرتكض الخيل وملعب
الصبيان ومناخ الإبل ومجتمع النادي فهو حريمها فليس لغيرهم إحياؤها
وما ينتشر إليه البهائم للرعي في وقت الخوف وهو على قرب القرية فيه تردد
أما الدار فحريمها إذا كانت محفوفة بالموات مطرح التراب والثلج
ومصب ماء الميزاب وفناء الدار وحق الاجتياز في جهة فتح الباب
وإن كانت محفوفة بالأملاك فلا حريم لها لأن الأملاك متعارضة فليس بعضهما
بأن يجعل حريما لها أولى من الآخر ولكل واحد أن ينتفع في ملكه بما جرت به
العادة
وإن تضرر به صاحبه فلا يمنع إلا إذا كانت العادة السكون
ولو اتخذ أحدهما داره مدبغة أو حماما أو حانوت قصار أو حداد
قال المراوزة يمنع نظرا إلى العادة القديمة
وقال العراقيون إذا أحكم الجدران واحتاط على العادة لا يمنع
وتردد الشيخ أبو محمد فيما إذا كان يؤذي بدخان الخبز وجعله  مخبزا على
خلاف العادة لأن هذا إيذاء المالك لا إيذاء الملك وحاصله ولا يمنع لا تمنع
ومع
أما البئر فإن حفرها في الموات للنزح فموقف النازح حواليها حريمها وإن
كان النزح بالدواب فموضع تردد الدواب وعلى الجملة ما يتم الانتفاع
ولو حفر آخر بئرا بجنبه بحيث ينقص ماؤها لم يجز بل حريمها القدر الذى
يصون ماءها وكأنه استحق بالحفر
وفي طريقة العراق القطع بأنه يجوز
والأول أظهر فإنه لو أحيا دارا في موات فليس لآخر أن يحفر بجنب جداره
بئرا يتوهم الإضرار بجداره وإن كان ذلك يجوز للجار المالك ولكن وضع البناء
في الموات أوجب حريما لصيانة الملك فكذلك لصيانة ماء البئر

### | النوع الثالث اختصاص المسلمين بعرفة لأجل الوقوف

وفي امتناع إحياء عرفة به ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها لا يمتنع إذ لا تضييق به
والثاني يمتنع إذ فتح بابه يؤدي إلى التضييق
والثالث يجوز وإن ضيق ثم يبقى في الدور حق الوقوف

### | النوع الرابع اختصاص المتحجر

ومن تقدم إلى موضع ونصب حجارة وعلامات للعمارة اختص به بحق السبق بشرط أن
يشتغل بالعمارة
فلو تحجر ليعمر في السنة الثانية لم يجز ومهما جاز التحجر ومنع غيره من
الإحياء فإن أحيا فهل يملك ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها نعم لأنه سبب قوي والتحجر ضعيف فكان كالبيع سوما على سوم غيره
والثاني لا لأنه اختصاص مؤكد
والثالث أن التحجر إن كان مع الإقطاع منع وإلا فلا
وهل يجوز للمتحجر بيع حقه من الاختصاص والاعتياض عنه فعلى وجهين
أحدهما يجوز كالملك
والثاني لا كحق الشفعة وحق الرهن

### | النوع الخامس من الاختصاص الإقطاع

ويجوز للإمام أن يقطع مواتا على قدر ما يقدر المقطع على عمارته وينزل
الإقطاع منزلة التحجر في الاختصاص

### | النوع السادس الحمى

وهو كان جائزا لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وهو أن يحمي الكلأ ببقعة
لإبل الصدقة
وكان يجوز لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن يحمي لنفسه وللمسلمين
وهل يجوز للإمام بعده فيه خلاف
والصحيح الجواز إذ حمى عمر رضي الله عنه لإبل المسلمين
ولكن لا يجوز أن يحمى الإمام لنفسه وإنما كان ذلك خاصية رسول الله صلى
الله عليه وسلم فإذا صح الحمى فإحياؤه كالإحياء بعد التحجر

### | فرع

ما حماه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لحاجة أو حماه غيره فزالت الحاجة
فهل لأحد بعد ذلك نقضه فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها لا لأنها بقعة أرصدت لخير فأشبه المسجد
والثاني نعم لأنه بني على مصلحة حالية ظنية
والثالث أن حمى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فلا يغير وهو حماه بالبقيع
وهو بلد ليس بالواسع لأن حماه كالنص وحمى غيره كالاجتهاد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح م ي (ḥ-m-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Protection, guarding, and preventing access; the act of securing something from encroachment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sacred inviolability and exclusive right, often applied to sanctuaries (ḥimā) and protected zones.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical guarding; metaphorical (majāz) for legal exclusivity and right of priority.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Clauses (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the syntactic linkage of legal conditions (e.g., "if... then...") and exceptions (e.g., "unless...") to preserve precise juridical distinctions.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second type of special right (ikhtiṣāṣ) is that a protected perimeter (ḥarīm) belongs to a constructed property. Its owner is exclusively entitled to it, and it cannot be acquired by reviving dead land (iḥyāʾ).

If it is said: "What is the limit of the protected perimeter (ḥarīm)?" — We reply: As for the town which we established the unbelievers upon by treaty (muṣālaḥah), whatever surrounding dead land (mawāt) lies around it, from which we repel the Muslims and which is not revived in fulfillment of the treaty, that is the protected perimeter of the town. As for a village inhabited in Islam, whatever adjoins it — such as the galloping ground of horses, the playground of children, the resting place of camels, and the gathering place of the council (nādī) — is its protected perimeter; no one other than its people may revive it. As for what extends to where beasts scatter for grazing in times of fear, being near the village, there is hesitation (taraddud) regarding it.

As for a house (dār), its protected perimeter — when it is surrounded by dead land — includes the place for discarding dust and snow, the outlet of rainwater from the spout (mīzāb), the courtyard (fināʾ) of the house, and the right of passage in the direction of the door's opening. But if it is surrounded by owned properties, then it has no protected perimeter, because the properties are mutually conflicting; it is no more fitting that one of them be made a protected perimeter for it than another. Each owner may benefit within his own property in whatever manner custom (ʿādah) has established. Even if this harms his neighbor, he is not prevented — unless the custom is one of tranquility (sukūn).

If one of them makes his house a tannery (madbaghah), a bathhouse (ḥammām), a fuller's shop (ḥānūt qaṣṣār), or a blacksmith's forge (ḥaddād) — the Marāwizah (jurists of Marw) said: He is prevented, in consideration of the ancient custom. The Iraqis said: If he has fortified the walls and taken precautions according to custom, he is not prevented. Shaykh Abū Muḥammad hesitated regarding the case where one harms by the smoke of baking bread, making it a bakery (makhbaz) contrary to custom, because this is harm to the owner (īdhāʾ al-mālik), not harm to the property (īdhāʾ al-milk). The upshot of it is: he is not prevented.

As for a well (biʾr) — if it is dug in dead land for drawing water (nazḥ), then the standing place of the drawer around it is its protected perimeter. If the drawing is by beasts, then the place where the beasts tread is [included]. In general, whatever completes the benefit [is part of the perimeter]. If another digs a well adjacent to it such that its water diminishes, that is not permissible. Rather, its protected perimeter is the extent that preserves its water, as if he had acquired it by the digging. In the Iraqi method (ṭarīqah), there is a definitive ruling that it is permissible. But the first [view] is more apparent (aẓhar), for if one revived a house in dead land, it is not permissible for another to dig a well beside its wall, fearing harm to the wall — even though this would be permissible for a neighboring owner. But placing a structure in dead land necessitated a protected perimeter for the preservation of the property; likewise, for the preservation of the well's water.

### | The Third Type: The Special Right of the Muslims over ʿArafāt for the Standing (wuqūf)

Regarding the prohibition of reviving ʿArafāt by building there, there are three views:
1. It is not prohibited, since there is no constriction (taḍyīq) thereby.
2. It is prohibited, since opening its door leads to constriction.
3. It is permissible even if it constricts; then the right of standing (ḥaqq al-wuqūf) remains in the dwellings.

### | The Fourth Type: The Special Right of the One Who Marks Land (taḥajjur)

Whoever proceeds to a place and sets up stones and markers for construction is exclusively entitled to it by right of precedence (ḥaqq al-sabq), on the condition that he engages in construction. If he marks it to build in the second year, it is not permissible. Whenever marking is permissible and he prevents others from reviving, then if another revives it — does he own it? Three views:
1. Yes, because revival is a strong cause, while marking is weak; it is like a sale (bayʿ) where one bids over another's bidding (sawm).
2. No, because it is an affirmed special right (ikhtiṣāṣ muʾakkad).
3. If the marking was with a grant from the Imam (iqṭāʿ), it prevents; otherwise, it does not.

Is it permissible for the marker to sell his right of speciality or to take compensation for it? Two views:
1. Yes, like ownership (milk).
2. No, like the right of preemption (shufʿah) and the right of pledge (rahn).

### | The Fifth Type of Special Right: The Grant (iqṭāʿ)

It is permissible for the Imam to grant dead land to the extent that the grantee is able to cultivate it. The grant (iqṭāʿ) is placed in the position of marking (taḥajjur) regarding special right.

### | The Sixth Type: The Sanctuary (ḥimā)

This was permissible for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — namely, that he could protect the pasture (kalāʾ) of a place for the camels of charity (ṣadaqah). It was permissible for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to protect it for himself and for the Muslims. Whether it is permissible for the Imam after him is a matter of disagreement. The correct view (ṣaḥīḥ) is permissibility, for ʿUmar رضي الله عنه protected [a pasture] for the camels of the Muslims. But it is not permissible for the Imam to protect it for himself; rather, that was a special prerogative (khaṣīṣah) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. When the sanctuary is established, reviving it is like reviving after marking.

### | Branch (Farʿ)

What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ protected for a need, or another protected it, and then the need ceased — is it permissible for anyone afterward to annul it? Three views:
1. No, because it is a place reserved for good, resembling a mosque (masjid).
2. Yes, because it was founded upon a transient, conjectural benefit (maṣlaḥah ḥāliyyah ẓanniyyah).
3. What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ protected is not to be changed — and he protected al-Baqīʿ, which is a land not vast — because his protection is like a text (naṣṣ), while the protection of another is like independent reasoning (ijtihād).
