- Root: ر د د (radda)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To return, restore, repel; core sense of turning something back to its origin or rightful place.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, the restitution of a trust (amānah) to its proprietor, entailing both physical return and juridical discharge of liability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in property law—actual delivery of the ʿayn (corpus); metaphorical (majāz) when extended to returning a claim or obligation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis Construction (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — the clause "if its owner appears" (idhā ẓahara mālikuhu) governs the apodosis, establishing a legal causality where the ruling is contingent upon verified appearance.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth ruling concerns the obligation of returning [the found object] when its owner appears. This is ascertained by evidence (bayyinah); for if [the claimant] elaborates extensively in his description [of the object] and it becomes overwhelmingly probable that he is truthful, it is permissible to hand it over to him. Concerning the obligation of returning it without establishing evidence, there is a divergence [of scholarly opinion]. Among them are those who deemed it obligatory, since burdening [the finder] with evidence is difficult. And among them are those who said: perhaps he may have learned the description from the description given by the owner who lost it. Perhaps the more appropriate [view] is to suffice with the statement of a single upright (ʿadl) person, because trustworthiness is thereby attained.

### Two Subsidiary Branches
The first: If he hands it over to the describer, and then the [true] owner appears, the owner may pursue whichever of the two he wishes—the describer or the finder—and the finder may seek recourse against the describer, unless he had previously acknowledged ownership [in favor of the describer], in which case he cannot seek recourse.

The second: If the owner appears after [the finder] had acquired ownership [through the lapse of time and proper procedure], then if [the object] has perished, he must pay its value on the day of acquisition. If it remains extant, there are two positions (wajhān) on whether returning the very corpus is obligatory, analogous to the case of the borrower (mustaqriḍ) seeking recourse. And if it is defective, and he wishes to return it while appending the compensation for the defect (arsh), but the owner refuses, saying, "I want the value," then which of the two is to be answered—there are two positions. The first: the owner, because the corpus, after acquisition, is augmented for the purpose of approximating full compensation, and the avenue of compensation has been lost through the defect. The second: the finder, because he does not exceed the usurper (ghāṣib), and the usurper has the right to return the corpus along with the defect-compensation. Then, if he returns it, and he were to demand from the owner the wage of returning it, he has no such right—unless the owner had publicly announced, "Whoever returns my lost object shall have such-and-such," in which case he is entitled to what was named, as we have detailed in the Book of Reward (Kitāb al-Jiʿālah) following the Book of Hire (al-Ijārah). And God knows best.

= The Book of the Foundling (al-Laqīṭ) = It contains two chapters.

### Chapter One: On the Pillars of Taking Up a Foundling and Its Rulings
As for the pillars, they are three.

### The First Pillar: The Act of Taking Up Itself
It is the taking of a lost child who has no caretaker. In itself, it is a communal obligation (farḍ ʿalā al-kifāyah), because it is cooperation in righteousness and rescue from destruction. Concerning the obligation of bearing witness upon it, there is a divergence, built upon the divergence regarding witnessing over found property—and it is more deserving of obligation, because the fear of enslavement is present therein. Among our companions (al-aṣḥāb) are those who deemed it obligatory upon the person of concealed [status] (al-mastūr) as opposed to the upright. Then, if we stipulate it, whenever he abandons it, he does not establish for himself the guardianship of custody, and it is permissible to seize [the child] from his hand—as if it were a guardianship that is not established except after witnessing.

### The Second Pillar: The Foundling
Nothing is stipulated for it except the need for a caretaker. For if he has a prior taker, or a father, or a mother, or a relative, then there is no meaning to taking him up. Likewise, if he is an adult. And if he is below the age of discernment (tamyīz), taking him up is obligatory. Regarding [the age] after discernment up to puberty, there is hesitation, for he is close in resemblance to a stray camel included among found property, since he has a kind of independence.

### The Third Pillar: The Taker
The eligibility for taking up is established for every free, legally responsible (mukallaf), Muslim, upright, and prudent person. As for the slave and the mukātab (slave under contract of manumission), they are not eligible for taking up. If they take [a child], it is seized from their hands, and they have no guardianship over custody—unless the master grants permission, in which case he is the taker, and the slave is a deputy in the act of taking. As for the disbeliever, he is eligible for taking up a disbeliever, not a Muslim, for it is a kind of guardianship. Yes, a Muslim may take up a disbeliever. As for the immoral person (fāsiq), the Law does not entrust him. The person of concealed status (mastūr) may take up. Then, if he intends to travel with him, the judge prevents him, unless his uprightness is known. As for the squanderer (mubadhdhir), even if he is not immoral, he is not fit for the trusts of the Law. As for the poor person—and upon God is their provision—the Iraqis mentioned another position that [the child] is seized from his hand, out of consideration for the child.

If it is said: What if two takers crowd [over the child]? We say: As for the ineligible, he does not compete with the eligible, as previously stated. If both are eligible, then the wealthy is preferred over the poor, out of consideration for the child; and the city-dweller over the villager; and the villager is preferred over the Bedouin, due to what lies therein of consideration for the child in the breadth of livelihood in the cities and the goodness of morals therein. A woman is not preferred over a man, even though the mother is preferred over the father in custody, because the mother is more compassionate than a stranger whom the father would hire—whereas here, the stranger encompasses both aspects. Concerning preferring the one of apparent uprightness over the one of concealed status, there is a divergence. Among them are those who said: the one of apparent wealth is not preferred over the middling, because the concealed-status person claims that the shortcoming lies with the one who did not investigate his uprightness. And among them are those who said: he is preferred, because the foundation of uprightness is a condition for eligibility, so its apparentness necessitates preference. If they are equal in attributes, the one who preceded in taking is preferred over the later taker. And whether the one who preceded in standing over his head is preferred before the taker—there is hesitation. If they are equal, lots are cast between them, for there is no way to division nor to alternation (muhāyāʾah), since the child is harmed by the changing of hands after familiarity. Ibn Abī Hurayrah said: The judge places him in the hand of whichever of the two he deems [fit]. And if the child chooses one of them, no consideration is given to that, for there is no basis for his inclination—unlike the child's choice of one of his parents, for that is based on experience and testing.

### Subsidiary Branch
If the need for lots arises, and one of the two withdraws, [the child] is handed to the other. There is another position that this is not permissible; rather, the judge casts the lot in his name, and if it falls upon him, he is compelled [to take him], for he was obligated to fulfill the preservation after taking—but this is remote here. Yes, in continuity: if the sole taker of the foundling wishes to return him to his place, it is not permissible. And if he hands him over to the judge due to his incapacity, it is permissible. And if he is vexed by him while capable, there are two positions. The position of prohibition is that it is a communal obligation, and he has entered into it and is capable of it, so it becomes personally incumbent upon him.

chapters.title_en: The Ruling on Foundlings (Luqṭah): Custody, Maintenance, and the Legal Status of the Foundling in Islam, Lineage, and Freedom
chapters.arabic_text:
### | أما حكم الالتقاط فهو الحضانة والإنفاق

أما الحضانة فواجبه وكيفيتها لا تخفى
ومهما التقط في بلد لم يجز أن يحول إلى بادية ولا إلى قرية لأن فيه تضييق
المعيشة ولو التقط في بادية أو قبيلة فنقل إلى البلد جاز لأنه أرفق به وفيه
وجه أنه لا يجوز لأن ظهور نسبه في محل التقاطه متوقع ولو نقل من بلد مثله
فوجهان
أحدهما الجواز لتساوي المعاش
والثاني المنع لتوقع ظهور النسب في محل الالتقاط مع اتساع المعيشة في محل
الالتقاط
لو وجده في صحراء خال فله أن ينقله إلى أي موضع شاء إذ سائر  المواضع إما
مثله أو أصلح منه
أما الإنفاق فإن كان له مال فهو من ماله
وماله بالوصية للقيط والوقوف عليه والهبة منه ويقبلها القاضي ويقبضها أو
بأن يوجد معه مال مشدود على ثوبه أو فرس مربوط عليه أو يوجد في دار فتكون
الدار له لأن أصل اللقيط على الحرية ومعنى اليد الاختصاص
وإن كان بالقرب منه مال موضوع أو بهيمة مشدودة بشجرة ففيها وجهان وهو
تردد في هذا القدر هل يعد اختصاصا
وإن كان المال مدفونا تحته فلا اختصاص له به فإن وجد معه رقعة فيها أن
المال المدفون تحته له فالأظهر أنه له وفيه وجه أنه لا تعويل على الرقعة
ثم الملتقط ليس له أن ينفق ماله عليه بغير إذن القاضي فإن فعل ضمن إذ لا
ولاية له إلا على نفسه بالحفظ وهل له حفظ ماله دون إذن القاضي وفيه وجهان
ووجه الجواز أنه تابع للمالك وله حفظ المالك
وإن أنفق بغير إذن القاضي لأنه لم يجد قاضيا وأشهد فالظاهر أنه لا يضمن
وإن لم يشهد فقولان ذكرنا نظيرهما في هرب الجمال
أما إذا لم يكن له مال فلا يجب على الملتقط من ماله بحال ولكن ينفق عليه
من بيت المال فإن لم يكن فيجمع من أهل اليسار من المسلمين لأنه عيال عليهم
ثم لا رجوع عليه بعده
ومن الأصحاب من قال إن القاضي يستقرض إما من بيت المال أو من موسر ينفق
عليه فإن ظهر أن اللقيط عبد رجع على مولاه وإن ظهر حرا موسرا أو مكتسبا رجع
عليه في كسبه ويساره وإن كان عاجزا قضاه من سهم المساكين والفقراء من
الصدقات إذ لا معنى لإلزامه من غير هذه الجهة
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في معرفة حال اللقيط في الإسلام
والنسب والحرية وغيرها وفيه أربعة أحكام - صلى الله عليه وسلم -

### | الحكم الأول الإسلام

وهو ينقسم إلى ما يعرف بمباشرة وإلى ما يعرف بتبعية
أما المباشرة فيصح من البالغ العاقل ولا يصح من الصبي في الظاهر المذهب
نعم نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن صبي الكافر إذا وصف الإسلام حيل بينه وبين
أبويه
فمنهم من قال هذا محتوم وهو حكم بصحة الإسلام فخرجوا منه قولا مثل مذهب
أبي حنيفة رحمه الله
ومنهم من قال هو استحباب بعد استعطاف الوالدين فإن أبيا لم نجبرهما عليه
وقال الأستاذ أبو إسحاق إذا أضمر الصبي الإسلام كما أظهره حكمنا له
بالفوز في الآخرة وإن كنا لا نحكم به لصبيان الكفار بسبب تعارض الأخبار
وعبر عن هذا بأن إسلامه صحيح باطنا لا ظاهرا
ومنهم من قال إن إسلامه موقوف فإن أعرب بعد البلوغ عن الإسلام تبينا صحته
من أصله أما التبعية فلها ثلاث وجهات
الجهة الأولى تبعية الوالدين فإن حصل العلوق من مسلم أو الولادة من مسلمة
فالولد مسلم قطعا
فإن أظهر الكفر بعد البلوغ فهو مرتد أما إذا انفصل على الكفر فأسلم أحد
أبويه حكم بإسلامه في الحال
وكذا إسلام الأجداد والجدات عند عدم من هو أقرب منه ومع وجود الأقرب فيه
خلاف وأحكام الإسلام جارية على هذا الصبي في الحال
فإن بلغ وأعرب عن الإسلام استقر أمره وإن أظهر الكفر فقولان مرتبان
أحدهما أنه مرتد لا يقر عليه فلا ينقض ما سبق من الأحكام المبينة على
الإسلام كالمنفصل من المسلمين
والثاني أنه كافر أصلي يقرر بالجزية ولا يجبر على الإسلام لأن التبعية في
الإسلام بعد الانفصال ضعيف وإنما حكم به في الحال بشرط أن يستمر
فإذا استقل فالنظر إلى استقلاله أولى
فعلى هذا ما سبق من أحكام الإسلام بعد البلوغ وقبل الإعراب من إجزاء عتقه
عن كفارة أو توريثه من مسلم أو نكاحه مسلمة كل ذلك منقوض
وما سبق في حالة الصبي هل يتبين إنتقاضه فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم كما بعد البلوغ
والثاني لا إذ لو حكمنا به لأوجب ذلك الوقف في الأحكام للتوقف في الإسلام
بل الحكم بالإسلام مجزوم ما دام سبب التبعية قائما وهو الصبي
وإنما ينقطع بالبلوغ فبعد البلوغ يتوقف إلى إعرابه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-ق-ط (la-qa-ṭa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pick up, to snatch, to gather from the ground; a foundling (laqīṭ) is one who is picked up, implying an object of care and legal guardianship.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, it denotes the act of assuming responsibility for a helpless being, shifting the moral obligation to the community (kifāyah) and the state treasury (bayt al-māl).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical picking up; metaphorical (majāz) for legal custody and the transfer of guardianship rights.
- Root: ح-ض-ن (ḥa-ḍa-na)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To embrace, to hold in one's lap; custody (ḥaḍānah) as physical and moral nurturing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The right and duty of care, tied to the child's welfare (maṣlaḥah), not merely a parental privilege.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical embrace; metaphorical for legal guardianship over a foundling's person and property.
- Root: ن-ف-ق (na-fa-qa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To spend, to expend; maintenance (nafaqah) as obligatory financial support.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal obligation to sustain life, derived from the principle of necessity (ḍarūrah) and communal responsibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for monetary expenditure; metaphorical for the moral duty of the community to provide for the destitute.
- Root: ت-ب-ع (ta-bi-ʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, to pursue; derivative (tabaʿiyyah) as legal attachment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, the derivative status of a child's religion following the parent, a key principle in Islamic jurisprudence (fiqh).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical following; metaphorical for legal subordination in matters of faith and status.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text frequently uses "لو" (law, if) and "فإن" (fa-in, for if) to establish hypothetical legal scenarios, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to determine the operative ruling (ḥukm) in each case.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the ruling on picking up a foundling (luqṭah), it entails custody (ḥaḍānah) and maintenance (nafaqah).

As for custody, it is obligatory, and its manner is not hidden. Whenever one picks up a foundling in a town, it is not permissible to transfer him to a desert or to a village, because that would constrict his means of living. If he is picked up in a desert or among a tribe, then transferring him to a town is permissible, because it is more compassionate for him. There is a view that it is not permissible, because the appearance of his lineage at his place of being picked up is anticipated. If he is transferred from a town to a similar town, there are two views: one is permissibility, due to the equality of livelihood; the second is prohibition, due to the anticipation of the appearance of lineage at the place of picking up, despite the spaciousness of living at that place. If he is found in an empty desert, then he may transfer him to any place he wishes, since all other places are either similar to it or better than it.

As for maintenance: if the foundling has wealth, it is from his own wealth. His wealth may be [acquired] by bequest (waṣiyyah) to the foundling, by endowments (waqf) upon him, or by gift (hibah) to him, which the judge accepts and takes possession of; or by his being found with wealth tied to his garment, or a horse tethered to him, or his being found in a house, in which case the house is his, because the foundational presumption regarding the foundling is freedom (aṣl al-laqīṭ ʿalā al-ḥurriyyah), and the meaning of "possession" (yad) is exclusive claim (ikhtiṣāṣ). If wealth is placed near him, or an animal is tethered to a tree [near him], there are two views — this is a hesitation over whether this amount constitutes an exclusive claim. If the wealth is buried beneath him, he has no exclusive claim to it. If a note (ruqʿah) is found with him stating that the wealth buried beneath him belongs to him, the more apparent view is that it is his, and there is a view that no reliance is placed on the note.

Then, the finder (multaqiṭ) is not permitted to spend his own wealth on the foundling without the judge's permission. If he does so, he is liable (ḍāmin), for he has no authority (wilāyah) except over himself, by way of preservation. Does he have the right to preserve the foundling's wealth without the judge's permission? There are two views. The view of permissibility is that he is a deputy of the owner, and he has the right to preserve the owner's wealth. If he spends without the judge's permission because he found no judge, and he called witnesses, the apparent view is that he is not liable. If he did not call witnesses, there are two sayings (qawlān), the likes of which we mentioned in the case of the runaway camels.

As for when the foundling has no wealth, it is not obligatory upon the finder to spend from his own wealth in any case. Rather, he spends on him from the public treasury (bayt al-māl). If there is none, then [funds] are collected from the wealthy Muslims, because the foundling is a dependent (ʿiyāl) upon them. Then, there is no recourse against him afterward. Among our companions (al-aṣḥāb) is one who said: The judge borrows — either from the public treasury or from a wealthy person — and spends on him. If it becomes apparent that the foundling is a slave, he has recourse against his master. If it becomes apparent that he is a free person who is wealthy or earning, he has recourse against him in his earnings and wealth. If he is incapable, he pays it from the share of the poor and needy (sahm al-masākīn wa al-fuqarāʾ) from the alms (ṣadaqāt), for there is no meaning in imposing it upon him from any other source.

— Peace be upon him — The Second Chapter: On Knowing the Status of the Foundling Regarding Islam, Lineage, Freedom, and Other Matters. It contains four rulings — Peace be upon him —

### | The First Ruling: Islam

It is divided into what is known by direct action (mubāsharah) and what is known by derivative status (tabaʿiyyah).

As for direct action, it is valid from an adult of sound mind, and it is not valid from a minor in the apparent [school] doctrine (al-madhhab). Indeed, al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — explicitly stated that if a minor of a disbeliever describes Islam, a separation is effected between him and his parents. Among them is one who said: This is mandatory, and it is a ruling on the validity of his Islam, and they derived from it a saying similar to the school of Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him. Among them is one who said: It is recommended (istiḥbāb) after seeking to soften the parents' hearts; if they refuse, we do not compel them to it. Al-Ustādh Abū Isḥāq said: If the minor conceals Islam in his heart just as he manifests it, we rule for him the attainment of salvation in the Hereafter, even though we do not rule by it for the minors of disbelievers due to the conflicting reports (taʿāruḍ al-akhbār). This was expressed as: his Islam is valid inwardly (bāṭinan), not outwardly (ẓāhirān). Among them is one who said: His Islam is suspended (mawqūf); if after reaching maturity he declares Islam, it becomes evident that it was valid from its origin.

As for derivative status (tabaʿiyyah), it has three aspects. The first aspect is derivative status from the parents: if conception (ʿalūq) occurs from a Muslim, or birth from a Muslim woman, then the child is definitively Muslim. If he manifests disbelief after reaching maturity, he is an apostate (murtadd). As for when he is born upon disbelief, and then one of his parents embraces Islam, he is ruled to be Muslim immediately. Likewise, the Islam of grandfathers and grandmothers [applies] when there is no one closer than them; and with the existence of a closer one, there is a divergence (khilāf). The rulings of Islam are applied to this minor immediately. If he reaches maturity and declares Islam, his affair is settled. If he manifests disbelief, there are two sayings (qawlān), arranged [in order]. One of them: he is an apostate who is not left upon it, and what preceded of the rulings built upon Islam — like the one born from Muslims — is not overturned. The second: he is an original disbeliever (kāfir aṣlī) who is allowed to remain upon payment of the poll-tax (jizyah), and he is not compelled to Islam, because derivative status in Islam after separation is weak; it was only ruled upon immediately on the condition that he continue. When he becomes independent, then consideration of his independence is more appropriate. Upon this [second view], what preceded of the rulings of Islam after maturity and before declaration — such as the validity of his manumission (ʿitq) for an expiation (kaffārah), or his inheritance from a Muslim, or his marriage to a Muslim woman — all of that is overturned. As for what preceded during the state of minority, is it evident that it is overturned? There are two views: one of them is yes, just as after maturity; the second is no, for if we ruled by that, it would necessitate suspension in the rulings due to suspension in Islam. Rather, the ruling of Islam is definitive (majzūm) as long as the cause of derivative status remains, which is minority. It is only severed by maturity; after maturity, it is suspended until his declaration.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع على هذا القول

أحدها  إذا بلغ وجرى تصرف يستدعي الإسلام كعتق عن كفارة أو موت قريب مسلم
فمات اللقيط قبل أن يعرب بالكفر أو الإسلام ففي نقض التصرف وجهان
أحدهما ينقض إذ الأصل بعد البلوغ الاستقلال ولم يستقل بالإسلام فكيف يقدر
إسلامه
والثاني أنه لم يعرب أيضا بالكفر والإسلام غالب وقد سبق الحكم به فيستصحب
إلى أن يظهر الإعراب عن الكفر
والثاني لو قتله مسلم قبل البلوغ فالقصاص لا يمتنع بسبب توهم الكفر بعد
البلوغ
ولو قتل بعد البلوغ وقبل الإعراب
فإن قلنا لو أعرب بالكفر لنقض الأحكام فلا قصاص
وإن قلنا لا ينقض ففيه تردد وميل النص إلى سقوطه للشبهة
ونص مع هذا على أن الواجب دية مسلم وهذا يدل على أن الإسلام مستصحب في
سائر الأحكام وإنما سقط القصاص للشبهة
الثالث قال القاضي حسين إن مات هو قبل الإعراب يرثه حميمه المسلم وإن مات
حميمه المسلم فإرثه موقوف
ومعناه أن يقال له أعرب فإن مات قبل الإعراب فينبغي أن نقضي بتقدير الأول
عليه بناء على استصحاب حكم الإسلام
الرابع المجنون إذا بلغ مجنونا فهو كالصبي في جملة هذه الأحكام
وإن بلغ عاقلا كافرا ثم جن ثم أسلم أحد أبويه ففي التبعية خلاف كما في
عود ولاية المال

### | الجهة الثانية تبعية السابي

فالمسلم إذا استرق صبيا حكم بإسلامه تبعا له فإن الاسترقاق كأنه إيجاد
مستأنف
وإن كان معه أبواه لم يحكم به لأن تبعية الأبوين أقوى من تبعية السابي
فلو مات بعد ذلك أبواه اطرد كفره لأن النظر إلى الابتداء في تبعية السابي
ولو استرقه ذمي فالظاهر أنه لا يحكم بإسلامه
ثم لو باعه بعد ذلك من مسلم لا يحكم بإسلامه لفوات الابتداء
وفيه وجه أنه يحكم بإسلامه لأنا نجعل وقوع الصبي في يد المسترقى كوقوعه
في دار الإسلام والذمي كالمسلم في كونه من دار الإسلام ثم مهما حكم بإسلامه
تبعا للسابي فبلغ وأعرض بالكفر فحكمه ما سبق في تبعية الأبوين

### | الجهة الثالثة تبعية الدار

وكل لقيط يوجد في دار الإسلام فهو محكوم  بإسلامه لغلبة الإسلام إلا في
بلدة كثر الكفار فيها وانجلي المسلمون عنه حتى لم يبق منهم واحد
وقال أبو إسحاق المروزي يحكم الإسلام إذ لا يخلو عن مسلم مستسر بالإسلام
أما ما يوجد في دار الكفر فهو كافر وإن كانوا مسلمون يجتازون بها مسافرين
وإن كان فيها سكان من الأسارى والتجار ففيه وجهان لتعارض غلبة نسبة الدار
مع تغليب الإسلام
ثم هذا الصبي إذا بلغ وأظهر الكفر
منهم من قال قولان كما في تبعية المسترق والوالدين
ومنهم من قطع هاهنا بأنه كافر أصلي لأن تبعية الدار في غاية الضعف ثم
هؤلاء ترددوا في تنفيذ أحكام الإسلام عليه في الصبي ومال صاحب التقريب إلى
التوقف وهذا يعكر على إطلاق القول بالإسلام
وأيد صاحب التقريب هذا باختلاف القول في وجوب القصاص على قاتله المسلم
وقال لا مأخذ له إلا هذا التوقف

### | فرع

المحكوم بإسلامه تابعا للدار لو أقام ذمي بينة على نسبه ألحق به وتبعه في
الكفر وتغير ما ظنناه من الإسلام وإن استلحق من غير بينة ثبت النسب وفي
الحكم بكفره وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن تبعية الأب أقوى من تبعية الدار والدين يتبع النسب هاهنا
والثاني أن ذلك أقوى إذا لم يسبق الحكم وأما تسليط الذمي على الاستقلال
بإبطال حكمنا فبعيد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ق-ض (naqada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To unravel, break apart, or reverse a binding construction; to undo what was firmly established.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical annulment of a prior legal or theological ruling (ḥukm) once its foundational premise is shown to be false.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical unraveling; metaphorical (majāz) for juridical revocation of a status.
- Root: ص-ح-ب (ṣaḥiba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To accompany, cleave to, or remain in constant association with something.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The juristic principle of istiṣḥāb — presuming the continuation of a previously verified ruling (ḥukm) until contrary evidence emerges.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical companionship; technical for legal continuity across time.
- Root: ت-ب-ع (tabiʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, trail behind, or be subordinated to another's directive.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Derivative legal status (tabaʿiyyah) whereby a minor's religious identity is annexed to a dominant party — parent, captor, or abode.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for walking behind; metaphorical for juridical subordination of one ruling to another.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Protasis-Apodosis Coordination (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The repeated "if... then" structures (law... fa-in qulnā...) govern the branching of legal outcomes, each protasis introducing a distinct hypothetical whose apodosis yields a separate ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now follow the branches arising from this position [that the foundling is presumed Muslim until he explicitly declares otherwise].

**The First Branch:** If the foundling reaches puberty and then performs an act requiring Islam — such as manumitting [a slave] as expiation (kaffārah) or [inheriting from] a deceased Muslim relative — and then he dies before declaring either unbelief (kufr) or Islam, then there are two positions (wajhān) concerning whether that act is annulled:

One position holds that it is annulled, for the foundational principle after puberty is independence (istiqlāl) [in religious self-determination], and he did not independently affirm Islam — so how can his Islam be presumed?

The second position holds that he likewise did not declare unbelief, and Islam is the predominant [presumption]; the ruling [of Islam] was already established for him, so it is carried forward (yustaṣḥab) until he manifests a declaration of unbelief.

**The Second Branch:** If a Muslim kills him before puberty, retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is not precluded merely because of the supposition that he might have declared unbelief after puberty. But if he is killed after puberty and before declaration, then: if we adopt the position that had he declared unbelief his prior rulings would be annulled, then there is no retaliation. If we adopt the position that [his Islam] is not annulled, then there is hesitation (taraddud), and the textual inclination (mayl al-naṣṣ) is toward dropping [the retaliation] due to the ambiguity (shubhah). Yet alongside this, the text (naṣṣ) affirms that the blood-money (diyah) due is that of a Muslim — and this indicates that Islam is carried forward (mustaṣḥab) in all other rulings, and only the retaliation is dropped due to the ambiguity.

**The Third Branch:** Judge Ḥusayn said: If he dies before declaration, his Muslim kinsman inherits from him; but if his Muslim kinsman dies [first], then his inheritance is suspended (mawqūf). The meaning of this is that one says to him: "Declare [your faith]." If he dies before declaring, then we should rule by presuming the former [i.e., his Islam] upon him, based on carrying forward the ruling of Islam (istiṣḥāb ḥukm al-Islām).

**The Fourth Branch:** The insane person who reaches puberty in a state of insanity is treated like the minor in all these rulings. But if he reaches puberty sane and an unbeliever, then becomes insane, and then one of his parents embraces Islam — then there is disagreement (khilāf) concerning his [legal] followership (tabaʿiyyah), just as in the case of the return of guardianship over wealth.

---

**The Second Direction: The Followership of the Captor (tabaʿiyyat al-sābī)**

When a Muslim enslaves a minor, the minor is ruled to be Muslim by followership of him — for enslavement (istirqāq) is, as it were, a fresh origination (ījād mustaʾnaf) [of his legal personhood]. But if both of his parents are with him, he is not so ruled, because followership of the parents is stronger than followership of the captor. If his parents die after that, his unbelief persists (yaṭṭaridu kufruhu), because consideration is given to the initial moment in the followership of the captor.

If a dhimmī enslaves him, the apparent [position] is that he is not ruled to be Muslim. Then, if the dhimmī later sells him to a Muslim, he is still not ruled to be Muslim, because the initial [moment of enslavement] has been lost. There is a position that he is ruled to be Muslim, for we treat the minor's falling into the hand of the enslaver as his falling into the Abode of Islam (dār al-Islām), and the dhimmī is like the Muslim in being of the Abode of Islam. Then, whenever he is ruled Muslim by followership of the captor, and he reaches puberty and declares unbelief, his ruling is as previously stated in the followership of the parents.

---

**The Third Direction: The Followership of the Abode (tabaʿiyyat al-dār)**

Every foundling found in the Abode of Islam is ruled to be Muslim, due to the predominance of Islam — except in a town where the unbelievers have multiplied and the Muslims have departed until not a single one remains. Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī said: He is ruled Muslim, for [such a town] is not devoid of a Muslim concealing his Islam. As for what is found in the Abode of Unbelief (dār al-kufr), he is an unbeliever — even if Muslims pass through it as travelers. And if there are residents among them who are captives or merchants, then there are two positions, due to the conflict between the predominance of the abode's attribution and the predominance of Islam [in presumption].

Then, if this minor reaches puberty and manifests unbelief: some say there are two positions (qawlān), as in the followership of the enslaver and the parents; others state definitively here that he is an original unbeliever (kāfir aṣlī), because followership of the abode is extremely weak. Then these [latter] hesitated concerning executing the rulings of Islam upon him during his minority, and the author of al-Taqrīb inclined toward suspension (tawaqquf) — and this undermines the unqualified assertion of his Islam. The author of al-Taqrīb supported this by the disagreement concerning the obligation of retaliation against his Muslim killer, saying: "This has no basis except this suspension."

---

**A Branch:**

For one ruled Muslim by followership of the abode: if a dhimmī establishes by evidence (bayyinah) his lineage [to the foundling], he is attached to him and follows him in unbelief, and what we presumed of his Islam is changed. But if he claims paternity (istilḥāq) without evidence, the lineage is established, yet there are two positions concerning ruling him an unbeliever:

One: Yes [he is ruled an unbeliever], because followership of the father is stronger than followership of the abode, and religion follows lineage here.

The second: That [fatherly followership] is stronger only when no prior ruling has been issued; but empowering the dhimmī to independently annul our [established] ruling is far-fetched.

chapters.title_en: The Second Ruling Concerning the Foundling (al-Laqīṭ): His Crimes and Retaliation
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الحكم الثاني في اللقيط

جنايته في الصبي وأرش خطئه على بيت المال وإن جنى عليه خطأ فالأرش له وإن
كان موجبا للقود نظر فإن كان في النفس فقد اختلف نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه
في القصاص أما وجوبه فظاهر لأنه معصوم مسلم وأما إسقاطه فاختلف في تقليه
فقال الأكثرون سببه أن لا وارث له وأنه يثبت للمجانين والصبيان وسائر
المسلمين فكيف يستوفى وعلى هاذ لو قتل من لا وارث له فلا قصاص وكذا كل
قصاص خلفه من لا وارث له فلا قصاص عليه
وزيف صاحب التقريب هذا لأن الاستحقاق لا ينسب إلى آحاد المجانين والصبيان
بل إلى جهة الإسلام وعلل بأن نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه يدل على توقفه في
الإسلام بتبعية الدار لانتظار تغيره بعد البلوغ
وأما إذا قطع طرفه فعلى طرقة الأصحاب يجب القصاص لتعين المستحق وعلى
طريقة صاحب التقريب يتوقف فإن أعرب عن نفسه بالإسلام إذا بلغ تبين الوجوب
وإلا فلا
هذا إذا كان القاطع مسلما فإن كان ذميا فلا توقف من جهة الإسلام
فإن قيل والإمام هل يستوفي القصاص
قلنا إن كان في النفس فيستوفيه إن رآه أو يأخذ الدية لبيت المال إذ لا
معنى للتوقف ولو منع من أخذ البدل لصار القصاص حدا
وإن كان في طرف فالمستحق هو اللقيط فلا يستوفيه لأن الولي عند الشافعي
رضي الله عنه لا يستوفي القصاص
وحكي عن القفال وجه أن السلطان يستوفي القصاص في طرف المجنون لأنه لا
ينتظر لإفاقته وقت مخصوص
وهل للإمام أن يأخذ الأرش في الحال
نظر فإن وجب لصبي غني فلا وإن وجب لمجنون فقير فيأخذ للحاجة وعدم
الانتظار فإن وجب لصبي فقير أو لمجنون غني فوجهان لوجود أحد المعنيين
فإن قلنا لا يأخذ فيحبس من عليه القصاص إلى الإفاقة والبلوغ ولا يبالي
بطول الحبس فإن تفويت الحق غير ممكن
وإن قلنا يأخذ فبلغ الصبي وانتهض لطلب القصاص ففيه وجهان منشؤهما أن
الأخذ للحيلولة أم هو إسقاط للقصاص بحكم ظهور المصالح
ثم قال الأصحاب ولاية أخذ المال إن جعلناه إسقاطا فلا يثبت للوصي وإن جعل
للحيلولة فيثب له

### | الحكم الثالث نسب اللقيط

وفيه مسائل
الأولى إن ظهر إنسان وزعم أنه والده الحق بمجرد الدعوى إذ لا منازع
وإقامة البينة على النسب عسير
نعم إن بلغ الصبي وأنكر فهل ينقطع وجهان
أحدهما لا إذ تم الحكم به
والثاني نعم كما إذا استلحق بالغا فأنكره فإنه لا يثبت وإن كان المستلحق
هو الملتقط نفسه يثبت النسب
وقال مالك رحمه الله لا يثبت لأنه لا ينبذ ولد نفسه ثم يلتقطه إلا إذا
كان لا يعين أولاده فقد يفعل ذلك تفاؤلا
الثانية لو جاء عبد واستلحقه نص هاهنا على أنه يلحقه ونص في الدعاوى على
أنه ليس أهلا  فقال الأصحاب قولين الصحيح أنه أهل إذ إمكان النسب للرقيق
حاصل
والثاني لا لأنه يقطع ولاء السيد به عن نفسه
ثم الصحيح على هذا أن الحر لو استلحق صبيا رقيقا لحقه
ومنهم من منع لهذه العلة وهو قطع الحر بدعواه ولاء السيد
الثالثة المرأة إذا استلحقت فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه يلحق بها كالرجل
والثاني لا لأنه لو ألحق بها للحق زوجها وقبول قولها على زوجها محال
والإلحاق بها دونه محال
والثالث أنه يلحق الخلية دون ذوات الزوج لما ذكرناه
الرابعة إذا تداعى رجلان نسب مولود فلا يقدم حر على عبد ولا مسلم على
كافر بل يتساويان نعم صاحب اليد يقدم بشرطين
أحدهما أن لا تكون يده يد التقاط فإن يد الالتقاط لا تدل على النسب نعم
تدل على الحضانة
والثاني أن يكون صاحب اليد قد استلحق من قبل
فإن لم يسمع استلحاقه إلا عند دعوى الثاني فوجهان
أحدهما لا يقدم إذا لا دلالة لليد إذ لم يقارنه استلحاق
والثاني نعم لأن اليد على الجملة دالة ولعل الاستلحاق كان ولم يبلغنا

### | فرعان

أحدهما إذا أقام كل واحد بينة على أنه ولده تعارضتا وتهاترتا إذ لا سبيل
إلى قول القسمة ولا إلى قول الوقف فإنه لا يزيد فائدة
ولا يجري قول الإقراع أيضا إذ النسب لا يثبت بالقرعة
ولو تنازعا في الحضانة وأقام كل واحد منهما بينة على الالتقاط فإن شهدت
لأحدهما بالسبق في الالتقاط فهو مقدم في الحضانة وإن كنا نتردد في مثله في
الإملاك لأن حق الحضانة لا ينتقل والملك قد ينتقل وكذلك لو كان أحدهما صاحب
يد قدمت بينته لأنها دلالة الالتقاط كبينة الداخل
وإن تعارضا من كل وجه فإما قول التهاتر وإما قول القرعة ولا سبيل إلى
التوقف والقسمة
الثاني إذا بلغ الغلام وقد تعارضت الدعاوى أو البينات خيرناه بينهما
وأمرناه بالتعويل على حركة الباطن من جهة الجبلة لا على محض التشهي
فإن التحق بأحدهما ثم رجع لم يمكن بخلاف الصبي المخير بين الأبوين لأن
ذلك يعتمد  الشهوة
فلو ظهر قائف فيقدم قول الفاسق على التحاقه لأنه أقوى
وإن القائف بينة على خلافة قدمت البينة لأنها أقوى من قول القائف
وفي حكم اختيار اللقيط بعد التمييز وقبل البلوغ خلاف

### | الحكم الرابع رقه وحريته

وللقيط أربعة أحوال
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ن-ي (j-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To commit an offense, transgression, or crime against another; the act of harming.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A culpable act (jināyah) entailing liability, whether against life or limb, distinct from mere sin (ithm) in its juristic consequence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in denoting the physical act of transgression; metaphorically (majāz) extended to any harmful deed.
- Root: ق-ص-ص (q-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, trace, or pursue; to cut evenly; hence retaliation (qiṣāṣ) as exact equivalence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Retributive justice (qiṣāṣ) as the divinely ordained equal recompense for homicide or wounding, rooted in the principle of equivalence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the sense of tracing the crime to its perpetrator; technical (ʿurfī) in the juristic sense of exact retaliation.
- Root: ب-ي-ت (b-y-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: House, abode; bayt al-māl: the public treasury as the communal abode of wealth.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The collective Muslim treasury (bayt al-māl) as the institutional embodiment of communal responsibility for the unprotected.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a physical house; metaphorical (majāz) for the fiscal institution of the community.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (in kāna... fa-) and exceptive particles (illā) to delineate juristic branches, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second ruling concerns the foundling (al-laqīṭ) regarding his crimes and the compensation for his errors.

His criminal act (jināyah) while a minor, and the indemnity (arsh) for his erroneous harm, falls upon the public treasury (bayt al-māl). If harm is inflicted upon him by error, then the indemnity belongs to him. If the act warrants retaliation (qiṣāṣ), then we examine the matter. If it concerns the life (al-nafs), then the text of al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—differs regarding retaliation. As for its obligation, it is apparent, for he is inviolable (maʿṣūm) and a Muslim. As for its abrogation, there is disagreement concerning its basis. The majority (al-aktharūn) said: The reason is that he has no heir, and that the right of retaliation is established for the insane (majānīn), minors, and all Muslims—so how can it be exacted? And upon this reasoning, if one kills a person who has no heir, then there is no retaliation; likewise, any retaliation (qiṣāṣ) whose claim is left to one who has no heir entails no retaliation upon the offender.

The author of al-Taqrīb (al-Qaffāl) refuted this, because the entitlement is not attributed to individual insane persons or minors, but rather to the aspect of Islam (jihat al-Islām). He reasoned that the text of al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—indicates his hesitation (tawaqquf) regarding the foundling's Islam, due to his following the domicile (dār), awaiting its change after he reaches maturity (bulūgh).

As for the case where his limb is severed, then upon the path of the companions (aṣḥāb), retaliation is obligatory, for the entitled claimant is specified. Upon the path of the author of al-Taqrīb, it is suspended (yatawaqqaf). If the foundling expresses his Islam upon reaching maturity, then the obligation becomes evident; otherwise, it does not.

This applies when the one who severed is a Muslim. If he is a dhimmī (protected non-Muslim), then there is no suspension from the aspect of Islam.

If it is said: Does the Imām exact the retaliation? We say: If it concerns the life, he exacts it if he deems it appropriate, or he takes the blood-money (diyah) for the public treasury, for there is no meaning to suspension. If he were prevented from taking the substitute, then retaliation would become a mere punitive limit (ḥadd).

If it concerns a limb, then the entitled claimant is the foundling himself, so the Imām does not exact it, because the guardian (walī)—according to al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—does not exact retaliation.

It is narrated from al-Qaffāl a view (wajh) that the sultan exacts retaliation for a limb on behalf of the insane person, because one does not await a specific time for his recovery.

And does the Imām have the authority to take the indemnity (arsh) immediately? We examine: If it is obligatory for a wealthy minor, then no. If it is obligatory for a poor insane person, then he takes it due to need and the absence of waiting. If it is obligatory for a poor minor or a wealthy insane person, then there are two views (wajhān), due to the presence of one of the two considerations.

If we say he does not take it, then the one upon whom retaliation is due is imprisoned until recovery and maturity, and no heed is paid to the length of imprisonment, for forfeiting the right is not permissible.

If we say he takes it, then the minor reaches maturity and rises to demand retaliation—there are two views concerning this, whose origin is whether the taking is for mere sequestration (al-ḥaylūlah) or whether it is an abrogation of retaliation by virtue of the apparent interests (maṣāliḥ).

Then the companions said: The authority to take the wealth—if we deem it an abrogation, then it is not established for the executor (waṣī); if we deem it for sequestration, then it is established for him.

---

### | The Third Ruling: The Lineage (Nasab) of the Foundling

This contains several questions.

The first: If a person appears and claims that he is the foundling's father, the lineage is established by the mere claim (daʿwā), for there is no disputant, and establishing proof (bayyinah) of lineage is difficult.

Yes, if the minor reaches maturity and denies it, does the lineage become severed? There are two views. One: No, for the ruling was already established. The second: Yes, just as when an adult is claimed (istilḥāq) and he denies it, for it is not established. If the claimant is the finder (multaqiṭ) himself, the lineage is established.

Mālik—may God have mercy on him—said: It is not established, because a man does not abandon his own child and then find him, unless he does not recognize his children—for he might do so as an auspicious omen (tafāʾulan).

The second: If a slave comes and claims the foundling (istilḥāq), the text here states that he is joined to him, while the text in the chapter of claims (daʿāwā) states that he is not qualified. The companions said two opinions. The correct one is that he is qualified, for the possibility of lineage for a slave is attainable. The second: No, because he severs the patronage (walāʾ) of his master from himself by this.

Then, upon the correct view, if a free man claims a slave child, he is joined to him. Some forbade this for the same reason—namely, that the free man severs, by his claim, the master's patronage.

The third: If a woman claims the foundling, there are three views. One: He is joined to her, like the man. The second: No, for if he were joined to her, he would be joined to her husband, and accepting her statement against her husband is impossible; joining him to her while excluding the husband is also impossible. The third: He is joined to an unmarried woman (khalīyah) but not to a married one, for the reason we mentioned.

The fourth: If two men dispute over the lineage of a newborn, a free man is not given precedence over a slave, nor a Muslim over a disbeliever; rather, they are equal. Yes, the one in possession (ṣāḥib al-yad) is given precedence, with two conditions. One: That his possession is not the possession of finding (yad al-iltiqāṭ), for the possession of finding does not indicate lineage—rather, it indicates custody (ḥaḍānah). The second: That the one in possession had claimed the foundling previously. If his claim is not heard except at the time of the second claimant's dispute, then there are two views. One: He is not given precedence, for the possession has no indication since it was not accompanied by a claim. The second: Yes, he is given precedence, for possession in general is indicative, and perhaps the claim had occurred but did not reach us.

---

### | Two Subsidiary Branches (Farʿān)

The first: If each of them presents proof (bayyinah) that the foundling is his child, the two proofs are mutually contradictory (taʿāraḍat) and cancel each other out (tahāratā), for there is no way to adopt the view of division (al-qismah) nor the view of suspension (al-waqf), for it yields no benefit. Nor is the view of casting lots (al-qurʿah) applicable, for lineage is not established by lot.

If they dispute over custody and each presents proof of finding (iltiqāṭ), and the proof testifies for one of them of precedence in finding, then he is given precedence in custody—even though we hesitate in a similar case concerning properties (imlāk)—because the right of custody does not transfer, while ownership may transfer. Likewise, if one of them is the one in possession, his proof is given precedence, for it is an indication of finding, like the proof of the one entering (al-dākhil). If they are contradictory in every respect, then either the view of cancellation (tahātur) or the view of casting lots applies; there is no way to adopt suspension or division.

The second: If the boy reaches maturity while the claims or proofs are contradictory, we give him the choice between them and command him to rely upon the inner inclination (ḥarakat al-bāṭin) from the aspect of innate disposition (jibillah), not upon mere whim (shahwah). If he aligns himself with one of them and then retracts, it is not permitted—unlike the minor who is given choice between his parents, for that relies upon desire.

If a physiognomist (qāʾif) appears, then the statement of the physiognomist is given precedence over his own choice, for it is stronger. If the physiognomist's proof conflicts with another proof, the proof is given precedence, for it is stronger than the statement of the physiognomist.

Concerning the ruling on the foundling's choice after discernment (tamyīz) and before maturity, there is disagreement.

---

### | The Fourth Ruling: His Enslavement and His Freedom

The foundling has four states.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الحالة الأولى إذا لم يدع أحد رقه

فالأصل فيه الحرية في كل ما يخصه ولا يتعلق بغيره فينبني فيه الأمر على
الأصل إذ يحكم له بالملك ويصرف ماله إلى بيت المال إذا مات
ولو جنى فالأرش على بيت المال لأنه لم يتوقف في توريث بيت المال منه فكذا
في تغريمه لأنه بإزائه
أما ما يتعلق بالغير فإن أتلف متلف ماله وغرمه له إذا الغرم لا بد منه
ولا أرب للغارم في مصرفه وإن قتله عبد قتل به
وإن قتله حر فحاصل الخلاف ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه يجب القصاص أو الدية فإن الأصل الحرية إلى أن يظهر نقيضه ولم
يظهر
والثاني أنه تجب الدية دون القصاص لأن القصاص يسقط بالشبهة وهذه شبهة
ظاهرة
والثالث أنه يجب أقل الأمرين من الدية أو القيمة إذ لا تشغل الذمة
البرئية إلا بيقين وقد ذكرنا قولا في سقوط قصاص من لا وارث له على التعيين
فذلك القول عائد هاهنا
وإنما الأوجه الثلاثة تفريع على القول الآخر

### | الحالة الثانية أن يدعي مدع نرقة بغير بينة

فإن لم يكن في يده فلا تقبل دعواه وكذا إن كان في يده واليد يد الالتقاط
لأنا عرفنا مستنده
وفيه وجه أنه يحكم له بالرق بيد الالتقاط كمن وجد ثوبا في طريق فادعى
ملكه
وهو ضعيف لأنه لا حق للثوب في الانفكاك عن الملك وللصبي حق فيه
وإن لم تكن يد الالتقاط بل وجدناه في يده وهو يزعم أنه رقيقه فهو مصدق
فإن بلغ الصبي فأنكر ففي احتياج السيد إلى البينة وجهان سبق نظيرهما في
النسب

### | الحالة الثالثة أن يقيم المدعي بينة على الرق مطلقا

فحاصل المذهب ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها أنها تسمع كالبينة على الملك
والثاني لا بد من ذكر السبب لأن  أمر الرق خطير وربما عولت البينة على
ظاهر
اليد
والثالث وهو الأصح أن يد المدعي إن كانت عن جهة الالتقاط
فلا بد من ذكر السبب لأن البينة ربما استندت إلى هذه اليد التى لا دلالة
لها
وإن لم يكن للمدعي يد أو لم يكن له يد التقاط سمعت البينة

### | التفريع

إن قلنا لا بد من التقيد فالقيد أن يقول هذا رقيقي ولدته جاريتي المملوكة
في ملكي وعلى ملكي
فلو اقتصر على أنها ولدته جاريته المملوكة فوجهان
أحدهما لا إذ قد تلد الجارية المملوكة ولدا حرا عن وطء بشبهة
والثاني نعم إذ غرض التقيد أن يأمن استناد البينة إلى ظاهر اليد
ثم لو قيدت البينة الرق بالسبي أو الشراء أو الإرث كان كما لو قيدته
بالولادة إذ المقصود دفع حيال الإطلاق

### | الحالة الرابعة أن يبلغ اللقيط ويقر على نفسه بالرق للمدعي

نظر فإن لم يسبق منه ما يناقض هذا الإقرار قبل قوله على الصحيح إذ لم تكن
الحرية مجزومة بل كان بناء على الظاهر
وذكر صاحب التقريب قولا أنه لا تقبل تفريعا على أنه لو أعرب بالكفر لم
يجعل كافرا أصليا مراعاة لاستصحاب حكم الإسلام وكذا استصحاب أصل الحرية وهو
بعيد
أما إذا سبق منه ما يناقضه نظر فإن سبق إقرار بالحرية قطع العراقيون
والقاضي حسين بأنه لا يقبل إقراره إذ لله عز وجل حق في حرية العباد وقد ثبت
بإقراره فليس له إبطاله
وقطع الصيدلاني بالقبول كما لو أنكر حق الغير ثم أقر وكالمرأة إذا أنكرت
الرجعة ثم أقرت
ولو كان يرعي حق الشرع لما قبل إقرار اللقيط ابتداءا وقد حكم بحريته بناء
على الظاهر
أما إذا سبق إقرار بالرق لإنسان فأنكر المقر له فأقر بالرق لغيره حكى
العراقيون من نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه لا يقبل إقراره الثاني لأنه إذا
رد إقراره الأول عاد إلى يد نفسه فكأنه قد تم الحكم بحريته والثاني نقض
وخرج ابن سريج قولا أنه يقبل إذ الإقراران متوافقان على الرق وإنما
الاختلاف في  الإضافة إلى السيد
أما إذا لم يسبق إقرار ولكن سبق تصرفات تستدعي الحرية من نكاح وبيع وغيره
فهذا لا يمنعه من أن يقر على نفسه فيقبل إقراره بالرق
ويظهر أثره في كل ما قدر عليه كما إذا لم يسبق التصرف وهل يقبل فيما يقر
بغيره فيه ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها أنه يقبل لأن الأمر فيه لا يتجزأ فيصير إقراره كقيام البينة
ولو قامت البينة على رقة لقبل مطلقا فيما له وعليه وسلك بتصرفاته السابقة
مسلك الصادر من الرقيق بغير إذنه
فذلك لا يخفى حكمه والتفريع عليه فكذلك هذا
والثاني انه لا يقبل فيما يضر بغيره إذ سبق منه تصرف هو التزام لحقوق
الأعيان فلا تقبل مناقضته
والثالث أنه لا يقبل فيما مضي لأن الالتزام مقصور عليه وفي المستقبل هو
رقيق مطلق فيما له وعليه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ر-ر (ḥ-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Freedom as the intrinsic, unmarked state of the human person; the opposite of servitude (riqq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Freedom (ḥurriyyah) as a presumptive legal continuity (istiṣḥāb al-aṣl) — a divinely ordained default that persists until a clear counter-proof (nāqiḍ) emerges.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Ḥaqīqah — freedom is the literal, operative presumption in all rulings; any claim of enslavement is a metaphorical/exceptional intrusion requiring explicit substantiation.
- Root: ل-ق-ط (l-q-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pick up, to find; a foundling (laqīṭ) is one who is picked up from the road, having no known lineage or status.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The foundling's freedom is a legal fiction rooted in the sanctity of the human person (ḥurmat al-ādamī), not a verified fact — hence it can be overturned by confession or evidence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The "hand" (yad) of the finder is a mere custodial hand (yad al-iltiqāṭ), not a proprietary hand — a distinction between literal possession and legal ownership.
- Root: ق-ر-ر (q-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To affirm, to confess, to establish firmly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Confession (iqrār) as a self-imposed legal obligation — binding upon the confessor but not upon third parties or divine rights (ḥuqūq Allāh).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Majāz — a confession against oneself is literal truth-telling; a confession affecting others is metaphorical extension, hence subject to restriction.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Sequencing (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The text repeatedly structures rulings as "if X, then Y," where the protasis (condition) determines the apodosis (ruling). The particle "fa" (ف) marks the apodosis, indicating that each case is a self-contained juridical unit whose outcome flows necessarily from its stated condition.
chapters.translation:
---

**I say:** The first case — when no one claims his enslavement.

The foundational principle is freedom (al-ḥurriyyah) in everything that pertains to him personally and does not involve another's right. The ruling is therefore built upon this principle: he is adjudged to have ownership (milk), and his wealth is disbursed to the public treasury (bayt al-māl) upon his death. Likewise, if he commits an injury (jināyah), the compensation (arsh) falls upon the public treasury — for since we did not hesitate to make the treasury inherit from him, so too we do not hesitate to charge it with his liabilities, because the one is in exchange for the other.

As for what involves another's right: if someone destroys his property, the destroyer must compensate him — for compensation is unavoidable, and the one who pays has no interest in where the payment goes. If a slave kills him, the slave is executed in retaliation. If a free man kills him, the dispute yields three positions (awjuh):

**First:** Retaliation (qiṣāṣ) or blood-money (diyah) is obligatory, for the principle of freedom persists until its contrary appears — and no contrary has appeared.

**Second:** Only blood-money is obligatory, not retaliation, because retaliation is dropped by doubt (shubhah), and this is a manifest doubt.

**Third:** The lesser of the two — blood-money or the slave's value — is obligatory, for an innocent liability (dhimmah) is not burdened except with certainty. We have already mentioned a position on the dropping of retaliation for one who has no designated heir; that position returns here. The three positions above are merely branches upon the other position.

---

**The second case** — when a claimant asserts his enslavement without evidence (bayyinah).

If the foundling is not in his possession, his claim is not accepted. Likewise, if he is in his possession but the possession is a custodial hand (yad al-iltiqāṭ) — for we know its basis. There is a position that he is adjudged enslaved by virtue of the custodial hand, like one who finds a garment on the road and claims ownership of it. But this is weak, because a garment has no right to be released from ownership, whereas the child has a right therein.

If the possession is not custodial — rather we find the child in his hand and he claims the child is his slave — then he is believed. If the child reaches maturity and denies this, then whether the master needs evidence is a question with two positions, the parallel of which has preceded in the chapter on lineage (nasab).

---

**The third case** — when the claimant produces evidence of enslavement in absolute terms (muṭlaqan).

The school's outcome is three positions (aqwāl):

**First:** It is heard, like evidence of ownership.

**Second:** The cause (sabab) must be mentioned, for the matter of enslavement is grave, and the witnesses might have relied upon the apparent possession (ẓāhir al-yad).

**Third — and this is the most correct (al-aṣaḥḥ):** If the claimant's possession is from the custodial channel, the cause must be mentioned — for the evidence might have been based upon this hand which carries no indication. But if the claimant has no possession, or his possession is not custodial, the evidence is heard.

---

**The branch (al-tafrīʿ):**

If we say that specification is required, then the specification is that he say: "This is my slave; my owned slave-girl bore him in my ownership and upon my ownership." If he limits himself to saying she bore him — his owned slave-girl — then there are two positions:

**One:** No — for an owned slave-girl might bear a free child from intercourse under doubt (waṭʾ bi-shubhah).

**Two:** Yes — for the purpose of specification is to guard against the evidence being based upon the apparent possession.

Then, if the evidence specifies enslavement by capture (saby), purchase (shirāʾ), or inheritance (irth), it is as if he specified it by birth — for the objective is to repel the danger of absolute assertion.

---

**The fourth case** — when the foundling reaches maturity and confesses (aqarra) to enslavement for the claimant.

We consider: if nothing preceded from him that contradicts this confession, his statement is accepted according to the correct position — for freedom was not a matter of certainty but was built upon the apparent (ẓāhir). The author of al-Taqrīb mentioned a position that it is not accepted, branching upon the rule that if he had expressed disbelief (kufr), he would not be deemed an original disbeliever — out of regard for the continuity of Islam's ruling (istiṣḥāb ḥukm al-Islām). Likewise the continuity of the principle of freedom. But this is remote.

As for when something contradictory preceded from him: if a confession of freedom preceded, the Iraqis and Judge Ḥusayn ruled definitively that his confession is not accepted — for Allah, exalted, has a right in the freedom of His servants, and it was established by his confession; he has no power to nullify it. Al-Ṣaydalānī ruled definitively for acceptance — just as one who denies another's right then confesses to it, and like a woman who denies the revocation (rajʿah) then confesses to it. For if the right of the Law were being observed, the foundling's confession would not have been accepted in the first place — yet his freedom was adjudged upon the apparent.

As for when a confession of enslavement to one person preceded, then the confessee denied it, and he confessed to enslavement for another — the Iraqis narrated from the text (naṣṣ) of al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, that his second confession is not accepted. For when his first confession was rejected, he returned to his own hand — as if his freedom had been adjudged — and the second is a nullification. Ibn Surayj derived a position that it is accepted, for the two confessions agree upon enslavement; the difference is only in attribution to the master.

As for when no confession preceded, but acts requiring freedom preceded — such as marriage (nikāḥ), sale (bayʿ), and the like — this does not prevent him from confessing against himself, and his confession of enslavement is accepted. Its effect appears in everything he is capable of, just as if no act had preceded. As for whether it is accepted regarding what involves another's right — there are three positions:

**First:** It is accepted, for the matter is indivisible; his confession becomes like the establishment of evidence. If evidence of his enslavement were established, it would be accepted absolutely regarding what is for him and against him, and his prior acts would be treated as acts emanating from a slave without permission. That ruling is not obscure, nor its branches — so likewise here.

**Second:** It is not accepted regarding what harms another, for he had previously engaged in acts that constituted an assumption of rights over specific objects (ḥuqūq al-aʿyān); contradicting that is not accepted.

**Third:** It is not accepted regarding the past, for the assumption was confined to him; but in the future he is an absolute slave regarding what is for him and against him.

### | ويتفرع على القولين الآخرين فروع

الأول لقيطة نكحت ثم أقرت بالرق فالناكح دائم لأن في قطعه إضرارا
بالزوج والوطء وإن كان مستقبلا فهو في حكم الماضي وولدها الذى انفصل منها
قبل الإقرار حر ولا قيمة على الزوج إذ فيه إضرار
وفي المستقبل ترق الأولاد إن فرقنا بين الماضي والمستقبل
ولا يجعل الولد كالمستوفى بالنكاح لأنه موهوم بخلاف استحقاق الوطء
وأما المهر فللسيد المطالبة بأقل الأمرين من المسمى أو من المثل
فإن كان المسمى أقل ففي الزيادة إضرار بالزوج وإن كان مهر المثل أقل
فالسيد لا يدعي أكثر منه
أما العدة فإذا طلقها الزوج طلاقا رجعيا اعتدت بثلاثة أقراء لأنه استحق
الرجعة في الثالثة وفيه إضرار به
وكذا إن كان الطلاق بائنا لأن نفس العدة حق للزوج وإلا إذا قبلنا إقرارها
فيما يضر بالغير في المستقبل
ويحتمل أن يقال هذا كالمستحق بالعقد السابق كما في الوطء
فإن مات الزوج قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه تعتد بشهرين وخمسة أيام إذ حق
الزوج إنما يحسن مراعاته في حياته
فمن أصحابنا من قال إن سقط حقه فلا عدة لأنها تدعي بطلان النكاح من الأصل
بل عليها الاستبراء إن وطئت وإلا فلا  شئ عليها والنص ما ذكرناه وكأن
الشافعي رضي الله عنه ينظر في أصل العدة إلى حق الشرع وفي تفصيله إلى حق
الزوج
أما تسلميها إلى الزوج نهارا فيجب لأنه مستحق بالعقد السابق ففي المنع
إضرار

### | الفرع الثاني لقيط نكح ثم أقر بالرق

فإن قبلنا الإقرار مطلقا فقد بان بطلان النكاح من أصله ولا يخفى حكم وطء
الرقيق في مهر المثل إن جرى
وإن لم نقبل فيما مضي فقد بطل حقه من بضعها في المستقبل في الحال فكأنه
طلاق فيجب نصف المهر متعلقا بذمته وكسبه إن لم يكن وطئ وإن كان وطئ فتمام
المسمى لأن الوطء جرى في نكاح لم يتبعه بالإبطال فيما مضى فلا يجب إلا مهر
المثل

### | الفرع الثالث لقيط باع واشترى ثم أقر

فهذا أمر قد مضى فإن لم يقبل قوله في الماضي لم يتبع ما مضى وإن قبل قوله
عموما قدرنا أن تيك التصرفات صدرت من عبد غير مأذون فيسترد أعيان الأموال
ويرد الأثمان
وما تلف في يدهم مضمونة للسيد وما تلف في يد العبد فيتعلق بذمة العبد لا
برقبته وكسبه كديون معاملة العبد ولا ينفع العامل ظنه حريته عند التصرف

### | الفرع الرابع جنى اللقيط ثم أقر بالرق

اقتص منه أو تعلق الأرش برقته
وإن جني عليه اقتص إن كان الجاني رقيقا وإن كان حرا عدل إلى الأرش
فإن قطع إحدى يديه وتساوت القيمة ونصف الدية فذاك
وإن كان نصف القيمة أقل فليس للسيد إلا ذاك فإنه لا يطلب مزيدا
وإن كان نصف القيمة أكثر فرع على الأقوال
فإن قلنا الإقرار مطلقا لزم
وإن بعضنا اقتصر على نصف الدية فإنه إضرار بالجاني
وفيه وجه أن التغليظ على الجاني أولى

### | فرع به الاختتام

إذا قذف لقيطا بالغا وادعى رقه فادعى اللقيط حرية نفسه فقولان
أحدهما القول قول القاذف لأن الأصل براءة ذمته
والثاني القول قول اللقيط لأن الأصل الحرية وهو من تقابل الأصلين
وإن قطع حر طرفه وجرى هذا النزاع فطريقان
أحدهما طرد القولين
والثاني القطع بالقصاص إذ  لو لم نوجب لعدلنا إلى القيمة وهي أيضا مشكوك
فيها
أما الحد إذا ترك فالتعزيز مستيقن بكل حال والله تعالى أعلم وأحكم
= كتاب الفرائض=
والأصل فيها قوله تعالى {يوصيكم الله في أولادكم} وقال صلى الله عليه
وسلم
إن الله تعالى لم يكل قسم مواريثكم إلى ملك مقرب ولا إلى نبي مرسل ولكن
تولى بيانها فقسمها أبين قسم
وقال عليه السلام
تعلموا الفرائض وعلموها الناس فإنها نصف العلم وإني امرؤ مقبوض وسينزع
العلم من أمتي حتى يختلف رجلان في فريضة فلا يجدان من يعرف حكم الله فيها
وقد اختلف الصحابة في تفصيل الورثة واختار الشافعي رضي الله عنه مذهب زيد
لأنه أقرب إلى القياس ولقوله عليه السلام أفرضكم زيد
فنقتصر على ذكر مذهبه
فالوراثة تارة تكون بسبب عام كجهة الإسلام وأخرى بسبب خاص كالنكاح
والولاء وتارة النسب
والوارثون من الرجال عندنا عشرة
من جانب العلو الأب وأب الأب وإن علا
ومن جانب السفل الابن وابن الابن وإن سفل
ومن الطرف الأخ وابنه إلا أن يكون ابن أخ لأم والعم وابنه إلا أن يكون
عما لأم فإنه لا يرث ولا ولده
فيبقى اثنان وهما المعتق والزوج
والوارثات من النساء سبع
الأم والجدة والبنت وبنت الابن والأخت والزوجة ومولدة المعتقة
ومن عدا هؤلاء كأب الأم وأولاد البنات وأولاد الإخوة من الأم وأولاد
الأخوات والعمات والخالات والأخوال وأولادهم فهم من ذوي الأرحام لا ميراث
لهم عندنا بل الفاضل من المستحقين المذكورين لبيت المال
وتفصيل النظر في الوارث المذكورين تحصره أبواب
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في مقادير أنصباء ذوي الفروض - صلى
الله عليه وسلم -
والورثة قسمان ذو فرض وعصبة
وذو الفرض من له سهم مقدر شرعا لا يزيد وهم أصناف

- Root: ق-ر-ر (q-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To affirm, establish, settle; confession (iqrār) as a legal acknowledgment of a binding fact.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, iqrār is a self-incriminating attestation whose validity is weighed against third-party harm (ḍarar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in judicial admission; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to future effects, since the past is settled but the future remains contingent.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Harm, injury, detriment; the legal maxim "no harm and no reciprocating harm" (lā ḍarar wa lā ḍirār).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A jurisprudential criterion for invalidating or upholding rulings; harm to others (ḍarar bi-l-ghayr) restricts the efficacy of one's own confession.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in physical injury; metaphorical in legal detriment, e.g., nullifying a marriage contract.
- Root: ف-ر-ض (f-r-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To determine, apportion, prescribe; farīḍah as a fixed share ordained by God.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In inheritance law, farāʾiḍ are the divinely legislated portions (e.g., half, third, sixth) that cannot be exceeded.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for ordained shares; metaphorical for the science of inheritance itself, as in "half of knowledge."
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text alternates between hypothetical clauses (fa-in qabilnā... fa-in lam naqbal...) and exceptions (illā idhā...), requiring precise tracking of protasis and apodosis to render legal consequences accurately.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now there branch off from the two aforementioned positions further subsidiary issues.

**The First Branch:** A foundling (laqīṭ) married, then confessed to being enslaved. The marriage contract remains valid, because annulling it would cause harm (ḍarar) to the husband. And though the sexual intercourse (waṭʾ) is yet future, it is treated as belonging to the past [in legal effect]. Her child that was separated from her before the confession is free, and there is no indemnity (qīmah) upon the husband, since [imposing it] would be harmful. As for the future, the children are enslaved if we distinguish between past and future [effects of the confession]. And the child is not treated like that which is already consumed through marriage, because [its existence] is merely conjectural (mawhūm), unlike the entitlement to intercourse.

As for the dowry (mahr), the master may claim the lesser of two amounts: the specified dowry (al-musammā) or the equivalent dowry (mahr al-mithl). For if the specified amount is less, then [demanding] the excess would harm the husband; and if the equivalent dowry is less, the master does not claim more than it.

As for the waiting period (ʿiddah): if the husband divorces her with a revocable divorce (ṭalāq rajʿī), she observes three menstrual periods (aqrāʾ), because he is entitled to take her back in the third period, and [denying this] would harm him. Likewise, if the divorce is irrevocable (bāʾin), because the waiting period itself is a right of the husband — unless we accept her confession in what harms others in the future. And it is plausible to say: this is like what is entitled by the prior contract, as in the case of intercourse.

If the husband dies, al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — said: she observes a waiting period of two months and five days, since the husband's right is only to be observed during his lifetime. Thus, some of our companions said: if his right lapses, then there is no waiting period, because she claims the marriage was void from its very origin; rather, she must observe a period of abstention (istibrāʾ) if she was sexually penetrated, and if not, then nothing is incumbent upon her. But the textual ruling (al-naṣṣ) is what we have mentioned. It is as though al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — considers, in the essence of the waiting period, the right of the Sacred Law (ḥaqq al-sharʿ), and in its details, the right of the husband.

As for her being handed over to the husband during the day, this is obligatory, because it is entitled by the prior contract, and preventing it would be harmful.

**The Second Branch:** A foundling married, then confessed to being enslaved. If we accept the confession absolutely, then the marriage is revealed to be void from its origin, and the ruling on intercourse with a slave regarding the equivalent dowry is not hidden, if it occurred. But if we do not accept it regarding the past, then his right to her sexual intimacy (buḍʿ) is nullified for the future immediately, as though it were a divorce. Thus, half the specified dowry is obligatory, attached to his liability (dhimmah) and his earnings (kasb), if he did not have intercourse. If he did have intercourse, then the full specified amount [is due], because the intercourse occurred in a marriage that he did not follow with annulment regarding the past; hence, only the equivalent dowry is not obligatory [but the specified one].

**The Third Branch:** A foundling sold and bought, then confessed [to enslavement]. This is a matter that has passed. If we do not accept his statement regarding the past, then what has passed is not undone. If we accept his statement absolutely, we deem those transactions to have issued from an unauthorized slave (ʿabd ghayr maʾdhūn); thus, the very properties (aʿyān al-amwāl) are reclaimed, and the prices (athmān) are returned. What perished in the hands of the buyers is guaranteed (maḍmūnah) to the master; what perished in the slave's hand attaches to the slave's liability, not to his person (raqabah) nor his earnings, like the debts of a slave's transactions (duyūn muʿāmalat al-ʿabd). And the acting slave's assumption of his freedom at the time of the transaction does not avail him.

**The Fourth Branch:** A foundling committed a tort (janā), then confessed to enslavement. Retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is exacted from him, or the compensation for injury (arsh) attaches to his person. If a tort was committed against him, retaliation is exacted if the offender is a slave; if he is free, one turns to the compensation. If he cut off one of his hands, and the value [of the slave] equals half the blood-money (diyah), then that is it. If half the value is less, the master has only that, for he does not seek more. If half the value is more, then it branches upon the [earlier] positions: if we say the confession is accepted absolutely, it is incumbent; if we distinguish, we restrict to half the blood-money, for [more] would harm the offender. And there is a view that imposing the heavier [liability] upon the offender is more appropriate.

**The Concluding Branch:** If someone accuses a mature foundling of illicit fornication (qadhf) and claims his enslavement, while the foundling claims his own freedom, there are two positions. One: the accuser's statement is given credence, because the default is the freedom of his liability (barāʾat dhimmah). The second: the foundling's statement is given credence, because the default is freedom — this being a case of two conflicting defaults (taqābul al-aṣlayn). If a free man cuts off his limb and this dispute arises, there are two paths. One: to extend the two positions. The second: to decisively affirm retaliation, for if we did not impose it, we would turn to the value (qīmah), which is also doubtful. As for the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), if it is abandoned, then discretionary punishment (taʿzīr) is certain in any case. And God — exalted and wise — knows best.

= The Book of Inheritances (Kitāb al-Farāʾiḍ) =

The foundational principle therein is the saying of God — exalted — {«God instructs you concerning your children»} (Q 4:11). And the Prophet — peace be upon him — said: "God — exalted — did not delegate the division of your inheritances to a proximate angel nor to a sent prophet, but rather undertook its explanation Himself, and divided it with the clearest division." And he — peace be upon him — said: "Learn the inheritances and teach them to the people, for they are half of knowledge; and I am a man who will be taken, and knowledge will be withdrawn from my community until two men will differ over an inheritance portion and find no one who knows God's ruling therein."

The Companions differed over the details of the heirs, and al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — chose the school of Zayd [ibn Thābit], because it is closest to analogical reasoning (qiyās), and due to his saying — peace be upon him — "The most knowledgeable of you in inheritance is Zayd." So we restrict ourselves to mentioning his school.

Inheritance (wirāthah) is sometimes due to a general cause, like the aspect of Islam; sometimes to a specific cause, like marriage (nikāḥ) and clientage (walāʾ); and sometimes to lineage (nasab).

The male heirs with us are ten: from the ascending side — the father, and the father's father however high; from the descending side — the son, and the son's son however low; from the lateral side — the brother and his son, except a maternal brother's son; and the paternal uncle and his son, except a maternal uncle, for he does not inherit, nor does his child. There remain two: the emancipator (muʿtiq) and the husband.

The female heirs are seven: the mother, the grandmother, the daughter, the son's daughter, the sister, the wife, and the female emancipator of an emancipated slave (muwallidat al-muʿtiqah).

Whoever is beyond these — like the maternal grandfather, the children of daughters, the children of maternal brothers, the children of sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, maternal uncles, and their children — these are among the kindred (dhawū al-arḥām); there is no inheritance for them with us. Rather, the surplus from the aforementioned entitled heirs goes to the public treasury (bayt al-māl).

The detailed examination of the aforementioned heirs is encompassed by chapters.

— Peace be upon him — **Chapter One: On the Amounts of the Shares of the Fixed-Portion Heirs (Aṣḥāb al-Furūḍ)** — Peace be upon him —

The heirs are of two kinds: a fixed-portion heir (dhū farḍ) and an agnatic heir (ʿaṣabah). The fixed-portion heir is one who has a share determined by the Sacred Law that does not increase. They are the following categories:
