chapters.arabic_text:
وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا قال للحائض أنت طالق للبدعة وقع في الحال وإذا قال للسنة من
يقع حتى تطهر وكذا إن قال للتي طهرت قبل الجماع أنت طالق للسنة وقع الطلاق
في الحال وإن قال للبدعة لم تطلق حتى تجامع أو تحيض
والمقصود أن اللام للتأقيت فيما يشبه الأوقات كالسنة والبدعة فهو كقوله
أنت طالق لرمضان فإن تأقيت برمضان وأما لا يشبه الأوقات فاللام فيه للتعليل
كقوله أنت طالق لرضي فلان فإنه يقع في الحال رضي فلان أو سخط وقوله أنت
طالق لدخول الدار فهو تعليق يقع في الحال بخلاف قوله لقدوم زيد فإنه تأقيت
بالقدوم لأن القدوم مما ينتظر كالحيض والطهر
وإنما صريح لفظ التعليق إن وإذا وأما اللام فهو للتعليل ظاهرا إلا فيما
يشبه الأوقات وحيث حملنا على التعليل فلو قال أردت التأقيت فيدين في الباطن
وهل يقبل ظاهرا في وجهان وهذا فيما إذا خاطب متعرضة للسنة والبدعة فإن خاطب
صغيرة أو آيسة أو غير مدخول بها فهو للتعليل حتى يقع الطلاق في الحال سواء
قال أنت طالق للسنة أو للبدعة وفيه وجه إنه لو قال للسنة وقع في الحال فإن
معناه طلاق لا تحريم فيه ولو قال للبدعة لم يقع حتى  تحيض الصغيرة وحتى يدخل
بغير المدخول بها
أما إذا قال لمتعرضة للحالتين إذا قدم زيد فأنت طالق للسنة فإن قدم وهي
حائض لم يقع حتى تطهر وإن قال للبدعة وقدم وهي في طهر لم يجامع فيه لم تطلق
حتى تحيض أو يجامع
وإن علق بمجرد القدوم فقدم وهي حائض نفذ طلاقا بدعيا وإن لم تكن في حالة
التعليق من أهل السنة والبدعة نظر إلى حالة الوقوع لا إلى التعليق
فرع لو قال في طهر لم يجامعها فيه أنت طالق للبدعة فإذا جامع وقع الطلاق
كما غابت الحشفة وهل يلزمه بدوام الوطء إن لم ينزع في الحال مهر آخر من حيث
يجب المهر بابتداء وطء الرجعية فيه قولان مأخذهما أن دوام الوطء هل هو
كابتدائه والأظهر أنه لا يجب لأن مهر النكاح تناول أول هذا الوطء فلا يبعض
حكمه وإن تغير الحل في أثنائه
الثانية إن قال أنت طالق ثلاثا بعضهن للسنة وبعضهن للبدعة فإن قال أردت
إيقاع طلقة ونصف في الحال قبل وكملت طلقتان وإن قال أردت وقوع ثنتين في
الحال قبل ولو قال أردت إيقاع ثلاثة أنصاف في الحال وقع الثلاث في الحال
وإن قال لم يكن لي نية حمل على التشطير ووقع في الحال طلقة ونصف ولكن تكمل
طلقتان وهو كما لو قال هذه الدار بعضها لزيد وبعضها لعمرو حمل مطلقه على
التشطير لأن الأكثر لا يسمى بعضا في الظاهر فلو قال أردت واحدة في الحال
وثنتين في المستقبل فالظاهر أنه يقبل وفيه وجه أنه لا يقبل لأن تسمية
الثنتين من الثلاث بعضا بعيد
وقال المزني قياس قول الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن لا يقع في الحال لا طلقة
إذا لم ينو
شيئا لأن البعض مجمل فينبغي أن ينزل على الأقل إذ يحتمل الواحد ويحتمل
واحدا ونصفا وليجعل هذا تخريجا منه على مذهب الشافعي رضي الله عنه
الثالثة إذا قال أنت طالق أحسن الطلاق أو أفضله أو أجمله أو غير ذلك من
صفات المدح فهو كما لو قال  أنت طالق للسنة فلو كانت في حال البدعة لم يقع
في الحال وإن كانت في حال سنة وقع في الحال
ولو كانت في حال بدعة فقال أردت بأحسن الطلاق أعجله وقع في الحال لأنه
إظهار احتمال في جانب الوقوع
ولو قال أنت طالق أقبح الطلاق وأسمجه فهو كقوله أنت طالق للبدعة ولو قال
أنت طالق طلقة حسنة قبيحة أو بدعية سنية وقع فيه الحال سواء كانت متعرضة
للحالتين أو لم تكن لأنه وصف متناقض فيلغو ويبقى قوله أنت طالق وهو كقوله
أنت طالق طلاقا لا يقع إنه يقع في الحال ولا نبالي بهذيانه
الرابعة إذا قال أنت طالق ثلاثا في كل قرء طلقة فلها أحوال خمس
إحداها أن لا تكون مدخولا بها فإن كانت في الحيض لم يقع شيء لأن القرء
عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه طهر محتوش بحيضتين فإذا طهرت أو كانت في الطهر
وقعت واحدة وبانت ولا تلحقها الأخرى فإن طهرت طهرين ثم جدد نكاحها فقد انحل
اليمين فلا يعود وقوع الطلاق وإن رأينا عود الحنث لأنه معلق على الإقراء
وقد انقضت وإن جدد نكاحها قبل الانقضاء ابتنى على عود العنث
الثانية أن تكون صغيرة فهل تقع في الحال واحدة فيه وجهان مأخذهما أن
الانتقال من الطهر إلى الحيض هل هو قرء أو القرء طهر محتوش بحيضتين
الثالثة أن تكون آيسة فهل تقع في الحال واحدة فيه أيضا وجهان كما في
الصغيرة
الرابعة أن تكون مدخولا بها من ذوات الإقراء وهي حائل فيقع في طهرها طلقة
وتشرع في العدة وتلحقها الثانية والثالثة في الطهرين الآخرين وهل يستأنف
العدة أو تبني على عدتها فيه خلاف
الخامسة أن تكون حاملا فإن كانت لا ترى الدم أو قلنا دم الحامل دم فاسد
وقع في الحال واحدة وتبين بالولادة وإن كانت ترى الدم وقضينا بأنه حيض وقعت
واحدة وهل يتكرر الطهر في مدة الحمل فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأنه طهر بين حيضتين
والثاني لا لأن القرء ما يدل على البراءة وهذا لا  دلالة له أصلا
المسألة الخامسة إذا قال أنت طالق ثلاثا للسنة ثم قال أردت التفريق على
الإقراء لم يقبل ظاهرا لأنه لا سنة في تفريق الطلاق عندنا واللفظ لا ينبئ
عنه وكذلك لو قال أنت طالق ثلاثا ولم يقل للسنة ثم فسرنا بالتفريق فهل يدين
باطنا فيه وجهان كما لو قال أنت طالق ثم قال أردت به إن دخلت الدار ومأخذه
أن مجرد النية لا تؤثر فإن لو طلق بالنية لم يقع خلافا لمالك رحمه الله وإن
ذكر لفظا ونوى معه أمرا ولو صرح به لا نتظم
مع المذكور فهل يؤثر في الباطن فيه وجهان كقوله أنت طالق ثم قال نويت إن
شاء الله تعالى أو نويت إن دخلت الدار والأقيس إنه لا يؤثر لأنه ليس يحتمله
اللفظ ولا ذكر ما يدل عليه فهو مجرد نية وليس هذا كما إذ قال أنت طالق ونوى
طلاقا عن وفاق فإنه يدين فإن اللفظ كالمجمل من حيث اللغة لولا تخصيص الشرع
ولا كقوله نسائي طوالق وعزل بعضهن بالنية فإن يدين لأنه تخصيص عموم وهل
يقبل ظاهرا فيه خلاف وما يقاضي إلى أنه يقبل
ولو عاتبت زوجها بنكاح جديدة فقال في جوابها كل امرأة لي فهي طالق فإن لم
يعزلها بنيته طلقت وإن عزلها بنيته فقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه لا يقع لأن
القرينة دلت على نيته وهذا ينبغي أن يقبل ظاهرا ومن الأصحاب من قال لا يقبل
لأنه قوله كل امرأة صريح في الاستغراق وميل القاضي إلى قبول ذلك ظاهرا
وكذلك في
قوله نسائي طوالق وإن لم تكن قرينة لأنه تخصيص عموم وكذلك إذا قال وهو
يحل عنها وثاقا أنت طالق فقال أردت عن الوثاق فيه خلاف وميل القاضي إلى أنه
يقبل ظاهرا وقد قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه لو قال إن كلمت زيدا فأنت طالق ثم
قال أردت به شهرا وكلمته بعده لم يقع الطلاق باطنا لأن اللفظ كالعام في
الأزمان كلها
ولا خلاف في أنه لو قال أنت طالق ثم قال  أردت عن الوفاق لم يقبل ظاهرا
ولكن يدين وكأن الموجب للقبول ظاهرا أما قصور في دلالة اللفظ مثل أن تكون
دلالته بالعموم أو قرينة ظاهرة كما لو كان يحل الوثاق كان يحل عنها الوثاق
أو كانت تنازعه في نكاح جديدة كما ذكرناه وأما الموجب للقبول باطنا فكل
احتمال قرب أو بعد
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في بيان أركان الطلاق - صلى الله
عليه وسلم -
ولا بد للطلاق من أهل ومحل ولفظ وقصد إلى اللفظ وولاية على المحل فهذه
خمسة أركان
الركن الأول الأهل وهو المطلق وشرطه أن يكون مكلفا فلا يقع طلاق الصبي
والمجنون
الركن الثاني اللفظ وما يسد مسده وفيه ثلاثة فصول
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ر-أ (q-r-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Menstrual cycle; the period of purity between two menses; reading/reciting.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal terminology (Sharʿ), al-qarʾ denotes the state of ṭuhr (purity) flanked by two menstrual periods — a technical specification of the root's temporal sense.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to the menses itself; metaphorical (majāz) extension to the intervening purity is rejected by Shāfiʿī jurists in favor of the technical definition.
- Root: ب-د-ع (b-d-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Innovation; something newly originated without prior example.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In divorce law, "bidʿī" (innovative) divorce is one violating the Sunnah's timing — i.e., pronouncing divorce during menstruation or during a purity in which intercourse occurred.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The term shifts from its ontological sense (origination ex nihilo) to a legal-technical sense (violation of prophetic practice), a metaphorical transfer (naql) sanctioned by juristic convention.
- Root: ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To suspend, hang, attach; a thing dependent upon another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Taʿlīq (suspension) in legal theory means making an effect contingent upon a future condition — a metaphysical dependency relation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense of physical hanging is extended metaphorically to conditional causation in legal speech acts.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Lām of Causation vs. Timing (Lām al-Taʿlīl wa-Lām al-Tawqīt) — The particle "li" governs a genitive noun; its semantic function is determined by the nature of the governed noun. When the noun denotes a temporal period (like Ramaḍān, menstruation, purity), the lām indicates temporal specification (tawqīt). When it denotes a person or event not inherently temporal, the lām indicates causation (taʿlīl). This distinction rests on the principle of contextual determination (taqyīd bi-l-qarīnah).
chapters.translation:
I say — and in this section there are several subsidiary questions.

**The First Question:** If a man says to a menstruating woman, "You are divorced with an innovational divorce (li-l-bidʿah)," the divorce takes effect immediately. But if he says to her, "with a sunnic divorce (li-l-sunnah)," it does not take effect until she becomes pure. Likewise, if he says to a woman who has become pure but before intercourse, "You are divorced with a sunnic divorce," the divorce takes effect immediately. But if he says to her, "with an innovational divorce," she is not divorced until she either has intercourse or menstruates.

The intended point is that the lām (preposition) serves temporal specification (tawqīt) when attached to what resembles temporal periods, such as "sunnah" and "bidʿah." This is like his saying, "You are divorced for Ramaḍān (li-Ramaḍān)" — for he has specified the time by Ramaḍān. As for what does not resemble temporal periods, the lām there indicates causation (taʿlīl), as in his saying, "You are divorced for the pleasure of so-and-so (li-riḍā fulān)" — for it takes effect immediately whether so-and-so is pleased or displeased. And his saying, "You are divorced for the entering of the house (li-dukhūl al-dār)" is a suspension (taʿlīq) that takes effect immediately, unlike his saying, "for the arrival of Zayd (li-qudūm Zayd)," for that is temporal specification by the arrival, because arrival is something awaited, like menstruation and purity.

The explicit particles of suspension (taʿlīq) are only "in" (إن) and "idhā" (إذا). As for the lām, it is ostensibly for causation, except in what resembles temporal periods. Where we have construed it as causation, if he then says, "I intended temporal specification," he is believed inwardly (yudayyan fī al-bāṭin). But is he accepted outwardly (ẓāhir)? There are two opinions. This applies when he addresses a woman subject to both sunnah and bidʿah states. If he addresses a minor girl, a menopausal woman, or a woman not yet consummated with, then the lām is for causation, so the divorce takes effect immediately — whether he says "for the sunnah" or "for the bidʿah." There is an opinion that if he says "for the sunnah," it takes effect immediately, for its meaning is "a divorce without prohibition therein." But if he says "for the bidʿah," it does not take effect until the minor menstruates, or until he consummates with the unconsummated woman.

As for when he says to a woman subject to both states, "When Zayd arrives, you are divorced with a sunnic divorce" — if he arrives while she is menstruating, it does not take effect until she becomes pure. And if he says "with an innovational divorce," and he arrives while she is in a purity in which he has not had intercourse, she is not divorced until she menstruates or he has intercourse.

If he suspends upon mere arrival, and he arrives while she is menstruating, it executes as an innovational divorce. If she was not, at the time of suspension, a person subject to sunnah and bidʿah states, then consideration is given to the state at the time of occurrence, not at the time of suspension.

**A Branch:** If he says during a purity in which he has not had intercourse, "You are divorced with an innovational divorce," then when he has intercourse, the divorce occurs — as when the glans disappears (ghābat al-ḥashafah). Is he obligated, by the continuation of intercourse if he does not withdraw immediately, to another dower (mahr) — on the basis that the dower is obligatory at the commencement of intercourse with a revocably divorced woman (rajʿiyyah)? There are two opinions. Their basis is whether the continuation of intercourse is like its commencement. The more apparent (aẓhar) opinion is that it is not obligatory, because the marriage dower encompassed the beginning of this intercourse, so its ruling is not parceled out, even if permissibility changes mid-course.

**The Second Question:** If he says, "You are divorced three times, some of them for the sunnah and some for the bidʿah" — if he says, "I intended to effect one and a half divorces immediately," he is believed, and two divorces are completed. If he says, "I intended the occurrence of two immediately," he is believed. If he says, "I intended to effect three halves immediately," all three occur immediately. If he says, "I had no intention," it is construed as division into halves (tasḥīṭ), and one and a half divorces occur immediately, but two are completed. This is like his saying, "This house is partly for Zayd and partly for ʿAmr" — his unqualified statement is construed as division into halves, because "most" is not called "some" (baʿḍ) ostensibly. If he says, "I intended one immediately and two in the future," the apparent position is that he is accepted. There is an opinion that he is not accepted, because calling two of three "some" is far-fetched.

Al-Muzanī said: The corollary of Imām al-Shāfiʿī's (may God be pleased with him) position is that if he does not intend anything, not even one divorce occurs immediately, because "some" (baʿḍ) is ambiguous (mujmal), so it should be construed as the minimum — for it could mean one, and it could mean one and a half. Let this be considered an inference (takhrij) from him upon al-Shāfiʿī's school.

**The Third Question:** If he says, "You are divorced with the best divorce (aḥsan al-ṭalāq)," or "the most virtuous," or "the most beautiful," or other such attributes of praise — it is as if he said, "You are divorced for the sunnah." So if she was in a state of bidʿah, it does not take effect immediately; if she was in a state of sunnah, it takes effect immediately.

If she was in a state of bidʿah and he says, "I meant by 'the best divorce' the swiftest," it takes effect immediately, because he has shown a possible interpretation favoring occurrence.

If he says, "You are divorced with the ugliest divorce (aqbaḥ al-ṭalāq)" or "the most repulsive" — it is like his saying, "You are divorced for the bidʿah." If he says, "You are divorced with a good-ugly divorce" or "a bidʿic-sunnic divorce," it takes effect immediately — whether she is subject to both states or not — because the description is self-contradictory, so it is nullified (yalghū), and his statement "You are divorced" remains. This is like his saying, "You are divorced with a divorce that does not occur" — it occurs immediately, and we pay no heed to his nonsense.

**The Fourth Question:** If he says, "You are divorced three times, in every qarʾ (period) one divorce" — she has five states:

**First:** That she is not consummated with. If she was menstruating, nothing occurs, because al-qarʾ according to al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) is a purity enclosed by two menses. So when she becomes pure — or if she was already pure — one divorce occurs, and she is separated (bāna), and the others do not follow. If she becomes pure for two purities, then he renews the marriage with her, the oath is dissolved (inḥalla al-yamīn), and the occurrence of divorce does not return — even if we hold the view that the violation (ḥinth) returns — because it was suspended upon the qurūʾ (periods), and they have elapsed. If he renews the marriage before the elapse, it builds upon the question of whether the violation returns.

**Second:** That she is a minor. Does one divorce occur immediately? There are two opinions. Their basis is whether the transition from purity to menstruation constitutes a qarʾ, or whether qarʾ is a purity enclosed by two menses.

**Third:** That she is menopausal. Does one divorce occur immediately? There are also two opinions, as with the minor.

**Fourth:** That she is consummated with, of those who have qurūʾ, and she is not pregnant. One divorce occurs in her purity, she commences her waiting period (ʿiddah), and the second and third follow in the other two purities. Is the ʿiddah renewed or does she build upon her existing ʿiddah? There is a disagreement.

**Fifth:** That she is pregnant. If she does not see blood, or if we hold that the blood of a pregnant woman is corrupt blood (dam fāsid), one divorce occurs immediately, and she is separated by giving birth. If she sees blood and we rule that it is menstruation, one divorce occurs. Does purity repeat during the duration of pregnancy? There are two opinions:
- One: Yes, because it is a purity between two menses.
- The second: No, because qarʾ is what indicates freedom of the womb (barāʾah), and this has no such indication at all.

**The Fifth Question:** If he says, "You are divorced three times for the sunnah," then says, "I intended the distribution over the qurūʾ," he is not accepted outwardly, because there is no sunnah in distributing divorce according to our school, and the wording does not indicate it. Likewise, if he says, "You are divorced three times" without saying "for the sunnah," and we interpret it as distribution — is he believed inwardly? There are two opinions, as in his saying, "You are divorced," then saying, "I intended by it 'if you enter the house.'" The basis is that mere intention has no effect — for if one divorced by intention alone, it would not occur, contrary to Mālik (may God have mercy on him). If he utters a word and intends with it something that, had he explicitly stated it, would not combine with what was uttered — does it affect inwardly? There are two opinions, as in his saying, "You are divorced," then saying, "I intended 'if God wills' (in shāʾ Allāh)," or "I intended 'if you enter the house.'" The more analogical (aqyas) view is that it has no effect, because the wording does not admit it, nor does he mention anything indicating it — it is mere intention. This is not like his saying, "You are divorced," intending a divorce by mutual consent (ʿan wifāq), for he is believed — because the wording is as if ambiguous (mujmal) linguistically, were it not for the Sharʿī specification. Nor is it like his saying, "My women are all divorced," and he excludes some by intention — for he is believed, because it is a specification of a general (takhṣīṣ al-ʿumūm). Is he accepted outwardly? There is a disagreement, and the inclination (al-qāḍī's) is toward acceptance.

If a woman reproaches her husband over a new marriage, and he says in response, "Every woman of mine is divorced" — if he does not exclude her by intention, she is divorced; if he excludes her by intention, al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said it does not occur, because the contextual indication (qarīnah) revealed his intention. This should be accepted outwardly. Some companions said it is not accepted, because his statement "every woman" is explicit in comprehensiveness (istiḥrāq). The Qāḍī's inclination is toward accepting it outwardly. Likewise in his saying, "My women are all divorced," even without a contextual indication, because it is a specification of a general. Similarly, if he says while untying a rope from her, "You are divorced," then says, "I meant from the rope (ʿan al-withāq)" — there is a disagreement, and the Qāḍī's inclination is toward accepting it outwardly. Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: If he says, "If you speak to Zayd, you are divorced," then says, "I meant by it 'for a month,'" and she speaks to him after that — the divorce does not occur inwardly, because the wording is like a general over all times.

There is no disagreement that if he says, "You are divorced," then says, "I meant by mutual consent (ʿan al-wifāq)," he is not accepted outwardly, but he is believed inwardly. It is as if what necessitates outward acceptance is either a deficiency in the wording's indication — such as its indication being by generality — or an apparent contextual indication, like his untying a rope from her, or her reproaching him over a new marriage, as we mentioned. As for what necessitates inward acceptance, it is any possibility, near or far.

— Peace be upon him — **Chapter Two: On Elucidating the Pillars of Divorce** — Peace be upon him —

Divorce necessarily requires: an eligible person (ahl), a locus (maḥall), a wording (lafẓ), an intent directed to the wording (qaṣd ilā al-lafẓ), and authority over the locus (wilāyah ʿalā al-maḥall). These are five pillars.

**The First Pillar:** The eligible person — namely, the divorcer. Its condition is that he be legally accountable (mukallaf). Thus, the divorce of a minor boy or an insane person does not occur.

**The Second Pillar:** The wording and what stands in its place. It contains three sections.

chapters.title_en: The First Chapter on Clarifying Explicit (Ṣarīḥ) and Allusive (Kināyah) Expressions of Divorce
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الأول في بيان الصريح والكناية

وصرائح الألفاظ ثلاثة الطلاق والفراق والسراح أما الطلاق فلشيوعه وتكرره
في القرآن العظيم وأما الفراق والسراح فلتكررهما في القرآن العظيم وقال أبو
حنيفة رحمه الله لا صريح إلا الطلاق وقيل هو قول قديم للشافعي رضي الله عنه
ولا بأس به
فإن قوله تعالى {أو تسريح بإحسان} لم يرد مورد بيان اللفظ وفي هذه
القاعدة مسائل
الأولى إن كل ما يشتق من لفظ الطلاق كقوله أنت مطلقة وطلقتك فكل ذلك صريح
وفي قوله أنت الطلاق وجهان والأظهر أنه كناية لأنه ليس بمستعمل على هذا
الوجه
وأما قوله أطلقتك فهو كناية لأنه ظاهر في رفع الحبس وحل الوثاق
الثانية الفعل من السراح والفراق كقول سرحتك وفارقتك صريح
أما الاسم كقوله أنت مفارقة ومسرحة ففيه خلاف ومأخذه أن الوارد في القرآن
العظيم منه صيغة الفعل فقط
الثالثة معنى هذه الألفاظ سائر اللغات فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنها ليست صريحا وإليه ذهب الإصطخري تغليبا لمعنى التعبد
والثاني هو الأصح أنه صريح لأنه في معناه
ثم معنى قوله أنت طالق توهشته أي
ومعنى قوله طلقتك دشت بازداشتم ترا
ومعنى قوله فارقتك ازتو جدا كردم
ومعنى قوله سرحتك تراكسيل كردم
والثالث قال القاضي كل ذلك غير صريح إلا قوله توهشته أي لأنه لا يستعمل
في العادة  إلا في الطلاق وأما سائر الألفاظ فشائع الاستعمال في غير الطلاق
الرابعة إذا شاع لفظ في العرف للطلاق كقوله حلال الله علي حرام فهل يصير
صريحا فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن المقصود تعين جهة التفاهم وقد حصل
والثاني لا بل مأخذه القرآن العظيم فقط
وقال القفال إن صدر ذلك من فقيه يعرف الكناية ولم ينو لم يقع طلاقه وإن
صدر من عامي يقال له ما الذي يسبق إلى فهمه إذا سمعت هذه الكلمة من غيرك
فإن كان يفهم الطلاق جعل منه طلاقا
وهذا إن عنى به القفال الاستدلال على نيته وأنه إذ كان يفهم ذلك فلا يخلو
ضميره عن معناه وإن لم يشعر به فله وجه وإن عنى وقوع الطلاق مع خلو قلبه عن
النية بينه وبين الله تعالى فلا وجه له إذ لم يجعل صريحا هذا حكم الصرائح
أما الكنايات فهي كل لفظة محتملة إما جلية كقوله أنت خلية وبرية وبتة
وبتلة وإما خفية وهي التي لا تنتظم إلا بتقدير استعارة وأضمار كقوله اعتدي
واستبرئي رحمه فإن معناه طلقتك فاعتدي وكذا قوله الحقي بأهلك وحبلك على
غاربك ولا أنده سربك
واعزبي واغربي واذهبي
وأخفى منها كقوله تجرعي أي كأس الفراق وذوقي وتزودي وترددوا في قوله
اشربي أي كأس الفراق وألحق به بعضهم كلي وهو أبعد وترددوا في قوله أغناك
الله أخذا من قوله تعالى {وإن يتفرقا يغن الله كلا من سعته}
وحد الكناية ما يحتمل الطلاق ولو على بعد لا الذي لا يحتمل كقوله اقعدي
واغزلي وغيره وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا قال لزوجته أنت حرة ونوى الطلاق وقع وكنايات الطلاق والعتاق
متداخلة متناسبة في الأكثر نعم لو قال لعبده اعتد واستبرئ رحمك ونوى العتق
لم ينفذ لأن ذلك غير متصور في حقه ولو قال ذلك لأمته ففيه وجهان ولو قال
ذلك لزوجته قبل الدخول ففيه وجهان أيضا لأنها ليست بصدد العدة كالأمة
الثانية لفظ الظهار ليس كناية في الطلاق ولا الطلاق في الظهار مع
الاحتمال لأن كل واحد منهما  وجد نفاذا في موضوعه الصريح فلا يعدل إلى غير
موضوعه بالنية ولا يمكن تنفيذهما جميعا لأن اللفظ لم يوضع لهما وضع العموم
فصرف إلى ما هو صريح فيه
الثالثة إذا قال لزوجته أنت علي حرام فإن نوى الظهار كان ظهارا وإن نوى
التحريم
كان يمينا وتلزمه كفارة وإن نوى الطلاق نفذ وإن أطلق فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أظهرها أنه صريح في إيجاب الكفارة
والثاني أنه يلغو لأنه محتمل لوجوه
والثالث أنه في الأمة صريح في الكفارة لأن الآية إنما وردت فيه وفي
المنكوحة كناية

### | قاعدتان

إحداهما إن القرينة عندنا لا تجعل الكناية صريحا وأبو حنيفة رحمه الله
جعل الكناية في الغضب وعند التخاصم وسؤال الفراق صريحا وهو ضعيف لأن اللفظ
محتمل وعدول الرجل عن لفظ الطلاق مشعر بإضمار غير الطلاق فكيف ينقلب صريحا
الثانية إن النية ينبغي أن تقرن بلفظ الكناية فلو تقدمت أو تأخرت لم تؤثر
وإن نوى مع ابتداء اللفظ ولكن انقطعت قبل تمام اللفظ فالظاهر أنه يقع وإن
خلا عن النية أول اللفظ ونوى في أثنائه ففيه وجهان مشهوران
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ص-ر-ح (ṣ-r-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "clarity, explicitness, and freedom from ambiguity"—a thing is ṣarīḥ when its meaning is manifest without need for interpretation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, ṣarīḥ denotes a term whose legislative import (ḥukm) is established by its very wording, not by contextual inference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage—the word is employed in its primary, settled sense; metaphorical (majāz) usage is excluded.
- Root: ك-ن-ي (k-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning is "to conceal, to use an indirect expression"—kināyah is speech that veils the intended meaning behind a permissible alternative.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A kināyah is a term that is probabilistically indicative (muḥtamal) of a legal meaning but not definitive; it requires intention (niyyah) or contextual evidence (qarīnah) for enforcement.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Rhetorical trope—the word is used in a transferred sense, remaining within the bounds of linguistic convention but not as the primary designation.
- Root: ط-ل-ق (ṭ-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning is "release, loosening, and being unrestricted"—ṭalāq is the dissolution of the marriage bond, releasing the wife from its constraint.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Quranic and legal usage, ṭalāq is the legislated act of repudiation, a definitive termination of marital union.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The term is used literally for the legal act; its metaphorical extension (e.g., "release" of an animal) is secondary.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAmal fī al-Ṣīghah (Operative Force of Verbal Forms)—the grammatical form (fiʿl vs. ism) determines the default legal efficacy; verbs (fiʿl) are more direct in their operative force than derived nouns (ism), which may carry ambiguity.
chapters.translation:
I say: The explicit expressions (ṣarāʾiḥ) of divorce are three: "divorce" (ṭalāq), "separation" (firāq), and "release" (sarāḥ). As for "divorce" (ṭalāq), it is due to its prevalence and frequent repetition in the Mighty Quran. As for "separation" (firāq) and "release" (sarāḥ), it is due to their repetition in the Mighty Quran. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: There is no explicit expression except "divorce" (ṭalāq). It was said that this is an old position of al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him), and there is no harm in it. For His statement, the Exalted, {«or release with kindness»} (Quran 2:229), was not revealed as an exposition of the linguistic term [itself]. Under this principle are several issues:

The first issue: Everything derived from the word "divorce" (ṭalāq)—such as his saying "You are divorced" (anti ṭāliqah) or "I have divorced you" (ṭallaqtuk)—all of that is explicit (ṣarīḥ). Regarding his saying "You are the divorce" (anti al-ṭalāq), there are two positions; the more apparent (aẓhar) is that it is allusive (kināyah), because it is not customarily used in this manner.

As for his saying "I have released you" (aṭlaqtuk), it is allusive (kināyah), because it is apparent in the sense of removing confinement and dissolving the bond (ḥall al-withāq).

The second issue: The verbal form of "release" (sarāḥ) and "separation" (firāq)—such as his saying "I have released you" (sarraḥtuk) and "I have separated from you" (fāraqtuk)—is explicit (ṣarīḥ). As for the nominal form—such as his saying "You are separated" (anti mufāraqah) or "You are released" (anti musarraḥah)—there is a disagreement concerning it. Its basis is that what occurs in the Mighty Quran from these [expressions] is only the verbal form.

The third issue: The meaning of these expressions in other languages has three aspects. One of them: They are not explicit (ṣarīḥ); this is the view of al-Iṣṭakhrī, giving preponderance to the meaning of devotional worship (taʿabbud). The second—and it is the more correct (aṣaḥḥ)—is that it is explicit (ṣarīḥ), because it is equivalent in meaning. Then the meaning of his saying "You are divorced" (anti ṭāliq) is "I have made you unlawful for myself" (tūhhishtuh). The meaning of his saying "I have divorced you" (ṭallaqtuk) is "I have taken you back from myself" (dāsht bāzdāshtam turā). The meaning of his saying "I have separated from you" (fāraqtuk) is "I have parted from you" (az tu judā kardam). The meaning of his saying "I have released you" (sarraḥtuk) is "I have sent you away" (turā kasīl kardam). The third: Al-Qāḍī said: All of that is not explicit (ṣarīḥ) except his saying "I have made you unlawful for myself" (tūhhishtuh), because it is not customarily used except for divorce. As for the other expressions, they are commonly used for other than divorce.

The fourth issue: If a word becomes prevalent in custom (ʿurf) for divorce—such as his saying "What Allah has made lawful for me is unlawful" (ḥalāl Allāhi ʿalayya ḥarām)—does it become explicit (ṣarīḥ) therein? There are two positions. One of them: Yes, because the purpose is to determine the means of mutual understanding (tafāhum), and that has been achieved. The second: No; rather, its basis is only the Mighty Quran. Al-Qaffāl said: If this [utterance] issues from a jurist (faqīh) who knows the allusive expressions (kināyah) and does not intend [divorce], his divorce does not occur. But if it issues from a common person (ʿāmmī), he is asked: "What comes first to your understanding when you hear this word from someone other than you?" If he understands divorce, then divorce is established from him. This—if al-Qaffāl meant by it the inference to his intention, and that since he understands that [meaning], his conscience is not devoid of its significance even if he is not conscious of it—then it has merit. But if he meant the occurrence of divorce while his heart is devoid of intention between him and Allah the Exalted, then it has no merit, since it has not been made explicit (ṣarīḥ). This is the ruling concerning explicit expressions (ṣarāʾiḥ).

As for the allusive expressions (kināyāt), they are every word that is probable [in meaning], either manifestly (jalīyah)—such as his saying "You are free" (anti khalīyah), "You are innocent" (barīʾah), "You are cut off" (battah), "You are severed" (battalah)—or hidden (khafīyah), which are those that are not coherent except by positing a metaphor (istiʿārah) and an implicit [intention] (iḍmār)—such as his saying "Observe your waiting period" (iʿtaddī) and "Declare your womb pure" (istabriʾī raḥimak), for its meaning is "I have divorced you, so observe your waiting period." Likewise his saying "Join your family" (alḥaqī bi-ahlik), "Your rope is on your camel's hump" (ḥabluki ʿalā ghāribik), "I will not pursue your path" (lā andahu sarbak), "Withdraw" (iʿzibī), "Depart" (ughrubī), and "Go away" (idhhabī). Even more hidden than these is his saying "Swallow" (tajarraʿī)—meaning the cup of separation—and "Taste" (dhūqī), and "Take provisions" (tazawwadī). They hesitated concerning his saying "Drink" (ishrabī)—meaning the cup of separation—and some appended to it "Eat" (kulī), which is even more remote. They hesitated concerning his saying "Allah has enriched you" (aghnāki Allāh), derived from His statement, the Exalted: {«But if they separate, Allah will enrich each from His abundance»} (Quran 4:130). The definition of kināyah is: what is probable of divorce, even if remotely—not that which is not probable, such as his saying "Sit" (uqʿudī) or "Spin" (ighzilī) and the like. Under this are several issues:

The first issue: If he says to his wife "You are free" (anti ḥurrah) and intends divorce, it occurs. The allusive expressions of divorce and of manumission (ʿitāq) are interpenetrating and proportionate in most cases. Yes, if he says to his male slave "Observe your waiting period" (iʿtadd) and "Declare your womb pure" (istabriʾ raḥimak) and intends manumission, it does not take effect, because that is not conceivable in his case. If he says that to his female slave (umm walad), there are two positions. If he says that to his wife before consummation (dukhūl), there are also two positions, because she is not in the position of observing a waiting period (ʿiddah), unlike the female slave.

The second issue: The word of ẓihār (injurious comparison) is not a kināyah for divorce, nor is divorce a kināyah for ẓihār, despite the probability [of cross-reference], because each one of them has found operative effect (nufūdh) in its own explicit subject matter (mawḍūʿ). Thus, it is not diverted to other than its subject matter by intention, nor is it possible to enforce both of them [simultaneously], because the word was not placed for both with a general placement (waḍʿ al-ʿumūm). So it is directed to what is explicit in it.

The third issue: If he says to his wife "You are unlawful for me" (anti ʿalayya ḥarām): if he intends ẓihār, it is ẓihār; if he intends prohibition (taḥrīm), it is an oath (yamīn) and the expiation (kaffārah) becomes obligatory upon him; if he intends divorce, it takes effect. If he leaves it unrestricted (muṭlaq), there are three positions. The most apparent (aẓhar) of them: It is explicit (ṣarīḥ) in obligating the expiation (kaffārah). The second: It is nullified (laghw), because it is probable of multiple meanings. The third: It is, regarding a female slave, explicit (ṣarīḥ) in [obligating] the expiation, because the verse was revealed only concerning her; and regarding a married free woman (mankūḥah), it is a kināyah.

### Two Principles

One of them: The contextual indicator (qarīnah) does not, in our view, make a kināyah into an explicit expression (ṣarīḥ). Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) made the kināyah explicit (ṣarīḥ) in [cases of] anger, during quarreling, and when asking for separation—and this is weak, because the word is probable [of other meanings], and the man's deviation from the word "divorce" (ṭalāq) indicates an implicit intention of other than divorce. So how can it be transformed into an explicit expression?

The second principle: The intention (niyyah) should be conjoined with the utterance of the kināyah. If it precedes or follows, it has no effect. If he intends at the beginning of the utterance but the intention is interrupted before the completion of the utterance, the apparent [position] is that it occurs. If he is devoid of intention at the beginning of the utterance and intends during its midst, there are two well-known positions.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثاني في الأفعال

اعلم أن اللفظ إنما يراد للتفهيم وقد يحصل التفهيم بالإشارة والكتابة
فلنذكرهما
أما الإشارة فهي معتبرة من الأخرس وتنقسم إلى صريح وكناية
فالصريح ما يتفق الكفة على فهمهه والكناية ما يفطن له بعض الناس وإذا أتى
بالصريح لم يقبل بعد ذلك تأوليه كما في النطق والصحيح أنه إن أشار بالطلاق
في الصلاة نفذ الطلاق ولم تبطل صلاته
وأما كتابة الأخرس فهو طلاق لأنها أظهر من الإشارة ومع ذلك فلا نكلف
الأخرس القادر على الكتابة بأن يكتب الطلاق بل نقنع بالإشارة
وأما القادر فإشارته وإن بالغ فيها لا نجعلها صريحا لأن عدوله إليها مع
القدرة موهم نعم هل تجعل كناية قال القفال هو فعل مترتب على الكتابة
والإشارة أولى بالاحتياط لأن الكتابة معتادة والإشارة من الناطق غير معتادة
أما الكتابة فليس بصريح وإن كتب اللفظ الصريح فهل هو كناية اضطربت فيه
النصوص وحاصلة ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها  أنه كناية لأن الكتابة معتادة والمقصود التفهيم
والثاني أنه لغو لأن الصيغ اللفظية هي الموضوعة للعقود في حق القادر
والثالث أنها تعتبر من الغائب دون الحاضر لأجل العادة
وفي شرح التلخيص وجه أن كتبه صريح الطلاق صريح من غير نية وهو بعيد
أما إذا كتب قوله كل زوجة لي فهي طالق وقرأ ونوى عند القراءة وقع وإن قرأ
ولم ينو وقال قصدت القراءة فهل يقبل ظاهرا فيه تردد كما لو حل الوثاق عن
زوجته وقال عند ذلك أنت طالق فإن فرعنا على اعتبار الكتابة فيتصدى النظر في
أمور ثلاثة
الأول في التصرفات فتعتبر في كل ما يستقل به المتصرف كالعتق والعفو
والإبراء أما ما يفتقر إلى القبول ففيه قولان وفي النكاح قولان مرتبان
وأولى بألا ينعقد لما فيه من التعبد ولأنه كناية والشاهد لا يطلع على النية
ولكن من جوز ذلك ربما احتمله لأجل الحاجة ثم إن كتب زوجت بنتي من فلان
وأشهد عليه عدلين وشهدا هما بأعيانهما على قبول الزوج صح وإن شهد آخران
فوجهان ثم إذا كتب بعت داري منك فبلغه الكتاب فينبغي أن يقول على الفور
اشتريت أو يكتب على الفور لأن الاتصال بين الجواب والخطاب
شرط وهو الاتصال اللائق بالكتابة وإن تخلل بينهما شهور
الثاني في ألفاظ الكاتب وهو ثلاث
إحداهما أن يكتب أما بعد فأنت طالق ونوى فيحكم بوقوعه في الحال
الثانية أن يكتب إذا بلغك كتابي هذا فأنت طالق فلا يقع إلا بالبلوغ
الثالثة أن يقول إذا قرأت كتابي هذا فأنت طالق فلا يقع ما لم تقرأ
فإن كانت أمية فإذا قرئ عليها طلقت وقيل لا تطلق لأنها ما قرأت وكأنه علق
على قراءتها وهو محال فلا يقع وهذا بعيد نعم لو كانت قارئة فقرأ عليها
غيرها فالظاهر أنها لا تطلق وقيل إنها تطلق كما إذا قال إذا رأيت الهلال
فأنت طالق فإنها تطلق برؤية غيرها وهو بعيد لأن الرؤية قد يراد بها العلم
دون القراءة
الثالث في المكتوب عليه وكل ما يثبت عليه  الخط من ثوب وحجر وعظم فهو
كالبياض أما لو كتب على الماء أو على الهواء لم يكن ذلك كتابة بل هي إشارة
من قادر وقد ذكرناه
ولو كتب على البياض ولكن علق الطلاق على البلوغ فبلغ وقد امحت الكتابة لم
يقع لأنه بلغ الكاغد دون الكتاب وإن لم ينمح إلا السطر الذي فيه الطلاق أو
سقط
ذلك القدر ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه لا يقع لأن الكتاب عبارة عن جميع الأجزاء
والثاني أنه يقع لأن الكتاب قد بلغ
والثالث أنه إن قال إن بلغك كتابي هذا لم يقع لأنه يتناول جميع الأجزاء
وإن قال إن بلغك الكتاب وقع
أما إذا امحى الجميع إلا سطر الطلاق فالخلاف مرتب وأولى بالوقوع وإن لم
ينجح إلا التسمية والصدر وبقيت المقاصد كلها فمرتب وأولى بالوقوع وإن لم
يسقط إلا الحواشي فأولى بالوقوع ومنهم من قطع في هذه الصورة بالوقوع لأن
الحاشية غير مقصودة ومن منع علل بأن الحاشية من الكتاب ولذلك لا يجوز
للمحدث مسه في المصحف
فرع إذا قال إن بلغك نصف كتابي فبلغ الجميع ففيه وجهان
أحدهما يقع لأن في الكل نصفا
والثاني لا لأن مفهومه التخصيص بالنصف

### | الفصل الثالث في التفويض إلى الزوجة

والنظر في ثلاثة أطراف
الأول ألفاظه فإذا قال طلقي نفسك فقالت طلقت نفذ ولو قال أبيني نفسك
فقالت أبنت ونويا وقع وإن لم ينو أحدهما لم يقع وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله
لا تعتبر نيتهما بل تكفي نية الرجل وقولها يبنى على قوله
ولو قال طلقي نفسك فقالت أبنت ونوت فالظاهر الوقوع وفيه وجه أنه لا يقع
لمخالفة اللفظ وقيل إن ذلك يجري أيضا في توكيل الأجنبي
ولو قال اختاري فقالت اخترت نفسي وقعت طلقة رجعية ولو قالت اخترت زوجي لم
يقع شيء وهو مذهب عمر وعائشة وابن عباس وابن مسعود رضي الله عنهم وقال علي
وزيد رضي الله عنهما إن اختارت نفسها فطلقة بائنة وإن اختارت زوجها فرجعية
واشتد إنكار عائشة رضي الله عنها فقالت خيرني رسول  الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
فاخترته أترى أن ذلك طلاق رجعي
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ه-م (f-h-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Comprehension, understanding; the act of making something understood (ifhām).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Intellectual grasp of meaning; in legal context, the conveyance of intent (qaṣd) through any perceptible medium.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in speech; metaphorical (majāz) when extended to gesture (ishārah) or writing (kitābah), as these are non-articulate indicators.
- Root: ش-ه-د (sh-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Presence, witnessing, testifying; a witness (shāhid) who attests to an event.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal acts, the presence of witnesses validates contracts; their testimony substitutes for public knowledge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical presence; metaphorical for the witness's inward knowledge of intention (niyyah).
- Root: خ-ي-ر (kh-y-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Choice, selection between alternatives; to grant someone the power of option.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In divorce law, the option (takhyīr) given to the wife—whether she chooses her husband or herself—determines the legal outcome.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for choosing; metaphorical in the prophetic tradition where the choice of the husband negates divorce.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Suspension (Taʿlīq al-Ḥukm ʿalā al-Sharṭ) — The apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is suspended on the fulfillment of the protasis (sharṭ), requiring precise temporal and causal connection (ittiṣāl) between the condition and its realization.
chapters.translation:
### | The Second Chapter on Acts

Know that speech (al-lafẓ) is intended only for conveying understanding (al-tafhīm), and understanding may be achieved through gesture (al-ishārah) and writing (al-kitābah). Let us mention both.

As for gesture, it is considered valid from the mute person (al-akhras) and divides into explicit (ṣarīḥ) and allusive (kināyah). The explicit is that which all people agree upon understanding; the allusive is that which only some people perceive. When one employs the explicit, no reinterpretation (taʾwīl) is accepted thereafter, just as in speech. The correct position is that if a mute person gestures divorce (al-ṭalāq) during prayer, the divorce takes effect, and his prayer is not invalidated.

As for the writing of the mute person, it is divorce, because it is more manifest (aẓhar) than gesture. Nevertheless, we do not oblige a mute person capable of writing to write the divorce; rather, we are satisfied with gesture.

As for the one capable of speech, his gesture—even if he exaggerates in it—we do not render it explicit (ṣarīḥ), because his turning to it despite capability suggests ambiguity (īhām). Rather, is it made allusive (kināyah)? Al-Qaffāl said: It is an act subordinate to writing and gesture, and gesture is more deserving of caution (al-iḥtiyāṭ), because writing is customary (muʿtādah) while gesture from the articulate person is not customary.

As for writing, it is not explicit, even if one writes the explicit wording. Is it then allusive? The texts (al-nuṣūṣ) have diverged on this, and the sum is three opinions:
One: It is allusive, because writing is customary and the purpose is conveying understanding.
Second: It is void (laghw), because verbal formulas are the established means for contracts (al-ʿuqūd) on behalf of the capable person.
Third: It is considered valid from the absent person (al-ghāʾib) but not from the present (al-ḥāḍir), due to custom.

In the commentary on al-Talkhīṣ, there is a view that if one writes the explicit wording of divorce, it is explicit without intention (niyyah)—but this is remote (baʿīd).

As for when he writes: "Every wife of mine is divorced," then reads it and intends at the reading, it occurs. If he reads without intending and says, "I intended only recitation," is it accepted outwardly? There is hesitation (taraddud) therein, just as if he untied the bond (al-withāq) from his wife and said at that moment, "You are divorced." For if we build upon the validity of writing, then we turn to examining three matters:

**First: In dispositions (al-taṣarrufāt).** Writing is considered valid in everything in which the disposing party acts independently, such as manumission (al-ʿitq), pardon (al-ʿafw), and acquittal (al-ibrāʾ). As for what requires acceptance (al-qabūl), there are two opinions. In marriage (al-nikāḥ), there are two opinions, arranged hierarchically—and it is more deserving that it not be concluded, because of its devotional nature (al-taʿabbud) and because it is allusive, and the witness does not gain access to the intention. But whoever permitted it perhaps tolerated it due to necessity. Then, if he wrote: "I have married my daughter to so-and-so," and he called two just witnesses, and they themselves testified to the husband's acceptance, it is valid. If two others testified, there are two views.

Then, if he wrote: "I have sold my house to you," and the letter reached him, he should say immediately, "I have bought," or write immediately, because the connection (al-ittiṣāl) between the response and the address is a condition—and it is the connection befitting writing. If months intervened between them, [it is invalid].

**Second: In the wording of the writer.** There are three [cases]:
One: He writes: "To proceed (ammā baʿd): You are divorced," and intends—then it is judged to occur immediately.
Second: He writes: "When my letter reaches you, you are divorced"—then it does not occur except upon reaching.
Third: He says: "When you read my letter, you are divorced"—then it does not occur unless she reads.

If she is illiterate (ummīyah), then when it is read to her, she is divorced. It was said: She is not divorced, because she did not read—as if he suspended it on her reading, which is impossible, so it does not occur. This is remote. Indeed, if she were literate and another read it to her, the apparent view is that she is not divorced. It was said: She is divorced, just as if he said, "If you see the crescent moon, you are divorced"—she is divorced by another's seeing. This is remote, because "seeing" (al-ruʾyah) may mean knowledge (al-ʿilm) rather than reading.

**Third: In what is written upon.** Everything on which writing is established—cloth, stone, or bone—is like blank paper (al-bayāḍ). As for writing on water or air, that is not writing; rather, it is a gesture from one capable [of speech], which we have already mentioned.

If he wrote on blank paper but suspended the divorce on reaching, and it reached [the addressee] while the writing had been erased, it does not occur, because what reached was the paper, not the writing. If only the line containing the divorce was erased, or that portion fell off, there are three views:
One: It does not occur, because the "book" (al-kitāb) denotes all its parts.
Second: It occurs, because the book has reached.
Third: If he said, "If my book reaches you," it does not occur, because it encompasses all parts; but if he said, "If the writing reaches you," it occurs.

As for when all is erased except the line of divorce, the disagreement is arranged [hierarchically], and it is more deserving of occurrence. If only the basmalah and the opening remained, while all the purposes (al-maqāṣid) remained, it is arranged and more deserving of occurrence. If only the margins (al-ḥawāshī) fell off, it is even more deserving of occurrence. Among them is one who decisively ruled occurrence in this case, because the margin is not intended. One who prohibited reasoned that the margin is part of the book, and therefore it is not permissible for one in ritual impurity (al-muḥdith) to touch it in the muṣḥaf.

**Branch:** If he said, "If half of my book reaches you," and the whole reached, there are two views:
One: It occurs, because in the whole there is a half.
Second: It does not, because its implication (mafhūmuhu) is specification to the half.

### | The Third Chapter on Delegation to the Wife

The examination concerns three aspects:

**First: Its wording.** If he says, "Divorce yourself," and she says, "I have divorced [myself]," it takes effect. If he says, "Separate yourself (bīnī nafsaki)," and she says, "I have separated," and both intended, it occurs. If either of them did not intend, it does not occur. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Their intentions are not considered; rather, the man's intention suffices, and her statement is built upon his statement.

If he said, "Divorce yourself," and she said, "I have separated," intending [divorce], the apparent view is occurrence. There is a view that it does not occur, due to the discrepancy in wording (mukhālafat al-lafẓ). It was said that this also applies to delegating a third party (al-ajnabī).

If he said, "Choose (khtārī)," and she said, "I have chosen myself," one revocable divorce (ṭalqah rajʿīyah) occurs. If she said, "I have chosen my husband," nothing occurs. This is the doctrine of ʿUmar, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with them). ʿAlī and Zayd (may Allah be pleased with them) said: If she chooses herself, it is an irrevocable divorce (bāʾinah); if she chooses her husband, it is revocable. ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) strongly objected, saying: "The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) gave me the choice, and I chose him—do you think that was a revocable divorce?"

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرع

إذا كان التفويض بالكناية وأنكر الزوج النية فالقول قوله وكذلك إذا إذا
أنكرت نيتها فالقول قولها ولو قالت نويت أنا وأنكر الزوج فالقول قولها وفيه
وجه بعيد أن القول قوله لأن الأصل بقاء النكاح وهو ضعيف
الطرف الثاني في حقيقة التفويض وفيه قولان
أحدهما أنه تمليك وكأنه ملكها نفسها
والثاني أنه توكيل كتوكيل الأجنبي
ويبتنى عليه أنها لو طلقت نفسها في مجلس آخر لا على الاتصال لم يجز إن
جعلناه تمليكا لأن اتصال القبول لا بد منه وقبولها هو قولها طلقت
وإن جعلناه توكيلا جاز وقال القاضي وإن جعلناه توكيلا يحتمل أن يشترط ذلك
في المجلس لأن هذه الصيغة تتاقضى جوابا ناجزا كقوله أنت طالق إن شئت فإنه
يختص بمشيئتها في المجلس وأجرى ذلك في قوله وكلتك وفوض إليك طلاقك بالوكالة
وعبر المحققون عن هذا بأنا إن جعلنا مطلق التفويض تمليكا فهل للزوج سبيل
إلى توكيلها أن ينزل توكيلها أيضا على التمليك فيه تردد
فرع لو رجع عن التفويض قبل قبولها جاز على القولين جميعا وقال ابن خيران
لا يجوز على قول التمليك وكأنه يضمن التعليق وهو بعيد لأنه ليس بأبلغ من
قوله أنت طالق على ألف وله الرجوع قبل قبولها
الطرف الثالث في حكم العدد فإذا قال طلقي نفسك ونوى الثلاث فإن طلقت ونوت
الثلاث نفذ وإن لم تنو لم يقع الثلاث بل وقعت واحدة وفيه وجه أنه يقع لأن
البناء في العدد أقرب من البناء في أصل النية وهذا يقوي مذهب أبي حنيفة
رحمه الله نعم لو قال طلقي نفسك ثلاثا فقالت طلقت ولم تذكر العدد ولم تنو
فيظهر البناء هاهنا لأنه صرح به لا سيما إن جعلناه تمليكا فإن مجرد قول
القائل قبلت يكفي وإن يعد تمام الكلام لأنه كالبناء على الإيجاب
وأما كلام الوكيل فلا يبنى على كلام الموكل نعم إن اشترطنا القبول في
المجلس على قول التوكيل فلا يبعد أيضا أن يحتمل البناء
فرع لو قال طلقي نفسك ثلاثا فطلقت واحدة طلقت بالاتفاق واحدة ولو قال
طلقي واحدة فطلقت ثلاثا وقعت عندنا واحدة وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لا يقع
هاهنا شيء أصلا والفرق مشكل عليه بين الصورتين

### | الركن الثالث القصد إلى لفظ الطلاق ومعناه

ويتوهم اختلال القصد بخمسة أسباب سبق اللسان والهزل والجهل والإكراه
واختلال العقل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-و-ض (f-w-ḍ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To entrust, delegate, commit a matter to another; root sense of returning a thing to its owner or agent.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal delegation where the husband empowers the wife to execute his repudiation — a transfer of authority (wilāyah) over the divorce act.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in contractual delegation; here used metaphorically (majāz) for the husband's verbal empowerment, since the wife does not own the divorce but acts as his proxy.
- Root: م-ل-ك (m-l-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Possession, ownership, dominion; to have power over something.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, tamlīk is the transfer of proprietary right — here, the husband makes the wife "owner" of her own divorce decision.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in property transactions; metaphorical in divorce, as the wife does not truly own herself but is granted a juridical power.
- Root: و-ك-ل (w-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To appoint an agent, to entrust a task; root sense of reliance and delegation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Agency (wakālah) — the wife acts as the husband's deputy, her utterance binding him as his own.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in commercial agency; extended here to divorce, where the wife's speech is attributed to the husband's authority.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Sentences (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The apodosis (jawāb) must be immediate and connected (ittiṣāl) to the protasis (sharṭ) in the same session (majlis), as in "You are divorced if you wish." This governs the temporal validity of the wife's acceptance.
chapters.translation:
### | Branch

If the delegation (tafwīḍ) was expressed by indirect allusion (kināyah) and the husband denies having intended divorce, then his word is accepted. Likewise, if she denies her intention [to accept], her word is accepted. But if she says, "I did intend [to divorce myself]," and the husband denies it, then her word is accepted. There is a remote opinion (wajh) that his word is accepted, because the original presumption (al-aṣl) is the continuance of the marriage — but this is weak.

The second aspect concerns the true nature of delegation (tafwīḍ), and there are two opinions:
One: It is a transfer of ownership (tamlīk) — as if he made her owner of herself.
The second: It is an agency (tawkīl), like the agency of a stranger.

Upon this distinction is built the following: If she divorced herself in another session (majlis), not connected [to the pronouncement], it is not valid if we deem it tamlīk, because the connection (ittiṣāl) of acceptance is indispensable — and her acceptance is her saying "I divorce myself." But if we deem it tawkīl, it is valid. Al-Qāḍī [Abū Ṭayyib al-Ṭabarī] said: Even if we deem it tawkīl, it is possible that connection to the session is required, because this formula demands an immediate response (jawāb nājiz), like his saying "You are divorced if you wish" — which is restricted to her wish within the session. He applied this [reasoning] to his saying "I appoint you as agent" and "I delegate to you your divorce by agency." The verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqūn) expressed this as: If we deem absolute delegation to be tamlīk, then does the husband have any means to appoint her as agent — such that her agency also reduces to tamlīk? There is hesitation (taraddud) on this.

Branch: If he retracts the delegation before her acceptance, it is valid [to do so] on both opinions. Ibn Khayrān said: It is not valid on the opinion of tamlīk — as if he analogized it to a suspended [conditional] divorce (taʿlīq). But this is remote, because it is not more emphatic than his saying "You are divorced for a thousand [dirhams]," where he may retract before her acceptance.

The third aspect concerns the rule of number (al-ʿadad). If he says "Divorce yourself" and intends three, then if she divorces herself intending three, it takes effect. If she does not intend [three], three do not occur — rather, one occurs. There is an opinion (wajh) that three do occur, because the construction (bināʾ) upon the number is closer [to the explicit wording] than construction upon the original intention. This strengthens the school of Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him). Yes — if he said "Divorce yourself three times," and she said "I have divorced myself" without mentioning the number and without intending [three], then construction [upon the number] is manifest here, because he explicitly stated it. Especially if we deem it tamlīk — for the mere utterance of the acceptor saying "I accept" suffices, even if it does not complete the speech, because it is like construction upon the offer (ījāb). As for the agent's speech, it is not constructed upon the principal's speech. Yes — if we require acceptance in the session on the opinion of tawkīl, then it is not far that construction [upon the number] may also be possible.

Branch: If he said "Divorce yourself three times," and she divorced herself once, then one divorce occurs by agreement. If he said "Divorce yourself once," and she divorced herself three times, then in our school one divorce occurs. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) said: Nothing occurs at all here. The distinction between the two cases is problematic for him.

### | The Third Pillar: The Intention (Qaṣd) Toward the Utterance of Divorce and Its Meaning

The soundness of intention is vitiated by five causes: slip of the tongue (sabq al-lisān), jest (hazl), ignorance (jahl), coercion (ikrāh), and mental derangement (ikhtilāl al-ʿaql).

chapters.arabic_text:
### | السبب الأول سبق اللسان

فإذا بدرت منه كلمة الطلاق في محاورته أو في النوم لم يقع طلاقه ولكن
يعسر قبول دعواه إذا لم يكن قرينة نعم يدين باطنا وإن شهدت قرينه قبل ظاهرا
مثل إن كان اسم امرأته طارق فقال يا طالق وزعم أنه التف بلسانه الكلام من
غير قصد قبل قطعا لا كشهادة حل الوثاق فإن فيه خلافا لأن كلمة الطلاق
مستنكر في غير النكاح
وإن كان اسم امرأته طالق واسم عبده حر فقال يا طالق ويا حر وقصد النداء
لم يقع وإن قصد الإيقاع وقع وإن أطلق من غير قصد فعلى أيهما يحمل فيه وجهان
وقد ظهر أن قصد حروف الطلاق لايكفي بل لابد من قصد لفظ الطلاق لمعنى
الطلاق
السبب الثاني الهزل فإذا قالت المرأة في ملاعبتها طلقني ثلاثا فقال نعم
أنت طالق ثلاثا كاللاعب المستهزىء وقع الطلاق لوجود فصد لفظ الطلاق ولم
يعدم إلا القصد إلى الحكم ولا يشترط بدليل أنه لو طلق بشرط الخيار لنفسه
نفذ وإن كان ذلك يعدم الرضا بالحكم وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلاث جدهن
جد وهزلهن جد الطلاق والنكاح والعتاق
ولم يحكم الشافعي رضي الله عنه بانعقاد نكاح الهازل وهو خلاف ظاهر الخبر
أما
البيع وسائر التصرفات فتردد بعض الأصحاب في انعقادها من الهازل
السبب الثالث الجهل وهو أن يخاطب امرأة بالطلاق وهو يظن أنها زوجة غيره
فإذا هي زوجته وقد رآها في ظلمة أو في جلباب أو كان أبوه زوجها منه في صغره
وهو لا يدري فالمشهور أنه يقع طلاقها وهذا فيه احتمال ظاهر لأنه إذا لم
يعرف الزوجية لم يقصد إلى قطعها وقد  ذكرنا في كتاب الغصب وجها في نظيره من
العتق أنه لا يقع وهو منقدح وبيانه أنه الأعجمي إذا لقن كلمة الطلاق وهو لا
يفهم لم يقع طلاقه بالاتفاق وأما بيع الجاهل فظاهر صحته وهو إذا ما باع مال
أبيه على ظن أنه حي وعلى هذا قالوا نفوذ الطلاق أولى والأقيس في البيع أنه
أيضا لا ينعكس ولأن القصد إلى المعنى المجهول محال
السبب الرابع الإكراه وطلاق المكره لا يقع عندنا لأن قصده مختل إذ
الإكراه بعث فيه القصد وكأنه فعل المكره وقال أبو حنيفة يقع
ثم نحن أيضا نوقعه مهما زعم المكره أنه كان راضيا أو ظهرت منه مخايل
الاختيار وذلك كمخالفته للمكره بزيادة أو نقصان أو تغيير لفظ
مثال الزيادة أن يكرهه على طلاق واحد فطلق ثلاث أو على طلاق زوجة واحدة
فطلق زوجتين
والنقصان أن يكلفه طلاق زوجتين فطلق واحدة أو على الثلاث فطلق طلقة أو
اثنتين أو قال قل طلقتها فقال فارقتها أو قال طلق إحدى زوجتيك فعين واحدة
وطلقها فإن التعليل دليل تبرمه بالمطلقة أما إذا ترك التورية وهو فقيه قادر
ومعترف بأن الإكراه لم يدهشه عن ذكر التورية ففيه خلاف والظاهر أنه يقع
ويجعل ذلك دليل الاختيار
والنظر بعد هذا في طرفين
أحدهما التصرفات المتأثرة بالإكراه والإكراه يسقط أثر التصرفات عندنا
قطعا إلا في خمسة مواضع
الأول الإسلام فإنه يجوز إكراه الحربي عليه فيصح إسلامه وإلا فتبطل فائدة
الإكراه وفي إسلام الذمي المكره خلاف والأصح أنه لا يصح
الثاني الإرضاع ولا يخرجه الإكراه عن كونه محرما لأنه منوط بوصول اللبن
إلى الجوف لا بالقصد
الثالث القتل على أحد القولين فإنه يوجب القصاص على قول لأن الإكراه لم
يرفع الإثم
الرابع المكره على الزنا على أحد القولين يحد لأن حصول الانتشار دلالة
الاختيار فإنه لا يحصل بالإكراه ومأخذ القولين تردد في تصور الإكراه
الخامس إذا علق الطلاق على الدخول فأكره على الدخول ففيه قولان مأخذهما
أن الصفة لا يشترط فيها القصد بل يكفي الاسم
أما البيع  فيبطل بالإكره وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله ينعقد ولا يلزم
واعلم أن الاستثناء بالتحقيق يرجع إلا الإسلام فقط وإلى القتل على قول
أما ما عداه فسببه عدم تصور الإكراه أو عدم اشتراط القصد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ب-ق (sabaqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Precedence, outrunning, that which comes before another in time or rank.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The prior occurrence of an act or utterance before intention attaches to it; in legal contexts, the unreflective precedence of speech over deliberation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for temporal priority; metaphorical (majāz) for the tongue's utterance outpacing the heart's intent.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The clause "فإذا بدرت منه" is a conditional sentence (sharṭiyyah) where the protasis (condition) is introduced by "idhā" (sudden occurrence), requiring the apodosis to be a non-volitional judgment, matching the legal ruling of non-occurrence.
chapters.translation:
### | The First Cause: The Slip of the Tongue

If a word of divorce (ṭalāq) escapes his tongue during his conversation or in his sleep, his divorce does not take effect. However, accepting his claim [that it was unintentional] is difficult if there is no corroborating circumstance (qarīnah). Nevertheless, he is inwardly truthful (yudayyin) in his conscience. But if a corroborating circumstance testifies to his claim, it is accepted outwardly (ẓāhir). For example, if his wife's name is Ṭāriq and he says, "O Ṭāliq!" (i.e., addressing her by a mispronounced name), and he claims that his tongue twisted the word without any intent, it is accepted absolutely — unlike the case of testifying to the release of a bond (ḥall al-withāq), for therein there is a divergence of opinion, because the word "divorce" is anomalous outside the context of marriage.

And if his wife's name is Ṭāliq and his slave's name is Ḥurr (free), and he says, "O Ṭāliq! O Ḥurr!" intending to call them by name, the divorce does not occur. But if he intends to effect the divorce (īqāʿ), it occurs. And if he utters it absolutely without any intent, there are two opinions (wajhān) as to which [intention] it should be attributed.

It has thus become evident that intending the mere letters of divorce is insufficient; rather, one must intend the very word "divorce" for the meaning of divorce (qasd lafẓ al-ṭalāq li-maʿnā al-ṭalāq).

### The Second Cause: Jest (Hazl)

If a woman says during her playful banter, "Divorce me three times!" and he replies, "Yes, you are divorced three times," like one who jests and mocks, the divorce takes effect — because the intent toward the word of divorce exists, and nothing is absent except the intent toward the legal ruling (al-qaṣd ilā al-ḥukm), which is not a condition. This is proven by the fact that if he divorces with a condition of option (khiyār) for himself, it is executed, even though that entails the absence of consent to the ruling. And the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: {«ثلاث جدهن جد وهزلهن جد: الطلاق والنكاح والعتاق»} — "Three things are serious in earnest and serious in jest: divorce, marriage, and manumission."

Yet al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) did not rule that a jester's marriage is contracted, which contradicts the apparent meaning of the hadith. As for sale (bayʿ) and other legal dispositions, some of our companions (al-aṣḥāb) hesitated regarding their validity from a jester.

### The Third Cause: Ignorance (Jahl)

This is when a man addresses a woman with divorce while supposing she is another man's wife, but she turns out to be his own wife — having seen her in darkness or in a cloak (jilbāb), or his father had married her to him in his childhood and he does not know. The well-known position (al-mashhūr) is that her divorce does take effect. Yet there is a manifest probability [against this], because if he did not recognize the marital bond (zawjiyyah), he did not intend to sever it. We have already mentioned in the Book of Usurpation (Kitāb al-Ghaṣb) a position (wajh) regarding its analogue in manumission (ʿitq) that it does not occur — and this is a cogent view. Its clarification is that if a non-Arab (aʿjamī) is prompted with the word of divorce while he does not understand it, his divorce does not occur by consensus. As for the sale by an ignorant person, its validity is apparent — that is, when one sells his father's property supposing him to be alive. On this basis, they said that the execution of divorce is more fitting [to be upheld]. But the more analogical (al-aqyas) view in sale is that it likewise does not take effect, because intent toward an unknown meaning is impossible.

### The Fourth Cause: Coercion (Ikrāh)

The divorce of one coerced does not occur in our school (ʿindanā), because his intent is corrupted — for coercion generates in him a [counter-]intent, and it is as if the act belongs to the coercer. Abū Ḥanīfah said: it does occur.

Then we too execute it whenever the coerced claims that he was consenting, or when signs of choice (makhāyil al-ikhtiyār) appear from him — such as his opposing the coercer by increase, decrease, or alteration of the wording.

An example of increase: he is coerced into one divorce, but he pronounces three; or coerced into divorcing one wife, but he divorces two.

An example of decrease: he is compelled to divorce two wives, but he divorces one; or compelled to [pronounce] three, but he pronounces one or two; or he is told, "Say: I have divorced her," but he says, "I have separated from her (fāraqtuhā)"; or he is told, "Divorce one of your two wives," but he specifies one and divorces her — for such specification is evidence of his aversion to the divorced one.

But if he abandons the dissimulative ambiguity (tawriyah) while being a jurist (faqīh) capable [of it], and he admits that the coercion did not daze him from mentioning the tawriyah, then there is a divergence of opinion (khilāf). The apparent position is that it does occur, and this is made evidence of his choice.

### The Consideration After This Concerns Two Aspects

**The First Aspect: Dispositions Affected by Coercion**

Coercion nullifies the effect of dispositions in our school, absolutely, except in five places:

**First:** Islam — for it is permissible to coerce a harbī (enemy combatant) to it, and his Islam is valid; otherwise, the benefit of coercion would be void. Regarding the Islam of a coerced dhimmī, there is a divergence, and the more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that it is not valid.

**Second:** Breastfeeding (riḍāʿ) — coercion does not remove it from being a cause of prohibition [of marriage], because it is contingent upon the arrival of milk into the stomach, not upon intent.

**Third:** Killing — on one of the two opinions, for it necessitates retaliation (qiṣāṣ) on one view, because coercion does not remove the sin.

**Fourth:** One coerced into fornication (zinā) — on one of the two opinions, he is subject to the prescribed punishment (ḥadd), because the occurrence of erection is evidence of choice, for it does not occur through coercion. The basis of the two opinions is the hesitation over whether coercion is conceivable [in such an act].

**Fifth:** If divorce is suspended upon entry [into the house], and he is coerced into entering — there are two rulings (qawlān) whose basis is that the attribute (ṣifah) does not require intent; rather, the mere name suffices.

As for sale, it is nullified by coercion. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: it is contracted but not binding (lā yalzam).

Know that the exception, upon verification, reverts only to Islam alone, and to killing on one opinion. As for the rest, their cause is either the inconceivability of coercion or the non-requirement of intent.

chapters.title_en: The Second Aspect: The Definition of Coercion (Ḥadd al-Ikrāh)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الطرف الثاني في حد الإكراه

وفيه مسلكان للأصحاب متباعدان
أحدهما أن يصير بحيث لا تبقى له طاقة في المخالفة بل يكون مضطرا إلى
اختيار الموافقة شاء أم أبى كالذي يفر من أسد ضار فيتخطى النار والشوك ولا
يبالي ومثل هذا لا يحصل إلا بسيف مسلول أو تخويف بالإلقاء في النار مثلا
والشرط أن يصير كالمدهوش الذي لا تبقى له روية واستصواب
ثم الجبان قد يدهش ويسقط اختياره بما لا يسقط به اختيار الشجاع فالمعتبر
سقوط خيرته في هذه الطريقة أما من يخوف بالحبس المخلد أو الجوع وما لا
يأخذه في الحال منه أمر لا يطيقه فالطلاق به واقع بناء للأمر على الحزم
والاستصواب وذلك عين الاختيار وهذه الطريقة أضم للنشر
المسلك الثاني أن ذلك لا يعتبر بل إذا خير بين الطلاق وبين أمر لا يحتمله
العاقل لأجل الطلاق فطلق لم يقع الطلاق به كالحبس المخلد والتهديد بالضرب
والجوع ممن يعلم أنه يحقق ذلك وكذلك صفع ذوي المروءة على ملأ من الناس
وكذلك التخويف بإتلاف المال وقتل الولد وعند هذا ينشأ النظر في المكره به
والمكره عليه
فإذا أكره على القتل بإتلاف المال أو الحبس فليحتمله وإن أكره على الطلاق
بذلك فربما لا يحتمله وربما يقال يحتمل إتلاف المال في الطلاق فإن أكره
بإتلاف مال على إتلاف مال فيتصدى النظر في القله والكثرة وضبط ذلك عسير ولا
تخلو طريقه عن غموض ويحصل منه أن المتفق عليه الإكراه بالقتل أو الجرح الذي
يخاف الموت منه كالقطع وما عدا ذلك فيخرج على الخلاف
السبب الخامس زوال العقل وذلك إن كان بإغماء أو جنون أو شرب دواء فيمنع
نفوذ الطلاق والتصرفات وإن كان بمسكر تعدى بشربه ولم يصب قهرا في حلقه
فنصوص الشافعي رضي الله عنه قديما وحديثا وقوع الطلاق ونص  في الظهار قديما
على قولين فقال بعض الأصحاب في المسألتين قولان ومعظم العلماء على وقوع
طلاق السكران ومذهب عثمان وابن عباس وأبي يوسف وزفر والمزني وابن سريج
رضوان الله عليهم أجمعين أنه لا يقع الطلاق وفي سائر تصرفاته طرق منهم من
طرد القولين حتى في أفعاله ومنهم من قال أفعاله كأفعال الصاحي وإنما
الخلاف في أقواله
ومنهم من قال ما عليه ينفذ والقول فيما له وأشهر الطرق طرد القولين في
الكل
ومن شرب البنج متعديا فزال عقله منهم من ألحقه بالسكران لعدوانه ومنهم من
ألحقه بالمجنون لأن ذلك لا يشتهى
فإن قيل ما حد السكر قلنا قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه إذا اختلط كلامه
المنظوم وانكشف سره المكتوم والمقصود أن يصير مثل المجنون الذي لا تنتظم
أموره أما ما دام في ابتداء نشاطه فهو كالعاقل وإن سقط كالمغشي عليه فهو
كالنائم والمغمى عليه ويبعد طرد الخلاف به وقد قيل به وهو ضعيف لأن ذلك
يعدم من أصل القصد
وطلاق المجنون والصبي كطلاق الهازل والجاهل وإنما لا يقع نظرا لهما
والسكران لا يستوجب النظر ولذلك لا يسقط عنه انقضاء العبادات بخلاف المجنون
والأقيس مذهب المزني وهو إلحاق السكران بالمجنون في التصرفات

### | الركن الرابع لنفوذ الطلاق المحل وهي المرأة

وفيه فصلان

### | أحدهما

أنه لو أضاف إلى بعضها نفذ وكمل ولو أضاف إلى عضو معين نفذ عندنا خلافا
لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله ثم له ثلاث درجات
إحداها أن يضيف إلى جزء متصل كاليد والرأس والكبد والظهر وسائر الأعضاء
الباطنة ولا خلاف في وقوعه نعم الأذن المنفصلة إذا عادت ملتحمة أو الشعرة
الساقطة إذا انغرست في موضع آخر ففي الإضافة إليه فيه خلاف
الثانية أن يضيف إلى فضلات بدنها كالبول واللبن والعرق والدمع والمني
فالصحيح أنه لا يقع وفيه وجه بعيد أنه يقع ولم يطرد ذلك الوجه في الجنين
لأنه كالمستقل نعم ترددوا في الدم والشحم أنه يلحق بالفضلات أو بالأجزاء من
حيث إن الدم
كالقوام للروح والشحم يشبه السمن ولو قال سمنك طالق  نفذ
الثالثة الإضافة إلى الصفة كقوله حسنك أو لونك أو بياضك طالق وذلك لاغ
لأن الصفة تابع لا تقبل الإضافة دون الموصوف نعم لو قال روحك أو حياتك طالق
قالوا إنه يقع لأن الروح جوهر وأصل والحياة كذلك ولا يحتمل نظر الفقهاء
الخوض في الفرق بين الروح والحياة
فرع لو قال إن دخلت الدار فيمينك طالق فقطع يمينها ثم دخلت ففي الطلاق
وجهان مبينات على أن تنفيذ الطلاق المضاف إلى الجزء بطريق التسرية منه أو
بطريق جعل ذكر البعض عبارة عن الكل وفيه خلاف فإن قيل بالتسرية فلم يصادف
اليمين حتى تنفذ فيه فلا يقع وإن جعل عبارة عن الكل نفذ
أما إذا قال لمقطوعة اليمين يمينك طالق فالصحيح أنه لا يقع على الوجهين
لأنه وإن جعل عبارة الجميع فحيث توجد
ولا خلاف أنه لو قال لها ذكرك أو لحيتك طالق لم يقع لأن المذكور مفقود
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-ر-ه (K-R-H)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "dislike" or "aversion" — the state of being compelled against one's inclination; al-karh (with fatḥa) denotes "compulsion" while al-kurh denotes "dislike" as an internal state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological-juridical usage, ikrāh is the imposition of a harmful alternative upon an agent such that their volitional capacity (ikhtiyār) is nullified or severely diminished — distinct from mere dislike, which does not negate choice.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to actual physical overpowering; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to threats and intimidation that produce a comparable psychological state of helplessness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Construction (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — the text repeatedly employs conditional clauses (idhā... fa...) where the protasis establishes a hypothetical scenario and the apodosis delivers the juridical ruling, requiring precise parsing of the condition's scope.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second aspect concerns the definition of coercion (ikrāh). There are two widely divergent approaches (maslakān) among our companions [the Shāfiʿīs].

The first approach: [A person is coerced] when he reaches a state where he retains no capacity (ṭāqah) to oppose [the command], but rather is compelled (muḍṭarr) to choose compliance, whether he wills it or refuses — like one fleeing a predatory lion who steps over fire and thorns without caring. Such a state is not attained except by a drawn sword or by intimidation through threat of being cast into fire, for example. The condition is that he becomes like one stupefied (madhūsh) who retains no deliberation (rawiyyah) or judgment of what is sound (istiswāb).

Then, the coward may be stupefied and lose his choice by what would not cause the brave man to lose his choice. Thus, what is considered in this approach is the [actual] loss of one's discernment (khīrah). As for one who is threatened with perpetual imprisonment or starvation — matters that do not seize him immediately with something he cannot bear — divorce pronounced [under such threats] takes effect, because the matter is built upon prudence (ḥazm) and sound judgment, and that is precisely choice (ikhtiyār). This approach is more conducive to the dissemination [of rulings].

The second approach: That [loss of choice] is not the criterion. Rather, if one is given the choice between divorce and a matter that a rational person cannot bear for the sake of [avoiding] divorce, and he then pronounces divorce, the divorce does not take effect — such as perpetual imprisonment, threats of beating, or starvation from one known to carry out such threats. Likewise, slapping a person of honor (dhawī al-murūʾah) in public view [constitutes coercion]. Similarly, intimidation through destruction of wealth or killing of one's child. At this point, the inquiry arises concerning the means of coercion (al-mukrah bihi) and the act coerced upon (al-mukrah ʿalayhi).

Thus, if one is coerced into killing by [threat of] destruction of wealth or imprisonment, let him endure it [and not comply]. But if coerced into divorce by such means, perhaps he cannot endure it [and may comply]. And it may be said: destruction of wealth can be endured in [avoiding] divorce. If one is coerced by destruction of wealth into destroying wealth [of another], then the inquiry turns to the question of little versus much [wealth], and establishing a precise measure for that is difficult, and its path is not free of obscurity. What emerges from this is that the agreed-upon [case of] coercion is by killing or wounding from which death is feared, such as amputation. Whatever falls outside that is adjudicated according to the divergent opinions.

The fifth cause: The loss of intellect (zawāl al-ʿaql). If this occurs through fainting (ighmāʾ), madness (junūn), or drinking a [mind-altering] medicine, then divorce and all legal dispositions are rendered inoperative. But if it occurs through an intoxicant (muskir) consumed transgresively — he drank it of his own accord, not being forced into his throat — then the texts of al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him), both early and late, affirm the occurrence of divorce. He also has an early text concerning ẓihār [that is transmitted] on two opinions. Some companions said concerning both matters: there are two opinions. The majority of scholars hold that the divorce of the intoxicated person takes effect. The school of ʿUthmān, Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Yūsuf, Zufar, al-Muzanī, and Ibn Surayj (may Allah be pleased with them all) is that the divorce does not take effect. Concerning his other dispositions, there are several paths: among them, one who extends the two opinions even to his physical acts; among them, one who says his physical acts are like the acts of the sober person, and the disagreement pertains only to his utterances; and among them, one who says what is against him takes effect, while what is in his favor [is suspended]. The most well-known path extends the two opinions to everything.

As for one who drinks banj (a narcotic) transgresively and loses his intellect: among them are those who liken him to the intoxicated person due to his transgression, and among them are those who liken him to the madman because [banj] is not something craved [by the soul].

If it is said: What is the definition of intoxication (sukr)? I say: al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: When his orderly speech becomes confused and his hidden secret is disclosed. The intended meaning is that he becomes like the madman whose affairs are not properly ordered. As long as he remains in the beginning of his exhilaration, he is like the sane person. If he collapses like one who has fainted, he is like the sleeper and the one who has lost consciousness — and it is far-fetched to extend the disagreement to this state, though it has been said, but it is weak, because that [state] eliminates intention (qaṣd) entirely.

The divorce of the madman and the minor is like the divorce of the joker and the ignorant person — it does not take effect, out of consideration (naẓar) for them. But the intoxicated person does not merit such consideration, and therefore the expiry of devotional obligations is not waived for him, unlike the madman. The more analogically sound (aqyas) [position] is the school of al-Muzanī, which is to liken the intoxicated person to the madman in all legal dispositions.

### The Fourth Pillar for the Effectiveness of Divorce: The Locus (al-Maḥall) — i.e., the Woman

This contains two chapters.

### Chapter One

If he [the husband] attributes [the divorce] to part of her, it takes effect and is complete. If he attributes it to a specific limb, it takes effect in our school, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him). Then [the attribution] has three degrees:

The first degree: He attributes it to a connected part, such as the hand, head, liver, back, and all internal organs. There is no disagreement concerning its occurrence. However, a detached ear that has reattached and healed, or a fallen hair that has been implanted in another place — concerning attribution to these there is disagreement.

The second degree: He attributes it to her bodily excretions (fuḍalāt), such as urine, milk, sweat, tears, and semen. The correct [position] is that it does not take effect. There is a remote view (wajh) that it does take effect, but that view was not extended to the fetus, because it is like an independent entity. However, they hesitated concerning blood and fat — whether they are classed with the excretions or with the parts — because blood is the constitution (qiwām) of the spirit, and fat resembles clarified butter (samn). If he said, "Your clarified butter is divorced," it takes effect.

The third degree: Attribution to an attribute (ṣifah), such as his saying, "Your beauty, or your color, or your whiteness is divorced." This is void, because the attribute is a dependent [accident] that does not admit attribution without its qualified subject (mawṣūf). However, if he said, "Your spirit (rūḥ) or your life (ḥayāh) is divorced," they said it takes effect, because the spirit is a substance (jawhar) and an origin (aṣl), and likewise life — and it is not fitting for jurists to delve into the distinction between spirit and life.

Branch: If he said, "If you enter the house, your right hand is divorced," and then he cut off her right hand, and she then entered [the house] — concerning the occurrence of divorce there are two views (wajhān), built upon whether the execution of divorce attributed to a part operates by way of transmission (tasriyah) from that part, or by way of making the mention of the part a figurative expression (ʿibārah) for the whole. There is disagreement on this. If it is said [to operate] by transmission, then [the divorce] did not encounter the hand [at the moment of entry] so as to take effect upon it — thus it does not occur. If it is made a figurative expression for the whole, it takes effect.

As for when he says to a woman whose right hand has been cut off, "Your right hand is divorced" — the correct [position] is that it does not take effect on either view, because even if it is made a figurative expression for the whole, [the whole] exists [but the named part does not].

There is no disagreement that if he said to her, "Your male organ (dhakar) or your beard is divorced," it does not take effect, because the thing mentioned is non-existent [in her].
