- Root: ش-ر-ط (sharṭa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To mark, condition, or stipulate; a condition (sharṭ) is that upon which something else depends.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, taʿlīq (suspension) renders an utterance contingent upon a future, unknown event—distinct from taʾqīt (temporal limitation).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in contracts of irrevocable effect; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to divine will, since God's will is not a conditional cause but an eternal attribute.
- Root: ع-ل-ق (ʿaliqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hang, suspend, or attach; taʿlīq is the attachment of a ruling to a condition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Suspension (taʿlīq) of an effect upon a condition implies uncertainty (taraddud) regarding the condition's occurrence—impossible for God's eternal will.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): In legal speech, taʿlīq is valid for future contingencies (mustaqbal), but invalid when the condition is impossible (muḥāl) or already determined.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-Istiṯnāʾ al-Muttaṣil (Connected Exception) — The exception particle (illā) or phrase (in shāʾ Allāh) must grammatically attach to the immediately preceding operative verb (al-ʿāmil), not to a noun or vocative, unless the noun itself carries operative force.
chapters.translation:
I say: Within this section are several subsidiary questions (masāʾil).

**The First Question:** If a man says to his wife, "You are divorced, if Allah wills," or to his slave, "You are free, if Allah wills," the divorce and the manumission do not occur. This is because the will of Allah is unseen (ghayb) and cannot be known; thus, the attribute upon which the utterance is suspended becomes unknown (majhūl). Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) held that the divorce does not occur, but the manumission does occur. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly stated that if a man says, "You are to me like the back of my mother, if Allah wills," he becomes a muẓāhir (one who pronounces ẓihār). Among our companions (aṣḥāb), some extended this ruling to divorce and all other contracts, while others distinguished by saying that ẓihār is an informative statement (ikhbār), and suspending an informative statement upon the will is invalid. Similarly, if one says, "So-and-so owes me ten, if Allah wills," the ten are still binding upon him, because a declarative acknowledgment (iqrār) does not admit suspension, whereas a performative utterance (inshāʾ) does admit suspension. Yet others equated contracts with acknowledgments and permitted the exception by the will in all of them; and upon this latter view, the subsidiary rulings are built.

**The Second Question:** If he says, "O divorced one, if Allah wills," the apparent ruling (al-ẓāhir) is that divorce occurs, because the exception cannot grammatically attach to a noun (ism); it only attaches to a performative utterance (inshāʾ). However, there is a consideration (naẓar) here, because this noun (i.e., "O divorced one") carries the meaning of a performative utterance. For this reason, some said that nothing occurs. But if he says, "O divorced one, you are divorced three times, if Allah wills," the exception reverts to the three, and one divorce occurs by virtue of his saying "O divorced one."

**The Third Question:** If he says, "You are divorced three times, O divorced one, if Allah wills," the companions (aṣḥāb) said that nothing occurs, because his saying "O divorced one" does not operate such that the exception attaches to it—this being a subsidiary branch upon the apparent view (ẓāhir). Rather, the exception reverts to the three, and the interposition of his saying "O divorced one" does not repel the exception, because it is of the same genus as the speech. This is like his saying, "You are divorced three times, O Ḥafṣah, if Allah wills."

**The Fourth Question:** If he says, "You are divorced, if Allah does not will," or "unless Allah wills," the import of the two expressions is one and the same, and its meaning is suspension upon the non-existence of the will. And just as the will is not known, so too its non-existence is not known. By analogy (qiyās), divorce should occur—and al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly ruled this. Indeed, here it is even more apt, because he has suspended it upon something impossible (muḥāl), since it is impossible for divorce to occur contrary to the will of Allah. This is like his saying, "You are divorced, if you ascend to the sky." The author of al-Talkhīṣ said: It may be said that divorce occurs, unlike suspension upon ascending, because ascending is possible in itself, whereas divorce contrary to the will of Allah is impossible. It is as if he said, "You are divorced with a divorce that does not occur." It was related from al-Qāḍī (Abū Ṭayyib al-Ṭabarī) that he chose the occurrence of divorce here. But this is far-fetched, because if he says, "You are divorced with a divorce, if blackness and whiteness combine," it does not occur, because it is suspension upon an impossibility. So too his saying, "If your divorce contradicts the will of Allah," is also impossible. However, he (al-Qāḍī) may have another avenue (māʾkhadh): namely, that if he says, "You are divorced, if Zayd does not enter the house," and Zayd does enter, it does not occur; but if Zayd dies before entering, it becomes evident that it occurred at the time of the pronouncement. If Zayd dies and the entry remains doubtful, there are two views (wajhān): One, that it does not occur, because the original presumption (al-aṣl) is non-occurrence. The second, that it does occur, because he executed the divorce and excepted from it, and the exception was not established. This second view is more apparent (aẓhar) in his saying, "You are divorced, unless Zayd enters the house," for this is the form of exception (ṣīghat al-istithnāʾ). The correct view is that there is no difference between the two formulations. On this basis, it is not far-fetched to say that the will of Allah is excepted, and thus divorce occurs for that reason. This is his strained (mutakallaf) avenue. The correct view is that it does not occur; for if it occurred, then Allah would have willed its occurrence, yet he only suspended divorce upon the non-existence of the will. However, if it does not occur, it becomes evident that Allah did not will it, and thus the attribute upon which he suspended is realized—so it ought to occur. Then, by its occurrence, the attribute is negated. Thus, the condition and the consequent here are mutually contradictory (mutadhāddān) and cannot coexist. The origin of the initial impression (badw al-naẓar) is whether suspension in this manner is valid. It is not like suspension upon the combination of blackness and whiteness, because the contradiction is between blackness and whiteness themselves, not between the combination and the divorce—so there is no contradiction between the consequent and the condition. This issue draws upon the question of circularity (al-dawr): For his saying to a woman not yet consummated with, "If I divorce you, then you are divorced before it," there is a contradiction between the condition and the consequent, and Abū Zayd (al-Marwazī) therefore nullified it, while Ibn al-Ḥaddād upheld it. This question is connected to that one.

If it is said: When he says, "You are divorced, if Allah wills," what is the meaning of hesitation (taraddud) regarding the will, given that His will is eternal (qadīmah) and admits no hesitation? If what is meant is its attachment (taʿalluq), then either it is attached to the utterance of divorce or to its ruling (ḥukm). If attached to the utterance, then He has willed the utterance, for it has already occurred. If attached to the ruling, then the ruling is eternal, and the will does not attach to the eternal, because the ruling is the speech of Allah (kalām Allāh taʿālā). We say: The meaning is the will of the ruling of divorce, and the will is eternal, but what is intended is that there occurs for it, at the time of the event's occurrence, a new attachment (taʿalluq ḥādith) to the eternal will. Even if it had, before the event, a certain type of attachment in another manner, that renewed attachment is doubtful. As for his saying, "The ruling is eternal," it is not meant that it is not so; rather, the woman's becoming forbidden (taḥrīm) is an originated attribute (waṣf ḥādith) that requires a new attachment of the eternal speech to it. For the eternal address (al-khiṭāb al-qadīm) has renewed attachments, just as the will does. And legal rulings are built upon renewed attachments, not upon the eternal origin.

**The Sixth Chapter: On Doubt (al-shakk) in Divorce and in Its Object (maḥall)**

As for doubt in divorce itself, its form is that one hesitates whether he divorced or not. The original presumption is that no divorce occurred, so we adhere to the principle of istiṣḥāb (presumption of continuity), just as when one is certain of purity and doubts whether an impurity occurred. This is because there is no room for ijtihād (independent reasoning) in matters of divorce and impurity, and istiṣḥāb suffices. This is not like a divorce over which jurists differ, for such is not treated as doubtful; rather, one must rely upon what ijtihād dictates. Similarly, if a bird flies by and he says, "If this is a crow, then my wife is divorced," and he doubts, the divorce does not occur unless it becomes clear that it is a crow. If another man says, "And if it is not a crow, then my wife is divorced," his divorce also does not occur, because if he had uttered it alone, it would not occur; so the prior utterance of another does not alter his ruling.

But if he has two wives and says, "If this is a crow, then ʿAmrah is divorced, and if it is not, then Zaynab is divorced," one of them is forbidden to him, and he must abstain from both, because the person (of the speaker) is one, and certainty is achieved with respect to him.

**Branch (farʿ):** If this occurs regarding two slaves belonging to two different masters, each master may dispose of his own slave. If one of them purchases the other's slave so that both come into his ownership, he is placed under interdiction (ḥajr) regarding both until the matter becomes clear. There is a view that the interdiction applies specifically to the purchaser, because the first owner was already disposing of his slave, and his ruling is not reversed by the other's purchase. The correct view is the first. If the first owner sells his slave, then the second purchases the other, it may be said that he may dispose of the second, because that first occurrence has concluded—just as one who prays toward one direction, then his ijtihād changes to another direction, prays toward the new direction and does not repeat the first prayer. It may also be said otherwise, because istiṣḥāb is weak relative to ijtihād.

As for doubt concerning the object of divorce (maḥall al-ṭalāq)—such as when he divorces one of two wives and then forgets which—he must refrain (tawaqquf) until he remembers.

If he says to his wife and a foreign woman, "One of you two is divorced," then says, "I meant the foreign woman," is he accepted? There are two views: One, no, because she is not a valid object of his divorce. The second, yes—and this is the more apparent (aẓhar)—because the utterance is ambiguous (mubham). On this view, he is made to clarify (yurājiʿ) until he specifies.

If he says to two wives, "One of you is divorced," he is required to specify (taʿyīn). If he had intended a specific one, he is required to disclose (kashf) it. The correct view is that her waiting period (ʿiddah) begins from the time of the ambiguous pronouncement (al-ibhām). If he had not intended a specific one, he is required to specify one for the divorce to take effect. When he specifies, does the divorce occur by the specification, or does it become evident that it occurred by the ambiguous pronouncement? There are two views: One, that it occurs by the ambiguous pronouncement, and the specification is like an explanation (bayān) and a designation of its object—so the waiting period is counted from that time, on the correct view, just as when he had intended. The second, that it occurs by the specification, because if it had occurred before, it would have occurred upon no specific object, for he has now clarified the object. But since he pronounced it without clarifying the object, we oblige him to clarify the object.

Then, regarding specification (taʿyīn), there is consideration (naẓar) in two states: during life and after death.

**The First Consideration: During Life.** Within it are several questions:

**The First:** He is obliged to specify, and is demanded to do so, and it is obligatory immediately (ʿalā al-fawr)—just as one who embraces Islam with ten wives. He sins by delaying. If he ambiguously pronounced a revocable divorce (ṭalqah rajʿiyyah), there are two views on whether specification is obligatory immediately, because the prohibition (taḥrīm) has occurred, but the means of return (al-najāḥ) has not been severed.

**The Second:** He is obliged to provide maintenance (nafaqah) for both wives before specification, even if the period is prolonged. Likewise, if he intended one but did not disclose, and likewise in the crow question until it becomes clear, because the interdiction of marriage (ḥajr al-nikāḥ) is continuous, so maintenance is indispensable.

**The Third:** If he has intercourse with one of them—if we say that divorce occurs by specification, then this is not a specification; but if we say it is like an explanation (bayān), then it is not far-fetched to make this an explanation designating the one with whom he had intercourse. The same disagreement applies if he has intercourse with one of his female slaves after ambiguously pronouncing manumission between them. Where we make intercourse a specification, she has no dower (mahr); where we do not make it a specification, he specifies the other for marriage, and there are two views on the obligation of dower, built upon the time of the divorce's occurrence.

**The Fourth:** If both wives die, or one of them, the demand for specification is not dropped on account of inheritance. This supports our view that divorce occurs by the ambiguous pronouncement. On the other view, they differed: some said that here, out of necessity (ḍarūrah), specification is treated as explanation (bayān), not as effectuation (īqāʿ); others said that we determine that the divorce occurred upon the specific one just before her death—just as we say regarding a sold object that perishes: we determine that the contract was rescinded just before the perishing, out of necessity.

**The Fifth:** On the formulations of specification (ṣiyagh al-taʿyīn). There are two forms:

**One:** He says, "I intended both of them." Then divorce does not occur upon both, because the utterance does not admit that. But it is an acknowledgment (iqrār) of divorce for both, and each may hold him to it. If he says, "I intended this one, then this one," al-Qāḍī said that the first is divorced, not the second, because his utterance does not admit conjunction. Al-Imām (al-Ghazālī's teacher, al-Juwaynī) said the correct view is that it is an acknowledgment regarding the second as well, and his saying "then" is nullified—just as when he says, "This house is for Zayd, then for ʿAmr," ʿAmr may hold him to it. If he says, "I intended this one after this one," then according to al-Qāḍī, divorce occurs upon the second, because she is prior in meaning though later in mention; and on al-Imām's doctrine, he is held to both.

**The Second Form:** He ambiguously pronounces divorce among three women, then seats two on one side and the third on another, then says, "I intended this one," pauses briefly, then says, "or this one." We say: He has not removed the ambiguity. If he specifies the third, the latter two are designated for marriage. If he specifies one of the two, her companion shares with her, because he joined her to her in the acknowledgment by his saying "this one or this one." The companion is only designated for sharing by his pause with the formulation. If he says, in continuous sequence (ʿalā al-sard), "this one or this one and this one," it is possible that the third shares with the first and shares with the second. His word is accepted in this, and his statement is credited.

All this applies when he had intended. But if he ambiguously pronounced divorce without any intention, and we demanded specification, and he said, "I specified this one or this one," his word is accepted. If he says, "I specified this one and this one," the first is specified, and his word regarding the second is nullified, because it is not an acknowledgment such that he is held to it—rather, it is a performative utterance (inshāʾ), and a performative utterance cannot stand alone as an effectuation unless preceded by an utterance admitting conjunction.

**The Sixth Question: On Dispute (al-nizāʿ).** It has three forms:

**One:** If he had intended, and one wife claims that he meant her, and he denies—then his word is accepted. If he refuses to swear (nukūl), she swears and is designated for divorce by her oath, and the other is designated by the husband's acknowledgment against himself in his denial.

**The Second Form:** If he had divorced a specific one of them but forgot which, and one says, "He divorced me"—his saying "I forgot" is not accepted. Rather, he must swear a decisive oath (al-batt) that he did not divorce her. If he refuses, she swears a decisive oath and judgment is given for her. If we accepted a man's oath denying knowledge and forgetfulness, this would lead to consequences in cases of loans (istiqrāḍ) and all other claims.

**The Third Form:** In the crow question, if one wife says, "If it was a crow, then I am divorced," and the husband denies—he must swear a decisive oath that it was not a crow, or refuse, so that she swears a decisive oath that it was a crow. If he suspended upon her entry or the entry of another, and they dispute, he is excused with an oath denying knowledge of the entry. Thus said my Imām (al-Juwaynī). But I do not see any difference between the two cases at all; rather, it should be said that he must swear a decisive oath or refuse in both questions alike.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | النظر الثاني فيما بعد الموت

وفيه ثلاث مسائل
إحداها إذا ماتا جميعا فعليه التعيين فإن كان قد نوى بقبله فبين للوارث
تحليفه لأجل الميراث وإن لم يكن قد نوى فعين لم يكن لهم التحليف لأنه إنشاء
منوط باختياره وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله ينحسم التعيين بالموت وللزوج نصف
حقه من ميراث كل واحدة
الثانية أن يموت الزوج أيضا فهل للوارث التعيين نظر فإن كانتا في الحياة
فيوقف ميراث كل واحدة بينهما حتى يصطلحا وليس لوارث الزوج التعيين
وإن ماتت إحداهما ثم مات الزوج ثم ماتت الأخرى فإن عين الوارث الأولى
للطلاق فهو مقر على نفسه إذ حرم مورثه عن الميراث فيقبل وإن عين الأخيرة
ليحرمها عن ميراث مورثه وليجوز ميراث الأولى فهذا محل غرضه ففي تعيينه
ثلاثة أقوال
أحدث أنه يقبل لأنه خليفة المورث في خيار الشفعة وغيره فكذلك في هذه
والثاني أنه لا أثر له لأن حقوق النكاح لا تورث
والثالث أنه إن قال إن الزوج قد نوى هذه فله ذلك فلعله سمعه أو فهمه
بقرينة وإن قال لم ينو ولكنه أراد  إنشاء التعيين لم يجز لأن هذا إلى الزوج
وكذا الخلاف في تعيين الوارث إذا أبهم العتق بين عبدين ومات لأن للوارث
غرضا فيه والعراقيون أرسلوا ذكر قولين في أن الوارث هل يعين حيث يعين الزوج
لو كان حيا ولم يفرقوا بين أن يكون له غرض أو لا غرض له وهذا التفصيل ذكره
القفال وهو أحسن
الثالثة إذا قال إن كان هذا غرابا فزوجتي طالق وإن لم يكن غرابا فعبدي حر
فيحجر عليه فيهما جميعا لأن المالك متحد وإن كان الجنس مختلفا فإن مات قبل
التعيين فهل للوارث التعيين فيه طريقان
أحدهما طرد القولين
والثاني القطع بأن لا يعين لأن لللقرعة مدخلا للعتق فهو أولى من التعيين
وإن لم يكن لها مدخل في الطلاق
وإذا وقع الإبهام في محض الإرقاق فلا خلاف في أن المحكم للقرعة فعلى هذا
لو أقرعنا فخرج على الرقيق عتق وتعينت المرأة للنكاح وورثت وإن خرج على
المرأة لم تطلق لأن القرعة لا تؤثر في الطلاق ولكن هل يتعين الرقيق للرق
فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن القرعة إن قصرت عن حكم الطلاق فتستعمل في الرق والعتق
والثاني لا لأن تعيينه للرق فرع تعيين المرأة للطلاق بالقرعة فإذا لم
تعمل القرعة في محلها كيف تعمل فيما يثبت ضمنا له فعل هذا يبقى الإبهام إذ
كنا نتوقع بالقرعة بيانا فلم يحصل

### | الشطر االثاني من الكتاب في التعليقات

والنظر فيه في فصول مطولة وفي فروع متعددة موجزة فلنقدم الفصول وهي ستة

### | الفصل الأول في التعليق بالأوقات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ي-ن (ʿ- y - n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to specify, designate, or determine" — the act of fixing a particular referent from among possibilities; also "eye" as the organ of discernment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological contexts, taʿyīn denotes the authoritative designation of an ambiguous term (mubham) by the one holding the right (ḥaqq), often tied to intention (niyya) and its evidentiary trace.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to physical pointing or ocular identification; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to legal designation where the "eye" of the judge or heir discerns the intended object.
- Root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to strike, smite, or cast" — from which derives "lot" (qurʿah) as the casting of lots, a decisive random selection.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, qurʿah is a procedural device for resolving ambiguity when human designation fails; it operates only where the law permits chance as a determinant (e.g., manumission), not in matters of personal status like divorce.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical striking; metaphorical: the "striking" of a decision upon an ambiguous case, akin to a divine or judicial decree.
- Root: و-ر-ث (w-r-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to inherit" — the transfer of property, rights, or obligations from the deceased to heirs.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Inheritance (irth) is a divinely ordained transfer; the heir (wārith) stands as a successor (khalīfah) to the deceased in certain legal capacities, but not in all — particularly not in personal rights like divorce (ṭalāq).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: succession to wealth; metaphorical: succession to legal authority (wilāyah), which is the contested extension here.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Suspension (Taʿlīq) — In Arabic syntax, a conditional clause (sharṭ) suspends the apodosis (jazāʾ) upon the occurrence of the protasis; legally, this mirrors the suspension of an effect (e.g., divorce, manumission) upon a future contingency, requiring designation (taʿyīn) when the contingency is ambiguous.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second consideration concerns what follows death. It contains three questions.

**The First Question:** If both [wives] die, then designation [of which was divorced] is incumbent [upon the husband]. If he had intended [the divorce] during his lifetime, then he must clarify [this] to the heir, who may administer an oath to him for the sake of inheritance. But if he had not intended [it] and [only] designated [after death], then they have no right to administer an oath to him, because this is an origination (inshāʾ) dependent upon his own choice. Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — said: Designation is foreclosed by death, and the husband [in such a case] takes half of his right from the inheritance of each [wife].

**The Second Question:** If the husband also dies, does the heir have the right of designation? Consider: If both [wives] are alive [at the husband's death], then the inheritance of each is suspended between them until they reach a settlement, and the husband's heir has no right of designation. But if one wife dies, then the husband dies, then the other wife dies — if the heir designates the first [as the one divorced], he is making an admission against himself, since he has barred his own predecessor (muwarith) from inheritance, so this is accepted. But if he designates the last [wife as divorced] in order to bar her from his predecessor's inheritance and to validate the inheritance of the first — this is the locus of his objective. Regarding his designation [in this case], there are three opinions:

The most recent [opinion of al-Shāfiʿī] is that it is accepted, because he is the successor (khalīfah) of the deceased in the option of preemption (shufʿah) and other matters, so likewise in this.

The second is that it has no effect, because the rights of marriage (ḥuqūq al-nikāḥ) are not inherited.

The third is that if he says, "The husband had indeed intended this [wife]," then he may [designate], for perhaps he heard it from him or inferred it from circumstantial evidence (qarīnah). But if he says, "He did not intend [it], yet I wish to originate a designation," then this is not permissible, because this [right] belongs to the husband [alone].

Likewise, there is a disagreement regarding the heir's designation when [the deceased] left ambiguous the manumission between two slaves and then died, because the heir has an objective in it. The Iraqis have transmitted two opinions on whether the heir may designate where the husband could designate were he alive, without distinguishing between whether the heir has an objective or not. This detailed distinction was mentioned by al-Qaffāl, and it is more sound.

**The Third Question:** If he says, "If this is a crow, then my wife is divorced; and if it is not a crow, then my slave is free" — then he is placed under interdiction (ḥajr) regarding both [matters], because the owner is one, even though the categories differ. If he dies before designation, is there for the heir a right of designation in this? There are two paths:

One: to extend the two opinions [mentioned above].

The second: to affirm definitively that he does not designate, because the lot (qurʿah) has an entry into manumission, so it is more appropriate than designation — even though it has no entry into divorce.

And when the ambiguity occurs in pure enslavement (irqāq), there is no disagreement that the lot is the arbiter. Thus, on this basis, if we cast lots and it falls upon the slave, he is freed and the woman is designated for marriage [i.e., not divorced] and inherits. But if it falls upon the woman, she is not divorced, because the lot has no effect in divorce. However, is the slave designated for enslavement [in that case]? There are two aspects:

One: Yes — because if the lot falls short of governing divorce, it is still employed in [matters of] enslavement and manumission.

The second: No — because his designation for enslavement is subsidiary to the woman's designation for divorce by the lot. So if the lot does not operate in its proper locus, how could it operate in what is established as subsidiary to it? Thus, the ambiguity remains, since we had expected clarification by the lot, and it was not achieved.

---

### | The Second Half of the Book: On Suspensions (Taʿlīqāt)

I say: The consideration therein concerns extended chapters (fuṣūl) and numerous concise branches (furūʿ). Let us present the chapters — and they are six.

### | Chapter One: On Suspension by Times

وهي أربعة
النوع الأول في التعليق بمجيء وقت منتظر وصيغة التعليق إن وفي معناه إذا
فلا فرق بين أن يقول إن طلعت الشمس أو إذا طلعت الشمس أو إن دخلت الدار أو
إذا دخلت الدار فالكل تعليق وقال مالك رحمه الله إذا علق بما يستيقن وقوعه
كطلوع الشمس وقع في الحال وهو ضعيف
فنقول لو قال أنت طالق في أول شهر رمضان طلقت كما أهل الهلال مقرونا بأول
جزء منه ولا نقول إن في  للظرف فيقضي وقتا محتوشا بوقتين من شهر رمضان بل لا
يشعر بالانطباق عليه ولو قال أنت طالق في شهر رمضان فكمثل ولو قال أنت طالق
في يوم السبت طلقت مع طلوع الفجر ولو قال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يقع في آخر
النهار وآخر الشهر التفاتا إلى أن الوجوب المعلق
بوقت موسع يستقر في آخره
ولو قال أنت طالق في آخر شهر رمضان طلقت في آخر جزء منه وفيه وجه آخر
أنها تطلق في أول جزء من ليلة السادس عشر لأن النصف الأخير كله آخر الشهر
ولو قال أنت طالق في أول آخر الشهر طلقت في أول يوم الأخير على وجه وفي أول
نصف الأخير على وجه ولو قال في آخر أول هذا الشهر ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه آخر النصف الأول
والثاني أنه آخر الليلة الأولى
والثالث أنه آخر يوم الأول
ولو قال في سلخ الشهر فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه آخر جزء من الشهر إذ به الانسلاخ
والثاني أنه أول اليوم الأخير
والثالث أنه أول جزء من الشهر لأنه منه يأخذ في الانسلاخ وهذا ركيك
ولو قال عند انسلاخ الشهر لم يتجه إلا في آخر جزء من الشهر
النوع الثاني التعليق بمضي الأوقات فلو قال إذا مضى يوم فأنت طالق وهو با
الليل فيقع مع الغروب من الغد وإن كان بالنهار فإلى أن يعود النهار إلى مثل
وقته ولو قال إذا مضت السنة فتطلق مع استهلال المحرم وإن لم يكن قد بقي إلا
يوم ولو قال إذا مضت سنة فلا بد من اثني عشر شهرا من وقت اليمين ويكفي
الأشهر العربية لكن الشهر الذي هو فيه إذا كان في وسطه يكمل ثلاثين من آخر
السنة وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله إذا انكسر شهر انكسر جميع الشهور لأنه لا
بد من التوالي
النوع الثالث التعليق بالزمان الماضي فإذا قال أنت طالق بالأمس قصدت الآن
إيقاع الطلاق بالأمس قلنا هذا محال لأن حكم اللفظ لا يتقدم على اللفظ وهل
يقع في الحال  فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن حكم لفظه لو تحقق شمل الوقت الحاضر فينفذ في القدر الممكن
والثاني وهو الأقيس أن هذا لغو من الكلام فلا يقع به شيئ
ولو قال أوقعت الآن طلقة ينتشر حكمها إلى الأمس لأنه محال
والثاني هو اختيار الربيع أنه لا يقع لأنه أوقع ما يتصف بهذه الصفة وما
وصفه به فهو محال فلا يقع شيئ
وترجع حقيقة الخلاف إلى أنه إذا وصف الطلاق بوصف جعل محالا يلغى أصل
الطلاق أو الوصف واستدل الربيع بقوله أنت طالق إن أحييت ميتا أو صعدت
السماء فإنه لا يقع فاختلف الأصحاب فيه على ثلاثة أوجه
منهم من وافقه
ومنهم من قال يقع في مسألة الصعود والإحياء وهو كقوله أنت طالق طلاقا لا
يقع عليك
ومنهم من فرق بين الإحياء والصعود وقال الإحياء محال من المخلوق فهو
كقوله طلاقا لا يقع عليك وأما الصعود فممكن في نفسه
والصحيح أن هذه التعليقات صحيحة والمقصود الإبعاد كقوله تعالى {حتى يلج
الجمل في سم الخياط} وأما قوله طلاقا لا يقع فهو متناقض في ذاته وقوله
طلاقا ينعكس حكمه على ما مضى ليس بمتناقض لكنه مخالف حكم الشرع فينقدح فيه
التردد ولا بأس بما ذكره الربيع فيه
ولو قال إذا مات فلان فأنت طالق قبله بشهر صح فإن مات قبل مضي الشهر لم
يقع الطلاق لأنه يؤدي إلى التقديم على اللفظ ولو مات بعد شهر تبينا وقوع
الطلاق قبله بشهر وكذلك لو قال قبل قدوم زيد وقبل دخول الدار بشهر وقال أبو
حنيفة رحمه الله يستند الطلاق في الموت دون القدوم والدخول وهو تحكم
ولو قال أنت طالق أمس غدا أو غدا أمس وقع في الحال لأن اليوم هو أمس غدا
وغدا أمس ولو قال أنت طالق في السنة الماضية ولم يبين فالظاهر الحكم
بالطلاق لأن ظاهره الإقرار بوقوع الطلاق ولو قال أردت أو زوجا آخر طلقك أو
طلقتك أنا في نكاح آخر ثم جددت فإن أقام بينة قبل وإلا حكم بالطلاق في
الوقت  ولو قال أردت طلقة رجعية فيقبل لأنه تقرير للطلاق في هذا النكاح
النوع الرابع التعليق بتكرير الأوقات وفيه مسألتان
أحدهما إذا قال أنت طالق ثلاثا في كل سنة طلقة طلقت طلقة واحدة في الحال
وواحدة في أول محرم السنة الثانية إن أراد السنين العربية والثالثة في أول
محرم السنة الثالثة إن بقيت العدة وإن لم يرد السنة العربية فلا تقع
الثانية ما لم تنقض سنة كاملة من الأولى
وإن أطلق فوجهان على حسب الاحتمالين
فلو أبانها ثم جدد النكاح في وسط الثانية وقلنا بعود الحنث طلقت كما
نكحها وإن كان أول السنة قد ما فات لأن جميع السنة وقت وإنما عجلنا في أول
السنة عند دوام النكاح لمصادفة الوقت
الثانية لو قال أنت طالق ثلاثا في كل يوم طلقة طلقت طلقة في الحال ووقعت
الثانية صبيحة اليوم الثاني فلو قال لو أردت أن يتخلل بين كل طلاقين يوم
كامل فيدين باطنا وهل يقبل ظاهرا فيه وجهان وهذا يخالف السنة لأن اليوم
مقدر محصور لا يوجب الحساب تداخله كما يوجب تداخل السنين

- Root: ع-ل-ق (ʿalāqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hang, suspend, attach; a thing suspended from another, implying dependence and connection.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal term for making an effect contingent upon a future condition (taʿlīq), where the occurrence of the condition triggers the effect.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in physical suspension; metaphorical (majāz) in legal causation, where the condition is the "rope" (ḥabl) that pulls the effect into existence.
- Root: و-ق-ت (waqata)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A time, period, or appointed moment; the measure of duration.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal discourse, a defined temporal boundary (waqt) that may be expansive (muwassaʿ) or constrained (muḍayyaq), affecting the moment of obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a fixed point; metaphorical for a span whose "ends" (ṭarafān) are conceptually distinguished, as in "first" (awwal) and "last" (ākhir).
- Root: س-ل-خ (salakha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To skin, flay, or strip off; the act of removing a covering, hence the "peeling away" of a month's days.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Used for the terminal phase of a time period, where the month "sheds" its remaining days.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for animal skinning; metaphorical for the end of a month, where the final part is "stripped" from the whole.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ẓarf (Apposition of the Adverbial) — When a time-adverb (ẓarf) like "in" (fī) governs a noun, its scope is determined by the intended semantic range, and ambiguity arises when the noun (e.g., "month") has divisible parts, requiring juristic specification of the precise moment.
chapters.translation:
I say: These are four types.

**The First Type: Suspension upon the Arrival of an Expected Time**

The formula of suspension is "if" (in) and its equivalent "when" (idhā). Thus, there is no difference between one saying, "If the sun rises," or "When the sun rises," or "If you enter the house," or "When you enter the house" — all of these are suspensions. Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) held that if one suspends upon something whose occurrence is certain, like the rising of the sun, it takes effect immediately — but this is weak.

We say: If he says, "You are divorced at the beginning of Ramadan," she is divorced with the sighting of the crescent, conjoined with its first part. We do not say that "in" (fī) here is a container (ẓarf) that necessitates a time enclosed between two times of Ramadan; rather, it does not indicate an overlapping application. If he says, "You are divorced in Ramadan," it is the same. If he says, "You are divorced on Saturday," she is divorced with the dawn. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) held that it occurs at the end of the day and the end of the month, with attention to the fact that an obligation suspended upon an expansive time is established at its end.

If he says, "You are divorced at the end of Ramadan," she is divorced in its last part. There is another view: she is divorced in the first part of the night of the sixteenth, because the entire latter half is the "end" of the month. If he says, "You are divorced at the beginning of the end of the month," she is divorced on the first day of the last [half] according to one view, and in the first part of the latter half according to another. If he says, "At the end of the beginning of this month," there are three views: one, that it is the end of the first half; two, that it is the end of the first night; three, that it is the end of the first day.

If he says, "At the sloughing (salkh) of the month," there are three views: one, that it is the last part of the month, for with it the month is "sloughed"; two, that it is the first of the last day; three, that it is the first part of the month, because from it the month begins to "slough" — and this is flimsy. If he says, "At the sloughing-off (insilākh) of the month," it does not apply except to the last part of the month.

**The Second Type: Suspension upon the Passage of Times**

If he says, "When a day has passed, you are divorced," and he is in the night, it occurs with sunset of the following day. If he is in the daytime, then [it occurs] when the daytime returns to the like of his time. If he says, "When the year has passed," she is divorced with the first sighting of Muḥarram, even if only a day remained. If he says, "When a year has passed," then twelve months from the time of the oath are necessary, and the Arabic months suffice. However, the month in which he is — if he is in its middle — is completed as thirty days from the end of the year. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: If one month is broken, all months are broken, because continuity is required.

**The Third Type: Suspension upon Past Time**

If he says, "You are divorced yesterday," intending now to effect a divorce yesterday, we say: This is impossible, because the ruling of an utterance cannot precede the utterance itself. Does it occur immediately? There are two views. One: Yes, because if the ruling of his utterance were realized, it would encompass the present time, so it executes to the extent possible. The second — which is the more analogical (aqyas) — is that this is idle speech (laghw), and nothing occurs by it.

If he says, "I have now effected a divorce whose ruling spreads back to yesterday," it is impossible. The second view — which is the choice of al-Rabīʿ — is that it does not occur, because he has effected something described by an impossible attribute, and what he described as impossible does not occur at all. The crux of the dispute reverts to: when one describes divorce with an attribute that renders it impossible, is the divorce itself nullified, or the attribute? Al-Rabīʿ argued with his saying, "You are divorced if you revive the dead or ascend to the sky" — for it does not occur. The companions (aṣḥāb) differed on this in three views: Some agreed with him; some said it occurs in the case of ascending and reviving, likening it to his saying, "You are divorced with a divorce that does not fall upon you"; and some distinguished between reviving and ascending, saying reviving is impossible from a creature, so it is like his saying, "A divorce that does not fall upon you," whereas ascending is possible in itself.

The correct view is that these suspensions are valid, and the intent is repulsion (ibʿād), as in His saying {«until the camel passes through the eye of the needle»} (Q 7:40). As for his saying, "A divorce that does not fall upon you," it is self-contradictory. His saying, "A divorce whose ruling reverses upon the past," is not self-contradictory, but it contravenes the ruling of the Sacred Law, so hesitation (taraddud) arises in it — and there is no harm in what al-Rabīʿ mentioned regarding it.

If he says, "When so-and-so dies, you are divorced a month before it," it is valid. If he dies before the month passes, the divorce does not occur, because it would lead to preceding the utterance. If he dies after a month, it becomes evident that the divorce occurred a month before him. Likewise, if he says, "Before the arrival of Zayd," or "Before entering the house, by a month." Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The divorce is retroactive (mustanid) in death but not in arrival or entry — and this is arbitrary (taḥakkum).

If he says, "You are divorced yesterday-tomorrow," or "Tomorrow-yesterday," it occurs immediately, because today is yesterday's tomorrow and tomorrow's yesterday. If he says, "You are divorced in the past year," without specification, the apparent ruling is divorce, because its apparent meaning is an acknowledgment of the occurrence of divorce. If he says, "I meant another husband divorced you," or "I divorced you in another marriage, then I renewed [the contract]," then if he produces evidence, it is accepted; otherwise, divorce is ruled in the present time. If he says, "I meant a revocable divorce," it is accepted, because it is a confirmation of divorce in this marriage.

**The Fourth Type: Suspension upon the Repetition of Times**

There are two issues here. First: If he says, "You are divorced three times, one divorce each year," she is divorced once immediately, once at the beginning of Muḥarram of the second year if he intended the Arabic years, and the third at the beginning of Muḥarram of the third year if the waiting period (ʿiddah) remains. If he did not intend the Arabic year, the second does not occur until a full year has elapsed from the first. If he leaves it unspecified, there are two views corresponding to the two probabilities.

If he irrevocably divorced her, then renewed the marriage in the middle of the second year, and we hold that the oath is re-triggered (ʿawd al-ḥinth), she is divorced upon his marrying her — even if the beginning of the year has passed, because the entire year is a time, and we only accelerated [the divorce] at the year's beginning during the continuance of marriage due to the coincidence of the time.

Second: If he says, "You are divorced three times, one divorce each day," she is divorced once immediately, and the second occurs on the morning of the second day. If he says, "I intended that a full day intervene between each two divorces," he is believed inwardly (bāṭinan). Whether he is accepted outwardly (ẓāhir) has two views. This differs from the year [case], because the day is a fixed, bounded measure that does not necessitate the calculation of overlap as the overlap of years necessitates.

### | الفصل الثاني في التعليق بالتطليق ونفيه

وفيه ثلاثة صيغ
الأولى أن يقول إن طلقتك فأنت طالق فإذا قال ذلك بعد الدخول فمهما طلقها
واحدة طلقت طلقة أخرى بالتعليق ولا يختص ذلك بالمجلس كقوله متى ما ومهما
وإذا فكل ذلك لا يقتضي فورا إلا إذا علق على مشيئتها أو بإعطائها مالا
فيختص بالمجلس لاقتضاء القرينة لا للفظ
وأما قبل الدخول فلا تقع الطلقة المعلقة لأنها بانت بالأولى ولذلك نص
الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه لو خالعها لم يقع الطلاق المعلق لأنها بانت
بالخلع فلا يلحقها طلاق
وقد ظن أكثر الأصحاب أن هذا يدل على أن الجزاء يترتب على الشرط ويقع بعده
لأنه لوقع معه لوقع قبل الدخول ويكون كما لوقال أنت طالق طلقتين ويشهد لهذا
أيضا أنه لو قال لغانم مهما أعتقتك فسالم حر ثم أعتق غانما في المرض والثلث
لا يفي بهما لم يعتق من سالم شيء بخلاف ما  لو أعتقهما جميعا فإنه يقرع
بينهما والصحيح أن الجزاء مع الشرط لأن الشرط جعل علة بالوضع فهو كالعلة
الحقيقية والمعلول مع العلة وإن كان بينهما ترتيب عقلي في السببية بل هو
كحركة الخاتم فإنه مع حركة اليد وإن كان معلولا له وإنما لم يقع قبل الدخول
لأن مقتضاه وقوع الطلاق مع أول حال البينونة وأول حال البينونة يضاد الطلاق
كما في حال البينونة وكذلك لو قال لها أنت طالق طلقة معها طلقة لم يقع إلا
واحدة على أدق الوجهين بخلاف ما لو قال أنت طالق طلقتين لأن البينونة معلول
مجموع الطلقتين وقوله طلقتين كالتفسير لقوله طالق وكذا لا يعتق سالم لأن
عتقه معلول عتق غانم وربما خرجت القرعة على سالم فيعتق دون عتق غانم فيكون
المعلول قد ثبت دون العلة وذلك محال وهذا كلام دقيق عقلي ربما يقصر نظر
الفقيه عنه
النظر الثاني في هذه المسألة أن التعليق هل يكون تطليقا فإذا قال إن
طلقتك فأنت طالق ثم قال إن دخلت الدار فأنت طالق فدخلت وقعت طلقة بيمين
الدخول وأخرى بيمين التعليق لأن التعليق مع الصفة تطليق نعم مجرد التعليق
ليس بتطليق وكذلك لو تقدم التعليق ولم يوجد بعد يمينه إلا مجرد الصفة لم
يكن تطليقا إلا إذا قال إذا وقع عليك طلاقي فأنت طالق وكأن التعليق بالدخول
مقدم على هذا التعليق فإنه إذا وقع بمجرد الصفة وقعت طلقة أخرى لأنه وقوع
وليس بإيقاع وعن العراقيين وجه أن التعليق مع الصفة ليس أيضا بتطليق وهو
بعيد لأن سيما فيما إذا علق بفعل نفسه وأتى بالفعل
chapters.anchors:
- Root: عَلِقَ (ʿaliqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hang, cling, or adhere; suspension of one thing upon another as its condition.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal suspension (taʿlīq) where an effect is made contingent upon a future condition, akin to causal dependency in theology.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal clinging (ḥaqīqah) versus juristic metaphor (majāz) of attaching a ruling to a conditional clause.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Protasis-Apodosis (sharṭ-jazāʾ) — The apodosis is grammatically and semantically ordered after the protasis, yet its ontological realization is simultaneous with the condition's fulfillment, not subsequent to it.
chapters.translation:
I say: This chapter contains three formulations.

**The First Formulation**: That he says, "If I divorce you, then you are divorced." When he says this after consummation, then whenever he divorces her once, another divorce occurs by virtue of the suspension; and this is not restricted to the session [of utterance] — just like his saying "whenever (matā mā)" and "at whatever time (mahmā)" and "if (idhā)." All of this does not necessitate immediacy, except when he suspends it upon her will or upon giving her wealth — then it is restricted to the session, due to the contextual indication (qarīnah), not due to the wording itself.

As for before consummation, the suspended divorce does not occur, because she has already become irrevocably separated (bāʾin) by the first [divorce]. For this reason, al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — explicitly ruled that if he had effected a khulʿ (divorce by redemption) with her, the suspended divorce would not occur, because she became irrevocably separated by the khulʿ, and no divorce can attach to her thereafter.

Most of our companions (al-aṣḥāb) have supposed that this indicates the apodosis (jazāʾ) is ordered upon the condition and occurs after it — because if it occurred simultaneously with it, it would occur before consummation, and it would be as if he said, "You are divorced twice." This is also supported by the case where he says to Ghānim: "Whenever I emancipate you, then Sālim is free," then he emancipates Ghānim during his terminal illness, and the third [of the estate] does not suffice for both — then nothing of Sālim is emancipated, unlike the case where he emancipates both together, for then lots are cast between them.

The correct [position] is that the apodosis is simultaneous with the condition, because the condition is made a cause (ʿillah) by convention (al-waḍʿ), so it is like a true cause, and the effect (maʿlūl) is with the cause — even though there is a rational ordering between them in causality. Rather, it is like the movement of the ring: it is with the movement of the hand, even though it is an effect of it. It merely did not occur before consummation because its requirement is the occurrence of divorce at the first moment of irrevocable separation (al-baynūnah), and the first moment of irrevocable separation contradicts divorce — just as in the state of irrevocable separation itself.

Likewise, if he said to her, "You are divorced with a divorce accompanying it," only one divorce occurs, according to the more precise of the two views — unlike his saying, "You are divorced twice," because irrevocable separation is the effect of the total of the two divorces, and his saying "twice" is like an interpretation of his saying "divorced." Similarly, Sālim is not emancipated, because his emancipation is the effect of Ghānim's emancipation; and perhaps the lot might fall upon Sālim, so he would be emancipated without Ghānim's emancipation — then the effect would be established without its cause, which is impossible. This is subtle rational discourse (kalām daqīq ʿaqlī) from which the jurist's vision might fall short.

**The Second Consideration** in this matter: Is the suspension itself a divorce? If he says, "If I divorce you, then you are divorced," then says, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced," and she enters — one divorce occurs by the oath of entry, and another by the oath of suspension, because the suspension with the attribute is a divorce. Yes, mere suspension is not a divorce. Likewise, if the suspension preceded and thereafter nothing of his oath occurred except the mere attribute, it would not be a divorce — except if he said, "When my divorce falls upon you, then you are divorced," as if the suspension by entry is advanced over this suspension; for when it occurs by the mere attribute, another divorce occurs, because it is an occurrence (wuqūʿ), not an effectuation (īqāʿ). And from the Iraqis there is a view that the suspension with the attribute is also not a divorce — but this is remote, especially in the case where he suspends it upon his own act and then performs the act.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرعان

الأول إذا قال إن طلقتك عمره فحفصة طالق ثم قال إن طلقتك حفصة فعمرة طالق
ثم بدأ بحفصة فطلقها طلقت حفصة بالتنجيز طلقة وطلقة عمرة بالتعليق طلقة
وعادت طلقة إلى حفصة من طلاق عمرة لأنه تعليق طلاق عمرة تراخى عن تعليق
طلاق حفصة فكان تطليقا لها وقد علق طلاق حفصة على تعليقها
ولا بدأ بعمرة فطلقها فيرجع الطلاق على حفصة ولم يرجع طلاق إلى  عمرة لأن
تعليق طلاق حفصة سبق تعليق طلاق عمرة فكان بالنسبة إلى تعليق طلاق عمرة
وقوعا محضا لا إيقاعا نعم لو أبدل لفظ الإيقاع بالوقوع وقع على المطلقة
طلقة تنجيزا وطلقة أخرى تعليقا ولم يقع على الأخرى إلا طلقة واحدة لأنه إن
حل اليمين لأن حرف إن ومهما لا يقتضي التقرار بخلاف كلما فينحل بوجود الصفة
مرة واحدة
الفرع الثاني إذا قال وله نسوة وعبيد إذا طلقت واحدة فعبد من عبيدي حر
وإذا طلقت اثنتين فعبدان حران وإذا طلقت ثلاثا فثلاثة وإذا طلقت أربعا
فأربعة ثم
طلق أربعة نسوة عتق عشرة أعبد لأنه حنث في الإيمان الأربعة لأن في
الأربعة أربعة وثلاثة واثنتين وواحدة وذلك عشرة
ولو أبدل إذا بكلما عتق خمسة عشر فيعتق بيمين الواحد أربعة لأن فيها
أربعة آحاد وبيمين الاثنين أربعة لأن فيها اثنين مرتين وبيمين الثلاثة
ثلاثة وبيمين الأربع أربعة وذلك خمسة عشر وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يعتق
ستة عشر لأنه حسب الثلاثة مرة فبقي الواحد فحسبه في يمين الواحد مرة أخرى
وهو خطأ لأنه قد حسب مرة في يمين الآحاد ومن الأصحاب من ذلك يعتق سبعة عشر
وإنما زاد اثنين بيمين الاثنين لأنه زعم أنه في الأربعة اثنين ثلاث مرات
لأنه حسب الثاني والثالث مرة وهذا خطأ لأنه لو جاز هذا لجاز أن يصير ثلاثة
أيضا مرتين فإن الثاني والثالث والرابع ثلاثة أخر سوى الأول والثاني
والثالث ولا قائل بهذا
الصيغة الثانية التعليق بنفي التطليق فإذا قال إن لم أطلقك فأنت طالق لم
تطلق في الحال وكذلك إذا قال إن لم أضربك فإنه يتوقع ذلك في الاستقبال ولا
يقتضي الفور ولو قال إذا لم أطلقك ومضى زمان يسير يسع التطليق ولم يطلق وقع
الطلاق لأن إذا ظرف زمان ومعناه أي وقت أطلقك فيه فأنت طالق
وقوله متى ومتى ما كقوله إذا في اقتضاء الفور وفي الأصحاب من لم يتضح له
الفرق فجعل المسألتين على قولين وهذا ضعيف إذ الفرق ظاهر نعم لو قال أردت
بإذا ما يريده المريد بقوله إن يدين وهل يقبل ظاهرا فيه وجهان
التفريع إذا قلنا لا يقع في صيغة إن على الفور فإنما يقع عند حصول اليأس
بخلو العمر عن الضرب والتطليق ولليأس ثلاث صور
إحداها موت أحد الزوجين فإذا مات قبل الطلاق والضرب تبينا وقوع الطلاق
قبيل الموت وكان يحتمل أن نتبين وقوعه عند اللفظ ولكن اللفظ مطلق يحتمل
الأمرين وتنزيله على إخلاء العمر محتمل والأصل نفي الطلاق من غير يقين ما
يوقعه وإنما يتحقق عدم الضرب لانقضاء العمر ففيه يقع
الصورة الثانية طرآن الجنون على الزوج وذلك لا يوجب اليأس لأنه ربما يفيق
فإن اتصل بالموت تبينا وقوع الطلاق قبيل الجنون وإن كان يمكن أن يوقع قبل
الموت إذ به يتحقق اليأس ولكن قبل الجنون يثبت اليأس إلا بانتظار الإفاقة
فإذا لم تقع الإفاقة فالجنون كالموت في اليأس وهذا في الطلاق أما في الضرب
فلا يأس لأن ضرب المجنون في تحقيق الصفة ونفيها كضرب العاقل على الصحيح
الصورة الثالثة انفساخ النكاح وذلك لا يوجب اليأس لأنه ربما ينكحها
فيطلقها ولا يشترط النكاح الأول لتحقيق الصفة فإن نكحها وطلقها فقد تحققت
الصفة وإن لم يطلقها وكانت في نكاحه عند الموت وقلنا بعود الحنث وقع الطلاق
قبيل الموت وإن لم نقل بعود الحنث أو لم تكن في نكاحه تبينا وقوع الطلاق
قبيل الفسخ ولتفرض في الطلاق الرجعي حتى لا نقع في الدور ونتصور الجمع بينه
وبين الفسخ
الصيغة الثالثة أن يقول أن طلقتك فأنت طالق وأن لم أطلقك فأنت طالق وقع
في الحال لأن أن للتعليل معناه أنت اطلقك لأن لم أطلق ويجوز في اللغة
الفصيحة حذف اللام واستعمال أن فهو إذا كقوله أنت طالق لرضا فلان فإنه يقع
في الحال ولو سخط وهذا في حق من يعرف اللغة ومن لا يعرف اللغة فلا فرق في
حقه بين إن وأن
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ل-ق (ʿ-l-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hang, suspend, attach; a thing suspended from another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Suspension of an effect upon a condition — the effect is "hung" upon the occurrence of the condition, not executed immediately.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical hanging; metaphorical (majāz) for legal suspension of an act upon a future contingency.
- Root: ح-ن-ث (ḥ-n-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To break an oath, to violate a vow.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The occurrence of the condition that triggers the penal consequence of a suspended oath.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for breaking a sworn oath; technical in jurisprudence for the realization of the suspended matter.
- Root: ي-أ-س (y-ʾ-s)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Despair, loss of hope.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal contexts, the point at which fulfillment of a condition becomes impossible (e.g., death, insanity, dissolution of marriage).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for emotional despair; metaphorical for legal impossibility of condition fulfillment.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿlīq al-Ḥukm ʿalā al-Sharṭ (Suspension of a ruling upon a condition) — The conditional particle (in, idhā, kullamā) governs the temporal and logical sequence of the suspended effect; the order of multiple conditions determines which effect is "pure occurrence" (wuqūʿ) versus "active execution" (īqāʿ).
chapters.translation:
### Two Subsidiary Branches

**The First Branch:** If a man says: "If I divorce you, ʿAmrah, then Ḥafṣah is divorced," then says: "If I divorce you, Ḥafṣah, then ʿAmrah is divorced," then he begins with Ḥafṣah and divorces her — then Ḥafṣah is divorced by immediate execution (tanjīz) one divorce, and ʿAmrah is divorced by suspension (taʿlīq) one divorce. And one divorce reverts upon Ḥafṣah from the divorce of ʿAmrah, because the suspension of ʿAmrah's divorce was delayed after the suspension of Ḥafṣah's divorce, so it was a divorce upon her (Ḥafṣah) — and the divorce of Ḥafṣah had been suspended upon her (ʿAmrah's) suspension. But if he begins with ʿAmrah and divorces her, then the divorce reverts upon Ḥafṣah, and no divorce reverts upon ʿAmrah, because the suspension of Ḥafṣah's divorce preceded the suspension of ʿAmrah's divorce. Thus, relative to the suspension of ʿAmrah's divorce, it was pure occurrence (wuqūʿ), not active execution (īqāʿ). Yes — if he substitutes the wording of "occurrence" (wuqūʿ) for "execution" (īqāʿ), then upon the divorced woman falls one divorce by immediate execution and another by suspension, and upon the other woman falls only one divorce, because the oath is dissolved — for the particle "in" and "mahmā" do not require repetition, unlike "kullamā" — so it dissolves by the existence of the attribute once.

**The Second Branch:** If a man says — while he has wives and slaves — "If I divorce one wife, then one of my slaves is free; if I divorce two, then two slaves are free; if I divorce three, then three; if I divorce four, then four," then he divorces four wives — ten slaves are freed, because he violated (ḥanitha) all four oaths, since in four there are four, three, two, and one — and that totals ten. But if he substitutes "kullamā" for "idhā," fifteen are freed: by the oath of one, four are freed (because in it there are four units); by the oath of two, four are freed (because in it there are two, twice); by the oath of three, three; by the oath of four, four — and that totals fifteen. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: sixteen are freed, because he counted the three once, then the one remained, so he counted it in the oath of one a second time. But this is an error, because it was already counted once in the oath of the units. And among our companions (al-aṣḥāb) is one who said seventeen are freed — he added two by the oath of two, claiming that in four there are two, three times, because he counted the second and third once. But this too is an error, because if this were permissible, then three could also become two times — for the second, third, and fourth are another three besides the first, second, and third — and no one holds this view.

**The Second Formulation:** Suspension by negation of divorce. If he says: "If I do not divorce you, then you are divorced," she is not divorced immediately. Likewise, if he says: "If I do not strike you," — for this is anticipated in the future and does not require immediacy (fawr). But if he says: "When (idhā) I do not divorce you," and a short time passes sufficient for divorce, and he does not divorce — then divorce occurs, because "idhā" is a particle of time, and its meaning is: "Any time I do not divorce you, you are divorced." And his saying "matā" and "matā mā" is like his saying "idhā" in requiring immediacy. Among our companions is one for whom the difference was not clear, so he made the two cases subject to two opinions — but this is weak, for the difference is manifest. Yes — if he says: "I intended by 'idhā' what one intends by 'in'," then whether he is believed outwardly — there are two views.

**The Ramification:** If we say that with the formulation "in" divorce does not occur immediately, then it occurs only upon the attainment of despair (al-yaʾs) — by the emptying of one's lifetime of striking or divorce. And despair has three forms:

**The First Form:** The death of one of the spouses. If one dies before divorce or striking, we ascertain that divorce occurred just before death. It would have been possible to ascertain its occurrence at the moment of utterance, but the utterance is absolute and admits both possibilities, and its interpretation upon the emptying of the lifetime is plausible. The default principle is the negation of divorce absent certainty of what would effect it — and the non-occurrence of striking is only verified by the expiration of the lifetime, so at that point it occurs.

**The Second Form:** The onset of insanity upon the husband. This does not necessitate despair, for perhaps he will recover. If it connects with death, we ascertain that divorce occurred just before the insanity — even though he could have effected it before death, for by death despair is verified. But before insanity, despair is not established except by awaiting recovery. So if recovery does not occur, insanity is like death in despair. This applies to divorce. As for striking, there is no despair, because the striking of an insane man in verifying or negating the attribute is like the striking of a sane man, according to the correct view.

**The Third Form:** The dissolution of the marriage (infisākh). This does not necessitate despair, for perhaps he will marry her again and divorce her — and the first marriage is not a condition for verifying the attribute. If he marries her and divorces her, the attribute is verified. If he does not divorce her, and she was in his marriage at death, and we hold the return of the violation (ʿawd al-ḥinth) — then divorce occurs just before death. If we do not hold the return of the violation, or she was not in his marriage, then we ascertain that divorce occurred just before the dissolution. Let this be posited in the case of revocable divorce (al-ṭalāq al-rijʿī), so that we do not fall into circularity (al-dawr) and can conceive of combining it with dissolution.

**The Third Formulation:** That he says: "Because (an) I divorce you, you are divorced, and because I do not divorce you, you are divorced" — then divorce occurs immediately, because "an" is for causation (al-taʿlīl), meaning: "You are divorced because I did not divorce you." And in eloquent Arabic, it is permissible to omit the lām and use "an" — so it is like his saying: "You are divorced for the pleasure of so-and-so," which occurs immediately even if he is displeased. This applies to one who knows the language. As for one who does not know the language, there is no difference for him between "in" and "an."

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثالث في التعليق بالحمل والولادة

وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا قال لها إن كنت حاملا فأنت طالق فلا يقع في  الحال لأن الحمل
لا يعلم بيقين فلو أتت بولد لأقل من ستة أشهر تبينا الوقوع عند اليمين وإن
كان لأكثر من أربع سنين تبينا أنه لم يقع وإن كان بين المدتين فإن كان
يطؤها فلا يقع وإن امتنع عنها فقولان
أحدهما يقع لأن النسب قد ثبت فيدل على وجود الحمل
والثاني لا لأن لحوق النسب يكفي فيه الاحتمال ولا يقع الطلاق بالاحتمال
واختلفوا في أنه هل يحرم الوطء قبل تحقق الحال فقيل أنه لا يحرم بالشك
كمسألة الغراب وقيل إنه يحرم لأن استكشافه ممكن على قرب وعلى هذا يجب
الاستبراء بالحيض ويتفرع عنه ثلاثة فروع
أحدها أنه هل يكتفي في الحرة بقرء واحد فيه وجهان
أحدهما لا كالعدة
والثاني نعم لأن الغرض مجرد استدلال وقد حصل
الثاني إذا استبرئها ثم وقال مرة أخرى قبل الوطء إن كنت حاملا فأنت طالق
فالظاهر أنه لا يجب إعادة الاستبراء وقيل إنه يجب لأن العدة الماضية لا
تؤثر فكذلك هذا
الثالث إذا خاطب بذلك صغيرة وهي في سن الحيض فيستبرئها بشهر أو أشهر وإن
خاطب آيسة فهل يكفي سن اليأس دلالة أو لا بد من الاستبراء فيه وجهان
المسألة الثانية إذا قال إن كنت حائلا فأنت طالق فهذه كتلك المسألة ولكن
حيث يحكم ثم بالوقوع فهاهنا يحكم بخلافه لأن الشرط هو عدم الحمل ويزيد
هاهنا أن تحريم الوطء هاهنا أقرب لأن الأصل الحيال وأيضا أثر الاستبراء ثم
في نفي الطلاق وهاهنا في الوقوع وقد قطعوا بأنه إذا انقضى ثلاثة أقراء يقع
الطلاق وفيه نظر لأنه لا يفيد يقين البراءة والشرط لا بد من استيفائة فإنه
لو علق على الاستيقان لم يقع بالاستبراء والمطلق يقتضي الحمل على اليقين
وقد مال إليه الشيخ أبو محمد ثم قال الأصحاب إذا أوقعنا بعد الإقراء فأتت
بولد لدون ستة أشهر تبينا أنه لم يكن الطلاق واقعا ونقضنا ذلك الحكم قطعا
وإن كان وطئها وطئا يمكن الإحالة عليه ففيه نقض ذلك الحكم وجهان
المسألة الثالثة في صيغ التعليق بالحمل فإذا  قال فقال إن كنت حاملا بذكر
فأنت طالق طلقة وإن كنا حاملا بأنثى فأنت طالق طلقتين فأتت بذكرين وقعت
طلقة واحدة ولم نزد
وإن أتت بذكر وأنثى وقعت ثلاث لأنه حنث باليمين وإن قال إن كان حملك ذكرا
فطلقه وإن كان أنثى فطلقتين لم يقع شيء أصلا فإن لفظه يقتضي حصر الجنس ولو
أتت بذكرين قال القاضي تقع طلقة لأن التنكير في لفظه لتنكير الجنس وقال
الشيخ أبو محمد لا يقع شيء لأنه لتنكير الواحد فلا يسمى ذلك ذكرا
المسألة الرابعة إذا قال إن ولدت ولدا فأنت طالق فأتت بولدين طلقت بالأول
وانقضت عدتها بالثاني فإن قال كلما ولدت ولدا فأنت طالق فهل يقع الطلاق
بالولد الثاني وبه تنقضي العدة الجديد أنه لا يقع لأنه يصادق أول وقت
البينونة وللشافعي رضي الله عنه نص في الإملاء أنه يلحق الثانية وليس له
وجه وتكلف القفال توجيهه فقال لو قال للرجعية أنت طالق مع انقضاء العدة
فيتجه قولان وزعم أنه يحتمل أن يقع مع الانقضاء لا في العدة ولا في
البينونة وشبه ذلك بما لو قال أنت طالق بين الليل والنهار فلا يقع في الليل
ولا في النهار بل يقع في الآن الفاصل بينهما والطلاق من جملة ما يقع دفعه
في الآن ولا يقع في زمان وهذا له وجه في التحقيق إذ فرق بين الآن وبين
الزمان الذي ينقسم ولكن في مسألة الولادة غير منقدح لأن مقتدى اللفظ أن يقع
مع الولادة والولادة تقارنها البينونة والبينونة تضاد الطلاق فالصحيح هو
القول الجديد
ولو قال إن ولدت ولدا فأنت طالق واحدة وإن ولدت ذكرا فاثنتين فولدت غلاما
طلقت ثلاثا لوجود الصفتين ولو قال إن ولدت أنثى فواحدة وإن ولدت ذكرا
فاثنتين فولدت خنثى لم يقع في الحال إلا واحدة لأنه المستيقن
فرع إذا قال وله أربعة نسوة حوامل كلما ولدت واحدة فصويحباتها طوالق
فولدن على التعاقب والتقارب طلقن جميعا أما الرابعة فثلاث إذ ولدت قبلها
ثلاث
نسوة وأما الثالثة فثنتان إذ ولد قبلها  اثنتان وانقضت عدتها بولادتها قبل
ولادة الرابعة أما الثانية فواحدة إذ طلقت بولادة الأولى وانقضت عدتها
بولادتها نفسها فلم يلحقها طلاق بعده وأما الأولى فثلاث طلقات لأنها بقيت
في العدة حتى ولدن جميع صواحباتها بعدها
