وهي مترددة بين المنكوحة والبائنة لأن الطلاق أوجب خللا في الملك ولم
يوجب زواله فلاختلاله قلنا إنه يحرم وطؤها وقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه يلزما
المهر بالوطء راجعها أو لم يراجعها ونص في المرتدة إذا وطئها ثم عادت إلى
الإسلام أنه لا مهر
فقيل قولان بالنقل والتخريج والفرق مشكل وغايته أن الرجعة في حكم ابتداء
أو استدراك وعودها إلى الإسلام يعيد الحل السابق وليس في حكم الابتداء
والصحيح أنه لا يجب الحد وإن وجب المهر لأن الملك بالكلية لم يزل وشبب
بعض الأصحاب بخلاف في وعلى الجملة يحرم الوطء وقطع الشافعي رضي الله عنه
بوجوب المهر يدل على اختلال أصل الملك إن لم يدل على زواله ويدل على بقاء
أصل الملك صحة الطلاق وصحة الخلع والظهار والإيلاء واللعان وجريان الميراث
ولزوم النفقة وفي الخلع قول قديم أنه لا يصح
ولو قال زوجاتي طوالق اندرجت الرجعية تحته وطلقت على الأصح لأنها زوجه في
خمس آي من كتاب الله تعالى هذا لفظ الشافعي رضي الله عنه وأراد به آياة
الإيلاء والظهار وغيرهما
ولا خلاف في لو أنه اشترى زوجته الرجعية لزمه الاستبراء لأنها كانت محرمة
وإن استبرئها في صلب النكاح فلا استبراء على الأظهر وقيل إنه يجب لتبدل جهة
الحل وقد قال بعض الأصحاب تردد قول الشافعي رضي الله عنه في الخلع يدل على
اختلاف قول الشافعي رضي الله عنه في أن الملك  زائل أم لا وقول بعض الأصحاب
إنه إن راجع بعد الوطء فلا مهر وإن لم يراجع يجب المهر يدل على أن الملك
موقوف فتحصل في زوال الملك ثلاثة أقوال
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في النزاع - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
وله صور خمس
الأولى أن يتفقا على انقضاء العدة يوم الجمعة لكن الزوج قال راجعت يوم
الخميس وقالت بل يوم السبت ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها وهو الذي ذكره المراوزة من عند آخرهم وهو القياس أن القول قولها
لأنهما إذا اتفقا على الطلاق وانقضاء العدة فالأصل انقطاع النكاح والزوج
يريد دفعه بدعوى الرجعة فعليه الإثبات
والوجه الثاني ذكره العراقيون أن القول قوله لأن الأصل بقاء النكاح
والرجعة إلى الزوج وليس لها قول إلا في انقضاء صورة الأقراء والزوج ينكر
بقاء العدة بعد يوم الخميس إذ الرجعة تقطع العدة ويحققه أن الزوج لو ادعى
الوطء في مدة العنة يصدق مع أن الأصل عدمه لتقرير النكاح فهذا أولى
والثالث ذكره صاحب التقريب أن المصدق هو السابق إلى الدعوى فإذا سبقت
بدعوى الإنقضاء الانقضاء فقد حكم الشرع بقولها بالتحريم فلا يرتفع بدعواه
من غير بينة وكذلك إذا سبق الزوج فعلى هذا إن تساوقا رجع الوجهين لأنه زال
المرجح له
الصورة الثانية ألا يقع التعرض لوقت العدة والرجعة ولكن اتفقا على جريان
الأمرين واختلفا في التقدم ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه المصدق لأن الأصل بقاء النكاح
والثاني أنها المصدقة لأنها مؤتمنة على ما في رحمها عاجزة عن الإشهاد
والزوج على قادر على الإشهاد على الرجعة
الصورة الثالثة أن يقع الوفاق على أن الرجعة جرت يوم الجمعة ولكن قالت
كانت العدة قد انقضت يوم الخميس وقال الزوج بل يوم السبت فهذا كصورة الأولى
فترجع الوجوه الثلاثة
الصورة الرابعة أن يقع الوفاق من وقت انقضاء العدة ويدعى الزوج رجعة
قبلها وأنكرت أصل الرجعة قال صاحب التقريب هي المصدقة بلا خلاف والأظهر
جريان الأوجه إذ لم تفارق هذه الصورة ما قبلها إلا أنها أنكرت لفظ الرجعة
وهناك إنما  أقرت بلفظ الرجعة لا بحقيقة الرجعة
الصورة الخامسة النزاع مع قيام العدة فإذا قال راجعتك أمس فأنكرت فالقول
قوله لأنه قادر على الإنشاء فيقبل قوله كقول الوكيل قبل العزل وقيل الأصل
عدم الرجعة فالقول قولها فإن أراد الإنشاء فلينشأ والصحيح أن إخباره لا
يجعل إنشاء وحكي عن القفال إنه إنشاء وهو بعيد لأن الشافعي رضي الله عنه
قال إن من أقر بالطلاق كاذبا لم يكن إن شاء
فرع إذا أنكرت الرجعة ثم أقرت قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه لم تمنع عنه فهو
كمن أقر بحق بعد الجحود وهذا فيه إشكال لأنها أقرت بالتحريم على نفسها ثم
رجعت
ولو أقرت بتحريم رضاع أو نسب لم تمكن من الرجوع ولكن الفرق أن الرجعة تصح
دونها
فلعلها أنكرت إذ لم تعرف ولا تقر بالرضاع والنسب وهو إثبات إلا على بصيرة
نعم من قال ما أتلف فلان مالي ثم رجع إلى الدعوى لم يمكن لأنه أقر على نفسه
وهاهنا جحدت حق الزوج فإذا توافقا لم يبطل حق الزوج ولو قالت ما رضيت في
النكاح ثم رجعت فهذا محتمل لأنها تحقق رضا نفسها ولذلك تحلف على البت
ولكنها جحدت حق الزوج فالأظهر أنه يغلب جانب الزوج وتمكن المرأة من الرجوع
= كتاب الإيلاء =
وفيه بابان
أحدهما في أركانه
والثاني في أحكامه
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في أركانه - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
وصورته أن يقول لزوجته والله لا أجامعك ولقد كان هذا طلاقا في الجاهلية
ثم غير الشرع حكمه وقضى بأن الزوج بعد مضي أربعة أشهر يجبر على الوطء أو
الطلاق
والإيلاء في اللغة مشتق من الألية وهي الحلف ولكن عرف الشرع خصصه باليمين
المعقود على الإمتناع من وطء المنكوحة
وأركانه أربعة الحالف والمحلوف به والمحلوف عليه والمدة المحلوف فيها
chapters.anchors:
- Root: خ-ل-ل (kh-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to pierce, perforate, or make porous"; a state of looseness or disorder in a structure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, denotes a defect or impairment that compromises the integrity of a right or contract without annihilating its essence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally here for the "loosening" of marital ownership (milk), not metaphorically; the impairment is real but partial.
- Root: ر-ج-ع (r-j-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To return, revert, or restore something to its prior state.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for the husband's right to reinstate the marriage during the ʿiddah (waiting period) without a new contract.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in legal usage—an act of restoration, not a metaphorical "return."
- Root: م-ل-ك (m-l-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Possession, ownership, or dominion over something.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, the legal authority (milk) the husband holds over the wife, which is impaired but not destroyed by a revocable divorce.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for legal ownership; the debate is whether this ownership is fully intact, impaired, or suspended.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Conditional Dependency) — The syntactic structure "because the divorce necessitated a defect (khallan) in ownership but did not necessitate its removal" establishes a causal hierarchy where the predicate (impairment) is affirmed while the contrary (removal) is negated, requiring careful parsing of the particle "lam" (not yet) versus "lā" (absolute negation).
chapters.translation:
I say: She (the revocable divorcée) is oscillating between the status of a married woman (mankūḥah) and a separated one (bāʾinah), because the divorce necessitated a defect (khallan) in the ownership (milk) but did not necessitate its complete removal. Due to this impairment, we say that sexual intercourse with her is prohibited. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: The dowry (mahr) becomes obligatory by intercourse, whether he revokes (rājaʿa) or does not revoke. And he explicitly ruled in the case of an apostate (murtaddah) wife—if he had intercourse with her and then she returned to Islam—that there is no dowry.

So it was said there are two opinions (qawlān): one transmitted (naql) and one derived (takhrij). The distinction (farq) between the two cases is problematic, and its ultimate basis is that revocation (rajʿah) is in the category of a new beginning (ibtidāʾ) or a corrective completion (istidrāk), whereas her return to Islam restores the prior permissibility (ḥill) and is not in the category of a new beginning. The correct position (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that the ḥadd punishment (for unlawful intercourse) is not obligatory even if the dowry is obligatory, because the ownership was not entirely removed. Some of our companions (al-aṣḥāb) raised a dispute (khilāf) on this point.

In summary: Intercourse is prohibited. Al-Shāfiʿī's (may Allah be pleased with him) definitive ruling on the obligation of the dowry indicates an impairment of the root of ownership, if not its removal; and it indicates the persistence of the root of ownership through the validity of divorce, the validity of khulʿ (divorce by redemption), ẓihār (injurious comparison), īlāʾ (vow of abstinence), liʿān (mutual imprecation), the operation of inheritance, and the obligation of maintenance (nafaqah). Regarding khulʿ, there is an old opinion (qawl qadīm) that it is not valid.

If he said: "My wives are all divorced," the revocable divorcée is included therein and is divorced according to the most correct opinion (al-aṣaḥḥ), because she is his wife in five verses of the Book of Allah. This is the wording of al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him), and he meant the verses of īlāʾ, ẓihār, and others.

There is no disagreement that if he purchased his revocable divorcée, he must observe the waiting period of the womb (istibrāʾ), because she had been prohibited to him. And if he had already observed istibrāʾ during the marriage itself, then no istibrāʾ is required according to the most apparent opinion (al-aẓhar). It was said it is required due to the change in the basis of permissibility. Some of our companions said: The fluctuation (taraddud) in al-Shāfiʿī's (may Allah be pleased with him) opinion regarding khulʿ indicates a divergence in his rulings on whether the ownership is removed or not. And the statement of some companions—that if he revokes after intercourse there is no dowry, but if he does not revoke the dowry is obligatory—indicates that the ownership is suspended (mawqūf). Thus, three opinions emerge regarding the removal of ownership.

— Peace be upon him — The Second Chapter: On Disputes (al-Nizāʿ) — Peace be upon him —

This has five forms (ṣuwar).

The First Form: They agree that the ʿiddah expired on Friday, but the husband says: "I revoked on Thursday," while she says: "Rather, on Saturday." There are three aspects (awjuh) here:

One of them—which is what the Khurāsānians (al-Marāwizah) mentioned unanimously, and it is the analogical one (al-qiyās)—is that her word is accepted, because when they agree on the divorce and the expiry of the ʿiddah, the default principle (al-aṣl) is the severance of the marriage, and the husband seeks to repel this by claiming revocation, so the burden of proof is upon him.

The Second Aspect—mentioned by the Iraqis (al-ʿIrāqiyyūn)—is that his word is accepted, because the default principle is the persistence of the marriage, and revocation belongs to the husband; she has no say except regarding the expiry of the ʿiddah in cases of menstrual cycles (aqrāʾ), and the husband denies the persistence of the ʿiddah after Thursday, since revocation cuts off the ʿiddah. This is corroborated by the fact that if the husband claimed intercourse during the period of impotence (ʿinnah), he would be believed despite the default principle being its non-occurrence, for the sake of affirming the marriage—so this is even more apt.

The Third Aspect—mentioned by the author of al-Taqrīb—is that the one believed is the one who preceded with his claim. If she preceded with the claim of expiry, then the Law (sharʿ) has already ruled by her word regarding prohibition, so it cannot be lifted by his claim without evidence. Likewise, if the husband preceded. On this basis, if they are simultaneous, the two aspects revert, because the preponderating factor has been removed.

The Second Form: Neither the time of the ʿiddah nor of the revocation is specified, but they agree that both events occurred and differ only on which preceded. There are two aspects:

One: He is believed, because the default principle is the persistence of the marriage.

The Second: She is believed, because she is entrusted (muʾtamanah) regarding what is in her womb, being unable to produce witnesses, whereas the husband is able to produce witnesses for the revocation.

The Third Form: They agree that the revocation occurred on Friday, but she says: "The ʿiddah had already expired on Thursday," while the husband says: "Rather, on Saturday." This is like the first form, so the three aspects apply.

The Fourth Form: They agree on the time of the ʿiddah's expiry, and the husband claims a revocation before it, while she denies the occurrence of revocation altogether. The author of al-Taqrīb said: She is believed without disagreement. The more apparent view (al-aẓhar) is that the aspects apply, for this form does not differ from the preceding one except that here she denies the very utterance of revocation, whereas there she affirmed the utterance of revocation but not its legal reality.

The Fifth Form: The dispute occurs while the ʿiddah is still running. If he says: "I revoked you yesterday," and she denies it, then his word is accepted, because he is capable of initiating (inshāʾ) the revocation, so his statement is accepted like the statement of an agent (wakīl) before his dismissal. It was said: The default principle is the non-occurrence of revocation, so her word is accepted; if he wishes to initiate, let him initiate. The correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that his mere report (ikhbār) does not constitute an initiation. It was narrated from al-Qaffāl that it is an initiation, but this is remote, because al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Whoever falsely confesses to divorce does not thereby effect a divorce.

Branch (farʿ): If she denies the revocation and then affirms it, al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: She is not prevented from it—this is like one who affirms a right after having denied it. There is a problem here, because she affirmed a prohibition upon herself and then retracted. If she had affirmed the prohibition of fosterage (riḍāʿ) or lineage (nasab), she could not retract. But the difference is that revocation is valid without her, so perhaps she denied it because she did not know, whereas she does not affirm fosterage or lineage except with certain knowledge. Indeed, if someone says: "So-and-so did not destroy my property," and then retracts to claim it, he cannot do so, because he affirmed against himself. Here, she denied the husband's right, so when they agree, the husband's right is not nullified. If she says: "I did not consent in the marriage," and then retracts, this is plausible, because she has certain knowledge of her own consent, and therefore she is made to swear an emphatic oath (al-batt). But since she denied the husband's right, the more apparent view is that the husband's side prevails, and the woman is permitted to retract.

= The Book of Īlāʾ (Vow of Abstinence) =

It contains two chapters:
One: On its Pillars (Arkān)
The Second: On its Rulings (Aḥkām)

— Peace be upon him — The First Chapter: On Its Pillars — Peace be upon him —

Its form is that he says to his wife: "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you." This was a form of divorce in the pre-Islamic era (Jāhiliyyah); then the Law changed its ruling and decreed that after four months have passed, the husband is compelled either to intercourse or divorce.

Īlāʾ linguistically is derived from al-āliyah, which means the oath, but the legal convention (ʿurf al-sharʿ) has specified it as the oath contracted upon abstaining from intercourse with the married wife.

Its pillars are four: the one who swears (al-ḥālif), the one sworn by (al-maḥlūf bih), the matter sworn upon (al-maḥlūf ʿalayh), and the duration sworn within (al-muddah al-maḥlūf fīhā).

chapters.title_en: The First Pillar: The One Who Takes the Oath of Ila' (al-Ḥālif)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الركن الأول الحالف

وهو كل زوج يتصور منه الجماع فقولنا زوج يشمل أصناف الأزواج من المسلم
والكافر والحر والعبد وأبو حنيفة رحمه الله وإن خالف في ظهار الذمي فقد
وافق في صحة إيلاء الذمي
ثم  إذا رفع الذمي إلينا حكمنا عليه بحكم الإسلام حتى في إيجاب الكفارة
ويخرج عن الضابط قول الرجل لأجنبية والله لا أجامعك أبدا فإنه إذا نكحها
لم يكن
مؤليا وإن كان الضرار حاصلا ولكن الإيلاء كان طلاقا وتصرفا في النكاح
فغير حكمه دون أصله فلا يصح من الأجنبي وليس كل ضرر يدفع وإنما المدفوع
إضرار من الزوج في حالة الزوجية وقد ذكر صاحب التقريب وجها غريبا أن هذا
إيلاء ولا يتجه إلا على قول غريب حكاه أيضا في تعليق الطلاق بالملك على
موافقة أبي حنيفة رحمه الله وهو غير صحيح
وأما الإيلاء عن الرجعية فصحيح وإنما يفيد إذا راجعها لأن العائد هو حل
النكاح الأول فهي في حكم الزوجات
وأما قولنا يتصور منه الجماع فيدخل فيه المريض المدنف والخصي والمجبوب
بعض ذكره فيصح إيلاء جميعهم لإمكان الوطء منهم على حال فأما الذي جب تمام
ذكره فقد اختلف فيه النصوص وللأصحاب فيه طرق ومنهم من قال قولان ووجه صحته
أنه إضرار باللسان فيمكنه الفيئة باللسان والإعتذار بالعجز كما في المريض
ومنهم من قطع بالبطلان وقال القولان فيه إذا حلف ثم جب
ومنهم من قطع القول بأنه وإن جب بعد الحلف أنه يبطل الإيلاء لأنه أيضا
حصل اليأس من الحنث فهو كما لو قال إن وطئتك فعبدي حر فمات العبد فإنه يبطل
الإيلاء لحصول اليأس
ثم إيلاء الرتقاء والقرناء كإيلاء المجبوب فيخرج على الخلاف

### | الركن الثاني المحلوف به
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ل-ف (ḥ-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The core meaning is "to take an oath" (al-yamīn), derived from the handshake (muḥālafah) in pre-Islamic pacts; also denotes the strength of the right side (al-yad al-yumnā) by which oaths were sworn.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, ḥalaf signifies a binding solemn vow invoking God or a sacred object, creating a moral and legal obligation (iltizām) that carries expiatory consequences (kaffārah) upon violation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to the verbal act of swearing; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to the person (ḥālif) as the agent whose capacity for sexual intercourse is the operative condition, not merely the oath's form.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Dependency (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The legal ruling (ḥukm) is parsed as a conditional sentence where the oath's validity (ṣiḥḥah) depends on the subject's marital status (zawjiyyah) at the time of utterance, with the apodosis (the iylā' effect) suspended on this condition.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first pillar is the one who takes the oath of iylā' (al-ḥālif). He is every husband from whom sexual intercourse is conceivable. Our statement "husband" (zawj) encompasses all categories of husbands — the Muslim and the disbeliever, the free man and the slave. Although Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) dissented regarding the ẓihār of a dhimmī, he concurred on the validity of iylā' from a dhimmī. Then, if a dhimmī raises his case to us, we adjudicate upon him according to Islamic law, even in the obligation of the expiation (kaffārah).

What falls outside this criterion is a man's statement to a foreign woman (ajnabiyyah): "By God, I will never have intercourse with you." For if he later marries her, he is not thereby an mu'lī (one who has taken iylā'), even though harm (ḍirār) has occurred. But iylā' was [legally constituted as] a form of divorce (ṭalāq) and a disposition (taṣarruf) within marriage; thus it alters the ruling of marriage without altering its essence. Hence it is not valid from a foreign man. And not every harm is repelled; rather, what is repelled is the harm inflicted by the husband within the state of marriage. The author of al-Taqrīb has mentioned a strange opinion (wajh gharīb) that this constitutes iylā', but this is only tenable on a strange position which he also narrated regarding the suspension of divorce upon ownership, in agreement with Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) — and it is not sound.

As for iylā' from a revocably divorced wife (al-rajʿiyyah), it is valid, though it only takes effect if he takes her back (rājaʿahā), because what returns is the license of the first marriage; thus she is in the ruling of wives.

As for our statement "from whom sexual intercourse is conceivable," this includes the gravely ill patient (al-marīḍ al-mudnif), the eunuch (al-khaṣī), and the one whose part of his male organ has been severed (al-majbūb baʿḍ dhakarihi). The iylā' of all of them is valid, due to the possibility of intercourse from them in some state. As for the one whose entire male organ has been severed (man jubba tamām dhakarihi), the texts (nuṣūṣ) have differed concerning him, and among the companions (al-aṣḥāb) there are multiple paths (ṭuruq). Some of them said: there are two opinions (qawlān). The basis for its validity is that it is harm inflicted by the tongue, so he can effect the return (al-fay'ah) by the tongue and excuse himself by incapacity, just as in the case of the sick man. Some of them definitively ruled its nullification (buṭlān), and said the two opinions apply only if he swore the oath and then was castrated. And some definitively ruled that even if he is castrated after the oath, the iylā' is nullified, because despair of the violation (al-ḥinth) has occurred — just as if he said: "If I have intercourse with you, my slave is free," and then the slave died, for the iylā' is nullified due to the occurrence of despair.

Then, the iylā' of the woman with an imperforate vagina (al-ratqā') and the woman with fused labia (al-qarnā') is like the iylā' of the castrated man, so it follows the same disagreement.

### | The Second Pillar: That By Which the Oath Is Taken

والنظر فيه في ستة أقسام
القسم الأول الحلف بالله أو بصفة من صفاته وهي الأصل وفيه مسألتان
إحداهما أنه لو وطىء هل يلزمه كفارة اليمين الجديد وهو القياس أنه يلزمه
لانه حنث في يمين بالله تعالى وفي القديم قولان ووجهه أن الإيلاء كان طلاق
الجاهلية فغيره الشرع وجعله موجبا للطلاق بعد مدة فكان حكمه بضرب المدة
وإيجاب الطلاق بدل عن الكفارة ويشهد له قوله تعالى {أشهر فإن فاؤوا فإن
الله غفور رحيم} فإن هذا لا يشعر بلزوم الكفارة بل يشعر بأنه يوجب المغفرة
والرحمة نعم  لو حلف على أن لا يطأها ثلاثة أشهر تلزمه كفارة اليمين إذا حنث
لأن هذا ليس بإيلاء وقيل بطرد القول القديم فيه أيضا وهو بعيد
المسألة الثانية أن صحة الإيلاء هل تختص باليمين بالله تعالى أم يصح
بالتزام العبادات وتعليق الطلاق وغيره الجديد أنه لا يختص لأنه منوط
بالإضرار والإضرار لانقطاع رجاء المرأة ورجاؤها ينقطع إذا ظهر مانع للزوج
وكما أن خوف الكفارة يمنع فكذلك خوف هذه اللوازم وتوجيه القديم أن الإيلاء
مأخوذ من عادة
العرب وهي اليمين بالله تعالى عندهم فلا ينبغي أن يتصرف فيه بالمعنى ولا
تفريع بعد هذا على هذا القول أصلا
فرع لو كرر الإيلاء بعد تخلل فصل وقال أردت التأكيد قبل على أحد الوجهين
لأنه إخبار فأشبه الإقرار دون الإنشاء وكذا في تعليق الطلاق خلاف مرتب
وأولى بأن لا يقبل لأنه بالإنشاء أشبه
القسم الثاني في الحلف بالتزام العبادات فإذا قال إذا جامعتك فلله علي
صوم أو صلاة أو عتق رقبة أو تصدق بمال فهو مؤل فإذا حنث ففيما يلزمه
الأقوال المعروفة في يمين الغضب واللحجاج نعم لو قال إن وطئتك فلله علي صوم
هذا الشهر لم يصح الإيلاء لأن المطالبة تتوجه بعد انقضاء الشهر وانحلال
اليمين
القسم الثالث الحلف بالعتق وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا قال إن جامعتك فعبدي حر فمات العبد أو باعه أو أعتقه انحل
الإيلاء بعد انعقاده لأنه خرج عن التعرض لالتزام شيء بالوطء ولو قال إن
جامعتك فعبدي حر قبله بشهر صار مؤليا ولكن تحسب مدة الإيلاء بعد مضي شهر
فتكون المطالبة في الشهر السادس إذ لو وطىء في الشهر الأول لم يلزمه شيء
فإن العتق لا يمكن تقديمه على اللفظ فبعد تمام الشهر يتعرض للالتزام فلو
باع العبد في منتصف الخامس طولب في
السادس لأنه لو وطىء لتبين بطلان البيع وتقدم العتق عليه ولو تركت
المطالبة حتى انقضى من وقت البيع شهر كامل سقطت المطالبة إذ سقط التعرض
التزام
الثانية إذا قال إن وطئتك فعبد حر عن ظهاري وكان قد  ظاهر صار مؤليا وعند
الوطء يعتق العبد عن الظهار ويكون الإلتزام الجديد في الإيلاء تعيين العبد
وتعجيل العتق فإن ذلك لم يوجبه الظهار وفيه وجه أنه يعتق ولا ينصرف إلى
الظهار لأنه يتأدى به حق الحنث فلا يتأدى به حق الظهار وطردوا هذا فيما لو
قال إن دخلت الدار فأنت حر عن ظهاري وهو بعيد فإن التعليق ليس فيه إلا
إضافة العتق إلى الزمان فهو كالتنجييز
أما إذا لم يكن قد ظاهر فلا يكون مؤليا بينه وبين الله تعالى ولو وطىء لم
يعتق عبده لأنه قال أنت حر عن ظهاري ولا ظهار ولكن في الظاهر يجعل مقرا
بالظهار ويعتق عبده عند الوطء ويجعل مؤليا لذلك
الثالثة إذا قال إن جامعتك فعبدي حر عن ظهاري إن تظهرت فهذا تعليق لعتق
العبد بصفتين بالوطء والظهار وحكمه أنه لو وطىء أولا لم يعتق ولكن يتعرض
للزوم لو ظاهر فيعتق العبد لا على جهة الظهار لأنه قدم تعليقه على الظهار
فلا ينصرف إليه ثم قالوا لا يصير مؤليا في الحال ولكن لو ظاهر أولا صار
مؤليا لأنه صار العتق متعلقا بالوطء ثم قالوا إنه يعتق لا من جهة الظهار
وهذا فيه نظر لأنه إذا لم ينصرف إلى الظهار فينبغي أن لا يعتق كما إذا قال
أنت حر عن ظهاري ولم يكن قد ظاهر فإنه لا يعتق باطنا كما ذكرناه ثم إذا لم
يعتق لا يصير مؤليا لأنه لا التزام إلا أن يقال يلغى قوله عن ظهاري لأنه
جعل العتق محالا وبقي قوله أنت حر فهذا له احتمال ولكن في
المسألتين جميعا أعني في التعليق وفي قوله أنت حر عن ظهاري إذا لم يكن قد
ظاهر
الرابعة إذا قال إن جامعتك فلله علي أن أعتق هذا العبد عن ظهاري فكونه
مؤليا يبني على أن العبد هل يتعين بالنذر ويعتق بعتق سبق لزومه فيه خلاف
سيأتي في النذور
القسم الرابع في الحلف بالطلاق وفيه مسائل
إحداها أنه لو قال إن وطئتك فأنت طالق ثلاثا فهو مؤل  على الجديد ثم يطالب
بالفيئة أو تنجيز الطلاق ويقال له في الفيئة عليك تغييب الحشفة والنزع في
الحال متصلا بالتغييب من غير مكث فإنه يقع به الثلاث وتحرم ويقع النزع في
حال التحريم ولكنه كالخروج من المعصية فلا بأس به وقال ابن خيران يحرم
الوطء إذ وصل النزع غير ممكن ويتجه مذهبه أيضا فإن النزع أيضا نوع مماسة
والخروج عن الملك المغصوب جائز للضرورة ولكن تعريض النفس لمثل ذلك
بالاختيار غير جائز
فرع لو قال لغير المدخول بها إن وطئتك فأنت طالق فهو مؤل فإن وطئها وقع
الطلاق رجعيا وإن كان الطلاق مقارنا للوطء غير متأخر عنه لأن الوطء مقرر
والطلاق مبين فقد اجتمعا فغلب جانب تقرير النكاح
الثاينة إذا قال إن وطئتك فضرتك طالق فهو مؤل فإن أبان الضرة انقطع
الإيلاء لزوال الإلتزام فإن جدد نكاحها وقلنا بعود الحنث عاد الإيلاء فتبنى
المدة على ما مضى من المدة قبل الطلاق وما تخلل في مدة الإبانة لا يحسب ولا
تستأنف المدة بخلاف الردة والرجعة إذا طرءا كما سيأتي
الثالثة إذا قال إن وطئت إحداكما فالأخرى طالق فهو مؤل قال ابن الحداد
إذا مضت المدة وجاءتا إلى القاضي طالبتين طلق القاضي إحداهما على الإبهام
ثم إن كان
الزوج قد نوى إحداهما نزل على المنوية وعلى الزوج البيان وإن كان قد أبهم
بقي مبهما ووجب على الزوج التعيين فلو قال قبل التعيين راجعت التي صادفها
الطلاق ففي صحة الرجعة مع الإبهام وجهان والأصح أنها إذا لم تقبل التعليق
فلا تقبل الإبهام قال القفال غلط ابن الحداد لأن الدعوى لا تصح مبهما وهما
معترفتان بالإشكال وهما كرجلين قالا عند القاضي لأحدنا على فلان ألف فإنه
لا يسمع لكن يتجه لابن الحداد أن الضرار قد تحقق بهما ولا بد من الرفع
عنهما
القسم الخامس في اليمين التي تقرب الوطء من الإلتزام وفيه صيغ
الأولى إذا آلى عن نسوة فقال والله لا أجامعكن فإنما تلزمه الكفارة إذا
جامع جميعهن فلا تتعلق كفارة بوطء واحدة ولكن  يتعلق به القرب من الحنث بوطء
الباقيات فالجديد أنه لا يصير مؤليا حتى يطأ ثلاثا منهن فيصير مؤليا في حق
الرابعة إذ تتوقف الكفارة على وطئها والقول القديم أنه مؤل لأن القرب من
اللزوم محذور كأصل اللزوم فعلى هذا لو وطىء واحدة سقط إيلاؤها دون البواقي
وكذلك لو طلق واحدة أما إذا ماتت واحدة سقط إيلاء الكل إذ حصل اليأس عن
جماع جميعهن وبه يقع الحنث
الصيغة الثاينة أن يقول والله لا أجامع كل واحدة منكن فهذا إيلاء إذ
يتعلق الحنث بكل واحدة ولو قال لا أجامع واحدة منكن فله ثلاثة أحوال
إحداها أن يريد به لزوم الكفارة بواحدة أي واحدة كانت على العموم فهو مؤل
إذ ما من واحدة يطؤها إلا وتلزمه الكفارة ولكن إذا وطىء واحدة انقطع إيلاء
الباقيات إذ
اليمين لا يتناول إلا واحدة
الثانية أن يقول أردت واحدة معينة مبهمة وعلي تعيينها او قال نويت واحدة
بعينها وعلي بيانها انعقد الإيلاء كذلك ويطالب بالبيان أو التعيين وقال
الشيخ أبو علي لا إيلاء لأن كل واحدة ترجو أن لا تكون هي المرادة أو
المعينة بالإيلاء فكيف يساوي هذا اليأس المحقق في معينة وهذا متجه إن
اعترفت بالإشكال فإن ادعت أنه عناها وجب عليه الجواب لا محالة
ثم إذا لم يكن قد عين فعين فتحسب المدة من وقت التعيين أو من وقت اليمين
فيه خلاف ينبني على أن الطلاق المبهم متى وقع كما ذكرناه في الطلاق
الحالة الثالثة أن يطلق هذه الصيغة فعلى أي المعنيين يحمل فيه وجهان
لتعارض الإحتمالين
الصيغة الثالثة إذا قال والله لا أجامعك في السنة إلا مرة واحدة فالوطء
يقربه من الحنث فيكون مؤليا على القديم دون الجديد وعلى الجديد إذا وطئها
صار مؤليا فينظر إلى بقية المدة من السنة فإن كانت دون أربعة أشهر فليس
بمؤل وإن زاد صار مؤليا من وقت الوطء ولو قال والله لا أجامعك في السنة إلا
مائة مرة أو ألف مرة فحكمه حكم المرة الواحدة لا تختلف بالكثرة  والقلة
الصيغة الرابعة إذا قال إن جامعتك مرة فوالله لا أجامعك بعدها فهذا تعليق
يمين بالوطء فمنهم من قطع بأنه ليس مؤليا لأنه ليس بحالف 7 في الحال حتى
يطأها مرة ومنهم من خرج على القولين لأن الوطء يعرضه لأن يصير حالفا
ولو قال إن وطئتك فأنت طالق إن دخلت الدار قال القاضي هو مؤل قطعا لأن
الوطء يصير مانعا لها عن الدخول ومنهم من خرج على القولين إذ لا فرق بين
المسألتين
فرع إذا قال إن وطئتك فوالله لا أطؤك فغيب الحشفة ثم عاد إلى الإيلاج
ثانيا ففي لزوم الكفارة خلاف والاوجه أن الوطء يتناول جميع الإيلاجات فلا
يحنث بالوطأة الأولى ويلتفت إلى خلاف في وجوب المهر إذا كان المعلق به ثلاث
طلقات
القسم السادس في شروط لفظ الإيلاء وفيه مسائل
الأولى أن الكناية لا تتطرق إلى لفظ اليمين من الإيلاء فلو آلى عن امرأة
ثم قال لأخرى أشركتك معها لم يصر مؤليا لأن عماد الإيلاء ذكر اسم الله
تعالى وفي مثله من الظهار خلاف مبني على أن المغلب فيه اليمين أو الطلاق
ولا خلاف في جواز الإشراك في نفس الطلاق وأما إذا قال إن دخلت الدار فانت
طالق ثم قال لغيرها أشركتك معها وأراد تعليق طلاق الثانية بدخولها في نفسها
لا بدخول الأولى ففي ذلك خلاف
ولو قال أنت علي حرام ونوى الإيلاء فالظاهر أنه لا ينعقد كلفظ الإشراك
والثانية أنه ينعقد لأن هذا اللفظ ورد في القرآن لإيجاب الكفارة
الثانية في تعليق الإيلاء وهو صحيح كقوله إن دخلت الدار فوالله لا أطؤك
ولو
قال والله لا أجامعك إن شئت فقالت شئت صار مؤليا وهل تختص المشيئة
بالمجلس فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم كما في الطلاق
والثاني لا كما في التعليق بالدخول
وقال مالك رحمه الله إذا علق بمشيئتها لم يكن مؤليا لأنها التي أضرت
بنفسها إلا أن الشافعي رضي الله عنه ليس يعتبر ذلك فإنها لو تركت المطالبة
بعد انقضاء المدة فلها العود إلى المطالبة لأنها تترك علي  توقع فلذلك تشاء
على توقع أن الزوج يخالف مشيئتها ويطؤها
الثالثة أنه لا يتشرط اقتران الغضب بالإيلاء عندنا وقال مالك رحمه الله
لا يكون مؤليا إلا في حالة الغضب وهو بعيد إذ الضرار حاصل بكل حال
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ل-و (a-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes swearing, vowing, or binding oneself; al-īlā' is the oath of abstinence from marital intercourse.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, it is a solemn vow (yamīn) that creates a legal impediment, distinct from mere intention.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to the oath itself; metaphorical extension applies to any binding commitment that produces the same legal effect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Sentence Structure (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) must be syntactically and semantically linked; the legal effect follows the fulfillment of the condition.
chapters.translation:
I say: The examination of this topic proceeds in six divisions.

**The First Division: The Oath by Allah or by One of His Attributes — This is the Foundational Principle**

This division contains two questions.

**The First Question:** If a man who has taken an oath of abstinence (īlā') actually has intercourse [with his wife], does the expiation (kaffārah) for a new oath become obligatory upon him? The analogical ruling (qiyās) is that it does become obligatory, because he has violated (ḥanitha) an oath taken by Allah the Exalted. However, according to the old doctrine (al-qadīm), there are two opinions. The rationale [for the old view] is that īlā' was originally a divorce of the pre-Islamic era (ṭalāq al-jāhiliyyah); the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ) then changed it and made it a cause for divorce after a specified period. Thus, its ruling became the imposition of a waiting period and the obligation of divorce as a substitute for expiation. This is supported by the saying of Allah the Exalted: {أشهر فإن فاؤوا فإن الله غفور رحيم} — "Four months; then if they return [to their wives], indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." This [verse] does not indicate the obligation of expiation; rather, it indicates that [returning] necessitates forgiveness and mercy. However, if he swore that he would not have intercourse with her for three months, then the expiation for breaking an oath becomes obligatory upon him if he violates it, because this is not īlā'. It was also said that the old doctrine is extended to this case as well, but this is remote.

**The Second Question:** Is the validity of īlā' restricted to oaths by Allah the Exalted, or is it valid through undertaking acts of worship (iltizām al-ʿibādāt) and suspending divorce and other things? The new doctrine (al-jadīd) is that it is not restricted [to oaths by Allah], because īlā' is contingent upon harm (iḍrār), and harm arises from the severance of the wife's hope [of intercourse]. Her hope is severed when an impediment appears on the husband's part. Just as the fear of expiation prevents [intercourse], so too does the fear of these necessary consequences [prevent it]. The rationale for the old doctrine is that īlā' is derived from the custom of the Arabs, and their custom was to swear by Allah the Exalted. Therefore, one should not reinterpret it by analogical reasoning (maʿnā), and no subsidiary rulings (tafrīʿ) are derived from this doctrine at all.

**Subsidiary Issue (Farʿ):** If he repeated the īlā' after an intervening separation (faṣl) and said, "I intended confirmation (taʾkīd)," it is accepted according to one of the two opinions, because it is an informative statement (ikhbār), thus resembling acknowledgment (iqrār) rather than a performative utterance (inshā'). Similarly, in the suspension of divorce, there is a related disagreement, and it is even more appropriate that it not be accepted, because it more closely resembles a performative utterance.

**The Second Division: The Oath by Undertaking Acts of Worship**

If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then upon me is an obligation to Allah to fast, or to pray, or to free a slave, or to give charity from my wealth," then he is a muʾlī (one who has taken the oath of abstinence). If he violates [the oath], then regarding what becomes obligatory upon him, there are the well-known opinions concerning the oath of anger (yamīn al-ghaḍab) and importunity (al-lijāj). However, if he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then upon me is an obligation to Allah to fast this month," the īlā' is not valid, because the claim [against him] would only arise after the month has elapsed and the oath has been dissolved.

**The Third Division: The Oath by Manumission (al-ʿitq)**

This division contains several questions.

**The First Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then my slave is free," and then the slave dies, or he sells him, or manumits him, the īlā' is dissolved after having been validly contracted, because [the slave] has exited from being subject to the obligation of something contingent upon intercourse. If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then my slave is free," one month before [the oath], he becomes a muʾlī, but the period of īlā' is calculated after the month has elapsed. Thus, the claim [against him] arises in the sixth month. For if he had intercourse in the first month, nothing would be obligatory upon him, since manumission cannot precede the utterance. After the completion of the month, he becomes subject to the obligation. If he sells the slave in the middle of the fifth [month], he is called to account in the sixth, because if he had intercourse, the sale would be revealed as void and the manumission would take precedence over it. If the claim is deferred until a full month has elapsed from the time of the sale, the claim is dropped, since the subjection to the obligation has ceased.

**The Second Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then this slave is free as expiation for my ẓihār (injurious comparison)," and he had indeed pronounced ẓihār, he becomes a muʾlī. Upon intercourse, the slave is manumitted as expiation for the ẓihār, and the new obligation in the īlā' is the designation of the slave and the acceleration of manumission, for that [specific designation] was not required by the ẓihār. There is an opinion that he is manumitted but not applied to the ẓihār, because by him the obligation of the violation (ḥanath) is fulfilled, so the obligation of the ẓihār is not fulfilled by him. They extended this to the case where he says, "If you enter the house, then you are free as expiation for my ẓihār," but this is remote, for in suspension (taʿlīq) there is nothing but the addition of manumission to a time, so it is like an immediate execution (tanjīz).

However, if he had not pronounced ẓihār, he is not a muʾlī between him and Allah the Exalted, and if he has intercourse, his slave is not manumitted, because he said, "You are free as expiation for my ẓihār," and there is no ẓihār. But in the external [legal] sense, he is treated as one who acknowledges ẓihār, and his slave is manumitted upon intercourse, and he is considered a muʾlī on that account.

**The Third Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then my slave is free as expiation for my ẓihār, if I pronounce ẓihār," this is a suspension of the slave's manumission upon two conditions: intercourse and ẓihār. Its ruling is that if he has intercourse first, [the slave] is not manumitted, but he becomes subject to the obligation if he then pronounces ẓihār, in which case the slave is manumitted — but not as expiation for ẓihār, because he placed the suspension [of manumission] before the ẓihār, so it does not apply to it. Then they said: he does not become a muʾlī at present, but if he pronounces ẓihār first, he becomes a muʾlī, because manumission becomes contingent upon intercourse. Then they said: he is manumitted, but not as expiation for ẓihār. This is subject to scrutiny, because if it does not apply to the ẓihār, then it should not be manumitted — just as when he says, "You are free as expiation for my ẓihār," and he had not pronounced ẓihār, for then he is not manumitted inwardly, as we have mentioned. Then, if he is not manumitted, he does not become a muʾlī, because there is no obligation. Unless one says: his statement "as expiation for my ẓihār" is rendered void, because he made manumission impossible, and his statement "you are free" remains. This has some plausibility, but [the issue applies] in both questions — namely, in the suspension and in his statement "you are free as expiation for my ẓihār" when he had not pronounced ẓihār.

**The Fourth Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then upon me is an obligation to Allah to manumit this slave as expiation for my ẓihār," then his being a muʾlī is built upon whether the slave becomes specifically designated (yataʿayyan) by the vow (nadhr) and is manumitted by a manumission that precedes its obligation — concerning which there is a disagreement that will come in the chapter on vows (al-nudhūr).

**The Fourth Division: The Oath by Divorce (al-ṭalāq)**

This division contains several questions.

**The First Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then you are divorced three times," he is a muʾlī according to the new doctrine. Then he is called upon to return (al-fayʾah) or to execute the divorce immediately. It is said to him regarding the return: upon you is the obligation to insert the glans (taghyīb al-ḥashafah) and withdraw immediately, continuously with the insertion, without any delay. For by this, the three divorces occur, and she becomes forbidden [to him]. The withdrawal occurs at the moment of prohibition, but it is like exiting from an act of disobedience, so there is no harm in it. Ibn Khayrān said: intercourse is forbidden, since withdrawal is not possible [without it], and his doctrine is also sound, for withdrawal is also a type of contact (mumāssah). Exiting from usurped property is permissible out of necessity, but exposing oneself to such [an act] voluntarily is not permissible.

**Subsidiary Issue (Farʿ):** If he said to a woman not yet consummated with, "If I have intercourse with you, then you are divorced," he is a muʾlī. If he has intercourse with her, the divorce occurs as a revocable divorce (rajʿī), even though the divorce is simultaneous with the intercourse and not subsequent to it, because intercourse is a confirmation (muqarrir) while divorce is a dissolution (mubayyin); since they have combined, the side of confirming the marriage prevails.

**The Second Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then your co-wife (ḍarrah) is divorced," he is a muʾlī. If he makes the co-wife irrevocably divorced (abāna), the īlā' is severed due to the removal of the obligation. If he renews his marriage to her, and we hold that the violation (ḥanath) returns, then the īlā' returns, and the period is built upon what has elapsed of the period before the divorce. The time intervening during the period of irrevocable divorce (ibānah) is not counted, and the period is not recommenced — unlike apostasy (riddah) and return (rujʿah) if they occur, as will come later.

**The Third Question:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with either of you, then the other is divorced," he is a muʾlī. Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: if the period elapses and both come to the judge seeking [their right], the judge divorces one of them indeterminately (ʿalā al-ibhām). Then, if the husband had intended one of them specifically, it applies to the one intended, and the husband must clarify. If he had left it indeterminate, it remains indeterminate, and the husband is obligated to specify. If he says before specifying, "I have taken back (rājaʿtu) the one whom the divorce befell," then regarding the validity of the return (rujʿah) with indeterminacy, there are two opinions. The more correct one is that if she does not accept suspension (taʿlīq), she does not accept indeterminacy. Al-Qaffāl said: Ibn al-Ḥaddād erred, because a claim (daʿwā) is not valid when indeterminate, and both [women] acknowledge the ambiguity. This is like two men who say before the judge, "One of us has a claim of a thousand [dirhams] against so-and-so" — this is not heard. However, Ibn al-Ḥaddād's view can be supported, because harm (ḍirār) has been realized against both of them, and it is necessary to remove it from both.

**The Fifth Division: The Oath That Brings Intercourse Close to Obligation**

This division contains several formulations (ṣiyagh).

**The First Formulation:** If he takes the oath of abstinence from multiple women and says, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with all of you," then expiation becomes obligatory upon him only if he has intercourse with all of them. No expiation attaches to intercourse with one [woman], but what attaches to it is the proximity to violation (qurb al-ḥanath) through intercourse with the remaining ones. According to the new doctrine, he does not become a muʾlī until he has intercourse with three of them, at which point he becomes a muʾlī with respect to the fourth, since expiation becomes contingent upon intercourse with her. The old doctrine holds that he is a muʾlī [from the start], because proximity to obligation is as prohibited as the obligation itself. According to this, if he has intercourse with one, her īlā' is dropped but not that of the remaining ones. Similarly, if he divorces one [of them]. However, if one of them dies, the īlā' of all is dropped, since despair of intercourse with all of them has been realized, and by this the violation occurs.

**The Second Formulation:** He says, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with each one of you." This is īlā', since violation attaches to each one. If he says, "I will not have intercourse with one of you," then he has three states:

*First State:* He intends by it the obligation of expiation by one [intercourse] — whichever one it may be, in a general sense. Then he is a muʾlī, for there is no woman with whom he has intercourse except that expiation becomes obligatory upon him. However, if he has intercourse with one, the īlā' of the remaining ones is severed, since the oath only applies to one.

*Second State:* He says, "I intended one specific woman, but indeterminately, and upon me is to specify her," or he says, "I intended one particular woman, and upon me is to clarify her." Then the īlā' is contracted accordingly, and he is called upon to clarify or specify. Shaykh Abū ʿAlī said: there is no īlā', because each woman hopes that she is not the one intended or specified by the īlā' — so how can this equal the realized despair [produced] by a specific [woman]? This is sound if [the wife] acknowledges the ambiguity. But if she claims that he meant her, he must answer, without doubt. Then, if he had not specified and then specifies, is the period calculated from the time of specification or from the time of the oath? There is a disagreement built upon when an indeterminate divorce (al-ṭalāq al-mubham) occurs, as we mentioned in the chapter on divorce.

*Third State:* He utters this formulation absolutely [without clarification]. Then upon which of the two meanings it is construed has two opinions, due to the conflict of the two probabilities.

**The Third Formulation:** If he says, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you in the year except once," then intercourse brings him close to violation, so he is a muʾlī according to the old doctrine but not the new. According to the new doctrine, if he has intercourse with her, he becomes a muʾlī, and then one looks at the remainder of the year's period. If it is less than four months, he is not a muʾlī; if it exceeds that, he becomes a muʾlī from the time of intercourse. If he says, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you in the year except a hundred times or a thousand times," its ruling is the same as the ruling for once — it does not differ by abundance or scarcity.

**The Fourth Formulation:** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you once, then by Allah I will not have intercourse with you after it," this is a suspension of an oath upon intercourse. Some have definitively ruled that he is not a muʾlī, because he is not swearing at present until he has intercourse with her once. Others have derived [his status] from the two opinions, because intercourse exposes him to becoming a swearer. If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then you are divorced if you enter the house," al-Qāḍī said: he is definitively a muʾlī, because intercourse becomes an impediment preventing her from entering. Some have derived [his status] from the two opinions, since there is no difference between the two questions.

**Subsidiary Issue (Farʿ):** If he says, "If I have intercourse with you, then by Allah I will not have intercourse with you," and he inserts the glans, then returns to penetration a second time, then regarding the obligation of expiation there is a disagreement. The most correct view is that "intercourse" encompasses all penetrations, so he does not violate by the first act of intercourse. Reference is made to the disagreement concerning the obligation of the dower (mahr) when what is suspended is three divorces.

**The Sixth Division: The Conditions of the Wording of Īlā'**

This division contains several questions.

**The First Question:** Allusion (kināyah) does not apply to the wording of the oath in īlā'. If he takes the oath of abstinence from one woman, then says to another, "I have made you a partner with her," he does not become a muʾlī [with respect to the second], because the foundation of īlā' is the mention of the name of Allah the Exalted. In the analogous case of ẓihār, there is a disagreement built upon whether the dominant element is the oath or divorce. There is no disagreement regarding the permissibility of making a partner in divorce itself. However, if he says, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced," then says to another, "I have made you a partner with her," intending the suspension of the second's divorce upon her own entry, not upon the first's entry, then there is a disagreement [as to its validity].

If he says, "You are forbidden to me (anti ʿalayya ḥarām)" and intends by it īlā', then the apparent [doctrine] is that it is not contracted, like the wording of partnership. The second [opinion] is that it is contracted, because this wording appears in the Qur'an for the obligation of expiation.

**The Second Question:** Concerning the suspension of īlā' — it is valid, as in his saying, "If you enter the house, then by Allah I will not have intercourse with you." If he says, "By Allah, I will not have intercourse with you, if you wish," and she says, "I wish," he becomes a muʾlī. Is the wish restricted to the session (majlis)? There are two opinions: one, yes, as in divorce; the second, no, as in suspension upon entry. Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: if he suspends it upon her wish, he is not a muʾlī, because she has harmed herself. However, al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) does not consider this, for if she abandons the claim after the period has elapsed, she may return to the claim, because she abandons it in anticipation (tarajjī) — and therefore she wishes [for intercourse] in anticipation that the husband will oppose her wish and have intercourse with her.

**The Third Question:** It is not a condition that anger (al-ghaḍab) be conjoined with īlā' in our doctrine. Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him) said: one is not a muʾlī except in a state of anger — but this is remote, for harm (ḍirār) is realized in every state.

### | الركن الثالث في المدة المحلوف عليها

والمطلق منه قوله لا اجامعك والمقيد قوله لا أجامعك سنة فإن حلف على
أربعة أشهر فما دونه لا يكون مؤليا لأنه قاصر عن المدة الشرعية ولو حلف على
خمسة أشهر فهو مؤل ويطالب في الشهر الخامس ولو حلف على أربعة أشهر ولحظة
فهو مؤل على معنى أنه يأثم ولكن لا تظهر فائدته في المطالبة ولو حلف على
أربعة أشهر فلما كان في الشهر الرابع حلف على أربعة أخرى ولم يزل كذلك يفعل
أبدا فليس مؤليا وإن كان الضرار حاصلا
ولو قال دفعة لا أجامعك أربعة أشهر فإذا انقضت فوالله لا أجامعك أربعة
أشهر وهكذا حتى استوفى مدة طويلة فالصحيح أنه ليس بمؤل لأنه إذا انقضى
أربعة أشهر فكيف يطالب بحكم اليمين الأولى وقد انحلت أو بحكم اليمين
الثانية ولم ينقضي منها إلا لحظة وفيه وجه أنه إذا فعل ذلك مرة واحدة فهو
مؤل لأنه يصير ذريعة إلى الإضرار ويلزم عليه ما لو فعل ذلك آخر كل أربعة
أشهر وهو بعيد
ولو قال إذا مضت خمسة أشهر فوالله لا أطؤك لا يصير مؤليا حتى تنقضي خمسة
أشهر فبعده تستفتح المدة ولو قال والله لا اطؤك خمسة أشهر وإذا انقضت
فوالله لا أطؤك سنة فإذا انقضى أربعة أشهر طولب بالفيئة في الشهر الخامس
فإن فاء انقطعت الطلبة في الشهر الخامس فإذا انقضى الشهر الخامس استفتحنا
مدة أربعة أشهر لليمين الثانية
ولو قال لا أطؤك حتى تصعدي السماء أو ينزل عيسى عليه السلام أو يخرج
الدجال أو يقدم فلان وهو على مسافة يعلم أنه لا يقدم في أربعة أشهر فهو مؤل
قطعا
ولو أقت بدخول دار أو قدوم زيد لم يكن مؤليا في الحال فإذا انقضى أربعة
أشهر فهل نطالبه بالفيئة  فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن الوطء في هذه الحال موجب للكفارة
والثاني أنه لا يطالب لأن القدوم والدخول منتظر في كل
حال ولو أقت بموت زيد فمنهم من قال هو كقدوم زيد ومنهم من قطع بأنه مطالب
لأنه كالمستبعد في الإعتقادات ولو أقت بموت الزوجين فهو إيلاء لا محالة
لأنه حصل اليأس في العمر وصيغته أن يقول لا أطؤك ما عشت أو عشت

### | الركن الرابع في ألفاظ المحلوف عليه

وهي ثلاثة أقسام الأول ما هو صريح لا يقبل التأويل ولا يدين كلفظ النيك
وإيلاج الذكر في الفرج وتغييب الحشفة في الفرج وكذلك قوله للبكر لا افتضتك
فلو فسر بالضم والأعناق لم يدين على الأصح
القسم الثاني ما هو صريح في الظاهر ويتطرق إليه التديين وهو الوطء وكذلك
الجماع لكثرة الإستعمال وأما الإصابة فألحقه الشيخ أبو علي بالجماع وهو
بعيد أما المباشرة والملامسة والمباضعة وما يجري مجراه ففيه قولان
أحدهما أنها صريحة كالجماع لأن العادة في الجماع التحاشي عن الصريح
والثاني أنها كنايات لأنها بالوضع غير صريح وعادة الإستعمال ليس يتضح فيه
كما في الجماع
القسم الثالث الكنايات قولا واحدا وهو كقوله لأبعدن عنك ولا يجمع رأسي
ورأسك وسادة ولا شئونك وفي لفظ القربان والغشيان وجهان
أحدهما أنهما كنايتان والثاني أنهما في معنى المباشرة والمباضعة
فأما إذا قال ووالله لا أجامعك في دبرك أو في الحيض والنفاس فهو محسن
وليس بمؤل
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في حكم الإيلاء الصحيح - صلى الله
عليه وسلم -
ومجموع ما يترتب عليه أحكام
أولها ضرب المدة
والثاني المطالبة بالفيئة
والثالث دفع المطالبة بفيأة أو طلاق
والرابع ما تقع به الفيئة فنشرحها في فصول
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-د-د (m-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Extension, prolongation, or a specified span of time; the measure of a thing's continuance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legally defined term (al-muddah al-sharʿiyyah) that determines whether a vow constitutes ila' — a period fixed by revelation, not by custom.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in denoting a temporal extent; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to the "term" of a legal obligation, as the duration itself is not the agent but the container of the ruling.
- Root: ف-ي-ء (f-y-')
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, reversion; specifically, the act of returning to a prior state or obligation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, the mandated return to sexual relations (al-waṭ') after a vow of abstinence, as a restorative act that nullifies the transgression of ila'.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in meaning "to come back"; legally technical (majāz mursal) for "fulfilling the conjugal duty," since the physical return is the sign of the intended compliance.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍ-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Harm, injury, or detriment inflicted upon another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The underlying rationale (ʿillah) for the legal sanction of ila' — the prohibition of persistent harm to the wife through indefinite abstention.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical harm; metaphorical for legal detriment, as the harm here is the deprivation of a contractual right, not bodily injury.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Sentence Structure (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazā') — The protasis (sharṭ) and apodosis (jazā') govern the timing of legal effects; the apodosis is suspended until the condition is fulfilled, and the legal consequence (ḥukm) attaches only upon the condition's realization, as in "If five months pass, then I swear..." where the vow's term begins only after the condition.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third pillar concerns the duration sworn upon. The unqualified form is one's saying, "I will not have intercourse with you," while the qualified form is, "I will not have intercourse with you for a year." If one swears for four months or less, he does not become an abstainer (mu'li), because it falls short of the legally prescribed term. If he swears for five months, he is an abstainer, and he is called to account in the fifth month. If he swears for four months and a moment, he is an abstainer in the sense that he commits a sin, but its legal benefit does not appear in the demand for restitution. If he swears for four months, and while in the fourth month swears another four, and continues doing so perpetually, he is not an abstainer, even though harm is realized.

If he says at once, "I will not have intercourse with you for four months, and when they elapse, by God, I will not have intercourse with you for four months," and so on until he has covered a long period, the correct ruling is that he is not an abstainer, because when the four months elapse, how can he be called to account by virtue of the first oath, which has already been dissolved, or by virtue of the second oath, of which only a moment has elapsed? There is a view that if he does this once, he is an abstainer, because it becomes a means to harm; but this entails the consequence that if he does so at the end of every four months, he would be an abstainer, which is remote.

If he says, "When five months pass, by God, I will not have intercourse with you," he does not become an abstainer until the five months elapse, after which the term begins. If he says, "By God, I will not have intercourse with you for five months, and when they elapse, by God, I will not have intercourse with you for a year," then when four months elapse, he is demanded to return (al-fay'ah) in the fifth month. If he returns, the demand ceases in the fifth month; when the fifth month elapses, we begin a new four-month term for the second oath.

If he says, "I will not have intercourse with you until you ascend to heaven, or until Jesus (peace be upon him) descends, or until the Antichrist emerges, or until so-and-so arrives," while that person is at a distance known not to be traversed within four months, he is an abstainer definitively.

If he conditions it upon entering a house or the arrival of Zayd, he is not an abstainer at present. When four months elapse, do we demand restitution from him? There are two views: One is yes, because intercourse in this state would necessitate expiation (kaffārah). The second is that he is not demanded, because the arrival and entry are expected at any moment. If he conditions it upon the death of Zayd, some say it is like the arrival of Zayd, while others definitively hold that he is demanded, because it is deemed improbable in common belief. If he conditions it upon the death of both spouses, it is ila' without doubt, because despair of life is realized. Its formulation is his saying, "I will not have intercourse with you as long as I live," or "as long as you live."

### The Fourth Pillar: The Expressions of the Sworn-Upon Act

These are three categories. The first is what is explicit (ṣarīḥ), admitting no interpretation, nor is the swearer believed in his interpretive claim — such as the word "copulation" (al-nayk), "inserting the penis into the vagina," and "concealing the glans in the vagina." Likewise, his saying to a virgin, "I will not deflower you." If he interprets it as "pressing" or "embracing," he is not believed, according to the soundest view.

The second category is what is explicit in appearance but admits interpretive belief — namely, "intercourse" (al-waṭ') and "coitus" (al-jimā') due to their frequent usage. As for "touching" (al-iṣābah), Shaykh Abu Ali attached it to coitus, which is remote. As for "direct contact" (al-mubāsharah), "touching" (al-mulāmasah), "bedding" (al-mubāḍa'ah), and what runs in their course, there are two views: One is that they are explicit like coitus, because custom in coitus avoids the explicit term. The second is that they are allusive (kināyāt), because by linguistic convention they are not explicit, and customary usage is not as clear in them as in coitus.

The third category is allusive expressions, by unanimous agreement — such as his saying, "I will distance myself from you," "My head and your head shall not share a pillow," and "I will have no concern with you." Regarding the terms "approach" (al-qurbān) and "covering" (al-ghishyān), there are two views: One is that they are allusive; the second is that they are in the meaning of direct contact and bedding.

If he says, "By God, I will not have intercourse with you in your anus," or "during menstruation or postpartum bleeding," he is virtuous and not an abstainer.

### The Second Chapter: On the Rulings of Valid Ila' — Peace be upon him —

The totality of what follows from it comprises rulings: The first is the prescription of the term; the second is the demand for restitution (al-fay'ah); the third is repelling the demand through restitution or divorce; and the fourth is what constitutes restitution. We shall explain these in sections.

### | الفصل الأول في المدة

وفيه مسائل
الأولى أن المدة تحسب من وقت الإيلاء من غير حاجة إلى القاضي بخلاف مدة
العنة فإنها تحسب من وقت ضرب القاضي المدة لأنها متعلقة بالإجتهاد وهذا
منصوص في الكتاب وسببه أن النسوة في غالب الأمر لا يصبرن عن الرجال مع
اليأس عن الوقاع في أكثر  من أربعة أشهر وإنما يشترط زيادة على الأربعة
لوقوع المطالبة بعد المدة وأن المدة مهلة للخيرة وأبو حنيفة رحمه الله رأى
الطلاق واقعا بمضي المدة فلم يشترط زيادة على أربعة أشهر
الثانية لا تختلف هذه المدة عندنا بالرق والحرية فإنه أمر يتعلق بالشهوة
والطبع فهو كمدة العنة وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله الحرة تتربص أربعة أشهر
والامة شهرين وقال
مالك رحمه الله تختلف برق الزوج وحريته
الثالثة في قواطع المدة فإن طلقها طلاقا رجعيا قبل مضي المدة انقطعت فإن
راجعها استأنفنا المدة لأنها قد حرمت بالطلاق ولا بد من إصرار على التوالي
في المدة
والردة بعد الدخول كالطلاق الرجعي والطلاق الرجعي بعد المدة يقطع المدة
فإن جرت رجعة فاستئناف المدة أولى فإن الطلاق إجابة إلى المطالبة فقد اجاب
مرة فلا يطالب حتى يمتنع أربعة أشهر أخر وألحقوا الردة أيضا بالطلاق وهو
أبعد لأنه ليس إجابة لمطالبته
أما الذي لا يقطع المدة كالصوم والإحرام من جهته فلا يؤثر لا طارئة ولا
مقارنة وكذلك الأعذار الطبيعية كمرضه وكونه محبوسا وكما لو طرأ الجنون عليه
فلا تمنع تيك الأعذار انعقاد المدة ولا دوامها أما الموانع فيما يمنع
احتساب المدة فكإحرامها وصغرها ونشوزها أو كونها محبوسة أو مجنونة أو مريضة
لا تحتمل الجماع
ثم هذه الأحوال إذا طرأت قطعت المدة فإن زالت تستأنف المدة أو تبنى على
ما مضى فيه وجهان
أحدهما الإستئناف كالطلاق والردة من الزوج والثاني أنه تبنى لأن هذا لم
يقطع النكاح حتى تنقطع المدة المبنية عليه وإنما هذه أعذار تمنع المطالبة
فإذا زالت عادت المطالبة والمذهب القطع بأنها إذا طرأت بعد المدة لم توجب
الإستئناف وقيل بطرد الوجهين وهو ضعيف
وأما صومها فلا يمنع الإحتساب لأن التمكين حاصل بالليل وفي التطوع
بالنهار فليس ذلك عذرا مانعا
الرابعة إذا تنازعا في انقضاء المدة فيرجع حاصله إلى النزاع في وقت
الإيلاء والقول فيه قوله مع يمينه

### | الفصل الثاني في المطالبة

وفيه مسائل
إحداها أن لها رفع الامر إلى القاضي فإن تركت المطالبة  أو رضيت فلها
العود مهما تشاء بخلاف ما إذا رضيت بعيب الزوج أو رضيت بعد مدة العنة لأن
ذلك عجز وعيب في حكم خصلة واحدة فرضاؤها به يسقط حقها وأما هذا فيحمل الرضا
فيه على توقع الحنث كما يحمل رضاها عند الإعسار بالنفقة على توقع اليسار
الثانية لا مطالبة لغير الزوجة فإذا رضيت لم يكن للولي ولا لسيد الأمة
المطالبة ولا لولي المجنونة والصغيرة لأن هذا لا يقبل النيابة
الثالثة لا مطالبة لها إذا كان فيها مانع طبعا كالمرض العظيم والرتق
والقرن أو شرعا كالحيض والعجب أن الحيض يمنع المطالبة ولا يقطع المدة لأن
ذلك يتكرر في الأشهر مرارا نعم إذا فرعنا على قول بعيد في صحة الإيلاء عن
الرتقاء كان لها المطالبة بالفيئة باللسان
الرابعة إذا كان المانع فيه
إن كان طبعا فلها مطالبته ليفيء باللسان ويعتذر ويعد الوطء وذلك يدفع
الضرار
فإن كان شرعا كالظهار والصوم والإحرام قطع المراوزة بأنه لا يكفيه الفيئة
باللسان وللمرأة المطالبة وعليه أن يطلق فإن وطيء اندفعت المطالبة مع كونه
حراما ونقول انت مخير بين أن تعصي بالوطء أو تطلق وأنت قد ورطت نفسك فيه
وقال
مالك رحمه الله الوطء في الإحرام لا يسقط المطالبة
أما العراقيون فبنوا على جواز التمكين وقالوا إذا كانت محرمة أو حائضا
فطالبها بالتمكين لم يحل لها
وإن كان الزوج محرما أو صائما عن فرض فطالبها فهل يحل التمكين فيه وجهان
أحدهما لا لأن هذا الوطء معصية فكيف يمكن منه
والثاني نعم لأن المعصية تختص بالزوج والوطء حقه فعليها التوفية وإن كان
المستوفي عاصيا
ولا خلاف في أن للرجعية الإمتناع لأن الطلاق متعلق بها واختلفوا في أن
الظهار كالإحرام أو كالطلاق ثم قالوا إن قلنا عليها التمكين فلها المطالبة
فإن قصد الزوج الوطء وامتنعت سقط طلبها وإن حرمنا التمكين فعليها الإمتناع
وهل لها الإرهاق إلى الطلاق فيه وجهان
أحدهما لها ذلك والزوج هو الذي ورط نفسه فيه والثاني لا بل يكتفي بوعد
كالمانع الطبعي
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-د-د (m-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Extension, prolongation, or a fixed span of time measured continuously.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A legally defined term (muddah) denoting a stipulated period whose completion triggers or extinguishes a right, tied to divine command (ḥukm sharʿī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for temporal extension; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to a legal grace period (muhlah) granting respite.
- Root: ط-ل-ب (ṭ-l-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Seeking, demanding, or pursuing a claim with persistence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal claim (muṭālabah) as a formal demand for a right, often before a judge (qāḍī), distinct from mere desire.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for verbal demand; metaphorical for the wife's right to compel the husband to either resume intercourse (fayʾah) or divorce.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses conditional clauses (idhā... fa-) to delineate legal outcomes, with exceptions (illā) marking interruptions of the duration, requiring precise parsing of temporal sequences.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first chapter concerns the duration (al-muddah), and therein are several issues.

The first issue: The duration is reckoned from the time of the oath of abstention (īlāʾ) without any need for the judge, unlike the duration for impotence (al-ʿunnah), which is reckoned from the time the judge imposes the period, because that latter is tied to juristic discretion (ijtihād). This is explicitly stated in the Book (al-Kitāb). The reason is that women, in most cases, cannot bear to be without men when despairing of intercourse for more than four months. An increase beyond four months is only stipulated because the claim (muṭālabah) occurs after the duration, and the duration is a grace period (muhlah) for deliberation. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) held that divorce occurs automatically upon the lapse of the duration, so he did not stipulate an increase beyond four months.

The second issue: This duration does not vary, in our view, between slavery and freedom, for it is a matter tied to lust and natural disposition, thus it is like the duration for impotence. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) said: A free woman waits four months, and a slave woman two months. Mālik (may God have mercy on him) said: It varies according to the slavery or freedom of the husband.

The third issue: Concerning what interrupts the duration. If he divorces her with a revocable divorce (ṭalāq rajʿī) before the lapse of the duration, it is interrupted. If he takes her back (rajʿah), we recommence the duration, because she has been rendered unlawful by the divorce, and there must be continuous persistence (iṣrār) throughout the duration. Apostasy (riddah) after consummation is like revocable divorce. A revocable divorce after the duration interrupts the duration; if a return (rajʿah) occurs, recommencing the duration is more appropriate, for the divorce is a response to the claim—he has already responded once, so he is not to be claimed until he abstains for another four months. They also analogized apostasy to divorce, though this is more remote, because it is not a response to her claim.

As for what does not interrupt the duration, such as fasting or iḥrām on his part, it has no effect whether it occurs during or alongside the duration. Likewise, natural excuses, such as his illness, his imprisonment, or if madness (junūn) suddenly afflicts him—these excuses do not prevent the commencement of the duration nor its continuity. As for impediments that prevent the reckoning of the duration, these are like her iḥrām, her minority, her recalcitrance (nushūz), or her being imprisoned, mad, or ill such that she cannot bear intercourse. Then, if these states arise suddenly, they interrupt the duration. If they cease, there are two views: either recommence the duration or build upon what has passed. One view is recommencement, like divorce and apostasy from the husband. The second is that she builds upon it, because this does not sever the marriage such that the duration built upon it is interrupted; these are merely excuses that prevent the claim, so when they cease, the claim returns. The established doctrine (al-madhhab) is the definitive ruling that if these arise after the duration, they do not necessitate recommencement. It was said that both views apply, but this is weak. As for her fasting, it does not prevent reckoning, because enabling (tamkīn) is achieved at night, and voluntary fasting during the day is not a preventing excuse.

The fourth issue: If they dispute over the lapse of the duration, the essence of the matter reduces to a dispute over the time of the oath of abstention (īlāʾ). The word therein is his word, with his oath.

I say: The second chapter concerns the claim (al-muṭālabah), and therein are several issues.

The first issue: She has the right to raise the matter to the judge. If she abandons the claim or is satisfied, she may return to it whenever she wishes, unlike the case where she is satisfied with a defect in the husband or is satisfied after the duration for impotence, because that is incapacity and defect in the ruling of a single trait, so her satisfaction with it extinguishes her right. As for this case, her satisfaction is interpreted as anticipating the husband's violation of his oath (ḥanīth), just as her satisfaction, when the husband is unable to pay maintenance, is interpreted as anticipating his future prosperity.

The second issue: There is no claim for anyone other than the wife. If she is satisfied, neither the guardian (walī) nor the master of a slave woman may claim, nor the guardian of a mad or minor woman, because this does not admit of delegation (niyābah).

The third issue: She has no claim if there is an impediment in her, either natural, like severe illness, closure (ratq), or obstruction (qarn), or legal, like menstruation. It is remarkable that menstruation prevents the claim but does not interrupt the duration, because it recurs multiple times within the months. Yes, if we proceed on a remote view regarding the validity of īlāʾ against a woman with closure (ratqāʾ), she would have the claim for resumption (fayʾah) verbally.

The fourth issue: If the impediment is in him—if it is natural, she may claim him to resume verbally, apologize, and promise intercourse, and this repels harm (ḍarar). If it is legal, like ẓihār, fasting, or iḥrām, the Marwazīs definitively ruled that verbal resumption does not suffice him, and the woman has the claim, and he must divorce. If he has intercourse, the claim is repelled despite its being unlawful, and we say: You are given the choice between disobeying by intercourse or divorcing, and you have ensnared yourself in this. Mālik (may God have mercy on him) said: Intercourse during iḥrām does not extinguish the claim. As for the Iraqis, they built upon the permissibility of enabling (tamkīn) and said: If she is in iḥrām or menstruating, and he claims enabling from her, it is not lawful for her. If the husband is in iḥrām or fasting an obligatory fast, and he claims her, are there two views on whether enabling is lawful for her? One view: No, because this intercourse is disobedience, so how can she enable it? The second: Yes, because the disobedience pertains specifically to the husband, and intercourse is his right, so she must fulfill it, even if the one fulfilling is disobedient. There is no disagreement that a woman under revocable divorce (rajʿiyyah) may refuse, because the divorce is attached to her. They differed on whether ẓihār is like iḥrām or like divorce. Then they said: If we hold that she must enable, she has the claim; if the husband intends intercourse and she refuses, her claim lapses. If we deem enabling unlawful, she must refuse. Does she have the right to pressure him toward divorce? There are two views. One: She has that right, and the husband is the one who ensnared himself. The second: No, rather a promise suffices, like the natural impediment.

chapters.title_en: The Third Chapter on Repelling the Claim (of Ila’)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثالث في دفع  المطالبة

ولا يندفع إلا بالطلاق أو الوطء من القادر والفيئة باللسان من العاجز كما
سبق فإن رفع إلى القاضي فامتنع من الأمرين طلق القاضي عليه في أصح القولين
وفي القول الثاني يلجئه بالحبس والتعزير إلى الطلاق وهو بعيد لأنه إكراه
على الطلاق وأنكر المزني هذا وقال لم يصر إليه أحد من العلماء نعم لو
استمهل الزوج من القاضي ثلاثة أيام في الفيئة باللسان لم يمهل وفي الوطء
وجهان أحدهما لا لأن مدة المهلة أربعة أشهر وقد تم
والثاني نعم لأنه ربما لا يجد قوة ونشطة في الحال فعلى هذا لو بادر
القاضي قبل مضي المدة لم تطلق لا كقتل المرتد قبل تمام المهلة فإنه مهدر
لأن الطلاق يقبل الرد وفيه وجه بعيد أنه يفنذ
والمهلة ثلاثة أيام تجري في سبعة مواضع المرتد وتارك الصلاة والفسخ
بالإعسار وبالعنة وخيار العتق والشفعة والإيلاء أما الرد بالعيب فهو على
الفور
ثم إذا استمهل فأمهلناه فادعى العنة فيستأنف مدة العنة ولا يطلق لأن
الطلاق كان تغليظا عليه لظننا به القدرة وذكر العراقيون وجها أنه يطلق
فرع إذا غاب الزوج إلى مسافة أربعة أشهر فلوكيلها في الخصومة أن يطالبه
بالطلاق أو الإنصراف إلى وطئها وخروجه إلى السفر في الرجوع ابتداء الفيئة
فلو صبر حتى انقضت مدة الإمكان ثم قال الآن أبتدىء السفر فلحاكم تلك البلدة
أن يطلق

### | الفصل الرابع فيما به الفيئة وهو الوطء

ويكفي تغييب الحشفة ولو نزلت على زوجها لم تحصل الفيئة إذ لا تنحل به
اليمين وليس هذا فيئة منه أما إذا أكره وقلنا يتصور على الوطء إكراه يدرأ
الحد ففي لزوم الكفارة به خلاف فإن قلنا يلزم فقد انحل الإيلاء وإن قلنا لا
فهل تنحل اليمين فيه خلاف
فإن قلنا تنحل فلا طلبة وإن قلنا لا ينحل فالصحيح أن الطلبة تبقى لبقاء
الإيلاء وفيه وجه أنه لا طلبة لاندفاع الضرار بحصول الوطء أما إذا آلى ثم
جن فوطىء فالمنصوص فيه أنه تنحل اليمين بفعله ولا كفارة وخرج من الناسي قول
في  وجوب الكفارة فيلتحق تفصيله بالمكره
فرع لو تنازعا في الوطء في المدة فالأصل عدم الوطء ولكن القول قوله على
خلاف قياس الخصومات وقد ذكرنا نظير ذلك في العنة ثم قال ابن الحداد لو
طلقها وأراد أن يراجعها وقال صدقتموني في الوطء فلي الرجعة قلنا لا بل نرجع
إلى القياس والأصل عدم الوطء والعدة والقول قولها في ذلك وإنما كان كذلك
لنوع ضرورة والله أعلم
= كتاب الظهار =
وفيه بابان الباب الأول في أركانه وموجب ألفاظه
وفيه فصلان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To repel, push back, ward off; core sense of thrusting away an impending harm or obligation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal sense of nullifying a claimant’s right or demand through a valid counter-action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical repulsion; metaphorical (majāz) for legal dismissal of a suit.
- Root: ف-ي-ء (f-y-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, reversion; specifically the return to conjugal relations after an oath of abstention.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Ila’ jurisprudence, the act of resuming sexual intimacy, thereby dissolving the oath’s effect.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical return; metaphorical for the verbal declaration of intent when incapable.
- Root: ع-ن-ن (ʿ-n-n) / ع-ج-ز (ʿ-j-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: ʿUnnah = impotence; ʿajz = incapacity, weakness.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Distinguishes physical incapacity (ʿunah) from legal incapacity (ʿajz) affecting the obligation of fi’yah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for bodily inability; metaphorical for legal concession granted to the incapable.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional-Resultative Construction (al-sharṭ wa al-jawāb) — The protasis (e.g., “if he refuses”) governs the apodosis (e.g., “the judge divorces”), with the judge’s action treated as a legal substitute (badal) for the husband’s obligation.
chapters.translation:
I say: The claim (of Ila’) is not repelled except by divorce or by intercourse from the one capable (of it), and by verbal return (fi’yah) from the one incapable, as previously established. If the matter is raised to the judge and the husband refuses both options, the judge pronounces divorce on his behalf — this is the sounder of the two opinions. In the second opinion, the judge compels him through imprisonment and discretionary punishment (taʿzīr) until he divorces; but this is remote, for it constitutes coercion (ikrāh) upon divorce. Al-Muzanī rejected this and said: No scholar has ever adopted it. Yes — if the husband requests a postponement from the judge of three days for verbal fi’yah, he is not granted it; but regarding intercourse, there are two views. One: No, because the grace period of four months has already elapsed. The second: Yes, for perhaps he lacks strength and vigor at that very moment. On this second view, if the judge acts hastily before the period elapses, the wife is not divorced — unlike the killing of an apostate before the completion of his grace period, for that is deemed wasted (no liability), because divorce admits of revocation. There is a remote view that it is executed (nonetheless). The three-day grace period applies in seven contexts: the apostate, the abandoner of prayer, rescission due to insolvency, rescission due to impotence, the option of emancipation, preemption (shufʿah), and Ila’. As for rescission due to defect, it is immediate. Then, if he requests postponement and we grant it, and he then claims impotence, a fresh period for impotence is commenced, and he is not divorced — because the divorce was a severity upon him due to our presumption of his capability. The Iraqis mentioned a view that he is divorced. Branch: If the husband is absent at a distance of four months’ travel, his wife’s agent in litigation may demand from him either divorce or return to intercourse with her; and his departure for travel upon returning constitutes the initiation of fi’yah. If he waits until the period of possibility elapses, then says, “Now I begin the journey,” the judge of that land may pronounce divorce.

THE FOURTH CHAPTER: On What Constitutes Fi’yah, Namely Intercourse

The insertion of the glans (ḥashafah) suffices. If she descends upon her husband, fi’yah is not achieved, for the oath is not thereby dissolved, and this is not a fi’yah from him. As for when he is coerced — and we hold that coercion upon intercourse is conceivable such that it averts the ḥadd penalty — there is a dispute over whether expiation (kaffārah) becomes obligatory thereby. If we say it is obligatory, then the Ila’ is dissolved; if we say it is not, then there is a dispute over whether the oath is dissolved. If we say it is dissolved, then no claim (of Ila’) remains; if we say it is not dissolved, the sound view is that the claim remains due to the persistence of Ila’, though there is a view that no claim remains because the harm is repelled by the occurrence of intercourse. As for when he makes Ila’, then becomes insane, and then has intercourse — the text (al-manṣūṣ) holds that the oath is dissolved by his act, with no expiation. From al-Shāfiʿī (regarding the forgetful person) a view is transmitted on the obligation of expiation, and its detail is annexed to the case of the coerced. Branch: If they dispute over intercourse during the period, the default is non-occurrence of intercourse, but the husband’s word is accepted — contrary to the analogy of ordinary litigation. We have mentioned the like of this in the chapter on impotence. Then Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: If he divorced her and wished to take her back, saying, “You have confirmed my intercourse, so I have the right of return (rajʿah),” we say: No — rather we revert to the analogy, and the default is non-occurrence of intercourse and of the waiting period (ʿiddah); her word is accepted therein. It is only so due to a kind of necessity. And God knows best.
