chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الأول في أركانه

وهو المظاهر والمظاهر عنها واللفظ والمشبه به
الركن الأول المظاهر وكل من يصح طلاقه يصح ظهاره وقد ذكرناه وذلك لأن
الظهار كان طلاقا في الجاهلية فجعله الشرع محرما للزوجة وموجبا للكفارة عند
العود إليها فيصح ظهار المجبوب والخصي والذمي ثم على الذمي الكفارة ويصح
منه الإعتاق مهما أسلم في ملكه عبد كافر وكذلك لو قال لمسلم أعتق عبدك
المسلم عن كفارتي جاز على وجه فإن عجز فالصوم غير ممكن في حقه فيعدل إلى
الإطعام وقال القاضي لا يعدل فإنه قادر فليسلم وليصم وهو بعيد لأنه مقرر
على دينه فلا يكلف تركه وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لا يصح ظهار الذمي لأنه
ليس من أهل الكفارة
الركن الثاني المظاهر عنها وهي كل من يلحقها الطلاق فإن ظاهر عن الرجعية
وتركها لم يكن عائدا فإن راجعها تعرض للزوم الكفارة كما سيأتي وإن ارتدت
وظاهر عنها فإن رجعت إلى الإسلام انعقد الظهار فالإيلاء والظهار والطلاق
متساوية إلا في المجبوب والرتقاء فإن الصحيح أن الإيلاء فيهما لا يصح
الركن الثالث اللفظ وصريحه أن يقول أنت علي كظهر أمي أو مثل ظهر أمي ولا
مناقشة في الصلات فلو قال أنت مني أو معي أو عندي مثل ظهر أمي فكل ذلك صريح
وكذا لو ترك الصلة وقال أنت كظهر أمي فلو قال أردت الإضافة إلى غيري لم
يقبل كما لو قال أنت طالق وقال أردت من غيري لأن الشيوع يمنع هذا التأويل
ثم يتصدى النظر في  أجزاء الأم وأجزاء الأم قسمان
أحدهما ما لا يذكر في معرض الكرامة كقوله كبطن أمي وشعرها ورجلها ويدها
وفيه قولان
القديم أنه ليس بظهار اتباعا لعادة الجاهلية
والثاني أنه ظهار اتباعا للمعنى لأنه كلمة زور تشعر بالتحريم كالظهر وكذا
لو أضاف إلى بعض الزوجة فقال يدك أو رجلك علي كظهر أمي يخرج
على القولين ومأخذه الإتباع أو النظر إلى المعنى فقد ظهر أن التصرفات
القابلة للتعليق كالطلاق والظهار والعتاق تصح إضافتها إلى البعض أما النكاح
والرجعة فلا وأما الإيلاء فإذا قال لا أجامع فرجك أو نصفك الأسفل فهو صريح
ولو اضاف إلى النصف الشائع فيه احتمال لأن ترك الجماع في النصف من ضرورته
تركه في الكل
القسم الثاني ما يذكر في معرض الكرامة كقوله أنت مثل أمي أو كأمي أو كروح
أمي فإن أراد الكرامة فليس بظهار وإن قصد الظهار فهو ظهار وإن أطلق فوجهان
لتعارض الإحتمالين ولو قال كعين أمي التفت إلى الجديد والقديم لأنه إضافة
إلى البعض واختلفوا أن الرأس كالبطن والعين والروح لأنه قد يذكر للكرامة
الركن الرابع في المشبه به فلو شبهها بمحللة أو محرمة تحريما مؤقتا
كالأجنبية
أو تحريما لا محرمية فيها كالكملاعن عنها لم يكن ظهارا أما المحرمة على
التأييد بقرابة أو مصاهرة أو رضاع ففيه أقوال
أحدها الإقتصار على الأم اتباعا لعادة الجاهلية وهو مأخذ القديم
والثاني أن كل ذلك ظهار اتباعا للمعنى لأن التحريم شامل
والثالث الإقتصار على الأم وإلحاق الجدة بها لأنها في معناها غير دونها
والرابع إلحاق كل محرمة بالنسب بالأم وكذا كل محرمة بالرضاع لم نعهد
تحليلها من أول وجودها دون من طرأ التحريم عليها ودون المحرمة بالمصاهرة
فإنها كانت محللة ولأن الرضاع يشبه النسب دون المصاهرة
أما إذا قال أنت علي كظهر أبي لم يكن ظهارا لأنه ليس في محل الإستحلال

### | الفصل الثاني في موجب الألفاظ
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ظ-ه-ر (Ẓ-H-R)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "back" (al-ẓahr), the physical rear part of the body; also denotes elevation, prominence, and manifestness (ẓuhūr).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, ẓihār is a pre-Islamic form of divorce (ṭalāq) repurposed by Sharīʿah as a prohibited declaration (muḥarram) requiring expiation (kaffārah) upon resumption of marital relations.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally, "back" is a body part; metaphorically (majāz), it signifies the entire woman in the context of conjugal intimacy, as the back is the locus of sexual approach.
- Sībawayh Rule: ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — The phrase "أنت علي كظهر أمي" employs a prepositional phrase (fī maḥall al-rafʿ) as predicate, with the particle "ka" (simile) governing a genitive, requiring syntactic parsing of the comparison as a complete nominal sentence.
chapters.translation:
I say: The pillars of ẓihār are four: the one who makes the declaration (al-muẓāhir), the woman against whom it is made (al-muẓāhar ʿanhā), the verbal formula (al-lafẓ), and the object of comparison (al-mushabbah bihī).

**The First Pillar: The Declarant (al-Muẓāhir)**
Anyone whose divorce (ṭalāq) is valid, his ẓihār is likewise valid — and we have already mentioned this. This is because ẓihār was a form of divorce in the pre-Islamic era (Jāhiliyyah), and the Sacred Law (al-Sharʿ) transformed it into a prohibition of the wife and an obligation of expiation (kaffārah) upon returning to her. Thus, ẓihār is valid from the impotent man (al-majbūb), the eunuch (al-khaṣī), and the dhimmī (protected non-Muslim). The dhimmī is obligated to pay the expiation, and it is valid for him to emancipate a slave — if, after embracing Islam, a non-Muslim slave comes into his possession, he may free him. Likewise, if he says to a Muslim: "Emancipate your Muslim slave on my behalf as expiation," this is permissible in one respect. If he is unable [to free a slave], then fasting (al-ṣawm) is not possible in his case, so he shifts to feeding the poor (al-iṭʿām). Al-Qāḍī [Abū Ṭayyib al-Ṭabarī] said: He does not shift [to feeding], for he is capable [of fasting] — let him embrace Islam and then fast. This view is remote, because he is confirmed upon his religion and is not obligated to abandon it. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) held that ẓihār from a dhimmī is invalid, because he is not among those qualified for expiation.

**The Second Pillar: The Woman Against Whom Ẓihār Is Made (al-Muẓāhar ʿanhā)**
She is any woman whom divorce can reach. If he declares ẓihār against a woman in revocable divorce (al-rajʿiyyah) and then leaves her, he has not become a "returner" (ʿāʾid). If he takes her back (rājaʿahā), he becomes exposed to the obligation of expiation, as will follow. If she apostatizes (irtaddat) and he declares ẓihār against her, then if she returns to Islam, the ẓihār is validly contracted. Thus, īlāʾ (vow of abstinence), ẓihār, and ṭalāq are all equal [in their rulings], except in the case of the impotent man and the woman with vaginal occlusion (al-ratqāʾ), for the sound opinion is that īlāʾ is not valid in these two cases.

**The Third Pillar: The Verbal Formula (al-Lafẓ)**
Its explicit (ṣarīḥ) form is that he says: "You are to me like the back of my mother" (anti ʿalayya ka-ẓahri ummī), or "like the back of my mother" (mithla ẓahri ummī). There is no dispute concerning the connective particle (al-ṣilah). If he says: "You are from me" (anti minnī), or "with me" (maʿī), or "in my presence" (ʿindī), like the back of my mother — all of this is explicit. Likewise, if he omits the connective and says: "You are like the back of my mother." If he then says: "I intended [the comparison] to refer to someone other than [my mother]," this is not accepted — just as if he said: "You are divorced" (anti ṭāliq) and claimed: "I intended [divorce] from someone other than [you]." This is because the general applicability (al-shuyūʿ) prevents such an interpretation.

Then we turn to examining the parts of the mother. The parts of the mother are of two categories:

**First Category:** What is not mentioned in the context of honor (al-karāmah), such as his saying: "Like the belly of my mother," "her hair," "her leg," or "her hand." There are two opinions (qawlān) concerning this:
- The old opinion (al-qadīm): It is not ẓihār, following the custom of the Jāhiliyyah.
- The second opinion: It is ẓihār, following the meaning (al-maʿnā), because it is an obscene utterance (kalimat zawr) that signifies prohibition, just like the back.

Likewise, if he adds [the comparison] to a part of the wife herself, saying: "Your hand" or "your leg is upon me like the back of my mother," this branches upon the two opinions. The basis of [the divergence] is either following [the custom] or considering the meaning. It has thus become clear that dispositions (al-taṣarrufāt) susceptible to suspension (al-taʿlīq) — like ṭalāq, ẓihār, and emancipation (al-ʿitāq) — are valid when attributed to a part [of the person]. As for marriage (al-nikāḥ) and revocation (al-rajʿah), they are not [valid when attributed to a part]. As for īlāʾ, if he says: "I will not have intercourse with your vagina" or "your lower half," it is explicit. If he attributes it to the undivided half (al-niṣf al-shāʾiʿ), there is a possibility [of invalidity], because abstaining from intercourse with half necessarily entails abstaining from the whole.

**Second Category:** What is mentioned in the context of honor, such as his saying: "You are like my mother," "like my mother," or "like the soul (rūḥ) of my mother." If he intends honor, it is not ẓihār. If he intends ẓihār, it is ẓihār. If he leaves it unqualified (muṭlaq), there are two faces (wajhān) due to the conflict of the two probabilities. If he says: "Like the eye of my mother," one looks to the new opinion (al-jadīd) and the old opinion (al-qadīm), because it is an attribution to a part. They differed concerning the head — whether it is like the belly, the eye, and the soul, because it may be mentioned for honor.

**The Fourth Pillar: The Object of Comparison (al-Mushabbah bihī)**
If he compares her to a woman who is lawful [for him] (muḥallalah), or to one prohibited by a temporary prohibition (taḥrīman muʾaqqatan) — like a foreign woman (al-ajnabiyyah) — or to one prohibited by a prohibition involving no kinship-barrier (muḥrimiyyah) — like the woman divorced by liʿān (al-mulāʿanah ʿanhā) — it is not ẓihār. As for one prohibited permanently (al-muḥarramah ʿalā al-taʾbīd) by kinship (qarābah), marriage-affinity (muṣāharah), or fosterage (riḍāʿ), there are several opinions (aqwāl):
1. The first: Restriction to the mother alone, following the custom of the Jāhiliyyah — this is the basis of the old opinion.
2. The second: All of that is ẓihār, following the meaning, because the prohibition is comprehensive.
3. The third: Restriction to the mother, with the grandmother (al-jaddah) annexed to her, because she is in her meaning, not below her.
4. The fourth: Annexing every woman prohibited by lineage (al-nasab) to the mother, and likewise every woman prohibited by fosterage — [but only] those whose permissibility was not known from the very beginning of their existence, not those upon whom prohibition supervened, and not those prohibited by marriage-affinity, for she was previously lawful. This is because fosterage resembles lineage, unlike marriage-affinity.

As for his saying: "You are to me like the back of my father" (ka-ẓahri abī), it is not ẓihār, because the father is not in the locus of seeking lawful sexual intercourse (maḥall al-istiḥlāl).

### | The Second Chapter on What the Verbal Formulas Necessitate

chapters.title_en: Section 415: On the Suspension, Conditions, and Rulings of Ẓihār (Injurious Comparison)
chapters.arabic_text:
وفيه مسائل
الأولى أنه لو قال مهما ظاهرت عن ضرتك فأنت علي كظهر أمي كان كما قال لأن
الظهار يقبل التعليق ولو  أشار إلى أجنبية وقال مهما ظاهرت عنها فأنت علي
كظهر أمي صح وتناول ظهارا عنها بعد نكاحها تنزيلا لموجب اللفظ على الصحيح
شرعا فلو أجرى مع الأجنبية لفظ ظهار لم يحنث ولو صرح وقال إن ظاهرت عن
فلانة وهي أجنبية فهذا لغو عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه وتعليق بمحال وقال
المزني رحمه الله ينزل ذلك على اللفظ وكذا الخلاف فيما لو قال إن بعت الخمر
فأنت علي كظهر أمي ثم باع لم يحنث عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه لأنه ليس ببيع
وعند المزني يحمل على المسمى بيعا بالعادة أما إذا قال إن ظاهرت عن فلانة
الأجنبية فيحتمل التعريف ويحتمل اشتراط كونها أجنبية فعلى أيهما يحمل فيه
وجهان
الثانية أن يظاهر عن امرأة ويقل للأخرى أشركتك معها ونوى ففيه خلاف مبني
على أن الظهار يغلب فيه مشابه الأيمان أو الطلاق
الثالثة إذا قال أنت طالق كظهر أمي وقع الطلاق بقوله أنت طالق ثم نراجعه
فإن أراد بالبقية التأكيد قبل وإن أراد الظهار لغا إن كان بائنا ونفذ إن
كان رجعيا
الرابعة أن يقول أنت علي حرام كظهر أمي فله أحوال
إحداها أن ينوي الطلاق دون الظهار وقصد التأكيد فهو كما نوى وكقوله أنت
طالق كظهر أمي وفيه وجه أن الظهار هو الحاصل لأنه أتى بصريحه دون صريح
الطلاق فهو أولى من الكناية ولا يخفى أنه لو عنى الظهار دون غيره فلا يحصل
إلا الظهار
الحالة الثانية أن يقول نويت الطلاق والظهار جميعا مقرونا بقولي أنت علي
حرام ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أن الجمع غير ممكن في لفظ واحد والطلاق أقوى فهو الواقع
والثاني أن الظهار أولى إذ أتى بصريحه
والثالث وهو اختيار ابن الحداد أن الرجل يخير حتى يختار أحدهما إذ ليس
أحدهما أولى من الآخر
الحالة الثالثة أن يقول أردت بقولي علي حرام طلاقا وبقولى ظهر أمي ظهارا
وقع الطلاق ونفذ الظهار إن كان رجعيا وفيه وجه أن الظهار لا يصح لأن قوله
كظهر أمي غير مستقل وقد انصرف أول  الكلام إلى الطلاق
أما لو عكس وقال أردت الظهار بالأول والطلاق بالآخر نفذ الظهار دون
الطلاق لأنه نواه بلفظ الظهار وقال الشيخ أبو محمد ينفذ الطلاق لأن قوله
كظهر أمي ليس مستقلا ولم يحصل به ظهار فيحصل به طلاق
الحالة الرابعة أن يقول لم أقصد بالمجموع إلا تحريم عينها فتحرم عليه
ولتزمه الكفارة
المسألة الخامسة لو قال أنت علي حرام وقال نويت الطلاق والظهار جميعا مع
اللفظة قال ابن الحداد إن نوى الظهار أولا يصح ويقع الطلاق ولم يكن عائدا
وإن نوى الطلاق أولا وكان رجعيا صح الظهار
قال الشيخ أبو علي هذا غلط لأن اللفظ واحد فينبغي أن يجعل كما لو نواهما
معا فيخرج على الخلاف في أن الأولى أيهما وهذا يلتفت على أن نية الكناية
إذا اقترنت ببعض اللفظ ما حكمه وقد ذكرناه في الطلاق
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في حكم الظهار الصحيح - صلى الله
عليه وسلم -
وله حكمان
أحدهما تحريم الجماع على الإقتران به إلى أن يكفر إما بالعتق أو الصيام
أو الإطعام وجوز أبو حنيفة رحمه الله الوطء للمكفر بالإطعام لأن الآية
مطلقة في حقه
لكن الشافعي رضي الله عنه ينزل المطلق على المقيد في مثل ذلك
ثم اختلف قول الشافعي رضي الله عنه في أن التحريم هل يقتصر على الجماع
فقال في المختصر أحببت أن يمنع القبلة وقال في موضع آخر رأيت أن تمنع
القبلة فقيل قولان
أحدهما التريم لقوله تعالى {من قبل أن يتماسا} والقائل الثاني يحمله على
الوقاع لقوله {من قبل أن تمسوهن} نعم
مسالك الأشباه متعارضة فنقول كل ما يحرم الوطء لخلل في الملك كالطلاق
والردة والإستبراء عن الغير كعدة الوطء بالشبهة أو لإباحة الغير كتزويج
السيد أمته فكل ذلك يحرم اللمس وأما الصوم والحيض فلا وقياس الإحرام أن
يكون كالصوم ولكنه يحرم اللمس تعبدا وأما الإستبراء في المسبية فيحرم الوطء
وفيما دونه خلاف وإن كان من جهة شراء أو تملك فيحرم الإستمتاع مطلقا لأنه
لو ظهر الحمل لحرم على  الإطلاق بخلاف جهة السبي والظهار مردد بين هذه
الأصول فإن لم نحرم إلا الوطء ففي الإستمتاع بما دون السرة والركبة خلاف
مبني على أنا إن حرمنا ذلك في الحائض عللنا بانتشار الأذى أو تخوف الوقوع
في الوقاع ويظهر تشبيه الظهار بالحيض لأنه يحرم مع دوام النكاح لكن من حيث
إنه كان طلاقا فأقت تحريمه بالكفارة فيحتمل أن يشبه بتحريم الرجعية
الحكم الثاني وجوب الكفارة وهو منوط بالعود قال الله تعالى {ثم يعودون
لما قالوا} فاختلف العلماء فيه على خمسة مذاهب
قال الثوري هو بنفس الظهار عائد وهو فاسد لقوله تعالى {ثم يعودون} وقال
داود أراد تكرار لفظ الظهار والعود إليه وقال الزهري
ومالك في إحدى الروايتين إنه الوقاع إذ به يعود لنقض كلامه وقال أبو
حنيفة ومالك رحمهما الله في رواية إنه العزم على الإمساك وقال الشافعي رضي
الله عنه هو نفس الإمساك
ومهما لم يطلق عقيب الظهار على الإتصال فهو ممسك ولا يكفيه العزم على
الطلاق دون تحقيقه لأن إمساكه عود لنقض كلامه فسبيله أن يقول أنت علي كظهر
أمي أنت طالق متصلا حتى لا يلزمه كفارة ويتفرع على هذا الأصل مسائل
الأولى إذا مات عقيب الظهار فلا كفارة إذ لم يتحقق الإمساك فإنه يفتقر
إلى زمان القدرة على الطلاق ولو طلقها طلاقا رجعيا فلا عود فإن راجع فنص
الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن نفس الرجعة عود ونص أنه لو ارتد وعاد لم يكن نفس
الإسلام عودا وكذا لو أبانها وجدد النكاح وقلنا بعود الظهار والحنث لم يكن
بمجرده عائدا لأن الإسلام يقصد به تبديل الدين والنكاح يقصد به تجديد الملك
والرجعة لا معنى لها إلا إمساك الزوجة ومن أصحابنا من خرج وجها إلى
الرجعة من النكاح وإلى النكاح والردة من الرجعة وطرد القولين لكن الفرق
وتقرير النص أظهر فإن قيل إذا آلى ثم أبان وجدد النكاح لزمته الكفارة
بالوطء وإن لم نقل بعود الحنث فلم لا تعود كفترة الظهار قلنا لأن اليمين
يستقل بنفسه دون النكاح والظهار لا  يتصور إلا في النكاح والكفارة هاهنا
كالمطالبة بالفيئة عن الإيلاء فإنها من الخواص فلا تعود في نكاح ثان
نعم لو ظاهر وعاد حتى حرمت عليه استقرت الكفارة فلو طلق وجدد استمر
التحريم إلى الكفارة وأما لو كانت رقيقة فاشتراها ففيه خلاف مبني على أن
تحريم الطلاق واللعان هل يتعدى إلى ملك اليمين كما ذكرناه
المسألة الثانية إذا ظاهر عن زوجته الرقيقة ثم اشتراها على الفور ففيه
وجهان
أحدهما أن الشراء ينفي العود كالطلاق لأنه قاطع
والثاني لا لأنه نقله من حل إلى حل فهو عائد وهذا يتجه إذا قلنا إنه
يتعدى تحريم الظهار إلى ملك اليمين
ثم قال ابن الحداد لا بد وأن يتصل قوله اشتريت بالظهار فلو تشاغل بأسبابه
حصل العود وقال الأصحاب إن كانت أسبابه متعذرة فهو كما قال وإن كانت متيسرة
على القرب لم يكن عائدا أما إذا علق طلاقها بعد الظهار على الدخول فهو عائد
وإن كان الدخول متيسرا إذ لا فائدة في التعليق وهو قادر على التنجيز ولو
كان قد علق من قبل فدخل على الإتصال فلا عود إن كان الدخول متيسرا
ولو لاعن عقيب الظهار فظاهر النص أنه يمنع العود ثم اختلف في تصويره
فمنهم من قال لو قذف بعد الظهار ولم يقصر في البدار إلى الرفع إلى القاضي
على العادة فلا عود ومنهم من قال ينبغي أن تتصل كلمات اللعان بالظهار ويكون
القذف والرفع سابقا وقال ابن الحداد ينبغي أن تتصل الكلمة الأخيرة بالظهار
فإنه القاطع وألزم عليه كما لو قال عقيب الظهار يا زينب أنت طالق وقيل قوله
يا زينب لا يوجب العود لأنه من جملة الكلام فكذا كلمات اللعان
المسألة الثالثة لو علق الظهار بفعل غيره فوجد ولم يعرف فليس بعائد فكما
يعرف فينبغي أن يبادر الطلاق ولو علق بفعل نفسه ففعل ونسي الظهار فهو عائد
لأنه في نسيان فعل نفسه غير معذور
المسألة الرابعة إذا قال أنت علي كظهر أمي خمسة أشهر لم يصح على القديم
لخروجه عن المعتاد وعلى  الجديد يصح إن غلبنا مشابه الأيمان وإن غلبنا مشابه
الطلاق فلا لأن الطلاق المؤقت أبد لغلبة الطلاق ولم يظهر ذلك للظهار وقد
قيل يصح مؤبدا تشبيها بالطلاق
التفريع إن شبهناه بالأيمان صح مؤقتا ويكون العود بالجماع نص الشافعي رضي
الله عنه عليه لأنه ينتظر تحليلا بعد الأشهر وإنما يمسك لذلك فلا يكون مجرد
إمساكه مناقضا واعترض المزني رحمه الله على هذا وقال لا فرق بينه وبين
المطلق فمن الأصحاب من قال للشافعي رضي الله عنه قول قديم أن العود هو
الجماع فيطرد في المطلق والمقيد وهو فساد لأنه نص عليه في الجديد والفرق ما
ذكرناه
فعلى النص إذا جامع حرم الجماع فعليه النزع متصلا بتغييب الحشفة وعلى
مذهب ابن خيران يحرم الجماع الأول أيضا كذلك قال الصيدلاني إذا جامع نتبين
أنه كان عائدا عقيب اللفظ وعليه يحمل إمساكه وفيه فقه يوافق النص ويدفع
اعتراض المزني رحمه الله فعلى هذا لا نبيح الوطء الأول إذ هو مبين للتحريم
قبله فهو كما لو قال أنت طالق قبل الوطء فإنه يحرم الوطء
المسألة الخامسة إذا قال لأربع نسوة أنتن علي كظهر أمي صار مظاهرا عن
جميعهن ولكن في تعدد الكفارة واتحادها خلاف لاتحاد اللفظ وهو كالخلاف فيما
لو قذف جماعة بكلمة واحدة أن الحد هل هو متعدد ومشابه الأيمان تقتضي
الإتحاد لأن الكلمة واحدة ومشابه الطلاق التعدد لتعدد المحل فإن قلنا يتعدد
فلا يخفى وإن قلنا يتحد فلو أمسكهن فعليه كفارة ولو طلق ثلاثا وأمسك واحدة
لزمه كفارة لأن مناقضة الظهار بالعود تتحقق بإمساك واحدة وليس كما لو قال
والله لا أجامعكن فإنه لا كفارة بجماع واحدة لأن مخالفته تتحقق بجماع
الجميع وتحقيقه أن الظهار هاهنا يتعلق بطلاق الجميع
فأما إذا ظاهر عنهن بأربع كلمات على التوالي فتجب أربع كفارات ويكون
بالظهار الثاني عائدا إلى الأول وبالثالث عائدا إلى الثاني وبالرابع عائدا
إلى الثالث فإن قال عقيب الرابع أنت طالق فعليه ثلاث كفارات فإن لم يقل
فأربع كفارات
المسألة السادسة إذا كرر لفظ  الظهار على الإتصال وقال قصدت بالثاني تأكيد
الأول قبل ولكن هل يكون عائدا فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأن اشتغاله بالتأكيد ترك للطلاق
والثاني لا لأنه لا يكون به ممسكا لأن التأكيد في حكم تمام الكلام
وإن قصد ظهارا آخر ففي تعدد الظهار مع اتحاد المرأة طريقان
أحدهما طرد القولين في تعدد الكفارة
والثاني القطع بالتعدد وتغليبا لجانب اللفظ
ولا خلاف أنه لو قذف شخصا واحدا مرتين فالحد واحد ثم إن طلق عقيب الثاني
لم يكن عائدا في الثاني وهل يكون عائدا في الأول لاشتغاله بالثاني فيه
وجهان مرتبان على صورة إرادة التأكيد وها هنا أولى بأن يكون عائدا لأنه
كلام مستقل بنفسه أما إذا تخلل زمان فهو عائد في الأول والظهار الثاني
منعقد إن قلنا بتعدد الكفارة وإلا فلا فائدة فيه
أما إذا قلنا تتعدد فقال أردت التأكيد مع تخلل الفصل هل يقبل ها هنا تردد
فيه جواب القفال كما ذكرناه في الإيلاء لأن فيه مشابه الإخبار
المسألة السابعة إذا جن عقيب الظهار فليس بعائد فلو أفاق لم تكن مجرد
الإفاقة عودا ولكن إن لم يطلق عقيب الإفاقة صار عائدا ولو قال إن لم أتزوج
عليك فأنت علي كظهر أمي فلا ظهار في الحال فإن مات قبل التزويج حصل اليأس
وصار مظاهرا عائدا قبيل الموت هكذا قاله ابن الحداد وقال بعض الأصحاب
الظهار حاصل ولا عود لانه مات عقيب انعقاد الظهار وإنما كان يستقيم ما قاله
لو استند انعقاد الظهار إلى الأول وما ذكره ابن الحداد أغوص فليتأمل
فإن قيل الوطء يحرم بنفس الظهار أو بالعود قلنا بالعود إذا لو كان بمجرد
الظهار لكان تستقر الكفارة وإن طلق عقيبه حتى لو أراد وطأها بنكاح جديد أو
ملك يمين لم يجز إلا بكفارة وليس كذلك لكنه إذا عاد حرم ووجبت الكفارة
واستقرت لا لاجل استحلال الوطء فإنه لو أبانها بعد العود لم تسقط الكفارة
لأنها استقرت بالعود المناقض للظهار كما يستقر بالحنث في اليمين فالكفارة
تجب بالظهار والعود جميعا والظهار أحد  سببيها كاليمين ولذلك قال ابن الحداد
لو قال إن دخلت الدار فأنت علي كظهر أمي ثم أعتق عن الظهار ثم دخلت وقع
العتق لتأخره عن أحد السببين وخالفه بعض الأصحاب وقالوا وزانه ما لو قال إن
دخلت الدار فوالله لا أكلمك ثم أعتق قبل الدخول لا يجزىء لأنه إنما يصير
حالفا عند الدخول ولكن يحتمل أن يقال السبب صيرورته حالفا ومظاهرا وقد وجد
فيكفي ذلك والله أعلم
= كتاب الكفارات=
وخصالها ثلاثة العتق والصوم والإطعام والعتق لا يدخل في فدية الحج
والإطعام لا يدخل في كفارة القتل على أحد القولين وكفارة الجماع والظهار
متساويتان في الترتيب العتق ثم الصيام ثم الإطعام وكذا كفارة القتل إن قلنا
يدخلها الإطعام وكفارة الأيمان على الخيرة بين العتق والكسوة والإطعام فإن
عجز فالصيام ثلاثة أيام وسيأتي في موضعه والمقصود كفارة الظهار ثم يندرج
فيه جمل من أحكام الكفارات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ظ-ه-ر (Ẓ-H-R)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "back" (al-ẓahr), the physical posterior; also "height" and "appearance." The verb ẓāhara ʿan means "to back away from" or "to turn one's back on," hence the pre-Islamic divorce formula.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, ẓihār is a specific oath-like utterance comparing one's wife to a prohibited woman (e.g., mother), entailing both a prohibition and an expiation (kaffārah). It is a suspended (muʿallaq) conditional act, akin to an oath (yamīn) but with marital consequences.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally (ḥaqīqah), it refers to the physical back; metaphorically (majāz), it denotes the act of declaring one's wife like one's mother's back, a trope for severing conjugal intimacy. The rhetorical shift from literal to legal-metaphorical is central.
- Root: ع-و-د (ʿ-W-D)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To return," "to repeat," "to revert." The noun ʿawd signifies a return to a prior state or action.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ẓihār, al-ʿawd is the juristic act of "returning" to the wife (i.e., resuming marital relations or intending to keep her), which triggers the obligation of expiation. It is a technical term for the condition that activates the kaffārah.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Distinguishes literal return (physical coitus) from metaphorical return (mere intention or retention of the wife), a key point of juristic disagreement.
- Root: ك-ف-ر (K-F-R)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To cover," "to conceal," "to expiate." Kaffārah is that which covers over a sin or violation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theologically, it is the prescribed act of atonement (manumission, fasting, or feeding) that removes the legal prohibition arising from a violated oath or ẓihār.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal covering (e.g., night covering day); metaphorical covering of sin through prescribed acts.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq (Conditional Suspension) and ʿAṭf (Conjunction): The syntactic structure of conditional sentences (sharṭ/jazāʾ) governs whether an utterance is suspended (muʿallaq) on a future event. Also, the rule of Istiʾnāf (resumption) applies when a speaker utters multiple clauses, determining whether the second clause is an independent sentence or a continuation (taʾkīd) of the first.
chapters.translation:
I say: Within this section are several subsidiary questions (masāʾil).

The first: If a man says, "Whenever I pronounce ẓihār against your co-wife (ḍarratak), then you are to me like the back of my mother," it is as he said, because ẓihār admits of suspension (taʿlīq) upon a condition. And if he pointed to a foreign woman (ajnabiyyah) and said, "Whenever I pronounce ẓihār against her, then you are to me like the back of my mother," it is valid, and it applies to a ẓihār against her after he marries her, by way of interpreting the utterance's import according to what is sound in Sacred Law (sharʿan). But if he uttered the word "ẓihār" with respect to a foreign woman [without marriage], he does not incur the violation (ḥanath). And if he specified, saying, "If I pronounce ẓihār against so-and-so," while she is a foreign woman, this is null (laghw) according to al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him), being a suspension upon an impossibility (taʿlīq bi-muḥāl). Al-Muzanī (may God have mercy on him) said: It is interpreted according to the literal utterance. Likewise, the disagreement applies if he said, "If I sell wine, then you are to me like the back of my mother," and then he sold it: he does not incur violation according to al-Shāfiʿī, because it is not a valid sale (bayʿ); but according to al-Muzanī, it is interpreted as what is customarily called a "sale." As for his saying, "If I pronounce ẓihār against so-and-so," where she is a foreign woman, the definite article (al-taʿrīf) admits of two interpretations: either it specifies the woman, or it stipulates her being foreign. On which of the two it is interpreted, there are two positions (wajhān).

The second: If a man pronounces ẓihār against one wife and says to another, "I have made you a partner with her," intending [to include her], there is a disagreement built upon whether ẓihār is more akin to oaths (aymān) or to divorce (ṭalāq).

The third: If he says, "You are divorced like the back of my mother," the divorce occurs by his saying "You are divorced." Then we examine the remainder. If he intended by the rest an emphasis (taʾkīd), it is accepted. If he intended a ẓihār, it is null (laghw) if the divorce was irrevocable (bāʾin), but it takes effect if the divorce was revocable (rajʿī).

The fourth: If he says, "You are to me forbidden (ḥarām) like the back of my mother," he has several states:

One state: He intends divorce without ẓihār, aiming at emphasis. It is as he intended, like his saying "You are divorced like the back of my mother." There is a position that ẓihār is what actually occurs, because he uttered its explicit wording (ṣarīḥ) without the explicit wording of divorce, so it takes precedence over a mere allusion (kināyah). It is obvious that if he meant ẓihār alone, nothing but ẓihār occurs.

The second state: He says, "I intended both divorce and ẓihār together, conjoined with my saying 'You are to me forbidden.'" There are three positions:
- One: Combining both is impossible in a single utterance, and divorce is stronger, so it is what occurs.
- Second: ẓihār takes precedence, since he uttered its explicit wording.
- Third, which is the choice of Ibn al-Ḥaddād: The man is given the option (takhīr) to choose either one, since neither is more deserving than the other.

The third state: He says, "By my saying 'forbidden to me' I intended divorce, and by my saying 'like the back of my mother' I intended ẓihār." The divorce occurs, and the ẓihār takes effect if the divorce was revocable. There is a position that the ẓihār is invalid, because his saying "like the back of my mother" is not an independent utterance (ghayr mustaqill), and the beginning of the speech has already turned toward divorce. But if he reversed it, saying, "I intended ẓihār by the first [phrase] and divorce by the last," the ẓihār takes effect without the divorce, because he intended it by the explicit wording of ẓihār. Shaykh Abū Muḥammad said: The divorce takes effect, because his saying "like the back of my mother" is not independent, and no ẓihār is achieved by it, so divorce is achieved by it.

The fourth state: He says, "I did not intend by the whole utterance anything but the prohibition of her person (taḥrīm ʿaynihā)." Then she is forbidden to him, and he must incur the expiation (kaffārah).

The fifth question: If he says, "You are to me forbidden," and then says, "I intended both divorce and ẓihār together with the utterance," Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: If he intended ẓihār first, it is invalid, and divorce occurs, and he is not considered a returner (ʿāʾid). If he intended divorce first, and it was revocable, then the ẓihār is valid. Shaykh Abū ʿAlī said: This is an error, because the utterance is one, so it should be treated as if he intended both together, and it is resolved according to the disagreement over which of the two takes precedence. This depends on the rule: when the intention of an allusion (niyyat al-kināyah) is conjoined with part of the utterance, what is its ruling? We have mentioned this in the chapter on divorce.

The second chapter: On the ruling of a valid ẓihār.

It has two rulings:

The first: The prohibition of sexual intercourse (jimāʿ) from the time of the utterance until he expiates, either by manumission, fasting, or feeding. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) permitted intercourse for one who expiates by feeding, because the verse is absolute (muṭlaq) in his regard. But al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) applies the absolute to the restricted (muqayyad) in such cases.

Then al-Shāfiʿī's position differed on whether the prohibition is limited to intercourse. In al-Mukhtaṣar he said: "I prefer that the kiss be prevented." In another place he said: "I hold that the kiss should be prevented." It was said these are two positions (qawlān):
- One: The prohibition extends [to kissing], due to His saying {before they touch one another} (Q. 58:3).
- The second: He interprets it as referring to coitus, due to His saying {before you touch them} (Q. 58:4).

Yes, the paths of similar cases (ashbāh) are conflicting. We say: Everything that prohibits intercourse due to a defect in ownership (khalal fī al-milk)—like divorce, apostasy (riddah), or istibrāʾ from another (like the waiting period after intercourse by mistake)—or due to the permissibility of another (like a master marrying his slave-girl)—all of these prohibit touching (lams). As for fasting and menstruation, they do not. The analogy of iḥrām (pilgrimage sanctity) would make it like fasting, but it prohibits touching by way of devotion (taʿabbudan). As for istibrāʾ in a captive woman (sabiyyah), it prohibits intercourse, but there is disagreement on what is less than that. If it is by way of purchase or ownership, then enjoyment is prohibited absolutely, because if pregnancy became apparent, it would be prohibited absolutely, unlike the case of captivity. Ẓihār is equivocal (mutaraddid) among these principles. If we do not prohibit except intercourse, then there is a disagreement on enjoyment of what is below the navel and above the knee, built upon whether, when we prohibit that in a menstruating woman, we do so due to the spread of harm or the fear of falling into coitus. The resemblance of ẓihār to menstruation appears because it prohibits while the marriage continues, but insofar as it was like divorce, its prohibition is lifted by expiation, so it may resemble the prohibition of a revocable divorcee.

The second ruling: The obligation of expiation, which is contingent upon the "return" (ʿawd). God Most High said {then they return to what they said} (Q. 58:3). The scholars disagreed on this in five schools:
- Al-Thawrī said: He is a returner by the very ẓihār itself. This is corrupt, due to His saying {then they return}.
- Dāwūd said: He meant the repetition of the ẓihār utterance and returning to it.
- Al-Zuhrī and Mālik, in one of two narrations: It is coitus, for by it he returns to breaking his word.
- Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik, in another narration: It is the resolve (ʿazm) to retain [the wife].
- Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him): It is the very act of retaining (imsāk).

Whenever he does not divorce immediately after the ẓihār, he is a retainer (mumsik), and his resolve to divorce without actualizing it does not suffice, because his retention is a return that breaks his word. So his course is to say, "You are to me like the back of my mother—you are divorced," consecutively, so that no expiation is incumbent upon him.

From this principle branch several questions:

The first: If he dies immediately after the ẓihār, there is no expiation, since retention was not actualized—for it requires a period of time in which he had the capacity to divorce. If he divorced her with a revocable divorce, there is no return. If he then took her back (rājaʿa), al-Shāfiʿī's text (naṣṣ) states that the very act of taking back is a return. He also stated that if he apostatized and then returned [to Islam], the very act of Islam is not a return. Likewise, if he irrevocably divorced her and renewed the marriage, and we say the ẓihār and the violation return, the mere renewal is not a return, because Islam aims at changing religion, and marriage aims at renewing ownership, whereas taking back (rajʿah) has no meaning other than retaining the wife. Among our companions, some derived a position (wajh) analogizing rajʿah to marriage, and marriage and apostasy to rajʿah, extending the two positions. But the distinction, and the establishment of the text, is more apparent. If it is said: If he took an oath of abstention (īlāʾ), then irrevocably divorced, and renewed the marriage, expiation becomes incumbent upon him by intercourse even if we do not say the violation returns—so why does the expiation of ẓihār not return? We say: Because the oath is independent in itself without marriage, whereas ẓihār is not conceivable except in marriage. And the expiation here is like the demand for return (fayʾah) in īlāʾ—it is among the specific properties (khaṣāʾiṣ) and does not return in a second marriage. Yes, if he pronounced ẓihār and then returned until she became forbidden to him, the expiation is settled (istaqarrat). If he then divorced and renewed [the marriage], the prohibition continues until expiation. As for if she was a slave-girl and he purchased her, there is a disagreement built upon whether the prohibition of divorce and liʿān extends to ownership by the right hand (milk al-yamīn), as we mentioned.

The second question: If he pronounces ẓihār against his slave-girl wife and then purchases her immediately, there are two positions:
- One: The purchase negates the return, like divorce, because it is a severance (qāṭiʿ).
- Second: It does not, because it transfers her from one lawful state to another, so it is a return. This applies if we say the prohibition of ẓihār extends to ownership by the right hand.

Then Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: His saying "I purchased" must be connected to the ẓihār. If he busied himself with its preliminaries, the return occurs. The companions (aṣḥāb) said: If its preliminaries were impossible, it is as he said; if they were readily available in the near term, he is not a returner. As for if he suspended her divorce after the ẓihār upon entry [into a house], he is a returner even if entry was readily available, since there is no benefit in suspension while he is capable of immediate execution. If he had suspended it beforehand and then entered consecutively, there is no return if entry was readily available.

If he pronounced liʿān (mutual imprecation) immediately after the ẓihār, the apparent text (ẓāhir al-naṣṣ) is that it prevents the return. Then they disagreed on its formulation. Some said: If he accused her of adultery after the ẓihār and did not delay in hastening to raise the matter to the judge, according to custom, there is no return. Others said: The words of the liʿān should be connected to the ẓihār, with the accusation and the raising being prior. Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: The last word should be connected to the ẓihār, for it is the severance. He was compelled on this, as if he said immediately after the ẓihār, "O Zaynab, you are divorced." It was said: His saying "O Zaynab" does not necessitate the return, because it is part of the speech—likewise the words of liʿān.

The third question: If he suspended the ẓihār upon an act of another, and it occurred without his knowledge, he is not a returner. When he learns of it, he should hasten to divorce. If he suspended it upon his own act, and he did it but forgot the ẓihār, he is a returner, because in forgetting his own act he is not excused.

The fourth question: If he says, "You are to me like the back of my mother for five months," it is invalid according to the old position (qadīm), because it departs from the customary. According to the new position (jadīd), it is valid if we give preponderance to the resemblance to oaths. If we give preponderance to the resemblance to divorce, then no, because a time-limited divorce is perpetual (abad), due to the dominance of divorce, and this is not apparent for ẓihār. It was said: It is valid as perpetual, by analogy to divorce.

The ramification: If we liken it to oaths, it is valid as time-limited, and the return is by coitus—al-Shāfiʿī's text states this, because he awaits a lawful release after the months, and he only retains for that purpose, so his mere retention is not contradictory. Al-Muzanī (may God have mercy on him) objected to this and said: There is no difference between it and the absolute [ẓihār]. Some companions said: Al-Shāfiʿī had an old position that the return is coitus, applied uniformly to the absolute and the restricted—but this is corrupt, because he stated the text on the new position, and the distinction is what we mentioned.

According to the text, if he has intercourse, intercourse becomes forbidden, so he must withdraw immediately upon the insertion of the glans (taghyīf al-ḥashafah). According to the school of Ibn Khayrān, the first intercourse is also forbidden likewise. Al-Ṣaydalānī said: If he has intercourse, we know that he was a returner immediately after the utterance, and his retention is interpreted accordingly. In this there is a jurisprudence that agrees with the text and repels al-Muzanī's objection. On this basis, we do not permit the first intercourse, for it reveals the prohibition before it—like if he said, "You are divorced before intercourse," for then intercourse is forbidden.

The fifth question: If he says to four wives, "You are all to me like the back of my mother," he becomes a muẓāhir against all of them. But there is a disagreement on whether the expiation is multiple or single, due to the unity of the utterance. This is like the disagreement on whether, if one accuses a group of adultery with a single word, the ḥadd (penalty) is multiple. The resemblance to oaths necessitates unity, because the word is one; the resemblance to divorce necessitates multiplicity, due to the multiplicity of the subjects. If we say it is multiple, it is obvious. If we say it is single, then if he retains all of them, one expiation is incumbent. If he divorces three and retains one, one expiation is incumbent, because the contradiction of ẓihār by return is realized by retaining one. It is not like his saying, "By God, I will not have intercourse with you all," for there is no expiation for intercourse with one, because his violation is realized by intercourse with all. The verification is that ẓihār here is attached to divorcing all.

As for if he pronounces ẓihār against them with four words consecutively, four expiations are obligatory. By the second ẓihār he is a returner to the first, by the third a returner to the second, and by the fourth a returner to the third. If he says immediately after the fourth, "You are divorced," then three expiations are incumbent. If he does not say it, then four expiations.

The sixth question: If he repeats the word of ẓihār consecutively and says, "I intended by the second an emphasis of the first," it is accepted. But is he a returner? There are two positions:
- One: Yes, because his occupation with emphasis is a neglect of divorce.
- Second: No, because he is not thereby a retainer, since emphasis is in the ruling of completing the speech.

If he intended another ẓihār, then on the multiplicity of ẓihār with a single woman there are two paths (ṭarīqān):
- One: Extending the two positions on the multiplicity of expiation.
- Second: Affirming multiplicity with certainty, giving preponderance to the side of the utterance.

There is no disagreement that if one accuses a single person of adultery twice, the ḥadd is one. Then if he divorces immediately after the second, he is not a returner in the second. Is he a returner in the first, due to his occupation with the second? There are two positions, arranged on the case of intending emphasis. Here it is more apt that he be a returner, because it is speech independent in itself. As for if time intervened, he is a returner in the first, and the second ẓihār is validly contracted if we say the expiation is multiple; otherwise, there is no benefit in it.

As for if we say it is multiple, and he says, "I intended emphasis," with an intervening interval—is he accepted here? There is hesitation in it, per the answer of al-Qaffāl, as we mentioned in īlāʾ, because it resembles a report (ikhbār).

The seventh question: If he goes mad immediately after the ẓihār, he is not a returner. If he recovers, the mere recovery is not a return. But if he does not divorce immediately after recovery, he becomes a returner. If he said, "If I do not marry over you, then you are to me like the back of my mother," there is no ẓihār at present. If he dies before marrying, despair (yaʾs) occurs, and he becomes a muẓāhir and a returner just before death—thus said Ibn al-Ḥaddād. Some companions said: The ẓihār is contracted, and there is no return, because he died immediately after the contraction of the ẓihār. His statement would only be sound if the contraction of the ẓihār were retroactive to the first [condition]. What Ibn al-Ḥaddād mentioned is more penetrating (aghwaṣ), so let it be pondered.

If it is said: Is intercourse forbidden by the ẓihār itself or by the return? We say: By the return. For if it were by the mere ẓihār, the expiation would be settled even if he divorced immediately after it, such that if he wished to have intercourse with her by a new marriage or by ownership of the right hand, it would not be permissible except with expiation—and it is not so. But when he returns, it becomes forbidden, and the expiation becomes obligatory and settled—not because of making intercourse lawful, for if he irrevocably divorced her after the return, the expiation does not lapse, because it was settled by the return that contradicted the ẓihār, just as it is settled by the violation (ḥanath) in an oath. Thus the expiation is obligatory by both the ẓihār and the return together, and the ẓihār is one of its two causes, like the oath. Therefore Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: If he said, "If I enter the house, then you are to me like the back of my mother," and then he manumitted [a slave] for the ẓihār, and then entered, the manumission is valid, because it came after one of the two causes. Some companions disagreed and said: Its parallel is if he said, "If I enter the house, then by God I will not speak to you," and then manumitted before entering—it does not suffice, because he only becomes a swearer upon entry. But it is possible to say: The cause is his becoming a swearer and a muẓāhir, and this has occurred, so it suffices. And God knows best.

= The Book of Expiations (Kaffārāt) =

Its means are three: manumission, fasting, and feeding. Manumission does not enter into the ransom (fidyah) of pilgrimage, and feeding does not enter into the expiation of homicide on one of the two positions. The expiation for intercourse [during Ramadan] and for ẓihār are equal in order: manumission, then fasting, then feeding. Likewise the expiation for homicide, if we say feeding enters it. The expiation for oaths is on the option between manumission, clothing, and feeding; if one is unable, then fasting three days. This will come in its place. The purpose here is the expiation of ẓihār, and within it are included several rulings on expiations.
