chapters.arabic_text:
### | القسم الثاني من الكتاب في عدة الوفاة وحكم السكنى

وفيه بابان - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في موجب العدة وقدرها
وكيفيتها وفيه فصول - صلى الله عليه وسلم -

### | الفصل الأول في الموجب والقدر

فنقول المتوفى عنها زوجها عليها عدة الوفاة ممسوسة كانت أو لم تكن وإن
كانت حاملا فمهما وضعت حلت ولو في الساعة ويحل لها غسل الزوج عندنا بعد
العدة وبعد نكاح زوج آخر وإن كانت حائلا فتعتد أربعة أشهر وعشرا والأمة
تعتد بشهرين وخمسة أيام وتنقضي العدة وإن لم تحض في هذه المدة خلافا لمالك
رحمه الله لأن الله تعالى لم يتعرض للحيض مع تعرض النساء له ومالك رحمه
الله يقول لا أقل من حيضة واحدة أو وقوع الحيض المعتاد مرة أو مرات

### | فرع

لو طلق إحدى امرأتيه على الإبهام ومات قبل البيان فعلى كل واحدة أربعة
أشهر وعشر للإحتياط إن كانتا حائلتين غير مدخول بهما وإن كانتا حاملتين
فعليهما التربص إلى حين الوضع وإن كانتا حائلتين من ذوات الأشهر فعليهما
أربعة أشهر وعشر إذ تنقضي الأشهر الثلاث أيضا وإن كانتا من ذوات الأقراء
فعلى كل واحدة التربص بأقصى الأجلين ويكفي غير المدخول بها تربص أربعة أشهر
وعشر

### | الفصل الثاني في المفقود زوجها

فإن وصل خبر موته ببينة فعدتها من وقت الموت عندنا وقال علي رضي الله عنه
من وقت بلوغ الخبر وإن اندرس خبره وأثره وغلب على الظنون موته فقولان
أحدهما أنها زوجته إلى أن تقوم البينة بموته وهو القياس لأن النكاح ثابت
بيقين فكيف يقطع بالشك
والثاني أنها تتربص أربع سنين ثم تعتد بعد ذلك عدة الوفاة وقد قلد
الشافعي فيه عمر رضي الله عنهما في القديم ورجع عنه في الجديد وقال لو قضى
به قاض نقضت قضاءه إذ بان له أن تقليد الصحابة لا يجوز للمجتهد
وقد طول الأصحاب في التفريع عليه وقد ذكرناه في المذهب البسيط فلا معنى
له مع  صحة الرجوع عنه
ثم على الجديد فلها طلب النفقة من مال الزوج أبدا فإن تعذر كان لها طلب
الفسخ بعذر النفقة على أصح القولين

### | الفصل الثالث في الإحداد

وذلك واجب في عدة الوفاة وغير واجب في عدة الرجعية وفي عدة البائنة قولان
وفي المفسوخ نكاحها طريقان منهم من قطع بأنها لا تجب كالمعتدة من شبهة وكأم
الولد إذا مات عنها سيدها ووجه حداد المطلقة البائنة القياس على عدة الوفاة
ووجه الفرق أنها مجفوة بالطلاق وإنما يليق الإحداد بالمتفجعة بالموت
والأصل في وجه الإحداد قول رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
لا يحل لامرأة تؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر أن تحد على ميت فوق ثلاث إلا على
زوج أربعة أشهر وعشرا فأفاد هذا جواز الحداد ثلاثة أيام على الجملة وتحريمه
بعد الثلاث وبعد العدة
ومعناه ترك الزينة والطيب على قصد الحداد وإلا فلا منع عن ترك الزينة فإن
قيل وما كيفية الحداد قلنا معناه ترك التزين والتطيب والحداد من الحد وهو
المنع والتزين إنما يكون بالتنظيف والثياب والحلي
أما التنظف بالقلم والإستحداد والغسل وإزالة الوسخ فلا يحرم وأما الثياب
فالنظر في جنسها ولونها أما الجنس فتحل كلها سوى الإبريسم فيحل الخز
الدبيقي والكتان وغيره مما يحل للرجال وإنما الإبريسم فإنما أحل لها لأجل
التزين للرجال وقال العراقيون الإبريسم في حقها كالقطن في حق الرجال وإنما
عليها ترك المصبوغات من الثياب والأول أصح
وأما الحلي فيحرم ما هو من الذهب لأنها خاصية النساء والظاهر أنه أيضا
يحرم التحلي باللآلىء المجردة لأنها للزينة وأما التختم بخاتم يحل مثله
للرجال فلا يحرم
وأما المصبوغ للتزين كالأحمر والأصفر والاخضر فهو حرام من القطن والكتان
وغيره
وإنما الأسود والأكهب الكدر وما لا يتزين به فهو جائز ولا فرق بين أن
يصبغ بعد النسج أو قبله وخصص أبو إسحاق المروزي رحمه الله التحريم بالمصبوغ
بعد النسج أما الثوب الخشن إذا صبغ على خلاف العادة صبغ الزينة حكى صاحب
التقريب فيه قولين ووجه المنع أنه من البعد تظهر به  الزينة
وأما الزينة في أثاث البيت والفرش فلا تحرم وإنما الحداد في بدنها وأما
الطيب فيحرم عليها ما يحرم على المحرم ويحرم عليها أن تدهن رأسها ولحيتها
إن كانت لها لحية كالمحرم ولا يحرم عليها أن تدهن بدنها إن لم يكن فيه طيب
وإنما يمنع في الشعر
وأما تصفيف الشعر وتجعيده بغير دهن ففيه تردد وأما الإكتحال فقد قال
الشافعي رضي الله عنه لا بأس بالإثمد فاتفقوا على أنه أراد به العربيات
فإنهن إلى السواد أميل فلا يزينهن الإثمد أما البيضاء فلا يجوز ذلك لها إلا
لعلة الرمد وعليها أن تكتحل ليلا وتمسح نهارا هكذا أمر رسول الله صلى الله
عليه وسلم أم سلمة رضي الله عنها إلا أن تحتاج إلى ذلك نهارا أيضا فيجوز
وعليها ملازمة المسكن إلا لحاجة
ولو تركت جميع ذلك عصت ربها وانقضت عدتها
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في السكنى - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
وفيه أربعة فصول
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-د-د (ʿ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Counting, enumeration; the appointed number of days or months prescribed by law.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legally prescribed term of waiting (ʿiddah) that bars remarriage, rooted in the divine ordinance of enumeration for a fixed duration.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is numerical counting; metaphorical extension to the legal waiting period as a "counted" span of ritual observance.
- Root: س-ك-ن (s-k-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Dwelling, tranquility, settled abode; the place of residence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The widow's mandated right to remain in the marital home during the ʿiddah, as a protective measure of dignity and mourning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal dwelling; legally, the enforced residence (suknā) as a distinct obligation from the ʿiddah itself.
- Root: ح-د-د (ḥ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Boundary, limit, prohibition; to prevent or restrain.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iḥdād—the widow's ritual abstention from adornment as a mark of mourning, derived from the root meaning "restraint."
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "barrier"; metaphorical transfer to the prohibition of beautification during the mourning period.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — Governing the nuanced legal conditions (e.g., "if pregnant, then upon delivery") and exceptions (e.g., "except for need") that structure the juristic rulings.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division of the book concerns the waiting period (ʿiddah) for widowhood and the ruling on residence (suknā). It comprises two chapters—peace be upon him. The first chapter addresses what necessitates the ʿiddah and its measure; the second addresses its modality. It contains several sections—peace be upon him.

### First Section: On What Necessitates the ʿiddah and Its Measure

We say: A woman whose husband has died is obligated to observe the ʿiddah of widowhood, whether she was consummated with or not. If she is pregnant, then whenever she delivers, she becomes lawful (to remarry), even if that occurs within the very hour. In our school, it is lawful for her to wash her deceased husband after the ʿiddah and after marrying another husband. If she is not pregnant, she observes a waiting period of four months and ten days. A slave woman observes two months and five days. The ʿiddah expires even if she does not menstruate during this period, contrary to Mālik—may God have mercy on him—because God Most High did not mention menstruation, despite women's frequent mention of it. Mālik—may God have mercy on him—holds that there must be at least one menstruation, or the occurrence of the customary menses once or several times.

### Branch

If a man divorced one of his two wives ambiguously and died before clarification, then each woman must observe four months and ten days as a precaution, if both are non-pregnant and unconsummated. If both are pregnant, they must wait until delivery. If both are non-pregnant and among those whose term is counted in months, they observe four months and ten days, since the three months also expire. If they are among those whose term is counted by menstrual cycles, each must wait the longer of the two terms. For the unconsummated one, waiting four months and ten days suffices.

### Second Section: On the Woman Whose Husband Is Missing

If news of his death arrives with valid testimony, her ʿiddah begins from the time of death in our school. ʿAlī—may God be pleased with him—said it begins from the time the news reaches her. If his news and trace have been effaced, and overwhelming conjecture suggests his death, there are two opinions. One: she remains his wife until evidence establishes his death—this is the analogical ruling (qiyās), because marriage is established with certainty, so how can it be severed by doubt? The second: she waits four years, then observes the ʿiddah of widowhood thereafter. Al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—had followed ʿUmar—may God be pleased with them both—in this in the old school (al-qadīm), but he retracted it in the new school (al-jadīd). He said: If a judge ruled by it, I would overturn his ruling, for it became clear to him that following the Companions (taqlīd) is not permissible for a mujtahid. The companions (of al-Shāfiʿī) have elaborated extensively on its ramifications, which I have mentioned in The Simple Compendium (al-Basīṭ); there is no point in repeating it given the soundness of the retraction. Then, according to the new school, she may seek maintenance from the husband's estate indefinitely. If that proves impossible, she may seek annulment of the marriage due to the lack of maintenance, according to the more correct of the two opinions.

### Third Section: On Iḥdād (Mourning Abstention)

This is obligatory during the ʿiddah of widowhood, not obligatory during the ʿiddah of a revocable divorce (rajʿī). Regarding the ʿiddah of an irrevocable divorce (bāʾin), there are two opinions. For a woman whose marriage is annulled, there are two paths: some definitively hold it is not obligatory, like the woman observing ʿiddah due to a doubtful marriage, and like the umm walad when her master dies. The basis for requiring iḥdād from the irrevocably divorced woman is analogy to the ʿiddah of widowhood. The basis for distinguishing is that she is repudiated by divorce, and iḥdād befits only one stricken by death. The foundational proof for iḥdād is the saying of the Messenger of God—peace be upon him: {«لَا يَحِلُّ لِامْرَأَةٍ تُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ أَنْ تُحِدَّ عَلَى مَيِّتٍ فَوْقَ ثَلَاثٍ إِلَّا عَلَى زَوْجٍ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْرًا»} ("It is not lawful for a woman who believes in God and the Last Day to mourn a dead person beyond three days, except for a husband—four months and ten days.") This establishes the permissibility of mourning for three days in general, and its prohibition beyond three days and beyond the ʿiddah.

Its meaning is the abandonment of adornment and perfume with the intent of mourning (iḥdād); otherwise, there is no prohibition on abandoning adornment. If it is asked: What is the modality of iḥdād? We say: Its meaning is abandoning beautification and perfuming. Iḥdād derives from al-ḥadd, which is prohibition. Beautification occurs through cleanliness, garments, and jewelry.

As for cleanliness—through trimming nails, shaving pubic hair, bathing, and removing filth—it is not prohibited. As for garments, consideration is given to their type and color. Regarding type: all are permissible except silk (ibrīsam). Thus, brocaded khazz, linen, and other fabrics permissible for men are lawful. Silk was only made lawful for her for the purpose of adornment before men. The Iraqis said: Silk for her is like cotton for men; she is only required to abandon dyed garments. The first opinion is more correct.

As for jewelry: what is made of gold is prohibited, for it is a particularity of women. The apparent position is that adorning with bare pearls is also prohibited, for they are for adornment. As for wearing a ring that is permissible for men, it is not prohibited.

As for garments dyed for adornment—like red, yellow, and green—they are prohibited, whether of cotton, linen, or other fabrics. Only black, dull gray, and what is not used for adornment are permissible. There is no difference between dyeing after weaving or before. Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī—may God have mercy on him—restricted the prohibition to dyeing after weaving. As for a coarse garment dyed contrary to custom with a dye of adornment, the author of al-Taqrīb reported two opinions. The basis for prohibition is that adornment appears through it from a distance.

As for adornment in household furnishings and carpets, it is not prohibited; iḥdād pertains only to her body. As for perfume: whatever is prohibited for a pilgrim in iḥrām is prohibited for her. It is prohibited for her to oil her head and her beard—if she has a beard—like the pilgrim. It is not prohibited for her to oil her body if there is no perfume in it; the restriction applies only to the hair.

As for arranging and curling the hair without oil, there is hesitation. As for kohl: al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—said there is no harm in using ithmid (antimony). They agreed that he meant Arab women, for they incline toward blackness, and ithmid does not adorn them. As for a fair-skinned woman, that is not permissible for her except for the ailment of ophthalmia. She must apply kohl at night and wipe it off during the day. Thus did the Messenger of God—peace be upon him—command Umm Salama—may God be pleased with her—unless she needs it during the day as well, in which case it is permissible.

She must remain in her dwelling except for a need. If she abandons all of this, she disobeys her Lord, yet her ʿiddah expires.

—Peace be upon him—The Second Chapter: On Residence (Suknā)—peace be upon him—
It contains four sections.

### | الفصل الأول فيمن تستحق السكنى

وتستحق المطلقة المعتدة بائنة كانت أو رجعية لقوله تعالى {لا تخرجوهن من
بيوتهن} ولا تستحق المعتدة عن وطء الشبهة ونكاح فاسد ولا المستولدة إذا
عتقت لأن الآية وردت في النكاح نعم هل تجب في عدة الوفاة قولان وفي عدة بعد
انفساخ النكاح طريقان منهم من قال قولان ومنهم من قطع بأنها لا تستحق إن
كان الفسخ منها بعيبه او عتقها او كان منه ولكن بعيبها أو ما يكون بسبب
منها أما ما ينفرد به الزوج كردته وإسلامه ففيه قولان ومأخذ التردد أن
الآية وردت في فراق الطلاق وهذا تردد في أن فراق الموت والفسخ هل هو في
معناه لأن إيجاب السكنى بعد البينونة كالخارج عن القياس
وأما الصغيرة التي لا تحتمل الجماع ففي سكناها من الخلاف ما في نفقتها في
صلب النكاح وكذلك الأمة إذا طلقت فإن قلنا الزوج يستحق تعيين المسكن في صلب
النكاح فعليها ملازمة المسكن بعد النكاح وإن قلنا إن السيد يبوئها
بيتا وطلقت في ذلك البيت فالظاهر أنها  لا يلزمها ملازمة المسكن لأن العدة
تلتفت على النكاح وقيل إنه يجب ذلك
ثم إذا أوجبنا ملازمة المسكن ففي وجوب لزوم السكنى على الزوج خلاف يلتفت
على النفقة في صلب النكاح فحيث كان يجب النفقة تجب السكنى بعد الطلاق
أما الناشزة إذا طلقت في دوام النشوز قال القاضي لا سكنى لها إذ لم يكن
لها نفقة وهذا فيه نظر لأنها إن طلقها في مسكن النكاح فيجب عليها شرعا لزوم
المسكن فإن أطاعت في ذلك فبالحري أن تستحق السكنى

### | الفصل الثاني في أحوال المعتدة وهل يباح لها مفارقة المسكن

فنقول يجب عليها لزوم المسكن حقا لله تعالى فلا يسقط برضا الزوج وإنما
يباح الخروج بعذر ظاهر والأعذار على ثلاث مراتب
الأولى ما يرجع إلى طلب الزيادة كزيارة وعمارة واستنماء مال وتعجيل حج
الإسلام ولا يجوز الخروج لمثل ذلك
الثانية ما ينتهي إلى حد الضرورة كوجوب الهجرة والتمكين من إقامة الحد أو
خافت على زوجها أو مالها لأن الموضع غير حصين أو كانت تتأذى بأحمائها أو
تؤذيهن وكل ذلك تسليط على الإنتقال لأن هذه المهمات أقوى في الشرع من لزوم
المسكن في العدة
الثالثة ما ينتهي إلى حد الحاجة كالخروج للطعام والشراب أو تدارك مال
أخبرت بأنه أشرف على الضياع فذلك أيضا رخصة في الخروج في حق من لا كافل لها
ونحو ذلك وإن كان هذا العذر نادرا وكذلك حكم ملازمة المنزل في السفر إذا
كانوا ينتجعون ويسافرون اعتيادا فلها المسافرة معهم ومهما خرجت لحاجة
فينبغي أن تخرج بالنهار لأن الليل مظنة الآفات
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ك-ن (sakana)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be still, to settle, to dwell"; al-sakan denotes a place of repose and residence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, suknā is a proprietary right of dwelling attached to the ʿiddah, tied to the sanctity of the marriage bond (ḥurmat al-nikāḥ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = physical dwelling; metaphorical (majāz) = the legal obligation of lūzūm al-maskan (confinement to the residence), which is a juristic construct, not mere physical presence.
- Root: ع-د-د (ʿaddada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Counting, enumeration; ʿiddah is the prescribed waiting period counted in days or menstrual cycles.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A period of ritual and legal purity (barāʾah al-dhimmah) and verification of the womb (barāʾah al-raḥim).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = numerical count; metaphorical = the entire legal regime of waiting, including housing and maintenance.
- Root: ن-ش-ز (nashaza)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Rising, elevation; nushūz is the wife's rebellion against marital duties.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A moral-legal state of disobedience (maʿṣiyyah) that suspends financial rights.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = physical elevation; metaphorical = spiritual/legal defiance.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The phrase "إذا طلقت" (when she is divorced) sets a conditional frame where the ruling (ḥukm) is suspended on the occurrence of the condition, requiring careful parsing of the protasis and apodosis in periodic legal sentences.
chapters.translation:
I say: The divorced woman undergoing her waiting period (al-muʿtaddah) is entitled to housing, whether the divorce is irrevocable (bāʾin) or revocable (rajʿī), due to His saying, the Exalted: {«Lā tukhrijūhunna min buyūtihinna»} ("Do not expel them from their houses") [Q. 65:1]. However, the woman observing the ʿiddah due to intercourse under a mistaken presumption (waṭʾ al-shubhah) or an invalid marriage (nikāḥ fāsid) is not entitled to housing, nor is the umm walad (slave-mother of a child) when she is emancipated, because the verse was revealed specifically concerning marriage. Yes, regarding whether housing is obligatory during the ʿiddah of death (ʿiddat al-wafāh), there are two opinions (qawlān). And regarding the ʿiddah following the dissolution of the marriage (infisākh al-nikāḥ), there are two paths (ṭarīqān): among the scholars are those who affirm two opinions, and among them are those who decisively rule that she is not entitled to housing if the dissolution originated from her side—whether due to a defect (ʿayb) in her, or her emancipation (ʿitq)—or if it originated from the husband's side but was caused by her defect or by something attributable to her. As for that which is exclusively the husband's act, such as his apostasy (riddah) or his conversion to Islam (islām), there are two opinions. The basis of the hesitation (taraddud) is that the verse was revealed concerning separation by divorce (farāq al-ṭalāq), and this hesitation concerns whether separation by death and dissolution are analogous to it in meaning, because imposing housing after irrevocable separation (baynūnah) is like an exception to analogical reasoning (khārij ʿan al-qiyās).

As for the minor girl who cannot bear intercourse, her entitlement to housing follows the same disagreement as her entitlement to maintenance (nafaqah) during the subsistence of the marriage. Likewise, the slave-woman (al-amah) when she is divorced: if we hold that the husband is entitled to designate the residence during the marriage, then she is obligated to confine herself to the residence after the marriage. But if we hold that the master (al-sayyid) assigns her a house, and she is divorced while in that house, then the apparent ruling (al-ẓāhir) is that she is not obligated to confine herself to the residence, because the ʿiddah is attached to the marriage. Yet it has been said that this obligation does apply.

Then, when we impose the obligation of confinement to the residence, there is a disagreement regarding the obligation of the husband to provide housing (luzūm al-suknā), which is attached to the ruling on maintenance during the marriage: wherever maintenance is obligatory, housing becomes obligatory after divorce.

As for the rebellious wife (al-nāshizah) who is divorced while in a state of persistent nushūz, al-Qāḍī [Abū Ḥāmid al-Marwazī] said: she has no right to housing, since she had no right to maintenance. But this view requires scrutiny, because if he divorced her in the marital residence, then she is legally obligated to confine herself to the residence; and if she obeys in that regard, then it is all the more fitting that she be entitled to housing.

---

ENGLISH_TITLE: The Second Chapter on the States of the Woman in ʿIddah and Whether She Is Permitted to Leave the Residence

QUAD_ANCHORS:
- Root: خ-ر-ج (kharaja)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To exit, to go out; ikhrāj is expulsion, takhrīj is permission to exit.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal context, khurūj is a physical act that may violate a divine command (ḥaqq Allāh) unless excused by a valid ʿudhr.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = spatial exit; metaphorical = legal dispensation (rukhṣah) that transforms prohibition into permissibility.
- Root: ع-ذ-ر (ʿadhara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Excuse, pretext; ʿudhr is a legitimate ground that lifts blame.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A cause (sabab) recognized by the Lawgiver as sufficient to suspend a strict obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = apology; metaphorical = juristic category of necessity (ḍarūrah) or need (ḥājah) that overrides default rules.
- Root: ض-ر-ر (ḍarra)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Harm, injury; ḍarūrah is a state of extreme necessity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A threshold where preservation of life, religion, or property (maqāṣid) outweighs a lesser obligation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = physical harm; metaphorical = legal principle "al-ḍarūrāt tubīḥ al-maḥẓūrāt" (necessities permit prohibitions).
- Sībawayh Rule: Gradation of Conditions (al-Tadrīj fī al-Shurūṭ) — The tripartite division of excuses (ḥājah, ḍarūrah, taḥṣīl al-ziyādah) is structured as a syntactic hierarchy of conditional clauses, each with distinct legal consequences, requiring precise parsing of "mā yarjiʿu ilā..." (that which pertains to...) constructions.

chapters.title_en: The Third Chapter on What is Obligatory Upon the Husband
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثالث فيما يجب على الزوج

وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا كانت الدار مملوكة للزوج لم يجز له إزعاجها ولا يجوز له
مداخلتها لتحريم الخلوة إلا في موضعين
أحدهما أن تكون هي في حجرة مفردة بالمرافق وعليها باب فإن لم يكن عليها
باب أو كان مرافقها واحدا كالمطبخ والمستراح في الدار لم تجز المداخلة لأن
التوارد على المرافق يفضي إلى الخلوة وكذلك تحرم المداخلة وإن كانت الدار
فيحاء مهما لم  تنفصل المرافق ولم يحجب الباب
الثاني أن يكون معها في الدار محرم لها فلا خلوة وكذلك إن كان مع الرجل
زوجة أخرى أو جارية أو محرم له ولو كان معها أجنبية أو معتدة أخرى فهل يمنع
ذلك الخلوة فيه تردد مأخذه أن النسوة المنفردات هل لهن السفر عند الامن
بغير محرم ولو استخلى رجلان بامرأة فهو محرم وليس ذلك كاستخلاء رجل
بامرأتين والوجه أن يقال إن كان ممن يحتشم أو يخاف من جانبه حكاية ما يجري
من فجور إن كان فهو مانع للخلوة وإلا فلا
فرع لو أراد الزوج بيع الدار وعدتها بالحمل أو الأقراء لم ينعقد لأن
المنفعة مستحقة لها وآخر المدة غير معلوم ولو كانت من ذوات الأشهر فهو كبيع
الدار المستأجرة إلا إذا كان يتوقع طرآن الحيض في الأشهر ففيه طريقان منهم
من لم يلتفت إلى ذلك بناء على الحال ومنهم من منع البيع لتوقع ذلك
فإن صححنا وطرأ الحيض كان كما لو اختلطت الثمار بالمبيع وقد ذكرناه في
البيع
المسألة الثانية إذ كانت الدار مستعارة فعليها الملازمة إلى أن يرجع
المعير فإن رجع فعلى الزوج أن يسلم إليها دارا يليق بها ويبذل الأجرة إن لم
يجد بعارية وكذلك إذا انتهت مدة الإجارة فإن مست الحاجة إلى الأجرة وأفلس
الزوج ضاربت الغرماء بأجرة ثلاثة أشهر إن كانت من ذوات الأشهر وإن كانت من
ذوات الأقراء وعادتها مختلفة ضاربت بالأقل وإن كانت مستقيمة فمقدار العادة
على الأصح وفيه وجه أنها بالأقل وهو ضعيف لأن حصتها لا تسلم إليها وما يخص
الغرماء يسلم إليهم فالإحتياط لجانبها أولى وكذلك الحامل تضارب لتمام تسعة
أشهر فإن الزيادة على ذلك نادر لا يعتبر هذا إذا كان الزوج حاضرا فإن كان
غائبا استقرض القاضي عليه فإن استأجرت من مالها بغير إذن القاضي ففي رجوعها
على الزوج خلاف ولا خلاف في أنها لو كانت في دار مملوكة فلا تباع لحق
الغرماء لأنها كالمرهونة فلا تخرج منها بحال
المسألة الثالثة إذا أسكنها في النكاح ضيقا  لا يليق بها ورضيت وطلقها
فلها أن لا ترضى في العدة وتطلب مسكنا لائقا بها وكذلك لو أسكنها دارا
فيحاء فله أن ينقلها
بعد الطلاق إلى موضع لائق بها لكن قال القاضي ينبغي أن يطلب لها أقرب
مسكن يمكن إلى مسكن النكاح حتى لا يطول ترددها في الخروج وما ذكره لا يبعد
أن يستحب ولا شك في أنه لا يخرجها عن البلدة
المسألة الرابع إن ألزمنا السكنى في عدة الوفاة فهي من التركة فإن لم يكن
وتبرع به الوارث وأراد إسكانها كان لها ذلك وإن قلنا لا تستحق فلو رضي
الوارث بملازمة مسكن النكاح فالظاهر أنه يجب عليها ذلك مطلقا وقيل إن كانت
مشغولة الرحم أو متوهمة الشغل فله ذلك مطلقا لأجل صيانة الماء وإن لم تكن
ممسوسة فلا يلزمها ذلك بل يجب عليها ملازمة أي مسكن شاءت ثم هذا التعيين
للوارث وليس للسلطان ذلك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-ع-ج (za-ʿa-j)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To drive away, expel, or dislodge from a place; forceful removal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Displacement from a rightful abode, violating the wife's established right of domicile (suknā).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical ejection; metaphorically, any act that nullifies her security of residence.
- Root: خ-ل-و (khal-wa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Solitude, seclusion; emptiness of a place from others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The prohibited private seclusion (khalwah) between a man and a non-maḥram woman, a legal impediment to licit interaction.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal spatial emptiness; legally, the specific state of being alone together that triggers rulings on permissibility.
- Root: م-ح-ر-م (maḥ-ram)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Forbidden; a person within the prohibited degrees of marriage.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The permanent unmarriageable kin whose presence negates the risk of seclusion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal prohibition; legally, the protective category of relatives.
- Root: ض-ر-ب (ḍa-ra-ba)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To strike, beat; to share, divide, or apportion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, the creditor's act of competing (muḍārabah) with other creditors for a share of the debtor's assets.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal striking; metaphorically, the equitable distribution of claims against insolvent estates.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (law, idhā, in) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal rulings, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the juristic distinctions.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third chapter concerns what is obligatory upon the husband.

It contains several issues.

**The First Issue:** If the house is owned by the husband, he is not permitted to dislodge her from it, nor is he permitted to enter upon her therein, due to the prohibition of seclusion (khalwah), except in two situations.

**The First Situation:** That she be in a separate chamber with her own conveniences (marāfiq) and with a door upon it. If there is no door upon it, or if her conveniences are shared—such as the kitchen and the lavatory within the house—then entering upon her is not permitted, because the shared use of conveniences leads to seclusion. Likewise, entering upon her is prohibited even if the house is spacious (fayḥāʾ), as long as the conveniences are not separated and the door does not screen [her].

**The Second Situation:** That there be with her in the house a maḥram of hers; then there is no seclusion. Likewise, if there is with the man another wife, or a slave-girl, or a maḥram of his. If there is with her an unrelated woman (ajnabiyyah) or another woman in her waiting period (muʿtaddah), does that prevent seclusion? There is hesitation (taraddud) therein, whose basis is: do women who are alone have the right to travel without a maḥram when security prevails? And if two men seclude themselves with one woman, that is prohibited, and it is not like a man secluding himself with two women. The sound view (al-wajh) is to say: if she is one who is modest (yaḥtashim) or fears that her side may report what transpires of immorality, then that is a preventive of seclusion; otherwise, it is not.

**A Branch (farʿ):** If the husband wishes to sell the house while her waiting period is counted by pregnancies or by menstrual cycles (aqrāʾ), the sale does not conclude, because the usufruct is due to her and the end of the period is unknown. If she is one whose waiting period is counted by months (dhawāt al-ashhur), then it is like selling a rented house—except if the onset of menstruation is anticipated during those months. On this, there are two paths (ṭarīqān): among them is one who does not heed that, based on the present state; and among them is one who prohibits the sale due to that anticipation. If we validate the sale and menstruation then supervenes, it is as if fruits had become mixed with the sold item—and we have already mentioned this in the Book of Sales.

**The Second Issue:** If the house is borrowed (mustaʿārah), then she must remain therein until the lender (muʿīr) returns. If he returns, then the husband must hand over to her a house befitting her, and must pay the rent if he cannot find one on loan. Likewise, if the term of the lease (ijārah) expires. If she is in need of rent and the husband becomes insolvent, she competes with the creditors (ghuramāʾ) for the rent of three months if she is one whose waiting period is counted by months. If she is one whose waiting period is counted by menstrual cycles and her habit is irregular, she competes for the lesser amount. If her habit is regular, then the amount is according to her habit, on the more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ). There is a view that it is the lesser amount, but that is weak, because her share is not delivered to her, whereas what belongs to the creditors is delivered to them—so exercising caution on her side is more appropriate. Likewise, the pregnant woman competes for the full nine months, for any increase beyond that is rare and not taken into account. This applies when the husband is present. If he is absent, the judge borrows on his behalf. If she rents from her own wealth without the judge's permission, there is disagreement (khilāf) on her recourse against the husband. There is no disagreement that if she were in a house owned [by the husband], it is not sold for the creditors' right, because it is like a pledged property (marhūnah)—she is not removed from it under any circumstance.

**The Third Issue:** If he housed her during the marriage in a cramped dwelling unbefitting her, and she consented, then he divorced her—she has the right not to consent during the waiting period and to demand a dwelling befitting her. Likewise, if he housed her in a spacious house, he has the right to move her after the divorce to a place befitting her. However, Judge [Abū Ṭayyib al-Ṭabarī] said: one should seek for her the nearest possible dwelling to the marital home, so that her going out is not prolonged. What he mentioned is not far from being recommended (mustaḥabb). There is no doubt that he does not remove her from the town.

**The Fourth Issue:** If we impose the dwelling (suknā) during the waiting period of death (ʿiddat al-wafāh), then it is from the estate (tarikah). If it is not [so imposed], and the heir voluntarily provides it and wishes to house her [there], she has that right. If we say she is not entitled [to it], and the heir consents to her remaining in the marital home, then the apparent view is that it is obligatory upon her absolutely. It is said: if she is occupied with pregnancy or suspected of being so, then he has that right absolutely, for the sake of preserving the seed (ṣiyānat al-māʾ). If she is not touched [by intercourse], then it is not obligatory upon her; rather, she must remain in whichever dwelling she chooses. Then this designation (taʿyīn) belongs to the heir, and the sultan does not have that authority.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الرابع في بيان مسكن النكاح

وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا أذن لها في الإنتقال إلى دار أخرى ثم طلقها قبل الإنتقال
لازمت المسكن الأول وإن طلق بعد الإنتقال لازمت المسكن الثاني والعبرة في
الإنتقال بدنها وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله العبرة بنقل الأمتعة
وإن صادفها الطلاق في الطريق فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها ترجيح الأول استصحابا
والثاني ترجيح الثاني لأنها انتقلت عن الأول
والثالث أنها تتخير بينهما للتعارض وكذا الكلام فيما إذا أذن لها في
الإنتقال إلى بلدة أخرى ففي جواز الإنصراف خلاف
الثانية لو خرجت إلى سفر بإذنه فطلقها بعد مفارقة عمارة البلد فليس عليها
الإنصراف لأن إبطال أهبة سفرها إضرار فإن فارقت المنزل دون البلد فوجهان
أحدهما يجب الإنصراف لأنها بعد لم تنقطع عن الوطن
والثاني لا لأن ذلك إضرار بإبطال الأهبة
ولا خلاف في أن لها الإنصراف
ثم إذا مضت لوجهها فلها التوقف إلى إنجاز حاجتها وعليها الرجوع لملازمة
المسكن بقية مدة تنقضي في الطريق ففي وجوب الإنصراف خلاف والظاهر أنه لا
يجب ولا فائدة فيه ولا يكلفها التقدم على الرفقة لأجل ذلك وإن  انقضت حاجتها
قبل ثلاثة أيام جاز لها استكمال الثلاث لأنها مدة مكث المسافر شرعا
الثالثة ما ذكرناه في سفر تجارة أو مهم فإن كان سفر نزهة أو ما لا مهم
فيه وقد أذن لها عشرة أيام مثلا فطلقها في أثناء المدة ففي جواز استيفاء
المدة قولان ويجري القولان في وجوب الإنصراف إن طلقها في الطريق وهكذا في
المدة الزائدة على حاجة التجارة في سفر التجارة لأنه ليس فيه مهم ولكن انضم
الإذن في أهبة السفر فاحتمل أن يقال في المنع إضرار
ولو أذن لها في الإعتكاف عشرة أيام فطلقها قبل المدة فإن قلنا لو خرجت
بمثل هنا العذر جاز البناء على الإعتكاف المنذور فعليها الخروج وإن كان
الإعتكاف منذورا لأنه لا ضرر وإنما هو مجرد إذن فهو كما لو أذن لها في
المقام في دار أخرى عشرة أيام فطلاقها يبطل ذلك الإذن وإن قلنا إن الإعتكاف
يبطل فيكون فيه
ضرار كما في أهبة السفر
ولا خلاف في أنها لو خرجت مع الزوج فطلقها في الطريق لزمها الإنصراف
لأنها خرجت بأهبة الزوج فلا تبطل عليها أهبتها والخروج لغرض التجارة غير
جائز لأنه طلب زيادة وإنما جاز ذلك في الدوام للضرار في فوات الأهبة
الرابعة إذا أذن لها في الإحرام وطلقها قبل الإحرام لم تحرم وإن كان بعد
الإحرام وكان بعمرة يمكن تأخيرها ففي وجوب التأخير وجهان ولعل الأصح جواز
الخروج لأن في مصابرة الإحرام ضرارا
الخامسة منزل البدوية كمسكن البلدية لكن إن رحلوا بجملتهم فلها الرحيل
وإن رحل غير أهلها فعليها المقام فإن رحل أهلها وهي آمنة في المقام ففيه
وجهان وهو راجع إلى أن ضرر مفارقة الأهل هل يعتبر
ولو كانوا يرجعون على قرب فعليها المقام إذ لا ضرر ولو ارتحلت معهم
فأرادت المقام بقرية في الطريق جاز فإن ذلك أحسن من السفر بخلاف المأذونة
في السفر فإن رجوعها إلى الوطن أولى من الإقامة في قرية
السادسة إذا صادفها الطلاق في دار أخرى أو بلدة أخرى فقال ارجعي فقالت
طلقت  بعد الإذن في النقلة فأنكر الزوج الإذن نقل عن الشافعي رضي الله عنه
أن القول قوله وهو القياس ولكن نقل أنه إن كان النزاع مع الورثة
فالقول قولها وإلى الفرق ذهب أبو حنيفة رحمه الله وابن سريج وكأن كونها
في غير مسكن النكاح يشهد لها على الورثة لا على الزوج ومن أصحابنا من جعل
المسألتين على قول ومنهم من جعلها على حالين فنقول إنما جعل القول قوله إذا
كان النزاع في اصل اللفظ وإن كان في معنى اللفظ بأن قالت أردت بالإذن
النقلة وقال بل النزهة فالظاهر تصديقها فيقبل قولها

### | القسم الثالث من الكتاب في الإستبراء بسبب ملك اليمين

وفيه ثلاثة فصول

### | الفصل الأول في قدر الإستبراء وشرطه وحكمه

أما قدره فهو قرء واحد لأنه نادى منادي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد
سبي أوطاس
ألا لا توطأ حامل حتى تضع ولا حائل حتى تحيض
وللمستبرأة ثلاثة أحوال
أحدها أن تكون من ذوات الأقراء واستبراؤها بقرء واحد وهو الحيض لقوله
عليه السلام
حتى تحيض ولأنه إذا لم يعتبر إلا قرء واحد فليعتبر الحيض فإنه دليل على
البراءة هذا هو الجديد
وفيه وجه آخر أنه الطهر قياسا على العدة لأن التعبد غالب عليه ولذلك يجب
مع يقين البراءة إذا استبرأها من امرأة أو صبي

- Root: س-ك-ن (s-k-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is stillness, tranquility, and settling; a dwelling (maskin) is where one abides and finds repose.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, maskin denotes the established domicile that grounds marital maintenance and post-divorce lodging obligations (suknā).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical dwelling; metaphorical (majāz) for the legal entitlement to residence as a right attached to the marriage contract.
- Root: ب-ر-ء (b-r-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be free, clear, or exonerated from a claim or impurity; barāʾah is acquittal.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In fiqh, istibrāʾ is the legally prescribed waiting period to ascertain the womb's freedom from pregnancy, thus establishing certainty of non-impregnation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical clearing; metaphorical for legal certification of the womb's vacancy.
- Root: ع-د-د (ʿ-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Counting, numbering; ʿiddah is the prescribed count of periods.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ʿiddah is a devotional (taʿabbudī) ordinance, not purely rational, as it is imposed even when certainty of non-pregnancy exists.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for numerical count; metaphorical for the entire waiting period as a legal construct.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The phrase "until she gives birth" (ḥattā taḍaʿa) and "until she menstruates" (ḥattā taḥīḍa) function as temporal limiters (ghāyah) that define the terminus of prohibition, requiring careful parsing of the governing verb's scope.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth chapter concerns clarifying the residence of marriage (maskin al-nikāḥ).

It contains several issues.

**The First Issue:** If he grants her permission to move to another house, then divorces her before the move, she remains bound to the first residence. But if he divorces her after the move, she is bound to the second residence. The criterion for the move is her physical person (badanuhā). Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — said: the criterion is the transfer of the household goods (amtiʿah).

If the divorce overtakes her while she is en route, there are three positions (wujūh):
1. One gives precedence to the first residence, by way of istiṣḥāb (presumption of continuity).
2. The second gives precedence to the second residence, because she has already departed from the first.
3. The third holds that she may choose between the two, due to the conflicting indicators.

The same discussion applies when he grants her permission to move to another town — there is a disagreement (khilāf) regarding whether she may turn back.

**The Second Issue:** If she departs on a journey with his permission, and he divorces her after she has left the built-up area of the town (ʿimārat al-balad), she is not obliged to turn back, because nullifying her travel preparations (uhbah) would cause her harm (ḍarar). If she has left the house but not yet the town, there are two positions (wajhān):
1. One holds that she must turn back, because she has not yet severed herself from the homeland.
2. The second holds that she need not, because that would be harmful by nullifying her preparations.

There is no disagreement that she has the right to turn back.

Then, if she proceeds on her way, she may pause to accomplish her need, and she must return to adhere to the residence for the remainder of the period that elapses during the journey. Regarding the obligation to turn back, there is a disagreement; the apparent position (al-ẓāhir) is that it is not obligatory, as there is no benefit in it, and she is not compelled to outpace her traveling companions for that sake. If her need is accomplished before three days elapse, she may complete the full three days, because that is the legally recognized duration of a traveler's stay (mukth al-musāfir).

**The Third Issue:** What we have mentioned applies to a journey of trade or of important purpose (muhimm). But if it is a pleasure trip, or one with no important purpose, and he has granted her permission for, say, ten days, then divorces her mid-term — there are two opinions (qawlān) on whether she may complete the full term. The same two opinions apply to the obligation of turning back if he divorces her en route. Likewise, this applies to a period exceeding the need of trade in a trade journey, because there is no important purpose in it; however, the permission for travel preparations is annexed, so it is plausible to say that preventing her would be harmful.

If he grants her permission for iʿtikāf (seclusion in the mosque) for ten days, then divorces her before the term ends — if we hold that when she departs with a valid excuse like this she may build upon a vowed iʿtikāf, then she must depart, even if the iʿtikāf is vowed (mandhūr), because there is no harm involved; it is merely a permission. This is like his granting her permission to reside in another house for ten days — his divorce nullifies that permission. But if we hold that the iʿtikāf is nullified, then there is harm in it, as in the case of travel preparations.

There is no disagreement that if she departs with her husband and he divorces her en route, she must turn back, because she departed with the husband's preparations, so her own preparations are not nullified against her. Departing for the purpose of trade is not permissible, because it seeks increase (ziyādah); rather, it was permitted in the case of continuity (al-dawām) due to the harm of losing preparations.

**The Fourth Issue:** If he grants her permission to enter iḥrām (the state of pilgrimage consecration) and divorces her before she enters iḥrām, she must not enter it. If it is after entering iḥrām, and it is for an ʿumrah that can be postponed, there are two positions on whether postponement is obligatory. Perhaps the more correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that she may depart, because persevering in iḥrām would cause her harm.

**The Fifth Issue:** The dwelling of a Bedouin woman is like the residence of a city woman. However, if her entire tribe departs, she may depart with them. If only those other than her family depart, she must remain. If her family departs while she is safe in remaining, there are two positions — this reverts to the question of whether the harm of separation from one's family is considered.

If they will return shortly, she must remain, as there is no harm. If she departs with them, then wishes to remain in a village along the way, that is permissible, for that is better than traveling — unlike the woman permitted to travel, for whom returning to the homeland is preferable to residing in a village.

**The Sixth Issue:** If the divorce overtakes her in another house or another town, and he says, "Return," while she says, "I was divorced after the permission to move," and the husband denies granting permission — it is transmitted from al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — that the husband's word is accepted, and that is the analogical position (al-qiyās). But it is transmitted that if the dispute is with the heirs (wurathāʾ), then her word is accepted. Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — and Ibn Surayj adopted this distinction. It is as though her being in a place other than the marital residence testifies on her behalf against the heirs, but not against the husband. Among our companions, some treat both cases under a single opinion, and some treat them as two distinct situations. We say: the husband's word is accepted only when the dispute concerns the very wording (aṣl al-lafẓ). But if it concerns the meaning of the wording — as when she says, "By permission I meant the move," and he says, "Rather, I meant a pleasure outing" — then the apparent position is to affirm her statement, and her word is accepted.

---

### The Third Part of the Book: On Istibrāʾ Due to Ownership of the Right Hand

It contains three chapters.

### The First Chapter: On the Measure of Istibrāʾ, Its Condition, and Its Ruling

As for its measure, it is a single qarʾ (menstrual period), because the herald of the Messenger of God — may God's peace and blessings be upon him — proclaimed after the captives of Awtās: «أَلَا لَا تُوطَأُ حَامِلٌ حَتَّى تَضَعَ وَلَا حَائِلٌ حَتَّى تَحِيضَ» ("Verily, no pregnant woman shall be approached until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant woman until she menstruates").

The woman undergoing istibrāʾ has three states:

1. She may be among those who menstruate regularly (dhawāt al-aqrāʾ), and her istibrāʾ is a single qarʾ, namely menstruation (al-ḥayḍ), due to his saying — peace be upon him — «حَتَّى تَحِيضَ» ("until she menstruates"), and because when only one qarʾ is considered, menstruation is the one to consider, for it is the indicator of freedom from pregnancy (barāʾah). This is the new position (al-jadīd).

2. There is another position that it is a period of purity (ṭuhr), by analogy with the ʿiddah, because devotional obligation (taʿabbud) predominates in it. For this reason, it is obligatory even with certainty of non-pregnancy, when one performs istibrāʾ upon a woman or a young girl (ṣabī).

### | التفريع

إذا قضينا بأنه حيض فلا بد من حيض كامل فلا يكفي بقبة حيض وإن قلنا إنه
طهر فهل يكفي بقية الطهر فيه خلاف لأن العدة تشتمل على عدد فجاز أن يعبر عن
شيئين وبعض الثالث بثلاثة ولأنه يجري فيه الحيض مرات ولو صادف الملك آخر
الحيض فانقضى طهر كامل بعده كفى على هذا القول وقيل إنه لا بد من حيض كامل
بعده لتحصل دلالة على البراءة في ملكه وهذا رجوع إلى القول الأول وشهادة
تضعيف هذا القول
الحالة الثانية أن تكون من ذوات الأشهر وفيه قولان
أحدهما أنه يكفي شهر واحد
والثاني أنه لا أقل من ثلاثة أشهر لأنه أقل مدة ضربت شرعا للدلالة على
البراءة والأمور الطبيعية لا تختلف بالرق
وأبو حنيفة رحمه الله يوجب على المستولدة إذا عتقت ثلاثة أقراء أو ثلاثة
أشهر نظرا إلى حريتها في الحال ونحن نكتفي بقرء واحد نظرا إلى جهة الملك
الحالة الثالثة أن تكون حاملا فعدتها بوضع الحمل وإن كان من الزنا لإطلاق
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قوله
حتى تضع ومنهم من قال لا تنقضي بالزنا كما في العدة وقيل هذا يلتفت على
أن المعتبر حيض أم طهر فإن اعتبرنا الحيض من حيث إنه دليل البراءة فكذلك
حمل الزنا دليل البراءة وإلا فلا
أما حكمه فهو تحريم لوجوه الإستمتاع قبل تمامه إلا في المسبية ولأنه لا
يحرم فيها إلا الوطء لأن المانع في الشراء توقع ولد من البائع يمنع صحة
الشراء وولد الحربي لا يمنع جريان الرق وإنما استبراؤها لصيانة ماء المالك
عن الإمتزاج بالحمل فيقتصر التحريم على الوطء ومنهم من سوى وحرم استمتاع
المسبية أيضا تبعا
أما شرطه فإنه يقع بعد القبض ولزوم الملك في مظنة الإستحلال فلو جرت حيضة
قبل قبض الجارية المشتراة ففيه خلاف لضعف الملك والظاهر أنه يجزىء للزوم
الملك نعم لم يعتد بها في الموهوبة قبل القبض وفي الموصى بها قبل القبول
فلا أثر للقبض في الوصية وفي مدة الخيار لا يجزىء إذا قلنا الملك للبائع
وإن قلنا للمشتري فهو كما قبل القبض لضعفه
ولو كانت مجوسية أو مرتدة فأسلمت بعد انقضاء الحيض فقد انقضى في الملك
ولكن لا في مظنة الإستحلال ففيه وجهان
ومن خاصية الإستبراء أنه ليس من شرطه الإمتناع عن الوطء بل لو وطئها
انقضى الإستبراء وعصى بالوطء فإن أحبلها وهي حائض حلت في الحال إذ ما مضى
كان حيضا كاملا وانقطع بالحيض فإن كانت طاهرا لم ينقض الإستبراء إلى وضع

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ر-ء (q-r-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A period of time; specifically, the time of menstruation or the time of purity between two menses — its sense is disputed, as it denotes both.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, it signifies the temporal marker by which the womb’s emptiness (barāʾah) is ascertained; its ambiguity (between purity and menses) generates juristic divergence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes a "turn" or "cycle" of time; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies it to the legal ruling attached to that cycle.
- Root: ب-ر-ء (b-r-ʾ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be free, clear, or exonerated from a claim or encumbrance.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal and theological "acquittal" of the womb from pregnancy — the underlying purpose (maqṣad) of the ʿiddah and istibrāʾ.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical healing from illness; metaphorical: legal certification of emptiness from conception.
- Root: م-ل-ك (m-l-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Possession, ownership, dominion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic discourse, the valid proprietary right (milk) that renders sexual use licit; its strength or weakness determines the validity of the disengagement period.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: holding something in one's hand; metaphorical: legal entitlement, whether firm (lāzim) or precarious (ḍaʿīf).
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa-l-Istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs conditional clauses (idhā, law, fa-in) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal outcomes; the protasis (sharṭ) and apodosis (jawāb) must be parsed to determine whether the condition governs the ruling or merely describes its context.

---

### Sub-Rulings (Tafrīʿ)

If we have ruled that it is menstruation (ḥayḍ), then a complete menstruation is required, and the remainder of a menstruation does not suffice. But if we say that it is purity (ṭuhr), then there is a divergence (khilāf) as to whether the remainder of the purity suffices — because the waiting period (ʿiddah) comprises a number [of cycles], and it is permissible that two full things and part of a third be expressed by the number three. Also, because menstruation runs through it multiple times. And if the ownership [of the slave-girl] coincides with the end of her menstruation, and then a complete purity elapses afterward, it suffices according to this view. But it was said: a complete menstruation after it is necessary, so that an indication of acquittal (barāʾah) is obtained within his ownership. And this is a return to the first view and a testimony to the weakness of this second view.

**The Second Case:** That she be among those who menstruate by months (dhawāt al-ashhur). There are two views on this:
- One: that a single month suffices.
- The second: that nothing less than three months suffices, because it is the minimum period set by the Law (sharʿ) as an indication of acquittal, and natural matters do not differ by reason of slavery.

Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) obliges upon the umm walad (slave-mother of a child), if she is freed, three menstrual cycles (aqrāʾ) or three months — looking to her freedom in the present state. But we suffice with a single cycle (qarʾ), looking to the aspect of ownership (milk).

**The Third Case:** That she be pregnant — her waiting period is concluded by giving birth (waḍʿ al-ḥaml), even if [the pregnancy] is from fornication (zinā), due to the absolute nature of the Messenger of God's (peace be upon him) saying: {«حَتَّى تَضَعَ»} ("until she gives birth"). And among them is one who said: it is not concluded by [birth from] fornication, just as in the ʿiddah. And it was said: this turns upon whether the consideration is menstruation or purity — if we consider menstruation insofar as it is an indication of acquittal, then likewise the pregnancy from fornication is an indication of acquittal; otherwise, not.

**As for its ruling (ḥukm):** It is the prohibition of all forms of enjoyment (istimtāʿ) before its completion — except in the case of the captive woman (sabiyyah). For in her case, only intercourse (waṭʾ) is prohibited, because the impediment in purchase is the anticipation of a child from the seller that would vitiate the validity of the purchase; whereas the child of a warring unbeliever (ḥarbī) does not prevent the operation of slavery (riqq). Rather, her istibrāʾ is only for the preservation of the owner's fluid (māʾ) from mixing with the pregnancy — so the prohibition is restricted to intercourse. And among them is one who equated [the two cases] and prohibited enjoyment of the captive woman as well, by way of following [the analogy].

**As for its condition (sharṭ):** It occurs after taking possession (qabḍ) and the binding of ownership (luzūm al-milk), in the context of presumptive licitness (maẓinnat al-istiḥlāl). So if a menstruation elapsed before taking possession of the purchased slave-girl, there is a divergence concerning it, due to the weakness of ownership. And the apparent [view] is that it suffices, because of the binding of ownership. Yes — it is not counted in the case of the gifted woman (mawhūbah) before possession, nor in the bequeathed woman (mūṣā bihā) before acceptance (qabūl), for possession has no effect in bequest (waṣiyyah). And during the period of option (khiyār), it does not suffice if we say ownership belongs to the seller; but if we say it belongs to the buyer, then it is as before possession, due to its weakness.

And if she were a Magian (majūsiyyah) or an apostate (murtaddah), and then embraced Islam after the completion of her menstruation — it has indeed completed within ownership, but not within the context of presumptive licitness. So there are two aspects (wajhān) concerning it.

And from the specific properties (khāṣṣiyyah) of istibrāʾ: it is not a condition of it to abstain from intercourse. Rather, if he had intercourse with her, the istibrāʾ is concluded, and he has sinned by the intercourse. If he impregnated her while she was menstruating, she becomes licit immediately — for what has passed was a complete menstruation, and [the istibrāʾ] is cut off by the menstruation. But if she was in a state of purity, the istibrāʾ is not concluded until the delivery of the pregnancy.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثاني في سبب الإستبراء

وهو جلب ملك أو زواله
الأول الجلب فمن تجدد له ملك على الجارية هي محل استحلاله توقف حلها على
الإستبراء بعد لزوم ملكه بقرء سواء كان الملك عن هبة أو  بيع وصية أو إرث أو
فسخ أو إقالة وسواء كانت صغيرة أو كبيرة أو حاملا أو حائلا وسواء كان
المالك ممن يتصور منه شغل أو لا يتصور كامرأة أو مجبوب أو صبي وسواء كانت
قد استبرأت قبل البيع أو لم تكن وقال داود لا يجب استبراء البكر وقال مالك
رحمه الله الصغيرة التي لا توطأ لا تستبرأ وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لا يجب
إذا عادت بخيار رؤية أو رد بعيب أو رجوع في هبة أو إقالة قبل القبض وأوجب
في الإقالة بعد القبض
وألحق أصحابنا بزوال الملك المكاتبة إذا عجزت وعادت إلى الحل لأنها صائرة
إلى حالة تستحق المهر على السيد ولذلك تحل أخت المكاتبة
ولا خلاف في أن التحريم بالصوم والرهن لا يؤثر أما زوال إحرامها
وإسلامها بعد الردة وطلاق زوجها إياها ففيه خلاف لتأكيد هذه الأسباب
وإيجاب ذلك في المزدوجة اولى لأن الزوج قد استحق منافعها ثم يرجع الإستحقاق
إليه أما إذا اشترى منكوحته الرقيقة ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه لا يجب لأن الحل دائم من شخص واحد
والثاني يجب لتبدل جهة الحل
ولو باع جاريته بشرط الخيار ثم رجعت إليه في مدة الخيار فإن قلنا لم يزل
ملكه فلا استبراء وإن قلنا زال الملك وحرم الوطء لزم الإستبراء وإن قلنا
زال الملك ولكن الوطء جائز لأنه فسخ فها هنا يحتمل أن يقال الحل مطرد
والجهة متحدة بخلاف شراء الزوجة فلا استبراء ويحتمل أن ينظر إلى تجدد الملك
وبه يعلل استبراء المنكوحة المشتراة
فرع لو اشترى محرمة أو معتدة أو مزوجة ففي وجوب استبرائها بعد انقضاء
العدة أو بعد طلاق الزوج من غير دخول نصوص مضطربة للشافعي رضي الله عنه
فقيل فيه قولان
أحدهما أنه يجب وهو القياس ولا يبعد أن يتأخر الإستبراء عن الملك إلى وقت
الطلاق ونزوال العدة
والثاني أنه لا يجب لأن الموجب جلب الملك ولم تكن إذ ذاك في مظنة
الإستحلال فهو كشراء الأخت من الرضاع لا يوجب الإستبراء ولما حصل الحل لم
يتجدد  ملك حتى يجب به
السبب الثاني زوال الملك فنقول الجارية الموطوءة مستولدة كانت أو لم تكن
فهي في حكم مستفرشة فإذا اعتقت بعد موت السيد أو بالإعتاق فعليها التربص
بقرء واحد وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله أما المستولدة فتتربص عند العتق ولكن
بثلاثة أقراء نظرا إلى كمالها في الحال وأما الأمة فلا تربص عليها وزاد
فقال لو وطئها السيد وأراد في الحال تزويجها جاز من غير استبراء وهذا هجوم
عظيم على خلط المياه وعندنا أن كل جارية موطوءة لا يحل تزويجها إلا بعد
الاستبراء وكأن هذا الإستبراء من نتيجة حصول ملك الزوج فإن ملك السيد لم
يزل إلا أنه يجب تقديمه على الملك لأن النكاح يقصد لحل الوطء فلا يمكن عقده
إلا بحيث يستعقب الحل وأما المشتري فيستبرىء بعد الملك لأن الشراء بقصد
الأغراض المالية فلا يقبل الحجر بسبب الوطء نعم إن عزم على الشراء قدم
الإستبراء عليه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ر-أ (barāʾa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be free/clear of something," from which istibrāʾ derives as "seeking/ensuring freedom" (of the womb from pregnancy).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, it denotes the prescribed waiting period to ascertain the non-pregnancy of a slave-woman (jāriyah) before a new master may lawfully have intercourse with her.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) sense is "seeking disengagement"; here it is a technical legal metaphor (majāz) for the temporal deferment of sexual permissibility pending uterine verification.
- Root: م-ل-ك (malaka)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root signifies "possession, ownership, dominion."
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, it distinguishes proprietary ownership (milk al-raqabah) from usufructuary right (milk al-manfaʿah), pivotal in the rulings below.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for transfer of title; metaphorically extended to the "acquisition" of a wife's usufruct via marriage.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs "سواء... أو..." (whether... or...) to enumerate exhaustive cases, and "لو" (if) for hypothetical counterfactuals, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second chapter concerns the cause of istibrāʾ, which is either the acquisition of ownership or its cessation.

**The First Cause: Acquisition of Ownership**
Whoever acquires new ownership over a slave-woman who is a lawful object of sexual enjoyment for him — her permissibility is suspended upon istibrāʾ after his ownership becomes binding, by the passage of one menstrual period (qarʾ). This applies whether the ownership arises through gift, sale, bequest, inheritance, rescission (faskh), or mutual revocation (iqālah); whether she is young or old, pregnant or non-pregnant; whether the owner is one from whom impregnation is conceivable or not — such as a woman, an impotent man (majbūb), or a child; and whether she had already undergone istibrāʾ before the sale or not.

Dāwūd (al-Ẓāhirī) held that istibrāʾ is not required for a virgin. Mālik (may God have mercy on him) held that a young girl who cannot be sexually penetrated need not undergo istibrāʾ. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) held that istibrāʾ is not required if the woman returns to the seller due to an option of inspection, rejection for a defect, revocation of a gift, or iqālah before delivery — but he required it in iqālah after delivery.

Our companions (the Shāfiʿīs) analogized to the cessation of ownership the case of a mukātabah (slave under manumission contract) who fails to pay and reverts to being a full slave — for she returns to a state in which the master may claim her dower (mahr), and therefore the sister of a mukātabah becomes lawful (for the master to marry).

There is no disagreement that prohibition through fasting or pledging (rahn) has no effect [on istibrāʾ]. As for the cessation of her iḥrām (pilgrimage sanctity), her re-embrace of Islam after apostasy, or her husband's divorce of her — there is disagreement [on whether istibrāʾ is required], due to the strength of these causes. Requiring it in the case of a married woman (who is purchased) is more appropriate, because the husband had acquired her usufruct, and then that right reverts [to the buyer].

As for one who purchases his own married slave-woman (i.e., his wife who is a slave): there are two views. One: istibrāʾ is not required, because the permissibility is perpetual from a single person. The second: it is required, because the basis of permissibility has changed.

If a man sells his slave-woman with an option (khiyār) and she reverts to him during the option period: if we say his ownership never ceased, then no istibrāʾ is required. If we say ownership ceased and intercourse became unlawful, then istibrāʾ is obligatory. If we say ownership ceased but intercourse remains lawful because it is a rescission (faskh) — then here it may be said that permissibility is continuous and the basis is unified, unlike the purchase of a wife, so no istibrāʾ is required; or it may be said that one looks to the renewal of ownership, and by this the istibrāʾ of a purchased wife is justified.

**Subsidiary Issue:** If one purchases a woman in iḥrām, or an ʿiddah-observing woman, or a married woman — whether istibrāʾ is obligatory for her after the ʿiddah expires or after the husband divorces her without consummation — there are conflicting texts from al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him). It is said there are two opinions. One: it is obligatory, and this is the analogical view; it is not far-fetched that istibrāʾ be deferred from the moment of ownership to the time of divorce or expiry of ʿiddah. The second: it is not obligatory, because the cause [of istibrāʾ] is the acquisition of ownership, and at that time she was not in a position of lawful enjoyment — just as purchasing a foster-sister (by radāʿ) does not necessitate istibrāʾ; and when permissibility is later attained, no new ownership is acquired to necessitate it.

**The Second Cause: Cessation of Ownership**
We say: a slave-woman who has been sexually used — whether she is an umm walad (mother of her master's child) or not — is in the ruling of one whose womb is presumed occupied. Thus, if she is freed after the master's death or by his manumission, she must wait one menstrual period. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) said: as for the umm walad, she waits upon manumission, but three periods, considering her full status at that time; as for the ordinary slave-woman, no waiting is required. He further said: if the master had intercourse with her and then wishes to marry her off immediately, that is permissible without istibrāʾ. This is a grave incursion into the mixing of lineages (khalṭ al-miyāh). In our view, no sexually-used slave-woman may be married off except after istibrāʾ. This istibrāʾ is, as it were, a consequence of the husband's acquisition of ownership [through marriage]; for the master's ownership has not ceased, yet istibrāʾ must precede that ownership, because marriage is intended for the lawfulness of intercourse, and thus cannot be contracted unless it immediately yields permissibility. As for the buyer, he performs istibrāʾ after ownership, because purchase is intended for financial purposes and is not restricted by considerations of intercourse. Indeed, if one resolves to purchase, he may perform istibrāʾ before the purchase.

chapters.title_en: Branches on the Umm Walad's Marriage and the Rules of Istiʾbrāʾ (Waiting Period for the Womb)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع

الأول لو اشترى المستفرشة المستبرأة تسلط على التزويج وأعتق قبل التزويج
أو باع وأراد المشتري التزويج أو أعتق المشتري قبل الوطء فأراد التزويج ففي
جواز ذلك ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها وهو الظاهر أنه يجوز إذ كان يجوز قبل زوال الملك فطرآن العتق أو
الشراء لم يحرم تزويجا كان ذلك جائزا
والثاني أنه لا يجوز لأن زوال ملك الفراش سبب يوجب عدة الإستبراء وقد طرأ
فامتنع بهذا الطارىء حتى يزول
والثالث أن ذلك يمنع في المستولدة دون الرقيقة لأنها بالمستفرشة أشبه
والثاني المستولدة المزوجة إذا طلقها زوجها واعتدت فأعتقها السيد وأراد
تزويجها قبل الوطء فهل له ذلك فيه قولان
أحدهما نعم إذ كان يجوز قبل العتق
والثاني لا لأن عتقها هو زوال ملك الفراش وقد صارت مستفرشة له بانقضاء
عدتها وإن لم يطأها إذ عادت إلى فراشه
أما إذا قال أنت حرة مع آخر العدة فها هنا لم ترجع إلى فراشه فمنهم من
قطع بجواز التزويج ومنهم من طرد القولين وجعل مجرد زوال الملك عن المستولدة
سببا للعدة
الثالث إذا أعتق المستولدة المزوجة  وهي في صلب النكاح أو عدته فالظاهر
أن الإستبراء لا يجب لأنه ليس الزائل فراشا له بل هي فراش للزوج وفيه قول
آخر أنه يجب لزوال ملك السيد وقد كانت مستفرشة من قبل فإن أوجبنا في العدة
فلا يخفى أنهما لا يتداخلان ويبقى النظر في التقديم والتأخير كما سبق
الرابع إذا أعتق مستولدته وأراد أن ينكحها في مدة الإستبراء ففي جوازه
خلاف والأظهر جوازه كما لو وطئها بالشبهة وأراد أن ينكحها والثاني المنع
لأن زوال الملك أوجب تعبدا بالإستبراء ولذلك منع من التزويج من الغير على
وجه مع أنه كان جائزا قبل العتق
الخامس المستولدة المزوجة إذا مات زوجها وسيدها جميعا فإن مات السيد أولا
فعليها عدة الوفاة أربعة أشهر وعشر فإن مات الزوج أولا فعليها نصف ذلك وإن
استبهم فعليها الأخذ بالأحوط وذلك ظاهر إذا فرعنا على الصحيح في أنه ليس
عليها استبراء للسيد وإن أوجبنا فبعد مضي عدة الوفاة لا بد من شهر آخر إلا
إذا كانت من ذوات الأقراء فتكفيها حيضة وإن جرت في مدة العدة لأن المقصود
وجود صورة الحيض بعد موت السيد وقد حصل وإن لم تجر فلا بد منها بعد العدة
وإن ماتا معا فلا استبراء لأنها ما عادت إلى فراشه والظاهر أن عدتها
شهران وشيء بخلاف ما لو تقدم موت السيد بلحظة على موت الزوج وفيه وجه أنها
لو عتقت في أثناء العدة استكملت عدة الحرائر فإذا أعتقت مع موته فهو أولى
بذلك

### | قاعدة

يجوز اعتماد قولها إني حضت فلا سبيل إلى تحليفها إذ لا يرتبط بنكولها حكم
فإن السيد لا يقرر على الحلف ولا اطلاع له على حيضها
ولو امتنعت عن غشيانه ورفعت إلى القاضي فقال قد أخبرتني بالحيض فالأوجه
تصديق السيد وتسليطه إذ لولا ذلك لوجبت الحيلولة بينهما كما في وطء الشبهة
فالإستبراء باب من التقوى فيفوض إلى السيد وذكر القاضي أنه لا يبعد أن يكون
لها المخاصمة والدعوى حتى إن الجارية الموروثة لو ادعت أن المورث وطئها
وطئا محرما على  الوارث فللوارث أن لا يصدقها وهل لها تحليفه فيه خلاف فكذلك
هذا ويتأيد بوجه ذكر أن لها الإمتناع عن وقاع السيد الأبرص فيشعر بأنها
صاحبة حق على الجملة

### | الفصل الثالث فيما تصير به الأمة فراشا

فنقول قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الولد للفراش فإذا استبرأ جارية
فأتت بولد قبل أن يطأها فلا يلحق به إذ لا فراش وتصير فراشا بالوطء وإنما
يلحقه الولد إذا استلحقه أو أتت به لزمان يحتمل أن يكون منه بعد الوطء
ويثبت الفراش بأن يقر بوطء عري عن دعوى الإستبراء والعزل
والصحيح أن دعوى العزل لا تنفي الولد لأن الماء سباق لا يدخل تحت
الإختيار والصحيح أن اعترافه بالوطء في غير المأتى لا يلحق الولد به أما
إذا قال وطئت واستبرأتها بعده بحيض فالمذهب أنه ينتفي عنه الولد بغير لعان
لأن فراش الأمة
ضعيف ومنهم من قال لا ينتفي إلا باللعان
فإن

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ف-ر-ش (farasha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The bed, spread, or place of cohabitation; the marital or concubinal bed that establishes lineage.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal "bed" (firāsh) as the basis for paternity attribution, per the prophetic hadith {«الْوَلَدُ لِلْفِرَاشِ»}.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for the physical bed; metaphorical (majāz) for the legal bond of ownership or marriage that makes a woman's womb subject to a man's paternity.
- Root: ب-ر-أ (baraʾa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be free from, to be cleared; the root of istibrāʾ (seeking clearance of the womb).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal obligation to verify the emptiness of the womb (barāʾat al-raḥim) before new cohabitation, to avoid mixing lineages.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical purity; metaphorical for legal exoneration from paternity claims.
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿataqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be free, to be released from bondage.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Manumission as a legal act that removes the master's ownership (milk) over the slave's body and womb.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical freedom; metaphorical for the termination of the "bed" (firāsh) of ownership.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses "لو" (if) and "فإن" (for if) to structure hypothetical legal cases, where the protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) must be parsed precisely to determine the legal ruling.

---

### | Branches

**The First Branch:** If a man purchases a slave-woman who has been given to him as a bed-fellow (mustafrashah) and who has already completed her istibrāʾ, and he gains the right to marry her, then he manumits her before marrying, or he sells her and the buyer wishes to marry her, or the buyer manumits her before intercourse and then wishes to marry her — concerning the permissibility of this, there are three views (awjuh):

**One of them** — and it is the apparent (al-ẓāhir) — is that it is permissible, for it was permissible before the removal of ownership; the occurrence of manumission or purchase did not render unlawful a marriage that was already permissible.

**The second** is that it is not permissible, because the removal of the ownership of the bed (milk al-firāsh) is a cause that necessitates the waiting period of istibrāʾ, and this cause has now arisen; thus it is prevented by this new occurrence until it is removed.

**The third** is that this prohibition applies to the umm walad (mother of a child) but not to the ordinary slave-girl (raqīqah), because the umm walad is more akin to the mustafrashah.

**The Second Branch:** If a man manumits his umm walad who is married (muzawwajah), and her husband divorces her and she completes her ʿiddah (waiting period), then the master manumits her and wishes to marry her before intercourse — does he have that right? There are two sayings (qawlān):

**One of them:** Yes, for it was permissible before the manumission.

**The second:** No, because her manumission is the removal of the ownership of the bed, and she has become a mustafrashah for him upon the expiry of her ʿiddah, even if he has not had intercourse with her, since she has returned to his bed.

But if he said, "You are free at the end of the ʿiddah," then here she does not return to his bed. Some scholars definitively ruled the permissibility of marriage; others extended the two sayings and made the mere removal of ownership over the umm walad a cause for the ʿiddah.

**The Third Branch:** If a man manumits his married umm walad while she is still in the bond of marriage (ṣulb al-nikāḥ) or in her ʿiddah from it, then the apparent ruling is that istibrāʾ is not obligatory, because what has been removed is not his bed; rather, she is the bed of the husband. There is another saying that it is obligatory due to the removal of the master's ownership, and she had previously been a mustafrashah. If we deem the ʿiddah obligatory, it is clear that the two do not overlap (lā yatadākhalān), and the consideration of precedence and delay remains as previously discussed.

**The Fourth Branch:** If a man manumits his umm walad and wishes to marry her during the period of istibrāʾ, there is a disagreement (khilāf) on its permissibility. The most apparent (al-aẓhar) is its permissibility, just as if he had intercourse with her by mistake (shubhah) and wished to marry her. The second view is prohibition, because the removal of ownership necessitated the devotional act (taʿabbud) of istibrāʾ; for this reason, she was prevented from marrying another, even though it was permissible before the manumission.

**The Fifth Branch:** If a married umm walad's husband and master both die — if the master dies first, then upon her is the ʿiddah of widowhood: four months and ten days. If the husband dies first, then upon her is half of that. If the order is unknown (istabhama), then she must adopt the more cautious (al-aḥwaṭ). This is apparent if we base it on the correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) that she owes no istibrāʾ to the master. But if we deem it obligatory, then after the expiry of the ʿiddah of widowhood, another month is necessary — unless she is among those who menstruate (dhawāt al-aqrāʾ), in which case a single menstruation suffices, even if it occurs during the ʿiddah period, because the purpose is the occurrence of the form of menstruation after the master's death, and this has been achieved. If it does not occur, then it must occur after the ʿiddah. If both die simultaneously, then no istibrāʾ is required, because she has not returned to his bed. The apparent ruling is that her ʿiddah is two months and a bit, unlike the case where the master's death precedes the husband's death by a moment. There is a view that if she were manumitted during the ʿiddah, she would complete the ʿiddah of a free woman; so if she is manumitted at the moment of his death, this is even more apt.

---

### | Principle (Qāʿidah)

It is permissible to rely on her statement, "I have menstruated," and there is no way to administer an oath to her, for no legal ruling is attached to her refusal to swear (nukūl). For the master is not compelled to swear, nor does he have any knowledge of her menstruation.

If she refuses to allow him to have intercourse with her and raises the matter to the judge, and he (the master) says, "She informed me of menstruation," then the most correct view (al-awjah) is to affirm the master's word and grant him authority (taslīṭ), for were it not so, separation between them would be obligatory, as in the case of intercourse by mistake (waṭʾ al-shubhah). Thus, istibrāʾ is a chapter of piety (taqwā), and it is delegated to the master. The judge (al-Qāḍī) mentioned that it is not far-fetched that she has the right to litigate and claim — for if an inherited slave-girl claims that the deceased had intercourse with her in a manner forbidden to the heir, the heir may refuse to believe her, and there is disagreement on whether she may demand an oath from him. Likewise here. This is supported by the view that she may refuse intercourse with a leprous (abraṣ) master, which indicates that she is, in general, a possessor of rights.

---

### | The Third Chapter: On What Makes a Slave-Woman a Bed (Firāsh)

We say: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: {«الْوَلَدُ لِلْفِرَاشِ»} ("The child belongs to the bed"). So if a man performs istibrāʾ on a slave-girl and she brings a child before he has intercourse with her, the child is not attributed to him, for there is no bed. She becomes a bed only through intercourse, and the child is attributed to him only if he acknowledges it (istalḥaqahu) or if she brings it at a time that could plausibly be from him after intercourse.

The bed is established by his acknowledgment of intercourse that is free from any claim of istibrāʾ or coitus interruptus (ʿazl). The correct view is that a claim of ʿazl does not negate the child, for the sperm is a "racer" (sabbāq) that is not subject to choice. The correct view is that his admission of intercourse in a place other than the vagina (ghayr al-maʾtā) does not attribute the child to him. But if he says, "I had intercourse and then performed istibrāʾ with a menstruation," then the school's ruling (al-madhhab) is that the child is negated from him without liʿān (mutual imprecation), because the bed of a slave-woman is weak. Some have said it is not negated except by liʿān.

Then—
