والحضانة عبارة عن حفظ الولد وتربيته وتجب مئونة الحضانة على من عليه
النفقة وعند الإزدحام يسلك بها مسلك الولاية لأنها سلطنة على الحفظ
والتربية لكن تفارق الولاية في أن الإناث أولى بالحضانة لأن الأنوثة تناسب
هذه الولاية لزيادة الرقة والشفقة
ولو عضل الأقرب أو غاب انتقل إلى الأبعد لا إلى السلطان لأن هذا يعتمد
الشفقة المجردة بخلاف ولاية النكاح ولو امتنعت الأم فأمها أولى من أب الطفل
لأن شفقتها كشفقة الأم وقيل ينتقل الحق بعضلها إلى الأب وكأنه في درجة
السلطنة في الولاية وهو بعيد
ومهما اجتمع الأب والأم فالأم أحق بالحضانة بشرط اتصاف الأم بخمس صفات
الإسلام والعقل والحرية والأمانة بالفراغ
أما الإسلام فإنما يشترط في ولد المسلم لأن تسليمه إلى الكافر يعرض دينه
للفتنة
وأما العقل فهو الأصل فلا ثقة بحفظ المعتوهة
وأما الحرية فلا بد منها لأن هذه ولاية ولا ولاية مع الرق ولا يؤثر رضا
السيد وكذلك من نصفها حر ونصفها رقيق إذ لا ولاية لمثلها ولكن عليها  نفقة
القريب لأن ذلك من قبيل الغرامات
وأما الأمانة فلا بد منها إذ الفاسقة لايؤمن من جانبها
وأما الفراغ فنعني به أن لا تكون في نكاح غيره فإذا نكحت سقط حقها من
الحضانة لأنه نوع رق ولا يؤثر رضا الناكح إلا إذا نكحت من له حق الحضانة
كعم الولد فالمشهور أنه لا يسقط حقها من الحضانة وفيه وجه أن الأب أولى من
الأم وإن نكحت العم
ومهما طلقت قبل المسيس عاد حقها كما إذا أفاقت من جنون أو عتقت من رق أو
تابت من فسق أو أسلمت بعد كفر فإن كانت رجعية فالمنصوص رجوع حقها لأنها
الآن فارغة معتزلة وفيه قول مخرج وهو اختيار المزني أنه لا حق لها لاستمرار
سلطنة الزوج
أما المعتدة البائنة فيعود حقها لكن إن كانت في مسكن الزوج فللزوج أن لا
يرضى بإدخال الولد ملكه فإن رضي رجع حقها لا كرضاه في صلب النكاح فإنه لا
يؤثر لأن هذا كرضا المعير للدار

### | الفصل الثاني فيمن يستحق الحضانة

وهو كل من لا يستقل إما لصغر أو جنون لكن الأم أولى بالصبي قبل التمييز
فإذا ميز خير بينها وبين الأب وسلم إلى من يختاره غلاما كان أو جارية وقال
أبو حنيفة رحمه الله الأب بالغلام أولى والأم بالجارية أولى وقد روى أبو
هريرة رضي الله عنه أنه صلى الله عليه وسلم خير غلاما
ولا ننظر إلى سبع سنين بل نتبع التمييز فإن استمرت الغباوة إلى ما بعد
البلوغ فالأم أولى وكذلك إن اتصل به جنون وكأن حقها لا ينقطع إلا باختيار
الصبي عن تمييز
ولو اختار أحدهما ثم رجع رد إلى الآخر لأن الحال قد يتغير في الرفق به
إلا إذا كثر تردده حتى دل على قلة التمييز فيرد إلى الأم وكذلك إذا سكت عن
الإختيار هذا في حق الصبي
أما البالغ إذا كان غير رشيد فهو كالصبي وإن كان رشيدا وهو ذكر استقل وإن
كانت جارية وهي بكر فالظاهر أن للأب أن يسكنها موضعا وليس لها  الإستقلال
وإن كانت رشيدة كما يجبرها على حبس النكاح وهو أعظم من حبس المسكن ثم هذا
يختص بالأب والجد ومن له ولاية الإجبار وفيه وجه أنها تستقل وإنما التزويج
بالجبر
أما البنت فإنها تستقل إذا تم رشدها بالممارسة لكنها إن كانت تتهم بريبة
فلعصباتها ولاية إسكانها وملاحظتها دفعا للعار عن النسب ولا يثبت هذا إلا
لمن له ولاية التزويج ولو ادعى الريبة فأنكرت فتبعد مطالبته بالإثبات
بالبينة فإن ذلك افتضاح يجر العار والإحتكام على عاقلة أيضا بمجرد الدعوى
بعيد ولكن إقامة البينة أبعد منه
فرعان
أحدهما هل يجري التخيير بين الأم ومن يقع على حاشية النسب كالعم والأخ
فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم كالأب والجد
والثاني أن الأم أولى وإنما التخيير مع الأب والجد لأن لهم درجة الولاية
والإجبار
ويجري هذا الخلاف في التخيير بين الأب والأخت والخالة إذا قلنا إن الأب
مقدم عليهما في الحضانة
الثاني أنه إذا اختار الأب لم يمنعها من الزيارة وإذا اختار الام لم يسقط
عن الأب مئونة الحضانة والقيام بتأديبه وتسليمه إلى الحرفة أو المكتب وكذلك
المجنون الذي لا تستقل الأم بضبطه يجب على الأب رعايته ومهما سافر الأب سفر
نقلة بطل تقديم الأم وكان له استصحاب الولد كيلا ينقطع النسب سواء كان قبل
التمييز أو بعده إذ فيه ضرار نعم لو رافقته الأم فهي أولى وليس له استصحابه
في سفر النزهة ولا في سفر التجارة وإن طالت المدة وفيه وجه لطول المدة
ولو انتقل إلى ما دون مرحلتين ففي جواز انتزاع الولد وجهان لأن تتابع
الرفاق يمنع اندراس النسب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ض-ن (ḥaḍana)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hold, embrace, or shelter in the lap/bosom; the physical act of nurturing an infant.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Custody (ḥaḍānah) as a protective guardianship over the child's physical and moral welfare, distinct from legal authority (wilāyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical embracing; metaphorical (majāz) for the legal right of nurturing and supervision.
- Root: و-ل-ي (waliya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be near, to take charge, to govern; the one who assumes authority.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Wilāyah as a delegated power of disposition over another's affairs, requiring competence and trustworthiness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for proximity; metaphorical for legal authority and coercive power (ijbār).
- Root: ر-ق-ق (raqqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Thinness, softness; slavery (riqq) as a state of legal incapacity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Riqq negates wilāyah because the slave lacks independent legal personality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical thinness; metaphorical for legal subjugation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clauses with Law (لو) and Idhā (إذا) — [The protasis introduces a hypothetical condition, and the apodosis states the legal consequence; the particle "wa-mahmā" (whenever) indicates a general conditional governing multiple legal rulings.]
chapters.translation:
I say: The first [topic] concerns the qualifying attributes [of the custodian].

Custody (ḥaḍānah) is the preservation of the child and his upbringing. The maintenance for custody is obligatory upon the one who bears the duty of support (nafaqah). When claimants are in competition, custody is treated according to the rules of guardianship (wilāyah), because it is a form of authority over preservation and upbringing. However, it differs from guardianship in that females are more entitled to custody, for femininity is suited to this authority due to greater tenderness and compassion.

If the nearest [relative] obstructs (ʿaḍala) or is absent, [custody] transfers to the next nearest, not to the ruler (sulṭān), because this [office] relies on pure compassion, unlike the guardianship of marriage. If the mother refuses, then her mother is more entitled than the child's father, for her compassion is like the mother's compassion. It is said that the right transfers by her obstruction to the father, as if he holds a degree of authority in guardianship — but this is remote.

Whenever the father and mother are both present, the mother is more entitled to custody, on the condition that the mother possesses five attributes: Islam, sanity, freedom, trustworthiness, and being unmarried (farāgh).

As for Islam, it is required only in the case of a Muslim child, because entrusting him to a disbeliever exposes his religion to temptation (fitnah).

As for sanity, it is the fundamental [requirement], for there is no reliance upon the preservation [of the child] by an insane woman (maʿtūhah).

As for freedom, it is indispensable, because this is a form of authority (wilāyah), and there is no authority with slavery (riqq). The consent of the master has no effect. Likewise, a woman who is half-free and half-slave [is disqualified], for there is no authority for one like her. However, she is obligated to pay the maintenance of the relative, because that falls under the category of financial liabilities (gharāmāt).

As for trustworthiness, it is indispensable, for a sinful woman (fāsiqah) is not safe from her side.

As for being unmarried (farāgh), we mean that she is not in the marriage of another. If she marries, her right to custody falls, because it is a type of subjugation (riqq). The consent of the husband has no effect — except if she marries one who has a right to custody, like the child's paternal uncle. Then the well-known [position] is that her right to custody does not fall. There is a view that the father is more entitled than the mother if she marries the paternal uncle.

Whenever she is divorced before consummation (qabla al-masīs), her right returns — just as when she recovers from insanity, or is freed from slavery, or repents from sin, or embraces Islam after disbelief. If the divorce is revocable (rajʿiyyah), the text (manṣūṣ) states that her right returns, because she is now unmarried and secluded. There is an extracted opinion (qawl mukharraj) — which is the choice of al-Muzanī — that she has no right, due to the continuation of the husband's authority.

As for the woman in an irrevocable waiting period (bāʾin), her right returns. However, if she is in the husband's dwelling, the husband may refuse to allow the child to enter his property. If he consents, her right returns — unlike his consent during the subsistence of the marriage, for that has no effect, because this is like the consent of one who lends a house.

### The Second Chapter: On Who Is Entitled to Custody

[The entitled custodian] is anyone who is not independent — either due to minority or insanity. However, the mother is more entitled to a young child before the age of discernment (tamyīz). When the child attains discernment, he is given the choice between her and the father, and he is handed over to whomever he chooses — whether boy or girl. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The father is more entitled to the boy, and the mother is more entitled to the girl. Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated that the Prophet (peace be upon him) gave a boy the choice.

We do not look to the age of seven years; rather, we follow discernment. If dullness (ghabāwah) persists beyond puberty, the mother is more entitled. Likewise, if insanity is continuous [with his condition], her right is not severed except by the child's choice upon discernment.

If he chooses one [parent] and then retracts, he is returned to the other, because the situation may change regarding kindness to him — unless his vacillation becomes excessive, such that it indicates a deficiency in discernment, in which case he is returned to the mother. Likewise, if he remains silent about choosing. This applies to the minor child.

As for the adult who is not prudent (rashīd), he is like a minor. If he is prudent and male, he is independent. If she is a maiden (bikr) [and prudent], the apparent [position] is that the father has the right to house her in a place, and she does not have independence — even if she is prudent — just as he may compel her to refrain from marriage, which is greater than confining her to a dwelling. This is specific to the father, the grandfather, and whoever holds the authority of compulsion (ijbār). There is a view that she is independent, and only marriage is by compulsion.

As for the [adult] daughter, she is independent when her prudence is perfected through experience. However, if she is suspected of suspicion (rībah), her agnates (ʿaṣabāt) have the authority to house her and supervise her, to repel disgrace from the lineage. This is established only for one who holds the authority of marriage. If he claims suspicion and she denies it, his demand for proof by evidence (bayyinah) is remote, for that is an exposure that drags disgrace. Adjudicating against a sane woman merely by a claim is also remote, but establishing evidence is even more remote.

Two subsidiary issues (farʿān):

First: Does the choice apply between the mother and one who falls on the periphery of lineage, like the paternal uncle and the brother? There are two views:
One: Yes, like the father and grandfather.
The second: The mother is more entitled, and the choice is only with the father and grandfather, because they hold a degree of authority and compulsion.
This disagreement applies to the choice between the father and the sister or the maternal aunt, if we say the father is preferred over them in custody.

Second: If he chooses the father, [the father] does not prevent her from visiting. If he chooses the mother, it does not absolve the father from the maintenance of custody, undertaking his discipline, and handing him over to a trade or school. Likewise, the insane child whom the mother cannot independently manage — the father must care for him. Whenever the father travels a journey of relocation (safar naqlah), the mother's precedence is voided, and he may take the child with him, so that lineage is not severed — whether before or after discernment, for therein is harm. Yes, if the mother accompanies him, she is more entitled, and he may not take the child on a pleasure trip (safar nuzhah) nor on a trade trip (safar tijārah), even if the duration is long. There is a view [that he may] due to the length of duration.

If he moves to a distance less than two stages (marḥalatayn), there are two views on the permissibility of seizing the child, because the succession of companions prevents the effacement of lineage.

chapters.title_en: The Third Chapter on Mutual Precedence and Conflict (al-Tazāḥum wa al-Tadāfuʿ)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثالث في التزاحم والتدافع

والنظر في أطراف
الأول في اجتماع النسوة فإن تدافعن فالحاضنة على من عليها النفقة وإن
تزاحموا وطلبت كل واحدة الحضانة فالنص في الجديد أن الأم أولى ثم أمهاتها
المدليات بالإناث لا بالذكور ثم أم الأب وجداته المدليات بالإناث وإن علون
ثم أم الجد وجداته على الترتيب المقدم في الأب ثم أم أب الجد وجداته كذلك
ثم الأخوات ثم الخالات ثم  بنات الإخوة لأن الخالة أم وشفقتها أكثر من شفقة
العمات وهن بعد الخالات لأن قرابة الأم أقوى في الحضانة والقديم يوافق
الجديد في جميع هذا الترتيب إلا أنه في القديم قدم الأخوات والخالات على
أمهات الأب لإدلائهن بالأم وهو ضعيف لأن شفقة الأصول أعظم
ويبقى النظر في ثلاث مسائل
إحداها أن الأخت من الأب مقدمة على الأخت من الأم في الجديد وذكر وجه في
التخريج على القديم أن الأخت للأم مقدمة لقرابة الأم وعلة الجديد أنهما
يستويان في الشفقة ولا تؤثر جهة الأم في زيادة الشفقة لكن هذه لها قوة في
الميراث ويصلح ذلك في الترجيح لكن هذا لا يطرد في خالة لأب وأخرى لأم وكذلك
لعمات إذ لا ميراث فمنهم من قدم الخالة للأب لأن الميراث بين لنا قوة هذه
الجهة فلا يرعى غير الميراث ومنهم من قدم الخالة للأم إذ لا ميراث وقرابة
الأم آكد
الثانية نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه لا مدخل في الحضانة لكل جدة ساقطة
في الميراث وهي كل جدة تدلي بذكر بين الأنثيين وهو مشكل لأنها وإن كانت
ساطقه في الميراث فالخالة والعمة أيضا كذلك ولعل سببه أن الذكر الذي ليس
بوارث ليس له ولاية الحضانة وهي تدلي به ولهذا الإشكال ذكر أصحابنا وجهين
آخرين
أحدهما أنهن لو انفردن فلهن الحضانة ولكنهن مؤخرات عن الخالات وجميع
المذكورات
والثاني أنهن مؤخرات عن الجدات الوارثات مقدمات على الاخوات والخالات
الثالثة القريبة الأنثى التي لا محرمية لها كبنات الخالات وبنات العمات
فيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه لا حضانة لهن إذ الحضانة تستدعي خبرة ببواطن الأمور فتستدعي
المحرمية
والثاني أنه تثبت وذكر الفوراني ذلك وقال الخالات مقدمات على بنات الإخوة
وبنات الإخوة مقدمات على العمات كما يقدم ابن الأخ في الإرث على العم وقال
بنات الخالات مقدمات على بنات العمات
الطرف الثاني في اجتماع الذكور وهم أربعة أقسام
الأول محرم وارث فله حق الحضانة ويترتبون ترتب العصبات في الولاية إلا
الأخ من الأم فإنه ليس بولي وهو متأخر  عن الأصول وعو الإخوة للأب مع أنه
محرم وارث وهل يؤخر عن العم فيه وجهان منهم من أخر للولاية ومنه من قدم
للقرب والشفقة وهو الأظهر
الثاني الوارث الذي ليس بمحرم كبني الأعمام لهم حق حضانة في الصبي وفي
الصغيرة التي لا تشتهي دون التي تشتهى
الثالث المحرم الذي ليس بوارث كالخال وأب الأم والعم من الأم وبني
الأخوات فهم مؤخرون عن الورثة وهل لهم حق عند فقدهم فيه وجهان
أحدهما تثبت للمحرمية كما تثبت للخالة وإن لم تكن وارثة
والثاني لا لأن الخالة أنثى وانضمام الأنوثة إلى القرابة مؤثر ثم لا خلاف
أن المستحب للسلطان أن يسلم إليهم
الرابع قريب ليس بمحرم ولا وارث كابن الخالة والخال فالصحيح أنه لا حق
لهم وإن ظهر الخلاف في بنات الخالات لأجل الأنوثة وفيه وجه
الطرف الثالث في اجتماع الذكور والإناث ولا شك أن الأم وأمهاتها مقدمات
إذا كن من جهة الإناث ثم بعدهن في الأب والجدات من قبل الأب قولان
ظاهر النص تقديم الأب فلا يقدم على الأب إلا الأم وأمهاتها كذلك قال
الشافعي رضي الله عنه
والثاني أنهن مقدمات وإن أدلين به لشفقة الأنوثة فعلى هذا في تقديم
الأخوات على الأب ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها التقديم للأنوثة
والثاني لا لأن الأب أصل
والثالث أنه يقدم على الأخت للأب فإنها فرعه دون الأخت للأم والأخت للأب
والأم
وهذا الوجه لا يجري في الخالة لأنها ليست فرعا ولكن يجري الوجهان في
تقديم الخالة على الأب بل تقديم الخالة عليه أولى من تقديم الأخت وكل جدة
ليست فاسدة فهي مقدمة على كل عصبة تقع على حواشي النسب
وأما الذكور والإناث على الحواشي إذا استووا في القرب والإرث فالأنثى
أولى والأخت أولى من الأخ
ولو كانت الأنثى بعيدة والذكر قريبا فوجهان لتعارض الأنوثة والقرابة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ز-ح-م (z-ḥ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is crowding, pressing together, or vying for a single space—implying competition over a shared object of claim.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, denotes competing claims where each party asserts a right, necessitating a rule of priority (tarjīḥ) based on strength of cause.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage is physical crowding; here it is metaphorical (majāz) for competing legal entitlements, where the "space" is the custodial right (ḥaḍānah).
- Root: د-ف-ع (d-f-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To push, repel, or thrust away—implying active opposition between claimants.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In kalām and fiqh, denotes mutual repulsion where one claim negates another, requiring resolution by textual or analogical preference.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is physical pushing; metaphorical here is the juridical "pushing off" of one claimant by another due to superior entitlement.
- Root: ح-ض-ن (ḥ-ḍ-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To hold in one's lap or bosom—core sense is physical embrace and protective care.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for legal custody of a child, entailing both physical care and moral guardianship, rooted in the Quranic image of maternal embrace.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is the lap; metaphorical extension is the legal right of nurturing custody, where proximity of kinship (qarābah) determines priority.
- Root: د-ل-و (d-l-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To lower a bucket into a well—core sense is reaching down through intermediaries.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In inheritance and custody law, denotes "tracing descent through" (al-idlāʾ bi), i.e., claiming kinship via an intermediate ancestor.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is drawing water; metaphorical is genealogical linkage through a chain of ancestors, distinguishing maternal-line (bi-al-ināth) from paternal-line (bi-al-dhukūr) tracing.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Precedence (Taqdīm al-Sharṭ ʿalā al-Jawāb) — In sentences like "فإن تدافعن فالحاضنة على من عليها النفقة" (if they conflict, then the custodian is the one upon whom maintenance is obligatory), the protasis (sharṭ) establishes the condition, and the apodosis (jawāb) assigns the ruling, requiring the reader to parse the conditional as a legal hypothetical with an implied universal quantifier over all conflicting female claimants.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third chapter concerns mutual precedence and conflict (al-tazāḥum wa al-tadāfuʿ). The examination proceeds through three aspects.

The first aspect concerns the concurrence of women. If they conflict, then the custodian (al-ḥāḍinah) is the one upon whom maintenance is obligatory. If they vie for precedence and each woman claims custody, then the text (al-naṣṣ) in the new doctrine (al-jadīd) is that the mother is most entitled, then her mothers—those tracing descent through females, not through males—then the father's mother and her grandmothers tracing through females, however high they ascend, then the grandfather's mother and her grandmothers in the order previously established for the father, then the paternal grandfather's mother and her grandmothers likewise, then the sisters, then the maternal aunts (al-khālāt), then the brothers' daughters. This is because the maternal aunt is like a mother, and her compassion is greater than the compassion of paternal aunts (al-ʿammāt). And they [the paternal aunts] come after the maternal aunts because the maternal kinship is stronger in custody. The old doctrine (al-qadīm) agrees with the new doctrine in all this order, except that in the old doctrine, the sisters and maternal aunts are given precedence over the father's mothers, due to their tracing through the mother. But this is weak, because the compassion of the roots (al-uṣūl) is greater.

There remain three subsidiary questions.

The first: The paternal sister is given precedence over the maternal sister in the new doctrine. A face (wajh) is mentioned in derivation (takhrīj) upon the old doctrine that the maternal sister is given precedence due to maternal kinship. The rationale of the new doctrine is that they are equal in compassion, and the maternal direction does not effect an increase in compassion. However, this one [the paternal sister] has strength in inheritance, and that suffices for preference (tarjīḥ). But this does not hold uniformly for a paternal maternal aunt versus a maternal maternal aunt, nor for paternal aunts, since there is no inheritance [between them]. Thus, some scholars give precedence to the paternal maternal aunt because inheritance clarifies for us the strength of that direction, so nothing other than inheritance is considered. And some give precedence to the maternal maternal aunt, since there is no inheritance and maternal kinship is more emphatic.

The second: Imam al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—stated that there is no entry into custody for any grandmother who is excluded (sāqiṭah) from inheritance—namely, every grandmother who traces through a male between two females. This is problematic, because even if she is excluded from inheritance, the maternal aunt and the paternal aunt are likewise [excluded], yet they have custody. Perhaps the reason is that the male through whom she traces is not an heir, and he has no guardianship of custody, while she traces through him. Due to this problem, our companions mentioned two other faces.

One of them: If they [such grandmothers] were alone, they would have custody, but they are deferred behind the maternal aunts and all those mentioned [in the order].

The second: They are deferred behind the inheriting grandmothers but given precedence over the sisters and maternal aunts.

The third: A close female relative who has no mahramiyyah (degree of unmarriageable kinship)—such as daughters of maternal aunts and daughters of paternal aunts—there are two faces.

One of them: They have no custody, because custody requires expertise in the inner states of affairs, and that requires mahramiyyah.

The second: It is established. Al-Fūrānī mentioned this and said: The maternal aunts are given precedence over the brothers' daughters, and the brothers' daughters are given precedence over the paternal aunts, just as the brother's son is given precedence in inheritance over the paternal uncle. And he said: The daughters of maternal aunts are given precedence over the daughters of paternal aunts.

The second aspect concerns the concurrence of males, and they are of four categories.

The first: A mahram who is also an heir. He has the right of custody, and they are ranked according to the ranking of the ʿaṣabāt (agnatic heirs) in guardianship—except the maternal brother, for he is not a guardian, and he is deferred behind the roots (al-uṣūl) and the paternal brothers, even though he is a mahram and an heir. As to whether he is deferred behind the paternal uncle, there are two faces: some defer him due to guardianship, and some give him precedence due to proximity and compassion—and this latter is the more apparent (al-aẓhar).

The second: An heir who is not a mahram—such as the sons of paternal uncles. They have a right of custody over the young boy and over the young girl who is not yet desired [sexually], but not over the one who is desired.

The third: A mahram who is not an heir—such as the maternal uncle (al-khāl), the mother's father, the paternal uncle through the mother, and the sons of sisters. They are deferred behind the heirs. As to whether they have a right when the heirs are absent, there are two faces.

One of them: It is established due to mahramiyyah, just as it is established for the maternal aunt even though she is not an heir.

The second: It is not, because the maternal aunt is female, and the conjunction of femininity with kinship is effective. Then there is no disagreement that it is recommended (mustaḥabb) for the ruler (al-sulṭān) to hand [the child] over to them.

The fourth: A relative who is neither a mahram nor an heir—such as the son of the maternal aunt and the maternal uncle. The correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that they have no right, even though the disagreement appeared regarding the daughters of maternal aunts, due to femininity. And there is a face [supporting them].

The third aspect concerns the concurrence of males and females. There is no doubt that the mother and her mothers are given precedence when they are from the female line. Then after them, regarding the father and the grandmothers from the father's side, there are two sayings (qawlān). The apparent import of the text is giving precedence to the father, so none is given precedence over the father except the mother and her mothers likewise—thus said al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him.

The second: They [the paternal grandmothers] are given precedence, even though they trace through him, due to the compassion of femininity. Upon this [second view], regarding giving precedence to the sisters over the father, there are three faces.

One of them: Precedence is given due to femininity.

The second: No, because the father is a root (aṣl).

The third: He is given precedence over the paternal sister, for she is his branch, but not over the maternal sister, nor over the paternal sister through the mother. This face does not apply to the maternal aunt, because she is not a branch. But the two faces apply to giving the maternal aunt precedence over the father—indeed, giving the maternal aunt precedence over him is more fitting than giving the sister precedence. And every grandmother who is not "corrupt" (fāsidah) in her lineage is given precedence over every ʿaṣabah that falls upon the fringes of the genealogy.

As for males and females upon the fringes, when they are equal in proximity and inheritance, the female is more entitled, and the sister is more entitled than the brother. But if the female is distant and the male is near, there are two faces, due to the conflict between femininity and proximity.

### | السبب الثالث للنفقة ملك اليمين

وفيه مسائل
الأولى أن نفقة المملوك إمتاع وهو على الكفاية ولا تسقط إلا بزوال الملك
أو الكتابة وليس عليه أن يطعمه ويكسوه من جنس ما يطعم  ويكتسي ولكن ما يليق
به ولو اقتصر من الكسوة على ما يستر به العورة لم يجز ذلك في بلادنا لأنه
إضرار وإن لم يكن يتأذى بحر وبرد وهل يجب تفضيل النفيس على الخسيس في
الكسوة فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه يجب إذ العادة تقتضي ذلك
والثاني لا لأن الرقيق يليق به الخشن وإن كان نفيسا
والثالث أنه لا يفرق في العبيد أما الجواري فيفضل السرية على الخادمة
الثانية قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
إذا كفى أحدكم طعامه خادمه حره ودخانه فليجلسه معه فإن أبى فليروغ له
لقمة وليناولها إياه فترددوا وفي ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أن ذلك واجب على الترتيب
والثاني أنه يجب إما الإجلاس او ترويغ اللقمة ولا يجب الترتيب والثالث
وهو الأظهر أن ذلك مستحب وهو من مكارم الأخلاق
الثالثة الرقيقة أو أم الولد إذا أتت بولد فعليها الإرضاع بخلاف الزوجة
فإنها رقيقة ولا يفرق بينه وبينها ولا تكلف أن ترضع غير ولدها مع ولده فإنه
إضرار بها وبولدها نعم له أن يستمتع بها ويضم الولد إلى غيرها في وقت
الإستمتاع
الرابعة ليس لها فطام ولدها قبل الحولين ولا الزيادة على الحولين إلا
برضاه والمتبع رضا السيد فيه إلا إذا كان إضرارا بالولد وأما الحرة فحقها
مؤكد في إرضاع ولدها فيتوقف الفطام على توافقهما فإن أرادت الفطام فله
المنع وإن أرادت الإرضاع بالأجرة وأراد الأب الفطام فعليه الأجرة وليس له
المنع
الخامسة لا أصل للمخارجة وهو ضرب خراج مقدر على العبد كل يوم بل على
العبد بذل المجهود وعلى السيد أن يحمله على ما يطيقه فلو امتنع السيد عن
الإنفاق يباع عليه فإن لم يرغب أحد في شرائه فهو من محاويج المسلمين
السادسة يجب عليه علف الدواب لأن أرواحها محترمة ولذلك لا يجوز تعذيبها
ولا ذبحها إلا لمأكله وكذلك لا ينزف ألبانها بحيث يستضر بنتاجها
ويجوز غصب العلف والخبط لحاجتها إذا أشرفت على الهلاك على المذهب الظاهر
والمسافر يقدم حاجة الدابة إلى الماء على الوضوء فيتيمم وإذا  أجدبت الأرض
فعليه علف السائمة
ولا يجب عليه عمارة داره وقناته وعقاره وإن أشرفت على الإنهدام لأن
الحرمة لذي الروح فإن امتنع من العلف فللقاضي أن يجبره على البيع أو يبيع
عليه والله تعالى أعلم وأحكم والحمد لله رب العالمين
= كتاب الجنايات=
اعلم أن أدلة الشريعة من الكتاب والسنة والإجماع متظاهرة على أن القتل
كبيرة متفاحشة موجبة للعقوبة في الدنيا والآخرة
وموجباته في الدنيا ثلاثة القصاص والدية والكفارة
أما القصاص فالنظر في حكمه عند العفو والإستيفاء وفي موجبه أما الموجب
فالنظر فيه يتعلق بالطرف والنفس أما النفس فالنظر فيها يتعلق بأركان وهو
القاتل والقتيل ونفس القتل

### | الركن الأول القتل نفسه

والموجب للقصاص منه كل فعل عمد محص عدوان مزهق للروح
وقولنا مزهق يتناول المباشرة والسبب فلزم تمييز العمد المحض عن غيره
وتمييز السبب عن غيره وينكشف بالنظر في أطراف خمسة

chapters.translation:
### | The Third Cause of Maintenance: Right-Hand Ownership

In this [section] are several questions.

**The First:** The maintenance of the owned slave is [a form of] enjoyment (imtāʿ), and it is [measured] by sufficiency (kifāyah). It does not lapse except by the removal of ownership or by kitābah (contractual manumission). It is not required of the master to feed him and clothe him from the same kind as what he himself eats and wears, but rather [he must provide] what is befitting (yalīq) for the slave. If he restricts the clothing to what merely covers the nakedness (ʿawrah), that is not permissible in our lands, because it is harmful (iḍrār), even if [the slave] is not afflicted by heat or cold. As to whether it is obligatory to prefer the fine over the coarse in clothing, there are three views:

One: It is obligatory, for custom (ʿādah) necessitates that.
The second: No, for the coarse befits the slave, even if he is noble.
The third: There is no distinction among male slaves; as for female slaves, the concubine (surriyyah) is preferred over the servant girl.

**The Second:** The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: {«When one of you has his servant suffice him his food, its heat and its smoke, let him seat him with him; and if he refuses, let him place a morsel in his hand and hand it to him.»} They differed concerning it, and there are three views:

One: That is obligatory in sequence (ʿalā al-tartīb).
The second: That it is obligatory either to seat him or to place the morsel in his hand, and the sequence is not obligatory.
The third — and it is the most apparent (al-aẓhar) — is that it is recommended (mustaḥabb) and is among the noble traits of character (makārim al-akhlāq).

**The Third:** The female slave, or the mother of a child (umm al-walad), when she gives birth to a child, it is upon her to nurse him — unlike the [free] wife. For she is a slave, and no distinction is made between him and her. She is not burdened to nurse a child other than her own along with her own child, for that is harmful to her and to her child. Yes, he may enjoy her (yastamtiʿ bihā) and place the child with another [nurse] at the time of enjoyment.

**The Fourth:** She does not have [the right] to wean her child before the completion of two years, nor to exceed two years, except with his consent. The consideration is the consent of the master (al-sayyid) therein — unless it is harmful to the child. As for the free woman, her right is confirmed (muʾakkad) in nursing her child, so weaning is contingent upon their mutual agreement. If she wishes to wean, he has the right to prevent her; and if she wishes to nurse for a wage and the father wishes to wean, then the wage is upon him, and he does not have the right to prevent her.

**The Fifth:** There is no basis for al-mukhārajah — which is the imposition of a fixed tribute (kharāj) upon the slave each day. Rather, upon the slave is the exertion of utmost effort (badhl al-majhūd), and upon the master is to burden him with what he can bear. If the master refuses to spend [on maintenance], [the slave] is sold against him. If no one desires to purchase him, then he is among the needy of the Muslims (maḥāwīj al-Muslimīn).

**The Sixth:** It is obligatory upon him to provide fodder (ʿalaf) for beasts of burden, for their souls are inviolable (muḥtaramah). For this reason, it is not permissible to torture them, nor to slaughter them except for [their] consumption. Likewise, their milk is not to be drained to the extent that their offspring are harmed. It is permissible to seize fodder and to strip leaves (khabṭ) for their need when they are on the verge of perishing, according to the apparent school (al-madhhab al-ẓāhir). And the traveler gives precedence to the animal's need for water over [his own] ablution (wuḍūʾ), so he performs tayammum. And when the land becomes barren, it is upon him to fodder the grazing livestock (al-sāʾimah).

It is not obligatory upon him to maintain his house, his aqueduct (qanāh), or his property, even if they are on the verge of collapse, for inviolability belongs to that which possesses a soul (dhū al-rūḥ). If he refuses to provide fodder, the judge (al-qāḍī) may compel him to sell, or sell on his behalf. And Allah Most High knows best and is Most Wise. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

= The Book of Crimes (Kitāb al-Jināyāt) =

Know that the evidences of the Sacred Law — from the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus (ijmāʿ) — are concurrent (mutazāhir) upon the fact that killing is a grave enormity (kabīrah mutafāḥishah), necessitating punishment in this world and the Hereafter.

Its necessitating causes (mūjibāt) in this world are three: retaliation (qiṣāṣ), blood-money (diyah), and expiation (kaffārah).

As for retaliation (al-qiṣāṣ), the consideration is in its ruling upon pardon (ʿafw) and execution (istīfāʾ), and in its cause (mūjib). As for the cause, the consideration therein pertains to the limb (al-ṭarf) and the soul (al-nafs). As for the soul, the consideration therein pertains to its pillars (arkān), namely: the killer (al-qātil), the killed (al-qatīl), and the act of killing itself (nafs al-qatl).

### | The First Pillar: The Act of Killing Itself

That which necessitates retaliation from it is every intentional (ʿamd), deliberate (muḥaṣṣal), transgressive (ʿudwān) act that extinguishes the soul (muzhiq li-l-rūḥ).

Our saying "extinguishing" (muzhiq) encompasses both direct causation (al-mubāsharah) and indirect causation (al-sabab). Thus it becomes necessary to distinguish pure intentionality (al-ʿamd al-maḥḍ) from other than it, and to distinguish the cause (al-sabab) from other than it. This is disclosed by consideration of five aspects (aṭrāf khamsah).

### | الطرف الأول في تمييز العمد عن شبه العمد

والقصد له ثلاث متعلقات
أحدها بالفعل فمن تزلق رجلاه فسقط على غيره فمات فهو خطأ محض
الثاني التعلق بالشخص فمن رمى إلى صيد فأصاب إنسانا فهو خطأ محض وإن كان
الفعل باختياره
الثالث القصد المتعلق بزهوق الروح وبهذا يتميز العمد عن شبه العمد
وفي ضبطه طريقان
أحدهما أن ما علم حصول الموت به بعد وجود قصد الفعل والشخص فهو عمد محض
سواء كان قصد الفاعل إزهاق الروح أو لم يكن قصد وسواء كان حصول الموت به
غالبا أو نادرا كقطع الأنملة
الطريقة الثانية أن الضابط ما يقصد به القتل غالبا في المثقل فأما في
الجراحات فكل جرح سار ذي غور لأن قطع الأنملة لا يقصد به القتل غالبا ثم
هو موجب للقصاص وهذا ضعيف لأن معنى العمد لا يختلف بالجرح والمثقل وللمثقل
أيضا تأثير في الباطن وغور في الترضيص
والطريقة الأولى أيضا مدخولة لأنه لو ضرب كوعه بعصا فتورم ودام الألم حتى
مات علم حصول الموت به ولا قصاص فيه لقوله عليه السلام
قتيل السوط والعصا فيه مائة من الإبل وأي فرق  بينه وبين ما لو غرز إبرة
فأعقبت ألما وورما حتى مات إذ يجب القصاص به ولو أعقبت ألما دون الورم
فوجهان فإن أمكن أن يقال المضروب بالعصا لعله مات فجأة بسبب في باطنه أمكن
ذلك في غرز الإبرة كيف وقد نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه لو أبان بعض
الأصابع فتأكل الباقي فلا قصاص في الباقي وقد علم حصول السراية به ونص على
أنه لو ضرب رأسه فأذهب ضوء عينيه وجب القصاص في الضوء لأن اللطائف تقصد
بالسراية دون الأجسام وقد علم حصول السراية في الموضعين وعن هذا تصرف بعض
الأصحاب في النصين بالنقل والتخريج وقالوا فيهما قولان فتخرج الطريقتان على
القولين
ولما عسر الضبط على أبي حنيفة رحمه الله إذ رأى القصد خفيا عول على
الجارح فلزمه إسقاط القصاص في التفريق والتخنيق والتحريق
فالأولى في تعليل مذهب الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن نترك الضبط ونقول حصول
الموت بالسبب إما أن يكون نادرا أو كثيرا أو غالبا وليس كل كثير غالبا فإن
المرض كثير وليس بنادر ولا غالب بل الغالب الصحة والجذام نادر لا كثير ولا
غالب فكل ما كان حصول الموت به نادرا فلا قصاص فيه كالعصا والسوط وغرز إبرة
لا تعقب ورما ولما كان
سقوط الأطراف بالسراية نادرا نص على سقوط القصاص فيه بخلاف زوال اللطائف
كالعقل والبصر
ويقابل هذه الرتبة ما كان حصول الموت به غالبا كالجراحات الكبيرة
والمثقلات فتلحق بما يكون حصول الموت به ضروريا كالتخنيق وحز الرقبة
والمتوسط الذي يكون حصول الموت به كثيرا لا غالبا كالجراحات الواسعة فوق
غرز الإبرة وكقطع الأنملة وكالعصا والسوط ففي هذا ينظر إلى السبب الظاهر
وهو الجرح مزهقا فيجب القصاص به لأن الجرح طريق سالك إلى الإزهاق غالبا وإن
لم يكن قدر هذا الجرح مزهقا غالبا وما لا يجرح فليس طريقا غالبا فاعتبر فيه
أن يتحقق كونه بالإضافة إلى الشخص والحال مهلكا غالبا ثم ذلك يختلف
بالأشخاص والأحوال فليحكم فيه بالاجتهاد
فإن قيل لو ضرب شخصا ضربا يقتل المريض  غالبا لكن ظنه صحيحا قلنا يجب
القصاص لأن هذا الظن إذا لم ينف العدوان في الفعل وهو في نفسه قاتل فلا
يكون
معذورا بجهله بخلاف ما لو صدر هذا من مؤدب أو أب أو من طبيب سقاه شيئا
يقتل ذلك المريض إلا أنه لم يعرف مرضه فلا يجب القصاص لأنه جهل أباح الفعل
فإن قيل إذا سقي غيره دواء يقتل كثيرا لا غالبا فهو كالجراحات أو
المثقلات قلنا ظاهر كلام الأصحاب أنه كغرز الإبرة فإن أعقب تغيرا أو تألما
وجب القصاص لأن أغشية الباطن رقيقة فينقطع بالدواء فكان إلحاقه بالجرح أولى
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ص-د (qaṣada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intent, aim, or direction of purpose toward an object; the deliberate orientation of will.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, the volitional targeting (qaṣd) of an act, person, or consequence, distinguishing culpable agency from mere causation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes direct aim; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to indirect causation, but here it is strictly literal—intentional direction.
- Root: ش-ب-ه (shabaha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Similarity, ambiguity, or resemblance; that which is not fully identical but approximates.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Quasi-deliberate (shibh al-ʿamd) denotes an act resembling intentional killing in its outward form but lacking full intent to kill.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Metaphorical extension—resemblance without identity; the legal category is a middle rank between pure accident and pure intent.
- Root: ز-ه-ق (zahaqa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Departure, passing away; specifically the soul's exit from the body.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical term for the expiration of the soul (zuhūq al-rūḥ), the defining criterion for homicide.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage for the soul's departure; metaphorical for the completion of death.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (law, idhā) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal categories, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis for correct juristic inference.
chapters.translation:
I say: Intent (al-qaṣd) has three objects of attachment (mutaʿalliqāt).

The first is attachment to the act (al-fiʿl). Thus, whoever's feet slip and he falls upon another, causing his death, this is pure error (khaṭaʾ maḥḍ).

The second is attachment to the person (al-shakhṣ). Thus, whoever shoots at game but strikes a human being, this is pure error, even though the act was performed by his own choice.

The third is the intent attached to the expiration of the soul (zuhūq al-rūḥ), and by this, deliberate homicide (al-ʿamd) is distinguished from quasi-deliberate homicide (shibh al-ʿamd).

In regulating this criterion, there are two methods (ṭarīqatān):

The first is that whatever is known to result in death through it, after the existence of intent toward the act and the person, is pure deliberate homicide—whether or not the agent intended the expiration of the soul, and whether death through it occurs predominantly (ghāliban) or rarely (nādiran), such as severing a fingertip (qaṭʿ al-anmulah).

The second method is that the criterion is what is predominantly intended for killing in the case of heavy objects (al-muthqal). As for wounds (al-jirāḥāt), every penetrating, deep wound (jirāḥ sārī dhī ghawr) [qualifies], because severing a fingertip is not predominantly intended for killing, yet it necessitates retribution (qiṣāṣ). This [second method] is weak, because the meaning of deliberateness does not differ between wounds and heavy objects; heavy objects also have an internal effect and deep penetration in crushing (al-tarḍīṣ).

The first method is also flawed, because if one struck another's wrist with a stick, causing swelling and continuous pain until death, death is known to result through it, yet there is no retribution therein, due to his saying, peace be upon him: {«قَتِيلُ السَّوْطِ وَالْعَصَا فِيهِ مِائَةٌ مِنَ الْإِبِلِ»} — "For the slain by whip and stick, one hundred camels [are due]." And what difference is there between this and one who pierces him with a needle, which produces pain and swelling until death, where retribution is obligatory? And if it produces pain without swelling, there are two aspects (wajhān). For if it could be said that the one struck by the stick perhaps died suddenly due to an internal cause, the same could be said of the needle's piercing. Moreover, al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, explicitly ruled that if one severed some fingers and the rest became gangrenous (taʾakkala), there is no retribution for the remaining [fingers], even though the spread (al-sarāyah) through it is known. And he explicitly ruled that if one struck his head and destroyed the light of his eyes, retribution is obligatory for the light, because subtle faculties (al-laṭāʾif) are intended to be affected by spread, unlike bodies. And the occurrence of spread is known in both cases. Due to this, some companions (al-aṣḥāb) manipulated the two texts through transmission (al-naql) and derivation (al-takhrīj), saying there are two opinions (qawlān) in both, and the two methods are derived upon the two opinions.

And since regulation was difficult for Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, because he saw intent as hidden, he relied upon the wounding instrument (al-jāriḥ), which necessitated his dropping retribution in cases of severing (al-tafrīq), strangulation (al-takhnīq), and burning (al-taḥrīq).

The most appropriate approach in explaining the school of al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, is to abandon [strict] regulation and say: The occurrence of death through a cause is either rare (nādir), frequent (kathīr), or predominant (ghālib). Not every frequent thing is predominant, for illness is frequent—neither rare nor predominant; rather, health is predominant. Leprosy is rare—neither frequent nor predominant. Thus, whatever causes death rarely entails no retribution, such as the stick, the whip, and the piercing of a needle that produces no swelling. And since the falling off of limbs through spread is rare, he explicitly ruled that retribution drops therein, unlike the removal of subtle faculties such as intellect and sight.

Opposing this rank is what causes death predominantly, such as large wounds and heavy objects, which are annexed to what causes death necessarily, such as strangulation and severing the neck (ḥazz al-raqabah). The intermediate [rank]—where death occurs frequently but not predominantly, such as wide wounds beyond needle-piercing, severing a fingertip, the stick, and the whip—in this case, one looks to the apparent cause, namely the wound as life-extinguishing (muzhiq), and retribution is obligatory through it, because the wound is a traversable path to extinguishing [life] predominantly, even if this particular wound's capacity is not predominantly life-extinguishing. What does not wound is not a predominant path, so it is considered therein that it be verified as predominantly lethal in relation to the person and the condition. Then this varies by persons and conditions, so judgment therein is by juristic reasoning (ijtihād).

If it is said: If one struck a person with a blow that predominantly kills a sick person, but he thought him healthy, we say: Retribution is obligatory, because this assumption, if it does not negate transgression (al-ʿudwān) in the act—and it is in itself lethal—he is not excused by his ignorance. This differs from the case where this issues from a disciplinarian (muʾaddib), a father, or a physician who gave him something that kills that sick person, except that he did not know his illness—then retribution is not obligatory, because ignorance rendered the act permissible.

If it is said: If one gave another a medicine that kills frequently but not predominantly, is it like wounds or heavy objects? We say: The apparent [import] of the companions' statements is that it is like needle-piercing. If it produces a change or pain, retribution is obligatory, because the inner membranes are delicate and are severed by the medicine, so annexing it to the wound is more appropriate.

chapters.title_en: The Second Branch: Distinguishing the Cause from Direct Agency
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الطرف الثاني في تمييز السبب عن المباشرة

وما يحصل الموت عقبه ينقسم إلى شروط وعلة وسبب
أما الشرط فهو الذي يحصل عنده لأنه كحفر البئر مع التردية فإن الموت
بالتردية لكن الحفر شرط وكذا الإمساك مع القتل والشرط لا يتعلق القصاص به
وأما العلة فما تولد الموت إما بغير واسطة كحز الرقبة وإما بواسطة كالرمي
فإنه يولد الجرح والجرح يولد السراية والسراية تولد الموت وهذا يتعلق
القصاص به
أما السبب فما له أثر في التولد ولكنه يشبه الشرط من وجه فهذا على ثلاث
مراتب
الأولى الإكراه على القتل وهو موجب للقصاص فإنه شديد الشبه بالعلة لأنه
يولد في المكره داعية القتل غالبا
الثانية شهادة الزور فإنها تولد في القاضي داعية القتل لكنه دون الإكراه
فإن هذا إلجاء شرعا والاول حسا لكن لما كان كل واحد يفضي إلى القتل غالبا
في شخص معين لم نفرق بينهما وأبو حنيفة رحمه الله لم يلحق الشهادة بالإكراه
الثالثة ما يولد المباشرة توليدا عرفيا لا حسيا ولا شرعيا كتقديم الطعام
المسموم إلى
الضيف ففيه قولان
أحدهما لا قصاص على المقدم لأن الأكل ليس ملجئا لا حسا ولا شرعا
والثاني يجب لأن هذا التغرير يفضي إلى القتل غالبا في معين ثم الصحيح أن
الدية تجب وقيل بطرد القولين
ولو وضع الطعام المسموم في داره اعتمادا على أن الداخل المقصود سيأكله
انبساطا فلا قصاص عليه وقيل  بطرد القولين فلو دعا الضيف وحفر في الدهليز
بئرا فتردى فيه ففي القصاص قولان فإن قيل لو جرى سبب وقدر المقصود على دفعه
ولم يدفع قلنا هذا على مراتب
الأولى أن لا يكون السبب مهلكا كما لو فتح عرقه بغير إذنه ولم يعصب حتى
نزف الدم أو ألقاه في ماء قليل فبقي مستلقيا حتى غرق أو حبسه في بيت فلم
يطلب طعاما مع القدرة حتى مات فهو الذي أهلك نفسه فلا دية له ولا قصاص
الثانية أن يكون السبب مهلكا والدفع عسيرا كترك مداواة الجرح فالقصاص
واجب
الثالثة أن يكون السبب مهلكا وكان الدفع سهلا كما لو ألقاه في ماء مغرق
فترك السباحة وهو يحسنها ففيه وجهان ووجه الإيجاب أنه قد يدهش عن السباحة
والسبب في نفسه مهلك وفي الدية وجهان مرتبان وأولى بالوجوب
ولو ألقاه في نار فوقف فوجهان مرتبان والظاهر وجوب القصاص لأن النار بأول
اللقاء تشنج الأعضاء فتعسر الحركة به
فإن قيل لو كان به بعض الجوع فحبسه ومنعه الطعام حتى مات قلنا إن علم وجب
القصاص كما لو قصد مريضا بضرب خفيف وإن كان جاهلا بجوعه ففي القود قولان
أحدهما يجب كما لو ضرب مريضا على ظن أنه صحيح فالجوع السابق وإن كان
معينا فهو كالمرض
والثاني لا يحب لأن هذا القدر من الجوع ليس مهلكا وزيادة الجوع الأول هو
الذي أهلك بخلاف الضرب فإنه ليس زيادة في المرض لأنه ليس من جنسه فلم يمكن
إحالة الهلاك عليه
وحيث لا نوجب القصاص فلا بد من الدية وفي قدرها قولان
أحدهما الكل إذ سقوط القصاص كان بالشبهة
والثاني النصف لأن الهلاك حصل بالجوعين فهو كما لو وضع في السفينة
المثقلة زيادة مغرقة ففي قدر الضمان ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها الكل والثاني النصف والثالث التوزيع لأن تأثير المثقلات في الإغراق
متناسب بخلاف تأثير الجوع والجرح
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ب-ب (sababa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A rope or cord by which one reaches water; extended to any means or pathway leading to an end
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): That which mediates between two things without being the efficient agent itself; in legal theory, the indirect conduit of effect
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a physical cord; metaphorical: any instrumentality that "ties" an outcome to an actor without direct contact
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿalla)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To drink a second time; the cause as that which "repeats" its effect through generative succession
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The efficient cause (ʿillah) that produces its effect either immediately or through intermediate stages; in jurisprudence, the operative ground of a ruling
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: second draught; metaphorical: the generative chain where each link drinks from the preceding
- Root: ش-ر-ط (sharata)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A mark or sign; a condition as that which is marked out as prerequisite
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The external precondition that must exist for the cause to operate, yet contributes nothing to the effect itself
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: branding mark on a camel; metaphorical: the stipulated prerequisite that "brands" the context without generating the outcome
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīr al-ʿāmil (Ellipsis of the Governing Operator) — The tripartite division (sharṭ/ʿillah/sabab) requires supplying an implicit governing verb (aʿnī, "I mean") to parse the appositional structure correctly.
chapters.translation:
I say: That after which death occurs is divided into conditions, causes, and means.

As for the condition (sharṭ), it is that which death occurs in conjunction with — like digging a well alongside the act of throwing someone into it. For death results from the throwing, but the digging is a condition. Likewise, restraint alongside killing [is a condition]. The condition does not entail retribution (qiṣāṣ).

As for the cause (ʿillah), it is that which generates death — either without an intermediary, like severing the neck, or through an intermediary, like shooting, for the shot generates the wound, the wound generates the spreading [of injury], and the spreading generates death. This entails retribution.

As for the means (sabab), it is that which has an effect in the generation [of death] but resembles the condition in some respect. This falls into three ranks:

The first: coercion (ikrāh) to kill — this mandates retribution, for it bears strong resemblance to the cause, since it generates in the coerced person the impulse to kill, predominantly.

The second: false testimony (shahādat al-zūr) — for it generates in the judge the impulse to kill, but it is below coercion. For this [false testimony] is a legal compulsion (iljāʾ sharʿī), while the former is a sensory compulsion. Yet since each leads predominantly to killing a specific person, we did not differentiate between them. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) did not annex false testimony to coercion.

The third: that which generates direct agency in a customary manner (tawlīd ʿurfī) — neither sensory nor legal — like presenting poisoned food to a guest. Concerning this, there are two opinions:
One: no retribution upon the presenter, because eating is not compulsive, neither sensorily nor legally.
The second: it is obligatory, because this deception leads predominantly to killing a specific person. Then the correct [view] is that the blood-wit (diyah) is obligatory. And it was said: the two opinions are carried through [consistently].

If he placed poisoned food in his house, relying on the fact that the intended entrant would eat it out of familiarity, then no retribution upon him. And it was said: the two opinions are carried through.

If he invited a guest and dug a well in the vestibule, and he fell into it, then concerning retribution there are two opinions.

If it is said: if a means occurred and the intended victim was able to repel it but did not repel it — we say: this falls into ranks:

The first: that the means is not destructive — like one who opened his vein without his permission and did not bandage it until the blood drained away; or threw him into shallow water and he remained lying until he drowned; or imprisoned him in a house and he did not seek food despite ability until he died — then it is he who destroyed himself, so neither blood-wit nor retribution [is due].

The second: that the means is destructive and repelling it is difficult — like neglecting to treat a wound — then retribution is obligatory.

The third: that the means is destructive and repelling it is easy — like throwing him into drowning water and he refrained from swimming despite being skilled at it. Concerning this, there are two aspects (wajhān). The aspect of obligation [argues] that he may be stunned away from swimming, and the means in itself is destructive. Concerning the blood-wit, there are two aspects, ranked — and the more appropriate is obligation.

If he threw him into fire and he stood still [and burned], then two aspects, ranked — and the apparent [view] is the obligation of retribution, because fire at the first contact contracts the limbs, making movement difficult for him.

If it is said: if he had some hunger and he imprisoned him and prevented food until he died — we say: if he knew, retribution is obligatory, just as if he intended a sick person with a light blow. If he was ignorant of his hunger, then concerning retaliation (qawad) there are two opinions:
One: it is obligatory, just as if he struck a sick person supposing him healthy — for the prior hunger, though contributory, is like illness.
The second: it is not obligatory, because this degree of hunger is not destructive, and the increase of the prior hunger is what destroyed — unlike the blow, for it is not an increase in the illness since it is not of its kind, so the destruction cannot be attributed to it.

Wherever we do not mandate retribution, the blood-wit is indispensable. Concerning its amount, there are two opinions:
One: the full amount, since the fall of retribution was due to ambiguity (shubhah).
The second: half, because the destruction occurred through both hungers — just as if he placed on an overloaded ship an additional sinking weight. Concerning the amount of liability, there are three sayings:
One: the full amount. The second: half. The third: apportionment — because the effect of weights in sinking is proportional, unlike the effect of hunger and wounding.

chapters.title_en: The Third Aspect: The Concurrence of Cause and Direct Agency
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الطرف الثالث في اجتماع السبب والمباشرة

أما الشرط فلا يخفى سقوطه معهما كالممسك مع القاتل والحافر مع المردي إذ
لا قصاص عليهما ولا ضمان  خلافا لمالك رضي الله عنه فإنه جعل الممسك شريكا
وأما المباشرة مع السبب فعلى مراتب
الأولى أن يغلب السبب المباشرة وذلك إذا لم تكن المباشرة عدوانا كقتل
القاضي والجلاد مع شهادة الزور فالقصاص على الشهود فإن كان عدوانا بأن
اعترف ولي القصاص بكونه عالما بالتزوير فلا قصاص على الشهود ولا دية لأنه
لم يلجأ حسا ولا شرعا فصار قولهم شرطا محضا كالإمساك
الثانية أن يصير السبب مغلوبا بالمباشرة كما إذا ألقاه من شاهق الجبل
فتلقاه إنسان بسيفه فقده بنصفين فلا قصاص على الملقي عرف أو لم يعرف لأن
إلقاءه صار شرطا محضا لما ورد عليه مباشرة مستقلة
الثالثة أن يعتدل السبب والمباشرة كالإكراه على القتل فالأقوى لا يحبط
مباشرة المكره خلافا لزفر وأبي يوسف وهل تصير المباشرة مغلوبة به حتى لا
يجب القصاص على المكره فيه قولان فإن لم نوجب القصاص ففي الدية قولان
مرتبان وأولى بالوجوب لأنها تثبت مع الشبهة ووجه الإسقاط نقل الفعل عن
المكره وجعله كالآلة وإن أوجبنا الدية ففي طريقها وجهان
أحدهما تجب عليهما جميعا ثم يرجع على المكره
والثاني يجب النصف لأن إيجاب القصاص عليهما كالتشريك فإن قلنا لا دية ففي
الكفارة وجهان وجه إثباتها أنه آثم بالقتل وفاقا وقد تجب الكفارة حيث لا
دية كما في الرمي إلى صف الكفار
وإن قلنا لا تجب ففي حرمان الميراث وجهان والظاهر الحرمان لأنه آثم
بالقتل والكفارة والدية غرم يمكن نقله إلى المكره بخلاف الحرمان
فإن قيل فما قولكم في أمر السلطان قلنا في نزوله منزلة الإكراه وجهان وجه
إلحاقه به أمران
أحدهما أنه يعلم من عادة السلطان السطوة عند المخالفة وإن لم يصرح به
وعلى هذه العلة يلتحق به كل متغلب هذه عادته وإن لم يكن سلطانا ثم وجه
التردد أن المعلوم من عادته
هل يكون كالملفوظ به على الإقتران
العلة الثانية أن طاعة السلطان واجبة على الجملة كيلا تؤدي مخالفته إلى
إثارة الفتنة ولذلك نقول لا ينعزل بالفسق ولو كان الإستبدال به يثير الفتنة
فلا  يستبدل فتزاحم على الفعل موجب ومحرم فإن لم نبح انتهض شبهة كالإكراه
بخلاف أمر السيد عبده فإنه يجب عليه مخالفة السيد إذ لو عاقبه دفع السلطان
ظلمه وليس وراء السلطان يد دافعة فمخالته تحرك الفتنة نعم لو كان العبد من
طباعه الضراوة فإذا أغراه بإنسان فالقصاص على السيد كما لو أغرى سبعا وكذا
لو أغرى مجنونا هذه حاله هل يتعلق الضمان برقبة هذا العبد وبمال هذا
المجنون أم ينزل منزلة البهيمة فيه وجهان من حيث إنه إنسان صورة لكنه بهيمة
في المعنى
فإن قيل وما حد الإكراه قلنا قد ذكرنا صورته في الطلاق لكنا نتعرض لصور
إحداها أنه لو أكره إنسانا على أن يكره ثالثا على قتل الرابع فعلى الأول
قصاص وفيمن بعده قولان
الثانية لو قال اقتل زيدا أو عمرا وإلا قتلتك فقتل زيدا فهو مختار لأن
ميله إلى زيد ليس إلا عن شهوة ويظهر ذلك إذا قال اقتل من أهل الدار واحدا
وإلا قتلتك
الثالثة أن يقول اقتل نفسك وإلا قتلتك فهذا ليس بإكراه ولو قال اقتلني
وإلا قتلتك فهذا إكراه وإذن فهل يؤثر الإذن في سقوط القصاص والدية فيه
ثلاثة أوجه
أصحها أنه يسقط لأنه صاحب الحق كما إذا قال اقتل عبدي
والثاني لا لأن القصاص والدية تثبت للورثة ابتداء لا إرثا
والثالث لا يجب القصاص للشبهة وتجب الدية
فإن قيل إذا رأيتم إيجاب القصاص عليهما فإن لم يكن أحدهما كفؤا للمقتول
قلنا يجب القصاص على الكفء لأن شريك غير الكفء يجب القصاص عليه كشريك الأب
وشريك العبد في قتل السيد
وإن كان أحدهما صبيا وقلنا إن فعل الصبي خطأ فالآخر شريك خاطىء لكن إن
كان المحمول صبيا فيحتمل أن يجب القصاص على الحامل لأن خطأه نتيجة الإكراه
فهو كما لو أكره إنسانا على أن يرمي إلى طلل عرفه المكره إنسانا وظنه
الرامي جرثومة ففي وجوب القصاص وجهان وجه الإيجاب جعل المكره مباشرا وجعل
المكره آلة له لأنه تولد من إكراهه وعن هذا اختبط الأصحاب في المكره  على
إتلاف المال هل يطالب بالضمان فعلى وجه لا يطالب أصلا لأنه كالآلة
ولو أكرهه على صعود شجرة فزلقت رجله فمات وجب القصاص على المكره ولم يجعل
كشريك الخاطىء لأن هذا الخطأ ولده إكراهه بخلاف جهل المكره وصباه فإن فيه
وجهين
فإن قيل فما الذي يباح بالإكراه قلنا لا يباح به القتل والزنا ويباح به
إتلاف المال بل يجب وتباح به الردة وفي وجوب التلفظ به وجهان منهم من لم
يوجب للتصلب في الدين ويباح شرب الخمر بالإكراه وفي وجوبه خلاف مرتب على
الردة وأولى بالوجوب والإفطار في الصوم ينبغي أن يقضى بوجوبه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ب-ب (sababa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A rope or cord by which one draws water; extended to any means, path, or connection leading to an end.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, that which mediates an effect without being the immediate efficient agent; a cause (sabab) stands in contrast to direct agency (mubāsharah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: a physical cord. Metaphorical: any linkage that draws an effect toward its terminus, as in "so-and-so is a means (sabab) to good."
- Root: ب-ش-ر (bashara)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To touch, contact directly with the skin; to take hold of something with immediate bodily contact.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Direct agency (mubāsharah) in jurisprudence: the act performed by the agent himself without an intervening instrument or human intermediary.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical touch. Metaphorical: the immediate causal connection between an agent and a deed, as opposed to indirect causation (tasbīb).
- Root: ق-ص-ص (qassa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow a trace, to track; to relate a narrative; from this, qiṣāṣ (retaliation) as the law of exact equivalence in following the crime.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Retributive justice (qiṣāṣ) as the divinely ordained equalization between transgression and punishment, rooted in the principle of equivalence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: tracing footsteps. Metaphorical: the legal institution of exact retaliation, where the punishment "follows" the crime in measure.
- Root: ك-ر-ه (kariha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To dislike, to find something repugnant; ikrāh: compelling someone against his inclination.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Coercion (ikrāh) as a legal impediment that transfers the juridical attribution of an act from the coerced agent to the coercer, while the coerced becomes a mere instrument (ālah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: aversion. Metaphorical: the legal state where one's will is overborne, rendering the act as if performed by another.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Concessive Clauses (al-ḥāl al-muʿarriḍah) — When a conditional or concessive clause (e.g., "whether he knew or did not know") follows a legal ruling, it signals that the ruling is indifferent to the condition, indicating the dominance of one causal factor over another.
chapters.translation:
I say: As for the mere condition (sharṭ), it is evident that liability falls away with both [the cause and the direct agent] — like the one who holds the victim while another kills him, and the one who digs a pit while another pushes the victim into it. For neither incurs retaliation (qiṣāṣ) nor indemnity (ḍamān), contrary to Mālik — may God be pleased with him — who made the holder a partner [in liability].

As for direct agency (mubāsharah) combined with causation (sabab), it falls into degrees:

**The First Degree:** That the cause overwhelms the direct agency — namely, when the direct agency is not an act of transgression, such as the killing by the judge and the executioner upon false testimony. The retaliation falls upon the witnesses. But if the direct agency was transgressive — namely, if the guardian of the retaliation right confessed that he knew of the falsification — then there is no retaliation upon the witnesses and no blood-wit (diyah), because the victim did not resort to them either by sense or by law. Their statement thus became a mere condition, like the act of holding.

**The Second Degree:** That the cause becomes overwhelmed by the direct agency — as when one throws a man from a mountain peak, and another person receives him upon his sword and cuts him in two. There is no retaliation upon the thrower, whether he knew or did not know, because his throwing became a mere condition when an independent direct agency intervened upon it.

**The Third Degree:** That the cause and the direct agency are balanced — as in coercion (ikrāh) to kill. The stronger [cause] does not nullify the direct agency of the coerced one, contrary to Zufar and Abū Yūsuf. And whether the direct agency becomes overwhelmed by it such that retaliation is not incumbent upon the coerced one — there are two opinions. If we do not impose retaliation, then concerning the blood-wit there are two opinions, arranged in order, and the blood-wit is more deserving of imposition because it is established even with ambiguity (shubhah). The ground for dropping it is the transfer of the act from the coerced one and making him like an instrument. If we impose the blood-wit, then concerning its mode there are two aspects:

One: It is incumbent upon both jointly, then the direct agent recovers from the coercer.

The Second: Only half is incumbent, because imposing retaliation upon both is like making them partners.

If we say there is no blood-wit, then concerning the expiation (kaffārah) there are two aspects. The ground for affirming it is that he is sinful by the killing, by agreement; and expiation may be incumbent where there is no blood-wit, as in shooting toward a rank of unbelievers.

If we say it is not incumbent, then concerning the deprivation of inheritance there are two aspects. The apparent [view] is deprivation, because he is sinful by the killing. The expiation and the blood-wit are a financial burden that can be transferred to the coercer, unlike the deprivation.

If it is said: "What then is your doctrine concerning the command of the Sultan?" — I say: Concerning its descending to the rank of coercion, there are two aspects. The ground for annexing it to coercion is two matters:

One: It is known from the custom of the Sultan that he exercises violence upon opposition, even if he does not explicitly state it. Upon this ground, every tyrant whose custom is such is annexed to him, even if he is not a Sultan. Then the ground for hesitation is whether what is known from his custom is like what is uttered, in conjunction [with the command].

The Second Ground: Obedience to the Sultan is obligatory in general, lest opposition to him lead to the stirring of sedition (fitnah). For this reason we say he is not removed from office by his wickedness; and if replacing him would stir sedition, he is not replaced. Thus there presses upon the act a factor that necessitates and one that prohibits. If we do not permit [the act], it raises an ambiguity like coercion. This differs from the command of a master to his slave, for the slave must disobey the master, since if the master punished him, the Sultan would repel his injustice; and there is no repelling hand beyond the Sultan. Thus disobeying him stirs sedition. Indeed, if the slave is of a nature prone to ferocity, and he incites him against a person, then retaliation falls upon the master — just as if he had incited a beast of prey. Likewise, if he incited a madman of this disposition — whether the indemnity attaches to the person of this slave and the property of this madman, or whether he descends to the rank of a mere animal — there are two aspects, inasmuch as he is human in form but a beast in meaning.

If it is said: "What is the definition of coercion?" — I say: We have already mentioned its form in the chapter on divorce, but we shall address its forms:

**One of them:** If he coerced a man to coerce a third to kill a fourth, then retaliation is upon the first, and concerning those after him there are two opinions.

**The Second:** If he said: "Kill Zayd or ʿAmr, or I will kill you," and he killed Zayd — then he is a free chooser, because his inclination toward Zayd arises only from desire. This becomes evident when he says: "Kill one of the people of the house, or I will kill you."

**The Third:** If he said: "Kill yourself, or I will kill you" — this is not coercion. But if he said: "Kill me, or I will kill you" — this is coercion combined with permission. Does the permission effect the dropping of retaliation and blood-wit? There are three aspects:

The most correct: It drops, because he is the possessor of the right — as when he says: "Kill my slave."

The Second: It does not drop, because retaliation and blood-wit are established for the heirs ab initio, not by inheritance.

The Third: Retaliation is not incumbent due to ambiguity, but the blood-wit is incumbent.

If it is said: "When you see the imposition of retaliation upon both, what if one of them is not a legal equal (kufʾ) to the slain?" — I say: Retaliation is incumbent upon the equal, because the partner who is not an equal — retaliation is incumbent upon him, like the partner of the father and the partner of the slave in killing the master.

If one of them is a minor, and we say that the act of the minor is an error, then the other is a partner in error. But if the one carried [and thrown] is a minor, then it is probable that retaliation is incumbent upon the carrier, because his error is the result of coercion — just as when one coerces a man to shoot at a ruin which the coercer knows contains a man, while the shooter supposes it to be a mound of earth. Concerning the imposition of retaliation there are two aspects. The ground for imposition is making the coercer the direct agent and making the coerced an instrument for him, because it was generated from his coercion. From this the companions (aṣḥāb) became perplexed concerning the one coerced to destroy property — whether he is pursued for indemnity. On one aspect, he is not pursued at all, because he is like an instrument.

And if he coerced him to climb a tree, and his foot slipped and he died, then retaliation is incumbent upon the coercer, and he is not treated as a partner in error — because this error was generated by his coercion. This differs from the ignorance and minority of the coerced one, for concerning those there are two aspects.

If it is said: "What is permitted by coercion?" — I say: Killing and fornication are not permitted by it. The destruction of property is permitted by it — nay, it becomes obligatory. Apostasy (riddah) is permitted by it, and concerning the obligation of uttering [the word of apostasy] there are two aspects: some did not impose it, for firmness in religion. The drinking of wine is permitted by coercion, and concerning its obligation there is a disagreement arranged upon [the question of] apostasy — and it is more deserving of being obligatory. And breaking the fast in Ramadan, by coercion, should be judged as obligatory.

chapters.title_en: Section 457: On the Fourth and Fifth Branches of Causation in Retaliation (Qiṣāṣ)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الطرف الرابع أن يكون السبب من الآدمي والمباشرة من بهيمة

كما إذا ألقاه في تيار بحر فالتقمه الحوت قبل الغرق فيلزمه القصاص وينزل
فعل الحوت منزلة جرح السكين
ولو ألقاه في بئر عميق وكان في عمقه نصل منصوب فمات به وجب القصاص وخرج
الربيع قولا أن الدية تجب دون القصاص اعتبارا باختيار الحيوان وكونه شبهة
في الدفع وإن ألقاه في ماء لا يغرق فالتقمه الحوت من حيث لم يشعر الملقي
فلا يجب عليه إلا الدية وإن عرف حضور الحوت لزمه القصاص
ولو أمسك إنسانا وعرضه للسبع حتى افترسه وجب القصاص والمجنون الضاري
بطبعه كالسبع والحوت وإن لم يكن ضاريا اعتبر اختياره في قطع السبب
فروع أربعة
الأول لو أنهشه حية أو عقربا يقتل مثله غالبا لزمه القصاص ونزلت الحية
منزلة السكين ولو كان لا يقتل غالبا كان كغرز الإبرة
الثاني لو ألقى عليه عقربا أو حية فنهشته فلا قود لأن الغالب أنه يفر وإن
كان ضاريا فهو كالإنهاش
الثالث لو جمع بينه وبين سبع في بيت فافترسه وجب القصاص وإن كان بدله حية
فلا قصاص لأن الحية تفر والسبع في المضيق يثب بطبعه فإن لم يكن الطبع كذلك
لم يكن الحكم كذلك
الرابع لو أغرى به كلبا أو سبعا في صحراء فلا قصاص بخلاف البيت فإن السبع
في المضيق يقصد وفي الصحراء يتوحش
فإن كان ضاريا في  الصحراء ولم يكن الهرب ممكنا لزم القصاص فإن كان الهرب
ممكنا فتخاذل فهو كترك السباحة

### | الطرف الخامس في طرآن المباشرة على المباشرة أو السبب على السبب

والحكم فيه تقديم الأقوى فإن اعتدلا جمعنا بينهما فلو جرح الأول وحز
الثاني الرقبة فالقاتل هو الثاني لانقطاع أثر الأول بخلاف ما إذا قطع هذا
من الكوع والثاني من المرفق فمات فإن القصاص عليهما لأن ألم الأول ينتشر
إلى الأعضاء الرئيسية ويبقى
ولو قطع الأول حلقومه ولم يبق إلا حركة المذبوحين فقده الثاني بنصفين
فالقصاص على الأول ولا نظر إلى حركة المذبوحين بخلاف ما لو حز رقبة المريض
المشرف على الموت لأن موته غير مقطوع به وبخلاف ما لو نزع أحشاءه وإن كان
بحيث يعلم أنه يموت بعد يوم أو يومين ولكنه في الحال يعقل بحياة مستقرة فإن
القصاص يجب على من حز الرقبة لأن عمر رضي الله عنه شاور في الخلافة في هذه
الحالة فكيف لا تعتبر حياته وقال مالك رحمه الله هو كحركة المذبوحين
فأما إذا جرح كل واحد جراحة فمات بالسراية أو حز أحدهما الرقبة والآخر قد
بنصفين معا فهما شريكان
فقد تنخل من هذا أن العمد المحض العدوان المزهق للروح سبب القصاص ولا يرد
على
الحد ما لو استحق حز رقبة إنسان فقده بنصفين لأنه لا عدوان به من حيث
كونه إزهاقا بل من حيث الإساءة في الطريق فلذلك لم يجب القصاص فإن قيل ظن
الإباحة هل يكون شبهة قلنا إذا قتل من ظنه مرتدا ولم تعهد له الردة فيجب
القصاص وإن كان قد عهد مرتدا ولكنه أسلم ولم يشعر به فقولان
أحدهما السقوط للظن المبتنى على الإستصحاب
والثاني يجب لأنه غير معذور في هذا الظن إذ لا يحل للآحاد قتل المرتد
وكذلك لو ظنه عبدا أو ذميا لزمه القصاص على المذهب لأن هذا ظن لا يبيح فهو
كما لو زنى مع العلم بالتحريم والجهل بوجوب الحد بخلاف ما إذا رأى مسلما في
دار الحرب على زي المشركين ولم يعهده  مسلما فقتله فإذا هو مسلم فلا قود
وتجب الكفارة وفي الدية قولان لأن القتل مباح بهذا الظن وهو معذور
أحدهما تجب لأنها ضمان المحل وذلك لا يختلف باختلاف حال المتلف
والثاني أنها لا تجب لأنها وإن كانت عوضا فليست على مذاق الأعواض المحضة
فإنها بدل للنفس وتجب الكفارة قولا واحدا لأنها تجب من غير تقصير
ولو قتل إنسانا على ظن أنه قاتل أبيه ففي وجوب القصاص قولان
أحدهما يجب لأنه غير معذور فيه
الثاني لا يجب لأن هذا الظن مما يمهد عذره لأن القتل مباح بهذا الظن لكنه
غير معذور ولهذا نقطع بالوجوب إذا قال تبينت أن أبي حي
ومن أصحابنا من قطع بأنه لو صدقه ولي الدم فلا قصاص وإنما القولان إذا
تنازعا
ومنهم من طرد القولين لأنه ظن من غير مستند شرعي

### | الركن الثاني القتيل

وشرط كونه مضمونا بالقصاص على الجملة كونه معصوما والعصمة تستفاد
بالإسلام والجزية والأمان يتنزلان منزلته والحربي مهدر والمرتد كذلك في حق
المسلم ولكن في حق الكافر الذمي والمرتد إذا قتله فيه خلاف
ومن عليه القصاص معصوم في حق غير المستحق والزاني المحصن معصوم بالقصاص
عن الذمي وعن المسلم فيه وجهان مثارهما التردد في أن الحد للمسلمين والإمام
نائبهم أو إضافة الحد إلى الله تعالى كإضافة القصاص إلى إنسان معين حتى لا
يظهر أثره في حق غيره
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-ق-م (la-qā-ma)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To swallow or gulp down wholly; the action of a beast seizing prey in its jaws.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes an act of consumption that terminates life, analogous to a lethal instrument in legal causation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for animal ingestion; metaphorical (majāz) extension to legal agency where the animal acts as a mere tool.
- Root: ض-ر-ي (ḍa-rā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Predatory ferocity; a beast's natural disposition to attack.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, distinguishes voluntary agency (ikhtiyār) from instinctual compulsion, affecting culpability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for wild beasts; metaphorical for a person whose aggression is habitual and uncontrollable.
- Root: ع-ص-م (ʿa-ṣa-ma)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Protection, inviolability; that which renders blood sacrosanct.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The juridical status of inviolability (ʿiṣmah) conferred by faith, covenant (dhimmah), or safe-conduct (amān).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for legal protection; metaphorical for the moral sanctity of life in divine law.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqdīm al-Aqwā (Prioritizing the Stronger Cause) — When two causal acts converge, the grammatically and logically stronger agent governs the ruling, mirroring the syntactic precedence of the primary verb over the subordinate.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth branch is that the cause (sabab) be from a human being while the direct act (mubāsharah) is from a beast. For example, if he cast him into a sea current and a fish swallowed him before drowning, then retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is incumbent upon him, and the fish's act is treated as the wound of a knife. Likewise, if he cast him into a deep well in whose depth an upright blade was fixed, and he died by it, retaliation is obligatory. Al-Rabīʿ has transmitted a saying that only blood-money (diyah) is due, not retaliation, considering the animal's choice and its being a source of doubt (shubhah) in repelling. If he cast him into water that does not drown, and a fish swallowed him from where the caster was unaware, then only blood-money is due; but if he knew of the fish's presence, retaliation is incumbent.

If he seized a person and exposed him to a beast until it tore him apart, retaliation is obligatory. A rabid madman by his nature is like the beast and the fish. If he was not rabid, his choice is considered in severing the cause.

There are four subsidiary branches. First: If he made a snake or scorpion bite him, of a kind that generally kills, retaliation is incumbent, and the snake is treated as a knife. If it does not generally kill, it is like the prick of a needle. Second: If he cast a scorpion or snake upon him and it bit him, there is no retaliation (qawad), because the norm is that he would flee; but if it was rabid, it is like the deliberate bite. Third: If he confined him with a beast in a house and it tore him apart, retaliation is obligatory. But if it was a snake instead, there is no retaliation, because the snake flees, whereas the beast in a narrow place leaps by its nature. If the nature is not so, the ruling is not so. Fourth: If he incited a dog or beast against him in an open desert, there is no retaliation, unlike the house, for the beast in a narrow place targets, but in the desert it grows wild. If it was rabid in the desert and flight was impossible, retaliation is incumbent. If flight was possible and he failed to act, it is like abandoning swimming.

The fifth branch concerns the supervenience of direct act upon direct act, or cause upon cause. The ruling therein is to prioritize the stronger. If they are equal, we combine between them. Thus, if the first wounded and the second severed the neck, the killer is the second, due to the cessation of the first's effect — unlike the case where one cut from the wrist and the second from the elbow, and he died: retaliation is upon both, because the first's pain spreads to the vital organs and persists. If the first cut his windpipe, leaving only the convulsive movement of the slaughtered, and the second cut him in half, retaliation is upon the first, with no regard to the convulsive movement — unlike the case of severing the neck of a sick man on the verge of death, for his death is not certain; and unlike the case of extracting his entrails, even if it is known he will die after a day or two, yet he presently possesses stable life. Retaliation is then obligatory upon the one who severed the neck, for ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) consulted regarding the caliphate in such a state — how then is his life not considered? Mālik (may God have mercy on him) said he is like the convulsive movement of the slaughtered.

As for when each wounds him with a wound and he dies by the spreading (sarāyah), or one severs the neck and the other cuts him in half simultaneously, they are partners.

It emerges from this that pure intentional aggression (al-ʿamd al-maḥḍ) that extinguishes the soul is the cause of retaliation. This is not refuted by the case of one who deserved the severing of his neck and another cut him in half, for there is no aggression therein in terms of extinguishing life, but rather in terms of misusing the method. Hence retaliation is not obligatory. If it is said: Does the presumption of permissibility (ẓann al-ibāḥah) constitute a doubt (shubhah)? We say: If he killed one he presumed to be an apostate, and no apostasy had been established from him, retaliation is obligatory. If apostasy had been established but he had embraced Islam without the killer's knowledge, there are two sayings: One is the dropping of retaliation, due to the presumption built upon istiṣḥāb (continuity of prior state); the second is that it is obligatory, for he is not excused in this presumption, since it is not lawful for individuals to kill an apostate. Likewise, if he presumed him a slave or a dhimmī, retaliation is incumbent upon him according to the school, for this is a presumption that does not permit — just as if he fornicated with knowledge of prohibition but ignorance of the ḥadd penalty. This differs from the case where he saw a Muslim in the abode of war dressed in the garb of polytheists, and had not known him to be Muslim, so he killed him, and he turned out to be Muslim: there is no retaliation, and expiation (kaffārah) is obligatory. Regarding blood-money there are two sayings, because the killing is permitted by this presumption and he is excused. One: It is obligatory, for it is a guarantee of the subject, which does not differ with the differing states of the destroyer. The second: It is not obligatory, for though it is compensation, it is not of the pure order of compensations, being a substitute for the soul. Expiation is obligatory by unanimous saying, for it is due without negligence.

If he killed a man presuming he was the killer of his father, there are two sayings on the obligation of retaliation. One: It is obligatory, for he is not excused therein. The second: It is not obligatory, for this presumption paves the way for his excuse, since killing is permitted by this presumption — but he is not excused, and for this we decisively affirm obligation if he says, "It became clear to me that my father is alive." Among our companions, some decisively held that if the heir of the blood confirms him, there is no retaliation, and the two sayings apply only when they dispute. Others extended the two sayings, for it is a presumption without a legal basis.

As for the second pillar, the slain person: The condition of his being guaranteed by retaliation, in sum, is his inviolability (ʿiṣmah). Inviolability is acquired by Islam; the poll-tax (jizyah) and safe-conduct (amān) are treated as its equivalent.
