chapters.arabic_text:
الأول لو قال المجني عليه نقص سمعي ولم يزل وجب أرش النقصان وقدر
بالمسافة وطريقه أن يجلس بجنبه من هو في مثل سنه وصحته ويبعد عنهما واحد
ويرفع الصوت فلا يزال يقرب إلى أن يقول السليم سمعت ثم يديم ذلك الحد في
الصوت ويقرب إلى أن يقول المجني عليه سمعت فإن سمع على النصف من تلك
المسافة فقد نقص نصف  السمع فإن قال الجاني سمع من قبل حلفنا المجني عليه
ولو قال لست أسمع من إحدى أذني فامتحانه أن تصم الأذن الثانية ويصاح به
صيحة منكرة
الثاني لو قال أهل الصنعة لطيفة السمع باقية لكن وقع في المنفذ الارتتاق
ففي كمال الدية وجهان
أحدهما أن تعطل المنفعة هل هو كزوالها ويجري فيما إذا ذهب سمع الصبي
فتعطل نطقه أو ضرب صلبه فتعطل رجله ففي تعدد الدية في نظائر ذلك خلاف
الثالثة البصر وفي إبطالها مع بقاء الحدقة كمال الدية يستوي فيه الأخفش
والأعمش ومن على حدقته بياض لا يمنع أصل البصر ثم يمتحن عند دعوى العمى
بتقريب حديدة من حدقته مغافصة وإن ادعى النقصان امتحن كما في السمع
الرابعة الشم وفي إبطاله كمال الدية ويجرب بالروائح المنتنة الحادة فإن
ادعى
النقصان فامتحان ذلك عسير فيكتفي باليمين وقيل إن الشم لا تكمل فيه الدية
لأن التأذي به مع كثرة الأنتان أكثر من التلذذ به مع قلة الطيب وهذا هوس إذ
هو طليعة كسائر الحواس
الخامسة النطق وفي إبطاله عن اللسان كمال الدية وإن بقي حاسة الذوق
والإعانة على المضع والحروف الشفهية والحلقية لأن الذي بطل جزء مقصود برأسه
فإن ذهب بعض الكلام فأقرب معيار فيه الحروف وهي ثمانية وعشرون متساوية في
الاعتبار وقال الاصطخري لا تدخل الشفوية والحلقية في التوزيع
فرعان
الأول لو كان لا يحسن بعض الحروف فهل يؤثر في نقصان الدية فيه وجهان
أحدهما لا لانه يرجع إلى ضعف النطق فهو كضعف البطش
والثاني نعم لأن البطش لا يتقدر والحروف صارت مقدرة للنطق بنوع من
التقريب فإن قلنا يحط فلو كان يقدر على الإعراب عن جميع مقاصده بتلك الحروف
لغزارة فضله ففي الحط خلاف والظاهر أنه يحط أما إذا كان نقصان الحروف
بجناية جان فالحط أولى
والقول الضابط في الفرق بين النقصان بجناية أو آفة أن المفوت جرم أو
منفعة فكل جرم مقدر فنقصان بعضه مؤثر سواء كان بجناية أو آفة كسقوط بعض
السن وبعض الأنملة وانشقاق لحم الرأس  إلى حد المتلاحمة وما لا يتقدر كفلقة
من الأنملة فسقوطها لا ينقص كانت بآفة سماوية أو جناية أبقى شيئا أو لم تبق
مهما لم ينقص البطش لأن الزينة ليست من خاصية هذا العضو
وأما نقصان المنفعة التي لا تتقدر إن كانت بآفة سماوية لم ينقص وإن كانت
بجناية وجميع جرم العضو باق فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها لا يعتبر كالآفة
والثاني نعم لأن الآفات لا تنضبط والجناية تنضبط كما في القروح والجراحات
والثالث أن الآخر إن قطع العضو لم يعتبر النقصان في حقه وإن أبطل بقية
البطش حط عنه ما وجب على الأول لأنهما جنايتان متناسبتان من وجه واحد وإنما
يظهر الخلاف في نقصان الحروف لأنها كالمقدرة للنطق
الفرع الثاني لو قطع بعض لسانه فأبطل كل كلامه فعليه الدية ولو أبطل بعض
كلامه وتساوت نسبة الجرم والحروف بأن قطع نصف الجرم وزال نصف الكلام فعليه
نصف الدية وإن تفاوتت النسبة فنأخذ بأكثر الشهادتين لأن كل واحد من الحروف
والجرم مبين مقدار الزائل من القوة النطقية التي لا يتقدر تحقيقها بنوع من
التقريب فنأخذ أكثر الشهادتين
فإن قطع ربع اللسان فزال نصف الحروف فعليه النصف
وإن قطع نصف اللسان فزال ربع الحروف فعليه النصف وقال أبو إسحاق النظر
إلى الجرم ولكن إذا قطع ربع اللسان فزال نصف الكلام فكأنه أشل ربعا من
الباقي فتظهر فائدة العبارتين فيمن اقتلع الباقي فإنه لو قطع ربع لسانه
وذهب نصف كلامه فاستأصل غيره باقي اللسان فعليه ثلاثة أرباع الدية نظرا إلى
الأكثر عند الأصحاب وعند أبي إسحاق عليه نصف الدية وحكومة ربع أشل
ولو قطع ربع اللسان فأذهب ربع الكلام فأوجبنا النصف فجاء الثاني واستأصل
وجب عليه ثلاثة أرباع الدية نظرا إلى الأكثر وعند الشيخ أبي إسحاق رحمه
الله نصف الدية نظرا إلى الجرم
وأما إذا قطع فلقة من لسانه ولم يذهب شيئا من الكلام فلا شيء لأن القوة
إذا نقصت رجعنا إلى الشهادتين ورجحنا وإذا لم ينقص فليس إلا حكومة كلسان
الأخرس
المنفعة السادسة الصوت وفي  إبطاله كل الدية وإن بطل معه حركة اللسان
فديتان وفيه وجه أن الواجب دية واحدة لأن مقصود الصوت النطق
وإن قلنا ديتان فلو كان حركة اللسان ناقصة فقد تعطل النطق ولم يزل ففيه
الخلاف السابق
السابعة الذوق وفيه كمال الدية لأنه أحد الحواس الخمسة ويجرب عند النزاع
بالأشياء المرة المقرة
الثامنة منفعة المضغ وفيها كمال الدية وفواتها بأن يتصلب مغرس اللحيين
فلا يتحرك بانخفاض وارتفاع ولا يحيا صاحبه إلا بالحسوة والإيجار
فرع لو جنى على سنه فاسود ولم يمكن المضغ به وجب كمال الأرش فإن لم يكن
إلا مجرد السواد ففيه حكومة لأنه إزالة جمال محض
التاسعة قوة الإمناء والإحبال به فإذا أبطل بجناية على صلبه وجب كمال
الدية ولو جنى على ثدي امرأة وأبطل منفعة الإرضاع قال القاضي رحمه الله فيه
حكومة لأن منفعة الإرضاع تطرأ وتزول بخلاف قوة منفعة المني فإنها ثابتة قال
الإمام
ويحتمل خلافه لانه مقصود في نفسه وإن كان يطرأ
العاشرة منفعة المشي والبطش وفيهما كمال الدية ولو ضرب صلبه فبطل مشيه
وجب كمال الدية ولو قطع رجله ففي كمال الدية فيه خلاف لأنها صحيحة في نفسها
وأنها تعطل بجناية على غيرها ولو ضرب صلبه فبطل مشيه ومنيه ففي الإندراج
خلاف من حيث إن الصلب محل المني ومبدأ الحركة للمشي فاقتضي اتحادا بينهما
من وجه
الحادية عشرة إذا بطل شهوة الجماع من غير شلل في الذكر ولا انقطاع في
المني لم يبعد تكميل الدية لانقطاع إحساسه باللذة وكذا إذا بطل شهوة الطعام
إن أمكن وكذا لو ضرب عنقه فارتتق منفذ الطعام وجب كمال الدية إذ تبقى حياة
مستقرة فإذا حز غيره رقبته كملت الدية على الأول
الثانية عشرة إذا أفضى ثيبا كان أو بكرا عليه ديتها ومعنى هذا أن يتحد
مسلك الجماع والغائط أو مسلك الجماع والبول ولا يندرج المهر تحتها لاختلاف
مأخذهما
ويجب على الزاني والزوج لأن الزوج لا يستحق إلا وطأ لا يوجب الإفضاء فإن
كان لا يحتمل إلا بالإفضاء لضيق المنفذ أو  كبر الآلة لم يستحق الوطء ونزل
الضيق من جانبها منزلة الرتق إن خالف العادة والكبر من جانبه ينزل منزلة
الجب في إثبات الفسخ
ولو انتزع بكرا على كره لزمه مهر المثل وأرش البكارة وقيل إذا أوجبنا مهر
مثل بكر فقد قضينا حق البكارة
والإفضاء بالخشبة والأصبع موجب للدية ولو أزال الزوج بكارة زوجته بالأصبع
لم يجب أرش البكارة لأنه مستحق وقيل يجب لعدوله عن طريق الإستحقاق
هذا حكم الأطراف إذا أفردت أو جمعت من غير سراية فيتصور أن يجب في شخص
واحد قريب من عشرين دية ولو مات بالسراية عاد إلى دية واحدة ولو حز الجاني
رقبته فالنص أنه يتداخل وخرج ابن سريج أنه لا يتداخل كما لو تعدد الجاني
فإن اختلف حكم الجناية بأن قطع خطأ وحز عمدا أو على العكس فقولان منصوصان
لأن تغاير الوصف يضاهي تغاير الجاني
فإن قلنا بالتداخل فإن قطع يدا خطأ وقتل عمدا قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه
إنه تجب دية واحدة نصفها على الجاني مغلظة ونصفها على العاقلة مخففة وكأنه
جعل الحز كجناية أخرى تممت سراية الأولى ومن الأصحاب من خالف النص وقال تجب
دية مغلظة إذ حز الرقبة يبطل أثر ما سبق
هذا حكم أطراف الحر الذكر أما الرقيق فنص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أن جراح
العبد من قيمته كجراح الحر من ديته استحسانا لقول سعيد بن المسيب رضي الله
عنه وخرج ابن سريج قولا أن الواجب قدر النقصان كما أن الواجب في الجملة قدر
القيمة وكما نص على قول في أنه لا تضرب على العاقلة بدله ولا تجري القسامة
فيه إلحاقا له بالبهائم
فإن قطع بإلحاقه بالحر في القصاص والكفارة فلو قطع ذكره وأنثييه فزادت
قيمته فيجب على النص قيمتان وعلى التخريج لا يجب شيء كما في البهيمة
وأما المرأة فترعى نسبة أطرافها إلى ديتها وفيها قول قديم أنها تعاقل
الرجل إلى ثلث ديته أي تساويها فإن جاوزت الثلث رد إلى قياس ديتها ففي ثلث
أصابعها ثلاثون من الإبل وفي أربع  لو أوجبنا أربعين لجاوزنا ثلث الدية
فنرجع إلى نسبة ديتها فنوجب عشرين وهو بعيد مرجوع عنه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-م-ع (s-m-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The faculty of hearing; the physical organ and its perceptive power.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Hearing as one of the five external senses (ḥawāss) — a divinely instituted means of knowledge acquisition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the auditory faculty; metaphorically (majāz) for obedience/acceptance — here strictly literal.
- Root: ن-ط-ق (n-ṭ-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Articulate speech; the power of utterance distinguishing humans.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Speech (nuṭq) as the faculty of expressing meanings — a rational perfection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for vocal articulation; the "letters" (ḥurūf) serve as its quantified measure.
- Root: ش-م-م (sh-m-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The sense of smell; inhaling odors.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): One of the five senses; its loss entails full blood-money (diyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sensory perception; the rhetorical objection to its valuation is dismissed as sophistry.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Governing the legal protases ("if he claims...") and apodoses ("then we administer the oath...") with precise modal sequencing.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first [case]: If the victim of the assault says, "My hearing has diminished and has not been restored," then the compensation for the diminution (arsh al-nuqsān) is obligatory. Its measure is determined by distance, and its method is that one who is similar to him in age and health sits beside him, and a third person distances himself from both of them and raises his voice. He [the caller] then keeps approaching until the healthy one says, "I have heard." Then he maintains that same limit of volume and keeps approaching until the victim says, "I have heard." If he hears at half of that distance, then half of his hearing has been lost. If the offender says, "He heard before [the injury]," we administer the oath to the victim. And if he says, "I do not hear from one of my ears," then his examination is that the second ear be plugged and a terrifying shout be made at him.

The second [case]: If the experts of the craft say, "The subtle faculty of hearing remains, but obstruction (irtitāq) has occurred in the passage," then regarding the completeness of the blood-money (diyah) there are two positions (wajhān):
One of them: Is the incapacitation of the benefit equivalent to its removal? This applies likewise to the case where the hearing of a young boy is lost and his speech is thereby incapacitated, or his spine is struck and his leg is thereby incapacitated — regarding the multiplicity of blood-monies in such analogous cases there is a divergence of opinion.

The third: Sight. In its abolition while the eyeball remains, the full blood-money is due. In this, the weak-sighted (akhfash) and the blear-eyed (aʿmash) are equal, as is one upon whose eyeball there is a whiteness that does not prevent the essence of sight. Then, when blindness is claimed, he is examined by bringing an iron [blade] near his eyeball suddenly (mughāfasah). And if he claims diminution, he is examined just as in the case of hearing.

The fourth: Smell. In its abolition, the full blood-money is due. It is tested with sharp, foul-smelling odors. If he claims diminution, then examining that is difficult, so the oath suffices. And it was said that the blood-money is not completed for smell, because the harm one suffers from it amid abundant stenches is greater than the pleasure one gains from it amid scarce perfumes. But this is delusion (hawas), for it is a vanguard (ṭalīʿah) like the rest of the senses.

The fifth: Speech. In its abolition from the tongue, the full blood-money is due, even if the sense of taste remains, along with assistance in chewing and the labial and guttural letters — because what has been abolished is a part intended in itself. If some of the speech goes, then the closest standard for it is the letters, which are twenty-eight, equal in consideration. Al-Iṣṭakhrī said: The labial and guttural [letters] do not enter into the distribution.

Two subsidiary branches:
The first: If he did not master some letters [even before the injury], does this affect the diminution of the blood-money? There are two positions:
One: No — because it reverts to a weakness of articulation, like the weakness of grip.
The second: Yes — because grip is not quantifiable, while the letters have become a quantified measure for speech by way of approximation. If we say that deduction applies, then if he were able to express all his purposes with those letters due to the abundance of his eloquence, there is a divergence regarding the deduction, and the apparent [view] is that deduction applies. But when the deficiency of letters is due to an assault by an aggressor, the deduction is more appropriate.

The governing principle (al-qawl al-ḍābiṭ) in distinguishing between deficiency caused by assault or by [divine] affliction is that what is lost is either a corporeal mass (jirm) or a benefit (manfaʿah). Every corporeal mass that is quantified, a deficiency in part of it is effective — whether by assault or affliction — like the falling of part of a tooth or part of a fingertip, or the splitting of the flesh of the head up to the point of the scalp [wound]. What is not quantified, like a sliver of a fingertip, its falling does not diminish [the blood-money] — whether it was by a heavenly affliction or an assault that left something or left nothing — as long as the grip is not diminished, because ornamentation is not a specific property of this member.

As for the diminution of a benefit that is not quantified: if it was by a heavenly affliction, it does not diminish; if it was by an assault and the entire corporeal mass of the member remains, then there are three positions:
One: It is not considered, like the affliction.
The second: Yes [it is considered], because afflictions cannot be regulated, while assault can be regulated, as in the case of ulcers and wounds.
The third: That the second [offender] — if he severed the member, the diminution is not considered against him; but if he abolished the rest of the grip, there is deducted from him what was obligatory upon the first — because they are two assaults proportionate from one aspect. The divergence only appears in the diminution of the letters, because they are like a quantified measure for speech.

The second subsidiary branch: If he cut part of his tongue and abolished all his speech, then the full blood-money is upon him. If he abolished part of his speech, and the proportion of the mass and the letters were equal — e.g., he cut half the mass and half the speech was removed — then half the blood-money is upon him. If the proportions differ, we take the greater of the two testimonies, because each of the letters and the mass indicates the amount of what has been removed of the speech-power (quwwah nāṭiqah), which cannot be verified exactly except by way of approximation — so we take the greater of the two testimonies.

If he cut a quarter of the tongue and half the letters were removed, then half [the blood-money] is upon him.
If he cut half the tongue and a quarter of the letters were removed, then half is upon him. Abū Isḥāq said: The consideration is to the mass. But if he cut a quarter of the tongue and half the speech went, it is as though he paralyzed a quarter of the remainder. The benefit of the two expressions appears in the case of one who extracts the remainder: if he cut a quarter of his tongue and half his speech went, then another completely removed the rest of the tongue — then upon him is three-quarters of the blood-money, in consideration of the greater [amount] according to the companions (al-aṣḥāb). And according to Abū Isḥāq, upon him is half the blood-money plus a discretionary assessment (ḥukūmah) for a paralyzed quarter.

And if he cut a quarter of the tongue and removed a quarter of the speech, and we thus obligated half, then a second person came and completely removed [the rest], then upon him is obligatory three-quarters of the blood-money, in consideration of the greater. And according to Shaykh Abū Isḥāq (may God have mercy on him), half the blood-money, in consideration of the mass.

But if he cut a sliver of his tongue and nothing of the speech was removed, then nothing is [obligatory], because when the power is diminished we revert to the two testimonies and give preponderance; and when it is not diminished, there is nothing but a discretionary assessment (ḥukūmah), like the tongue of a mute.

The sixth benefit: The voice. In its abolition, the full blood-money [is due]. If the movement of the tongue is abolished along with it, then two blood-monies. And there is a position that only one blood-money is obligatory, because the purpose of the voice is speech. If we say two blood-monies, then if the movement of the tongue was deficient — speech being incapacitated but not removed — then the previous divergence applies.

The seventh: Taste. In it, the full blood-money, because it is one of the five senses. At the time of dispute, it is tested with bitter and astringent things.

The eighth: The benefit of chewing. In it, the full blood-money. Its loss occurs when the roots of the jaws become rigid so that they do not move up and down, and its owner cannot survive except by sipping and forced feeding (ījār).

A subsidiary branch: If he injured his tooth and it blackened, and chewing with it became impossible, then the full compensation (arsh) is obligatory. If there is nothing but mere blackness, then a discretionary assessment (ḥukūmah), because it is the removal of pure beauty.

The ninth: The power of ejaculation and procreation through it. If it is abolished by an assault upon his spine, then the full blood-money is obligatory. If he injured the breast of a woman and abolished the benefit of nursing, al-Qāḍī (may God have mercy on him) said: In it is a discretionary assessment, because the benefit of nursing arises and ceases, unlike the power of the seminal benefit, which is constant. Al-Imām said: Its contrary is probable, because it is intended in itself, even if it arises [and ceases].

The tenth: The benefit of walking and grip. In both of them, the full blood-money. If he struck his spine and his walking was abolished, the full blood-money is obligatory. If he cut his leg, there is a divergence regarding the full blood-money, because it is sound in itself yet incapacitated by an assault upon something else. If he struck his spine and his walking and his semen were abolished, there is a divergence regarding inclusion [under one diyah], from the aspect that the spine is the locus of semen and the origin of the movement of walking — so an unity between them is necessitated from one aspect.

The eleventh: If the desire for intercourse is abolished without paralysis in the penis or interruption in the semen, it is not far that the full blood-money is completed, due to the cessation of his sensation of pleasure. Likewise, if the desire for food is abolished, if that is possible. Likewise, if he struck his neck and the passage of food became obstructed, the full blood-money is obligatory, since a stable life remains. Then if another severed his neck, the blood-money is completed upon the first.

The twelfth: If he caused ifḍāʾ (perforation of the vaginal septum) — whether to a previously married woman (thayyib) or a virgin — then upon him is her blood-money. The meaning of this is that the passage of intercourse and excrement become one, or the passage of intercourse and urine become one. The bridal gift (mahr) is not included under it, because their sources differ.

It is obligatory upon the fornicator and upon the husband, because the husband is not entitled except to intercourse that does not cause ifḍāʾ. If she cannot tolerate [intercourse] except with ifḍāʾ due to the narrowness of the passage or the largeness of the organ, then he is not entitled to intercourse; and the narrowness on her side is treated like the condition of ratq (vaginal occlusion) if it deviates from the norm, and the largeness on his side is treated like the condition of jab (penile amputation) in establishing the annulment [of marriage].

If he deflowered a virgin against her will, then upon him is the equivalent bridal gift (mahr al-mithl) and the compensation for the hymen (arsh al-bakārah). And it was said: If we have obligated the equivalent bridal gift of a virgin, we have already discharged the claim of the hymen.

Ifḍāʾ by a wooden implement or a finger is a cause for the blood-money. If a husband removed the hymen of his wife with his finger, the compensation for the hymen is not obligatory, because he is entitled [to it]. And it was said: It is obligatory, because he deviated from the path of entitlement.

This is the ruling for the limbs when they are isolated or combined without transmission (sarāyah). Thus it is conceivable that upon a single person nearly twenty blood-monies become obligatory. If he dies by transmission, it reverts to a single blood-money. If the offender severed his neck, the text (naṣṣ) is that they merge (tadākhul). Ibn Surayj derived the position that they do not merge, just as when the offenders are multiple. If the ruling of the assault differs — e.g., he cut by mistake and severed deliberately, or the reverse — then there are two stated positions (qawlān mansūṣān), because the difference of description resembles the difference of the offender.

If we say merging applies: if he cut a hand by mistake and killed deliberately, al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said that one blood-money is obligatory — half of it upon the offender, aggravated (mugallaẓah), and half upon the ʿāqilah (kinsmen), mitigated (mukhaffafah). It is as though he made the severing another assault that completed the transmission of the first. Among the companions is one who opposed the text and said: An aggravated blood-money is obligatory, because severing the neck abolishes the effect of what preceded.

This is the ruling for the limbs of a free male. As for the slave, al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) stated in the text that the wounds of a slave are [reckoned] from his value, just as the wounds of a free man are from his blood-money — by way of juristic preference (istiḥsān), following the saying of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib (may God be pleased with him). Ibn Surayj derived a position that the obligatory [amount] is the measure of the diminution, just as the obligatory [amount] in total is the measure of the value. And just as he stated a position that no blood-money is imposed upon the ʿāqilah for him, nor does qasāmah (compurgation oath) apply to him — likening him to animals.

If [one adopts] likening him to the free man in retaliation (qiṣāṣ) and expiation (kaffārah): if he cut his penis and his testicles and his value thereby increased, then according to the text two values are obligatory, and according to the derivation nothing is obligatory, as in the case of an animal.

As for the woman, the proportion of her limbs to her blood-money is observed. And there is an old position (qawl qadīm) that she equals the man up to a third of his blood-money — i.e., she matches him. If it exceeds the third, it reverts to the measure of her blood-money. Thus in three of her fingers [the compensation] is thirty camels; in four, if we obligated forty we would exceed the third of the blood-money, so we revert to the proportion of her blood-money and obligate twenty. But this [old position] is far-fetched and has been abandoned.

chapters.title_en: The Second Division of the Book: Elucidating the Causative (Mūjib) Among Causes (Asbāb) and Direct Acts (Mubāshirāt)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | القسم الثاني من الكتاب في بيان الموجب من الأسباب والمباشرات

والنظر في أربعة أطراف
الأول في تمييز السبب عما ليس بسبب وكل ما يحصل الهلاك معه فإما أن يحصل
به فيكون علة كالتردية في البئر أو يحصل عنده بعلة أخرى ولكن لولاه لم تؤثر
العلة كحفر البئر مع التردية فهو سبب وإما أن يحصل معه وفاقا ولا تقف العلة
على وجوده فلا عبرة به كما إذا كلم غيره او صفعه صفعة خفيفة فمات فهذا لا
يجعل سببا بل هو موافقة قدر
والإحتمال يظهر في ثلاث صور
الأولى إذا صاح على صغير وهو على طرف سطح فارتعد وسقط ومات وجب الضمان
لأنه سبب ظاهر وفي القصاص قولان مرتبان على ما لو حفر بئرا في داره ودعا
إليه غيره وهذا أولى بالإيجاب لأن الإفضاء إلى الهلاك ها هنا أغلب
ولو تغفل بالغا بصوت منكر فسقط من السطح ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه يحمل على موافقة القدر لأن الرعدة لها أسباب والكبير لا يسقط
بالصياح غالبا
والثاني يجب الضمان لأن هذا ممكن والسبب ظاهر فيحال عليه
والثالث إن جاءه من ورائه وجب وإن واجهه فلا
والصحيح أنه إن ظهر أنه سقط به وجب وإن شك فيه احتمل أن يقال الأصل برءاة
الذمة واحتمل أن يقال الأصل حمله على السبب المقارن به
الثانية لو صاح على صبي موضوع على الأرض فمات أو على بالغ فزال عقله ففيه
وجهان منشؤهما التردد في الإحالة عليه
الثالثة التهديد والتخويف إذا أفضى إلى سقوط الجنين وجب الضمان إذ وقوع
ذلك غالب وقع لعمر رضي الله عنه فشاور الصحابة رضي الله عنهم فقال عبد
الرحمن بن عوف رضي الله عنه إنك مؤدب فلا شيء عليك وقال علي رضي الله عنه
إن لم يجتهد فقد غشك وإن اجتهد فقد أخطأ أرى عليك الدية
الطرف الثاني في اجتماع العلة والشرط كالحفر والتردي ومهما كانت العلة
عدوانا انقطعت الحوالة عن الشرط فالضمان على المردي لا على الحافر وإن لم
يكن عدوانا بأن تخطى الإنسان فتردى جاهلا نظر إلى الحفر فإن لم يكن عدوانا
أهدر الضمان وإن كان عدوانا أحيل الهلاك عليه
وإن تزلق رجله بقشر بطيخ أو بماء مرشوش فهذه الأسباب كحفر البئر

### | فروع

الأول إذا وضع صبيا في مسبعة فافترسه سبع فإن قدر على الإنتقال فلا ضمان
كما لو فصد بغير إذنه فتركه حتى نزف الدم وإن كان عاجزا فوجهان
أحدهما الحوالة على السبع لأنه مختار ولم يسبق منه إلا وضع يد والصبي
الحر لا يضمن باليد
والأصح أنه يحال عليه لأن هذا يعد في العرف إهلاكا
الثاني إذا اتبع إنسانا بسيفه فولى هاربا فألقى نفسه في نار أو ماء أو
بئر أو مسبعة وافترسه سبع فلا ضمان على المتبع لأنه مختار في هذه الأفعال
وغايته أن يكون مكرها
ولو قال اقتل نفسك وإلا قتلتك فقتل نفسه لم يضمن المكره إذ لا معنى
للخلاص عن الإهلاك أصلا
أما إذا تردى في بئر جاهلا لكونه أعمى أو لظلام الليل أو لكون البئر
مغطاة فالضمان على المتبع لأن هذا الإلجاء أقوى من مجرد الحفر
ولو ألقى نفسه على سطح فانخسف به فيحال الضمان عليه لاختياره إلا إذا كان
انخسافه لضعفه وهو لا يدري فهو كالبئر المغطاة
الثالث إذا سلم صبيا إلى سابح فغرق وجب الضمان على أستاذه لأنه لا يغرق
إلا بتقصير بأن يهمله في غير محله
فلو قال له ادخل الماء فدخل مختارا فيحتمل أن يقال لا ضمان لأنه لا يضمن
الحر باليد والصبي مختار ولكن قال العراقيون يجب لأنه ملتزم للحفظ وأما
البالغ فلا يضمن في هذه الصورة
وإن خاض معه اعتمادا على يده فأهمله احتمل إيجاب الضمان وقال العراقيون
لا يجب لأنه مقصر في الإغترار بقوله
فإن قيل إذا كان حفر البئر سببا عند العدوان فبماذا يكون العدوان عدوانا
قلنا نذكر محل العدوان من البئر وإيقاد النار وإشراع الجناح وإلقاء قشر
البطيخ وقمامة السوق  ورش الماء حتى يعرف به ما عداه
أما البئر فلا عهدة فيه على من حفره في ملكه أو في موات فإن كان في ملك
الغير فهو عدوان وإن كان في الشوارع نظر فإن أضر بالطارقين فهو عدوان وإن
لم يضر فإن فعله لمصلحة الطريق وبإذن الوالي وأحكم رأسه فلا ضمان على
الحافر وإن كان بغير إذن الوالي فقولان ووجه الإيجاب أن الإستقلال للآحاد
إنما يباح بشرط سلامة العاقبة فإن فعل لمصلحة نفسه فله ذلك ولكن بشرط سلامة
العاقبة
وكذلك إشراع القوابيل والأجنحة جائز إذا لم يضر بالمجتازين ولكنه بشرط
سلامة العاقبة فهو في عهدته دواما وابتداء وليس هذا كما لو حفر بئرا في
داره فنسقط جدار دار جاره فلا ضمان لأن تصرفه في نفس الملك لو قيد بشرط
السلامة لأورث حرجا على الناس فقيد بالعادة وأسقط عهدته
وأما الإرتفاق بالاجنحة فمستغنى عنها ومهما حفر بئرا في أرض جوارة ولم
يحكم أطرافها بالخشب أو وسع رأسها بحيث خرج عن العادة فهو مطالب بعهدته
وكذلك لو أوقد نارا على السطح في يوم ريح كان في عهدة الشرار وإن كان على
العادة فعصفت ريح بغتة فلا ضمان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ب-ب (s-b-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A rope or cord by which water is drawn; extended to any means, path, or connection leading to an end.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological discourse, a cause (sabab) is that whose existence entails the existence of the effect but whose non-existence entails its non-existence—distinct from the efficient agent (fāʿil).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes a physical tether; metaphorical (majāz) usage transfers this to any nexus of imputation in liability (ḍamān).
- Root: ع-ل-ل (ʿ-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Recurring illness; secondary drinking after the first quenching; hence, that which is secondary and dependent.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ʿillah (efficient cause) is that through which (bihi) the effect occurs—directly and intrinsically—as opposed to the sabab which merely accompanies it.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The ʿillah is the proximate agent; the sabab is the remote enabler. The distinction is rhetorical-legal, not merely lexical.
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, to be responsible for, to include within oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Liability (ḍamān) is the legal obligation to compensate for harm (itlāf) whether by direct act or by causation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for financial surety; metaphorically for tortious responsibility.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Protasis (al-sharṭ al-muḍmar) — The phrase "wa-kullu mā yaḥṣulu al-halāku maʿahu" (and everything with which destruction occurs) sets up a universal conditional whose apodosis is distributed across the three ensuing categories, requiring careful parsing of the particle "immā" (either/or) as disjunctive specification.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division of the book concerns the elucidation of the causative (mūjib) among causes (asbāb) and direct acts (mubāshirāt).

The investigation proceeds through four extremities (aṭrāf).

**The First Extremity: Distinguishing the Cause from What Is Not a Cause**

Everything with which destruction (halāk) occurs is either:
- That which occurs **through it** (bihi), in which case it is an efficient cause (ʿillah)—like the act of pushing someone into a well (al-tardiyah);
- Or that which occurs **in its presence** (ʿindahu) through another cause, but had it not been, that other cause would not have taken effect—like digging the well (ḥafr al-biʾr) in conjunction with the pushing; this is a cause (sabab);
- Or that which occurs **coincidentally alongside it** (wifāqan), where the efficient cause does not depend on its existence—then no regard is given to it, as when one speaks to another or gives him a light slap and he dies; this is not made a cause but is rather a concurrence of fate (muwāfaqat qadar).

The problematic cases (iḥtimāl) appear in three scenarios:

**Scenario One:** If a man shouts at a small child who is at the edge of a roof, and the child trembles, falls, and dies—liability (ḍamān) is obligatory, for this is an apparent cause (sabab ẓāhir). Regarding retaliation (qiṣāṣ), there are two opinions (qawlān) arranged upon the analogy of one who digs a well in his own home and then summons another to it. This case is even more strongly warranting of obligation, for the progression toward destruction (ifḍāʾ ilā al-halāk) here is more predominant (aghlab).

If one startles an adult (bāligh) with an alarming sound and he falls from the roof, there are three aspects (awjuh):
1. That it is borne upon concurrence of fate, for trembling has its own causes, and an adult does not typically fall due to shouting;
2. That liability is obligatory, for this is possible and the cause is apparent, so the death is imputed to it;
3. That if the shout came from behind him, liability is obligatory; but if he faced him, then not.

The sound (ṣaḥīḥ) position: If it becomes apparent that he fell because of it, liability is obligatory. If there is doubt, it may be said—on the principle of the presumption of innocence of the liability (barāʾat al-dhimmah)—that no liability attaches; or it may be said—on the principle of imputing the effect to its concomitant cause—that liability attaches.

**Scenario Two:** If one shouts at a small child placed upon the ground and he dies, or at an adult whose reason departs (zāla ʿaqluhu), there are two aspects (wajhān) whose origin is the hesitation in imputing the harm to him.

**Scenario Three:** Threatening and intimidation (al-tahdīd wa al-takhwīf), if it leads to the miscarriage of a fetus (isqāṭ al-janīn), obligates liability, for such an occurrence is predominant (ghālib). This occurred in the time of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), who consulted the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "You are a discipliner (muʾaddib), so nothing is upon you." ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "If he did not exert his judgment (ijtihād), he has deceived you; and if he exerted his judgment, he has erred—I hold that the blood-wit (diyah) is upon you."

**The Second Extremity: The Conjunction of the Efficient Cause and the Condition**

This is like the digging and the pushing. Whenever the efficient cause (ʿillah) is an act of transgression (ʿudwān), the imputation (ḥawālah) is cut off from the condition (sharṭ); thus liability falls upon the pusher (al-murdī), not the digger. If it was not an act of transgression—as when a man steps over and falls in ignorantly—then one examines the digging: if the digging was not transgressive, the liability is nullified (uhdira); if it was transgressive, the destruction is imputed to it.

If his foot slips upon a watermelon rind (qishr biṭṭīkh) or upon sprinkled water (māʾ marshūsh), these causes are like digging the well.

**Branches (Furūʿ)**

**Branch One:** If a man places a small child in a place of predators (masbaʿah) and a beast devours him: if the child was able to move away, there is no liability—just as if one performed phlebotomy (faṣd) on him without his permission and then left him until he bled out. If the child was incapable, there are two aspects:
1. Imputation upon the beast, for it is a free agent (mukhtār), and nothing preceded from the man except the placing of his hand; and a free person (al-ḥurr) is not guaranteed by mere touch (yad);
2. The more correct (aṣaḥḥ) view: imputation upon the man, for this is reckoned in customary practice (ʿurf) as destruction (ihlāk).

**Branch Two:** If a man pursues another with his sword, and the pursued turns fleeing and casts himself into fire, water, a well, or a place of predators and a beast devours him—there is no liability upon the pursuer, for the pursued is a free agent (mukhtār) in these acts; at most, the pursuer is a coercer (mukrih).

If he said to him: "Kill yourself, or else I will kill you," and he killed himself, the coercer is not liable, for there is no meaning to deliverance (khalāṣ) from destruction at all in this case.

However, if he fell into a well ignorantly—due to being blind, or due to the darkness of night, or because the well was covered—then liability is upon the pursuer, for this compulsion (iljāʾ) is stronger than mere digging.

If he cast himself upon a roof and it collapsed beneath him, liability is imputed to him for his choice—unless the collapse was due to its weakness and he did not know, in which case it is like the covered well.

**Branch Three:** If a man entrusts a small child to a swimmer (sābiḥ) and the child drowns, liability is obligatory upon his teacher (ustādh), for he would not drown except through negligence (taqṣīr)—such as neglecting him in an unsuitable place.

If he said to him: "Enter the water," and he entered voluntarily, it may be said that there is no liability, for a free person is not guaranteed by mere touch, and the child is a free agent. But the Iraqis (al-ʿIrāqiyyūn) said: liability is obligatory, for he has undertaken the duty of safeguarding (iltizām al-ḥifẓ). As for an adult, there is no liability in this scenario.

If he waded in with him relying upon his hand and he neglected him, it is possible to affirm liability. The Iraqis said: it is not obligatory, for the one who entrusted him was negligent in being deceived by his statement.

**On the Locus of Transgression (Maḥall al-ʿUdwān)**

If it is said: "When digging the well is a cause (sabab) in cases of transgression, then by what does the transgression become transgression?" I say: We shall mention the locus of transgression with respect to the well, the kindling of fire, the protrusion of a projecting beam (jirnāḥ), the throwing of watermelon rind, the refuse of the marketplace (qumāmat al-sūq), and the sprinkling of water—so that what is beyond these may be known by analogy.

As for the well: there is no liability (ʿuhdah) upon the one who digs it in his own property (milk) or in dead land (mawāt). If it is in another's property, it is transgression. If it is in the public thoroughfares (shawāriʿ), one examines: if it harms the passersby (ṭāriqīn), it is transgression; if it does not harm, then if he did it for the benefit of the road and with the permission of the governor (wālī), and he secured its mouth firmly (aḥkama raʾsahu), there is no liability upon the digger. If it was without the governor's permission, there are two opinions (qawlān). The aspect affirming liability is that the independent action of individuals (istiqlāl al-āḥād) is only permitted upon the condition of safety of consequence (salāmat al-ʿāqibah). If he acted for his own benefit, he may do so, but upon the condition of safety of consequence.

Likewise, the protrusion of projecting structures (qawābīl) and beams (ajniḥah) is permissible if it does not harm those passing by—but it is upon the condition of safety of consequence. Thus it remains within his liability (ʿuhdah) perpetually and from the outset. This is not like the case of one who digs a well in his own home and then the wall of his neighbor's house collapses—there is no liability, for his disposal within his own property, if restricted by the condition of safety, would cause hardship (ḥaraj) upon people; so it is restricted by customary practice (ʿādah) and his liability is dropped.

As for the use of projecting beams (irtifāq bi-al-ajniḥah), it is dispensable (mustaghnā ʿanhā). Whenever one digs a well in adjacent land (arḍ jawwārah) and does not secure its edges with wood, or widens its mouth beyond customary practice, he is held to its liability.

Likewise, if one kindles a fire upon the roof on a windy day, he is liable for the sparks (sharār)—even if he acted according to custom, but an unexpected wind (rīḥ baghtah) blew, there is no liability.

### | فرعان

أحدهما لو حفر بئرا في ملكه ودعا إليه إنسانا في ظلمة فسقط فيه فإن لم
يكن عنه معدل ففي الضمان قولان فإن اتسع الطرق فقولان مرتبان منشؤهما تعارض
الغرور والمباشرة وكذا الخلاف في تقديم طعام مسموم أو أطعمة فيها طعام
مسموم
الثاني إذا سقط ميزاب لإنسان على رأس إنسان فإن كان الساقط هو القدر
البارز فهو كالجناح وإن سقط الكل ففي وجوب الضمان وجهان وجه الإسقاط كونه
من مرافق الملك لا كالجناح فإن قلنا يجب فيقسط الضمان على القدر البارز
والقدر الداخل في الملك تنصيفا على أحد الوجهين وتقسيطا في الوجه الثاني
على الوزن بخلاف ما لو ضربا بعمودين متفاوتين في الثقل فإنهما يتساويان في
الدية لأن ذلك يختلف بقوة الضارب ولا ينضبط
والجدار المائل إلى الشارع كالقابول فإن مال إلى ملكه وسقط فلا ضمان  وإن
مال إلى الشارع وسقط من غير إمكان تدارك فلا ضمان فإن مال أولا وأمكنه
التدارك ولم يفعل فوجهان لتعارض النظر إلى أصل البناء وما طرأ من بعد
فأما قشور البطيخ وقمامات البيوت ففي المنع من إلقائها على الشوارع عسر
لأنها
من مرافق الملك وتشبه الميزاب ففي ضمان المتعثر بها ثلاثة أوجه يفرق في
الثالث بين إلقاء إلى وسط الطريق وبين الرد إلى الطرف
وأما رش الماء فإن كان لتسكين الغبار فهو لمصلحة عامة فيضاهي حفر البئر
لمصلحتهم فإن لم تكن مصلحة فهو سبب ضمان في حق الماشي إذا لم ير موضع الرش
فإن تخطاه قصدا فلا ضمان
الطرف الثالث في ترجيح سبب على سبب فإذا اجتمع سببان مختلفان قدم الأول
على الثاني فلو حفر بئرا ونصب آخر حجرا على طرف البئر أو وضع قشرة بطيخ على
طرفه فتعثر به إنسان وسقط في البئر فالضمان على صاحب الحجر لأن التردي
نتيجته فهي العلة الأولى وكذا لو جرف السيل حجرا وتركه على طرف البئر سقط
الضمان عن الحافر كما لو وضعه آخر
وكذلك لو نصب سكينا ونصب آخر أمامه حجرا فتعثر بالحجر ووقع على السكين
وكذا لو حفر بئرا ونصب آخر في قعر البئر سكينا ونصب آخر أمامه حجرا فالضمان
على الحافر
ولو حفر بئرا قريب العمق فعمقها غيره وهلك المتردي فيها فوجهان
أحدهما الإحالة على الأول
والثاني أنهما يشتركان لتناسب الجنايتين

- Root: غ-ر-ر (gh-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Deception, delusion, or exposing someone to peril through misleading circumstances.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Moral and legal causation where one party induces another into harm, distinct from direct physical agency.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for deliberate enticement; metaphorical (majāz) for indirect inducement via environmental conditions.
- Root: ب-ر-ز (b-r-z)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: That which protrudes, emerges, or stands out from a surface.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In liability law, the projecting part of a structure (e.g., a waterspout) that extends beyond property boundaries, treated as an independent cause.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical protrusion; metaphorical for the legal distinction between the projecting and embedded portions.
- Root: ق-س-ط (q-s-ṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Dividing equitably, apportioning, or distributing proportionally.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Proportional allocation of liability based on causal contribution, not equal shares.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for fair division; metaphorical for legal apportionment of damages.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Disjunctive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-taqsīm) — The text uses "if... then" constructions and bifurcated alternatives (e.g., "two opinions," "two faces") to structure legal rulings, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
I say: This section contains two subsidiary issues.

**The First Subsidiary Issue:** If a person digs a well on his own property and then calls another person to it in darkness, and that person falls into it, then if there is no alternative path for the invited person, there are two opinions regarding liability. But if the roads are numerous, then there are two ordered opinions, whose origin is the conflict between the principle of inducement (al-ghurūr) and the principle of direct causation (al-mubāsharah). Likewise, the disagreement applies to presenting poisoned food, or presenting foods among which there is poisoned food.

**The Second Subsidiary Issue:** If a person's waterspout (mīzāb) falls onto another person's head, then if what fell is only the protruding portion, it is like the projecting canopy (al-janāḥ). But if the entire spout falls, then there are two faces (wajhān) regarding the obligation of liability. One face holds that liability is dropped, because it is among the conveniences of property ownership (marāfiq al-milk), not like the projecting canopy. If we say liability is obligatory, then the damages are apportioned between the protruding portion and the portion embedded within the property—either by halving according to one of the two faces, or by proportional division according to weight in the second face. This differs from the case where two persons strike with two pillars of differing weight, for they are equal in the blood-money (diyah), because that varies with the strength of the striker and cannot be precisely regulated.

As for a wall that leans toward the public road, it is like the projecting canopy. If it leans toward one's own property and falls, there is no liability. If it leans toward the public road and falls without any possibility of repair, there is no liability. But if it leaned initially and repair was possible, yet the owner did not act, then there are two faces, due to the conflict between considering the original construction and considering what subsequently arose.

As for melon rinds and household refuse, there is difficulty in prohibiting their disposal onto public roads, because they are among the conveniences of property ownership and resemble the waterspout. Regarding liability for one who trips over them, there are three faces. In the third face, a distinction is made between throwing them into the middle of the road and pushing them to the side.

As for sprinkling water: if it is to settle dust, then it serves the public interest, and thus it parallels digging a well for their benefit. If there is no such benefit, then it is a cause of liability with respect to the passerby who does not see the place of sprinkling. But if he deliberately steps over it, there is no liability.

**The Third Topic: On Preponderating One Cause Over Another.** When two different causes converge, the first is given precedence over the second. Thus, if one person digs a well, and another places a stone at the edge of the well, or places a melon rind at its edge, and a person trips over it and falls into the well, then liability falls upon the owner of the stone, because the fall is its result—it is the primary cause (al-ʿillah al-ūlā). Likewise, if a flood sweeps a stone and leaves it at the edge of the well, liability is dropped from the digger, just as if another had placed it there.

Similarly, if one person erects a knife, and another places a stone in front of it, and a person trips over the stone and falls onto the knife, [liability is on the stone's owner]. Likewise, if one digs a well, another places a knife at the bottom of the well, and yet another places a stone in front of it, then liability falls upon the digger.

And if one digs a well of shallow depth, and another deepens it, and the one who falls in perishes, then there are two faces. One face refers liability to the first [digger]. The second holds that they share liability, due to the proportionality of the two offenses.

الأول لو وضع حجرا في الطريق فتعثر به من لا يراه ضمن ولو قعد على الطريق
فتعثر به
غيره وهلكا فالنص أن ضمان القاعد مهدر وضمان الماشي على عاقلة القاعد ولو
تعثر ماش بواقف وماتا فالهلاك مضاف إلى الماشي بالنص وقيل في المسألتين
قولان بالنقل والتخريج
أحدهما أن الإحالة على الماشي في المسألتين لانه المتحرك
والثاني على الساكن لأن الطريق للمشي لا للسكون
ومن قرر النص فرق بأن الماشي قد يفتقر إلى الوقوف لحظة فأما القعود فليس
من مرافق الطريق
الثاني إذا تردى في بئر في محل عدوان  فتردى وراءه آخر فسقط عليه وماتا
فالأول مات بسببين الحفرة وثقل الثاني ولكن يستقر أيضا ضمانه على الحافر
لأن وقوع الثاني كان من الحفر أيضا إلا أن لورثة الأول مطالبة عاقلة الثاني
بنصف الدية ثم يرجع على عاقلة الحافر ويحتمل أن يقال الثاني كالمكره فلا
يتعلق بعاقلته شيء وهذا يضاهي المتردد في أن المكره على إتلاف المال هل
يطالب ثم يرجع أم لا يطالب أصلا
الثالث لو انزلق على طرف البئر فتعلق بآخر وجذبه وتعلق ذلك الآخر بثالث
وجذبه ووقع بعضهم على بعض فالأول مات بثلاثة أسباب بصدمة البئر وثقل الثاني
وثقل الثالث وهو منتسب من جملتها إلى واحد وهو ثقل الثاني بجذبه إياه فهدر
ثلث الدية وثلثها على الحافر وثلثها على الثاني لجذبه الثالث
وأما الثاني فهلك بجذبه الأول وثقل الثالث فنصف ديته على الأول لأنه جذبه
ونصفه مهدر لأن الثالث سقط بجذبه وأما الثالث فكل ديته على الثاني فلو
زاد رابع فيجتمع لهلاك الأول أربعة أسباب فالمهدر ربع الدية ولا يخفى طريقه
هذا مذهب علي بن أبي طالب كرم الله وجهه واختيار الجمهور وفيه وجوه أخر
مزيفة ذكرناها في البسيط
الطرف الرابع في الأسباب المتشابهة التي تثبت بها شركة من غير ترجيح ولها
صور
الأولى إذا اصطدم حران في المشي وماتا فكل واحد شريك في قتل نفسه وقتل
صاحبه ففي تركه كل واحد منهما كفارتان لأن الشريك في قتل نفسين يلتزم
كفارتين لأنها لا تتجزأ وفي تركة كل واحد نصف دية صاحبه إن كان التصادم
عمدا وإلا فعلى
العاقلة فإن كانا راكبين ففي تركه كل واحد نصف قيمة دابة صاحبه فأما حكم
نفسيهما فكما سبق
وإن غلبت الدابة راكبها فاصطدما قهرا فقولان
أحدهما أن هلاك النفس والدابة مهدر لحصوله بفعل الدابة
والثاني أنه منسوب إلى اختيارهما في الركوب وهما مخطئان
فإن كانا صبيين ركبا بأنفسهما فكالبالغين إلا إذا قلنا لا عمد للصبي
فيخالف البالغ فيه فإن أركبهما أجنبي واحد متعديا فعليه كفارتان وقيمة
الدابتين وعلى عاقلته دية النفسين  وإن أركبهما أجنبيان فنصف الهلاك في الكل
مضاف إلى كل واحد منهما
فإن أركبه الولي عند مسيس الحاجة من غير تفريط فهو كما لو ركب الصبي
بنفسه ولا عهدة على الولي وإن لم تكن حاجة ولكن أركبه لغرض التفرج والزينة
حيث يغلب الأمن ففي إحالة الضمان على الولي ووجهان الحوالة أن مثل ذلك يجوز
بشرط سلامة العاقبة
ولو تعدى المركب وتعدى الصبي فقد قيل الإحالة على المركب ويحتمل الإحالة
على الصبي فإذا قلنا له عمد إذ المباشرة أولى من السبب لكن لما لم تكن
مباشرته عدوانا لصباه أمكن أن يجعل كالمتردي مع الحفر
فإن كانا عبدين فهما مهدران وإن كان أحدهما عبدا فنصف قيمة العبد في تركة
الحر أو على عاقلته على قول ونصف دية الحر تتعلق بتلك القيمة لأنه كان
يتعلق برقبته لو بقي فيتعلق بقيمته
وإن كانتا حاملين ففي تركة كل واحدة أربع كفارات بناء على أن قاتل نفسه
تلزمه
الكفارة وأن الشريك تلزمه كفارة كاملة وأن الجنين فيه كفارة وفي تركة كل
واحدة نصف غرة جنينها ونصف دية صاحبتها ونصف غرة جنين صاحبتها فتجب غرتان
كاملتان في التركتين ودية واحدة ويهدر النصف منهما لا من الجنين
وإن كانتا مستولدتين حاملتين وتساوت قيمتهما فقد تقاصا وإن كانت إحداهما
تساوي مائتين والأخرى مائة فصاحب المائتين يستحق مائة وصاحب المائة يستحق
خمسين فبقي لصاحب النفيسة خمسون على صاحب الخسيسة لأن جناية المستولدة تجب
على السيد لانه بالإستيلاد السابق صار مانعا بخلاف القن وكان يحتمل ها هنا
أن لا تلزمه لانه إنما يكون مانعا إذا بقي المحل حيا قابلا للتفويت وقد كان
موته مع الجناية لا بعدها
وإن كانتا حاملتين والقيمة بحالها وقيمة كل غرة أربعون فصاحب النفيسة
يستحق مائة وعشرين من جملة مائتين وأربعين ولكن قيمة الخسيسة مائة وهي أقل
من الأرش فلا يجب على السيد إلا أقل الأمرين فالواجب على صاحب الخسيسة مائة
ويستحق صاحب الخسيسة سبعين خمسون لمستولدته وعشر للغرة فيبقى عليه ثلاثون
الصورة الثانية إذا اصطدمت سفينتان  بأجراء ملاحين فالسفينة كالدابة
والملاح كالراكب وغلبة الرياح كغلبة الدابة حتى يخرج على القولين ونزيد ها
هنا إن كان في كل سفينة عشرة أنفس مثلا فهما شريكان في قتل العشرين وكذلك
في إتلاف المال الذي في السفينة فإن هلك المال وتنازعوا فقال الملاح حصل
بغلبة الريح وقال المالك بل بفعلكما فالقول قول الملاح إذ الأصل براءة
الذمة
ولو ثقب الملاح السفينة وغرق أهلها فقد يكون عمدا محضا وقد يكون شبه
العمد وقد يكون خطأ ولا يخفى حكمه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-م-ن (ḍ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To guarantee, be liable, or undertake responsibility for a thing; the core sense is that of a binding obligation attaching to one's person or estate.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, damān denotes the jurisprudential liability for harm (itlāf) or loss, whether arising from direct action (mubāsharah) or indirect causation (sabab).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for financial liability; metaphorically (majāz) extended to the "burden" of blood-wit (diyah) borne by the ʿāqilah.
- Root: ع-ق-ل (ʿ-q-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The intellect; also the blood-wit paid by the kin-group (ʿāqilah), as it "restrains" retaliation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ʿāqilah are the male agnatic heirs who bear the diyah for unintentional homicide, a collective obligation rooted in tribal solidarity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for "binding" or "restraining"; metaphorical for the group that assumes the compensatory duty.
- Root: ك-ف-ر (k-f-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cover, conceal; expiation (kaffārah) as an act that "covers" the sin.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The expiatory act mandated for unintentional homicide, freeing a slave or fasting, which cannot be divided or shared.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for covering; metaphorical for the ritual expiation that effaces the moral stain of the offense.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional and Circumstantial Clauses (al-sharṭ wa al-ḥāl) — The text frequently employs conditional constructions (law, idhā) and circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) to delineate the precise causal sequence, requiring the translator to preserve the temporal and conditional logic of the original.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first [case]: If a man places a stone upon the road, and one who does not see it trips over it, then he is liable. And if he sits upon the road, and another trips over him, and both perish, then the text (naṣṣ) [of the school] holds that the liability of the sitter is nullified (mahdar), while the liability of the walker falls upon the ʿāqilah of the sitter. And if a walker trips over a standing person, and both die, then the destruction is attributed to the walker by the text. And it was said concerning the two cases that there are two opinions, by transmission (naql) and by derivation (takhrij):

One of them: that the attribution is to the walker in both cases, because he is the moving agent.
The second: that it is attributed to the stationary one, because the road is for walking, not for standing still.

And whoever affirms the text distinguishes [between the cases] by [saying] that the walker may need to pause for a moment, whereas sitting is not among the amenities (marāfiq) of the road.

The second [case]: If one falls into a well located in a place of transgression (maḥall ʿudwān), and another falls in behind him, landing upon him, and both die, then the first died by two causes: the pit and the weight of the second. Nevertheless, his liability is also settled upon the digger of the well, because the fall of the second was also a consequence of the digging. However, the heirs of the first may claim against the ʿāqilah of the second for half the blood-wit (diyah), and then [the ʿāqilah of the second] may seek recourse against the ʿāqilah of the digger. And it is possible to say that the second is like one compelled (mukrah), so that nothing attaches to his ʿāqilah. This resembles the disputed question of whether one compelled to destroy property is sued [directly] and then seeks recourse, or is not sued at all.

The third [case]: If one slips at the edge of a well and clings to another, pulling him down, and that other clings to a third, pulling him down, and they fall upon one another, then the first died by three causes: the impact of the well, the weight of the second, and the weight of the third. And of these, only one is attributed to a single agent — namely, the weight of the second, by his pulling him. Thus one-third of his blood-wit is nullified, one-third is upon the digger, and one-third upon the second, for his pulling the third.

As for the second: he perished by the pull of the first and the weight of the third. So half his blood-wit is upon the first, because he pulled him, and half is nullified, because the third fell by his own pulling. As for the third: his entire blood-wit is upon the second. If a fourth is added, then four causes converge upon the death of the first, and the nullified portion is one-fourth of the blood-wit — and its method is not obscure.

This is the doctrine of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God honor his face) and the choice of the majority (al-jumhūr). And there are other, refuted (muzayyafah) aspects which we have mentioned in al-Basīṭ.

The fourth topic: On similar causes (al-asbāb al-mutashābihah) by which shared liability is established without preponderance (tarjīḥ). And it has several forms:

The first form: If two free men collide while walking and both die, then each one is a partner (sharīk) in the killing of himself and the killing of his companion. Thus, from the estate of each, two expiations (kaffāratān) are due — because the partner in the killing of two persons is obligated to two expiations, since expiation cannot be divided. And from the estate of each, half the blood-wit of his companion is due, if the collision was intentional (ʿamd); otherwise, it falls upon the ʿāqilah. If they were riders, then from the estate of each is due half the value of the mount of his companion. As for the ruling on their own persons, it is as previously stated.

And if the mount overpowered its rider, and they collided by force (qahran), then there are two opinions:
One: that the destruction of the person and the mount is nullified, because it occurred by the act of the mount.
The second: that it is attributed to their choice in riding, and they are both mistaken (mukhṭiʾān).

If they were two boys who rode by themselves, then [the ruling] is like that of adults — except if we hold that there is no intentional act (ʿamd) for a boy, in which case he differs from the adult therein. If a single outsider mounted them [upon the animals] transgressively (mutʿaddiyan), then upon him are two expiations and the value of the two mounts, and upon his ʿāqilah is the blood-wit of the two persons. If two outsiders mounted them, then half the destruction in all [categories] is attributed to each one of them.

If the guardian (walī) mounted them at a time of pressing need, without negligence (tafrīṭ), then it is as if the boy rode by himself, and there is no claim (ʿuhdah) upon the guardian. But if there was no need, and he mounted them for the purpose of amusement and adornment, where safety generally prevails, then there are two aspects (wajhān) concerning the attribution of liability to the guardian: the attribution [is upheld] because such an act is permissible only on the condition of a safe outcome.

And if the one who mounted [the boy] transgressed, and the boy also transgressed, then it was said: the attribution is upon the one who mounted him. And it is possible that the attribution is upon the boy. For if we say he has intentional act (ʿamd), since direct action (mubāsharah) takes precedence over causation (sabab) — yet, since his direct action was not transgressive due to his minority, it becomes possible to treat him like one who falls into a pit alongside the digging.

If they were two slaves, then their [deaths] are nullified. If one of them was a slave, then half the value of the slave is in the estate of the free man, or upon his ʿāqilah, according to one opinion; and half the blood-wit of the free man attaches to that value — because it would have attached to his person (raqabah) had he survived, so it attaches to his value.

If they were two pregnant women, then in the estate of each are four expiations — based on the [principle] that the killer of himself is obligated to expiation, that the partner [in homicide] is obligated to a full expiation, and that the fetus entails an expiation. And in the estate of each is half the ghurrah (fetal compensation) for her own fetus, half the blood-wit of her companion, and half the ghurrah of her companion's fetus. Thus two full ghurrahs are due from the two estates, and one full blood-wit; and half of them is nullified — but not [anything] of the fetuses.

If they were two pregnant umm walad (mothers of a child by her master), and their values were equal, then they offset each other (taqāṣā). If one was worth two hundred and the other one hundred, then the owner of the two-hundred [slave] is entitled to one hundred, and the owner of the one-hundred [slave] is entitled to fifty. Thus there remains for the owner of the more valuable one fifty [dirhams] against the owner of the less valuable one — because the injury (jināyah) of the umm walad is owed by the master, since by the prior istīlād (bearing a child to the master) he became a barrier (māniʿ) [to her liability], unlike the mere slave (qinn). And it was possible here that he should not be liable, because he is a barrier only if the subject remains alive and susceptible to being forfeited; but her death occurred with the injury, not after it.

And if they were both pregnant, with their values as stated, and the value of each ghurrah is forty, then the owner of the more valuable one is entitled to one hundred and twenty out of a total of two hundred and forty. But the value of the less valuable one is one hundred, which is less than the compensation (arsh); so the master is not obligated beyond the lesser of the two amounts. Thus what is owed by the owner of the less valuable one is one hundred. And the owner of the less valuable one is entitled to seventy: fifty for his umm walad and twenty for the ghurrah. So there remains thirty against him.

The second form: If two ships collide, with their crews of sailors [at the helm], then the ship is like the mount, and the sailor is like the rider, and the overpowering of the winds is like the overpowering of the mount — such that it is adjudicated according to the two opinions [mentioned above]. And we add here: if each ship had, for example, ten persons, then they are partners in the killing of the twenty, and likewise in the destruction of the property within the ships. If the property perishes and they dispute — the sailor saying, "It occurred by the overpowering of the wind," and the owner saying, "Rather, by your act" — then the word is the sailor's, because the default principle (aṣl) is the exoneration of the liability (barāʾat al-dhimmah).

And if the sailor pierced the ship and its people drowned, then it may be pure intentionality (ʿamd maḥḍ), or quasi-intentional (shibh al-ʿamd), or erroneous (khaṭaʾ) — and its ruling is not obscure.
