- Root: غ-ر-ر (gh-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "heedlessness" or "that which is fresh and new"; in legal terms, al-ghurrah is the standard blood-money for a fetus — a fixed payment of one-twentieth of full diyah (five camels or equivalent).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, al-ghurrah denotes a compensatory value for a life not fully established in personhood (the fetus), reflecting graded inviolability (ʿiṣmah) across developmental stages.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to a "pledge" or "valuable thing"; here it is metaphorical (majāz) transference to the fixed indemnity for fetal death, as the term shifts from object to obligation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Ellipsis (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb bi-ḥadhf) — The phrase "if nothing remains but the pain" (fa-in lam yakun illā al-alam) implies an omitted apodosis (e.g., "then it is subsumed"), requiring the reader to supply the governing verb from context.
chapters.translation:
I say: A subsidiary branch — If there remains upon the mother a blemish or a wound [from the assault that caused miscarriage], then a discretionary assessment (ḥukūmah) is added to the fixed indemnity (al-ghurrah) for her. But if there is nothing except the pain [of the miscarriage itself], then it is subsumed under the fixed indemnity.

This completes the examination of the blood-money (al-diyah) and retaliation (al-qiṣāṣ) among the causes that necessitate [liability for] homicide. Let us now mention the third cause, namely the expiation (al-kaffārah).

= The Book of Expiation for Homicide =

It consists of freeing a believing slave (raqabah muʾminah). If one cannot find [such a slave], then fasting for two consecutive months. There is no role for feeding [the poor] in it, nor is it to be analogized (qiyās) to the expiation of ẓihār [injurious comparison], because the [Quranic] verse {«فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ مُّؤْمِنَةٍ»} and {«فَإِطْعَامُ سِتِّينَ مِسْكِينًا»} has distinguished the two matters entirely and differentiated between them. It is not like the slave in ẓihār, for there it was left unrestricted [without the qualifier "believing"], so it was permissible to analogize it to the explicit text (al-naṣṣ) in homicide. The author of al-Taqrīb reported a [dissenting] view (wajh) in homicide that feeding [the poor] is established therein by analogy to ẓihār.

Then, upon the [dominant] school (al-madhhab), if one dies before [completing] the fast, then one discharges [the obligation] for each day by giving a mudd [of staple food] — not by way of the feeding being a substitute [for the fast], but rather just as one discharges [missed days] of Ramaḍān [upon death].

This is the description of the obligatory act. As for that which necessitates it, its pillars are three: the killing (al-qatl), the killer (al-qātil), and the killed (al-qatīl).

As for the killing, it is every killing that is not permissible (ghayr mubāḥ). Thus it is obligatory [to expiate] due to causation (al-sabab), direct commission (al-mubāsharah), digging a well [that causes death], error (al-khaṭaʾ), and intentionality (al-ʿamd). It is not obligatory in the killing of an aggressor (al-ṣāʾil), a rebel (al-bāghī), or one upon whom retaliation (al-qiṣāṣ) or stoning (al-rajm) is due, because that is permissible [killing]. Error, however, is not permissible, even if it is also not forbidden [in the strict sense].

As for the killer, its condition is that he be a legally obligated (multazim) living person. Thus it is not obligatory upon the ḥarbī [enemy combatant], but it is obligatory upon the dhimmī [protected non-Muslim], the child, and the insane person.

If a child engages in intercourse during the daytime of Ramaḍān, there is no expiation upon him, since there is no transgression (ʿudwān) [on his part]; yet transgression is not a condition in homicide [for expiation to apply].

Regarding the expiations of iḥrām [pilgrimage violations], there are two views (wajhān), because they are the result of a bodily act of worship (ʿibādah badaniyyah), and bodily worship has been validly performed by him [the child]. Regarding the validity of his fasting for expiation before puberty, there are two views, because it is a bodily act of worship, but it was incumbent upon the child [in the case of homicide].

As for the "living" [condition], we guarded thereby against the case of one who digs a well, and then after his death a person falls into it and dies. Regarding the obligation of expiation from his estate, there are two views. The view of dropping [the obligation] is that expiation is a bodily act of worship, so its obligation cannot arise after death. Upon this is built the disagreement concerning one who kills himself — whether his expiation is discharged from his estate. And due to the predominance of the aspect of worship (shāʾibat al-ʿibādah), we ruled that when a group jointly participates in killing one person, each one owes a complete expiation. There is a view that it is divisible, as in the case of the penalty for hunting [in iḥrām] (jazāʾ al-ṣayd).

As for the killed, its condition is that he be an inviolable human being (ādamī maʿṣūm). The fetus is a human being. Excluded from this are [severed] limbs and animals. Included under the inviolable (al-maʿṣūm) are the dhimmī, the muʿāhad [one with a treaty], and the slave — if his master kills him, expiation is incumbent upon the master.

Excluded from this is the ḥarbī, and the women and children of the unbelievers, since there is no inviolability for them; the prohibition against killing them is for the sake of [preserving] property [i.e., potential enslavement].

Included under it is the Muslim in the abode of war (dār al-ḥarb), however he is killed. Yes, the blood-money may definitively lapse whenever one shoots toward the unbelievers without knowing that a Muslim is among them, and [the arrow] strikes a Muslim. But if one knew that a Muslim was among them and intended [to strike] the unbeliever, yet struck the Muslim, then the blood-money is obligatory definitively. If one intended a specific person whom he thought to be an unbeliever, but he had actually converted to Islam before that and remained in the dress of the unbelievers, then there are two opinions (qawlān) regarding the blood-money. Shaykh Abū Muḥammad extended the two opinions to the case where one knew that a Muslim was among them, but the arrow deviated to someone other than the one intended.

This completes the examination of the causes that necessitate [liability for] homicide. Let us now specify, among the proofs that establish it, the Book of Blood-Claims (daʿwā al-dam), the Oath of Compurgation (al-qasāmah), and Testimony therein.

= The Book of Blood-Claims, the Oath of Compurgation, and Testimony Therein =

These are three matters.

The first: the claim (al-daʿwā). It has five conditions.

The first condition: that it be attached to a specific person. If one says, "So-and-so killed my father," it is not heard [if unspecified]. If one says, "These people all killed [him]," and their joint commission of the killing is conceivable, it is heard. If one says, "One of these ten [killed him], but I do not know his exact identity," there are two views (wajhān):
One of them: it is not heard, due to the ambiguity (al-ibhām).
The second: it is heard, due to necessity (al-ḥājah), and there is no harm to the defendant — rather, each one is able to take a truthful oath. But if they all refuse [to swear] collectively, then the returned oath (al-yamīn al-mardūdah) becomes problematic for the ambiguous claim. These two views apply in claims of usurpation (al-ghaṣb), destruction (al-itlāf), and theft (al-sariqah). They do not apply in confession (al-iqrār) or sale, when one says, "I forgot," because he is negligent (muqaṣṣir). It was said: they apply in commercial transactions. And it was said: they apply only in blood [claims].

The second condition: that the claim be detailed as to whether the killing was intentional or erroneous, solitary or joint. If he leaves his claim vague, the judge asks for clarification (al-istifṣāl). It was said: he should turn away from him, because asking for clarification is [a form of] prompting (talqīn) — and this [latter view] is weak.

chapters.title_en: Section 488 — Conditions of the Claim (Daʿwā) and Its Validity
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرع

لو قال قتل هذا أبي مع جماعة ولم يذكر عددهم فإن كان مطلوبه المال لم تصح
الدعوى لأن حصة المدعى عليه إنما تبين بحصة الشركاء وإن كان مطلوبه الدم
وقلنا يوجب العمد القود المحض فالظاهر صحته
وإن قلنا أحدهما لا بعينه فوجهان
الثالث أن يكون المدعي مكلفا ملتزما حاله الدعوى وكونه صبيا أو مجنونا أو
جنينا حالة القتل لا يضره إذ يعرف ذلك بالتسامع
الرابع أن يكون المدعى عليه مكلفا فلا دعوى على صبي ولا مجنون وتصح
الدعوى على السفيه فيما ينفذ به إقراره كالقصاص وبإقراره بإتلاف المال
قولان
فإن رددناه سمعنا الدعوى لينكر فيقيم البينة وهل تعرض اليمين إذا أنكر إن
قلنا إن اليمين المردودة كالبينة تعرض عليه رجاء النكول وإن قلنا كالإقرار
فلا فائدة في نكوله ولكن هل تعرض اليمين فعساه يحلف فتنقطع الخصومة في
الحال فيه وجهان الأصح أنه تعرض
الخامس أن تنفك الدعوى عما يكذبها فلو ادعى على شخص أنه منفرد بقتل أبي
ثم ادعى على غيره بأنه شريك لم تسمع الثانية لأن الأولى تكذبه فإن أقر
الثاني وقال المدعي كذبت في الأولى أو أخطأت فالصحيح أن له مؤاخذته لأن
الغلط ممكن والحق لا يعدوهما
ولو ادعى العمد واستفسر فذكر ما ليس بعمد ففي بطلان دعواه لأصل القتل
وجهان الأظهر أنه لا تبطل لأن الكذب في التفصيل ليس من ضروره الكذب في
الأصل
ولو قال ظلمته فيما أخذت فنستفصله فإن قال كنت كاذبا في دعواي استرد
المال وإن قال اخذت بالقسامة وأنا حنفي لا يسترد إذ لا يعتبر في الأحكام
رأي الخصمين بل رأي الحاكم

### | النظر الثاني في القسامة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: د-ع-و (da-ʿa-wa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to call, summon, or invoke"; in legal context, it denotes the formal assertion of a right before a judge (daʿwā = claim).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juridical-theological usage, daʿwā is the verbal assertion of a right (ḥaqq) that requires proof (bayyinah) or oath (yamīn) for its establishment; it is distinct from mere narration (khabar) due to its adversarial structure.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage is the act of calling; metaphorical (majāz) usage is the legal claim, where the "call" is to the judge's jurisdiction over the opposing party.
- Root: ق-س-م (qa-sa-ma)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes division, distribution, or apportionment; also the oath of compurgation (qasāmah) taken by fifty men in homicide cases.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, qasāmah is a procedural device for establishing liability in ambiguous homicide, where oaths substitute for direct evidence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning is "swearing" or "dividing"; in legal context, it is a technical term (majāz) for the collective oath procedure.
- Root: ن-ك-ل (na-ka-la)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to abstain, refrain, or recoil"; in legal usage, it is the refusal to take an oath (nukūl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Nukūl is a juridical act of omission that, in some schools, functions as an admission (iqrār) or as evidence (bayyinah) against the refuser.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is "shrinking back"; metaphorical is the legal consequence of refusing the oath, which shifts the burden of proof.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses conditional clauses (law, in) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal outcomes; parsing requires identifying the protasis (condition) and apodosis (result) to preserve the logical structure of juristic reasoning.
chapters.translation:
### | Branch

If he says, "This man killed my father along with a group," without specifying their number, then if his demand is for property (māl), the claim is not valid (lā taṣiḥḥ), because the share of the defendant is only clarified by the shares of the partners. But if his demand is for blood (dam), and we hold that intentional killing (ʿamd) necessitates pure retaliation (qawad maḥḍ), then the apparent ruling is its validity. If we hold that it necessitates one of two things, unspecified, then there are two faces (wajhān).

The third [condition] is that the claimant (muddaʿī) be legally responsible (mukallaf) and committed [to the religion] at the time of the claim. His being a child (ṣabī), insane (majnūn), or a fetus (janīn) at the time of the killing does not harm him, for that is known through hearsay (tasāmuʿ).

The fourth [condition] is that the defendant (muddaʿā ʿalayh) be legally responsible. Thus, there is no claim against a child or an insane person. The claim is valid against a prodigal (safīh) regarding matters in which his admission (iqrār) is effective, such as retaliation (qiṣāṣ) and his admission of destroying property. There are two sayings (qawlān) on this.

If we reject [his admission], we hear the claim so that he may deny, and then he may produce evidence (bayyinah). Should the oath (yamīn) be offered when he denies? If we say that the refused oath (al-yamīn al-mardūdah) is like evidence, then it is offered to him, hoping for his refusal (nukūl). If we say it is like an admission, then there is no benefit in his refusal. But should the oath be offered, perhaps he will swear, and the dispute will be terminated immediately? There are two faces; the more correct (aṣaḥḥ) is that it is offered.

The fifth [condition] is that the claim be free of what contradicts it. Thus, if he claims against one person that he alone killed his father, then claims against another that he was a partner, the second claim is not heard, because the first contradicts it. If the second [defendant] admits, and the claimant says, "I lied in the first [claim]" or "I erred," then the correct ruling is that he may hold him liable, because error is possible, and the right does not extend beyond the two of them.

If he claims intentional killing (ʿamd), and upon being questioned, he mentions what is not intentional, then regarding the invalidation of his claim to the basis of killing (aṣl al-qatl), there are two faces. The more apparent (aẓhar) is that it is not invalidated, because lying in the detail (tafṣīl) does not necessitate lying in the basis (aṣl).

If he says, "I wronged him regarding what I took," then we question him further. If he says, "I was lying in my claim," he returns the property. If he says, "I took it by qasāmah, and I am a Ḥanafī," he does not return it, for in legal rulings, the opinion of the two litigants is not considered; rather, the opinion of the judge (ḥākim) is considered.

### | Second Consideration: On the Qasāmah

chapters.title_en: The Intermediate Compendium in Jurisprudence — Section 489: The Qasāmah (Compurgatory Oath) and Its Conditions
chapters.arabic_text:
والنظر في أربعة أركان
الأول بيان مظنته وهو قتل الحر في محل اللوث فلا قسامة في الأموال
والأطراف لأن البداية بالمدعي وتعديد اليمين خمسين خارج عن القياس ثبت
لحرمة الدم فلا يقاس عليه الطرف والمال وفي قتل العبد قولان لتردده بين
الدم  والمال وإذا جرح مسلما فارتد ومات وقلنا الواجب بعض الدية جرت القسامة
فيه لأنه بعض بدل الدم
وأما اللوث فنعني به علامة تغلب على الظن صدق المدعي وهو نوعان قرينة حال
وإخبار
أما الحال فهو أن يصادف قتيلا في محلة بينه وبينهم عداوة أو دخل عليهم
ضيفا فوجد قتيلا أو تفرق جماعة محصورون عن قتيل أو تفرق صفان متقاتلان عن
قتيل في صف الخصم أو وجد قتيل في الصحراء وعلى رأسه رجل ومعه سكين متضمخ
بالدم فهذا وأمثاله هو اللوث وقول المجروح قتلني فلان ليس بلوث لأنه مدع
خلافا لمالك رحمه الله
وأما الإخبار فشهادة عدل واحد تقبل شهادته لوث وكذا من تقبل روايته على
الأقيس وقيل لا بد في النسوان والعبيد من عدد
وأما العدد من الصبية والفسقة ففيهم خلاف لأنه يحصل بقولهم ظن لكن الشرع
لا يلتفت إليه فيضاهي من أوجه قرينة عدالة المدعي في صدق لهجته
وأما مسقطات اللوث فخمسة
الأول أن يتعذر إظهاره عند القاضي فلا فائدة فيما ينفرد المدعي بدعواه
نعم لو ظهر عند القاضي لوث على جمع فللمدعي أن يعين شخصا منهم إذ يعسر
إثبات اللوث في المعين ولو كان اللوث في قتيل خيبر متعلقا بجميع اليهود نعم
لو قال القاتل واحد منهم ولست أعرفه لم تمكنه القسامة
فإن حلفوا إلا واحدا كان نكوله لوثا فيجوز له أن يحلف على تعيينه فلو نكل
جميعهم وأراد أن يعين واحدا وزعم أنه ظهر له الآن لوث معين ففي تمكينه منه
وجهان وجه المنع أنه سبق الاعتراف منه في الجهل
الثاني إذا ثبت اللوث في أصل القتل دون كونه خطأ أو عمدا ففي القسامة على
أصل القتل وجهان وجه المنع أن القتل المطلق لا موجب له فإن العاقلة لا
يلزمها شيء ما لم يكن خطأ والجاني لا يلزمه ما لم يكن عمدا
الثالث أن يدعي المدعى عليه كونه غائبا عن البلد عند القتل فالقول قوله
مع يمينه وتسقط يمينه أثر اللوث
فإن تعارضت بينتان في حضوره وغيبته  تساقطتا إلا إذا تعرض بينة الغيبة
لعدم الحضور فقط فيكون ذلك شهادة النفي بخلاف ما إذا ذكر مكانه الذي غاب
إليه
ولو كان وقت القتل محبوسا أو مريضا مدنفا ولم يمكن كونه قاتلا إلا على
بعد ففي
سقوط اللوث به وجهان
ومهما حكم بالقسامة فأقام بينة على الغيبة نقض الحكم لأن القسامة ضعيفة
الرابع لو شهد شاهد بأن فلانا قتل أحد هذين القتيلين لم يكن لوثا ولو قال
قتل هذا القتيل أحد هذين الرجلين فهو لوث هكذا قاله القاضي مفرقا بين إبهام
القاتل وإبهام القتيل
وقيل بإسقاط اللوث في المسألتين والفرق أوضح لأن تعيين القاتل غير عسير
دون تعيين القتيل
الخامس تكاذب الورثة فلو ادعى أحد الإثنين في محل اللوث فكذبه الآخر فيه
قولان
اختيار المزني رحمه الله أن اللوث لا يبطل لأن للورثة أغراضا في التكذيب
والتصديق
والثاني أنه يبطل لأن اللوث ضعيف وهذا يضعف الظن
فإن قلنا يبطل فلو قال أحدهما قتل أبانا زيد ورجل آخر لا نعرفه وقال
الآخر قتله عمرو ورجل آخر لا نعرفه فلا تكاذب فلعل من لا يعرفه هو الذي
ادعاه أخوه إلا أن يصرح بنفي ما ادعاه
ثم مدعي زيد اعترف بان الواجب على زيد نصف الدية وحصته منها الربع فلا
يطالب إلا بالربع وكذا مدعي عمرو
وليس من مبطلات اللوث عندنا أن لا يكون على القتيل أثر خلافا لأبي حنيفة
رحمه الله لأن القتل بالتخنيق ممكن بحيث لا يظهر أثره
الركن الثاني في كيفية القسامة
وهو أن يحلف المدعي خمسين يمينا متوالية بعد التحذير والتغليظ وتفصيل
الدعوى في اليمين كما في سائر الأيمان وهل يشترط أن تكون في مجلس واحد فيه
وجهان منشؤهما أن للموالاة وقعا في النفس فيحتمل أن تكون واجبا
فإن قلنا واجب فإذا جن ثم أفاق بنى لأنه معذور
ولو عزل القاضي استأنف عند قاض آخر ولو مات في أثنائه فالوارث لا يبني بل
يستأنف وقال الخضري يبني الوارث
وفي جواز القسامة في غيبة المدعى عليه وجهان وجه المنع  أن اللوث إنما
يظهر إذا سلم عن قدح الخصم فيضعف في غيبته
هذا إذا كان الوارث واحدا فإن كانوا جمعا فنوزع عليهم الخمسين أو يحلف كل
واحد خمسين فعلى قولين
أحدهما أنه يوزع لأن جملتهم في حكم شخص واحد
والثاني لا لأن قدر حق كل واحد لا يثبت بيمين المدعي إلا بخمسين إذ لا
خلاف أنه لو نكل واحد وجب على الآخر أن يحلف تمام الخمسين فكيف يستحق بيمين
غيره
وإن قلنا بالتوزيع فلننبه على ثلاثة أمور
الأول أنهم لو كانوا ثلاثة والواحد حاضر والآخران صغيران أو غائبان
فغيبتهم كنكولهم فيحلف الحاضر خمسين ويأخذ ثلث الدية فإذا حضر الآخر حلف
نصف الأيمان وأخذ ثلث نفسه والثالث يحلف ثلث الأيمان ويأخذ حصة نفسه
الثاني أن التوزيع بالميراث فمن يستحق الثمن أو السدس حلف بقدره فإن
انكسر كمل المنكسر فإن كانوا ستين حلفوا ستين كل واحد يمينا ولا يمين على
إخوة الأب في مسائل المعادة
الثالث لو كان في الورثة خنثى حلف كل واحد أكثر ما يتوهم أن يكون نصيبه
ويعطى أقل ما يتوهم أخذا بالأحوط في الجانبين
فلو خلف ولدا خنثى وأخا لأب حلف الخنثى خمسين لاحتمال أنه مستغرق وأخذ
نصف الدية لاحتمال أنه أنثى
فإذا أراد الأخ أن يحلف فيحلف خمسا وعشرين وفائدته أن ينتزع النصف من يدي
الجاني ويوقف بينه وبين الخنثى فإن بانت أنوثته سلم إلى الأخ بيمينه السابق
وإن بانت الذكورة سلم إلى الخنثى باليمين السابقة
ولو خلف ولدا خنثى وبنتا حلف الخنثى ثلثي الأيمان لاحتمال أنه ذكر وأخذ
ثلث الدية لاحتمال أنه أنثى وحلفت البنت نصف الأيمان لاحتمال أن الخنثى
أنثى ولم يعتد من أيمانها إلا بالنصف ثم تأخذ ثلث الدية والثلث الباقي
متروك في يد المدعى عليه موقوف بينهما وبين بيت المال وليس لبيت المال نائب
حتى يحلف عنه فنعود إلى القياس في
تصديق المدعى عليه
هذا كله في يمين المدعي فأما سائر الأيمان في الدم فكيمين المدعى عليه
واليمين مع الشاهد ففي تعدده خمسين  قولان منشؤهما أن علة العدد الميل عن
القياس بتصديق المدعي أو حرمة الدم والقولان جاريان في الأطراف مع القطع
بأن القسامة غير جارية فيها فإن قلنا لا تتعدد فلو بلغ الأرش مبلغ الدية
فقولان وإن قلنا تتعد فلو نقص ففي التوزيع قولان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-و-ث (lawtha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be stained, polluted, or entangled"; a place of ambiguity or suspicion where blood is found.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, it denotes a circumstantial indicator (amārah) that tilts judicial presumption toward the plaintiff's veracity in homicide claims.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally for physical staining (e.g., blood on a garment); metaphorically (majāz) transferred to a "stain" of suspicion attaching to a defendant or locale.
- Root: ق-س-م (qasama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To divide, distribute, or swear an oath; the noun qasāmah is a juristic term for repeated oaths.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A divinely legislated exception to normal evidentiary procedure, rooted in the sanctity of blood (ḥurmat al-dam).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "division" (of oaths among heirs); metaphorical sense is the oath-procedure itself as a "portion" of proof.
- Root: ن-ك-ل (nakala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To refrain, abstain, or refuse; in law, the refusal to take an oath.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Refusal (nukūl) functions as an admission or as a corroborating indicator (lawth) against the refuser.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: "to turn away"; juristic: the legal consequence of a party's unwillingness to swear.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly uses "فإن" (if/then) and "إلا" (except) to structure legal conditionals, where the protasis states a hypothetical and the apodosis its ruling; the exceptive particle restricts the scope of a general claim (e.g., "except one" in the oath of the accused).
chapters.translation:
I say: The examination [of qasāmah] proceeds upon four pillars.

The first pillar is the exposition of its proper locus (maẓinnah), namely, the killing of a free person in a place of suspicion (lawth). Thus, there is no qasāmah concerning property or limbs, because the initiation [of oaths] by the plaintiff and the enumeration of fifty oaths is an anomaly (khārij ʿan al-qiyās) established solely for the inviolability of blood (ḥurmat al-dam); hence, it cannot be analogically extended to a limb or to property. Concerning the killing of a slave, there are two opinions, due to its oscillation between [the category of] blood and [that of] property. And if [the victim] wounded a Muslim, who then apostatized and died, and we hold that the obligatory [compensation] is a portion of the blood-wit (diyah), then qasāmah applies therein, because it is a part of the blood-recompense.

As for the lawth, we mean by it a mark (amārah) that predominantly overcomes conjecture (ghalabat ʿalā al-ẓann) as to the truthfulness of the plaintiff. It is of two types: a circumstantial indication (qarīnat ḥāl) and a report (ikhbār).

As for the circumstantial [type], it is that [the plaintiff] finds a slain person in a quarter (maḥallah) between whose inhabitants and [the victim] there was enmity; or [the victim] entered upon them as a guest and was found slain; or a confined group (jamāʿah maḥṣūrūn) dispersed from a slain person; or two opposing ranks (ṣaffān mutaqātilān) dispersed from a slain person found in the rank of the adversary; or a slain person is found in the desert with a man standing over his head holding a blood-stained knife. This and its like constitute lawth. The statement of the wounded person, "So-and-so killed me," is not lawth, because he is a claimant [in his own cause] — contrary to Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him.

As for the report [type], it is the testimony of a single just witness (shahādat ʿadl wāḥid); such testimony is accepted as lawth. Likewise, [the report of] one whose narration (riwāyah) is accepted, according to the stronger analogy (al-aqyas). It was said: with respect to women and slaves, a number [of reporters] is required.

As for the number [of reporters] among boys and sinners (fussāq), there is a divergence [of opinion], because their statement produces conjecture (ẓann), but the Law (al-sharʿ) does not pay heed to it; thus it resembles, in some respects, the indication of the plaintiff's justice (ʿadālah) in the truthfulness of his speech.

As for the nullifiers of lawth (musqiṭāt al-lawth), they are five:

The first: that its manifestation before the judge is impossible (taʿadhdhara iẓhāruhu). For there is no benefit in what the plaintiff alone asserts by his mere claim. Indeed, if a lawth appears before the judge against a group (jamāʿah), the plaintiff may designate a specific individual among them, since proving the lawth against a particular person is difficult. Even if the lawth concerning a slain person in Khaybar pertained to all the Jews collectively, [still,] if [the plaintiff] said, "The killer is one of them, but I do not know him," qasāmah would not be available to him. But if they all took an oath except one, his refusal (nukūl) becomes a lawth, and it becomes permissible for [the plaintiff] to swear to his designation. If they all refused and he wished to designate one, claiming that a specific lawth has now become manifest to him, then there are two faces (wajhān) concerning enabling him [to do so]. The face of prevention is that he has previously confessed to ignorance.

The second: if the lawth is established concerning the fact of killing (aṣl al-qatl) without [establishing] whether it was erroneous (khaṭaʾ) or intentional (ʿamd), then there are two faces concerning qasāmah upon the bare fact of killing. The face of prevention is that an unqualified killing entails no [fixed] obligation; for the ʿāqilah (kinsman group) is not liable for anything unless it was erroneous, and the perpetrator is not liable unless it was intentional.

The third: if the defendant claims that he was absent from the town at the time of the killing, then his statement is accepted with his oath, and his oath nullifies the effect of the lawth. If two evidences (bayyināt) conflict concerning his presence and absence, they cancel each other out — except when the evidence of absence is limited to [asserting] non-presence only, in which case it is a testimony of negation (shahādat nafy), unlike [the case] where [the witness] mentions the specific place to which he had gone. And if at the time of the killing [the defendant] was imprisoned, or gravely ill (marīḍ muḍnif) such that his being the killer was only remotely possible, then there are two faces concerning the nullification of the lawth by this. And whenever a judgment is rendered by qasāmah, and then [the defendant] produces evidence of his absence, the judgment is overturned, because qasāmah is weak [in evidentiary force].

The fourth: if a witness testified that "So-and-so killed one of these two slain persons," this is not lawth. But if he said, "One of these two men killed this slain person," it is lawth. Thus said the Judge (al-Qāḍī), distinguishing between the ambiguity of the killer (ibhām al-qātil) and the ambiguity of the slain (ibhām al-qatīl). And it was said [by others] that the lawth is nullified in both cases. The distinction is clearer, because designating the killer is not difficult, unlike designating the slain.

The fifth: the mutual denial (takādhub) of the heirs. If one of two [heirs] claims [qasāmah] in a place of lawth, and the other denies him therein, there are two opinions. The choice of al-Muzanī, may Allah have mercy on him, is that the lawth is not invalidated, because the heirs have motives for both denial and affirmation. The second [opinion] is that it is invalidated, because the lawth is weak, and this [denial] weakens the conjecture. If we say it is invalidated, then if one of them says, "Zayd and another man we do not know killed our father," and the other says, "ʿAmr and another man we do not know killed him," there is no mutual denial — perhaps the one he does not know is the very one his brother claimed, unless he explicitly denies what his brother claimed. Then, the claimant of Zayd has admitted that the obligation upon Zayd is half the blood-wit, and his share of it is one-quarter; thus he may only claim one-quarter. Likewise for the claimant of ʿAmr.

It is not among the nullifiers of lawth in our view that there be no trace (athar) upon the slain person — contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him — because killing by strangulation (takhnīq) is possible in such a way that no trace appears.

The second pillar concerns the modality of the qasāmah. It is that the plaintiff swears fifty consecutive oaths, after admonition (taḥdhīr) and solemnization (taghlīẓ), with the specification of the claim (tafṣīl al-daʿwā) in the oath, as in all other oaths. Is it required that they be in a single session (majlis wāḥid)? There are two faces, the origin of which is that consecutiveness (muwālāh) has an effect upon the soul; thus it is possible that it is obligatory. If we say it is obligatory, then if [the swearer] becomes insane (junna) and then recovers, he continues [from where he left off], because he is excused. And if the judge is dismissed, he starts anew before another judge. And if he dies in the midst of it, the heir does not continue but rather starts anew. Al-Khaḍirī said: the heir continues. Concerning the permissibility of qasāmah in the absence of the defendant, there are two faces. The face of prevention is that the lawth only manifests when it is safe from the adversary's objection (qadḥ), and it is weakened in his absence.

This [applies] when the heir is one. If they are a group, then [the fifty oaths] are either distributed among them, or each one swears fifty — upon two opinions. One of them is that it is distributed, because the totality of them is, in legal effect, like a single person. The second is that it is not [distributed], because the measure of each one's right is not established by the plaintiff's oath except by fifty; for there is no disagreement that if one of them refuses, the other must swear the remaining fifty. How then could [one] deserve [a share] by the oath of another? And if we say distribution [applies], let us draw attention to three matters:

First: if they are three, with one present and the other two minors or absent, then their absence is like their refusal (nukūl). Thus the present one swears fifty and takes one-third of the blood-wit. When the other [heir] appears, he swears half the oaths and takes his own third; and the third swears one-third of the oaths and takes his own share.

Second: the distribution is according to inheritance shares. Thus, whoever inherits an eighth or a sixth swears in proportion to it. If a fraction results, the fraction is completed [by rounding up]. If they are sixty [heirs], they swear sixty oaths, each one swearing one oath. And there is no oath upon the paternal brothers (ikhwat al-ab) in the cases of return (masāʾil al-muʿādah).

Third: if among the heirs there is a hermaphrodite (khunthā), each one swears the maximum that could conceivably be his share, and is given the minimum that could conceivably [be his share], taking the more cautious [course] (al-aḥwaṭ) in both directions. Thus, if [the deceased] leaves a hermaphrodite child and a paternal brother, the hermaphrodite swears fifty [oaths], due to the possibility that he is [a male] exhausting [the inheritance], and takes half the blood-wit, due to the possibility that she is female. Then, when the brother wishes to swear, he swears twenty-five [oaths]; its benefit is that he extracts the half from the hands of the perpetrator, and it is held in suspense between him and the hermaphrodite. If her femaleness becomes evident, it is handed to the brother by his prior oath; if his maleness becomes evident, it is handed to the hermaphrodite by the prior oath. And if [the deceased] leaves a hermaphrodite child and a daughter, the hermaphrodite swears two-thirds of the oaths, due to the possibility that he is male, and takes one-third of the blood-wit, due to the possibility that she is female. The daughter swears half the oaths, due to the possibility that the hermaphrodite is female; but only half of her oaths are counted. Then she takes one-third of the blood-wit, and the remaining third is left in the hands of the defendant, held in suspense between them and the public treasury (bayt al-māl). And the public treasury has no deputy to swear on its behalf; thus we revert to the analogical principle (al-qiyās) of crediting the defendant's [denial].

All this concerns the oath of the plaintiff. As for the other oaths in blood [cases], they are like the oath of the defendant. Concerning the oath with a single witness (al-yamīn maʿa al-shāhid), there are two opinions on whether it is multiplied to fifty. The origin of both is whether the cause (ʿillah) of the number is the deviation from analogy by crediting the plaintiff, or the inviolability of blood. These two opinions apply also to limbs, while it is certain that qasāmah does not apply therein. If we say it is not multiplied, then if the compensation (arsh) reaches the amount of the full blood-wit, there are two opinions. And if we say it is multiplied, then if it falls short, there are two opinions concerning its distribution.

chapters.title_en: Two Subsidiary Points, the Third Pillar (Ruling on Qasāmah), and the Fourth Pillar (Those Who Swear the Oaths of Qasāmah), Followed by the Third Section on Establishing Homicide by Testimony
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرعان

أحدهما لو شهد واحد على اللوث وقلنا يتحد اليمين مع الشاهد فإن استعملنا
الشهادة في القتل وجاء بصيغة الشهادة حلف معه يمينا واحدة وإن جاء بصيغة
الإخبار أو شهد على اللوث حلف معه خمسين يمينا
الثاني إذا ادعى على اثنين أنهما قتلا ففي توزيع الخمسين على قول التعدد
من القولين ما في التوزيع على الوارثين
الركن الثالث في حكم القسامة وفيه قولان
القديم أنه يناط به القصاص كما يناط به حد المرأة بلعان الزوج
والجديد أنه لا يناط به إلا الدية لأن سفك الدم بقول المدعي بعيد وأما
المرأة فإنها تقدر على دفع لعانه بلعانها
ثم إن حلف على القتل خطأ طالب العاقلة وإن حلف على العمد طالب الجاني وإن
نكل عن القسامة ومات لم يكن لوارثه أن يحلف
ولا يسقط حقه عن تحليف المدعى عليه لنكوله عن القسامة فإن نكل المدعى
عليه فأراد المدعي أن يحلف اليمين المردودة ففيه قولان
أحدهما المنع لأنه نكل مرة والثاني لا لأنه نكول عن القسامة وهذه يمين
أخرى وكذا إذا أراد أن يحلف مع الشاهد بعد النكول عن اليمين المردودة أو
القسامة
ومنشؤه أن المدعي عليه بعد أن صرح بالنكول ليس له الرجوع إلى اليمين لانه
تعلق به حق المدعي أما نكول المدعي عن اليمين المردودة في الحال لا تمنعه
من الرجوع إليه فإنه حقه فلا يسقط بالتأخير ويمين القسامة من حيث إنه يتعلق
بها حق المدعى عليه في انقلاب التصديق إليه يشبه يمين المدعى عليه
الركن الرابع فيمن يحلف أيمان القسامة وهو كل من يستحق بدل الدم وفيه
أربعة فروع
الأول إذا قتل عبد المكاتب وأجرينا القسامة في العبد حلف المكاتب لأنه
المستحق فإن عجز عن النجوم قبل النكول  حلف السيد إذ صار مستحقا فإن عجز بعد
النكول لم يحلف السيد كما لا يحلف الوارث بعد نكول الموروث
الثاني لو قتل عبده فأوصى بقيمته لمستولدته ومات فللورثة أن يقسموا وإن
كانت
القيمة للمستولدة لأن لهم حظا في تنفيذ وصية مورثهم
ولو أوصى بعين لغيره فادعاه مستحق ففي حلف الوارث لتنفيذ الوصية تردد
ووجه الفرق أن المستولدة مدعية وتصديقها بالقسامة على خلاف القياس ولم تكن
صاحبة حق عند القتل فكان الوارث أولى به
ومهما حلف الورثة سلمت القيمة لأم الولد فإن نكلوا ففي قسامة المستولدة
قولان وكذا في الغرماء إذا أرادوا أن يحلفوا أيمان القسامة عند نكول الوارث
لتقضي من الدية ديونهم ووجه المنع أن القسامة لإثبات القتل ممن يدلي بسبب
الحق عند القتل وهؤلاء تجدد حقهم بعد القتل
وإن قلنا لا يحلفون أو نكلوا فللوارث ولهم طلب يمين المدعي أما الوارث
فلغرض التنفيذ وأما هم فلغرض الإستحقاق
الثالث إذا قطع يد العبد فعتق ومات فعلى الجاني كل الدية فإن كانت الدية
مثل نصف القيمة انفرد السيد بالقسامة لأنه مستحق الجميع وإن فرعنا على أنه
لا قسامة في بدل الرقيق فها هنا وجهان لأنه دية حر بالإعتبار الآخر ولكن
صرف إليه لأنه جناية على الرقيق
ثم إن كان الواجب فاضلا عن أرش اليد فيصرف الفاضل إلى الورثة ويتصدى
النظر في توزيع اليمين أو تكميلها
الرابع إذا ارتد الولي ثم أقسم فإن قلنا لا ملك للمرتد بطل يمينه وإن
قلنا له الملك صح وثبت الدية وإن قلنا موقوف فالنص أنه يصح ويصرف إلى بيت
المال فيئا إن قتل المرتد
وفيه إشكال إذ بان أنه لم يكن مستحقا فكيف يثبت بحلفه فمنهم من قال فرع
الشافعي رضي الله عنه على قول بقاء الملك ومنهم من علل بأنه على الجملة سبب
استحقاق الدية لانه كان مسلما حال القتل فلا يكون يمينه كيمين الأجنبي

### | النظر الثالث من الكتاب في إثبات الدم بالشهادة

ولها شروط
الأول الذكورة فلا يثبت القصاص برجل وامرأتين ويثبت القتل الموجب  للمال
برجل وامرأتين فإن كان موجبا للقود عند الشهادة ثم رجع إلى المال لم يستوف
المال بتلك الشهادة لأنها كانت باطلة في الحال ولو أنشئت الشهادة بعد العفو
على مال فوجهان وجه المنع أن أصل القتل كان موجبا للقصاص
فرع نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنه لو شهد رجل وامرأتان على هاشمة مسبوقة
بإيضاح فكما لا يثبت الإيضاح الموجب للقصاص لا يثبت الهشم في حق الأرش ونص
على أنه لو شهدوا على أنه رمى عمدا إلى زيد فمرق السهم وأصاب غيره خطأ أن
الخطأ يثبت فقيل قولان بالنقل والتخريج ومنشؤهما أن الشهادة واحدة وقد سقط
بعضها فهل يسقط الباقي ومنهم من فرق لأن قتل عمرو منفصل عن قتل زيد والهشم
لا ينفصل عن الإيضاح
ولا خلاف على أنه لو ادعى قتل عمرو خطأ فشهدوا وذكروا هذه الكيفية وهو
مروق السهم من زيد لم يقدح في الشهادة لأن زيدا ليس مقصودا بالشهادة وكذلك
إذا قالوا نشهد أنه أوضح ثم عاد بعد ذلك وهشم

### | التفريع
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-و-ث (lawatha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to soil, defile, or entangle"; in legal context, it denotes strong circumstantial evidence that "taints" the accused with suspicion.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, al-lawth is the presumptive indicator (amārah) that shifts the burden of proof, aligning with the principle of ẓann (predominant conjecture) over certainty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) is physical soiling; metaphorical (majāz) is the "staining" of a defendant's credibility through evidence, making the oath of the claimant admissible.
- Root: ق-س-م (qasama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes division, distribution, or swearing; qasāmah is the collective oath-taking (fifty oaths) to establish blood-vengeance or diyah.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technically, it is a legislated oath (yamīn mashrūʿah) that substitutes for witnesses in homicide cases, rooted in the Quranic principle of tathbīt (establishing) claims.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is "to divide" (e.g., dividing an estate); metaphorical is the "division" of oaths among heirs or claimants, as per the distribution rules.
- Root: ن-ك-ل (nakala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to abstain, refuse, or recoil"; in law, it is the refusal to take an oath, which has specific procedural consequences.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Nakūl is a legal act of omission that transfers the right of oath to the opponent (radd al-yamīn), reflecting the principle of istiḥqāq (entitlement).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is "to shrink back" (e.g., from a fight); metaphorical is the "shrinking" from a sworn assertion, which legally inverts the burden of proof.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses conditional particles (in, idhā) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal outcomes, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to avoid ambiguity in rulings.
chapters.translation:
---

### | Two Subsidiary Points

One of them: If a single witness testifies to the strong circumstantial evidence (al-lawth), and we hold the position that the oath is combined with the witness, then if we employ the testimony regarding the killing and he comes with the formula of testimony (ṣīghat al-shahādah), he swears with him a single oath. But if he comes with the formula of mere information (ṣīghat al-ikhbār), or testifies to the lawth itself, he swears with him fifty oaths.

The second: If he claims against two persons that they both killed, then regarding the distribution of the fifty oaths—according to the position of multiplicity (qawl al-taʿaddud) from the two positions—there applies what applies in the distribution [of oaths] among the two heirs.

### The Third Pillar: Concerning the Ruling of Qasāmah

There are two positions (qawlān) on this:
The old position (al-qadīm): That retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is made contingent upon it, just as the punishment of the woman is made contingent upon the imprecation (liʿān) of the husband.
The new position (al-jadīd): That nothing is made contingent upon it except the blood-wit (diyah), because the shedding of blood based on the mere claim of the plaintiff is far-fetched. As for the woman, she is able to repel his imprecation by her own imprecation.

Then, if he swears that the killing was accidental (khaṭaʾ), he seeks [compensation] from the ʿāqilah (the paternal relatives liable for blood-wit). If he swears it was intentional (ʿamd), he seeks [retaliation] from the killer himself. If he refuses the qasāmah (nukūl) and dies, his heir has no right to swear [in his place].

Nor does his right to demand the oath of the defendant fall away due to his (the claimant's) refusal of the qasāmah. If the defendant refuses [the oath], and the claimant wishes to swear the returned oath (al-yamīn al-mardūdah), there are two positions:
One: Prohibition, because he (the defendant) refused once.
The second: No prohibition, because that refusal was regarding the qasāmah, and this is a different oath. Likewise, if he wishes to swear alongside the witness after the refusal of the returned oath or the qasāmah.

The source of the divergence (manshaʾ) is that the defendant, after explicitly refusing, has no recourse to the oath, because the claimant's right has become attached to it. As for the claimant's refusal of the returned oath at that moment, it does not prevent him from returning to it, for it is his right and is not nullified by delay. The oath of qasāmah, insofar as the defendant's right becomes attached to it in the inversion of attestation (inqilāb al-taṣdīq) toward him, resembles the oath of the defendant.

### The Fourth Pillar: Concerning Who Swears the Oaths of Qasāmah

It is everyone who is entitled to the blood-recompense (badal al-dam). It contains four subsidiary points:

The first: If a mukātab (a slave under a contract of manumission) is killed, and we apply qasāmah in the case of a slave, then the mukātab swears, because he is the entitled party. If he becomes incapable (of paying his installments) before the refusal (nukūl), the master swears, since he has become the entitled party. If he becomes incapable after the refusal, the master does not swear, just as the heir does not swear after the refusal of the testator.

The second: If a man kills his own slave, then bequeaths his value to his umm walad (slave-mother of his child), and then dies, the heirs may take the qasāmah, even though the value is for the umm walad, because they have a share in executing the bequest of their testator.
If he bequeaths a specific chattel to another, and a claimant claims it, there is hesitation (taraddud) regarding the heir's swearing to execute the bequest.
The basis of the distinction is that the umm walad is a claimant, and attesting her claim via qasāmah is contrary to analogy (khilāf al-qiyās), and she was not a right-holder at the time of the killing, so the heir is more entitled to it.
Whenever the heirs swear, the value is delivered to the umm walad. If they refuse, there are two positions regarding the qasāmah of the umm walad. Likewise, regarding creditors (ghuramāʾ) if they wish to swear the oaths of qasāmah upon the heir's refusal, so that their debts may be settled from the diyah. The basis of prohibition is that qasāmah is for establishing the killing by one who holds a cause of right (sabab al-ḥaqq) at the time of the killing, whereas these parties' rights arose after the killing.
If we say they do not swear, or they refuse, then the heir and they may demand the oath of the defendant—the heir for the purpose of execution, and they for the purpose of entitlement.

The third: If a person cuts off the hand of a slave, then the slave is emancipated and dies, then the full diyah is upon the injurer. If the diyah equals half the value, the master alone takes the qasāmah, because he is entitled to the entirety. If we branch upon the position that there is no qasāmah for the recompense of a slave (badal al-raqīq), then here there are two aspects (wajhān), because it is the diyah of a free person by the other consideration, but it is directed [to the master] because it is an injury upon the slave.
Then, if the obligatory [amount] exceeds the compensation for the hand (arsh al-yad), the excess is directed to the heirs, and consideration is given to the distribution or completion of the oath.

The fourth: If the guardian (walī) apostatizes and then swears the oath: If we hold that the apostate has no ownership, his oath is void. If we hold he has ownership, it is valid and the diyah is established. If we hold it is suspended (mawqūf), the text (al-naṣṣ) is that it is valid and is directed to the public treasury (bayt al-māl) as spoils (fayʾ) if the apostate is killed.
There is a difficulty here, for if it became clear that he was not entitled, how is it established by his oath? Some said this is a branch of al-Shāfiʿī's (may God be pleased with him) position on the persistence of ownership. Others reasoned that he is, in general, a cause of entitlement to the diyah, because he was a Muslim at the time of the killing, so his oath is not like the oath of a stranger (ajnabī).

### | The Third Section of the Book: On Establishing Homicide by Testimony

It has conditions:
The first: Masculinity (al-dhukūrah). Retaliation is not established by one man and two women, but homicide that necessitates wealth (i.e., diyah) is established by one man and two women. If it was necessitating retaliation (qawad) at the time of testimony, then reverted to wealth, the wealth is not collected by that testimony, because it was invalid at that moment. If the testimony were newly initiated after the pardon (al-ʿafw) regarding wealth, there are two aspects. The basis of prohibition is that the origin of the killing was necessitating retaliation.

A subsidiary point: Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) stated in the text (naṣṣ) that if one man and two women testify to a fracturing of the skull (hāshimah) preceded by a wound exposing the bone (īḍāḥ), then just as the īḍāḥ necessitating retaliation is not established, so too the hāshimah is not established with respect to the compensation (arsh). He also stated in the text that if they testify that he shot intentionally at Zayd, but the arrow pierced through and struck another accidentally, then the accidental [killing] is established. It was said there are two positions, by transmission (naql) and by derivation (takhrij). Their source is whether the testimony is one, and part of it has fallen away—does the remainder fall away? Some distinguished, because the killing of ʿAmr is separate from the killing of Zayd, whereas the hāshimah is not separate from the īḍāḥ.
There is no disagreement that if he claimed the accidental killing of ʿAmr, and they testified mentioning this manner—namely, the arrow's piercing through from Zayd—it does not vitiate the testimony, because Zayd is not the object of the testimony. Likewise, if they said, "We testify that he exposed the bone, then returned afterward and fractured it."

### | The Ramifications (al-Tafrīʿ)

chapters.title_en: On the Conditions of Testimony in Homicide and the Chapter on Crimes Requiring Punishments
chapters.arabic_text:
إذا أثبتنا أرش الهاشمة فقد ذكر في إثبات قصاص الموضحة وأرشها على سبيل
التبعية خلاف وهو بعيد
الشرط الثاني أن تكون صيغة الشهادة صريحة فلو قال أشهد أنه جرح وأنهر
الدم ومات المجروح لم يقبل ما لم يقل قتله إذ ربما يموت بسبب آخر والموت
عقيب الجراحة يعرف أنه بالجراحة بقرائن خفية فلا يغني إلا ذكر القتل وذكر
العراقيون وجها أنه يكفي كما تقوم الشهادة على اليد والتصرف مقام الملك
لأنه مستند العلم
ولو قال أشهد أنه أوضح رأسه لم يكف ما لم يصرح بالجراحة وإيضاح العظم
فإن صرح وعجز عن تعيين محل الموضحة لالتباسها بموضحات على رأسه سقط
القصاص وفي الأرش وجهان أحدهما لا كما إذا شهد رجل وامرأتان على موضحة عمدا
فإنه إذا لم يثبت المقصود لم يثبت غيره
والصحيح أنه يثبت لأنه لا قصور في نفس الشهادة وإنما التعذر في استيفاء
القصاص
ولو شهد على أنه قتله بالسحر لم يقتل لأن ذلك مما لا  يشاهد وجه تأثيره
فالقتل بالسحر لا يثبت إلا بالإقرار ثم قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه لو قال
الساحر أمرضه سحري ولكن مات بسبب آخر فلولي الدم القسامة واعترافه بالمرض
لوث وهذا يدل على أن المقر بالجرح إذا ادعى أن الموت بسبب آخر يجعل إقراره
لوثا وقد قيل إن القول قول الجاني وهو جار في السحر
فإن قيل تعلم السحر حرام أم لا قلنا إن كان فيه مباشرة محظور من ذكر سخف
أو ترك صلاة فذلك هو الحرام فأما تعرف حقائق الأشياء على ما هي عليها فليس
بحرام وإنما الحرام الإضرار بفعل السحر لا بتعلمه
الشرط الثالث أن لا تتضمن جرا ولا دفعا فلو شهد على الجراحة من يرث
المجروح ردت شهادته لأنه سبب استحقاقه
ولو شهد الوارث للمريض بدين أو عين فوجهان والفرق أن جرح المشهود عليه
سبب الإستحقاق دون الدين ولو شهدوا على الجرح وهما محجوبان حال الشهادة ثم
مات الحاجب أو بالعكس فالصحيح أن النظر إلى حالة الشهادة للتهمة وقيل قولان
كخما في الإقرار للوارث
فإن رددنا فلو أعاد بعد الحجب لا تقبل كالفاسق إذا أعاد
فأما الشهادة الدافعة فصورتها أن تشهد العاقلة على فسق بينة القتل الخطأ
ولو شهد اثنان من فقراء العاقلة نص أنه لا تقبل ولو شهد اثنان من الأباعد
مع أن الواجب مستوفى بالأقارب نص أنه تقبل فقيل قولان بالنقل والتخريج وقيل
إن الفقير أمله في الغني قريب وتقدير موت الأقارب بعيد فلا يورث تهمة
الشرط الرابع أن تسلم الشهادة عن التكاذب وفيه صور
الأولى إذا شهدا على رجلين بالقتل وشهد المشهود عليهما بأنهما قتلا هذا
القتيل نقدم على هذا مقدمة وهو أن شهادة الحسبة تقبل في حقوق الله تعالى
وفي القصاص
ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها نعم صيانة للحقوق عن الضياع
والثاني لا لأن للدم طالبا كما للمال
والثالث أنه إن لم يعرف المستحق قبلت الشهادة
فإن قلنا تقبل فتساوق أربعة إلى مجلس القاضي فشهد اثنان على الآخرين
بالقتل فشهد الآخران على الأولين بذلك القتل  ففيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها الرد وإن قبلنا شهادة الحسبة إذ هي متكاذبة فلا ترجح
والثاني أنا نراجع صاحب الحق ونحكم بشهادة من صدقهما
والثالث أن الأولى صحيحة وشهادة الآخرين غير مقبولة لأنهما دافعان
ولأنهما صارا عدوين للأولين ولكن إثبات العدواة بمجرد الشهادة ضعيف
وإن فرعنا على رد شهادة الحسبة فلو جاء المدعي بعد ذلك لم تنفع تلك
الشهادة وهل تقبل إعادتها فيه ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها لا كما لو رد بعلة الفسق
والثاني نعم لانه لم ترد بتهمة
والثالث أنهما إن تابا عن المبادرة قبلت الإعادة
رجعنا إلى مسألتنا فإذا شهد المشهود عليهما على الشاهدين واستمر المدعي
على تكذيبهما فلا أثر لشهادتهما لانهما دافعان وعدوان ومبادران وإن صدقهما
بطل حقه بتناقض الدعويين
فإن كان ذلك من وكيل فلا يؤخذ بإقرار لم يؤثر في إبطال الدعوى الأولى فإن
صدق الموكل الآخرين انبنى على أنهما مبادران أو دافعان
المسألة بحالها لو شهد المشهود عليهما على أجنبي سوى الشاهدين فهما
مبادران ودافعان وليسا عدوين وإن شهد أجنبيان على الشاهدين فهما مبادران
وليسا دافعين ولا عدوين
الصورة الثانية لو شهدوا على القتل فشهد أحد الورثة بعفو بعضهم سقط
القصاص بقوله من حيث إنه إقرار لا من حيث إنه شهادة حتى تسقط ولو كان فاسقا
الصورة الثالثة إذا شهد أحدهما أنه قتله غدوة وقال الآخر عشية فهو تكاذب
وكذا إذا نسبا إلى مكانين أو آلتين وكذا لو شهد أحدهما على الإقرار والآخر
على القتل لم يثبت لأنهما لم يتفقا على شيء
ولو شهد أحدهما على الإقرار بالقتل المطلق والآخر على الإقرار بالقتل
العمد ثبت أصل القتل فالقول قول المدعى عليه في نفي العمدية إلا أن يكون ثم
لوث يشهد للعمدية فتثبت القسامة
وإن قال أحدهما قتله عمدا وقال الآخر خطأ فوجهان
أحدهما أنه تكاذب
والآخر أنه يثبت القتل ومن يشهد بالخطأ فكأنه يشهد بعدم العمد فيبقى
النزاع في العمدية
وحيث يثبت التكاذب في الآلة والمكان والزمان قال المزني رحمه الله يفيد
قولهما لوثا فاتفقت المراوزة على  تغليطه لأنهما تساقطا بالتكاذب ونقل
العراقيون فيه قولين للشافعي رضي الله عنه

- Root: ش-ه-د (sh-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Presence, witnessing, giving testimony; al-shahādah is the declaration of what one has observed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Testimony (shahādah) as the conveyance of certain knowledge (ʿilm) regarding a witnessed event, distinct from mere report (khabar).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes ocular presence; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to juridical attestation.
- Root: ق-ص-ص (q-ṣ-ṣ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow, to trace, to cut; qiṣāṣ as retributive equivalence in kind.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Retaliation (qiṣāṣ) as the measured recompense for intentional homicide or wounding, grounded in the principle of equivalence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense of "following the trace" (taqaṣṣuṣ) is metaphorically applied to exacting like-for-like punishment.
- Root: ل-و-ث (l-w-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cling, to adhere; lawth as the strong circumstantial evidence that attaches suspicion to a defendant.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, lawth denotes the preponderant indication (dalālah) that shifts the burden of proof, permitting qasāmah (compurgatory oath).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literally "adhesion"; metaphorically, the clinging of suspicion to a party based on contextual indicators.
- Root: ج-ر-ح (j-r-ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To wound, to injure; al-jirāḥah is the infliction of bodily harm.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act of wounding as a legal cause (sabab) for entitlement to retaliation or compensation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical wounding; metaphorically extended to any injurious act.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Ellipsis (al-sharṭ maʿa al-ḥadhf) — The text frequently employs conditional constructions where the apodosis is implied by context, requiring careful reconstruction of the logical sequence.
chapters.translation:
I say: When we have established the compensation (arsh) for the wound that lays bare the bone (hāshimah), it has been mentioned that regarding the establishment of retaliation (qiṣāṣ) for the wound that exposes the bone (mūḍiḥah) and its compensation, there is a difference of opinion mentioned by way of subsidiary consequence, and that view is remote.

The second condition is that the wording of the testimony be explicit (ṣarīḥah). Thus, if a witness says: "I testify that he wounded him and made the blood flow, and the wounded person died," it is not accepted unless he says "he killed him," for perhaps he died due to another cause. The death occurring immediately after the wound is known to be caused by the wound only through subtle circumstantial indicators (qarāʾin khafiyyah). Therefore, nothing suffices except the explicit mention of killing. The Iraqis mentioned a view that it suffices, just as testimony regarding a hand (i.e., possession) and disposition (taṣarruf) stands in place of ownership, because it is the basis of knowledge.

And if he says: "I testify that he exposed his bone (awḍaḥa raʾsahu)," it does not suffice unless he explicitly mentions the wounding and the exposure of the bone. If he explicitly mentions it but is unable to specify the location of the mūḍiḥah due to its being confused with multiple mūḍiḥahs on his head, then retaliation (qiṣāṣ) falls. Regarding the compensation (arsh), there are two views: one is that it does not stand, just as when a man and two women testify regarding an intentional mūḍiḥah — for when the intended object is not established, what is other than it is not established either. The correct view is that it does stand, because there is no deficiency in the testimony itself; rather, the impediment lies only in the execution of retaliation.

And if he testifies that he killed him by sorcery (siḥr), he is not executed, because the manner of its effect is not observable. Thus, killing by sorcery is not established except by confession (iqrār). Then al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — said: If the sorcerer says, "My sorcery made him ill, but he died due to another cause," then the guardian of the blood has the right to qasāmah (compurgatory oath), and his admission of causing illness constitutes lawth (strong circumstantial evidence). This indicates that the one who confesses to wounding, if he claims that death was due to another cause, his confession is made a lawth. And it has been said that the statement (al-qawl) is that of the offender (al-jānī), and this applies in the case of sorcery.

If it is asked: Is learning sorcery forbidden or not? We say: If it involves the commission of a prohibited act — such as uttering foolish speech or abandoning prayer — then that is what is forbidden. As for knowing the realities of things as they are, that is not forbidden. Rather, what is forbidden is causing harm by performing sorcery, not by learning it.

The third condition is that the testimony must not entail a benefit (jarr) or a repulsion (dafʿ). Thus, if the heir of the wounded person testifies regarding the wound, his testimony is rejected, because it is a cause of his entitlement.

And if the heir testifies for the sick person regarding a debt or a specific chattel (ʿayn), there are two views. The difference is that the wounding of the one testified against is a cause of entitlement, unlike the debt. And if they testify regarding the wound while they are veiled from inheritance (maḥjūbān) at the time of testimony, then the veiling person dies — or the reverse — the correct view is that consideration is given to the state at the time of testimony, due to the suspicion (tuhmah). It was said: two views, like the two views regarding confession (iqrār) in favor of an heir.

If we reject it, then if he repeats the testimony after the removal of the veil, it is not accepted — just as when a sinner (fāsiq) repeats testimony after his repentance.

As for the repelling testimony (al-shahādah al-dāfiʿah), its form is that the ʿāqilah (the kin who pay blood-money) testify to the sinfulness (fisq) of the witnesses of accidental killing. If two poor members of the ʿāqilah testify, the text (naṣṣ) states that it is not accepted. If two distant relatives testify while the obligation is already fulfilled by the close relatives, the text states that it is accepted. It was said: two views, by transmission (naql) and by derivation (takhrij). And it was said: The poor person's hope in the rich is near, while the estimation of the death of the close relatives is remote, so no suspicion is engendered.

The fourth condition is that the testimony be free from mutual contradiction (takādhub). This involves several cases:

The first case: If two witnesses testify against two men for homicide, and the two testified-against men testify that those two killed this slain person — we preface this with an introduction: namely, that testimony of public concern (shahādat al-ḥisbah) is accepted in the rights of Allah — may He be exalted — and in retaliation (qiṣāṣ). There are three views:
One: Yes, it is accepted, to safeguard rights from being lost.
The second: No, because blood has a claimant just as property does.
The third: If the entitled person is not known, the testimony is accepted.

If we say it is accepted, and four persons come together to the judge's council, and two testify against the other two for homicide, and the other two testify against the first two for that same killing — then there are three views:
One: Rejection, even if we accept the testimony of public concern, because they are mutually contradictory, so neither is given preponderance.
The second: We refer back to the right-holder and judge by the testimony of whichever of them he affirms.
The third: The first testimony is valid, and the testimony of the others is not accepted, because they are repellers (dāfiʿān) and because they have become enemies of the first two. However, establishing enmity merely by testifying is weak.

If we build upon the rejection of the testimony of public concern, and the claimant comes afterward, that testimony does not benefit him. Is its repetition accepted? There are three views:
One: No, just as when it is rejected due to the cause of sinfulness (fisq).
The second: Yes, because it was not rejected due to suspicion.
The third: If they repent of their hastiness (mubādarah), the repetition is accepted.

We return to our original question: If the two testified-against men testify against the two witnesses, and the claimant persists in declaring them both liars, then their testimony has no effect, because they are repellers, enemies, and hasteners. If he affirms them, his right is voided due to the contradiction between the two claims.

If this is done by an agent (wakīl), he is not held liable for a confession that did not effect the nullification of the first claim. If the principal affirms the others, it is built upon whether they are hasteners or repellers.

The question remains as it was: If the two testified-against men testify against a third party other than the two witnesses, they are hasteners and repellers but not enemies. If two outsiders testify against the two witnesses, they are hasteners but neither repellers nor enemies.

The second case: If they testify regarding homicide, and one of the heirs testifies to the pardon (ʿafw) of some of them, retaliation falls by his statement — insofar as it is a confession (iqrār), not insofar as it is testimony — such that it falls even if he were a sinner (fāsiq).

The third case: If one of them testifies that he killed him in the morning (ghudwah) and the other says in the evening (ʿashiyyah), this is mutual contradiction. Likewise, if they attribute it to two different places or two different instruments. Likewise, if one testifies to a confession and the other to the killing, it is not established, because they did not agree upon a single matter.

If one testifies to a confession of absolute killing and the other testifies to a confession of intentional killing (qatl al-ʿamd), the basis of the killing is established. Then the statement is that of the defendant in negating intentionality, unless there exists a lawth that indicates intentionality, in which case qasāmah is established.

If one says, "He killed him intentionally," and the other says, "By mistake (khaṭaʾ)," there are two views:
One: It is mutual contradiction.
The other: The killing is established, and the one testifying to mistake is as if testifying to the absence of intent, so the dispute remains over intentionality.

Wherever mutual contradiction is established regarding the instrument, place, or time, al-Muzanī — may Allah have mercy on him — said: Their two statements yield a lawth. The people of Marw agreed in declaring him mistaken, because the two testimonies cancel each other out by the contradiction. The Iraqis transmitted two views of al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — regarding this.

= The Book of Crimes (Jināyāt) That Mandate Punishments =

They are seven: transgression (baghy), apostasy (riddah), fornication (zinā), slander (qadhf), drinking (shurb), theft (sariqah), and highway robbery (qaṭʿ al-ṭarīq).
