chapters.arabic_text: ### | الركن الثالث السارق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ر-ق (s-r-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning — taking another’s property covertly (akhdh al-māl khufyatan); the act of theft (sariqah) implies concealment and violation of trust.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic-theological usage, sariqah denotes the specific legal act triggering the ḥadd (fixed corporal punishment), distinguished from mere usurpation (ghaṣb) by the element of stealth and the threshold of nisāb (minimum value).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) — physical covert taking; metaphorical (majāz) — any clandestine breach of sacred limits (ḥudūd Allāh), as in spiritual theft of rights.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal Predication (al-ibtidā’ wa al-khabar) — The phrase “الركن الثالث” is a definite subject (mubtada’) with “السارق” as its predicate, forming a complete nominal sentence; the definiteness of both terms signals categorical specification, not mere description.
chapters.translation: I say: The third pillar [of the fixed punishment for theft] is the thief [himself, whose conditions and legal definition are now to be examined].

chapters.title_en: The Intermediate Compendium in Jurisprudence — Section 504: On Theft (Sariqah), Its Conditions, and Its Proof
chapters.arabic_text:
ولا يشترط فيه التكليف والإلتزام ويستوي في وجوب القطع الحر والعبد
والذكر والأنثى ولا قطع على الصبي والمجنون ويجب على الذمي لإلزامه أحكامنا
نعم هذا إذا سرق مال مسلم فإن سرق مال ذمي فهو موقوف على ترافعهم إلينا فإن
زنى بذمية فلا يحد ما لم يرضوا بحكمنا وإن زنى بمسلمة أقمنا الحد قهرا كما
سرق مال مسلم وقيل لا بد من رضاهم لأن حد الزنا حق الله ولا خصم فيه بخلاف
السرقة وهذا ركيك إذ يجر ذلك فضيحة عظيمة فإنه لا يرضى بحكمنا وغايتنا نقض
عهده ويجب تجديده إذا التزم وتاب
أما المعاهد إذا سرق ففي قطعه نصوص مضطربة وحاصلها ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها أنه كالذي لأجل العهد
والثاني أنه لا حد أصلا لأنه حربي دخل لسفارة
والثالث أنه يقطع إذا شرط ذلك عليه في ابتداء الأمان وإلا فلا
وسرقة المسلم ماله يخرج على سرقته مال المسلم إذ يبعد أن يقطع المسلم
بسرقة ماله ولا يقطع بسرقة مال المسلم ولو زنى بمسلمة  فطريقان منهم من قال
كالسرقة ومنهم
من قطع بانه لا يقام الحد لأنه حق الله تعالى لا يتعلق بطلب العبد ولا
خلاف في أنه يطالب بضمان الأموال وإنما النظر في الحدود
النظر الثاني من الكتاب في إثبات السرقة ومعرفتها بيمين مردودة أو إقرار
أو بينة
أما اليمين فإذا أنكر السرقة وحلف انقطعت الخصومة وإن نكل وحلف المدعي
ثبت الغرم وثبت القطع أيضا كما يثبت القصاص باليمين المردودة
ولو ادعى استكراه جاريته على الزنا ثبت المهر باليمين المردودة ويبعد
إثبات الرجم به لأن اليمين المردودة وإن جعلت بينة فلا تتعدى حق الحالف
والرجم حق الله تعالى ومن هذا ينقدح احتمال أيضا في قطع السرقة
وأما الإقرار فإن كان بعد الدعوى ثبت به القطع بشرط الإصرار فإن رجع لم
يسقط الغرم وفي سقوط الحد قولان
أحدهما أنه يسقط كحد الزنا
والثاني لا لارتباطه بحق الآدمي وبقاء الغرم الذي هو ملازم له ومنهم من
عكس وقال القطع ساقط وفي الغرم قولان ووجه إسقاطه تبعية القطع وهو فاسد
أما إذا أقر باستكراه جارية على الزنا ثم رجع فالأصح أنه يسقط الحد ويجب
المهر وقيل يحتمل أن يجعل كالسرقة ولكن مفارقة الحد للمهر أقرب من مفارقة
القطع للغرم فلذلك يتردد فيه
وإن رجع السارق بعد القطع فلا تدارك فإن رجع في أثنائه كف الجلاد عن
البقية إن قلنا يؤثر رجوعه
أما إذا أقر قبل الدعوى فهل يقطع دون حضور المالك وطلبه فيه وجهان ووجه
اعتبار طلبه أنه ربما يقر له بالملك أو بالإباحة فإنه يسقط الحد وإن كذبه
السارق
والصحيح أنه لو أقر بالزنا بجارية الغير فإنه يحد في الحال إذ لا مدخل
للطلب فيه ومساق هذا يشعر بأن مالك الجارية لو قال كنت ملكته الجارية قبل
ذلك فأنكر أن الحد يجب ولا يؤثر قول مالك الجارية فإنه لا يتعلق بخصومته
فهو كما لو قالت الحرة كنت زوجته وكذبها فإنه يحد
فإن قلنا إنه لا يقطع في الحال ففي حبسه إلى حضور المالك خلاف يلتفت  على
أنه هل يسقط برجوعه
هذا كله في الحر أما في العبد إذا أقر بسرقة لا توجب القطع فلا يقبل في
المال ولا نعلقه برقبته دون تصديق السيد فإن أقر بما يوجب القطع قطعت يمينه
وإن كذبه السيد خلافا للمزني وأبي يوسف رحمهما الله وإنما قبل لأنه غير
متهم فيه
ثم هل يتعلق غرم المال برقبته تابعا لثبوت القطع فيه نصوص مضطربة وحاصلها
أربعة أقوال
أحدها أنه لا يقبل لأنه إقرار على السيد لا على
العبد والثاني أنه يقبل لأن رقبته أيضا مملوكة للسيد فإن قبل في قطع يده
لنفي التهمة فليقبل في الغرم أيضا ورد المال
والثالث أنه إن أقر بعين هي في يده قبل لأن ظاهر اليد للعبد فإن أقر
بالإتلاف فلا يقبل لأن رقبته في يد السيد وهذا يوجب التعلق فيكون كما لو
قال جميع ما في يد السيد أنا سرقته وسلمته إليه فإنا لا نقبل قطعا
والرابع عكسه وهو أنه يقبل إقراره بالإتلاف فإن السيد على الأصح يفدي
بأقل الأمرين من قيمته أو قيمة العبد فقيمة العبد مرد الإضرار بالسيد أما
الأعيان إن فتح باب الإقرار بها تضرر به السيد إذ لا مرد له
فإن قيل هل للقاضي أن يحث السارق على ستر السرقة أو الرجوع عن الإقرار
قلنا أما الستر فيجوز مع رد المال لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم للسارق
ما إخالك سرقت وهذا كالتلقين للإنكار وقوله
أسرقت قل لا لم تصححه الأئمة وأما الرجوع عن الإقرار
فلا يحث عليه القاضي لقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم
من ارتكب شيئا من هذه القاذورات فليستتر بستر الله فإن من أبدى لنا صفحته
نقيم عليه حد الله فدل ذلك على الفرق ما بين قبل الظهور وما بعده
الحجة الثالثة للسرقة الشهادة ولا يثبت القطع إلا بشهادة رجلين فإن شهد
رجل وامرأتان ثبت الغرم دون القطع بخلاف ما لو شهدوا على القتل العمد فإنه
لا يثبت القصاص ولا الدية لأن الدية كالبدل عن القصاص والغرم ليس بدلا عن
القطع  بل يجب معه وفيه وجه أن الغرم أيضا لا يثبت كالدية وهو ضعيف
ثم البينة الكاملة لا توجب القطع بالشهادة على السرقة مطلقا بل لا بد من
التفصيل فيه فكم من سرقة لا توجب قطعا ولذلك يشترط التفصيل في الإقرار أيضا
ويشترط في بينة الزنا وهل يشترط في الإقرار بالزنا فيه خلاف وسببه أن حد
الزنا ظاهر ووجوده
عند الزاني محقق وأما الشاهد فإنما يعول فيه على المخايل وحد السرقة غير
ظاهر للسارق ولا شك أن النسبة إلى الزنا المطلق قذف لأن التعيير حاصل به
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ط-ع (qaṭʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Severance, cutting off; the prescribed amputation of the hand for theft.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The penal consequence (ḥadd) ordained by divine law as a deterrent, distinct from mere retaliation (qiṣāṣ) in its fixed, non-negotiable character.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) physical severance; metaphorically (majāz) used for the legal penalty itself, as the act of cutting is the defining ritual of the punishment.
- Root: ذ-م-م (dhimma)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Covenant, protection, obligation; the pact of protection granted to non-Muslim subjects.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The contractual bond (ʿahd) that renders the protected person (dhimmī) subject to Islamic legal rulings in matters of mutual dealings, while preserving their religious autonomy.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of blame (dhamm) inverted into a technical term for the protected status; the covenant itself is the operative legal fiction.
- Root: غ-ر-م (ghurm)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Debt, liability, financial compensation for loss or damage.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The pecuniary restitution (ḍamān) owed to the victim, distinct from the penal ḥadd; it is a right of the human claimant (ḥaqq ādamī).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal financial obligation; metaphorically extended to any liability that attaches to the offender's estate or person.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text frequently employs conditional clauses (in, law, idhā) and exceptions (illā) to delineate legal outcomes, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to determine the operative ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: It is not a condition for the thief that he be legally accountable (mukallaf) or that he have undertaken a binding commitment (iltizām). The obligation of amputation (qaṭʿ) applies equally to the free man and the slave, and to the male and the female. No amputation is imposed upon the minor or the insane person. It is, however, imposed upon the dhimmī, because he is bound by our legal rulings [in such matters]. Indeed, this [ruling] applies when he steals the property of a Muslim. But if he steals the property of a dhimmī, then [the penalty] is suspended upon their bringing the case to us for adjudication. Similarly, if he commits fornication (zinā) with a dhimmī woman, he is not subjected to the ḥadd punishment unless they consent to our judgment. But if he fornicates with a Muslim woman, we impose the ḥadd upon him by force, just as [we do] when he steals the property of a Muslim. Some have said that their consent is indispensable, because the ḥadd for fornication is a right of God (ḥaqq Allāh) and involves no human adversary, unlike theft. This [view] is flimsy, for it would lead to a great scandal: he would never consent to our judgment, and our ultimate recourse would be to annul his covenant (naqḍ ʿahdih). It must then be renewed if he submits [to our rule] and repents.

As for the muʿāhid (a non-Muslim with a temporary truce), if he steals, there are conflicting textual reports (nusūṣ) concerning his amputation. The gist of them is three opinions:
First, that he is like the dhimmī, [and is amputated] by virtue of the covenant.
Second, that no ḥadd is imposed upon him at all, because he is a ḥarbī (enemy combatant) who entered [our territory] for the purpose of embassy.
Third, that he is amputated if this condition was stipulated upon him at the inception of the safe-conduct (amān), and not otherwise.
The case of a Muslim stealing his property is subsumed under the case of his stealing a Muslim's property, for it is far-fetched that a Muslim be amputated for stealing his property yet not be amputated for stealing a Muslim's property. If he fornicates with a Muslim woman, there are two paths (ṭarīqān): among them are those who say it is like theft; and among them are those who decisively affirm that the ḥadd is not imposed, because it is a right of God, which is not contingent upon the claim of a human servant. There is no disagreement that he is pursued for financial liability (ḍamān) regarding property; the consideration pertains only to the ḥudūd.

The second inquiry (naẓar) of the book concerns the establishment of theft and its verification by a returned oath (yamīn mardūdah), confession (iqrār), or testimony (bayyinah).

As for the oath: if [the accused] denies the theft and swears, the litigation is terminated. If he refuses to swear (nukul) and the claimant swears, the financial liability (ghurm) is established, and the amputation is also established, just as retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is established by the returned oath. If he claims that he coerced his slave-girl into fornication, the dowry (mahr) is established by the returned oath. But it is far-fetched to establish stoning (rajm) thereby, because the returned oath, even if it is treated as testimony (bayyinah), does not extend beyond the right of the one who swears. Stoning is a right of God. From this, a possibility also arises concerning the amputation for theft.

As for confession: if it occurs after the claim [has been filed], the amputation is established by it, on the condition of persistence (iṣrār). If he retracts, the financial liability is not dropped. Regarding the dropping of the ḥadd, there are two opinions:
One is that it drops, like the ḥadd for fornication.
The second is that it does not drop, because it is linked to the right of a human being, and the financial liability—which is inseparable from it—remains. Among them are those who reversed this, saying: the amputation is dropped, and there are two opinions concerning the financial liability. The rationale for dropping it is its subordination to the amputation—but this is corrupt.

As for when he confesses to coercing a slave-girl into fornication and then retracts: the most correct (aṣaḥḥ) view is that the ḥadd drops and the dowry becomes obligatory. Some said it is possible to treat it like theft. However, the separation of the ḥadd from the dowry is more plausible than the separation of the amputation from the financial liability; therefore, there is hesitation concerning it.

If the thief retracts after the amputation has been carried out, there is no redress. If he retracts during its execution, the executioner desists from the remainder, if we hold that his retraction has effect.

As for when he confesses before any claim [is filed]: is he amputated without the presence of the owner and his demand? There are two aspects (wajhān). The rationale for considering his demand is that perhaps he (the owner) might acknowledge the thief's ownership or grant him permission (ibāḥah), which would drop the ḥadd—even if the thief denies this. The correct view is that if he confesses to fornication with another's slave-girl, he is subjected to the ḥadd immediately, for there is no room for a demand in it. The drift of this suggests that if the owner of the slave-girl were to say, "I had given him the slave-girl before that," and the thief denies it, the ḥadd is still obligatory, and the owner's statement has no effect, for it is not tied to his litigation. This is like the case of a free woman who says, "I was his wife," and he denies her—he is still subjected to the ḥadd.

If we hold that he is not amputated immediately, then there is a disagreement concerning his imprisonment until the owner's arrival, which turns on whether his retraction drops [the ḥadd].

All this pertains to the free man. As for the slave: if he confesses to a theft that does not necessitate amputation, his confession is not accepted regarding the property, nor do we attach it to his neck (raqabah) without the master's confirmation. If he confesses to what necessitates amputation, his right hand is amputated, even if the master denies him—contrary to al-Muzanī and Abū Yūsuf, may God have mercy on them. It is accepted [against him] because he is not suspect (mutahham) in it.

Then, does the financial liability attach to his neck as a consequence of the establishment of the amputation? There are conflicting textual reports, and the gist of them is four opinions:
One: it is not accepted, because it is a confession against the master, not against the slave.
Second: it is accepted, because his neck is also owned by the master. If it is accepted regarding the amputation of his hand, to negate suspicion, then let it be accepted regarding the financial liability and the restitution of the property.
Third: if he confesses to a specific chattel (ʿayn) that is in his own hand, it is accepted, because the apparent possession (ẓāhir al-yad) is the slave's. But if he confesses to destruction (itlāf), it is not accepted, because his neck is in the master's hand. This would necessitate attachment [to the neck], as if he said, "All that is in my master's hand, I stole it and delivered it to him"—we would never accept that.
Fourth: the reverse of this—namely, that his confession to destruction is accepted, for the master, on the most correct view, ransoms him with the lesser of two amounts: his value or the value of the slave. The value of the slave is the means of redressing the harm to the master. As for specific chattels, if the door of confession regarding them is opened, the master would be harmed thereby, for there is no recourse [for him].

If it is asked: may the judge urge the thief to conceal the theft or to retract his confession? We say: as for concealment, it is permissible with the restitution of the property, due to his saying, peace be upon him, to the thief: "I do not think you stole" — and this is like prompting him to deny. And his saying, "Did you steal? Say: No" — the imams have not authenticated this. As for retracting the confession, the judge does not urge him to it, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Whoever commits any of these abominations, let him conceal himself with the concealment of God. For whoever exposes his page to us, we establish upon him the ḥadd of God." This indicates the distinction between before appearance and after it.

The third proof for theft is testimony (shahādah). The amputation is not established except by the testimony of two men. If a man and two women testify, the financial liability is established without the amputation—unlike the case where they testify to intentional homicide (qatl ʿamd), for then neither retaliation nor blood-money (diyah) is established, because the blood-money is a substitute for retaliation. The financial liability is not a substitute for the amputation; rather, it is obligatory alongside it. There is an aspect (wajh) that the financial liability is also not established, like the blood-money—but this is weak.

Then, complete testimony does not necessitate the amputation by testifying to theft absolutely; rather, detail (tafṣīl) is indispensable in it. For how many a theft does not necessitate amputation! For this reason, detail is also required in confession. It is required in the testimony for fornication. Is it required in the confession for fornication? There is a disagreement about it. The cause is that the ḥadd for fornication is apparent, and its occurrence is certain for the fornicator himself. As for the witness, he relies only on circumstantial indications (makhāyil). The ḥadd for theft is not apparent to the thief. There is no doubt that attributing absolute fornication is slander (qadhf), because the defamation is achieved by it.

chapters.title_en: Two Subsidiary Issues, The Third Consideration on the Obligation, Four Subsidiary Branches, and the Sixth Offense: Highway Robbery
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرعان

أحدهما لو قامت شهادة حسبة على أنه سرق مال فلان الغائب فالنص أنه لا
يقطع ما لم يحضر ولو شهدوا على أنه زنى بجاريته قال يحد في الحال فقيل
قولان بالنقل والتخريج وطردوا ذلك في الإقرار في المسألتين ومنهم من فرق
وهو الأصح لأنه أباحه الملك فإقراره بالملك يدرأ حد السرقة دون حد الزنا
وله على الجملة تعلق بطلبه
فإن قلنا لا يقطع فهل يحبس يبني على أن شهادة الحسبة مقبولة في حق الله
تعالى والظاهر أنه مردود في حقوق الآدميين والسرقة كالمترددة بينهما فينقدح
فيه خلاف فإن لم تقبل لم يحبس وإن قلنا تقبل فيحبس ثم يكفي المالك إذا رجع
أن يدعي ويستوفي المال فإن قلنا لا تسمع فيجب إعادة البينة لأجل المال
والظاهر أنه لا تعاد لأجل القطع
الثاني دعوى السارق الملك تدفع عنه القطع إذا لم تكن بينه فإن قامت
البينة نظر فإن لم يكن في دعواه تكذيب الشهادة اندفع أيضا كما إذا شهدوا
على أنه سرق من حرزه متاعا أو شهدوا على أنه سرق ملكه ولكن قال السارق كان
قد وهب مني في السر والشاهد اعتمد على الظاهر
فأما إن قال كان ملكي أصلا وغصبته فهذا تكذيب للبينة ففي سقوط القطع ها
هنا تردد ويحتمل أن يبنى على أن المدعى عليه بعد قيام البينة عليه لو قال
المدعي يعلم سرا أنه ملكي وإنما الشاهد اعتمد ظاهر اليد فهل له تحليف
المدعي فيه خلاف فإن قلنا له ذلك فها هنا يرجع وجوب القطع إلى يمين المالك
وهو بعيد فلا يبعد إسقاطه

### | النظر الثالث من الكتاب في بيان الواجب

وهو الغرم والقطع والحسم والتعليق
أما رد العين فواجب بالاتفاق مع القطع فإن تلف وجب الغرم عندنا مع القطع
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله القطع والغرم لا يجتمعان
ثم الواجب القطع من الكوع وقال بعض أهل الظاهر من المنكب
ثم الواجب أولا قطع اليمين وفي الكرة الثانية قطع الرجل اليسرى حذرا من
استيعاب جنس البطش أو المشي أو استيعاب أحد الجانبين فيتعذر المشي وفي
الثالثة تقطع اليد اليسرى وفي الرابعة رجله اليمنى واقتصر أبو حنيفة رحمه
الله في الثالثة على التعزير وقد ورد الخبر بما ذكرناه وورد في بعض
الروايات فإن عاد خامسة فاقتلوه وقيل هو قول قديم للشافعي رضي الله عنه لكن
هذه الزيادة شاذة
وأما الحسم فهو غمس محل القطع في الزيت المغلي لتنسد أفواه العروق
والصحيح أن ذلك واجب نظرا للسارق كيلا يسري وهو إلى اختياره وعليه مئونته
وفيه وجه أنه زيادة عقوبة حفا لله تعالى إذ لم تزل الأئمة يفعلون ذلك مع
كراهية السارق
وأما التعليق فهو أن تعلق يده في رقبته وتترك ثلاثة أيام للتنكيل وقد ورد
به خبر ولم يصحح ثم هو استحباب إن صح التنكيل إن رآه الإمام

### | فروع أربعة

الأول من سقطت يده اليمنى بآفة سماوية فإذا سرق قطعنا رجله اليسرى ولو
سرق أولا ثم سقطت يده سقط القطع لأنه تعين الإستحقاق وقيل إنه يعدل إلى
الرجل اليسرى وهو غلط
الثاني لو بادر الجلاد وقطع اليسرى فإن قصد فعليه القصاص وقطع اليمين باق
وإن دهش وغلط فقد نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه في الأم على سقوط القطع ونقل
أيضا أن الدية تجب باليسرى ثم يطقع يمينه فتحصلنا على قولين
وقال أبو إسحق المروزي لو سقطت يسراه بآفة سماوية قبل قطع اليمين فلا
يبعد أن يجعل كغلط الجلاد وهو بعيد
الثالث لو كانت على يده أصبع  زائدة قطعنا اليد ولا نبالي ولو كان ناقصا
اكتفينا بالموجود ولو وجدنا أصبعا واحدة فإن لم نجد إلا الكف فالظاهر
الاكتفاء به تنكيلا بقطع المعصم وفيه وجه أنه يعدل إلى الرجل اليسرى إذا لم
يبق من آلة البطش شيء واليد عبارة عنها وأما اليد الشلاء فيكتفى بها إلا
إذا خيف الهلاك لنزف الدم فيعدل إلى الرجل
الرابع لو كان للمعصم كفان قطعنا الأصلية وتركنا الزائدة إن أمكن وإلا
قطعناهما وإن كانتا متساويتين ولا تبين الأصلية قال الأصحاب نقطعهما جميعا
لنتيقن استيفاء الأصلية ولا نبالي بالزيادة

### | الجناية السادسة قطع الطريق

والنظر في صفة قطاع الطريق وفي عقوبتهم وفي حكم العفو
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-ه-د (shahida)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be present, to testify; shahāda is information given with certainty of presence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Testimony as legal proof (bayyinah) establishing rights of God (ḥuqūq Allāh) vs. rights of men (ḥuqūq al-ādamiyyīn).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: presence at an event; metaphorical: bearing witness in court as if present.
- Root: ق-ط-ع (qaṭaʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cut off, sever; amputation as a fixed penalty (ḥadd).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The ḥadd of theft—severance of the hand as divinely ordained deterrence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical severance; metaphorical: cutting off the thief's means of gain.
- Root: غ-ر-م (gharima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pay a debt or fine; indemnity (ghurm) for loss.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Financial liability distinct from corporal punishment; the debate on combining ghurm with qaṭʿ.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: financial compensation; metaphorical: bearing the consequence of one's act.
- Root: ح-س-م (ḥasama)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To cut off, stop, seal; cauterization of veins.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Medical sealing of blood vessels post-amputation as a protective measure.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical sealing; metaphorical: preventing harm from spreading.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses "لو" (if) clauses to set hypothetical legal scenarios, and "إلا" (except) to carve out exceptions, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis.
chapters.translation:
### | Two Subsidiary Issues

One of them: If testimony given voluntarily (shahādat ḥisbah) is established that he stole the property of an absent person (fulān al-ghāʾib), the text (naṣṣ) holds that he is not amputated until the owner appears. But if they testify that he committed fornication with his slave-girl, he [al-Shāfiʿī] said: he is punished with the ḥadd immediately. It was said: there are two opinions, by transmission (naql) and by derivation (takhrīj), and they extended this to confession (iqrār) in both cases. Among them is one who distinguished—and this is the soundest (al-aṣaḥḥ)—because ownership made her lawful for him, so his confession of ownership repels the ḥadd of theft but not the ḥadd of fornication. And he has, in general, a connection to his claim (ṭalab).

If we say he is not amputated, is he imprisoned? This builds on whether testimony given voluntarily (shahādat al-ḥisbah) is accepted regarding the rights of God (ḥuqūq Allāh) — and the apparent view (al-ẓāhir) is that it is rejected regarding the rights of men (ḥuqūq al-ādamiyyīn). Theft is as if wavering between the two, so a disagreement arises therein. If it is not accepted, he is not imprisoned. But if we say it is accepted, he is imprisoned. Then it suffices for the owner, when he returns, to claim and recover the property. If we say it is not heard, then the evidence must be re-presented for the sake of the property. And the apparent view is that it is not re-presented for the sake of the amputation.

The second: The thief's claim of ownership repels amputation from him if there is no evidence against him [on that claim]. If evidence is established, we consider: if his claim does not entail a denial of the testimony (takdhīb al-shahādah), it is also repelled—as when they testify that he stole goods from his [the owner's] custody (ḥirz), or they testify that he stole his own property, but the thief says: "He had gifted it to me in secret," and the witness relied on the apparent state (al-ẓāhir).

But if he says: "It was originally my property and he usurped it from me"—this is a denial of the evidence. Regarding the dropping of amputation here, there is hesitation (taraddud). It is possible to build on the question: after evidence is established against the defendant, if he says, "The plaintiff knows secretly that it is my property, and the witness only relied on the apparent possession (ẓāhir al-yad)"—is he entitled to administer an oath to the plaintiff? There is disagreement therein. If we say he is entitled to that, then here the obligation of amputation reverts to the oath of the owner—and that is far-fetched (baʿīd), so it is not far-fetched to drop it [the amputation].

### | The Third Consideration of the Book: On Explaining the Obligation

It is: the financial indemnity (ghurm), the amputation (qaṭʿ), the cauterization (ḥasm), and the suspension (taʿlīq).

As for returning the stolen object (radd al-ʿayn), it is obligatory by consensus (ittifāq) along with amputation. If it is destroyed, the indemnity (ghurm) becomes obligatory with us, along with amputation. Abū Ḥanīfah—may God have mercy on him—said: amputation and indemnity are not combined.

Then the obligation is amputation from the wrist (al-kūʿ). Some of the Ẓāhirīs said: from the shoulder (al-mankib).

Then the obligation is first to cut the right hand. In the second offense, the left foot is cut—out of caution against exhausting the entire genus of grasping (al-baṭsh) or walking, or exhausting one of the two sides, which would render walking impossible. In the third, the left hand is cut. In the fourth, his right foot. Abū Ḥanīfah—may God have mercy on him—restricted the third to discretionary punishment (taʿzīr). The report (khabar) has come with what we mentioned, and in some narrations it came: "If he returns a fifth time, kill him." It was said this is an old opinion (qawl qadīm) of al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—but this addition is anomalous (shādhdhah).

As for cauterization (ḥasm), it is dipping the place of amputation in boiling oil so that the mouths of the veins are sealed. The correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that this is obligatory, out of consideration for the thief, lest [the bleeding] spread (yasrī). It is subject to his choice, and its expense is upon him. There is a face (wajh) that it is an additional punishment, out of zeal for God—may He be exalted—since the imams have not ceased doing this despite the thief's aversion.

As for suspension (taʿlīq), it is that his hand is hung from his neck and he is left for three days for deterrence (tankīl). A report has come regarding it but was not authenticated (ṣaḥḥaḥa). Then it is recommended (istihbāb) if the deterrence is authenticated, if the imam sees fit.

### | Four Subsidiary Branches

The first: If his right hand fell [was lost] due to a heavenly affliction (āfah samāwiyyah), then if he steals, we cut his left foot. But if he stole first, then his hand fell, the amputation drops, because the entitlement (istiḥqāq) was fixed. It was said: he shifts to the left foot—and this is an error (ghalaṭ).

The second: If the executioner (jallād) hastened and cut the left [hand]—if he intended [to err], then retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is upon him, and the cutting of the right remains. But if he was bewildered (dahisha) and erred, al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—stated in al-Umm that the amputation drops. It was also transmitted that the blood-money (diyah) is obligatory for the left, then his right is cut—so we arrive at two opinions. Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī said: If his left hand fell due to a heavenly affliction before the cutting of the right, it is not far-fetched to treat it like the executioner's error—but it is far-fetched.

The third: If there is on his hand a supernumerary finger (iṣbaʿ zāʾidah), we cut the hand and do not care. If it is deficient [missing a finger], we suffice with what exists. If we find only one finger—if we find nothing but the palm (kaf)—the apparent view is to suffice with it, as deterrence by cutting at the wrist. There is a face that he shifts to the left foot when nothing remains of the instrument of grasping (ālat al-baṭsh), and the hand is what is meant by it. As for the paralyzed hand (al-yad al-shallāʾ), it suffices, unless destruction is feared from blood loss (nazf al-dam), in which case he shifts to the foot.

The fourth: If the wrist has two palms, we cut the original and leave the supernumerary, if possible. Otherwise, we cut both. If they are equal and the original cannot be distinguished, the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: we cut both, to be certain of fulfilling the original, and we do not care about the excess.

### | The Sixth Offense: Highway Robbery (Qaṭʿ al-Ṭarīq)

The consideration is in the description of highway robbers (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq), in their punishment, and in the ruling on pardon (ʿafw).

chapters.arabic_text:
### | النظر الأول في صفتهم

والأصل فيهم قوله تعالى {إنما جزاء الذين يحاربون الله ورسوله} الآية
فذكر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم تفسيره فقال
أن يقتلوا إذا قتلوا أو يصلبوا إذا قتلوا وأخذوا الأموال أو تقطع أيديهم
وأرجلهم إذا أخذوا المال أو يلحق الطلب بهم إذا هربوا لينفوا من الأرض
وقال داود يجمع بين هذه العقوبات لظاهر الآية وقال مالك رحمه الله الشاب
يقطع والشيخ ذو الهرم يقتل ومن ليس له نجدة الشباب ولا رأي الشيوخ ينفى
ثم يعتبر عندنا فهيم صفتان النجدة والبعد عن محل الغوث
أما النجدة فلأنه إن لم يكن لهم شوكة بل كان اعتمادهم على الإختلاس
والهرب فلا يجب به إلا التعزير ثم لا يشترط للنجدة الذكورة ولا السلاح ولا
العدد بل لو اجتمع نسوة وكانت لهن شوكة فهن قطاع الطريق وقال أبو حنيفة
رحمه الله لو كان في جميع القطاع امرأة سقط الحد
والضرب واللطم كإشهار السلاح بالإتفاق
والواحد إذا قاوم واحدا أو جمعا بفضل قوة فهو قاطع طريق ولا نقول إن
المسافر الواحد مضيع لماله بل ماله محفوظ به إلا أن يقصد فمن قصده فهو قاطع
وقال الإمام ينبغي أن يرد ذلك إلى العادة فحيث يعد الواحد مفرطا فلا يجب
على سالب ماله إلا التعزير

### | فرع

لو هجم على الرفاق قوم تستقل الرفقة بدفعهم من  غير ضرر بين فاستسلموا فهم
المضيعون وليسوا قطاعا لانهم لم يأخذوا بشوكتهم بل بتسليم الملاك إليهم وإن
علموا أنهم لا يقاومون فهربوا منهم فهم قطاع وكذلك إذا كان الأمر في قوة
الجانبين كالمتقاوم إذا تقاتلوا وانكف الفريقان من غير ظفر فالظاهر أنهم
قطاع إن جرى قتل وسلب لأن الشوكة قد تحققت
وأما الصفة الثانية فهو بعدهم عن محل الغوث أما ما يجري من الأخذ على
أطراف العمران فيعتمد فيه الهرب والاختلاس دون الشوكة إلا إذا فترت قوة
السلطان وثار ذوو العرامة في البلاد فهم قطاع عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه وإن
كانوا في البلاد أما إذا دخلوا في وقت قوة السلطان دار بالليل مع المشاعل
مكابرين ومنعوا أهل الدار من الاستغاثة وانصرفوا وهم متلثمون ففيهم وجهان
أحدهما أنهم قطاع ونزل منعهم من الإستغاثة كبعدهم عن محل الغوث
والثاني أنهم سراق فإن الطلب يلحقهم على القرب وإنما اعتمادهم على
التواري والاختفاء
ولم يذهب أحد إلى أنهم مختلسون مع انهم لم يأخذوه في خفية واختزال
فإذن قد حصل أن قطاع الطريق من يعتمد على الشوكة في الحال مع بعد الغوث
لا على الاختلاس والهرب في الوقت

### | النظر الثاني في العقوبة الواجبة

ويمتزج به النظر في جرائمهم ولهم في الجرائم أحوال
الأولى أن يقتصر على أخذ ربع دينار فصاعدا فتقطع يده اليمنى ورجله اليسرى
سواء كان الربع ملكا لواحد أو لجماعة الرفقة وكذلك في السرقة لا يفرق بين
الخالص والمشترك في النصاب مهما كان الحرز واحدا وقال ابن خيران لا يشترط
النصاب
الثانية أن يقتصر على القتل المجرد فيقتل وليس فيه زيادة تغليظ إلا كون
القتل محتوما كما سيأتي
الثالثة أن يقتصر على الإرعاب وتكثير الشوكة وكان ردءا للقوم فعليه تعزير
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله هو شريك
الرابعة أن يجمع بين الأخذ والقتل فالمذهب المشهور أنه يصلب ويقتل ولا
يقطع ويكون الصلب زيادة تنكيل وتغليظ لأجل الجمع وقال أبو الطيب بن سلمة
تقطع يده ورجله لأخذه ويقتل لقتله ويصلب لجمعه بينهما وذكر  صاحب
التقريب وجها أنه إن أخذ نصابا وقتل قطع وقتل ولم يصلب وإن أخذ أقل منه
قتل وصلب ولم يقطع ويكون الصلب لأجل الأخذ والمذهب هو الأول وقال أبو حنيفة
الإمام بالخيار إن أحب قتل وصلب ولم يقطع وإن أحب قطع وقتل ولم يصلب
ثم إذا جمعنا بين القتل والصلب فالمذهب أنه يقتل على الأرض ثم يصلب
مقتولا وفيه وجه أنه يقتل مصلوبا إما بأن يترك حتى يموت جوعا على وجه أو
يقصد مقتله بحديدة مذففه على وجه وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله
ثم كم يترك على الصليب فيه قولان
أحدهما أنه يترك ثلاثة أيام
وعلى هذا إن كان يتعرض للتهري قبله فهل يترك فعلى وجهين
أحدهما لا يترك ثلاثة أيام لأن التنكيل قد حصل فيصان عن التفتت والنت
والقول الثاني أنه يترك حتى يتهرى ويسيل ودكه لأن الصليب اسم الودك ومنه
اشتق اسم الصليب
والصحيح أنه يقتل أولا ويغسل ويصلى عليه ثم يصلب ولا سبيل إلى ترك الصلاة
بكل حال خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله ويتعذر على قول من يقتله بعد الصليب ثم
يترك حتى يتهرى نعم وإن قلنا يقتل بعد الصليب ولكن ينزل بعد ثلاث فيمكن أن
يسلم إلى أهله للغسل والصلاة بعد الاسترسال فأما عقوبة النفي فالصحيح أنها
غير مقصودة بل إن وجدوا أقيم الحد والتعزير وإلا لحق بهم طلب أعوان السلطان
حتى يتشردوا في البلاد وينتفوا من تلك الأرض ومنهم من قال هي عقوبة مقصودة
في حق من اقتصر على الإرعاب ثم منهم من قال ينفيهم الإمام إلى بلد معين
ويعزرهم بها إما ضربا أو حبسا ومنهم من قال له أن يقتصر على النفي
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ر-ب (ḥ-r-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to take property by force" or "to wage war"; the form III verb ḥāraba denotes mutual hostility and armed confrontation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In the Qur'anic context, "those who wage war (yuḥāribūn)" against God and His Messenger refers to armed brigands (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq) who corrupt the earth through violence and plunder, not merely political enemies.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The literal sense is armed combat; metaphorically extended to any act of open aggression that destabilizes public security, distinguishing it from covert theft (sariqah).
- Root: ش-و-ك (sh-w-k)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The root denotes thorns; metaphorically, "shawkah" signifies martial strength, formidable power, or the capacity to resist.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal discourse, shawkah is the operative criterion for brigandage—the possession of sufficient force to overcome victims without reliance on stealth or flight.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: thorns; metaphorical: the "pricking" power of an armed band. The term shifts from physical plant anatomy to social-military capability.
- Root: ن-ف-ي (n-f-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To banish, expel, or drive away; also to negate or deny.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The Qur'anic phrase "or they be expelled from the land" (أو ينفوا من الأرض) denotes exile as a punitive measure removing the criminal from the locus of his harmful activity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: physical expulsion; metaphorical: the negation of the criminal's presence in the social order, rendering him a fugitive.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Conditional Protasis (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — In the phrase "if they kill, they are killed; if they kill and take wealth, they are crucified," the conditional structure (in... fa...) establishes a one-to-one correspondence between criminal acts and their prescribed punishments, with the apodosis determined by the protasis's cumulative content.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first examination concerns their attributes (ṣifātuhum).

The foundational proof concerning them is the saying of God the Exalted: {«The recompense of those who wage war against God and His Messenger»} — the verse. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, mentioned its interpretation, saying: "They are to be killed if they kill; or crucified if they kill and seize wealth; or their hands and feet are to be cut off if they seize wealth; or pursuit is to be attached to them if they flee, so that they be expelled from the land." Dāwūd (al-Ẓāhirī) held that these punishments are to be combined, due to the apparent meaning of the verse. Mālik, may God have mercy on him, held that the young man is to have his limb amputated, the decrepit elder is to be killed, and the one who possesses neither the vigor of youth nor the counsel of elders is to be exiled.

Then, in our school (ʿindanā), two attributes are considered: prowess (al-najdah) and distance from the place of succor (al-buʿd ʿan maḥall al-ghawth).

As for prowess: because if they possess no formidable force (shawkah), but rather their reliance is upon snatching (al-ikhtilās) and flight, then nothing is incumbent upon them except discretionary chastisement (al-taʿzīr). Moreover, for prowess, masculinity is not stipulated, nor weaponry, nor numbers. Rather, if women gathered and possessed formidable force, they are highway robbers (quṭṭāʿ al-ṭarīq). Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: if among all the robbers there is a single woman, the ḥadd punishment is dropped.

Striking and slapping are, by agreement, equivalent to the brandishing of weapons.

The single individual, if he resists one person or a group by virtue of superior strength, is a highway robber. And we do not say that the lone traveler is one who squanders his wealth; rather, his wealth is preserved through him, unless someone intends him — for whoever intends him is a highway robber. The Imām (al-Ghazālī's teacher, al-Juwaynī) said: this ought to be referred to custom (al-ʿādah); wherever the single individual is deemed negligent (mufriṭ), then upon the one who seizes his wealth nothing is incumbent except discretionary chastisement.

### | Branch

If a group storms upon a company of travelers, and the company is able to repel them without any harm between them, yet they surrender — then they are the squanderers (al-muḍayyiʿūn), and the attackers are not highway robbers, because they did not take by their force, but rather by the owners' surrender to them. But if they know that they cannot resist them, and they flee from them, then they are highway robbers. Likewise, if the matter is in the strength of both sides, like two mutually resisting parties when they fight and both groups are repelled without victory — the apparent position is that they are highway robbers if killing and plundering occurred, because force (al-shawkah) has been realized.

As for the second attribute: it is their distance from the place of succor. As for what occurs of seizure at the outskirts of civilization (aṭrāf al-ʿumrān), reliance therein is upon flight and snatching, not upon force — except when the power of the Sultan has weakened and the turbulent ones (dhawū al-ʿarāmah) have risen in the lands; then they are highway robbers according to al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, even if they are within the lands. As for when they enter, at a time of the Sultan's strength, a house by night with torches, overpowering (mukābirīn), preventing the inhabitants of the house from seeking aid, and departing while masked — concerning them there are two faces (wajhān). One of them: they are highway robbers, and their prevention of seeking aid is treated like their distance from the place of succor. The second: they are thieves (saraqah), for pursuit can reach them at close range, and their reliance is only upon concealment and hiding.

No one has held that they are snatchers (mukhtalisūn), given that they did not take it in secrecy and covertness. Thus it has been established that the highway robber is the one who relies upon force (al-shawkah) in the moment, combined with distance from succor — not upon snatching and flight at the time.

### | The Second Examination: The Mandated Punishment

And with it is intermixed the examination of their crimes. They have, regarding crimes, several states:

The first: that he confines himself to taking a quarter of a dīnār or more — then his right hand and left foot are cut off, whether the quarter is the property of one person or of the whole company collectively. Likewise in theft (al-sariqah), no distinction is made between the exclusive and the shared in the nisāb (minimum threshold), as long as the place of safekeeping (al-ḥirz) is one. Ibn Khayrān said: the nisāb is not stipulated.

The second: that he confines himself to bare killing — then he is killed, and there is no additional aggravation therein except that the killing is obligatory (maḥtūm), as will come.

The third: that he confines himself to intimidation (al-irʿāb) and the multiplication of force, being a supporter (radʾ) for the group — then upon him is discretionary chastisement. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: he is a partner.

The fourth: that he combines taking and killing. The well-known position of the school (al-madhhab al-mashhūr) is that he is crucified and killed, and not amputated; and the crucifixion is an additional humiliation (tankīl) and aggravation on account of the combination. Abū al-Ṭayyib ibn Salamah said: his hand and foot are cut off for his taking, and he is killed for his killing, and he is crucified for his combining of the two. The author of al-Taqrīb mentioned a face: if he took the nisāb and killed, he is amputated and killed but not crucified; and if he took less than it, he is killed and crucified but not amputated — the crucifixion being on account of the taking. The madhhab is the first. Abū Ḥanīfah said: the Imām has the choice — if he wishes, he kills and crucifies without amputation; and if he wishes, he amputates and kills without crucifixion.

Then, when we combine killing and crucifixion, the madhhab is that he is killed on the ground, then crucified dead. There is a face that he is killed crucified — either by being left until he dies of hunger, in one manner, or by his death being intended with a penetrating iron instrument, in another manner — and this is the madhhab of Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him.

Then, how long is he left upon the cross? There are two sayings (qawlān). One of them: he is left for three days. According to this, if he is exposed to putrefaction before that, is he left? There are two faces. One of them: he is not left for three days, because the humiliation (al-tan kīl) has already been achieved, so he is protected from disintegration and stench. The second saying: he is left until he putrefies and his marrow (wadak) flows, because the cross (al-ṣalīb) is the name of the marrow, and from it the name of the cross is derived.

The correct position (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that he is killed first, washed, and the funeral prayer is performed over him, then he is crucified. There is no way to omit the prayer in any case, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him. And it becomes impossible on the saying of the one who kills him after the crucifixion, then leaves him until he putrefies. Yes — if we say he is killed after the crucifixion, but is brought down after three days, then it is possible that he be handed to his family for washing and prayer after the decomposition (al-istirsāl).

As for the punishment of exile (al-nafy), the correct position is that it is not an intended punishment in itself; rather, if they are found, the ḥadd and discretionary chastisement are established against them; otherwise, the pursuit of the Sultan's agents is attached to them until they are scattered throughout the lands and expelled from that territory. Among them are those who said it is an intended punishment in the case of the one who confines himself to intimidation. Then among them are those who said: the Imām exiles them to a specific land and chastises them therein — either by flogging or imprisonment. And among them are those who said: he may confine himself to exile alone.

chapters.title_en: The Third Inquiry: The Ruling on the Penalty (Ḥukm al-ʿUqūbah)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | النظر الثالث في حكم العقوبة

وله حكمان
الأول أن التوبة قبل الظفر مؤثر فيها لنص القرآن العظيم فيسقط بها تحتم
القتل دون أصله على الظاهر ويسقط به الصلب وقطع الرجل أما قطع اليد هل يسقط
إذا كان المأخوذ نصابا فيه وجهان أحدهما لا كأصل القتل وإنما الذي يسقط
خاصية قطع الطريق
والثاني وهو الأصح أنه يسقط لأن هذا يخالف صورة السرقة واليد والرجل كعضو
واحد هاهنا وكذلك إن وجدنا رجله اليسرى دون يده اليمنى اكتفينا به ولم نقطع
يده اليسرى ومهما عاد ثانيا قطعنا اليد اليسرى والرجل اليمنى
أما التوبة بعد الظفر ففيه قولان يجريان في جميع حدود الله تعالى
أحدهما أنه لا يؤثر لأن القرآن خصص ما قبل التوبة
والثاني أنه يسقط لأنه إن خصص هاهنا فقد أطلق في آية السرقة فقال تعالى
{فمن تاب من بعد ظلمه وأصلح}
وقال القاضي قرنت التوبة هاهنا بالإصلاح فيدل على أن التوبة بعد الظفر لا
تؤثر إلا بعد الإستبراء وصلاح الحال إذ يمكن أن يكون للهيبة
وعلى الجملة فمن ظهر تقواه وحسنت حاله امتنع مؤاخذته بما جرى له في
الجاهلية أما إذا أنشأ التوبة حيث أخذ لإقامة الحد فهو متهم والتوقف إلى
استبرائه مشكل إن حبس وإن خلي فكيف نتبع أحواله
الحكم الثاني أن هذا القتل قد ازدحم عليه حق الله تعالى ولأجله تحتم وإن
عفا ولي القتيل عن حق القتيل فإنه معصوم ولا شك في أنه إذا جرح خطأ أو شبه
العمد فلا يقتل
وإن تمحض العمد فقد تعلق به حق الله تعالى قطعا فإنه يقتل وإن عفا ولي
القتيل ولكن هل يثبت للقتيل حق مع حق الله تعالى للشافعي رضي الله عنه فيه
قولان وتظهر فائدته في خمس مسائل
إحداها لو قتل ذميا أو عبدا أو أمة ومن لا يكافئه بالجملة فإن محضنا حق
الله تعالى قتل وإن قلنا فيه قصاص لم يقتل وهكذا لو قتل عبد نفسه قال
القاضي يخرج على القولين وقطع الصيدلاني بأنه لا يقتل وإن جعلناه حدا لأنه
مملوكه فلا يصلح لمقاتلته ومخاصمته في القتال
الثانية إن مات القاتل وقلنا إنه محض حد فلا دية للقتيل وإن قلنا فيه حق
الآدمي فله الدية
الثالثة إذا قتل جماعة اكتفي به إن جعلناه حدا وإلا قتل بواحد وللآخرين
الدية
الرابعة لو عفا الولي على مال فلا أثر له إن  جعلناه حدا وإلا فله الدية
ويقتل حدا وهو كمرتد استوجب القصاص وعفي عنه
الخامسة لو تاب قبل الظفر سقط الحد وبقي القصاص حتى يسقط بعفوه إن جعلنا
له حقا وإلا فيسقط بالكلية
ولعل الأصح الجمع بين الحقين ما أمكن فإن سقط الحد بالتوبة أو القصاص
بالعفو فيبقى الآخر خاليا عن الزحمة فيستوفى فأما إسقاط القصاص والحد أو
الدية فبعيد جدا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ت-و-ب (t-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Return, turning back; repentance as reverting from sin to obedience.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Repentance (tawbah) as the pivotal act of moral restoration, nullifying the punitive claim of the divine law when sincere.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of 'returning' (rujūʿ); metaphorically, the soul's reorientation toward God, distinct from mere verbal confession.
- Root: ظ-ف-ر (ẓ-f-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Victory, attainment, overcoming; here, the authorities' capture of the offender.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The moment of judicial seizure, marking the transition from fugitive status to legal accountability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal 'gaining the upper hand'; metaphorically, the state's jurisdictional reach over the criminal.
- Root: ق-ت-ل (q-t-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Killing, slaying; the capital penalty for highway robbery (ḥirābah).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The divinely ordained punishment (ḥadd) as distinct from private retaliation (qiṣāṣ), each carrying distinct juristic consequences.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal 'causing death'; metaphorically, the legal extinction of the offender's claim to life through judicial decree.
- Root: ع-ف-و (ʿ-f-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Pardon, remission; the victim's kin relinquishing their right to retaliation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Forgiveness as a human act that interacts with divine punitive claims, revealing the dual nature of the penalty.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal 'erasure'; metaphorically, the legal nullification of a claim, whether divine or human.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text employs conditional clauses (in/ idhā) and exceptions (illā) to delineate juristic outcomes, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to determine when repentance or pardon alters the penalty.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third inquiry concerns the ruling on the penalty (ḥukm al-ʿuqūbah). It carries two rulings.

The first: That repentance (tawbah) before capture (ẓafar) is effective upon it, by virtue of the text of the Mighty Qurʾān, and thereby the obligation of killing (taḥattum al-qatl) is dropped — though not its foundational basis (aṣluhu) according to the apparent view — and thereby crucifixion (ṣalb) and the amputation of the leg (qaṭʿ al-rijl) are dropped. As for the amputation of the hand (qaṭʿ al-yad), whether it is dropped when the stolen amount constitutes a nisāb (threshold), there are two views (wajhān): One — that it is not dropped, like the foundational basis of killing, and only the specific characteristic of highway robbery (khāṣṣiyyat qaṭʿ al-ṭarīq) is what drops. The second — and it is the more correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) — is that it is dropped, because this differs from the form of theft (ṣūrat al-sariqah), and the hand and leg are like a single limb (ʿuḍw wāḥid) here. Likewise, if we find his left leg without his right hand, we suffice with it and do not amputate his left hand. And whenever he returns a second time, we amputate the left hand and the right leg.

As for repentance after capture, there are two sayings (qawlān) that apply to all the prescribed penalties of God Most High (ḥudūd Allāh taʿālā): One — that it has no effect, because the Qurʾān specified what precedes repentance. The second — that it drops, because if it was specified here, it was made absolute in the verse of theft, where He Most High said: {فمن تاب من بعد ظلمه وأصلح} ("Then whoever repents after his wrongdoing and makes amends"). And al-Qāḍī said: Repentance is here coupled with making amends (iṣlāḥ), indicating that repentance after capture has no effect except after exoneration (istibrāʾ) and the rectification of one's state, since it could be due to intimidation (haybah). In sum, whoever manifests his piety and whose state becomes good, his being held accountable for what transpired in his pre-Islamic ignorance (jāhiliyyah) is prevented. But if he initiates repentance at the moment of seizure for the execution of the penalty, he is suspect (mut taham), and deferring until his exoneration is problematic — if he is imprisoned, and if he is released, how do we track his conditions?

The second ruling: That this killing has been crowded upon by the right of God Most High (ḥaqq Allāh taʿālā), and for its sake it is obligatory (taḥattam). Even if the guardian of the slain (walī al-qatīl) pardons the right of the slain, he is still inviolable (maʿṣūm). There is no doubt that if he wounds by mistake (khaṭaʾ) or quasi-intentional (shibh al-ʿamd), he is not killed. But if it is purely intentional (maḥḍ al-ʿamd), the right of God Most High attaches to it definitively, for he is killed even if the guardian of the slain pardons. However, whether a right of the slain (ḥaqq al-qatīl) is established alongside the right of God Most High — for al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, there are two sayings. Its benefit appears in five issues:

The first: If he kills a dhimmī, a slave, a female slave, or one who is not his equivalent (mukāfiʾ) in general — if we make it purely the right of God Most High, he is killed; but if we say there is retaliation (qiṣāṣ) in it, he is not killed. Likewise, if a man kills his own slave — al-Qāḍī said it is derived from the two sayings, and al-Ṣaydalānī decisively held that he is not killed, even if we make it a penalty (ḥadd), because he is his property, so he is not suited for his combat or his dispute in battle.

The second: If the killer dies, and we say it is purely a penalty (ḥadd), then there is no blood-money (diyah) for the slain; but if we say there is a human right (ḥaqq al-ādamī) in it, then he has the blood-money.

The third: If a group kills one person, he suffices for it if we make it a penalty; otherwise, he is killed for one, and the others receive blood-money.

The fourth: If the guardian pardons in exchange for wealth, it has no effect if we make it a penalty; otherwise, he has the blood-money, and he is killed as a penalty — like an apostate (murtadd) who incurs retaliation and is pardoned.

The fifth: If he repents before capture, the penalty drops and retaliation remains, until it drops by his pardon if we establish a right for him; otherwise, it drops entirely.

Perhaps the more correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) is to combine the two rights (al-jamʿ bayn al-ḥaqqayn) as much as possible. If the penalty drops by repentance, or retaliation by pardon, the other remains free of the crowding (zahmah) and is thus exacted. As for dropping both retaliation and the penalty, or the blood-money, that is very far-fetched (baʿīd jiddan).

chapters.title_en: Branches Concerning the Combination of Penalties for Highway Robbery and Other Offenses
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فروع

الأول إذا جرح المحارب جرحا ساريا فهو كالقتل في التحتم وإن كان الجرح
واقفا فلا قصاص فيه كالجائفة فلا يجرح فإن قطع عضوا فيه قصاص استوفى وهي
يتحتم فيه ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها نعم كالنفس
والثاني لا لأن القتل عهد حدا فلذلك يتحتم بخلاف القطع
والثالث أن قطع اليدين والرجلين يتحتم إن عهد حدا في السرقة بخلاف الأذن
والعين وسائر الأعضاء
الثاني يثبت قطع الطريق بشهادة أهل الرفقة يشهد كل واحد لرفيقه لا لنفسه
ولا يصرح ولو قال تعرضوا لنا ولرفقائنا فسدت صيغة الشهادة وكذا لو قال
الشاهد قذفني مع أم فلان فلاتقبل شهادته
الثالث يوالي بين قطع اليد والرجل بخلاف ما لو استحق يسراه في القصاص
ويمناه في السرقة فإنه يقدم القصاص ويمهل ريثما يندمل لأن الموالاة عظيم
الضرر لكن
القطعين في المحاربة عقوبة واحدة ولو استحق يمينه قصاصا قطعت اليمين في
القصاص ويكتفي بالرجل اليسرى وهل يمهل ريثما يندمل فيه وجهان
أحدهما يمهل لاختلاف العقوبة
والثاني لا لأن الموالاة كانت مستحقة فإن فاتت اليد فيبقى استحقاق
الموالاة
وإنما يقدم القصاص على حد السرقة والحراب ولا يبني على الخلاف في تقديم
حق الآدمي وحق الله تعالى إذا اجتمعا لأن الخلاف في الأموال التي لا يسقط
عنها حق الله تعالى بالشبهة وأما حدود الله تعالى فتسقط بالشبهة والرجوع عن
الإقرار فيقدم عليها حق الآدمي
الرابع إذا اجتمعت عقوبات للآدميين كحد القذف وقطع الطريق والقتل فإن
ازدحموا على الطلب يجلد ثم يقطع ثم يقتل ولا يبادر بالقطع عقيب الجلد إن
كان مستحق القتل غائبا إبقاء على روحه حتى لا يفوت القصاص  ولو كان حاضرا
وقال لا تتركوا الموالاة لأجلي فإني أبادر بعد القطع وأقتل ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه يبادر ولا يمهل لأن النفس مستوفاة فلا معنى للتأخير لأجل
المقتول ولا لأجل المستحق وقد رضي
والثاني أنه يمهل فإنه ربما يعفو مستحق القتل فتصير النفس هدرا بالموالاة
أما إذا أخر بعضهم حقه فإن كان المؤخر مستحق النفس قدم الجلد ويمهل ثم
يقطع وإن كان المؤخر مستحق الطرف فلا يمكن البدار إلى القتل ففيه تفويت
الطرف فيجب على مستحق النفس الصبر وهذا يؤدي إلى أن يصير مستحق الطرف إلى
غير نهاية ويندفع
القتل ولا صائر إلى أن مستحق النفس يسلط على القتل ويقال لصاحب الطرف
بادر إن شئت وإلا ضاع حقك ولو قيل به لكان منقدحا لكنه لو بادر وقتل بغير
إذن وقع الموقع ورجع صاحب الطرف إلى الدية
أما إذا كان المجتمع حدود الله تعالى كحد الشرب وجلد الزنا وقطع السرقة
والقتل فالبداية بالأخف وهو ترتيب مستحق ثم يمهل إلى الإندمال حتى لا يفوت
القتل بالموت بالسراية فإن لم يبق إلا القتل فلا إمهال
ولو كان بدل جلد الزنا جلد القذف فجلد الشرب أخف منه ولكن هل حق الآدمي
مقدم ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أن البداية في الشرب لأنه اخف
والثاني أنه يبدأ بحد القذف لأنه حق الآدمي
وكذا الخلاف لو كان بدل حد القذف قطع قصاص للآدمي
ولو زنى وهو بكر ثم زنى وهو ثيب فقد اجتمع الجلد والرجم فالظاهر الاكتفاء
بالرجم واندرج الجلد تحته وفيه وجه أنه يجلد ثم يرجم لأنه لا تداخل مع
الاختلاف
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ر-ح (jarḥa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Wounding, inflicting a bodily injury that breaks the skin or penetrates the body
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Physical harm as a legal category distinct from killing, yet sharing its causal continuum when the wound proves fatal by extension (sāriy)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal wounding vs. metaphorical "wounding" of honor or rights; here strictly literal
- Root: و-ل-ي (waliya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To follow consecutively, to be adjacent in sequence without interruption
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Sequential execution of punishments as a single penal act (muwālāh) versus separate acts requiring intervals
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal temporal adjacency; metaphorical in "guardianship" contexts—here literal
- Root: ش-ب-ه (shubhah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ambiguity, resemblance, uncertainty that clouds clear legal determination
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The jurisprudential principle that divinely prescribed penalties (ḥudūd) are suspended by doubt, unlike private claims
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal resemblance vs. technical legal ambiguity that nullifies punishment
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs layered conditionals (law, in) and exceptions (illā) to articulate juristic alternatives, requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the logical force of each ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first branch: If the highway robber inflicts a wound that spreads [through the body and proves fatal], it is like killing in its obligatory character (taḥattum). But if the wound is stationary [non-spreading], there is no retaliation (qiṣāṣ) therein—like the penetrating wound (jāʾifah)—so he is not to be wounded [in kind]. If he cuts off a limb for which retaliation is due, and it is exacted, is there obligatory character therein? Three opinions:

One: Yes, like the life [itself].

Second: No, because killing is a prescribed penalty (ḥadd) by covenant, and therefore it is obligatory, unlike amputation.

Third: That amputation of the two hands and the two feet is obligatory if it is a prescribed penalty by covenant in [the crime of] theft, unlike the ear, the eye, and the rest of the limbs.

The second branch: Highway robbery is established by the testimony of the traveling companions, each one testifying for his fellow, not for himself, and he does not specify [the details]. If he said, "They accosted us and our companions," the formulation of the testimony is corrupted. Likewise, if the witness said, "He slandered me along with the mother of so-and-so," his testimony is not accepted.

The third branch: One must maintain continuity (muwālāh) between the amputation of the hand and the foot [in highway robbery], unlike the case where one owes his left hand for retaliation and his right hand for theft—then retaliation is given precedence, and [the execution of the theft penalty] is delayed until [the wound] heals, because continuity entails grave harm. But the two amputations in highway robbery are a single punishment. If he owes his right hand for retaliation, the right hand is amputated in retaliation, and the left foot suffices [for the highway robbery penalty]. Is there a delay until healing? Two opinions:

One: He is delayed, because the punishments differ.

Second: No, because the continuity was already due; if the hand is lost, the entitlement to continuity remains.

Retaliation is given precedence over the penalty for theft and highway robbery, and this is not built upon the disagreement concerning the precedence of the right of a human being versus the right of God—when they converge—because that disagreement concerns property rights from which the right of God is not dropped by doubt (shubhah). As for the divine penalties (ḥudūd), they are dropped by doubt and by retraction of confession, so the human right takes precedence over them.

The fourth branch: If penalties for human beings converge—such as the penalty for slander (ḥadd al-qadhf), highway robbery, and killing—and they press together in demanding [execution], he is flogged, then amputated, then killed. He is not hastened to amputation immediately after flogging if the one deserving death is absent, preserving his life so that retaliation is not lost. If he is present and says, "Do not abandon the continuity for my sake, for I will hasten after amputation and kill myself," there are two opinions:

One: He hastens and is not delayed, because the life is already exacted, so there is no meaning in delaying for the sake of the slain one, nor for the sake of the one entitled [to retaliation], and he has consented.

Second: He is delayed, for perhaps the one entitled to killing may pardon, and then the life becomes wasted (hadar) through the continuity.

As for when some of them defer their right: if the deferrer is the one entitled to the life, then flogging is given precedence, and he is delayed, then amputated. If the deferrer is the one entitled to a limb, then one cannot hasten to killing, for therein lies the loss of the limb. Thus the one entitled to the life must be patient. This leads to the one entitled to the limb continuing indefinitely, and killing being repelled. And it leads to the one entitled to the life being empowered over the killing, and it is said to the owner of the limb: "Hasten if you wish; otherwise your right is lost." If this were adopted, it would be sound, but if he hastened and killed without permission, he would fall in place [validly], and the owner of the limb would revert to blood-money (diyah).

As for when the converging penalties are divine penalties—like the penalty for drinking, the flogging for fornication, the amputation for theft, and killing—then the beginning is with the lightest, which is the order of entitlement, then he is delayed until healing, so that killing is not lost through death by the spreading [of the wound]. If nothing remains but killing, there is no delay.

If instead of the flogging for fornication there were the flogging for slander, then the flogging for drinking is lighter than it, but is the human right given precedence? Two opinions:

One: The beginning is with drinking, because it is lighter.

Second: One begins with the penalty for slander, because it is a human right.

Likewise the disagreement if instead of the penalty for slander there were retaliatory amputation for a human being.

If he fornicated while a virgin, then fornicated while previously married (thayyib), then flogging and stoning converge. The apparent [view] is that stoning suffices, and flogging is subsumed within it. There is an opinion that he is flogged then stoned, because there is no interpenetration (tadākhul) with differing [penalties].

chapters.title_en: The Seventh Offense: Drinking Wine (Shurb al-Khamr)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الجناية السابعة شرب الخمر

والنظر في الموجب والواجب
أما الموجب فنقول يجب الجلد على كل ملتزم شرب ما أسكر جنسه مختارا من غير
ضرورة وعذر
أما قولنا ملتزم احترزنا به عن الحربي والمجنون والصبي فلا حد عليهم
وقولنا أسكر جنسه إشارة إلى أن ما أسكر كثيره فقليله وإن لم يسكر يوجب
الحد ككثيره وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يجب الحد بقليل الخمر وإن لم يسكر
وسائر  الأشربة لا يحد فيها إلا في القدر المسكر
وقولنا مختارا احترزنا به عن المكره فإنه يباح له الشرب لدفع ضرر الإكراه
فلا يحد بخلاف الزنا فإن فيه خلافا ولا خلاف أن الزنا لا يباح بالإكراه
وقولنا من غير ضرورة أردنا به أن من غص بلقمة ولم يجد غير الخمر فله أن
يسيغها بها وكذلك إذا خاف الهلاك من العطش وأما التداوي بالخمر في علاج
الأمراض فلا يجوز لنهي رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن ذلك وقوله
إن الله تعالى لم يجعل شفاءكم فيما حرم عليكم ولأن الشفاء به مظنون بخلاف
دفع العطش وإساغة اللقمة
ولكن يجوز التداوي بالأعيان النجسة كلحم السرطان والحية والمعجون الذي
فيه الخمر لأن تحريم الخمر المسكر مغلظ وتركه مقصود لا يقاومه ظن الشفاء
وأما الزجر عن تناول النجاسات مع أن مصير الأطعمة إلى النجاسة فهو من
قبيل المروءات المستحسنة فيجوز أن تزول بعذر المرض وقد قال القاضي لا يحد
الشارب إن قصد التداوي بها فكأنه جعل ذلك شبهة في الإسقاط ولم يصرح أحد
بجواز التداوي بها
وقولنا من غير عذر احترزنا به عن التداوي إذ الظاهر أنه لا حد وإن عصى
وعن حدث العهد بالإسلام إذا لم يعلم التحريم وكذا الغالط إذا ظنه شرابا آخر
قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه لو سكر مثل هذا الرجل لم يلزمه قضاء الصلوات لأنه
كالمغمى عليه وقال لو شرب الحنفي النبيذ حددته ونص أن الذمي لا يحد وإن رضي
بحكمنا وسببه أن الحنفي في قبضة الإمام والحاجة قد تمس إلى زجره بخلاف
الذمي الذي لم يلتزم حكمنا ومن أصحابنا من
قال لا يحد في المسألتين ومنهم من قال يحد في المسألتين
ثم الموجب بقيوده يجب أن يظهر للقاضي بشهادة رجلين أو إقرار صحيح ولا
يعول على النكهة والرائحة فلعله غلط أو أكره
ولو قال مطلقا شربت المسكر أو قال الشاهد شرب مسكرا أو شرب شرابا شربه
غيره فسكر كفى ذلك ولو تقدر احتمال الإكراه مع ظاهر الإضافة

### | الطرف الثاني  في الواجب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ل-د (j-l-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Striking with a whip; the act of flogging as a prescribed punishment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal corporal punishment (ḥadd) ordained for specific transgressions, distinct from discretionary chastisement (taʿzīr).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal physical striking; metaphorically denotes the enforcement of divine limits.
- Root: س-ك-ر (s-k-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Intoxication; the state of being veiled from sound reason.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The intoxicating substance itself; the legal criterion for prohibition is the intoxicating quality of the genus.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the effect of wine; metaphorical for any substance that clouds the intellect.
- Root: أ-ك-ر-ه (ʾ-k-r-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Compulsion; forcing someone against their will.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal duress (ikrāh) that negates culpability when it threatens life or limb.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal coercion; distinguished from necessity (ḍarūrah) which arises from circumstance, not another's force.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Restriction (al-Taqyīd bi-al-Sharṭ) — The repeated qualifiers ("every committed person," "choosing," "without necessity or excuse") function as restrictive conditions (ḥurūf al-sharṭ) that progressively narrow the scope of the legal obligation (wujūb), each clause operating as a new syntactic boundary for the ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: The seventh offense is the drinking of wine. The examination concerns both the cause (al-mūjib) and the obligation (al-wājib).

As for the cause, I say: Flogging is obligatory upon every committed person (multazim) who drinks that whose genus intoxicates, doing so voluntarily, without necessity or excuse.

By my saying "committed person," I exclude the harbī (non-Muslim at war), the insane, and the minor — for no prescribed punishment (ḥadd) applies to them. By my saying "that whose genus intoxicates," I indicate that whatever intoxicates in large quantity, its small quantity — even if it does not intoxicate — incurs the ḥadd just as its large quantity does. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) held that the ḥadd is incurred by a small amount of wine even if it does not intoxicate, but for all other beverages, punishment applies only at the intoxicating quantity.

By my saying "voluntarily," I exclude the one compelled (mukrah), for he is permitted to drink to repel the harm of compulsion, and thus no ḥadd is imposed upon him — unlike fornication (zinā), where there is disagreement, though there is no disagreement that fornication is not permitted under compulsion.

By my saying "without necessity," I intend the case of one who chokes on a morsel and finds nothing but wine — he may swallow it with it. Likewise, one who fears death from thirst. As for medicinal treatment with wine for curing diseases, it is not permissible, due to the Prophet's (peace be upon him) prohibition of that and his saying: {«Indeed God has not made your cure in what He has forbidden to you»}, and because healing through it is merely conjectural (maẓnūn), unlike the repelling of thirst or the swallowing of a morsel.

However, medicinal treatment with impure substances (al-aʿyān al-najisah) is permissible — such as crab flesh, snake, or an electuary containing wine — because the prohibition of intoxicating wine is intensified, and its abandonment is an intended objective that conjectural healing does not counterbalance. As for the deterrence from consuming impurities, given that foods ultimately become impurity, it belongs to the category of commendable manliness (murūʾāt) that may be waived due to the excuse of illness. Al-Qāḍī said: The drinker is not flogged if he intended medicinal treatment thereby — as if he made that a doubt (shubhah) for dropping the punishment — though no one has explicitly declared the permissibility of medicinal treatment with it.

By my saying "without excuse," I exclude medicinal treatment, for the apparent ruling is that no ḥadd applies, even if he disobeys. Also excluded is the recent convert to Islam who does not know the prohibition, and likewise the one mistaken who thought it was another beverage. Al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him) said: If such a man became intoxicated, he would not be required to make up the prayers, for he is like one who has lost consciousness. He also said: If a Ḥanafī drank nabīdh (date-wine), I would flog him. And he explicitly stated that a dhimmī is not flogged even if he consents to our jurisdiction. The reason is that the Ḥanafī is under the Imam's authority, and the need may arise to deter him — unlike the dhimmī who has not committed himself to our ruling. Among our companions, some said: No ḥadd in either case; and some said: Ḥadd in both cases.

Then the cause, with its restrictions, must be established before the judge by the testimony of two men or a valid confession (iqrār ṣaḥīḥ). One does not rely on breath odor or smell, for perhaps he was mistaken or compelled. If one said absolutely: "I drank an intoxicant," or a witness said: "He drank an intoxicant," or "He drank a beverage that intoxicated him," that suffices — even if the possibility of compulsion remains alongside the apparent attribution.

### | The Second Aspect: Concerning the Obligation

chapters.title_en: On the Quantity and Manner of the Fixed Punishment, and the Chapter on Discretionary Punishment (Taʿzīr), and the Book of Obligations of Compensations
chapters.arabic_text:
والنظر في قدره وكيفيته
أما القدر فأربعون جلدة وأصله ما روي أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أتي
بشارب فقال
اضربوه بالنعال فضربوه بالنعال وأطراف الثياب وحثوا عليه التراب ثم قال
بكتوه أو عيروه ونحوه ثم قال أرسلوه فلما كان في زمان أبي بكر رضي الله عنه
أحضر الذين شاهدوا ذلك فعدلوه بأربعين جلدة فكان يجلد أربعين وكذلك عمر رضي
الله عنه في صدر خلافته حتى تتايع الناس بشرب الخمر واستحقروا ذلك فشاور
الصحابة فقال علي رضي الله عنه من شرب سكر ومن سكر هذى ومن هذى افترى فأرى
عليه حد المفترين فكان عمر رضي الله عنه يجلد ثمانين وعثمان رضي الله عنه
يجلد ثمانين ثم عاد
علي رضي الله عنه إلى أربعين وروي عنه أنه عليه السلام أمر حتى جلد
الشارب أربعين وروي أنه قال إن شرب فاجلده فإن عاد فاجلدوه فإن عاد فاقتلوه
ولا خلاف أن القتل منسوخ في الشرب
ثم اختلف الأصحاب في شيئين
أحدهما أنه هل يكفي الضرب بالنعال وأطراف الثياب والحديث يدل على جوازه
ومن منع قال ذلك لا ينضبط فقد كفينا مئونة التعديل فيتبع
الثاني أن الإمام لو رأى أن يجلد ثمانين هل له ذلك فمنهم من منع لرجوع
علي رضي الله عنه ومنهم من جوز
أما الكيفية فالنظر في السوط ورفع اليد والضرب والزمان
أما السوط فليكن وسطا ويقوم مقامه الخشبة الزائدة على القضيب الناقصة من
العصا ولا ينبغي أن يكون في غاية الرطوبة ولا في غاية اليبس
وأما رفع اليد فلا يرفعه فوق الرأس فيعظم الألم ولا يكتفي بالرفع اليسير
فلا يؤلم بل يراعي التوسط
وأما الضرب فيفرقه على جميع بدنه ويتقي المقاتل كالقرط والأخدع وثغرة
النحر والفرج ويتقي الوجه ففيه نهي في البهائم فكيف في الآدمي ولا يتقي
الرأس عندنا خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله لقول أبي بكر رضي الله
عنه للجلاد اضرب الرأس فإن الشيطان في الرأس
ولا تشد اليدان من المجلود بل يترك حتى يتقي إن شاء  بيديه
ولا يتل للجبين بل يضرب وهو قائم
وتضرب المرأة وهي جالسة ويلف عليها ثيابها لكيلا تنكشف
وأما الزمان فلا بد من موالاة الضرب فلو فرق مائة سوط على مائة يوم لم
يجز ولو ضرب خمسين في يوم وخمسين في يوم آخر قال إنه جائز والضبط فيه عسير
فالوجه أن يقال إذا انمحى أثر الألم الأول لم يجز وإن كان باقيا جاز
هذا هو القول في الجناية الموجبة للحدود ولا بد من الاختتام بباب في
التعزير
- صلى الله عليه وسلم - باب في التعزير - صلى الله عليه وسلم -
والنظر في الموجب والمستوفي والقدر وأصل الوجوب
أما الموجب فكل جناية سوى هذه السبعة مما يعصي العبد بها ربه فيستوجب بها
التعزير سواء كان على حق الله تعالى أو على حق الآدمي إذ حق الآدمي أيضا لا
يخلو عن حق الله تعالى
وأما المستوفي فهو الإمام وليس ذلك للآحاد إلا الأب والسيد والزوج أما
الأب فلا يعزر البالغ والصغير لا يعصى لكن للأب الضرب تأديبا وحملا على
التعلم وردا عن سوء الأدب وللمعلم أيضا ذلك بإذن الأب وكل ذلك جائز بشرط
سلامة العاقبة فإن أفضى إلى الهلاك وجب الضمان على العاقلة ويكن شبه عمد
ويتبين أنهم جاوزوا حد الشرع إلا ما يظهر كونه عمدا محضا ففيه القصاص
وأما السيد فالصحيح أن له تعزير عبده في حق الله تعالى وأما في حق نفسه
فجائز بلاخلاف
وأما الزوج فلا يعزر زوجته إلا على النشوز على الترتيب الوارد في القرآن
العظيم فإن كانت لا تنزجر بالضرب اليسير بل بضرب مخوف فلا يعزر أصلا لأن
المبرح مهلك والخفيف غير مفيد
أما أصل الموجب فقد قال العلماء ما يتمحض لحق الله تعالى فالاجتهاد فيه
إلى الإمام فإن رأى الصلاح في سحب ذيل العفو والتغافل عنه في بعض المواضع
فعل وإن رأى الاقتصار على الزجر بمجرد الكلام فعل إذ المصلحة تختلف باختلاف
الأشخاص والأحوال وكم تجاوز رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن أقوام أساءوا
آدابهم
أما المتعلق بحق  الآدمي فلا يجوز إهمال أصله مع طلب المستحق لكن هل يجوز
للإمام ترك الضرب والاقتصار على الزجر بالكلام إن رأى ذلك فيه وجهان

والنظر في موجب الضمان ومحله
أما الموجب فالصادر عن الإمام إما تعزير وإما حد أو استصلاح
أما التعزير  فمهما سرى وجب الضمان وتبين خروجه عن المشروع إذ المشروع ما

وأما الحدود فهي مقدرة فيما عدا الشرب فإذا اقتصر فمات قلنا الحق قتله
أما إذا مال عن المشروع فلا يخلو إما أن يكون في وقت أو قدر أو جنس

أما الجنس فشارب الخمر إذا ضرب بالنعال وأطراف الثياب قريبا من أربعين

فإن أوجبنا فالصحيح إيجاب كل الضمان وفيه وجه أنه يوزع على التفاوت بين

والثاني أنه يجب النصف نظرا إلى الحق والباطل إذ ربما أثر آلام السياط لا
