chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-م-ن (Ḍ-M-N)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "inclusion" and "encompassing"; from it derives liability (ḍamān) as that which encompasses the obligation of compensation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, ḍamān signifies the transfer of liability for loss or damage onto the responsible party, a concept rooted in the Quranic principle of personal responsibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for financial liability; metaphorically (majāz) for penal responsibility (damān al-jināyāt).
- Root: ذ-ب-ح (Dh-B-Ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "slaughter" or "ritual throat-cutting"; the root also denotes the act of splitting or cleaving.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Islamic law, it signifies the ritual slaughter (tadhkiyah) that renders an animal lawful (ḥalāl) for consumption, a condition for the validity of sacrifice (uḍḥiyah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the physical act of cutting the throat; metaphorical for the complete severance of life's passage.
- Root: ج-ر-ح (J-R-Ḥ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "wounding" or "inflicting a bodily injury"; also used for earning or acquiring (kasb).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, it denotes a wound that breaks the skin or flesh, and by extension, the act of causing harm that incurs liability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical wounds; metaphorical for any act of aggression or transgression against another's property or person.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Condition and Consequence (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jazā') — The syntactic structure of conditional sentences (e.g., "If he preceded... then...") is used to establish legal causality and temporal sequence in liability.
chapters.translation:
I say: The hunted animal has various states [regarding liability].

**The First State: Sequential Wounding in the Kill**
If two hunters shoot at game and one arrow hits, and one of the two [hunters] is one who causes a mortal wound (muzmin) while the other is one who causes a fatal, immediate wound (jāriḥ), then the game belongs to the one who caused the mortal wound. If the fatal wound [of the second] preceded [the mortal wound], then there is no liability upon the one who inflicted the fatal wound. But if the fatal wound followed [the mortal wound], then he has wounded the property of another, and upon him is the compensation for the deficiency (arsh al-nuqsān) if he did not finish it off (yudhaffif). If he did finish it off, and the game had stable life (ḥayāh mustaqirrah) and the finishing blow did not strike the throat (madbāḥ), then it is [considered] carrion (maytah), and upon him is its full value, because he slaughtered an animal that was within [another's] lawful control (maqdūr ʿalayh) in a place other than the throat. If he struck the throat, it becomes lawful. Here there is a subtle point of consideration (naẓar), for if someone shot a sheep and struck its throat, there is a possibility regarding its lawfulness, especially if he did not intend the throat but it was struck accidentally. Perhaps the more apparent (aẓhar) ruling is its lawfulness.

However, if the second wound was not a finishing blow and fell upon a place other than the slaughtering place, and the game was left until it died from both wounds, then regarding the obligatory amount of liability upon the second [hunter], there is a consideration (naẓar) that is built upon a foundational issue. This is: if someone wounds a slave or an animal worth ten [dirhams] with a wound whose compensation (arsh) is one dinar, and then another wounds it after him with a wound whose compensation is also one dinar, and it dies from both wounds, then there are five opinions (awjuh) regarding what is obligatory upon them, and no opinion is free from difficulty.

**The First Opinion:** It is obligatory upon the first to pay five, because he is a partner in a slave whose value at the time of his injury was ten, and upon the second four and a half, because he is a partner in a slave whose value at the time of his wounding was nine. This is definitively false (bāṭil qaṭʿan), because it entails a loss of half a dinar to the owner, since the slave's value was ten and it was lost due to their combined injuries.

**The Second Opinion:** It is obligatory upon each one to pay five. This is also false, because equating the second with the first is impossible, since at the time of the second's injury the value was nine. How then could he be liable for more than four and a half?

**The Third Opinion** — and this is the choice of al-Qaffāl — is that upon the first is five, by virtue of his being a partner, and also upon him is half a dinar, which is half the compensation of his injury, because from him resulted half of the killing. Thus, only half of the compensation is subsumed under his act, and the other half remains. Upon the second is five and a half dinars: half a dinar being half the compensation of his wound, and four and a half being half the value of the slave at the time of his injury. He said: "There is nothing in this except an increase over the ten, and that is not improbable, for if someone cut off the hands of a slave and another killed him, what is obligatory upon them would be more than the value." This is corrupt (fāsid), because of the increase it entails, and because the compensation (arsh) is not considered at all when the injury spreads (sarāyah) to cause death, whether the wound was with a partner or not.

**The Fourth Opinion:** Abū al-Ṭayyib ibn Salmah said: What al-Qaffāl mentioned is suitable for us to make it a basis for division, such that it does not lead to an increase. So the parts are expanded into units, making the total twenty-one parts. The ten is then distributed over them. Thus, upon the first is eleven parts out of twenty-one parts of ten, and upon the second is ten parts out of twenty-one parts of ten. This does not lead to an increase. But this is corrupt, because it is built upon distinguishing the compensation (arsh) and considering it alongside the spread of the injury (sarāyat al-jināyah).

**The Fifth Opinion** — and this is the choice of the Imām [al-Shāfiʿī] and the author of al-Taqrīb — is that the second is not liable for more than four and a half. As for the first, upon him is five and a half to complete the value, because he was the cause of the loss (tafaswut) had it not been for the second. What cannot be established upon the second remains upon him. This also is not free from impossibility, but it is closer [to correctness]. As for the increase over ten, or the decrease from it, or the equating between the two partners, these are all manifestly false.

The issue remains the same if one of the two wounds was inflicted by the master [of the slave]. All the opinions apply, but what corresponds to the master's injury is nullified (hādir), and the rest is obligatory.

**Returning to the Hunting Issue:** Among them are those who said [the owner] is like the master and the stranger [in liability]. And among them are those who definitively held that everything is obligatory upon the second, because the owner's act upon the game is not corruption (ifsād) but rather a cause of lawfulness (sabab ḥill). It only becomes corruption due to the second's injury. As for the master's act, it is corruption. The correct view is a third opinion: if the owner was able to hasten the slaughter but did not do so until it died from both wounds, then his act is corruption, and he is like the master. If he was not able [to hasten], then his act is excused (mukhallan), and upon the second is the full value of the game that was mortally wounded (muzmin).

If the game was not mortally wounded and was worth ten, but as a mortally-wounded animal it is worth nine, the companions (aṣḥāb) said: nine is obligatory. The author of al-Taqrīb added: If it were slaughtered, it would be worth eight, so eight is obligatory upon him. However, the dirham that decreased due to slaughter should consider the owner's partnership therein, for if the owner's act is not considered in the corruption, he is still a partner in the slaughter. This is a good emendation (istidrāk ḥasan).

**The Second State: Simultaneous Wounding**
If they both hit [the game] simultaneously, then the game is between them if they are equal in finishing off (tadhfīf) and mortally wounding (īzmān), or in the absence thereof. If one of them, had he been alone, would have caused a mortal wound, and the second would not have, then al-Ṣaydalānī said: The game belongs to the one who causes the mortal wound, and there is no liability upon the second, because his wound did not lag behind the [first's] acquisition of ownership.

If one of them inflicted a finishing blow and the other a mortal wound, it is as if both had inflicted finishing blows or both had inflicted mortal wounds — it belongs to both of them, for each one has an independent cause (ʿillah) for acquisition.

If it is possible that the mortal wounding was caused by both of them or by one of them, and if it was by one of them but it is not known which one, then the game is between them. However, one of them must seek the other's permission to make it lawful (yastaḥill), distancing themselves from ambiguity (shubhah).

If we know that one of them inflicted a finishing blow and we are doubtful about the other, al-Qaffāl said: It is between them. He added: In such a case, retaliation (qiṣāṣ) is obligatory upon the two wounders. This is far-fetched regarding retaliation given the ambiguity. The truth here is that half belongs to the one who inflicted the finishing blow with certainty, and the other half is suspended between them. If we despair of clarification, the correct view is to divide the other half, such that the one who inflicted the finishing blow gains three-quarters of the game.

**The Third State:** We know the sequence of the two wounds, and one is a mortal wound and the other a finishing blow, but we do not know whether the mortal wound preceded, thus making it unlawful (ḥarām) by the finishing blow that followed it, or the opposite. There are two paths (ṭarīqān): One is the definitive ruling of unlawfulness (taḥrīm), giving precedence to prohibition (taghlīb al-ḥaẓr). The second is to apply the two opinions (qaulayn), as in the issue of growth (al-inmā'). The more correct is the first. As for the issue of growth, we have not witnessed the cause of lawfulness, and the other [cause] is merely conjectural. But here, it is not so.

**The Fourth State:** The two wounds occurred in sequence, and the mortal wounding resulted from both of them. Al-Ṣaydalānī said: The game is between them, and this is the analogical ruling (qiyās). Another said: It belongs to the second, since the mortal wounding occurred immediately after his act, while the first was hastening toward a resting place. On this basis, if the first returned and wounded a second time, then his first wound is nullified (hādir) and his second wound is subject to liability (muḍamman). The game has been corrupted by all three wounds. Regarding the obligatory amount, there are two paths: One is that the full value of the game is obligatory, along with the first wound, for it is nullified, and the second wound, for it is from the owner. Among them are those who said: This is like the case of someone who wounds an apostate slave, who then embraces Islam, and his master wounds him, then the first returns and wounds him a second time. Regarding what is obligatory upon him, there are two opinions: One is a third of the blood-money (diyah), distributed according to the state of nullification and inviolability (ʿiṣmah), then the share of inviolability is divided between the two wounds. We have mentioned this in the chapter on retaliation (qiṣāṣ). Likewise here. And God Almighty knows best.

---

**= The Book of Sacrificial Animals (Kitāb al-Ḍaḥāyā) =**

Sacrificial animals (ḍaḥāyā) are among the rites (shaʿā'ir) and confirmed Sunnahs (sunan mu'akkadah). The sacrifice consists of slaughtering one of the cattle (naʿam) on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Naḥr) and the Days of Tashrīq. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: «عظموا ضحاياكم فإنها على الصراط مطاياكم» ("Glorify your sacrifices, for they are your mounts upon the Path [al-Ṣirāṭ]").

Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: It is obligatory upon every resident who owns the nisāb [threshold of wealth]. In our school, it is not obligatory except by a vow (nadhr) or by saying: "I have made this sheep a sacrifice (uḍḥiyah)." If he bought it with the intention of sacrifice, it does not become obligatory upon him by mere intention alone.

Then, whoever resolves to sacrifice, it is recommended (yustaḥabb) for him not to shave [his head] or trim [his nails] during the first ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah — not as a resemblance to the Pilgrimage (ḥajj), for he is not prohibited from perfume — but rather for the most complete fulfillment of its parts, for he, peace be upon him, said: «أكبر ضحيتك يعتق الله بكل جزء منها جزءا منك من النار» ("Magnify your sacrifice, for God will free a part of you from the Fire for every part of it").

The consideration is in the pillars (arkān) of the sacrifice and its rulings. The pillars are four: the sacrificial animal (al-dhabīḥ), the slaughterer (al-dhābiḥ), the act of slaughter (al-dhabḥ), and the time (al-waqt).

**The First Pillar: The Sacrificial Animal**
The consideration is in its species (jins), its qualities (ṣifah), and its amount (qadr).

**As for the species:** Only cattle (naʿam) suffice, which are camels, cattle, and sheep/goats.

**As for the age (sinn):** It is the jadhaʿah from sheep — which is one that has completed one year and entered its second — and the thaniyyah from goats and cattle — which is one that has entered its third year — and the thanī from camels — which is one in its sixth year. These ages are the point of maturity for these animals, for they do not carry [young] or mount before them. The report (khabar) has come regarding this. The male and female are equal by consensus (ittifāq).

**As for the qualities:** The deficient animal does not suffice. Deficiency (nuqṣān) is divided into deficiency of quality and deficiency of a part.

**As for deficiency of quality:** He, peace be upon him, said: «أربع لا تجزىء العوراء البين عورها والعرجاء البين عرجها والمريضة البين مرضها والعجفاء التي لا تنقي» ("Four do not suffice: the one-eyed whose blindness is evident, the lame whose lameness is evident, the sick whose sickness is evident, and the emaciated which has no marrow"). He also forbade the thawlā' — which is the mad one that circles in the pasture and does not graze. It is necessary to explain these qualities.

**As for sickness (marad):** If it has not yet led to emaciation but is in its beginning, the apparent ruling is prohibition (manʿ) due to the hadith. There is an opinion that it only has effect if emaciation appears with it. As for the mangy (jarbā'), if its mange is abundant and the meat is corrupted, it is prohibited. Its initial stages have no effect.

**As for lameness (ʿaraj):** Its lowest degree is what prevents frequent movement in the pasture. What is less than that does not prevent. If its leg breaks and it is laid down for sacrifice, due to its agitation, there are two opinions: One is that it does not suffice, due to the hadith. The second is that it suffices, because what results from the preliminaries of slaughter is not considered.

**As for one-eyedness (ʿawar):** It does not vitiate as long as it can see with both eyes, even if there is blackness over it. If vision is lost by gouging (faq'), it does not suffice. If the eyeball remains, the apparent ruling is prohibition due to the hadith. Abū al-Ṭayyib ibn Salmah said: It has no effect on emaciation nor on the apparent form. He would also be bound by [the ruling for] total blindness, except that blindness affects emaciation quickly, unlike one-eyedness.

**As for the emaciated (ʿajfā'):** It is the one that the fastidious reject in times of cheap prices and due to the poor quality of its meat. It was said: This has no effect.

**As for the thawlā' (mad):** It does not suffice, because it affects emaciation quickly, and also as an act of devotion (taʿabbud).

**As for the female and the stud male,** even if its births and mounts are numerous, it suffices, unless emaciation becomes excessive due to that. The fact that its meat is disliked does not prevent [validity].

**As for the kharqā' (torn-eared), the sharqā' (split-eared), the muqābalah (with a hanging front piece), and the mudābarah (with a hanging back piece):** ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, forbade them and said: "We were commanded to examine the eye and the ear," i.e., to scrutinize them and seek their soundness. The kharqā' is the one with a torn ear; the sharqā' is the one with a split ear; the muqābalah is the one from which a piece of its ear was cut and hangs from the front of its ear; and the mudābarah is the one that hangs from the back of its ear. Regarding all of this, there are two paths: One is that there are two opinions — one permitting by analogy (qiyās), and one prohibiting due to the prohibition of ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him. Among them are those who said: All of that suffices, except if most of the ear is cut, or the amount that is visible from a distance — that is a deficiency in a limb intended for eating, and the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, forbade the maṣlūmah (with a severed ear) and the musta'ṣalah (with a completely removed ear). If a small amount of the ear is cut, there are two opinions. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God be pleased with him, estimated it as a third of the ear, and Abū Yūsuf, may God have mercy on him, estimated it as half. For al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, there is a difference in his texts (naṣṣ) regarding the one with no ear: It was said that if it is small in creation, it is permissible, and if it is born without ears (sakkā'), then no.

**As for deficiency of parts (nuqṣān al-ajzā'),** it has several forms:

**The First:** What a wolf cuts from the thigh of a sheep — this prevents validity, because it is an original limb. If its tail (aliyah) is pulled out, there are two opinions. If it had no tail in its creation, there are two opinions, ranked, with the one favoring validity being more appropriate. The basis for validity is that goats have no tail and yet suffice. But it may be answered that the abundance of its fat substitutes for it.

**The Second:** The small-uddered [animal] suffices. Regarding the one with a cut udder, there are two paths: One is that it is like the tail [in preventing validity]. The other is that it suffices, because the udder is not among the desired choice parts; it is like castration, which does not prevent validity definitively.

**The Third:** Deficiency of the horn and its breakage has no effect. Likewise, the scattering of teeth, since it has no effect on the meat, and no hadith has been reported regarding it, unlike the ear. It was said: If all the teeth scatter, it does not suffice; if some scatter, it suffices. This is far-fetched.

**As for the amount (qadr):** A sheep suffices only for one person. If two people share in one sheep, it is not valid. Yes, the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said when he sacrificed: "This is on behalf of Muhammad and the nation of Muhammad." This is sharing in the reward (thawāb), which is permissible. If two people share in two sheep as undivided shares (mushāʿ), there are two opinions. A camel (badanah) suffices for seven, and likewise a cow. If seven sheep were obligatory upon him for different reasons (asbāb), a camel or cow would suffice for him, except if it is from the compensation for hunting (jazā' al-ṣayd), where similarity of form is considered; thus, a camel does not substitute for seven gazelles.

It is not a condition for sharing in a camel or cow that they be from one household, contrary to Mālik, may God have mercy on him. Nor that all of them be seeking nearness [to God], contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him. Rather, whoever seeks meat may share, if we say division (qismah) is separation (ifrāz). If we say it is a sale (bayʿ), there are two opinions, with the opinion of permissibility being based on need.

This is the explanation of the obligatory. **As for the recommended (istihbāb):** Sheep are more beloved than goats; seven sheep are more beloved than a cow or camel; a camel is more beloved than a cow; the white is more beloved than the black. In the report: «لدم عفراء أحب عند الله من دم سوداوين» ("The blood of a white [animal] is more beloved to God than the blood of two black ones"). Al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, said: The female is more beloved than the male. It was said: He meant this regarding the compensation for hunting (jazā' al-ṣayd), where value is sought, and the female's value is higher. Otherwise, the male's meat is more delicious, so it is more appropriate. It was also said: He meant the female that has not given birth, for its meat is more delicious than the male's. In general, it is recommended to select a good sacrifice and fatten it, as a glorification of the rites (shaʿā'ir), for they are from the piety of hearts, and {لن ينال الله لحومها ولا دماؤها ولكن يناله التقوى منكم} ("Neither their flesh nor their blood reaches God, but piety from you reaches Him") [Q. 22:37].

**The Second Pillar: The Time**
The sacrifice is not valid except on the Day of Sacrifice and the Days of Tashrīq. The blood [offerings] for expiations (dimā' al-jabrānāt) in the Pilgrimage are not restricted to a specific time. Regarding vowed blood offerings of the Pilgrimage, there is a difference of opinion.

Then the consideration is in the beginning of the time and its end. **Its beginning:** After the passage from the Day of Sacrifice, following sunrise, of the amount of time needed for the dislike of prayer to cease, plus two rakʿahs and two sermons. There is an opinion that two rakʿahs are considered in which one recites Qāf and "Iqtarabat" [Sūrahs 50 and 54], and two lengthy sermons, as the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, did. Another opinion holds that two light rakʿahs and two light sermons suffice, but it does not reach the point of being content with the minimum that suffices. The Marāwizah said: Lightness is considered in the sermon; the difference is only regarding the lightness of the two rakʿahs, due to his saying, peace be upon him: «قصر الخطبة وطول الصلاة مئنة عن فقه الرجل» ("Shortening the sermon and lengthening the prayer is a sign of a man's understanding"). It was said: The sermon is not considered at all, for it is not a pillar.

**As for its end:** It is the sunset of the last day of Tashrīq. The sacrifice is valid during these days, by night and by day. Mālik, may God have mercy on him, said: It is not valid at night. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: It is not valid on the third day of Tashrīq.

Then, whoever misses it, there is no meaning to making it up (qaḍā'), for he must wait until the next festival (ʿīd), and at that time it falls as an obligation for the [current] time.

**The Third Pillar: The Slaughterer**
Whoever's slaughter is lawful, his direct performance of the sacrifice is valid. But sacrifice is not conceivable from a slave, a umm walad (mother of a child), or a mudabbar (whose freedom is deferred), for they have no ownership, on the correct view. It is not valid from a mukātib (slave under contract of manumission) without his master's permission. With his permission, there are two opinions. If he deputizes a Christian (kitābī) to slaughter the sacrifice without the intention [of sacrifice], it is permissible, and the deputy must intend, just as if he deputized him to pay the zakāh, it is permissible if he intends. It is recommended that he perform the slaughter himself. If he is unable, he should witness his sacrifice and intend at the time of slaughter. If he deputizes a Muslim to slaughter and intend, it is permissible.

**The Fourth Pillar: The Manner of Slaughter**
The consideration is in the obligations (wājibāt), the Sunnahs (sunān), and what is specific to sacrifices.

**As for the obligations:** It is the finishing off (tadhfīf) by completely cutting the windpipe (ḥulqūm) and the esophagus (marī') with an instrument that is not a bone from an animal with stable life.

**As for the cutting:** By this we guard against the case of snapping a bird's head with a pellet, for that does not make it lawful.

**As for the windpipe and esophagus:** They are apparent, and by cutting them the two jugular veins (wadajān) are severed. But if he goes to the trouble and does not cut them, it is permissible. Mālik, may God have mercy on him, said: It is not permissible. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: These are four [passages], and cutting three of them suffices, while cutting two does not suffice.

**As for completeness (tamām):** By this we guard against the case where a small piece of skin remains on the throat, and the animal reaches the movement of the slaughtered (ḥarakat al-madhbūḥ), and then he cuts it afterward — it is unlawful (ḥarām). If he cuts from the back of the neck and hastens until it does not reach the movement of the slaughtered before cutting the throat, it is permissible.

**As for the finishing off (tadhfīf):** We mean by it that if he begins the slaughter and another begins pulling out its entrails, it is carrion. Likewise, any wound that accompanies the slaughter and affects the finishing off [prevents validity].

**As for the bone:** It is prohibited, such that game wounded by an arrow whose head is made of bone is unlawful.

**As for stable life (ḥayāh mustaqirrah):** It is indispensable. If we extract a sheep from water or from beneath a collapsed wall and it has the movement of the slaughtered, we do not permit its slaughter. If we doubt whether its life was stable or not, the correct view is to give precedence to prohibition (taghlīb al-taḥrīm). If it is strongly presumed by signs of stable life, it is lawful. Al-Muzanī, may God have mercy on him, said: Among its signs is that it moves after slaughter. It was said: That blood flows out. These are not definitive signs, for the entrails of a slaughtered animal may come out while it still moves afterward. However, a combination of these signs with circumstantial evidence (qarā'in al-aḥwāl) that cannot be described may produce a strong presumption (ẓann ghālib) that is acted upon, while the original principle is the continuation of life.

**As for the Sunnahs:** It is recommended to sharpen the blade (shafrah), to press down upon it with force, to hasten the cut, to face the sacrificial animal toward the qiblah as is customary, and to pronounce the tasmiyah (saying "In the name of God"). There is no harm in saying "In the name of God, and Muhammad is the Messenger of God" with the nominative case (bi-al-rafʿ). It is not permissible to say "In the name of Muhammad," nor to say "In the name of God and Muhammad is the Messenger of God," for that is associating partners (tashrīk). It is recommended to slaughter the camel at the upper chest (labbah), for if slaughtered at the neck, its suffering is prolonged due to its long neck. Then the nahr (slaughter at the chest) at the labbah is by cutting the windpipe and esophagus as well. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: Deliberately omitting the tasmiyah is unlawful (muḥarram).

**As for what is specific to the sacrifice:** One should say: "O God, from You and to You, so accept from me." The intention (niyyah) of sacrifice is indispensable at the time of slaughter, unless he had already designated the sheep for sacrifice beforehand. In that case, the school holds that that intention suffices him.

The explicit wording of designation (taʿyīn) is to say: "I have made this a sacrifice." If he says: "For God upon me is a sacrifice," then says: "I have designated this sheep for my vow," there are two opinions regarding designation. If he says: "For God upon me is to sacrifice with this sheep," there are two opinions, ranked, with the one favoring designation being more appropriate. Likewise, the difference applies to its analogue in manumission (ʿitq), with the slave being more deserving of designation because he has a right in it. The basis of our saying that it is not designated is that the right is established in the liability (dhimmah) and does not transfer from it to the specific object except by performance (adā'). If he says: "I have made these dirhams a charity (ṣadaqah)," there are two opinions regarding designation. If he had a vow and said: "I have made this for my vow," his designation is nullified due to the weakness of the wording, and the purpose of designation is [to specify the object]. If he says: "For God upon me is to give charity to this person," this is more deserving of designation than designating dirhams; indeed, it is close to manumission.

Then, if the sheep is designated, it becomes specific to the time of sacrifice. If he says: "For God upon me is to sacrifice a sheep," there are two opinions regarding the designation of the time, based on whether it resembles the expiation blood (dimā' al-jabrānāt) because it is in the liability. The correct view is that mentioning the description of sacrifice necessitates the designation of the time. If we say the time is not designated, then if he says: "I have made this sheep for the sake of my vow," there are two opinions regarding time-restriction (ta'qīt). The analogical ruling is that it is not binding, because he designated it for the sake of what he had committed to.

### | القسم الثاني من الكتاب النظر في أحكام الضحايا

وهي ثلاثة
الأول التلف فإذا قال جعلت هذه الشاة ضحية فماتت فلا شيء عليه إلا أن
يكون قد عينها عن نذر سابق وقلنا إنها تتعين ففي وجه أنه كان تعيينه بشرط
الوفاء فإن ماتت فعليه الإبدال
وأما إذا أتلفها أجنبي فعليه قيمتها يشتري بها ضحية فإن لم يف فليس عليه
التكميل
أما المالك إذا أتلف ففي وجوب التكميل وجهان من حيث إنه كالملتزم للضحية
والشقص لا يجزىء فلا بد من الإتمام وإن زادت القيمة فيشتري بها كريمة وإن
تعذر فوجهان أحدهما أنه يشتري به شقص للضرورة وكذلك إذا كان ما غرمه
الأجنبي أقل من ضحية والثاني أنه يصرف مصرف الضحايا حتى لو اشترى منه خاتما
يقتنيه ولا يبيعه جاز
هذا في الإهلاك أما إذا ذبحه أجنبي في وقت الضحية فحيث لا تشترط النية
اكتفاء بالتعيين السابق فقد وقع الموقع وإن قلنا لا بد من النية فقد فاتت
القربة وفي لحمه وجهان أحدهما أنه يعود إلى مالكها وتنقل عنه الضحية وعلى
الذابح أرش نقصان الذبح والثاني أنه يصرف مصرف الضحية وإن لم تكن ضحية
وإنما تفوت القربة دون الإستحقاق ولا يجب على الأجنبي إلا نقصان الذبح وحيث
قلنا يقع الموقع ففي لزوم أرش الذبح قولان أحدهما نعم لعدوانه والثاني لا
لتأدي الواجب به
هذا إذا لم يفرق الأجنبي اللحم فإن فرق فاللحم مسترد ممن أخذه لأن
التعيين إلى المضحي فإن تعذر فعلى الذابح قيمة اللحم وأرش الذبح جميعا
وإنما سقط أرش الذبح على قول  إذا تأدت القربة به والآن فقد فات بتفريقه
ثم في كيفية تغريم كل من ذبح شاة غيره وأكل لحمه وأتلف قولان
أحدهما أنه تجب قيمتها حية والثاني أنه يجب أرش نقصان الذبح وقيمة اللحم
لأنه ذبح ملكه وأكل ملكه وهذا قد يقتضي زيادة قيمة
الحكم الثاني التعيب ومهما لم يلزمه شيء بالتلف فلا يلزمه بالتعيب ولكن
لو كان العيب بحيث يمنع الإجزاء في الضحية فهل ينفك عن الضحية والشاة معينة
فوجهان أحدهما نعم كالتلف والثاني لا بل تجري مجرى الضحايا
ولو قال ابتداء لشاة معيبة جعلت هذه أضحية وجب صرفها إلى مصرف الضحايا
على الصحيح إذ لا محمل لكلامه إلا هذا ولو قال لظبية جعلت هذه أضحية لغا
قوله ولو قال لفصيل فوجهان وكأن السن دائر بين العيب والجنس
ولو قال لله علي أضحية ثم عين معيبة للنذر لا تبرأ بها ذمته وهل يلزمه
تفرقة لحمها فيه وجهان ولو زال العيب ففي براءة الذمة بها وجهان وأما إذا
كان تعيب المعينة بفعله فعليه التضحية بشاة صحيحة بدلا عنها وفي انفكاك
المعينة الوجهان المذكوران

### | فروع

الأول طرآن العيب والإنكسار حالة قطع الحلقوم لا يؤثر وقبله وبعد الإضجاع
للشاة وجهان ذكرناهما في انكسار الرجل وإنما يليق التردد بما يكون من
اضطراب الذبح أما إذا
كان بسبب آخر فيظهر تأثيره وقد قال القفال ما يطرأ على الهدي المسوق إلى
الحرم بعد بلوغ الحرم لا يؤثر لأنه قد بلغ محله وخالفه الأصحاب لأن من
اشترى في الحرم الهدي فتعيب قبل الذبح أثر ذلك فيه فأي أثر للسوق
الثاني لو قال لله علي أن أضحي بعرجاء ففيما يلزمه ثلاثة أوجه أحدها أنه
تلزمه صحيحة والثاني أنه لا شيء عليه كنذر الظبية والثالث أنه لا يلزمه إلا
العرجاء
الثالث ضلال الشاة كتلفها وإنما نريد أنها لو وجدت بعد أن أوجبنا عليه
البدل وقد ضحاه ففي انفكاك الضالة قولان أحدهما أنه ينفك إذ لا وجه للتضعيف
وقد ضحى البدل والثاني أنه يضحي أيضا لأنه الأصل
وإن لم  يكن قد ضحى البدل اقتصر على الأصل إلا أن يكون قد عين البدل بلفظه
فأي الشاتين تذبح فيه أربعة أوجه أحدها البدل والثاني الأصل والثالث كلاهما
والرابع يتخير أيهما شاء
الحكم الثالث الأكل وهو جائز من المتطوع به وهل يجوز أكل الجميع أم لا
تتأدى
السنة إلا بتصدق شيء منه فيه وجهان أحدهما أنه يجوز لأن المقصود إراقة
الدم والضيافة وقد يستوي في ضيافة الله تعالى المالك وغيره والثاني أنه
يتصدق بما ينطلق عليه الإسم لقوله تعالى {فكلوا منها وأطعموا البائس
الفقير}
ولا يكفي في هذا القدر الإطعام بل لا بد من التمليك للفقير ولا يكفي
تمليك الغني للفقير أن يملك من شاء من غني وفقير ويجوز إطعام الأغنياء من
الضحية وعلى كل قول فالتصدق بالكل أحسن وكان من شعار الصالحين تناول لقمة
من كبد الضحية أو غيرها وقال علي رضي الله عنه في خطبته بالبصرة أما إن
أميركم رضي من دنياكم بطمريه لا يأكل اللحم في السنة إلا الفلذة من كبد
أضحيته
ثم كمال الشعار يتأدى بالتصدق بالنصف لقوله تعالى {فكلوا منها وأطعموا}
إلى وقيل تتأدى بالثلث لقوله عليه السلام كلوا منها وادخروا واتجروا أي
اطلبوا الأجر بالتصدق
وما يجوز أكله فلا يجوز إتلافه ولا أن يملك الأغنياء ليتصرفوا فيها
بالبيع لأن الضيافة مقصودة

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ض-ح-و (ḍ-ḥ-w)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to appear in the height of the sun" (ḍaḥā); a sacrificial animal (ḍaḥiyyah) is so named because it is slaughtered at the time of forenoon (al-ḍuḥā) when the sun has risen high.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The term denotes the ritual offering (qurbah) of an animal specifically for drawing near to God, distinct from ordinary slaughter (dhabḥ) or charity (ṣadaqah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage refers to the animal itself; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to the act of slaughtering at that time, and to the legal obligation (wujūb) attached to a vow (nadhr).
- Root: ت-ل-ف (t-l-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning is "to perish, be destroyed, or become null"; in legal usage it denotes the complete destruction of the object such that it can no longer serve its purpose.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, talaf contrasts with baqāʾ (permanence); in jurisprudence it triggers liability (ḍamān) for replacement or value.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical destruction; metaphorical for legal nullification of the designation (taʿyīn).
- Root: ع-ي-ب (ʿ-y-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is a defect, blemish, or imperfection that diminishes the object's value or fitness.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In ritual law, a ʿayb is a disqualifying flaw that prevents the animal from fulfilling the sacrificial requirement (ijzāʾ).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical defects; metaphorical for legal disqualification of the designation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditionality (al-Sharṭ) — The particle "fa" (ف) in conditional sentences marks the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), indicating that the ruling follows directly upon the condition, as in "fa-mātat" (then it died) and "fa-in lam yufarriq" (then if he did not distribute).
chapters.translation:
I say: The second division of the book concerns the examination of the rulings on sacrificial animals (al-ḍaḥāyā). They are three.

**The First Ruling: Destruction (al-talaf).** If a man says, "I have designated this sheep as a sacrificial animal (ḍaḥiyyah)," and it then dies, nothing is incumbent upon him — unless he had designated it for a prior vow (nadhr) and we hold that it becomes specifically bound (taʿyīn). In that case, there is a view (wajh) that his designation was conditional upon fulfillment; if it dies, then replacement (ibdāl) is incumbent upon him.

As for when a stranger (ajnabī) destroys it, he is liable for its value (qīmah), with which a sacrificial animal is to be purchased. If that value is insufficient [for a complete animal], he is not obligated to complete the remainder.

As for the owner himself, if he destroys it, there are two views (wajhān) concerning whether completion (takmīl) is obligatory — based on the fact that he is like one who has committed himself to the sacrifice, and a share (shiqṣ) does not suffice, so completion is necessary. If the value has increased, he purchases a noble (karīmah) animal with it. If that is not possible, there are two views: one, that he purchases a share with it due to necessity — and likewise if what the stranger was made to pay is less than a [full] sacrificial animal; the second, that he spends it in the channels of sacrificial distribution (maṣrif al-ḍaḥāyā), such that even if he bought a ring with it for his own use and did not sell it, that would be permissible.

This concerns destruction. As for when a stranger slaughters it during the time of sacrifice — where intention (niyyah) is not required, being satisfied with the prior designation — then it has fallen in its proper place (waqaʿa al-mawqiʿ). But if we say intention is indispensable, then the act of devotion (qurbah) has been lost. Regarding its meat, there are two views: one, that it reverts to its owner, the sacrifice is transferred away from him, and upon the slaughterer is the compensation for the diminution caused by the slaughter (arsh naqṣān al-dhabḥ); the second, that it is spent in the channels of sacrifice — even though it is not [valid as] a sacrifice — and only the devotion is lost, not the entitlement (istiḥqāq); and nothing is incumbent upon the stranger except the diminution of slaughter. Where we say it has fallen in its proper place, there are two positions (qawlān) on whether the compensation for slaughter is binding: one, yes, due to his transgression (ʿudwān); the second, no, because the obligation was discharged through him.

This applies when the stranger has not distributed the meat. If he did distribute it, then the meat is reclaimed (mustaradd) from whoever took it, because the designation belongs to the one offering the sacrifice (al-muḍḥī). If that is not possible, then upon the slaughterer is the value of the meat and the compensation for slaughter together. The compensation for slaughter is only dropped on the view [that it is not owed] when the devotion was discharged through it; now it has been lost by his distribution.

Then, concerning the manner of liability for one who slaughters another's sheep, eats its meat, and destroys it, there are two positions: one, that its value while alive is obligatory; the second, that the compensation for the diminution of slaughter plus the value of the meat is obligatory — because he slaughtered his [the owner's] property and ate his property, and this may entail an increase in value.

**The Second Ruling: Defect (al-taʿyīb).** Whenever nothing is incumbent upon him due to destruction, nothing is incumbent upon him due to defect. But if the defect is such that it prevents the animal from sufficing (manʿ al-ijzāʾ) in the sacrifice, then does it become released from the sacrifice while the sheep remains specifically designated? There are two views: one, yes, like destruction; the second, no — rather, it follows the course of sacrificial animals.

If he says at the outset regarding a defective sheep, "I have made this a sacrificial animal," then it must be spent in the channels of sacrifice, according to the sound (al-ṣaḥīḥ) view — for his speech has no other import. If he says regarding a gazelle (ẓabiyyah), "I have made this a sacrificial animal," his statement is void (laghā). If he says regarding a young weaned camel (faṣīl), there are two views — as if age (al-sinn) hovers between defect and genus.

If he says, "Upon God is a sacrifice for me" (lillāhi ʿalayya uḍḥiyyah), then designates a defective animal for the vow, his obligation (dhimmah) is not discharged by it. Whether he is obligated to distribute its meat — there are two views. If the defect is removed, then concerning the discharge of the obligation by it, there are two views.

As for when the specifically designated animal becomes defective by his own act, then he must offer a sound sheep in its place; and concerning the release of the designated animal, the two views already mentioned apply.

### Branches (Furūʿ)

**First Branch:** The occurrence of a defect or breakage (al-inqisār) at the moment of cutting the windpipe (ḥalqūm) has no effect. Before that, and after laying the sheep down (al-iḍjāʿ), there are two views — which we have mentioned regarding the breaking of a man's leg. Such hesitation is only fitting for what arises from the disturbance of the slaughter itself. As for when it is due to another cause, its effect is manifest. Al-Qaffāl has said: What occurs to a sacrificial animal (hadī) being driven to the Sanctuary (al-ḥaram) after reaching the Sanctuary has no effect, because it has reached its place (maḥall). But the companions (al-aṣḥāb) disagreed with him — because one who buys a hadī within the Sanctuary and it becomes defective before slaughter, that defect has effect upon it; so what effect could the driving have?

**Second Branch:** If he says, "Upon God is an obligation that I sacrifice a lame (ʿarjāʾ) animal," then concerning what is incumbent upon him there are three views (awjuh): one, that a sound animal is incumbent; the second, that nothing is incumbent upon him — like the vow of a gazelle; the third, that nothing is incumbent except the lame one itself.

**Third Branch:** The straying (ḍalāl) of the sheep is like its destruction. What we mean is that if it is found after we have made replacement obligatory upon him and he has already sacrificed [the replacement], then concerning the release of the strayed animal there are two positions: one, that it is released — for there is no justification for doubling, and he has already sacrificed the replacement; the second, that he sacrifices it as well, because it is the original (al-aṣl). If he has not yet sacrificed the replacement, he confines himself to the original — unless he had designated the replacement by his explicit utterance (bi-lafẓihi). In that case, concerning which of the two sheep is to be slaughtered, there are four views: one, the replacement; the second, the original; the third, both; the fourth, he chooses whichever he wishes.

**The Third Ruling: Eating (al-akl).** It is permissible for the one who volunteers the sacrifice (al-mutatawwiʿ). As for whether eating all of it is permissible, or whether the Sunnah is not discharged except by giving some of it in charity — there are two views: one, that it is permissible, because the purpose is the shedding of blood (irāqat al-dam) and hospitality (al-ḍiyāfah), and in the hospitality of God most high, the owner and others are equal; the second, that he gives in charity that to which the name [of meat] applies, due to His saying, exalted: {فكلوا منها وأطعموا البائس الفقير} ("So eat of it and feed the destitute, the poor"). For this amount, mere feeding (iṭʿām) is not sufficient; rather, transfer of ownership (tamlīk) to the poor person is indispensable. Nor is it sufficient for a rich man to transfer ownership to a poor man so that the latter may give to whomever he wishes, rich or poor. It is permissible to feed the rich from the sacrificial animal. On every view, giving all of it in charity is more excellent (aḥsan). It was among the marks of the righteous (shiʿār al-ṣāliḥīn) to partake of a morsel from the liver (kabad) of the sacrificial animal or other parts. ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said in his sermon at Baṣrah: "Indeed, your commander is content from his worldly life with two worn garments, and does not eat meat in the year except the slice (falhadhah) from the liver of his sacrificial animal."

Then the perfection of the mark (kamāl al-shiʿār) is discharged by giving half in charity, due to His saying, exalted: {فكلوا منها وأطعموا} ("So eat of it and feed"). And it was said that it is discharged by a third, due to his saying, peace be upon him: "Eat of it, store it, and trade" — i.e., seek reward by giving in charity.

What is permissible to eat is not permissible to destroy, nor to give ownership to the rich so that they may dispose of it by sale — because hospitality is the intended purpose.

### Branch

chapters.title_en: The Intermediate Compendium in Jurisprudence — Section 535: Sacrificial Animals, 'Aqīqah, and the Law of Foods
chapters.arabic_text: لو أكل الكل على قولنا يمتنع ذلك ففيما يلزمه من الغرم وجهان أحدهما قدر ما ينطلق عليه الإسم وهو الصحيح والثاني النصف أو الثلث هذا كله في المتطوع به أما المنذورة ففي جواز الأكل منها وجهان أحدهما أنها كالمتطوعة والثاني أنه لا يجوز الأكل منها كدماء الجبرانات فإن قيل ما حكم جلد الضحية قلنا الصحيح أنه لا يباع لكن ينتفع به في البيت أو يتصدق به وحكى صاحب التقريب قولا بعيدا أنه يباع ويصرف ثمنه مصرف الضحايا وهو ضعيف نعم قال لو تصدق بالجلد بدلا عن اللحم إذا قلنا إن عليه التصدق لم يجزه ذلك وهو أحسن فرع ولد الضحية المعينة لها حكم الأم والصحيح أن التصدق بجزء من الأم يسلط على أكل جميع الولد كما يسلط على أكل جميع اللبن فإنه في حكم جزء وفيه وجه أنه لا بد من التصدق بشيء من الولد لأنه حيوان مستقل فرع آخر لو اشترى شاة ثم قال جعلتها ضحية ثم وجد عيبا امتنع ردها وله طلب الأرش كما بعد العتق وقال العراقيون يسلك بالأرش مسلك الضحايا وهو بعيد لأنه لم يعين إلا المعيبة وظنه السلامة لا ينبغي أن يلزمه أرش السلامة واختتام الكتاب بباب العقيقة وهي سنة عندنا واجبة عند داود بدعة عند أبي حنيفة رحمه الله وحكمها حكم الضحية في الأكل والتصدق والسلامة من العيوب لكنها عبارة عن شاة تذبح في سابع ولادة المولودة لا تتأقت بيوم النحر بل يدخل وقتها بالولادة كما يدخل وقت دماء الجبرانات بأسبابها وفي الخبر يعق عن الغلام بشاتين وعن الجارية بشاة ثم تكفي الشاة عن الغلام وفاقا نعم تختص العقيقة بأنه لا يكسر منها عظام الشاة فقد ورد فيها خبر ولعله تفاؤل بسلامة أعضاء المولد فتنضج وتفصل المفاصل وتفريق اللحم أولى من دعاء الناس إليه وقال الصيدلاني يجوز التصدق بالمرقة وهذا إن أراد به أن يكفي عن التصدق بمقدار من اللحم إذا قلنا لا بد منه ففيه نظر قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه وعادة العرب تلطيخ رأس الصبي بدم العقيقة وهو مكروه نعم يستحب أن يسمى الصبي في السابع ويحلق شعره ويتصدق بزنته ذهبا أو فضة = كتاب الأطعمة = وفيه بابان - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الأول في حالة الاختيار - صلى الله عليه وسلم - والحيوان والجمادات أكثر من أن تحصى لكن الأصل فيه الإباحة لقوله تعالى {قل لا أجد فيما أوحي إلي محرما} الآية فجميع ما يمكن أكله مباح إلا ما يستثنيه عشرة أصول الأول ما حرم بنص الكتاب كالخمر والخنزير والدم والمنخنقة والموقوذة وكذلك ما حرم بالنص عليه في السنة كالحمر الأهلية الأصل الثاني ما في معنى المنصوص عليه كالنبيذ الذي هو في معنى الخمر المنصوص عليه الأصل الثالث كل ذي ناب من السباع وكل ذي مخلب من الطير إذ نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عنه ويحرم الفيل لأنه ذو ناب مكاوح وكذا الدب ومن ذوات المخلب البازي والشاهين والصقر والعقاب والنسر وجميع جوارح الطير والثعلب والضبع والضب حلال عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله لورود أحاديث فيها وترددوا في ثلاثة حيوانات أحدها ابن آوى قطع المراوزة بتحريمه وذكر العراقيون خلافا والثاني ابن عرس تردد العراقيون فيه لتردد شبهه بين الثعلب والكلب والثالث الهرة الوحشية فيها تردد لترددها بين الهرة الأهلية والأرنب وربما يظن أن أصلها إنسية فتوحشت في سني القحط ولا يحل السنور لما روي أنه عليه السلام قال الهرة سبع ولأنه يصطاد بالناب وتأكل الجيف فأشبه الأسد ويحل أكل الخيل لما روى جابر قال ذبحنا يوم خبير الخيل والبغال والحمير فنهانا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن البغال والحمير ولم ينهنا عن الخيل وأما الدلدل قطع الشيخ أبو محمد بتحريمه وأما السمور والسنجاب وما يشبههما فالأظهر إلحاقهما بالثعلب وقيل هو كابن عرس الأصل الرابع ما أمر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بقتله في الحل والحرم وهي الفواسق الخمس الغراب والحدأة والفأر والحية وفي معنى المنصوص كل سبع ضار كالذئب والأسد والفهد والنمر والكلب العقور وما ليس عقورا فهو محرم لأنه ذو ناب يعدو به كالهر الأصل الخامص ما نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن قتله فإن ذلك يدل على التحريم إذ لو حل لحل ذبحه كما أن الأمر بالقتل يدل على التحريم إذ لو حل لأمر بالذبح لا بالقتل وقد نهى عن قتل الهدهد والخطاف والنحل والصرد ولنملة وقد نص رضي الله عنه على أن المحرم يفدي الهدهد بالجزاء ولا يفدي عنده إلا حلال واختلف الأصحاب في حله لذلك وأما اللقلق فالأظهر أنه يحل لأنه كالكركي وأنواع الحمامات حلال وهن كل ذات طوق وأنواع العصافير وإن اختلفت ألوانها حلال وهي كثيرة والفاختة واليمام والقمري من الحمامات والزرزور والصعوة من العصافير وإنما ينظر فيه إلى تقارب الأشكال لا إلى الألوان وأما الغربان فإنها من الفواسق مع الحدأ والبغاثة في معنى الحدأة وهي ذات مخلب ضعيف ولكنها تقرب من الحدأة والغراب الأبقع هو المقطوع بتحريمه أما الأسود الكبير فألحقه المراوزة بالأبقع وتردد فيه العراقيون وأما غراب الزرع وفيه غبرة ليست كثيرة ومنه المحمرة المناقير والأرجل ففيها تردد وأما طير الماء فمباح كله وكذا في جميع حيواناته إلا ماله نظير في البر محرم ففيه قولان ذكرناهما الأصل السادس كل ما استخبثته العرب فهو حرام قال الله تعالى {يسألونك ماذا أحل لهم قل أحل لكم الطيبات} وإنما خرج على ما هو طيب عندهم فالحشرات كلها مستخبثة وكانت العرب تستخبث الباز والشاهين والنسر والصقر كما تستخبث العظاية واللحكاء والخنافس واللحكاء دويبة تغوص في الرمل مثل الأصبع والعظاية مثل الوزغ والضفدع والسلحفاة من المستخبثات وكذا السرطان ولا يحل من الحشرات شيء إلا الضبة وفي أم حبين تردد وفي الآثار أنها تفدي بحلان وكأنه ولد الضب وذوات الأجنحة من الحشرات كالذباب فإنها مستخبثة وإنما يحل منها الجراد وفي الصرارة تردد لتردده بين الخنافس والجراد وهو بالخنفساء أشبه وفي القنفذ تردد لما روي أن ابن عمر رضي الله عنه أفتى بحله واستدل بقوله تعالى {قل لا أجد فيما أوحي إلي محرما على طاعم يطعمه} الآية فقام شيخ وقال أشهد أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إنها من الخبائث فقال ابن عمر رضي الله عنه إن قال فهو كما قال فسبب التردد في قول الشيخ وعدالته ثم لا وجه فيما أشكل خبثه إلا الرجوع إلى العرب فإنها وإن كانت أمة كبيرة فطباعها متقاربة الأصل السابع ما أخبر الله تعالى عنه ورسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه كان حراما على الأمم السالفة فهو حرام على أحد القولين وإن لم يكن في شرعنا ذكر تحريمه علينا ولا نرجع في ذلك إلى قول أهل الكتاب إذ لا يوثق بقولهم والقول الثاني أن الإعتماد على عموم آية الإباحة أولى من اعتماد استصحاب حال الشرائع السابقة الأصل الثامن ما حكم بحله إذا خالطته نجاسة فهو حرام كالزيت النجس وبيعه حرام وإن ماتت فأرة في سمن ذائب أو غيره فكذلك وإن كان جامدا قور وطرح ما حوله والباقي طاهر كذلك أمر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم والجلالة وهي الحيوان الذي يتعاطى العذرة والأشياء القذرة حلال إن لم يظهر النتن في لحمه فإن ظهر النتن فهو نجس وحرام وإن تكلف بالعلف إزالة رائحتها حلت وإن تكلف بالطبخ فلا وجلدها يطهر بالدباغ والذكاة إن لم تبق الرائحة في الجلد وذكر العراقيون أن الجلالة تكره ولا تحرم أما الزرع فحلال وإن كثر الزبل فيه فإنه لا يظهر الرائحة فيه الأصل التاسع ما حكم بحله فميتته ومنخنقته حرام وبالجملة كل ما لم يذبح ذبحا شرعيا كما وصفناه ولا يستثنى عن ميتته إلا الجراد وحيوانات البحر لقوله عليه السلام الحل ميتته وعن المنخنفة إلا الجنين الذي يوجد ميتا في بطن المذبوح فإنه حلال ورد فيه الخبر الأصل العاشر ما اكتسب بمخامرة نجاسة ككسب الحجام فقد نهى رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عنه فروجع مرارا فقال أطعمه عبدك وناضحك وهذه كراهية وليس بتحريم وقد علل بأن ذلك مكتسب من حرفة خسيسة جائزة ومخامرة نجاسة وعندي أن التعليل بذلك يوجب إلحاق أجرة الكناس والدباغ به ولم يذهب إليه أحد ولعل السبب فيه أن الحجامة والفصد جرح مفسد للبنية وهو حرام في الأصل وإنما يباح بتوهم المنفعة وذلك مشكوك فيه ويطرد هذا في أجرة من يقطع يدا متآكلة لاستبقاء النفس ولا يطرد في أجرة الجلاد الذي يقطع في السرقة وقد أوردت هذه العلة في كتاب الحلال والحرام من كتب إحياء علوم الدين وقد ذكر الشافعي رضي الله عنه في آخر هذا الكتاب الودك النجس والإنتفاع به وبيعه وقد ذكرناه في البيع - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في حالة الإضطرار - صلى الله عليه وسلم - قال الله تعالى {إلا ما اضطررتم إليه} فيباح تناول الحرام للضرورة والنظر في حد الضرورة وجنس المستباح وقدره أما الضرورة فنعني بها أن يغلب على ظنه الهلاك إن لم يأكل وكذلك إن خاف مرضا يخاف منه الموت لجنسه لا لطوله ون كان يخاف طول المرض وعسر العلاج ففيه قولان ولا شك في أنه لا يشترط أن يصبر حتى يشرف على الموت فإن الأكل بعد ذلك لا ينعشه والظن كالعلم هاهنا كما في المكره على الإتلاف ثم إذا جاز الأكل وجب أن لا يجوز السعي في الهلاك وفيه وجه أنه يجوز الإستسلام تورعا عن الحرام في الصيال وهو ضعيف لأن ذلك إيثار مهجة على مهجة وأما تحريم الميتة فلا ينتهي إلى هذه الرتبة نعم يتجه ذلك ما دام المضطر غير قاطع بأن ترك الأكل يضره بل ظانا ظنا قريبا من الشك فإن ذلك يدرك بنوع اجتهاد النظر الثاني في قدر المستباح وفي جواز الشبع بعد تحقق الضرورة نصوص مضطربة حاصلها ثلاثة أقوال أحدها أنه يجب الإقتصار على سد الرمق إذ رجع إلى حالة لا يجوز ابتداء الأكل على مثله وزال الخوف والإضطرار والثاني أنه يشبع إذ نبيح للمضطر الأكل مطلقا وتحققت الضرورة أولا والثالث أنه إن كان في بلد اقتصر على سد الرمق وإن كان في بادية وخاف إن لم يشبع أن لا يتقوى على المشي ويهلك فيشبع وهذا يستدعي مزيد تفصيل فإن من علم في البادية أنه لو لم يشبع ولم يتزود لا يقوى ولا يجد غيره ويهلك فيجب القطع بأنه يشبع ويتزود ولا يفارق الإبتداء الدوام في هذا ون كان في بلد ولو سد الرمق ثم توقع طعاما مباحا قبل عود الضرورة وجب القطع بالإقتصار إذ الضرورة تبيح إزالة الخوف دون الشبع فإن كان لا يتوقع طعاما ولكن يمكنه الرجوع إلى الميتة إن لم يجد مباحا فهاهنا يتجه التردد إذ لو شبع لم يعاود على قرب وإن اقتصر عاد على القرب فيحتمل أن يقال هذا وإن لم يجز في الإبتداء ولكن بعد أن وقع في الأكل فالأكل دفعة أقرب من المعاودة كل ساعة والأقيس ما اختاره المزني رحمه الله وهو سد الرمق إلحاقا للدوام بالإبتداء النظر الثالث في جنس المستباح ويباح الخمر لتسكين العطش لأنه مستيقن كإساغة اللقمة بخلاف التداوي ويباح كل حرام إلا ما فيه سفك دم معصوم وليس له قتل ذمي أو معاهد ولا قتل عبده وولده ويجوز له قتل المرتد والزاني المحصن وإن كان ذلك منوطا بالإمام تقاوم هذا القدر وكذلك قتل الحربية جائز على الظاهر وإباحة قتل ولد الحربي وهو صغير فيه نظر والأظهر جوازه لأنه لا يقاوم تحريمه روح مسلم
chapters.anchors:
- Root: غ-ر-م (gh-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be burdened with a debt or liability; to incur a financial obligation as recompense.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, the imposition of a compensatory payment (ghurm) for a right that has been violated or consumed.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is the obligation itself; metaphorically extends to any liability incurred by one's action.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-Sharṭ) — The phrase "لو أكل" (if he ate) introduces a hypothetical protasis whose apodosis ("ففيما يلزمه") presents the legal consequence, requiring careful parsing of the dual-face (wajhān) construction.
chapters.translation:
I say: If he eats the whole [sacrificial animal] — and on our view this is prohibited — then regarding what he owes as compensation, there are two faces (wajhān): one is the amount to which the name [of the obligation] applies, and this is the sound (ṣaḥīḥ) position; the second is half or a third. All of this pertains to the voluntary offering (al-mutaṭawwaʿ bihi). As for the vowed offering (al-mandhūrah), there are two faces regarding the permissibility of eating from it: one is that it is like the voluntary offering; the second is that eating from it is not permissible, like the blood of expiatory compensations (dimāʾ al-jabrānāt).

If it is said: What is the ruling on the skin of the sacrificial animal? I say: The sound position is that it is not sold, but one may benefit from it in the home or give it as charity. The author of al-Taqrīb related a remote opinion (qawl baʿīd) that it is sold and its price is disbursed in the channels of sacrificial offerings — and this is weak (ḍaʿīf). Yes, he said: If one gives the skin in charity in place of the meat — when we hold that charity is obligatory upon him — this is not permissible, and this is the better (aḥsan) view.

A Branch (Farʿ):
The offspring of a designated sacrificial animal (al-muʿayyanah) has the same ruling as its mother. The sound position is that the obligation to give charity from a part of the mother authorizes eating all of the offspring, just as it authorizes drinking all of the milk, for the offspring is in the ruling of a part [of the mother]. There is a face that one must give charity from the offspring itself, because it is an independent animal.

Another Branch:
If a man buys a sheep, then says, "I have made it a sacrificial offering," and then finds a defect in it, he is prevented from returning it, and he may seek the compensation for the defect (al-arsh), just as after manumission [of a slave]. The Iraqis said: The compensation for the defect is to be channeled in the ways of sacrificial offerings — and this is remote, because he only designated the defective animal, and his assumption of soundness should not oblige him to [pay] the compensation for soundness.

The book concludes with the chapter on the ʿAqīqah (sacrifice for a newborn). It is a Sunnah (sunna) in our school, obligatory (wājibah) according to Dāwūd, and an innovation (bidʿah) according to Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him.

Its ruling is the same as the sacrificial offering regarding eating, giving in charity, and freedom from defects. But it refers to a sheep slaughtered on the seventh day after the birth of the newborn. It is not restricted to the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-naḥr); rather, its time enters with the birth, just as the time for the blood of expiatory compensations enters with their causes.

In the report (al-khabar): "For a boy, two sheep are sacrificed; for a girl, one sheep." Then one sheep suffices for a boy, in agreement [among us]. Yes, the ʿAqīqah is distinguished by the fact that the bones of the sheep are not broken — a report has been transmitted regarding this, perhaps as an auspicious omen (tafāʾul) for the soundness of the newborn's limbs. Thus, it is cooked and the joints are separated. Distributing the meat [raw] is preferable to inviting people to it. Al-Ṣaydalānī said: It is permissible to give the broth in charity. If he means by this that it suffices for the charity of an amount of meat — when we hold that it is obligatory — then there is consideration (naẓar) in this.

Al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — said: The custom of the Arabs was to smear the head of the boy with the blood of the ʿAqīqah, and this is disliked (makrūh). Yes, it is recommended (mustaḥabb) that the boy be named on the seventh day, his head shaved, and charity given of the weight of his hair in gold or silver.

= The Book of Foods (Kitāb al-Aṭʿimah) =
It contains two chapters.

Chapter One: On the State of Choice (ḥāl al-ikhtiyār).

Animals and inanimate things are too numerous to be enumerated, but the principle regarding them is permissibility (ibāḥah), due to His saying — may God bless him and grant him peace: {Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden"} (Q. 6:145) — the verse. Thus, everything that can be eaten is permissible, except what is excluded by ten principles (uṣūl).

The First Principle: What is forbidden by the text of the Book, such as wine, pork, blood, the strangled, and the beaten to death. Likewise, what is forbidden by the text of the Sunnah, such as domesticated donkeys.

The Second Principle: What is in the meaning of the textually forbidden, such as nabīdh (date-wine) which is in the meaning of the textually forbidden wine.

The Third Principle: Every beast with a fang (dhū nāb) and every bird with a talon (dhū mikhlab), for the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — forbade these. The elephant is forbidden because it has a fighting fang (nāb mukāwiḥ), and likewise the bear. Among those with talons are the falcon (bāzī), the shāhīn (peregrine), the hawk (ṣaqr), the eagle (ʿuqāb), the vulture (nisr), and all birds of prey. The fox and the hyena are permissible according to al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah — may God have mercy on him — due to reports (aḥādīth) transmitted regarding them. They hesitated regarding three animals:

One: The jackal (ibn āwā) — the Marwazīs definitively ruled its prohibition, while the Iraqis mentioned a disagreement.
Two: The weasel (ibn ʿirs) — the Iraqis hesitated regarding it due to the ambiguity of its resemblance between the fox and the dog.
Three: The wild cat (al-hirrah al-waḥshiyyah) — there is hesitation regarding it due to its ambiguity between the domestic cat and the rabbit. Perhaps one might think its origin is domestic and it became wild during the years of drought. The cat (al-sinnawr) is not permissible, because it was reported that he — peace be upon him — said: "The cat is a beast of prey," and because it hunts with its fang and eats carrion, thus resembling the lion.

The horse is permissible to eat, due to what Jābir reported: "We slaughtered on the day of Khaybar horses, mules, and donkeys. The Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — forbade us from the mules and donkeys, but did not forbid us from the horses."

As for the duldul (porcupine), Shaykh Abū Muḥammad definitively ruled its prohibition. As for the sable (sammūr) and squirrel (sinjāb) and what resembles them, the most apparent (aẓhar) view is to attach them to the fox. It was said: It is like the weasel.

The Fourth Principle: What the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — commanded to be killed in the sacred precinct (al-ḥill) and the sanctuary (al-ḥaram) — these are the five corrupters (al-fawāsiq): the crow, the kite, the mouse, and the snake. In the meaning of the textually specified is every harmful beast of prey, such as the wolf, lion, leopard, panther, and the biting dog. What is not biting is forbidden, because it has a fang with which it attacks, like the cat.

The Fifth Principle: What the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — forbade killing. This indicates prohibition, for if it were permissible, its slaughter would be permissible — just as the command to kill indicates prohibition, for if it were permissible, he would have commanded slaughter, not killing. He forbade killing the hoopoe (hudhud), the swallow (khuttāf), the bee (naḥl), and the shrike (ṣurad). He — may God be pleased with him — explicitly stated that the pilgrim in iḥrām compensates for the hoopoe with a penalty (jazāʾ), and he only requires a penalty for what is permissible [to hunt]. The companions (aṣḥāb) differed regarding its permissibility for that reason. As for the stork (laqlaq), the most apparent view is that it is permissible, because it is like the crane (kurkī).

The various types of pigeons are permissible — they are all those with a neck-ring (dhāt ṭawq). The various types of sparrows, despite their differing colors, are permissible — and they are numerous. The ringdove (fākhitah), the turtle-dove (yamām), and the collared dove (qumrī) are among the pigeons. The starling (zarzūr) and the wren (ṣaʿwah) are among the sparrows. Consideration is given to the similarity of forms, not colors.

As for crows, they are among the corrupters along with the kite. The buzzard (bughāthah) is in the meaning of the kite — it has a weak talon but resembles the kite. The piebald crow (al-ghurāb al-abqaʿ) is definitively forbidden. As for the large black one, the Marwazīs attached it to the piebald, while the Iraqis hesitated. As for the field crow (ghurāb al-zarʿ) — in which there is a grayness that is not extensive — and from it the red-beaked and red-legged ones, there is hesitation regarding them.

As for waterfowl, all of it is permissible, and likewise all its animals, except what has a forbidden counterpart on land — regarding which there are two opinions (qawlān) that we have mentioned.

The Sixth Principle: Everything that the Arabs deemed foul (istakhbathathu) is forbidden. God — exalted is He — said: {They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: "Lawful for you are the good things (al-ṭayyibāt)"} (Q. 5:4). This is based on what is good in their estimation. Thus, all insects (ḥasharāt) are deemed foul. The Arabs deemed foul the falcon, shāhīn, vulture, and hawk, just as they deemed foul the lizard (ʿaẓāyah), the sand-swimmer (laḥkāʾ), and the beetles (khanāfis). The laḥkāʾ is a creature that burrows in the sand, about the size of a finger. The ʿaẓāyah is like the gecko (wazaġ). The frog and the turtle are among the foul things, and likewise the crab.

Nothing from the insects is permissible except the ḍabb (spiny-tailed lizard). Regarding um ḥubayn (a type of lizard), there is hesitation. In the traditions (āthār), it is reported that it is compensated with a ḥulān (a young ḍabb) — as if it is the offspring of the ḍabb. Winged insects, like flies, are foul. From them, only the locust (jarād) is permissible. Regarding the cricket (ṣarṣarah), there is hesitation due to its ambiguity between the beetle and the locust — and it resembles the beetle more. Regarding the hedgehog (qunfudh), there is hesitation because it was reported that Ibn ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — gave a legal opinion (fatwā) of its permissibility, adducing His saying — exalted is He: {Say: "I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden for a eater to eat"} (Q. 6:145) — the verse. Then an old man stood up and said: "I bear witness that the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — said that it is among the foul things (al-khabāʾith)." Ibn ʿUmar — may God be pleased with him — said: "If he said it, then it is as he said." Thus, the cause of hesitation is the statement of the old man and his reliability (ʿadālah). Then, there is no recourse for what is ambiguous regarding its foulness except to the Arabs — for even though they are a great nation, their natural dispositions (ṭibāʿ) are similar.

The Seventh Principle: What God — exalted is He — and His Messenger — may God bless him and grant him peace — informed us was forbidden upon previous nations. It is forbidden according to one of the two opinions, even if there is no mention of its prohibition upon us in our Law. We do not rely in this on the statement of the People of the Book, for their statement is not trustworthy. The second opinion is that relying on the general import (ʿumūm) of the verse of permissibility is more appropriate than relying on the continuation of the state of previous laws (istiṣḥāb ḥāl al-sharāʾiʿ al-sābiqah).

The Eighth Principle: What is ruled permissible, but when impurity (najāsah) mixes with it, it becomes forbidden — like impure oil (al-zayt al-najis). Its sale is forbidden. If a mouse dies in melted butter (samn dhāʾib) or other [liquids], then likewise. If it is solid (jāmid), the area around it is cut off and discarded, and the rest is pure — thus the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — commanded.

The jallālah — which is an animal that feeds on dung and filthy things — is permissible if the stench does not appear in its meat. If the stench appears, it is impure and forbidden. If one takes pains with fodder to remove its odor, it becomes permissible. If one takes pains with cooking [to remove it], then no. Its skin is purified by tanning (dibāgh) and proper slaughter (dhakāh) if the odor does not remain in the skin. The Iraqis mentioned that the jallālah is disliked (makrūhah), not forbidden. As for crops (zarʿ), they are permissible even if much manure is in them, for the odor does not appear in them.

The Ninth Principle: What is ruled permissible, its carrion (maytah) and strangled [meat] are forbidden. In short, everything not slaughtered with a legally valid slaughter (dhakāh sharʿiyyah) as we have described [is forbidden]. Nothing is excepted from its carrion except the locust and sea animals, due to his saying — peace be upon him: "Its carrion is lawful" (al-ḥill maytatuhu). From the strangled, nothing is excepted except the fetus found dead in the belly of the slaughtered [mother] — it is permissible, and the report (al-khabar) has been transmitted regarding it.

The Tenth Principle: What is earned through mixing with impurity (mukhāmarah najāsah), like the earnings of the cupper (ḥajjām). The Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — forbade it. He was asked repeatedly, and he said: "Feed it to your slave and your camel." This is a dislike (karāhah), not a prohibition. It has been reasoned that this is because it is earned from a base profession that is permissible, but mixed with impurity.

In my view (ʿindī), this reasoning would necessitate attaching to it the wages of the dung-clearer (kannās) and the tanner (dabbāgh) — and no one has held this. Perhaps the reason is that cupping and phlebotomy are wounds that corrupt the constitution (al-binyah), which is forbidden in origin, and only permitted due to the presumption of benefit — and that is doubtful. This applies consistently to the wages of one who cuts off a gangrenous hand to preserve life, but does not apply to the wages of the executioner (jallād) who cuts [the hand] for theft. I have presented this reasoning in the Book of the Lawful and the Unlawful from the books of Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn. Al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — mentioned at the end of this book the impure fat (al-wadak al-najis), benefiting from it, and selling it — and we have mentioned it in the Book of Sales.

Chapter Two: On the State of Necessity (ḥāl al-iḍṭirār).

God — exalted is He — said: {Except what you are compelled to} (Q. 6:119). Thus, partaking of the forbidden is permitted for necessity. The inquiry concerns the limit of necessity (ḥadd al-ḍarūrah), the genus of what is permitted (jins al-mubāḥ), and its amount (qadruhu).

As for necessity, we mean by it: that it dominates his presumption (ghalaba ʿalā ẓannihi) that he will perish if he does not eat. Likewise, if he fears a disease from which death is feared due to its kind, not due to its prolongation. If he fears the prolongation of the disease and the difficulty of treatment, there are two opinions (qawlān). There is no doubt that it is not required that he wait until he is on the verge of death, for eating after that would not revive him. Presumption (al-ẓann) is like knowledge (al-ʿilm) here, just as in the case of one compelled to destroy [another's property].

Then, when eating becomes permissible, it is not permissible to strive toward destruction. There is a face that surrendering [to death] is permissible, out of scrupulousness (waraʿ) regarding the forbidden in the face of aggression (al-ṣiyāl) — and this is weak, because that is preferring one life over another. The prohibition of carrion does not reach this rank. Yes, this [surrender] is plausible as long as the one in necessity is not certain that abstaining from food will harm him, but rather presuming with a presumption close to doubt — for this is grasped by a kind of ijtihād.

The Second Inquiry: On the amount of what is permitted, and on the permissibility of satiety (al-shabaʿ) after the realization of necessity. The texts (nuṣūṣ) are inconsistent. Their sum is three opinions:
One: It is obligatory to limit oneself to sustaining the breath of life (sadd al-ramaq), for he has returned to a state in which beginning to eat in his like is not permissible, and fear and necessity have ceased.
Two: He may eat his fill, for we permit the one in necessity to eat absolutely, and necessity was realized at the outset.
Three: If he is in a town, he limits himself to sustaining the breath of life; if he is in a desert and fears that if he does not eat his fill he will not have the strength to walk and will perish, then he eats his fill. This requires further detail: For one who knows that in the desert, if he does not eat his fill and does not take provisions, he will not have strength and will find nothing else and will perish — then it is definitive that he eats his fill and takes provisions, and the beginning does not depart from the continuation in this. If he is in a town, and if he sustains the breath of life, then expects permissible food before the return of necessity, it is definitive that he limits himself, for necessity permits the removal of fear, not satiety. If he does not expect food, but can return to carrion if he finds no permissible [food], then hesitation is plausible here: for if he eats his fill, he will not return [to carrion] soon; if he limits himself, he will return soon. It may be said: This, even if not permissible at the beginning, yet after he has fallen into eating, eating at once is closer than returning every hour. The most analogically sound (al-aqyas) is what al-Muzanī — may God have mercy on him — chose: sustaining the breath of life, attaching the continuation to the beginning.

The Third Inquiry: On the genus of what is permitted. Wine is permitted to quench thirst, because it is certain (mustayaqqan), like swallowing a morsel — unlike medication (tadāwī). Every forbidden thing is permitted except what involves the shedding of protected blood (dam maʿṣūm). He may not kill a dhimmī or a covenanted person (muʿāhad), nor kill his own slave or his child. He may kill an apostate (murtadd) and a married adulterer (zānī muḥṣan), even if that is vested in the Imam — this amount is counterbalanced. Likewise, killing a belligerent woman (ḥarbiyyah) is permissible on the apparent view. The permissibility of killing the child of a belligerent — while he is a minor — has consideration (naẓar), and the most apparent view is its permissibility, because it does not counterbalance the prohibition of the soul of a Muslim.
