### | الفصل الأول في التولية
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-د-ل (badala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Exchange, substitution, replacement of one thing for another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theology, pertains to permissibility of substituting vowed offerings, contingent on juristic discretion (ijtihād).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in transactional exchange; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to ritual vows, indicating flexibility of obligation.
- Root: ه-د-ي (hady)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Guidance; also the sacrificial animal sent to the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Quranic term for offering (hady), tied to pilgrimage rites (manāsik) and expiation (dam).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for the animal; metaphorical for the act of sending, emphasizing destination (al-Ḥaram) as constitutive.
- Root: ن-ذ-ر (nadhr)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Vow; making an obligation upon oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A solemn pledge (nadhr) creating legal duty (wujūb) in worship (qurbah).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for verbal commitment; metaphorical extension to any act deemed meritorious, per juristic disagreement.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — Parsing phrases like "if we permit substitution" (in jawwaznā) as protasis, with apodosis governing legal consequence; also "except that it be real estate" (illā an yakūna ʿiqāran) as restrictive exception limiting the general obligation of transport.
chapters.translation:
I say: Now, regarding the sub-rulings (tafrīʿ): If we permit substitution (ibdāl) of the vowed animal, then equivalence in value is not a condition; yet there is a remote opinion (wajh) that it is required. As for the quality (ṣifah) [of the vowed animal], the correct position (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is that it must be specifically a mature camel (al-baʿīr al-thanī) that suffices for the sacrificial offering (uḍḥiyah), by virtue of his saying: "Upon me is an obligation to sacrifice." The Iraqis mentioned an opinion that it descends upon whatever is called a "sacrificial camel" (badanah), even if defective. Indeed, a young weaned camel (faṣīl) does not suffice, for it is not termed a "badanah."

The third expression: If he says, "Upon me is an obligation of a hady (offering)," and we interpret it as the minimal obligatory act of the Law (aqall wājib al-sharʿ), then he owes an animal from the grazing livestock (naʿam), free from defects, and he is obligated to transport it to the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram). There is an opinion that transport is not obligatory, because the blood of confinement (dam al-iḥṣār) and the blood of an animal [offering] suffice outside the Sacred Precinct. If we say it descends upon what is permissible in the Law (jāʾiz al-sharʿ), then anything to which the name "hady" or "gift" (minḥah) applies suffices, even a small coin (dāniq) given in charity wherever it may be. There is an opinion that delivery to the Sacred Precinct is indispensable for the name "hady," but this is remote.

The fourth expression: If he says, "Upon me is an obligation to offer this gazelle (ẓabyah) to Mecca," then delivery is incumbent upon him, and he must give it in charity alive in Mecca, for there is no act of devotion (qurbah) in slaughtering it — just as if he vowed ten cubits of linen cloth (karbās) without sewing it into a shirt. If he vowed a defective camel that does not suffice for the uḍḥiyah, then there are two opinions (wajhān) regarding the obligation of slaughtering it in Mecca, because it is of the same genus as the uḍḥiyah, though not of its requisite quality. If he designated a specific property and said, "Upon me is an obligation to offer it to Mecca," then transport of that very item is incumbent, unless it be real estate (ʿiqār) or a millstone (ḥajar raḥā) that cannot be transported; in that case, he sells it and transports the value. From this it is derived that Mecca is specified (taʿayyun) for charity (ṣadaqah) and prayer (ṣalāh) when designated. As for whether it is specified for fasting (ṣawm), the apparent position is that it is not specified, for no particular merit of Mecca has been established for fasting, unlike prayer and charity.

The fifth expression: If he says, "Upon me is an obligation to cover the Kaʿbah (kiswah) or to perfume it (ṭīb)," then it is incumbent upon him, because covering was a recognized practice (ʿahd) in the first era (al-ʿaṣr al-awwal) and was not denounced. This indicates that even an act not intrinsically a devotional goal (qurbah maqṣūdah) becomes obligatory by vow. It is permissible to cover the Kaʿbah with silk (ḥarīr), for that is forbidden to men to wear upon themselves, not [forbidden] in adornment [of the House]. Regarding undertaking to perfume the other two mosques [of Medina and Jerusalem], there is hesitation (taraddud). And God Most High knows best.

= The Book of the Etiquette of Judgeship (Kitāb Adab al-Qaḍāʾ) =
It contains four chapters (abwāb).

Chapter One: On Appointment (al-tawliyah) and Dismissal (al-ʿazl), containing two sections (faṣlān).

وفيه ست مسائل
الأولى في فضيلة القضاء والقيام بمصالح المسلمين
والإنتصاف للمظلومين من أفضل القربات وهو من فروض الكفايات وهو أفضل من
الجهاد وأهم منه لأن الجهاد لطلب الزيادة والقضاء لحفظ الموجود وقد قال
رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ليوم واحد من إمام عادل أفضل من عبادة ستين
سنة وحد يقام في أرض بحقه أزكى من مطر أربعين خريفا فلأجل فضيلة الولاية
وكونها مهما لنظام الدين والدنيا تجب الإجابة على من دعي إلى الحكم
والمستحب أن يقول إذا دعي سمعا وطاعة
الثانية في جواز طلب القضاء والولايات
وقد ورد فيه التحذير مع ما ذكرناه من الفضل فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم
من ولي القضاء فقد ذبح بغير سكين وقال لعبد الرحمن بن سمرة لا تسأل الإمارة
فإنك إن أعطيتها عن
مسألة وكلت إليها وإن أعطيتها من غير مسألة أعنت عليها وقال عمر رضي الله
عنه ما من أمير ولا وال إلا ويؤتى يوم القيامة مغلولة يداه إلى عنقه أطلقه
عدله أو أوبقه جوره
وإنما هذه التحذيرات لأن هذه الولاية تستخرج من النفس خفايا الخبث حتى
يميل على العدو وينتقم منه وينظر للصديق ويتبع الأغراض وقد يظن بنفسه
التقوى فإذا ولي تغير فنقول للطالب أربعة أحوال
إحداها أن يكون متعينا بأن لا يوجد غيره ممن يصلح فالطب فرض عليه وإن كان
خاملا فعليه أن يشهر نفسه عند الإمام حتى يولى ثم إن كان يخاف على نفسه
الخيانة والميل لم يكن هذا عذارا بل عليه أن يجاهد نفسه ويلازم سمت التقوى
فإن تولى ومال عصى وإن امتنع من القبول خوفا من الميل عصى وهو متردد بين
إحدى معصيتين لا محالة
الثانية أن يكون في الناحية من هو أصلح منه ففي انعقاد إمامة المفضول
خلاف
فإن منعنا ففي انعقاد قضاء المفضول وتوليته خلاف والأصح أنه ينعقد لأن ما
يفوت من مزية الإمامة لا جبر لها ونقصان القاضي يجبره نظر الإمام من ورائه
فإن قلنا لا ينعقد حرم عليه القبول وحرم على الإمام التولية فإن قلنا ينعقد
جاز للمفضول القبول إن ولي بغير مسأله وأولى أن لا يقبل وأما الطلب فمكروه
ولا ينتهي إلى التحريم وقيل إنه يحرم وهذا كله في الواثق بنفسه الذي اختبر
ورعها وتقواها فإن كان معه استشعار خيانة فيحرم الطلب
الثالثة أن يكون في البلد من هو دونه فإن قلنا لا تنعقد ولاية المفضول
التحق بالصورة الأولى وإن قلنا تنعقد جاز القبول بل هو الأولى لتحصيل تلك
المزية للمسلمين وأما الطلب فهو جائز وإن قلد بغير سؤال فهل يلزمه القبول
فيه وجهان ولكن هذا إذا كان واثقا بنفسه فإن كان خائفا فهذا لا يوازيه مزية
الفضيلة فليمتنع
الرابعة أن يكون في الناحية مثله فالقبول جائز وإن ولي بغير سؤال فلا يجب
القبول على الأظهر لأنه غير متعين لكن الأولى القبول لأنه أتاه من غير
مسألة فيعان عليه وأما الطلب فيحتمل أن يكره للخطر ويحتمل أن يستحب للفضيلة
وكل هذا إذا لم يخف على نفسه فإن خاف خوفا ظاهرا فعليه الحذر
وإن كان لا يستشعر ميلا ولكنه لم يجرب نفسه في الولايات فإن كان له حاجة
لطلب رزق وكفاية فلا تطلق له الكراهية بالتوهم مع الحاجة فله الطلب وإن لم
تكن حاجة فيكره له الطلب بمجرد هذا الإستشعار ولا ينتهي إلى التحريم
المسألة الثالثة في صفات القضاة ولا بد أن يكون حرا ذكرا مفتيا بصيرا إذ
لا ولاية للعبد ولا للمرأة وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يجوز تولية المرأة
فيما لها فيه شهادة
وقولنا مفتي أردنا المجتهد الذي تقبل فتواه ويخرج عنه الصبي والفاسق إذ
لا تقبل فتواهما نعم الفاص مفت في حق نفسه حتى لا يجوز له تقليد غيره ولكن
لا يوثق بفتواه ونعني المجتهد المتمكن من درك أحكام الشرع استقلالا من  غير
تقليد غيره ويستقصى تفصيل ذلك في علم الوصول أما المقلد فلا يصلح للقضاء
وأما من بلغ مبلغ الإجتهاد في مذهب إمام لا في أصل الشرع ففي جواز الفتوى
له خلاف مبني على أن من قلده كان قد قلد إمامه الميت أم قلده في نفسه فمن
جوز تقليد الميت وهو الصحيح جوز له
الفتوى ومع هذا فلا تجوز توليته مع القدرة على مجتهد مستقل وإذا لم يوجد
غيره وجب تقديمه على الجاهل والذي لم يبلغ مبلغ الإجتهاد في المذهب
وينبغي أن يعتبر مع هذه الخصال الكفاءة اللائقة بالقضاء فمجرد العلم لا
يكفي لهذه الأمور
وفي تولية الأمي الذي لا يحسن الكتابة وجهان أصحهما الجواز إذ كان صلى
الله عليه وسلم أميا وأما العمى فمينع القضاء لأنه لا يميز بين الخصوم
والشهود
ثم هذه الشروط أطلقها أصحابنا وقد تعذر في عصرنا لأن مصدر الولايات خال
عن هذه الصفات وقد خلا العصر أيضا عن المجتهد المستقل والوجه القطع بتنفيذ
قضاء من ولاه السلطان ذو الشوكة كيلا تتعطل مصالح الخلق فإنا ننفذ قضاء أهل
البغي للحاجة فكيف يجوز تعطيل القضاء الآن نعم يعصي السلطان بتفويضه إلى
الفاسق والجاهل ولكن بعد أن ولاه فلا بد من تنفيذ أحكامه للضرورة
المسألة الرابعة في الإستخلاف والأولى بالإمام أن يصرح بالإذن فيه فإن
نهى
امتنع وإن أطلق فثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه يمتنع لأنه لم يفوض إليه وولاية القضاء عند الشافعي رضي الله
عنه تتجزأ حتى لو فوض إليه قضاء الرجال دون النساء أو قضاء الأموال دون
النفوس أو استثنى شخصا واحدا عن ولايته نفذ عندنا خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه
الله فكذلك إذا لم يفوض إليه الإستخلاف
والثاني أن المطلق ينزل على المعتاد فيجوز له الإستخلاف
والثالث أنه إن اتسعت خطة الولاية بحيث لا يقدر على القيام بنفسه جاز
وإلا فلا
وتشترط صفات القضاة في النائب إلا إذا لم يفوض إليه إلا تعيين الشهود أو
التزكية فإنه لا يشترط من العلم إلا ما يليق به وقال الشيخ أبو  محمد نائب
القاضي في القرى إذا لم يفوض إليه إمضاء الحكم بل سماع البينة ونقلها فلا
يشترط منصب الإجتهاد بل العلم اللائق بأحكام البينات

- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā-yā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes cutting, deciding, and executing a matter definitively; al-qaḍāʾ is the final judgment that severs dispute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological-juridical usage, it is the authoritative determination of God's command in specific cases; carries weight of divine delegation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is 'cutting through'; metaphorically extended to the judge's role as one who cuts through contention with binding verdicts.
- Root: و-ل-ي (waliya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity, guardianship, and assuming charge of an affair.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Wilāyah is the power of disposal over another's affairs, whether by nature (God's lordship) or by delegation (human authority).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is 'being near'; metaphorical is 'having authority over', as the wālī stands in the place of oversight.
- Root: خ-ل-ف (khalafa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To succeed, come after, or stand in another's place.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Istikhlāf is the appointment of a deputy who assumes the delegated functions of the principal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal is temporal succession; metaphorical is deputyship in office.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs conditional clauses (in/fa-in) and exceptions (illā) to delineate juristic cases; the protasis sets the hypothetical scenario and the apodosis the ruling, requiring precise parsing of the particle fa- to mark the result.
chapters.translation:
I say: This section contains six questions.

**The First Question: On the virtue of judgeship and undertaking the welfare of the Muslims.**

Rendering justice to the oppressed is among the most excellent acts of drawing near to God (qurubāt), and it is one of the communal obligations (furūḍ al-kifāyāt). It is superior to jihad and more important than it, for jihad seeks increase (of territory or dominion), whereas judgeship preserves what already exists. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: {«لَيَوْمٌ وَاحِدٌ مِنْ إِمَامٍ عَادِلٍ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ عِبَادَةِ سِتِّينَ سَنَةً»} — "A single day of a just ruler is better than sixty years of worship" — and: {«حَدٌّ يُقَامُ فِي أَرْضٍ بِحَقِّهِ أَزْكَى مِنْ مَطَرِ أَرْبَعِينَ خَرِيفًا»} — "A prescribed punishment carried out in a land in its due right is purer than forty autumns of rain." Therefore, on account of the virtue of authority and its being a pillar for the order of religion and the world, it is obligatory to accept when one is called to adjudicate. And it is recommended that one say, when called, "Hearing and obedience" (samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan).

**The Second Question: On the permissibility of seeking judgeship and positions of authority.**

Warnings have been transmitted concerning it, despite the virtue we have mentioned. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: {«مَنْ وَلِيَ الْقَضَاءَ فَقَدْ ذُبِحَ بِغَيْرِ سِكِّينٍ»} — "Whoever undertakes judgeship has been slaughtered without a knife." And he said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Samurah: {«لَا تَسْأَلِ الْإِمَارَةَ فَإِنَّكَ إِنْ أُعْطِيتَهَا عَنْ مَسْأَلَةٍ وُكِلْتَ إِلَيْهَا وَإِنْ أُعْطِيتَهَا مِنْ غَيْرِ مَسْأَلَةٍ أُعِنْتَ عَلَيْهَا»} — "Do not seek the position of authority, for if you are given it due to asking, you will be entrusted to it; but if you are given it without asking, you will be aided in it." And ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, said: "There is no governor or official who will not be brought on the Day of Resurrection with his hands chained to his neck — either his justice releases him or his injustice destroys him."

These warnings are only because this authority extracts from the soul its hidden corruptions (khafāyā al-khubth), until one leans against the enemy and takes vengeance upon him, shows favor to the friend, and follows personal inclinations. A man may think himself pious, but when he is appointed, he changes. So we say: The seeker has four states:

**First state:** That he is uniquely qualified — namely, no one else exists who is fit. Then it is an individual obligation (farḍ ʿayn) upon him. Even if he is obscure, he must make himself known to the ruler until he is appointed. Then, if he fears for himself betrayal or inclination (to bias), this is not an excuse; rather, he must struggle against his soul and adhere to the path of piety. If he assumes office and inclines, he disobeys; and if he refuses acceptance out of fear of inclination, he disobeys — he is inevitably caught between one of two acts of disobedience.

**Second state:** That in the region there is someone more qualified than him. Then there is disagreement concerning the validity of the imamate of the lesser qualified (al-mafḍūl). If we forbid it, then there is disagreement concerning the validity of the judgeship of the lesser qualified and his appointment. The more correct view (al-aṣaḥḥ) is that it is valid, because what is lost of the excellence of the imamate cannot be compensated, whereas the deficiency of the judge can be compensated by the oversight of the ruler behind him. If we say it is not valid, then acceptance is forbidden for him, and appointment is forbidden for the ruler. If we say it is valid, then it is permissible for the lesser qualified to accept if appointed without his asking — though it is more proper that he not accept. As for seeking it, it is disliked (makrūh) and does not reach the level of prohibition; and it was said it is forbidden. All this applies to one confident in himself who has tested his scrupulousness (waraʿ) and piety. But if he senses within himself betrayal, then seeking is forbidden.

**Third state:** That in the town there is someone inferior to him. If we say the authority of the lesser qualified is not valid, then this case joins the first scenario. If we say it is valid, then acceptance is permissible — rather, it is more proper, to secure that excellence for the Muslims. As for seeking, it is permissible. And if he is appointed without asking, is acceptance obligatory upon him? There are two views (wajhān). But this is when he is confident in himself; if he fears, then the excellence of virtue does not outweigh this, so he should refrain.

**Fourth state:** That in the region there is someone equal to him. Then acceptance is permissible. If he is appointed without asking, acceptance is not obligatory on the stronger view (al-aẓhar), because he is not uniquely qualified. But acceptance is more proper, because it came to him without asking, so he will be aided in it. As for seeking, it is possible that it is disliked due to the risk, and possible that it is recommended for the virtue. All this applies when he does not fear for himself; if he fears with a manifest fear, then he must be cautious.

And if he does not sense inclination but has not tested himself in positions of authority — then if he has a need to seek sustenance and sufficiency, dislike is not unleashed upon him merely by conjecture (tawahhum) when there is need; he may seek. But if there is no need, then seeking is disliked for him merely on this sensing, and it does not reach prohibition.

**The Third Question: On the qualifications of judges.**

It is necessary that the judge be free, male, a muftī (one qualified to issue legal opinions), and discerning (baṣīr). For there is no authority for a slave, nor for a woman. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: It is permissible to appoint a woman in matters in which her testimony is accepted.

By our saying "muftī," we mean the mujtahid whose legal opinion is accepted. This excludes the minor and the sinner (fāsiq), for their opinions are not accepted. Yes, the sinner is a muftī with respect to himself, in that he may not imitate (taqlīd) another, but his opinion is not relied upon. By "mujtahid" we mean one capable of attaining the rulings of the Law independently, without imitating another. The detailed exposition of this belongs to the science of uṣūl (legal theory). As for the mere imitator (muqallid), he is not fit for judgeship.

As for one who has reached the level of ijtihad within the school (madhhab) of an imam, but not in the fundamentals of the Law itself — there is disagreement on the permissibility of his issuing legal opinions, built upon whether one who imitates him has imitated his dead imam, or imitated him in himself. Whoever permits imitation of the dead — which is the correct view — permits him to issue legal opinions. Nevertheless, his appointment is not permissible when an independent mujtahid is available. And if no one else exists, he must be preferred over the ignorant one and over one who has not reached the level of ijtihad within the school.

It is fitting that, along with these qualities, competence (kifāʾah) befitting judgeship be considered; mere knowledge is not sufficient for these matters.

Concerning the appointment of an illiterate person (ummī) who cannot write, there are two views; the more correct of them is permissibility, since he, peace and blessings be upon him, was illiterate. As for blindness, it prevents judgeship, because he cannot distinguish between litigants and witnesses.

Then, these conditions were stated absolutely by our companions (aṣḥābunā), yet they have become unattainable in our era, because the source of appointments is devoid of these qualities, and the era is also devoid of the independent mujtahid. The decisive view is to enforce the judgments of whomever the ruler of force (dhū al-shawkah) has appointed, so that the welfare of creation is not suspended. For we enforce the judgments of the people of rebellion (ahl al-baghy) out of necessity — so how could it be permissible to suspend judgeship now? Yes, the ruler disobeys by delegating to the sinner and the ignorant, but after he has appointed him, his judgments must be enforced out of necessity (ḍarūrah).

**The Fourth Question: On delegation (al-istikhlāf).**

The more proper course for the ruler is to explicitly authorize delegation. If he forbids it, it is impermissible. If he leaves it unrestricted, there are three views:

**One:** That it is impermissible, because he has not delegated it to him. And judgeship, according to al-Shāfiʿī, may God be pleased with him, is divisible — such that if he delegated to him judgment over men but not women, or over property but not persons, or excluded a single individual from his authority, it is valid in our view, contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him. So likewise, if he has not delegated delegation to him, it is not permitted.

**Two:** That the unrestricted grant is interpreted according to customary practice, so delegation is permissible for him.

**Three:** That if the scope of the office has expanded such that he cannot undertake it himself, delegation is permissible; otherwise, it is not.

The qualifications of judges are required in the deputy — except when he has been delegated only the appointment of witnesses or their certification (tazkiyah); then only the knowledge befitting that task is required. And Shaykh Abū Muḥammad said: The deputy judge in the villages, when he has not been delegated the execution of judgment but only the hearing of evidence and its transmission, does not require the rank of ijtihad, but rather knowledge befitting the rules of evidence.

### | فرع

ليس له أن يشترط على النائب الحكم بخلاف اجتهاده أو بخلاف اعتقاده حيث
يجوز تولية المقلد للضرورة بل اعتقاد المقلد في حقه كالإجتهاد في حق
المجتهد فإن شرط حنفي على نائبه الشافعي الحكم بمذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله
جاز له الحكم في كل مسألة توافق فيها المذهبان وما فيه خلاف لا يحكم فيه
أصلا لا بمذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه
الله فإنه خلاف اعتقاده ولا بمذهب الشافعي رضي الله عنه فإنه لم يفوض
إليه
المسألة الخامسة إذا نصب في بلدة قاضيين على أن لا يستقل أحدهما دون
الآخر لم يجز لأن الإختلاف يكثر في الإجتهاد فيؤدي إلى بقاء الخصومات ناشئة
ولو خصص كل قاض بطرف من أطراف البلد جاز كما يعتاد في بغداد وإن أثبت لكل
واحد الإستقلال في جميع البلد فوجهان
أحدهما لا إذ يتنازع الخصمان في اختيار أحدهما وكذلك في إجابة داعيهما
بخلاف داعي الإمام والقاضي أو خليفته فإن داعي الأصل يقدم وكذلك من اختاره
والثاني أنه يجوز ويحكم عند النزاع بالقرعة في التقديم
المسألة السادسة في التحكيم
إذا حكم رجلان اختصما في مال هل ينفذ حكمه عليهما فيه قولان والنكاح مرتب
على المال وأولى بأن لا ينفذ والعقوبات مرتبة على النكاح وأولى بأن لا تنفذ
ثم اختلف في محل القولين قيل إنه إذا لم يكن في البلد قاض فإن كان لم يجز
وقيل إن لم
يكن فهو جائز وإن كان فقولان وقيل بطرد القولين مطلقا والأصح المنع بكل
حال وقد ذكرنا توجيه ذلك في مسألة مفردة التمس بعضه الفقهاء بالشام

### | التفريع

إن جوزنا ذلك فليكن المحكم على صفة تجوز للقاضي توليته ثم لا ينفذ إلا
على من رضي فلو تعلق بثالث كما إذا كان في قتل الخطأ لم يضرب الدية على
العاقلة إذا لم يرضوا بحكمه وفيه وجه أن رضا القاتل كاف فيه  لأنهم تبع له
وهو بعيد لأن إقرار القاتل لا يلزمهم فكيف يلزمهم رضاه والمذهب أنه لا يحكم
في الإستيفاء بل ليس إليه إلا الإثبات وفيه وجه
ولا شك أنه ممنوع من استيفاء العقوبات لأنه يخرم أبهة الولاية ثم للمحكم
أن يرجع عن التحكيم قبل تمام الحكم وبعده فلا ينفع وإن لم يجدد رضا بعد
الحكم فهل يلزم بمجرد الرضا السابق ذكر العراقيون وجهين

### | الفصل الثاني في العزل وحكمه

وفيه خمس مسائل
الأولى في الإنعزال وينعزل بكل صفة لو قارنت التولية لامتنع كالعمى
والجنون والنسيان أما الفسق فالإمام الأعظم لا ينعزل بطرآنه إذ فيه خطر
ويجر ذلك فسادا أما القاضي إذا فسق وجب على الإمام عزله وقطع الفقهاء
المعتبرون بانعزاله وقال بعض الأصوليين لا ينعزل إلا أن يعزل

- Root: ش-ر-ط (sharṭ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A mark, sign, or condition; in legal usage, a stipulation that binds an act to a requisite.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A conditional clause (sharṭ) that renders an obligation contingent upon its fulfillment, akin to a divine ordinance’s conditionality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in contractual stipulations; metaphorical (majāz) when applied to divine decrees, as no human can truly bind God.
- Root: ح-ك-م (ḥukm)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Judgment, governance, or decisive arbitration between disputants.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act of applying divine law (ḥukm Allāh) to particular cases; in jurisprudence, the judge’s authoritative determination.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for a judge’s verdict; metaphorical for God’s eternal decree, as human judgment is a shadow of divine wisdom.
- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿazl)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Separation, removal, or dismissal from a position.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Termination of judicial authority, either by disqualifying attribute or by explicit removal.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical separation; metaphorical for stripping an office, as the office is an abstract trust.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause (al-sharṭ wa-l-jawāb) — The protasis (sharṭ) governs the apodosis (jawāb), as in “if he stipulates X, then the judgment is Y,” requiring precise syntactic linkage to preserve legal causality.
chapters.translation:
### | Branch

He may not stipulate upon the deputy judge to rule contrary to his own juristic reasoning (ijtihād) or contrary to his personal conviction (iʿtiqād), even where appointing a taqlīd-follower (muqallid) is permissible out of necessity. Rather, the conviction of the muqallid in his own case is like the ijtihād of the mujtahid in his. Thus, if a Ḥanafī appoints a Shāfiʿī deputy and stipulates that he rule according to the school of Abū Ḥanīfa (may God have mercy on him), then the deputy may rule in any matter where the two schools agree; but in any matter of disagreement, he may not rule at all — neither by the school of Abū Ḥanīfa (may God have mercy on him), for that would contradict his conviction, nor by the school of al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him), for that was not delegated to him.

**Fifth Issue:** If two judges are appointed in a single city on the condition that neither acts independently without the other, this is not permissible, for disagreement would abound in their ijtihād, leading to disputes remaining unresolved. But if each judge is assigned a specific district of the city, this is permissible, as is customary in Baghdad. If each is granted full independence over the entire city, there are two views:
- One: No, for the two litigants would dispute over choosing one of them, and likewise over responding to their summons — unlike the summons of the Imam, the judge, or his deputy, for the summons of the original authority takes precedence, as does the one he selects.
- The second: Yes, it is permissible, and in case of conflict, the matter is decided by lot (qurʿah) for precedence.

**Sixth Issue: On Arbitration (taḥkīm)**
If two men dispute over property and they appoint an arbitrator to judge between them, does his judgment bind them? There are two views. Marriage is ranked above property and is even more deserving of non-enforcement; penal sanctions (ʿuqūbāt) are ranked above marriage and are even more deserving of non-enforcement. Then there is disagreement over the scope of the two views. It is said: [the permissibility applies] only if there is no judge in the city; if there is, it is not permissible. And it is said: if there is no judge, it is permissible; if there is, there are two views. And it is said: the two views apply absolutely. The most correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) is prohibition in all cases. We have already explained the reasoning for this in a separate issue that some jurists in Syria requested.

### | Sub-branches

If we permit arbitration, then the arbitrator must possess the qualifications that would permit a judge to appoint him. Then his judgment is only enforceable against those who consent to it. Thus, if it affects a third party — as in the case of accidental homicide (qatl al-khaṭaʾ) — the blood-wit (diyah) is not imposed upon the ʿāqilah (the killer’s male agnatic relatives) if they do not consent to his judgment. There is a view that the killer’s consent suffices, for they are his followers. But this is far-fetched, for the killer’s own admission does not bind them — how then would his consent bind them? The established school (al-madhhab) is that he does not rule over execution (istīfāʾ); rather, he has only the power of establishing the claim (ithbāt). There is a view [allowing execution]. There is no doubt that he is prohibited from executing penal sanctions, for that would breach the dignity of authority (haybat al-wilāyah). Then the arbitrator may retract his arbitration before completing the judgment, but not after, for retraction would be futile. If he does not renew consent after the judgment, does the prior consent alone bind him? The Iraqis mention two views.

### | Chapter Two: On Dismissal and Its Ruling

It contains five issues.

**First: On Automatic Dismissal (al-inʿizāl)**
A judge is automatically dismissed by any attribute that, had it accompanied his appointment, would have prevented it — such as blindness, insanity, or forgetfulness. As for immorality (fisq), the Supreme Imam is not dismissed by its occurrence, for therein lies danger, and it would lead to corruption. But if a judge becomes immoral, the Imam is obligated to dismiss him. The authoritative jurists (al-fuqahāʾ al-muʿtabirūn) ruled that he is automatically dismissed, while some theologians (uṣūliyyūn) said he is not dismissed unless explicitly removed.

chapters.arabic_text: ### | فرع لو جنالقاضي ثم أفاق فهل يعود قضاؤه فيه وجهان والأصح أنه لا يعود كالوكالة لأن القضاء أيضا جائز إذ للقاضي أن يعزل نفسه الثانية في جواز العزل فللإمام عزل القاضي إذا رابه منه أمر ويكفي غلبة الظن فإن لم يظهر سبب فعزله بمن هو أفضل نفذ وإن عزله بمن هو دونه لم ينفذ على الأظهر وإن عزله بمثله فوجهان واختار الإمام نفوذ عزله بكل حال إذ ربما يرى من هو دونه أصلح لهم منه نعم عليه فيما بينه وبين الله تعالى أن لا يعزل إلا لمصلحة المسلمين فإن خالف المصلحة عصى ولكن ينبغي أن ينفذ عزله فإن ذلك يجر فسادا في الأقضية فرع حيث ينفذ العزل فهل يقف على بلوغ الخبر إليه طريقان أحدهما أنه على قولين كالوكيل والثاني القطع بأنه لا ينعزل لما فيه من الضرر أما إذا كتب إذا قرأت كتابي هذا فينعزل عند القراءة وكذلك إذا قرىء عليه بخلاف الطلاق فإن ذلك ينبني على اللفظ وهذا ينبني على المقصود ولا يقصد الإمام الجاد في العزل قراءته بنفسه وفيه وجه أن هذا كالطلاق الثالثة إذا انعزل الإمام لم ينعزل القضاة وكذا إذا مات إذ يعظم الضرر في خلو الخطة عن القضاة ولو انعزل القاضي بعزل أو موت أو غيره انعزل كل من فوض إليه شغلا معينا كمن يصغي إلى شهادة معينة وأما خليفته ونوابه في القرى وقيم الأطفال ففي انعزالهم ثلاثة أوجه أحدها أنهم لا ينعزلون كما لا ينعزل القاضي بموت الإمام الثاني ينعزلون كما ينعزل الوكيل والثالث أنه إن استخلف بالإذن الصريح لم ينعزلوا وإن استقل بالإستخلاف انعزلوا الرابعة إذا قال القاضي بعد العزل كنت قضيت لفلان لم يقبل قوله كالوكيل بعد العزل ويقبل بمجرد قوله قبل العزل وإن لم تكن بينة وإن قضينا بأنه لا يحكم بمجرد علمه وهذا متفق عليه لأنه أهل الإنشاء في الحال ولو شهد عدلان بعد العزل على قضائه ثبت وإن كان هو أحد العدلين وقال أشهد أني قضيت لم يقبل ولو قال أشهد أن قاضيا قضى ففيه وجهان أحدهما تقبل كما تقبل شهادة المرضعة كذلك والثاني لا لأن نسبة القضاء إليه ظاهر فكأنه صرح به الخامسة من ادعى على قاض معزول أنه أخذ منه رشوة حمله إلى القاضي المنصوب ليفصل بينهما الخصومة بطريقها وإن ادعى أنه أخذ مني المال بشهادة عبدين أو معلنين بالفسق فكذلك وإن ادعى مجرد الحكم دون أخذ المال ففي قبول الدعوى وجهان ينبنيان على أن القاضي إذا أقر على نفسه بذلك هل يغرم أم يختص الغرم بالشهود لو حاسب الصارف الأمناء فادعى واحد منهم أنه أخذ منه أجرة قدرها له المعزول فلا أثر لتصديق المعزول ولكن الزائد على أجرة المثل يسترد وهل تصدق يمينه في قدر أجرة المثل فيه وجهان أحدهما لا لأنه مدع والثاني نعم لأن الظاهر أنه لا يعمل مجانا وقد فاتت منافعه فلا بد من عوض - صلى الله عليه وسلم - الباب الثاني في جامع آداب القضاء وفيه فصول - صلى الله عليه وسلم -

- Root: ع-ز-ل (ʿazala)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is separation, removal, or setting apart; in juridical context, it denotes the act of dismissing or removing someone from an office.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological-juridical terms, ʿazl signifies the cessation of delegated authority (wilāyah) by the superior, entailing a reversion of the subordinate's competence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage (ḥaqīqah) refers to physical or positional removal; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to annulment of legal capacity or jurisdiction.
- Root: ج-ن-ن (junūn)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Concealment of intellect; insanity as a veiling of rational faculty.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A state negating legal accountability (taklīf) and suspending the validity of juridical acts.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: covering of the mind; metaphorical: any condition that voids legal efficacy.
- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Decisive execution of a matter; judgment that settles a dispute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The authoritative pronouncement of a ruling (ḥukm) by one vested with jurisdiction (wilāyat al-qaḍā).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: fulfillment and completion; metaphorical: the judge's binding adjudication.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Conditional Suspension (al-Taʿlīq bi-al-Sharṭ) — The validity of an act (e.g., dismissal) may be suspended upon a future condition (e.g., reading of a letter), and its effect is realized upon fulfillment, unlike utterances whose effect is tied to the moment of pronunciation.
chapters.translation:
I say: Section 558

### | Branch

If the judge becomes insane, then recovers, does his prior judgment return? There are two views (wajhān), and the more correct (aṣaḥḥ) is that it does not return—just as in the case of agency (wakālah)—because the judgeship is also revocable (jāʾiz), since the judge may dismiss himself.

The second [issue]: concerning the permissibility of dismissal. The Imām (ruler) may dismiss a judge if something about him arouses his suspicion, and a preponderant conjecture (ghalabat al-ẓann) suffices [as grounds]. If no cause appears, and he dismisses him in favor of one who is more excellent (afḍal), the dismissal is effective (nafadha). If he dismisses him in favor of one inferior to him (dūnahu), it is not effective according to the more apparent view (al-aẓhar). If he dismisses him in favor of an equal (mithl), there are two views. The Imām [al-Ghazālī] chose the effectiveness of his dismissal in every case, for perhaps he sees that one inferior to him is more suitable for the people than he. Indeed, between him and God most high, he must not dismiss except for the welfare of the Muslims (maṣlaḥat al-muslimīn). If he contravenes the [public] interest, he sins, yet his dismissal ought to be effective, for [declaring it void] would lead to corruption in the judiciary (fasād fī al-aqḍiyah).

### Branch
Where the dismissal is effective, does it depend upon the news reaching him [the judge]? There are two paths (ṭarīqān):
One: that it is [decided] on two opinions (qawlān), like the agent (wakīl).
The second: the definitive assertion (qaṭʿ) that he is not dismissed, due to the harm [that would ensue].

As for when he writes: "When you read this letter of mine, you are dismissed"—then he is dismissed upon the reading. Likewise, if it is read to him. This differs from divorce (ṭalāq), for that is built upon the utterance (lafẓ), whereas this is built upon the intent (maqṣūd). The Imām, being earnest in dismissal, does not intend his own reading [by himself]. There is a view that this is like divorce.

The third [issue]: If the Imām is dismissed, the judges are not dismissed. Likewise, if he dies, for great harm would result in the vacancy of the office (khilwat al-khiṭṭah) from judges. But if the judge is dismissed—by dismissal, death, or otherwise—then everyone to whom he delegated a specific task is dismissed, such as one who listens to a specific testimony. As for his deputy (khalīfah), his representatives (nuwwāb) in the villages, and the custodians of orphans (qayyim al-aṭfāl), there are three views (awjuh) concerning their dismissal:
One: they are not dismissed, just as the judge is not dismissed by the Imām's death.
Second: they are dismissed, just as the agent is dismissed.
Third: if he appointed them with explicit permission (idhn ṣarīḥ), they are not dismissed; but if he acted independently in appointing them (istaqalla bi-al-istikhilāf), they are dismissed.

The fourth [issue]: If the judge, after dismissal, says: "I had ruled for so-and-so," his statement is not accepted—like the agent after dismissal. But before dismissal, his mere statement is accepted, even without evidence (bayyinah), even though we rule that he does not adjudicate on the basis of his mere knowledge. This is agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh), because he is the one competent to originate [the judgment] at that time. If two just witnesses testify after dismissal to his ruling, it is established—even if he is one of the two witnesses. If he says: "I testify that I ruled," it is not accepted. If he says: "I testify that a judge ruled," there are two views:
One: it is accepted, just as the testimony of the wet-nurse (murḍiʿah) is accepted likewise.
Second: no, because attributing the ruling to himself is apparent (ẓāhir), as if he had explicitly stated it.

The fifth [issue]: If someone claims against a dismissed judge that he took a bribe (rishwah) from him, he brings him to the newly appointed judge to adjudicate the dispute between them in the proper manner. If he claims: "He took my wealth on the testimony of two slaves or two openly immoral persons (muʿlinān bi-al-fisq)," it is likewise. If he claims mere judgment without taking wealth, then concerning the acceptance of the claim there are two views, built upon [the question]: if the judge confesses to that against himself, does he incur liability (ghurm), or is liability confined to the witnesses?

If the disburser (ṣārif) settles accounts with the trustees (umanāʾ), and one of them claims that he took from him a fee (ujrah) which the dismissed [judge] had set for him, then the dismissed judge's confirmation has no effect. However, the excess over the equivalent fee (ujrat al-mithl) is recovered. As for whether his oath is believed regarding the amount of the equivalent fee, there are two views:
One: no, because he is a claimant (muddaʿī).
Second: yes, because the apparent [circumstance] is that he does not work for free, and his benefits have lapsed, so compensation is necessary.

— Peace be upon him — The Second Chapter: On the Comprehensive Etiquettes of Judging (Ādāb al-Qaḍā), containing sections — Peace be upon him —

chapters.title_en: Section 559: On Miscellaneous Etiquettes of the Judge — First Chapter
chapters.arabic_text: ### | الفصل الأول في آداب متفرقة وهي عشرة الأول أن من قبل الولاية في الحضرة فليقدم إلى البلد من يشيع ولايته فإن انصرف على الفور وقدم فجأة ولم يستفض فادعى أنه قاض فلهم الإمتناع من الطاعة إن لم يكن معه كتاب وإن كان كتاب من غير استفاضة ولا شهادة عدلين ففيه وجهان أحدهما أنه يجب اعتماد الكتاب مع مخايل الصدق وبعد الجرأة على التلبيس في مثل هذا على السلطان والثاني أن ابتداء الأمور العظيمة لا بد من الإحتياط فيها فلا بد من عدلين يخبران عن التولية وإن لم تكن على صيغة الشهادة فإنه ليس لذلك خصم معين حتى تقام عليه ولا ثم قاض آخر تثبت عنده وإن ظهرت مخايل الخيانة فلا حرج على الناس في التوقف أصلا الأدب الثاني أنه كما قدم فينبغي أن لا يشتغل بشيء حتى يفتش عن المحبوسين فمن كان محبوسا ظلما أو في تعزير أطلقه ومن أقر بأنه محبوس بحق رده إلى الحبس فإن لم يعترف سأله عن خصمه فإن ذكر خصما حاضرا أحضره فطالبه بابتداء الخصومة فإن أقام الحجة على أن القاضي الأول حكم عليه رده إلى الحبس وإلا خلاه حتى يستأنف الخصومة فإن قال المحبوس حبست ظلما قال بعضهم يخلى فإن إمسكانه من غير حجة لا وجه له وخصمه يحتاج إلى ابتداء الخصومة لا محالة وقال الأكثرون لا بد أن يحضر خصمه أولا ويسأل فإن لم يظهر له خصم أطلق فإن قال لا أدري لم حبست ينادى عليه إلى حد الإشاعة فإن لم يظهر له خصم أطلق وفي مدة الإشاعة لا يحبس ولا يخلى بل يراقب وهل يطالب بكفيل ببدنه فيه وجهان والأكثرون على أنه لا يلزمه ذلك فإن ذكر خصما غائبا وقال أنا مظلوم فمنهم من قطع بأنه يخلى ومنهم من ذكر وجهين أحدهما أنه يكتب إلى خصمه حتى يجتهد في التعجيل ويحضر فإن تخلف أطلق والثاني أنه يطلق لأن انتظار الغائب يطول بخلاف الحاضر ثم ينبغي أن يبادر بعد الفراغ من المحبوسين إلى النظر في أموال الأيتام والأوصياء ومحاسبتهم فإنها وقائع لا رافع لها إليه فإن وقعت حادثة في أثناء ذلك ولم يتفرع لفصلها مع شغل الأوصياء استخلف من يقوم بأحد المهمين والغرض مبادرة هذه الأمور الأدب الثالث أن يتروى بعد ذلك في ترتيب الكتاب والمزكين والمترجمين أما الكاتب فليكن عدلا عاقلا نزها عن الطمع ويكفي كاتب واحد ولا أقل من مزكيين وستأتي صفاتهم وأما المترجم فلا بد أيضا من عددهم وأما المسمع وهو الذي يسمع القاضي الأصم ففي اشتراط العدد ثلاثة أوجه أحدها أنه يشترط كالمترجم فإنه ينقل عين اللفظ كما أن ذلك ينقل معنى اللفظ والثاني لا لأن المسمع لو غير عرفه الخصمان والحاضرون بخلاف الترجمة والثالث أن العدد لا يشترط إلا أن يكون الخصمان أصمين فإن القوم قد يغفلون عن تغييره والخصم هو الذي يعتني به ### | التفريع إن لم نشترط العدد فلا نرعى لفظ الشهادة وهل تشترط الحرية فيه خلاف كما في شهادة رؤية الهلال لرمضان والصحيح أنه يسلك به مسلك الرواية وإن شرط العدد ففي لفظ الشهادة وجهان وعلى الجملة ليست هذه شهادة محققة ولكن لا يبعد الإستظهار فيها بالعدد واللفظ وقد حصل أن العدد شرط في الشاهد والمزكى والمترجم والمقوم ولا يشترط في القائف للخبر وهل يشترط في الخارص والقاسم والمسمع فيه وجهان ثم إن شرطنا العدد في المسمع فلا بد من رجلين وإن كانت الخصومة في مال وكذا في الشهادة على الوكالة بالمال لأن المشهود عليه ليس بمال في نفسه وإن كان إليه يئول ### | ### | فرع إذا طلب المسمع أجرة فهي على صاحب الحق أم هي من بيت المال على وجهين الأدب الرابع أن يتخذ القاضي مجلسا رفيقعا يكون مهب الرياح في الصيف وفي الشتاء كما كسا والمقصود أن لا يتسارع إليه الملل فيستضر الخصوم ولا ينبغي أن يتخذ المسجد مجلسا للقضاء فإن فعل ذلك فهو مكروه وليس بمحرم وسبب الكراهة إفضاؤه إلى رفع الأصوات ودخول النساء الحيض والصبيان وقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه إذا كنت أكره ذلك فإقامة الحدود أكره ولا بأس بفصل قضية أو قضايا في أوقات متفرقة وقد فعل ذلك رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ولكن لم يتخذه مجلسا وكلام المزني يشير إلى أن اتخاذه مجلسا لا يكره لكن الأولى تركه والصحيح الكراهية
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ل-ي (waliya)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is proximity and governance — wilāyah denotes the authority of one who stands in charge of another's affair, whether by appointment or natural guardianship.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic-theological usage, wilāyah is the delegated mandate to execute rulings (tanfīdh al-aḥkām) on behalf of the community, entailing both duty and liability.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is 'nearness' (qurb); the metaphorical extension to 'governance' is a settled majāz, since the governor is 'near' to the governed in oversight.
- Root: ش-ي-ع (shāʿa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To spread, become public, be widely known; ishtihār and istifāḍah derive from this — the latter meaning the diffusion of news until it becomes common knowledge.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Istifāḍah in legal contexts is the public notoriety that substitutes for formal testimony (shahādah) in matters of general appointment, as it removes doubt of collusion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: the spreading of water or dust; metaphorical: the propagation of a report until it fills the horizon of public awareness.
- Root: خ-ل-و (khalā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be empty, vacant; takhliyah is the act of releasing, setting free from restraint.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In judicial procedure, takhliyah of a prisoner is the restoration of his original liberty (barāʾah al-dhimmah) when no valid claim against him is established.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: emptying a vessel; metaphorical: discharging a person from custody, as if emptying him of the burden of detention.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text repeatedly employs conditional clauses (in kāna, fa-in) to structure legal rulings, where the protasis states the factual condition and the apodosis the juridical consequence; the exceptive particles (illā, ghayr) delimit the scope of obligation, as in 'no less than two witnesses' (lā aqall min muzakkiyayn).
chapters.translation:
I say — may Allah guide us and you to the truth:

### | First Chapter: On Miscellaneous Etiquettes

These are ten in number.

**The First Etiquette:** Whoever receives a judicial appointment (wilāyah) in the presence of the sovereign should send ahead to the town someone who will publicize his appointment. If he departs immediately, arrives suddenly without prior announcement, and his appointment has not become widely known (istafāḍa), then if he claims to be a judge, the people are entitled to refuse obedience — provided he has no written decree (kitāb) with him. If he has a written decree but without public notoriety or the testimony of two upright witnesses, there are two positions (wajhān):

One: that the written decree must be relied upon, given the indications of truthfulness (makhāyil al-ṣidq) and the improbability of anyone daring to forge such a document against the sovereign.

The second: that the commencement of grave matters requires caution; thus two upright witnesses must inform of the appointment, even if not in the formal formula of testimony — for there is no specific adversary against whom it must be established, nor another judge before whom it must be proven. However, if indications of treachery (makhāyil al-khiyānah) appear, the people are under no blame whatsoever in withholding obedience.

**The Second Etiquette:** Just as he arrives, he should not occupy himself with anything until he investigates the prisoners. Whoever is imprisoned unjustly or for discretionary punishment (taʿzīr) — he releases him. Whoever confesses that he is imprisoned by right — he returns him to prison. If he does not confess, he asks him about his adversary. If he names an adversary who is present, he summons him and demands the initiation of litigation. If the adversary establishes proof that the previous judge ruled against the prisoner, he returns him to prison; otherwise, he releases him until litigation is renewed. If the prisoner says, 'I was imprisoned unjustly,' some scholars say he is released — for detaining him without proof has no justification, and his adversary must initiate litigation in any case. The majority (al-aktharūn) say: his adversary must first be brought and questioned; if no adversary appears, he is released. If he says, 'I do not know why I was imprisoned,' a public announcement (nidāʾ) is made over him until the matter becomes widely known (ḥadd al-ishāʿah). If no adversary appears, he is released. During the period of announcement, he is neither imprisoned nor released, but kept under surveillance. Whether he may be required to provide a surety for his person — there are two positions; the majority hold that this is not incumbent upon him. If he names an absent adversary and says, 'I am wronged,' some scholars rule definitively that he is released; others mention two positions:

One: that a letter is written to his adversary so that he strives to hasten and appear; if he fails to come, the prisoner is released.

The second: that he is released immediately, for waiting for an absent party is prolonged, unlike one who is present.

Then, after finishing with the prisoners, he should hasten to examine the wealth of orphans and guardians (awṣiyāʾ) and hold them to account — for these are matters that have no one else to raise them to him. If an incident occurs during that time and he cannot attend to its resolution while occupied with the guardians, he appoints a deputy to handle one of the two important tasks. The objective is to hasten these matters.

**The Third Etiquette:** After that, he should deliberate carefully in arranging the scribe (kātib), the witnesses (muzakkiyūn), and the interpreters (mutarjimūn). As for the scribe — he should be upright, intelligent, and free from covetousness. A single scribe suffices, and no fewer than two witnesses for character-assessment (muzakkiyān) are required; their qualities will come later. As for the interpreter — their number is also required. As for the hearer (musmiʿ) — who conveys speech to a deaf judge — regarding the requirement of number, there are three positions:

One: that number is required, like the interpreter — for he transmits the very wording (ʿayn al-lafẓ), just as the interpreter transmits the meaning of the wording.

The second: that it is not required — for if the hearer altered the speech, the two adversaries and those present would recognize it, unlike translation.

The third: that number is not required unless both adversaries are deaf — for then the people might be heedless of alteration, whereas the adversary is the one who attends to it.

### | Ramification (Tafrīʿ)

If we do not require number, we do not observe the formula of testimony (lafẓ al-shahādah). Whether freedom is required of him is disputed, as in the testimony of sighting the crescent for Ramadan. The correct view is that he is treated according to the rules of transmission (riwāyah). If number is required, there are two positions on the formula of testimony. In sum, this is not a fully-fledged testimony, but it is not far-fetched to seek caution (istiẓhār) in it through number and formula.

It has thus been established that number is required for the witness, the character-assessor, the interpreter, and the appraiser (muqawwim), but not for the lineage-examiner (qāʾif), due to the report (khabar). Whether it is required for the land-assessor (khāriṣ), the divider (qāsim), and the hearer (musmiʿ) — there are two positions.

Then, if we require number for the hearer, two men are necessary — even if the litigation concerns property. Likewise in testimony regarding an agency over property (wakālah bil-māl), because the object testified upon is not property in itself, even if it ultimately leads to it.

### | Branch (Farʿ)

If the hearer demands a fee, is it upon the claimant (ṣāḥib al-ḥaqq) or from the public treasury (bayt al-māl)? — Two positions.

**The Fourth Etiquette:** The judge should take a lofty assembly-place (majlis rafīʿ) that is airy in summer and sheltered in winter, as it is clothed. The purpose is that weariness should not quickly overtake him, harming the litigants. He should not take the mosque as a place for adjudication. If he does so, it is disliked (makrūh) but not forbidden (muḥarram). The reason for the dislike is that it leads to raising voices, and the entry of menstruating women and boys. Imam al-Shāfiʿī — may Allah be pleased with him — said: 'If I dislike that, then I dislike the execution of prescribed punishments (ḥudūd) even more.' There is no harm in settling one case or several cases at scattered times [in the mosque], for the Messenger of Allah — peace be upon him — did so, but he did not take it as a permanent assembly-place. The statement of al-Muzanī suggests that taking it as a permanent assembly-place is not disliked, but leaving it is preferable. The correct view is that it is disliked.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرع

ذكر الصيدلاني وجهين في أن القاضي هل يتخذ حاجبا وبوابا والوجه أن يقال
له ذلك إن كان في خلوة وإن جلس للحكم وخشي الرحمة فله ذلك وإلا فلينظر إلى
المصلحة نعم ينقدح التردد إن لم يخمش الزحمة من حيث إن فيه توقفا لصاحب
الحق إلى الإستئذان فيجوز أن يمنع منه ويجوز أن يحتمل ذلك ليستعد القاضي
ويترك انبساطه في البيت ويتصدى له
الأدب الخامس أن لا يقضي في حال غضب وحزن بين وألم مبرح وجوع غالب إذ
يسوء خلقه فيمتد غضبه قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لا يقضي القاضي وهو
غضبان وفي
معناه كل ما يمنع من التؤدة واستيفاء الفكر
الأدب السادس أن لا يخرج حتى يجتمع علماء الفريقين ليشاورهم فيكون أبعد
من التهمة قال تعالى {وشاورهم في الأمر} قال الحسن البصري رحمه الله كان
عليه الصلاة والسلام مستغنيا عن مشاورتهم ولكن أراد أن تصير سنة للحكام
الأدب السابع أن لا يبيع ولا يشتري بنفسه ولا بوكيل معروف لأنه يستحيا
منه أو يخاف فيحابى فيكون مرتشيا بقدر المسامحة
الأدب الثامن إذا أساء واحد أدبه في مجلسه بمجاوزة حد الشرع في الخصام أو
مشافهة الشهود بالتكذيب زجره باللسان فإن عاد عزره وراعى التدريج فيه فإن
ظهر له شهادة زور عزر المزور على ملأ من الناس ونادى عليه حتى لا يحمل
الشهادة بعده
الأدب التاسع أن لا يقضي لولده ولا على عدوه بعلمه وإن قلنا يقضي بالعلم
وهل يقضي بالبينة فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لأنه أسير شاهدين فليس إليه شيء بخلاف الشاهد فإنه يقدر على
الكذب
والثاني وهو الأصح أنه لا يقضي إذ إليه الإستقصاء في دقائق أداء الشهادة
والرد بالتهمة وإليه التسامح فيه فولده كنفسه فيرفع إلى الإمام فإن رفع إلى
نائبه وحكم به ففيه وجهان يلتفتان على أنه هل ينعزل بموته فإنه إن لم ينعزل
يشابه قاضيا مستقلا
ووصى اليتيم إذا ولي القضاء فلا يقضي له لأنه خصم في حقه  كما في حق نفسه
وولده وقال القفال يقضي لأن كل قاض فهو ولي الأيتام وهو الصحيح
الأدب العاشر أن لا ينقض قضاء نفسه ولا قضاء غيره بظن واجتهاد يقارب ظنه
الأول قضى عمر رضي الله تعالى عنه بإسقاط الأخ من الأب والأم في مسألة
المشركة بعد أن شرك في العام الأول فروجع فيه فقال ذاك على ما قضينا وهذا
على ما نقضي وينقض في أربعة مواضع
الأول أن يخالف نص الكتاب أو سنة متواترة أو إجماعا وهذا ظاهر
الثاني أن يخالف قياسه واجتهاده خبر الواحد الصحيح الصريح الذي لا يحتمل
إلا تأويلا
بعيدا ينبو الفهم عن قبوله فينقض قضاء الحنفي في مسألة خيار المجلس
والعرايا وذكاة الجنين وألحق الأصحاب به النكاح بلا ولي والحكم بشهادة
الفاسق وبيع أمهات الأولاد وأمثاله وقالوا لا نبالي بتنزيل المتبايعين في
خيار المجلس على المتقاولين وتنزيل المرأة في النكاح بلا ولي على الأمة
والصغيرة فإنه جلي البطلان
الثالث أن يخالف القياس الجلي فينقض قضاء أصحاب الظاهر المعتقدين بطلان
القياس لأنه باطل بدليل أصولي قاطع
وينقض قضاء الحنفي إن قضى بالإستحسان المخالف للقياس الجلي إلا أن يعنى
به اتباع الخبر أو القياس الخفي فمن استحسن بغير ذلك فقد شرع نعم قد استحسن
الشافعي رضي الله عنه الحلف بالمصحف ولكنه مصلحة من غير مخالفة خبر وقياس
فهو جائز
وينقض مذهب الحنفي في مسألة القتل بالمثقل ومعظم مسائل الحدود والغصب
لأنه على خلاف القانون الكلي وقال الشافعي رضي الله عنه أنقض قضاء من حكم
لزوجة المفقود بأن تنكح بعد تربص أربع سنين وإن كان ذلك مذهب عمر رضي الله
تعالى عنه
الرابع أن يقاوم القياس الجلي قياس خفي يستند إلى واقعة شاذة لا يمكن
تلفيقه إلا بتكلف كقول أبي حنيفة رحمه الله إن المأذون في التجارة لا يقتصر
على الإذن بل يتعدى لقياس يتكلف استنباطه من مسألة العهدة بالحيلة وقولنا
إنه يتبع إذن المالك قياس جلي يعلم الأصولي سقوط خيالهم بالإضافة إليه
وعلى الجملة فإذا لم ينقدح عنده  إمكان الإصابة عند الله عز وجل بعد إحالة
وقع فينقضه
وهذا مما يختلف بالمجتهدين والوقائع وإنما لا ينقض القضاء حين يتقارب
النظران تقاربا لا يبعد وهم الإصابة أو المصير إلى أن كل واحد مصيب
ثم القضاء وإن لم ينقض فلا يتغير به الحكم باطنا وإنما ينفذ القضاء عندنا
ظاهرا وإن وقع في محل الإجتهاد وقال القفال يحل باطنا وقطع الأصوليون بأنه
لا يتغير أمر الباطن وهو الصحيح فلا يحل للشفعوي شفعة الجار وإن قضى له
الحنفي بها
وهل يمنعه الحنفي عن طلبه على خلاف اعتقاده فيه تردد والظاهر أنه لا يمنع
إذ القاضي لا يلتفت إلى مذهب غيره
فرع لو ظهر له خطأ في واقعة فليتتبع وإن لم ترفع إليه وإن ظهر له خطأ
القاضي المعزول لا يلزمه التتبع ما لم ترفع إليه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ق-ض (naqada)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To unravel, break apart, demolish a structure; to invalidate a binding contract or judgment by reversing its effect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal term for annulment of a judicial ruling (naqḍ al-qaḍāʾ) when it contradicts a definitive textual proof or an unequivocal analogy (qiyās jaliyy).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in construction contexts; metaphorical (majāz) in juristic usage, denoting the nullification of a judgment's binding force.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional sentence with implicit protasis (sharṭ muqaddar) — "If he overturns, it is only in four places" — where the apodosis is governed by the restrictive particle (innamā), indicating exclusivity.
chapters.translation:
---

**Branch**

Al-Saydalānī mentioned two views as to whether a judge may employ a chamberlain and a doorkeeper. The correct view is that he may do so if he is in seclusion; but if he sits for judgment and fears overcrowding, he may do so as well. Otherwise, he should consider the public interest. Indeed, hesitation arises if the crowd is not excessive, because this entails delaying the claimant's access until he seeks permission — so it is permissible to prevent it, and it is also permissible to tolerate it so that the judge may prepare himself, refrain from informal conduct at home, and devote himself to the matter.

**The Fifth Etiquette**: That he not judge while in a state of anger, manifest grief, severe pain, or overpowering hunger, for these corrupt his character and prolong his wrath. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«لَا يَقْضِي الْقَاضِي وَهُوَ غَضْبَانُ»} — "The judge shall not judge while he is angry." Included in its meaning is everything that prevents deliberation (al-tuʾadah) and the full exercise of thought.

**The Sixth Etiquette**: That he not go out [to the court] until the scholars of both parties have gathered, so that he may consult them — this being further from suspicion of bias. Allah Most High said: {«وَشَاوِرْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْرِ»} — "And consult them in the matter." Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) was independent of their counsel, but He intended it to become a sunnah for judges.

**The Seventh Etiquette**: That he neither sell nor buy personally, nor through a known agent, because he would be treated with deference or feared, and thus favored — becoming a bribe-taker to the extent of the indulgence shown him.

**The Eighth Etiquette**: If someone misbehaves in his assembly by exceeding the legal bounds in disputation or by addressing witnesses with accusations of falsehood, he should rebuke him verbally. If he repeats it, he should administer discretionary punishment (taʿzīr), observing gradualism therein. If perjured testimony becomes evident to him, he should punish the perjurer publicly before the people and proclaim against him, so that no one will bear false witness thereafter.

**The Ninth Etiquette**: That he not judge in favor of his child nor against his enemy on the basis of his own knowledge, even if we hold that he may judge by knowledge. As for judging by [the testimony of] witnesses in such cases, there are two views:

One of them: Yes, he may, because he is bound by two witnesses and has no discretion in the matter — unlike the witness, who is capable of lying.

The second — and this is the more correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) — is that he may not, because he has the discretion to scrutinize the fine points of testimony and to reject on grounds of suspicion, and he has the discretion to be lenient therein. Thus his child is like his own self, and the matter is referred to the supreme Imam. If it is referred to his deputy and he rules on it, there are two views, turning on whether the deputy is dismissed by the Imam's death — for if he is not dismissed, he resembles an independent judge.

And the guardian of an orphan, if he assumes the judiciary, may not judge in the orphan's favor, because he is an adversary regarding the orphan's right, just as regarding his own right and his child's. Al-Qaffāl said: He may judge, because every judge is a guardian of orphans — and this is the correct view.

**The Tenth Etiquette**: That he not overturn his own judgment nor that of another judge on the basis of mere conjecture and ijtihād that approximates his initial opinion. ʿUmar (may Allah Most High be pleased with him) ruled to exclude the full brother from the inheritance in the case of al-musharrakah, after having included him in the first year. When he was challenged on it, he said: "That was according to what we ruled then, and this is according to what we rule now."

He overturns in four places:

**First**: That the judgment contradict the explicit text of the Book, an unbroken (mutawātir) sunnah, or consensus (ijmāʿ) — this is evident.

**Second**: That it contradict, against his own analogy and ijtihād, a sound and explicit solitary report (khabar wāḥid) that admits of no interpretation except a far-fetched one that the understanding recoils from accepting. Thus one overturns the judgment of the Ḥanafī in the case of the option of the session (khiyār al-majlis), the ʿarāyā transaction, and the slaughter of the fetus. The companions (al-aṣḥāb) appended to these: marriage without a guardian, judgment on the testimony of a sinner, the sale of ummahāt al-awlād, and similar cases. They said: We do not care about the attempt to analogize the two contracting parties in the option of the session to two negotiators, nor the analogy of a woman in marriage without a guardian to a slave-girl or a minor — for its nullity is manifest.

**Third**: That it contradict an unequivocal analogy (al-qiyās al-jaliyy). Thus one overturns the judgment of the Ẓāhirīs who believe in the nullity of analogy, because it is void by a decisive usūlī proof. And one overturns the judgment of the Ḥanafī if he rules by juristic preference (istiḥsān) contrary to unequivocal analogy — unless by it he means following a report or a subtle analogy. Whoever employs istiḥsān otherwise has legislated anew. Indeed, al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) approved of administering an oath on the Muṣḥaf, but that is a public interest (maṣlaḥah) without contradicting any report or analogy, so it is permissible.

And one overturns the Ḥanafī doctrine in the case of killing with a heavy object (al-muthaqqal) and most of the cases of ḥudūd penalties and usurpation (ghaṣb), because it contradicts the universal legal principle. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I overturn the judgment of one who rules that the wife of a missing husband may marry after waiting four years, even if that was the doctrine of ʿUmar (may Allah Most High be pleased with him)."

**Fourth**: That an unequivocal analogy be opposed by a subtle analogy (qiyās khafiyy) resting on an anomalous case that cannot be reconciled except by artificial contrivance — as when Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) held that one permitted to trade is not restricted to the explicit permission but extends beyond it, based on an analogy laboriously derived from the case of the guarantee (al-ʿuhdah) by a trick. Our view — that he follows the owner's permission — is an unequivocal analogy, and the usūlī scholar knows that their conjecture collapses in comparison to it.

In sum: When, after due consideration, he cannot conceive of the possibility of correctness before Allah (glorified and exalted be He), he overturns it.

This varies according to the mujtahids and the cases. The judgment is not overturned only when the two considerations are so closely balanced that the likelihood of correctness is not remote, or when one adopts the position that each [mujtahid] is correct.

Then, even if the judgment is not overturned, the underlying ruling is not altered inwardly. Rather, the judgment is executed, in our view, only outwardly (ẓāhir), even if it falls within the domain of ijtihād. Al-Qaffāl said: It becomes lawful inwardly. But the usūlīs have definitively held that the inward matter is not altered — and this is the correct view. Thus, the Shāfiʿī is not permitted the preemption right of a neighbor (shufʿat al-jār) even if the Ḥanafī judge ruled in his favor.

And whether the Ḥanafī judge prevents him from seeking it contrary to his own belief — there is hesitation. The apparent view is that he does not prevent him, for the judge does not pay attention to the doctrine of another school.

**Branch**: If an error in a case becomes apparent to him, he should pursue it even if it was not brought before him. But if an error of a dismissed judge becomes apparent to him, he is not obliged to pursue it unless it is brought before him.

chapters.title_en: The Second Chapter on the Basis of His Adjudication
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثاني في مستند قضائه

ولا يخفى استناده إلى الحجج والغرض القضاء بالعلم والخط أما القضاء بما
ينفرد بعلمه ففيه قولان
أحدهما أنه يقضي به وهو أقوى من شاهدين
والثاني لا لأنه يتعرض للتهمة ويوغر الصدور ولا يليق بالإيالة فتح هذا
الباب فيصير أيضا وسيلة لقضاة السوء وفي العقوبات قولان مرتبان وأولى بأن
لا يقضي والصحيح أنه لا معنى للترتيب مع حصول حقيقة العلم والعقوبات فيه
كالمال
فإن قلنا يقضي فلا خلاف أنه لا يقضي بظنه الذي لا يستند إلى بينة ويقضي
بعلمه كيف كان وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لا يقضي إلا بعلم حصل في زمان
ولايته ومكان ولايته وإن قلنا لا يقضي فيستثنى عنه أربعة أمور
الأول أنه يتوقف عن القضاء إذا علم كذب الشهود يقينا بل يجب عليه التوقف
عند الريبة فكيف يقضي على خلاف معلومه
الثاني أنه يقضي به في عدالة الشهود ومنهم من قال يحتاج إلى مزكين على
هذا القول لأنه يتهم وكيف لا والعدالة لا تعلم يقينا
الثالث يقضي على من أقر في مجلس القضاء وإن رجع المقر فإنه أقوى الحجج
وأما إن أقر عنده سرا فيخرج على القولين ومنهم من  جوز أيضا على الإقرار سرا
قولا واحدا
الرابع أنه لو شهد شاهد واحد فهل يغني علمه عن الشاهد الثاني حتى يكون هو
كشاهد آخر فيه وجهان والأصح أنه
لا يكفي أما الخط فإذا رأى القاضي خطه بأني قضيت بكذا لم يجز له إمضاؤه
وكذا الشاهد
بل لا بد وأن يتذكر الواقعة بجميع حدودها وقال أبو يوسف يجوز الإعتماد
على الخط كما في اليمين فإنه رأى خط أبيه جاز له أن يحلف على البت في طلب
الحقوق وإسقاطها إذا وثق به وقطع أصحابنا بالفرق لأن التزوير على الخط بحيث
لا يختلف ممكن وفي فتح هذا الباب خطر عام بخلاف اليمين فإنه يباح بغالب
الظن ولا تؤدي إلى ضرر عام
فإذن الإعتماد على ثلاث درجات أوسعها الحلف وأضيقها القضاء والشهادة فإنه
لا يعتمد فيه مجرد الخط دون التذكر وبينهما رواية الأحاديث فإنه لا يعتمد
فيه مجرد الخط إن أمكن التحريف لكن إن صحت النسخة وحفظها بنفسه وأمن من
التغير جازت الرواية على الأظهر وعليه عمل علماء الأمصار وسوى الصيدلاني
بينهما وقال لا يحل للمحدث إلا رواية ما حفظ وتذكر فليرو كذلك أو ليترك
الرواية وسوى الشيخ أبو محمد على العكس من هذا وقال الشاهد إذا نسخ الواقعة
وحفظ النسخة في خزانة ووثق بأنه لم تحرف جاز له الشهادة وإن لم يذكر
والمشهور بين الأصحاب الفرق بين درجة الشهادة والرواية في صورة حفظ النسخة
وما ذكره الشيخ أبو محمد أقرب مما ذكره الصيدلاني

### | فروع

الأول لو شهد شاهدان عند القاضي بأنه قضى لم يجز له الحكم إذا لم يتذكر
ويشهدان عند غيره فيثبت قضاؤه وإن لم يذكره ولم يكذبهما ولكن القاضي ينبغي
أن يطلب من نفسه اليقين ولا يمكنه طلب اليقين من قاض آخر ويجوز هذا في
الرواية فمن المشايخ من كان يقول حدثني فلان عني وقال أبو يوسف يقبل ذلك في
القضاء أيضا
الثاني أنه لو ادعى خصم على قاض أنك قضيت لي فأنكر القضاء فليس له أن
يرفعه إلى قاض آخر  ويحلفه بل هو كالشاهد لا يحلف إذا أنكر الشهادة وقال
القاضي حسين إن قلنا إن اليمين المردودة كالإقرار فله ذلك حتى إن نكل حلف
الخصم وكان كإقرار القاضي وهذا ضعيف
الثالث إذا التمس صاحب الحق من القاضي أن يعطيه خطه بأنه قضى له ويسلم
إليه محضرا ديوانيا هل تجب الإجابة فيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه يجب إذ به إحكام الأمر وإتمامه
والثاني لا إذ لا اعتماد على الخط وإنما الخط مذكر فقط
فإن قلنا يكتب فالكاغد على الملتمس إن لم يطلق الإمام للقراطيس شيئا وذلك
مستحب إطلاقه ثم اعلم أنا وإن لم نوجب كتبة المحضر فيستحب للقاضي استحبابا
مؤكدا مهما جرت قضية أن يكتب محضرا يذكر فيه الواقعة وأسماء الخصمين فإن
كانا غريبين كتب الحلية ثم يجمع محاضر كل أسبوع في إضبارة ومحاضر الشهر في
قمطرة
ومحاضر السنة في خريطة ويكتب عليه التواريخ ويختم القاضي على الخريطة
بنفسه ويحفظه بنفسه أو بعدل لا يتمارى فيه ويدفع نسخة أخرى إلى صاحب الحق
حتى إن ضاعت واحدة سهل الرجوع إلى الأخرى وهذا هو العادة فإن التذكر من غير
خط بعيد ومن جوز للأمي أن يكون قاضيا فلا يمكنه إيجاب الكتبة وإن التمس
صاحب الحق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā-yā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To settle, decide, execute, or complete a matter; judicial decree and final determination.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The authoritative issuance of a legal ruling (ḥukm) that binds the parties, rooted in divine command and prophetic delegation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for judicial verdict; metaphorical (majāz) for divine decree (qaḍāʾ) as cosmic ordainment.
- Root: ع-ل-م (ʿalima)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Certain knowledge, perception, or cognition; the opposite of ignorance (jahl).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Certainty (yaqīn) attained through direct apprehension or valid inference; the epistemic basis for judicial action.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for verified cognition; metaphorical for mere assumption (ẓann) when unqualified.
- Root: خ-ط-ط (khaṭṭa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To draw, write, or inscribe; a line or script.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Written record as evidentiary artifact; distinguished from oral testimony in probative weight.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical writing; metaphorical for the act of recording as a memorial (tadhkirah).
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text employs layered conditionals (fa-in qulnā...) and exceptions (yustathnā ʿanhu...) requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve legal nuance.
chapters.translation:
I say: It is not hidden that his [the judge's] basis [in adjudication] rests upon proofs (ḥujaj), and the objective is adjudication by knowledge (ʿilm) and by the written record (khaṭṭ). As for adjudication based on what he alone knows [privately], there are two opinions (qawlān):

One of them: He adjudicates by it, and it is stronger than two witnesses.

The second: He does not, because it exposes him to accusation (tuhmah) and embitters hearts, and it is unbefitting for governance (siyāsah) to open this door, for it would also become a means for corrupt judges. Regarding penal sanctions (ʿuqūbāt), there are two opinions arranged in order [of priority], and it is more proper that he not adjudicate [by private knowledge]. The correct view is that there is no meaning to ordering [the opinions] when the reality of knowledge is attained, and penal sanctions therein are like property [in this regard].

If we say he adjudicates [by private knowledge], there is no disagreement that he does not adjudicate by his mere assumption (ẓann) that is not based on evidence (bayyinah), and he adjudicates by his knowledge however it was [acquired]. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: He does not adjudicate except by knowledge acquired during the time of his tenure and within the place of his jurisdiction.

If we say he does not adjudicate [by private knowledge], then four matters are excepted from this:

First: He withholds from adjudication if he knows with certainty that the witnesses are lying — rather, he must withhold upon mere suspicion (raybah). So how could he adjudicate contrary to what he knows?

Second: He adjudicates by it [private knowledge] regarding the probity (ʿadālah) of witnesses. Among them [the scholars] is one who said: He needs character accreditors (muzakkūn) on this opinion, because he is accused [of bias]. And how not, when probity is not known with certainty?

Third: He adjudicates against one who confesses (aqarra) in the court session, even if the confessor retracts — for it is the strongest of proofs. As for if he confessed before him privately, it follows the two opinions. Among them is one who also permitted [adjudication] on a private confession as a single opinion (qawl wāḥid).

Fourth: If a single witness testifies, does his [the judge's] knowledge suffice in place of the second witness, such that he is like another witness? There are two aspects (wajhān), and the most correct is that it does not suffice.

As for the written record (khaṭṭ): If the judge sees his own writing, [stating] "I adjudicated such-and-such," it is not permissible for him to execute it — and likewise the witness. Rather, he must recall the incident with all its particulars. Abū Yūsuf said: Reliance on the writing is permissible, as in the oath (yamīn), for if one sees his father's writing, it is permissible for him to swear with certainty (al-batt) in seeking rights or dropping them, if he trusts it. Our companions (aṣḥābunā) decisively affirmed the distinction, because forgery (tazwīr) upon writing, such that it is not altered, is possible, and in opening this door is a general danger — unlike the oath, for it is permitted based on predominant assumption (ghālib al-ẓann) and does not lead to general harm.

Thus, reliance is upon three degrees: the broadest is the oath, and the narrowest is adjudication and testimony, for therein mere writing is not relied upon without recollection. Between them is the narration of ḥadīth (riwāyah), for therein mere writing is not relied upon if alteration (taḥrīf) is possible. But if the copy (nuskhah) is sound, and he preserved it himself, and is secure from change, then narration is permissible on the most apparent [view], and upon this is the practice of the scholars of the regions. Al-Ṣaydalānī equated between them and said: It is not lawful for a ḥadīth narrator except to narrate what he has memorized and recalls — so let him narrate thus, or abandon narration. Shaykh Abū Muḥammad equated on the contrary of this and said: The witness, if he copies the incident and preserves the copy in a repository, and is confident it has not been forged, it is permissible for him to testify even if he does not recall [it]. The well-known [view] among the companions is the distinction between the degree of testimony and narration in the case of preserving the copy. What Shaykh Abū Muḥammad mentioned is closer [to correctness] than what al-Ṣaydalānī mentioned.

### | Branches (Furūʿ)

First: If two witnesses testify before a judge that he [the judge] adjudicated [a case], it is not permissible for him to rule [on it] if he does not recall [it]. And they testify before another [judge], then his adjudication is established even if he does not recall it and does not deny them. But the judge should seek certainty from himself, and he cannot seek certainty from another judge. This is permissible in narration — among the shaykhs was one who would say: "So-and-so narrated to me from me." Abū Yūsuf said: This is accepted in adjudication as well.

Second: If a litigant claims against a judge, "You adjudicated for me," and the judge denies the adjudication, it is not for him [the litigant] to raise it to another judge and have him swear the judge [to deny]. Rather, he is like a witness — he is not sworn when he denies testimony. Judge al-Ḥusayn said: If we hold that the rejected oath (al-yamīn al-mardūdah) is like a confession, then he has that [right], such that if the judge refuses [to swear], the litigant swears and it is like the judge's confession. This is weak.

Third: If the right-holder seeks from the judge that he give him his writing that he adjudicated for him, and he submits to him a court record (maḥḍar) of the dīwān — is answering [this request] obligatory? There are two aspects:

One of them: It is obligatory, for through it the matter is fortified and completed.

The second: No, for there is no reliance on writing — rather, writing is only a reminder (mudhakkir).

If we say he writes, then the paper is upon the seeker, unless the Imām has allocated something for papers — and such allocation is recommended (mustaḥabb). Then know that even if we do not obligate the writing of the record, it is strongly recommended (mustaḥabb muʾakkad) for the judge, whenever a case occurs, to write a record mentioning the incident and the names of the two litigants. If they are strangers, he writes their descriptions (ḥilyah). Then he gathers the records of each week in a folder (iḍbārah), the records of the month in a chest (qamṭarah), and the records of the year in a pouch (kharīṭah). He writes the dates upon them, and the judge seals the pouch with his own hand, and preserves it himself or with a trustworthy person (ʿadl) about whom there is no dispute. He gives another copy to the right-holder, so that if one is lost, recourse to the other is easy. This is the custom, for recollection without writing is far-fetched. And whoever permits an illiterate person (ummī) to be a judge cannot obligate the writing, even if the right-holder seeks it.
