chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرعان

الأول لو أقام الخارج بينة على الملك المطلق وأقام الداخل بينة على أنه
ملكه اشتراه من الخارج تقدم بينة الداخل كما لو أطلق ولا تزال يده قبل
إقامة البينة وقال القاضي تزال يده إذا ادعى ذلك إذ يقال اعترفت له بالملك
فسلم إليه ثم أثبت ما تدعيه من الشراء وكذلك لو قال أدعي أنه أبرأ عن الدين
المدعى به يقال له سلم الدين ثم أثبت الإبراء فقد انتهضت الخصومة الأولى
كما إذا ادعى على الوكيل بالخصومة إبراء موكله الغائب وجماهير القضاة على
أنه لا يطالب بالتسليم إذا كانت البينة حاضرة بخلاف الموكل الغائب فإن
تأخير ذلك يطول وكذا لو قال لي بينة غائبة فيكفيه تسليم العين والدين في
الحال
الفرع الثاني من أقر لغيره بملك ثم عاد إلى الدعوى لم تقبل دعواه حتى
يدعى تلقي الملك منه أما إذا أخرج من يده بينة فجاء يدعى مطلقا ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه لا يقبل إذ البينة في حقه كالإقرار
والثاني أنه يقبل لأن الرجل يؤاخد بإقرار نفسه في الإستقبال ولولاه لم
يكن في الأقارير فائدة
أما حكم البينة فلا يلزم بكل حال ولا خلاف أن  دعوى ثالث بالملك مطلقا
تسمع إذ لم يلزمه حكم البينة المقامة على غيره فهذا ثلاث مراتب فلتفهم
الحالة الثالثة أن تكون الدار في يدهما وادعى كل واحد جميعها
فإن لم تكن بينة فيتحالفان إذ كل واحد مدع في النصف مدعى عليه في النصف
فيبدأ القاضي بمن يراه أو بالقرعة فإن حلفا أو نكلا بقي الدار في يدهما كما
كان وإنما يحلف كل واحد على النفي بخلاف المتحالفين في البيع إذ كل واحد
يحلف على إثبات ما يدعيه ونفي ما يدعى عليه لأنه ليس يميز في البيع المدعي
عن المدعى عليه أما ها هنا فالتمييز ظاهر إذ نصف الدار مميز عن النصف الآخر
ومنهم من قال في المسألتين قولان بالنقل والتخريج
أما إذا حلف الأول ونكل الثاني ردت اليمين على الأول فيحلف على الإثبات
في النصف الآخر لأن هذه يمين المدعي المردودة
فلو أقام الناكل بينة بعد اليمين المردودة ففيه وجهان ينبنيان على أن
اليمين المردودة كالإقرار أو البينة فإن قلنا إنها كالإقرار لم تقبل أما
إذا نكل الأول فتعرض على الثاني يمين النفي واليمين المردودة وفي تعدد
اليمين وجهان
أحدهما أنه يتعدد لتعدد الجهة
والثاني أنه تكفي يمين واحدة جامعة بين النفي والإثبات للإيجاز فيحلف أن
جميع الدار له ليس لصاحبه فيها حق فلو قال والله إن النصف الذي يدعيه ليس
له فيه حق والنصف الآخر هو لي اكتفي بذلك
أما إذا كان لأحدهما بينة فتسمع ابتداء وإن كان داخلا في النصف ولكن تسمع
تابعا للنصف الآخر وإنما ينقدح الرد على رد بينة الداخل وحده إذا أنشأ مع
الإستغناء عنه وههنا احتاج لأجل النصف ولكن لو أقام الثاني بينة فقد قيل
الآن يجب على الأول إعادة بينته ليقع بعد بينة
الخارج ولا يبعد التساهل فيه أيضا
المدرك الثالث اشتمال إحدى البينتين على زيادة تاريخ أو سبب ملك والنظر
في أطراف
الأول في التاريخ فإن تساويا في التاريخ فيتعارضان وإن شهدت إحداهما على
الملك منذ سنة والأخرى منذ سنتين ففيه قولان
أحدهما أنها يتعارضان إذ المطلوب هو الملك في الحال فلا تأثير للسبق
والثاني ترجح السابقة وهو اختيار المزني ومذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله لأن
ما سبق ثبوته فالأصل بقاؤه فيصلح للترجيح واستدل المزني بما لو شهدت
إحداهما النتاج في يده أو سبب آخر من أسباب الملك فإنه يقضي بتقديمها وقضى
الأصحاب بطرد القولين وإن شهدت إحداهما على سبب الملك أيضا
ويجري القولان في بينة الزوجين على الزوجية إذا سبق التاريخ فإن كانت
إحدى البنتين مطلقة والأخرى مؤرخة فقولان مرتبان وأولى بأن لا ترجح لأن
المطلقة كالعامة
أما إذا كالن السبق في جانب واليد في جانب فإن قلنا السبق لا ترجيح به
فاليد مقدمة وإن رجحنا به فهاهنا ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أن السبق أولى
والثاني اليد أولى
والثالث أنهما يتعارضان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ب-ي-ن (bayyina)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Clarity, separation, and manifest distinction; bayyina is that which makes truth evident and separates it from falsehood.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Judicial proof that renders a claim manifestly established; in legal theology, it is the evidentiary instrument by which a right (ḥaqq) is actualized.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense is "clear evidence"; metaphorically extended to any proof (including oath or admission) that discloses hidden matters.
- Root: ق-ر-ر (iqrār)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To affirm, establish, or settle; iqrār is the acknowledgment that fixes a right against oneself.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A self-incriminating declaration that binds the declarant, treated as conclusive against him but not against others.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "making firm"; legally, it is the voluntary confession that operates like proof (bayyina) against the confessor alone.
- Root: ن-ك-ل (nukūl)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To abstain, withdraw, or refuse; in oath-contexts, refusal to swear.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Refusal of the oath (yamīn) which, in judicial procedure, converts the opponent's oath into a decisive proof.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal "turning away"; metaphorically, the litigant's abstention from swearing, which yields the same effect as an admission.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text's legal distinctions hinge on conditional clauses (law, idhā) and exceptions (illā), requiring precise parsing of protasis and apodosis to preserve the juristic gradations.
chapters.translation:
### Two Subsidiary Branches

**The First Branch:** If the outsider (al-khārij) produces evidence of absolute ownership, and the insider (al-dākhil) produces evidence that the property is his, having purchased it from the outsider, the insider's evidence takes precedence — just as if he had made an unqualified claim, and his hand (possession) is not removed before the evidence is presented. Al-Qāḍī (Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him) said: His hand is removed when he claims that, for it is said: "You have acknowledged ownership to him, so surrender it to him, then prove what you claim of purchase." Likewise, if he says: "I claim that he released me from the debt claimed against me," it is said to him: "Surrender the debt, then prove the release." Thus the first litigation is concluded — just as when one claims against an agent (wakīl) that his absent principal released him. The majority of judges hold that he is not required to surrender when the evidence is present, unlike the case of the absent principal, for delaying that would be prolonged. Similarly, if he says: "I have absent evidence," it suffices for him to surrender the chattel and the debt immediately.

**The Second Branch:** Whoever acknowledges ownership of something to another, then reverts to claiming it, his claim is not accepted unless he claims that he acquired ownership from him. However, if he produced evidence while the property was in his hand, then comes forward with an unqualified claim, there are two aspects (wajhān):
- One: It is not accepted, for evidence in his case is like an acknowledgment (iqrār).
- The second: It is accepted, for a man is bound by his own acknowledgment in the future; and were it not so, there would be no benefit in acknowledgments.

As for the ruling of the evidence, it is not binding in every case. And there is no disagreement that a third party's unqualified claim of ownership is heard, for the ruling of evidence presented against another does not bind him. These are three ranks — so understand them.

**The Third Case:** That the house is in the hands of both, and each claims the whole of it.
- If there is no evidence, they both take oaths (taḥāluf), for each is a claimant (muddaʿī) regarding half and a defendant (muddaʿā ʿalayh) regarding half. The judge begins with whomever he deems fit, or by lot (qurʿah). If both swear or both refuse, the house remains in their hands as it was. Each swears only to negation (nafy) — unlike the two parties taking oaths in a sale, where each swears to affirm what he claims and negate what is claimed against him, because in a sale the claimant is not distinguished from the defendant. Here, however, the distinction is evident, for half of the house is distinguished from the other half.
- Some said that in both cases there are two opinions, by transmission (naql) and by derivation (takhrij).

If the first swears and the second refuses, the oath is returned (radd) to the first, who swears to affirmation (ithbāt) regarding the other half — for this is the returned oath of the claimant (yamīn al-muddaʿī al-mardūdah).

If the one who refused produces evidence after the returned oath, there are two aspects, built upon whether the returned oath is like an acknowledgment or like evidence. If we say it is like an acknowledgment, it is not accepted.

If the first refuses, the second is offered the oath of negation and the returned oath. Regarding the multiplicity of oaths, there are two aspects:
- One: They multiply due to the multiplicity of aspects (jihāt).
- The second: A single comprehensive oath suffices, combining negation and affirmation, for brevity. He swears: "All of the house is mine; the other has no right in it." If he says: "By Allah, the half he claims — he has no right in it, and the other half is mine," that suffices.

If one of them has evidence, it is heard initially, even if he is an insider regarding half — but it is heard as a corollary (tābiʿan) to the other half. Objection to rejecting the insider's evidence alone arises only when he initiates it while independent of it; here he needs it for the half. But if the second produces evidence, it is said: Now the first must repeat his evidence, so that it falls after the outsider's evidence. And leniency in this is not far-fetched.

**The Third Consideration (al-mudrak al-thālith):** That one of the two evidences includes an additional date (tārīkh) or a cause of ownership (sabab al-milk). The examination concerns its peripheries.

**The First Periphery — Regarding the Date:** If the dates are equal, they conflict (taʿāruḍ). If one testifies to ownership since one year and the other since two years, there are two opinions:
- One: They conflict, for what is sought is ownership in the present, so precedence has no effect.
- The second: The earlier one is preferred (tarjīḥ) — this is the choice of al-Muzanī and the school of Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him), because what has been established earlier, its continuance is the default (al-aṣl baqāʾuhu), so it is fit for preference. Al-Muzanī argued by the case where one evidence testifies to the birth of livestock in his hand, or another cause of ownership — for judgment is given by preferring it. The companions (al-aṣḥāb) extended the two opinions to the case where one evidence testifies to a cause of ownership as well.
- The two opinions also apply to the evidence of spouses regarding marriage (zawjiyyah) when the date precedes. If one of the two evidences is unqualified (muṭlaqah) and the other dated (muʾarrakhah), there are two opinions, arranged — and it is more fitting that no preference is given, for the unqualified is like the general (al-ʿāmmah).

If precedence is on one side and possession (yad) on the other: If we say precedence gives no preference, then possession is given priority. If we prefer by it, then here there are three aspects:
- One: Precedence is more fitting.
- The second: Possession is more fitting.
- The third: They conflict.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | تنبيهات

الأول إذا شهدت البينة على ملك إنسان بالأمس ولم تتعرض له في الحال لم
تقبل على الجديد بخلاف ما لو شهد على إقراره بالأمس فإنه يثبت الإقرار
والإقرار الثابت مستدام حكمه وعليه عمل الأولين وإلا لبطلت فائدة الأقارير
لأن المقر يخبر عن تحقيق فيظهر استصحابه والشاهد يشهد على تخمين في الملك
فإذا لم ينضم إليه الجزم في الحال لم يؤثر وكذلك لو شهدت البينة على أنه
كان ملكه بالأمس اشتراه من صاحب اليد فتقبل لأنه يدرك يقينا بخلاف ما لو
قال اشتراه من غيره لأنه لا يكون حجة على صاحب اليد أما إذا أقر المدعى
عليه بملك سابق وقال للمدعي كان ملكك أمس فهل يلزمه التسليم استصحابا فيه
وجهان
أحدهما أنه يلزمه كما لو ثبت إقراره بالأمس
والثاني لا كما لو شهدت البينة على ملكه بالأمس فإنه مردد بينهما ثلاث
مراتب وهاهنا قول قديم أن البينة وإن شهدت على الملك بالأمس فتقبل كالإقرار
بالأمس ووجه غريب مال إليه القاضي أن الإقرار السابق إذا شهدت عليه البينة
لا يسمع ما لم يتعرض الشاهد للملك في الحال والمشهور الفرق كما سبق

### | التفريع

إذا فرعنا على الجديد فسبيل الشاهد أن يقول كان ملكه  بالأمس ولم يزل أو
هو الآن ملكه ويكون مستنده فيه الإستصحاب ويجوز ذلك إذا لم يعلم مزيلا فلو
صرح بأني مستصحب ملكه فإني لا أعلم مزيلا قال الأصحاب لا تقبل كشهادة
الرضاع على صورة الإمتصاص وحركة الحلقوم وقال القاضي تقبل إذ نعلم أنه لا
مستند له سواه بخلاف الرضاع إذ يدرك ذلك بقرائن لا تعرب العبارة عنه نعم لو
قال الشاهد في معرض مرتاب لا أدري أزال ملكه أو لم يزل لم تسمع لفساد
الصيغة
أما إذا قال لا أعلم مزيلا كفاه وأكثر الأصحاب على أنه لا بد من الجزم في
الحال
ولا خلاف أن البينة لو شهدت بأنه كان في يد المدعي بالأمس قبل وجعل
المدعي صاحب اليد
التنبيه الثاني لا توجب الملك لكن تظهره ومن ضرورته التقدم بلحظة على
الإقامة فلو كان المدعى دابة فنتاجها الذي نتج قبل الإقامة للمدعى عليه وما
نتج بعد الإقامة وقبل التعديل فللمدعي فلو كانت
شجرة ثمرتها بادية فهي للمدعى عليه
وفي الحمل احتمال إذ انفصال الملك فيه ممكن بالوصية وهذا في البينة
المطلقة التي لا تتعرض لملك سابق
التنبيه الثالث أن مقتضى ما ذكرناه أن لا يرجع المشتري بالثمن إذا أخذ
منه المبيع ببينة مطلقة لأنه ليس يقتضي الزوال إلا من الوقت قال القاضي
يحتمل أن يقال لا يرجع إذا كانت الدعوى والبينة مستندة إلى ملك سابق وإطلاق
الأصحاب يحمل على
أنهم أرادوا ذلك فإنه غير نادر لكنه قال في كلام الأصحاب ما يدل على خلاف
ما قلته إذ قالوا لو أخذ من المشتري أو المتهب من المشتري فللمشتري الأول
الرجوع على البائع منه ولعل سببه أن البينة إذا كانت مطلقة لا تشهد على
إزالة الملك فيحمل على الصدق المطلق فالحاجة تمس إلى ذلك في عهدة العقود
أما إذا ادعى عليه أنك أزلت الملك فأنكر وقامت البينة على إزالته فلا
رجوع له وأما مجرد دعوى المدعي للإحالة عليه فلا تمنع الرجوع إذا لم تشهد
البينة عليه
التنبيه الرابع لو ادعى أرضا وزرعا  فيها وأقام بينة عليها وأنه زرعها
وأقام صاحب اليد بينة أما الأرض فلصاحب اليد وأما الزرع فيبنى على أن السبق
واليد إذا اجتمعا أيهما يقدم
الخامس إذا ادعى ملكا مطلقا فذكر الشاهد الملك وسببه لم يضر لكن إن طلب
الخصم تقديم حجته لاشتمالها على ذكر السبب فلا يجاب إليه إلا بأن تعاد
البينة بعد دعواه فإن الذكر قبل الدعوى لاغ ولا تجرح البينة بخلاف ما لو
ادعى ألفا فشهدت البينت على ألفين رد في الزيادة لأنها زيادة مستقلة وهل
ترد في الباقي كيلا تتبعض البينة فيه وجهان
فإن قلنا ترد فهل يصير الشاهد مجروحا به فيه وجهان يجري في كل شهادة تؤدي
قبل الدعوى
ولو ذكر المدعي سببا وذكر الشاهد سببا آخر فالصحيح أنه لا يقبل للتناقض
وقيل تقبل على الملك ويلغى السبب
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ش-ه-د (sh-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be present, to witness, to testify; the root implies direct presence and perceptual certainty (muʿāyana).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological usage, shahāda is a formal attestation of a fact, requiring certainty (yaqīn), not conjecture (ẓann) or presumption.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) = eyewitness presence; metaphorical (majāz) = testifying to a legal state (e.g., ownership) based on evidentiary inference.
- Root: ق-ر-ر (q-r-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To settle, affirm, confess; the root conveys establishment and persistence.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iqrār (confession) is an informative utterance (khabar) about a prior state of fact, which by its nature endures (istishāb) until counter-evidence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = verbal acknowledgment; metaphorical = the legal effect of that acknowledgment as a continuing obligation.
- Root: ص-ح-ب (ṣ-ḥ-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Companionship, association; the root denotes being with or attached to something.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ṣāḥib al-yad (possessor in fact) — one whose physical control (yad) over an object is the presumptive basis of ownership.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal = physical accompaniment; metaphorical = legal possession and its evidentiary weight.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The text's distinctions hinge on whether the testimony's scope (mutʿallaq) is temporally restricted (e.g., "yesterday") or absolute (muṭlaq), affecting the predicate's validity.
chapters.translation:
### | Cautions

**First Caution:** If the witnesses testify to a person's ownership "yesterday" but do not address his ownership at the present moment, their testimony is not accepted according to the new doctrine (al-jadīd) — unlike the case where they testify to his confession made yesterday; for the confession is thereby established, and an established confession has a continuing legal effect (ḥukm mustadām), and upon this the practice of the early scholars proceeded. Otherwise, the utility of confessions would be nullified — because the confessor reports about a verified matter (taḥqīq), so its continuance (istishāb) becomes manifest; whereas the witness testifies to a conjecture (takhmin) regarding ownership, and if present-tense certainty is not joined to it, it has no effect. Likewise, if the witnesses testify that the object was his property yesterday, having purchased it from the current possessor (ṣāḥib al-yad), it is accepted — because it is grasped with certainty. This differs from the case where they say he purchased it from someone else, for that is not a proof against the current possessor.

As for when the defendant confesses to prior ownership and says to the plaintiff, "It was your property yesterday" — is he obliged to surrender it on the basis of continuance (istishāb)? There are two views:
- One: He is obliged, just as if his confession of yesterday had been established.
- The second: He is not obliged, just as if witnesses had testified to his ownership of yesterday — for it is undetermined between them.

There are three ranks here. And there is an old doctrine (qawl qadīm) that even if witnesses testify to ownership of yesterday, it is accepted, like a confession of yesterday. There is also a strange view, favored by al-Qāḍī [Abū Ṭayyib al-Ṭabarī], that a prior confession, if witnesses testify to it, is not heard unless the witness addresses present ownership — while the well-known distinction is as previously stated.

### | Derivation

If we proceed on the new doctrine, the proper course for the witness is to say: "It was his property yesterday and has not ceased to be," or "It is now his property" — his basis being continuance (istishāb). This is permissible if he knows of no annulling factor (muzīl). But if he explicitly says, "I am continuing his ownership, for I know of no annulling factor," the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: It is not accepted — like testimony to fosterage (riḍāʿ) based on the mere form of sucking and throat movement. Al-Qāḍī said: It is accepted, for we know he has no other basis than this — unlike fosterage, which is grasped through circumstantial indicators (qarāʾin) that expression cannot articulate. Indeed, if the witness says in a hesitant manner, "I do not know whether his ownership has been annulled or not," it is not heard, due to the corruption of the formulation (fasād al-ṣīgha).

But if he says, "I know of no annulling factor," it suffices him. The majority of the companions hold that present-tense certainty (jazm fī al-ḥāl) is indispensable.

There is no disagreement that if witnesses testify that the object was in the plaintiff's hand yesterday, it is accepted, and the plaintiff becomes the possessor in fact (ṣāḥib al-yad).

**Second Caution:** Testimony does not effect ownership (tūjib al-milk); rather, it manifests it (tuẓhiruhu). And from its necessity is that it precedes by a moment the establishment (iqāma) [of the claim]. Thus, if the claimed object is a beast, its offspring born before the establishment belongs to the defendant; what is born after the establishment but before the attestation (taʿdīl) belongs to the plaintiff. If it is a tree whose fruit is already apparent, it belongs to the defendant. As for the fetus (ḥaml), there is a probability — because the separation of ownership therein is possible through bequest (waṣiyya). This concerns the absolute testimony (bayyina muṭlaqa) that does not address prior ownership.

**Third Caution:** The implication of what we have stated is that the purchaser does not recover the price if the sold object is taken from him by absolute testimony — because it does not imply annulment (zawāl) except from that time. Al-Qāḍī said: It may be said that he does not recover if the claim and testimony are based on prior ownership; and the unqualified statements of the companions are to be understood as intending that — for it is not uncommon. However, he noted in the companions' discourse something indicating the contrary of what I said: for they said, if it is taken from the purchaser, or from the donee of the purchaser, the first purchaser has recourse against his seller. Perhaps the reason is that when the testimony is absolute, it does not testify to the annulment of ownership, so it is construed upon absolute truthfulness — and necessity demands this in the warranty of contracts (ʿuhdat al-ʿuqūd).

As for when he claims against him, "You annulled the ownership," and he denies, and testimony is established upon his annulment — then he has no recourse. As for the mere claim of the plaintiff to refer [the liability] upon him, it does not prevent recourse if the testimony does not establish it against him.

**Fourth Caution:** If he claims land and crops therein, and establishes testimony upon both and that he planted it, and the possessor in fact establishes testimony — as for the land, it belongs to the possessor in fact; as for the crops, it is built upon the question: when priority (sabq) and possession (yad) are combined, which is given precedence?

**Fifth:** If he claims absolute ownership, and the witness mentions the ownership and its cause (sabab), it does no harm. But if the opponent requests the presentation of his evidence because it includes the mention of the cause, he is not answered — except that the testimony be repeated after his claim; for the mention before the claim is void (lāgh). And the testimony is not thereby discredited. This differs from the case where he claims one thousand and the two witnesses testify to two thousand — the excess is rejected, because it is an independent addition. Is it rejected in the remainder as well, so that the testimony is not divided (lā tatabbaʿaḍ)? There are two views.

If we say it is rejected, does the witness thereby become discredited (majrūḥ)? There are two views — applicable to every testimony rendered before the claim.

If the claimant mentions one cause and the witness mentions another cause, the correct view is that it is not accepted, due to contradiction (tanāquḍ). And it was said: It is accepted upon the ownership, and the cause is annulled.

### | الطرف الثاني التنازع في العقود

وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا قال صاحب الدار أكريت بيتا من الدار بعشرة وقال المكتري بل
اكتريت الكل بعشرة وأقام كل واحد بينة قال ابن سريج بينة المكتري أولى
لاشتماله على ذكر زيادة حتى لو قال المكري اكتريت جميع الدار بعشرين وقال
المكتري بل بعشرة فبينة المكري أولى لأن فيه زيادة وهو ضعيف بل الصحيح
التعارض لأن هذه زيادة في مقدار المشهود به وليس فيه زيادة إيضاح بخلاف
استناد الملك إلى سبب أو تاريخ سابق فإن فرعنا على التعارض ورأينا التهاتر
فيتحالفان وكأنه لا بينة ولا تجعل الزيادة مرعية وبه يتبين ضعف رأي ابن
سريج وإن قلنا بالوقف فلا وجه له إذ المنافع تفوت وإن قلنا بالقسمة فكذلك
فإن الزيادة يدعيها واحد وينفيها الآخر وإنما يمكن القسمة إذا ادعى كل واحد
لنفسه وأما القرعة فممكن ولكن استعمالها ضعيف لأنها لا تستعمل إلا في إفراز
الحقوق المشتركة لينقطع النزاع أو في العتق للخبر
ومن رأى القسمة أو الوقف وتعذر عليه اختلفوا منهم من رجع إلى قول التهاتر
لعسر
الإستعمال ومنهم من رجع إلى الطريق الممكن في الإستعمال وهو القرعة فيرى
الإستعمال بأحد الطرق أولى  من التهاتر
الثانية إذا ادعى رجلان دارا في يد ثالث يزعم كل واحد أن الثالث قد باعه
وقبض منه مائة في ثمنها فتجري الأقوال الأربعة في بينتيهما لكن لا بد من
البينة لأمور
أحدها أنا على قول القرعة نسلم الدار إلى من خرجت قرعته ونسلم الثمن إلى
الثاني لأن القرعة مؤثرة في محل التناقض وهو رقبة الدار أما اجتماع الثمنين
عليه فممكن لا تضاد فيه
وعلى قول الوقف تخرج الدار والثمن من يده ويتوقف فيهما
وعلى قول القسمة يأخذ كل واحد نصف الدار ونصف الثمن ثم لكل واحد أن يمتنع
عن النصف لتبعض المبيع عليه فيرجع إلى جميع الثمن فإن فسخ
أحدهما فللآخر أن يطلب جميع الدار إذ يقول كانت القسمة لأجل المزاحم وقد
اندفع وفيه وجه أنه يقتصر على النصف
الثاني أن الشيخ أبا محمد قال لا أجري قول القرعة إذا كانتا مطلقتين غير
مؤرختين حتى يؤرخا بتاريخ واحد يظهر تناقضه إذ هي لتمييز الكاذب وصدقهما
ممكن بتعاقب عقدين بعد تخلل ملك وهذا ضعيف بل هي لتقديم أحد المتساويين
الثالث أن الربعي خرج قولا خامسا وهو أن تستعمل البينتان لفسخ العقدين إذ
تعذر عقد كل واحد بسبب بينة الآخر
الرابع أن الأقوال تجري إذا كانتا مطلقتين أو مؤرختين بتاريخ واحد أما
إذا سبق تاريخ إحداهما فهي مقدمة لأن البيع إذا ثبت سبقه منع صحة ما بعده
المسألة الثالثة عكس الثانية وهو أن يدعي كل واحد منهما بيع الدار من
الثالث بألف ومقصودهما طلب الألف وترك الدار في يده فالصحيح أن الأقوال لا
تجري لأن الذمة متسعة لإثبات الثمنين فيلزمه توفيتهما بخلاف ما إذا كان
المطلوب منه رقبة الدار لأنها واحدة تضيق ومن الأصحاب من أجرى الأقوال
لأنهما ربطا الثمنين بعين واحدة ولا يصح ذلك إلا إذا عينا وقتا واحدا
يستحيل تقدير الجمع وإلا فلزوم الثمنين في عقدين بينهما ببدل ملك ممكن إلا
أن تعيين وقت واحد لا يتسع لكلمتين أيضا لا يدركه الحس إلا إذا اكتفينا
بجواز شهادة النفي  مهما استند إلى وقت معين فإن السكوت عن البيع يشاهد
فنعلم أنه نفى البيع وفي مثل تلك الشهادة خلاف
المسألة الرابعة ادعى عبد أن مولاه أعتقه وادعى آخر أن مولاه باعه منه
وأقام كل واحد بينة فإن كان فيهما تاريخ قدم السابق لأنه يمنع صحة ما بعده
وإن لم يكن جرى الأقوال كلها
وعلى قول القسمة يعتق نصف العبد ويحكم بالملك في النصف والصحيح أنه لا
يسري إليه العتق لأنه محكوم به قهرا وذكر العراقيون قولين وزعموا أنه يسري
إليه العتق في قول لأنه حكم عليه باختياره العتق واعترض المزني وقال ينبغي
أن تقدم بينة العتق لأن العبد كصاحب اليد في حق رقبته وهو ضعيف لأنه في يد
سيده ما لم يثبت عتقه فهو يدعي اليد ولم تثبت بعد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ن-ز-ع (n-z-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To pull away, snatch, or contest; mutual contention over a single object of claim.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Disputation (tanāzuʿ) implying opposing claims over one right, distinct from mere difference (ikhtilāf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in legal context—actual conflicting assertions; metaphorical extension to competing evidences.
- Root: ت-ه-ا-ت-ر (t-h-a-t-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Mutual nullification; each party's claim cancels the other's.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic method, the doctrine of taḥātur—when two conflicting proofs are equal, both are disregarded.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: mutual destruction; here technical: annulment of both claims.
- Root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Casting lots; drawing straws.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A procedural device for allocating shared rights when evidence fails.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: striking; metaphorical: the lot's "strike" upon one claimant.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional apodosis with fa- (fa-l-tahātur) — the protasis (if we branch on taʿāruḍ) governs the apodosis, marking legal consequence.
chapters.translation:
### The Second Aspect: Disputes Concerning Contracts

Within it are several questions.

**The First Question:** If the owner of a house says, "I rented out a room of the house for ten," and the tenant says, "Rather, I rented the whole [house] for ten," and each produces evidence, Ibn Surayj said: The tenant's evidence takes precedence, because it includes mention of an increase [in the object]. Even if the owner said, "I rented the entire house for twenty," and the tenant said, "Rather, for ten," then the owner's evidence takes precedence, because it contains an increase [in the price]. But this is weak. Rather, the correct [view] is mutual conflict (taʿāruḍ), because this is an increase in the quantity of what is testified to, not an increase in clarification—unlike attributing ownership to a cause or an earlier date. If we branch upon mutual conflict and adopt the doctrine of mutual nullification (taḥātur), then both parties take an oath, as if there were no evidence at all, and the increase is not given consideration. By this, the weakness of Ibn Surayj's opinion becomes evident. If we say [the matter] is suspended (waqf), there is no basis for it, since the usufructs are lost. And if we say [the matter] is divided (qisma), likewise—for the increase is claimed by one and denied by the other; division is only possible when each claims [a share] for himself. As for casting lots (qurʿa), it is possible, but its use is weak, because it is only employed in allocating shared rights to cut off dispute, or in manumission, due to the report [hadith]. Among those who favor division or suspension and find it impracticable, they differ: some revert to the doctrine of mutual nullification due to the difficulty of application; others revert to the practicable method of application, namely casting lots. Thus, they hold that application by either method is preferable to mutual nullification.

**The Second Question:** If two men claim a house in the possession of a third, each claiming that the third sold it to him and that he paid him one hundred as its price, then the four doctrines apply regarding their two evidences. But evidence is indispensable for several reasons:

**First:** On the doctrine of casting lots, we surrender the house to the one whose lot emerges, and we surrender the price to the second—because the lot is effective in the locus of contradiction, namely the corpus of the house. As for the two prices being incumbent upon him [the seller], that is possible, with no contradiction therein.

**Second:** On the doctrine of suspension, the house and the price both leave his hand and are held in abeyance.

**Third:** On the doctrine of division, each takes half the house and half the price. Then each may refuse the half due to the partition of the sold object upon him, and thus revert to claiming the entire price. If one of them rescinds, the other may demand the entire house, saying: "The division was due to the rival claimant, and he has now been repelled." There is a view that he is limited to the half.

**Fourth:** Shaykh Abū Muḥammad said: I do not apply the doctrine of casting lots when the two evidences are absolute (muṭlaqatān), without dates, until they are dated with a single date showing their contradiction—for the lot is meant to distinguish the liar, and their both being truthful is possible through two successive contracts after an intervening ownership. But this is weak; rather, it is for giving precedence to one of two equals.

**Fifth:** Al-Rabʿī advanced a fifth doctrine: that both evidences are used to rescind both contracts, since each contract is rendered impracticable by the other's evidence.

**Sixth:** The [four] doctrines apply when the evidences are absolute or dated with a single date. But if one's date precedes the other's, it takes precedence, because if the earlier sale is established, it prevents the validity of what follows it.

**The Third Question:** The converse of the second—namely, that each of the two claims the sale of the house from the third for one thousand, their purpose being to claim the thousand and leave the house in his hand. The correct [view] is that the doctrines do not apply, because the liability (dhimmah) is capacious enough to establish both prices, so he is obligated to pay both—unlike the case where the corpus of the house is sought, for it is single and constrained. Some of our companions applied the doctrines, because they tied both prices to a single entity, and that is only valid if they specify a single time at which the conjunction is impossible to conceive. Otherwise, the obligation of both prices in two contracts, each with a distinct consideration, is possible—except that specifying a single time does not accommodate two utterances either, nor does the senses perceive it, unless we are content with the permissibility of negative testimony (shahādat al-nafy) when based on a specific time. For silence about a sale is observable, so we know he negated the sale. Regarding such testimony, there is disagreement.

**The Fourth Question:** A slave claims that his master manumitted him, and another claims that the master sold him to him, and each produces evidence. If both are dated, the earlier takes precedence, because it prevents the validity of what follows. If undated, all the doctrines apply.

On the doctrine of division, half the slave is manumitted and ownership is decreed over the other half. The correct [view] is that manumission does not carry over (yasrī) to him, because it is decreed coercively. The Iraqis reported two views, claiming that manumission carries over to him in one view, because he is adjudged [to have chosen] manumission by his own choice. Al-Muzanī objected, saying: The evidence of manumission should take precedence, because the slave is like the possessor with respect to his own corpus. But this is weak, because he is in his master's hand until his manumission is established; he claims possession, and it is not yet established.

### | الطرف الثالث في النزاع في الموت والقتل

وفيه مسائل ثلاثة
الأولى رجل معروف بالتنصر مات وله ابن مسلم يدعي أنه مات مسلما والإبن
النصراني يدعي أنه لم يسلم فالقول قول النصراني لأن الأصل عدم الإسلام
ولو أقام كل واحد بينة قدمت بينة المسلم لاشتمالها على زيادة ناقلة عن
الإستصحاب وكذلك إذا ادعى الإبن الإرث في دار فأقامت زوجة أبيه بينة أنه
أصدقها الدار أو اشترتها من أبيه قدمت بينتها
أما إذا شهدت بينة النصراني أنه نطق بتنصر ومات عقيبه فقد تعارضا فتجري
الأقوال الأربعة وقال أبو إسحق المروزي لا يجري قول القسمة إذ لا يشترك في
الميراث مسلم وكافر وهذا ضعيف إذ كل بينة تقتضي كمال الملك لصاحبها فاندفع
في النصف بالأخرى إذ ليس أحدهما بأولى فيكفي إمكان الشركة في جنس الملك
أما إذا كان الميت مجهول الدين فقال كل واحد منهما لم يزل على ديني حتى
مات فليس أحدهما أولى بأن يجعل القول قوله فتجعل التركة كمال في يد اثنين
تنازعاه وقال القاضي إن كان في يد أحدهما كان القول قوله وهذه زلة لأنه
معترف بأن يده من جهة الميراث فلا أثر ليده مع ذلك
فإن أقام كل واحد بينة  جرت الأقوال الأربعة وقيل بينة الإسلام تقدم لأنه
الظاهر في
دار الإسلام وهذا بعيد إذ لو كان كذلك لجعل القول قوله نعم نص الشافعي
رضي الله عنه أن هذا الشخص يغسل ويصلى عليه إذا أشكل أمره والصلاة على
نصراني أهون من ترك الصلاة على مسلم
المسألة الثانية مات نصراني وله ابن مسلم يدعي أنه أسلم بعد موته فيرث
وابنه النصراني يدعي أنه أسلم قبل موته فلا يرث فللمسألة حالتان
إحداهما أن يتفقا على أنه أسلم في رمضان ولكن ادعى أن الأب مات في شعبان
وقال الأخ النصراني بل مات في شوال فالقول قول النصراني لأن الأصل بقاء
الحياة فإن أقام كل واحد بينة قال الأصحاب تقدم بينة المسلم لاشتمالها على
زيادة علم بالموت في شعبان أما كونه ميتا في شوال فمشترك قال الإمام هذا
ضعيف لأن من يشهد على الموت في شوال يشهد على موته عن حياة وإذا ثبت الحياة
حصل التعارض فتجري الأقوال
الحالة الثانية اتفقا على أنه مات في رمضان ولكن قال المسلم أسلمت في
شوال وقال النصراني بل أسلمت في شعبان فالقول قول المسلم إذ الأصل بقاء
الكفر وإن كان لهما بينة فتقدم بينة النصراني لأن الناقلة أولى من
المستصحبه

### | فرع

زوجة مسلمة وأخ مسلم وابنان كافران تنازعوا في إسلام الميت وتعارضت
بينتان فإن رأينا القسمة فالنصف للإثنين فإنهما فريق والنصف للزوجة والأخ
ثم الزوجة تأخذ الربع من هذا النصف لأن الإبن محجوب بقولهما فلا نردها إلى
اليمين
ولو خلف أبوين كافرين وابنين مسلمين وتنازعوا في دين الميت فوجهان
أحدهما أن القول قول الأبوين لأن الظاهر أن الولد يكون على دين الأبوين
والثاني أن القول قول الإبنين لأن الإسلام ينبغي أن يغلب بالدار
المسألة الثالثة قال لعبده إن قتلت فأنت حر فشهد اثنان أنه قتل وشهد
آخران أنه مات حتف أنفه فقولان
أحدهما التعارض
والثاني تقديم بينة القتل لاشتمالها على زيادة إذ كل قتيل ميت وليس كل
ميت قتيلا ولو قال لسالم إن مت في رمضان فأنت  حر وقال لغانم إن مت في شوال
فأنت حر وأقام كل واحد بينة فقولان
أحدهما التعارض
والثاني تقديم بينة رمضان لزيادة علمها بتقديم الموت وقال ابن سريج بينة
شوال أولى لأنه ربما يغمى عليه في رمضان فيظن موته
فرع إذا تنازع الزوجان في متاع البيت فهو في يدهما ولا يختص السلاح
بالرجل ولا آلة الغزل بالمرأة خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله
chapters.anchors:
- Root: م-و-ت (m-w-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Cessation of vital functions; death as the opposite of life (ḥayāh)
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Death as the separation of the soul from the body; in legal contexts, the factual event triggering inheritance (irth) and manumission (ʿitq)
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for biological death; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual ignorance or dormancy
- Root: ق-ت-ل (q-t-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The act of killing; causing death through direct agency
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Killing as a legal category distinct from natural death; relevant to qisāṣ, diyah, and evidentiary priority
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for homicide; metaphorical for subjugation or severe humiliation
- Root: أ-ص-ل (a-ṣ-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Foundation, root, origin; that upon which something is built
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal presumption of continuity (istisḥāb al-ḥāl) — the baseline state that remains until proven otherwise
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for physical root; technical legal sense for the presumptive default in evidentiary conflicts
- Root: ب-ي-ن-ة (b-y-n-h)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Clear evidence; proof that makes a matter manifest
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, the testimony of two upright witnesses establishing a claim
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for clarity; technical for legal proof, often contrasted with the mere presumption (aṣl)
- Sībawayh Rule: Taʿāruḍ al-Bayyināt (Conflict of Evidences) — When two opposing proofs are presented, the one containing an additional element (ziyādah) that transfers the case from the presumptive state (nāqilah ʿan al-istisḥāb) takes precedence; if both are equal in probative force, the four juristic opinions on conflicting evidence apply.
chapters.translation:
I say: The third branch concerns disputes over death and killing. It contains three questions.

**The First Question:** A man known for Christianity dies, leaving a Muslim son who claims that he died as a Muslim, while the Christian son claims that he never embraced Islam. The statement of the Christian is accepted, because the presumption (al-aṣl) is the absence of Islam. If each of them produces evidence (bayyinah), the evidence of the Muslim is given precedence, because it contains an additional element (ziyādah) that transfers the case from the presumption of continuity (istisḥāb). Likewise, if the son claims inheritance in a house, and the wife of his father produces evidence that the father had given her the house as dower (ṣadāq) or that she had purchased it from him, her evidence is given precedence.

However, if the Christian's evidence testifies that he uttered Christianity and died immediately thereafter, then the two evidences conflict, and the four opinions apply. Abū Isḥāq al-Marwazī said that the opinion of division (qawl al-qismah) does not apply, since a Muslim and an infidel do not share in inheritance. This is weak, for each evidence entails complete ownership for its proponent, and each is repelled in half by the other, since neither is more deserving. It suffices that sharing is possible in the genus of ownership.

If the deceased's religion was unknown, and each of the two says, "He remained upon my religion until he died," then neither is more deserving that his statement be accepted. The estate is thus treated as if it were in the hands of two claimants disputing it. Al-Qāḍī said: If it is in the hands of one of them, his statement is accepted. This is a lapse (zallah), because he admits that his possession derives from inheritance, so his possession has no effect despite that.

If each produces evidence, the four opinions apply. It was said that the evidence of Islam is preferred because Islam is the apparent norm in the Abode of Islam (dār al-Islām). This is far-fetched, for if that were so, his statement would have been accepted. Indeed, al-Shāfiʿī — may Allāh be pleased with him — explicitly stated that this person is washed and prayed over if his case is ambiguous. Praying over a Christian is less harmful than omitting prayer over a Muslim.

**The Second Question:** A Christian dies leaving a Muslim son who claims that he embraced Islam after his death, and thus he inherits, while his Christian son claims that he embraced Islam before his death, and thus he does not inherit. This question has two states:

**First State:** They agree that he embraced Islam in Ramaḍān, but the Muslim claims that the father died in Shaʿbān, while the Christian brother says, "Rather, he died in Shawwāl." The statement of the Christian is accepted, because the presumption is the continuation of life. If each produces evidence, the companions (al-aṣḥāb) said that the Muslim's evidence is preferred, because it contains additional knowledge of death in Shaʿbān. As for his being dead in Shawwāl, that is shared. The Imām said: This is weak, because whoever testifies to death in Shawwāl testifies to his death after life, and when life is established, conflict arises, and the opinions apply.

**Second State:** They agree that he died in Ramaḍān, but the Muslim says, "I embraced Islam in Shawwāl," while the Christian says, "Rather, he embraced Islam in Shaʿbān." The statement of the Muslim is accepted, because the presumption is the continuation of disbelief (kufr). If they have evidence, the Christian's evidence is preferred, because the transferring evidence (al-nāqilah) takes precedence over the one affirming the presumption (al-mustasḥabah).

### Branch

A Muslim wife, a Muslim brother, and two infidel sons dispute over the Islam of the deceased, and two evidences conflict. If we adopt the opinion of division, then half goes to the two sons, for they are one party, and half to the wife and brother. Then the wife takes one-fourth of this half, because the son is barred (maḥjūb) by their testimony, so we do not refer her to the oath.

If he leaves two infidel parents and two Muslim sons, and they dispute over the religion of the deceased, there are two views (wajhān):
- One: The statement of the parents is accepted, because the apparent norm is that the child follows the religion of the parents.
- The second: The statement of the two sons is accepted, because Islam ought to prevail by virtue of the Abode.

**The Third Question:** He said to his slave: "If you are killed, you are free." Two witnesses testify that he was killed, and two others testify that he died a natural death. There are two opinions:
- One: Conflict (taʿāruḍ).
- The second: The evidence of killing is preferred, because it contains an additional element, for every killed person is dead, but not every dead person is killed.

If he said to Sālim: "If you die in Ramaḍān, you are free," and to Ghānim: "If you die in Shawwāl, you are free," and each produces evidence, there are two opinions:
- One: Conflict.
- The second: The evidence of Ramaḍān is preferred, due to its additional knowledge of the earlier death. Ibn Surayj said: The evidence of Shawwāl is more deserving, because he might fall unconscious in Ramaḍān and be thought dead.

**Branch:** If spouses dispute over the household goods (matāʿ al-bayt), they are in both their hands. Weapons are not exclusively the man's, nor spinning tools exclusively the woman's — contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah — may Allāh have mercy on him.

### | الطرف الرابع في النزاع في الوصية والعتق

وفيه مسائل
الأولى إذا قامت بينة على أنه أعتق في مرضه عبدا وهو ثلث ماله وقامت بينة
أخرى لعبد آخر فالقياس أن يجعل كأنه أعتقهما معا فيقرع بينهما لكن نص
الشافعي رضي الله عنه على أنه يعتق من كل واحد نصفه فيجب تنزيله على موضع
لا تجري فيه القرعة وذلك بأن يتقدم عتق أحدهما فإنه لا قرعة ولو تقدم عتق
أحدهما ولكن أشكل السابق فهو كالإعتاق معا أو كالتعاقب فيه قولان فإن قلنا
لا يقرع فيحمل تعارض البينتين على هذه الصورة ونقول الغالب أنه أعتقهما
ترتيبا وأشكل الأمر فلا قرعة فيقسم عليهما
الثانية المسألة بحالها لكن أحد البعدين سدس المال فحيث يقرع لو خرج على
الخسيس يعتق بكماله ويعتق من النفيس نصفه لتكملة الثلث ولو خرج على النفيس
اقتصر عليه فإنه كمال الثلث وحيث نرى القسمة على قول ففي كفيته وجهان
أحدهما أنه يعتق من كل واحد ثلثاه لأن النفيس يضارب بضعف ما يضارب به
الخسيس كما لو أوصى لزيد بكل ماله ولعمرو بثلث ماله وأجاز الورثة الوصايا
إذ يقسم المال بينهما أرباعا فإن زيدا يضارب بثلاثة أمثال ما يضارب به عمرو
والوجه الثاني وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله أنه يعتق من النفيس ثلاثة
أرباع ومن الخسيس نصفه لأن النفيس يقول إن أعتقت أولا فجميعي حر وإن تأخرت
فنصفي حر فنصف مسلم لا خلاف فيه إنما النزاع في النصف الآخر وهو قدر سدس
بيني وبينك فيقسم عليهما وهذا أيضا ينبغي أن يطرد في مسألة الوصية فيقول
زيد أما الثلثان فهو مسلم  لي وإنما التزاحم في الثلث فيقسم علينا فيحصل زيد
على خمسة أسداس وعمرو على سدس وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله
الثالثة شهد أجنبيان أنه أوصى بعتق عبده غانم وهو ثلث المال وشهد وارثان
بأنه رجع عنه وأوصى بسالم وهو أيضا ثلث ثبت بقول الوارثين عتق سالم والرجوع
عن غانم إذ لا تهمة عليهما في تبديل محل العتق ولا نظر إلى تبدل الولاء فلا
يتهم العدل بمثله أما إذا كان سالم سدس المال فهو متهم بتنقيص السدس فترد
في قدر السدس والشهادة إذا ردت في بعض فهل ترد في الباقي قولان فإن قلنا
إنها ترد فيعتق العبدان جميعا الأول بالشهادة إذ ردت شهادة الرجوع والثاني
يعتق بإقرار الوارث وقد نص الشافعي رضي الله عنه على عتقهما
وإن قلنا لا ترد في الباقي فقد شهد على الرجوع عن جميع غانم وهو متهم في
النصف إذ لم يثبت له بدلا ولا يتهم في النصف في نصف غانم ويعتق نصفه مع
جميع سالم لأن نصف غانم سدس وجملة سالم سدس والثلث يفي بهما فكأنه أوصى
بعتق نصف غانم وجميع سالم ويحتمل أن يقال الرجوع لا يتجزأ فتبطل الشهادة
على الرجوع عن عتق غانم وتبقى الشهادة بالعتق لغانم وشهادة الورثة كشهادة
الأجانب فكأنه ثبت عتقهما جميعا فيقرع بينهما فإن خرج على غانم عتق فقط وإن
خرج على سالم عتق وعتق معه من غانم نصفه ليكمل الثلث
الرابعة شهدت بينة أنه أوصى لزيد بالثلث وشهدت أخرى لعمرو بالثلث وشهدت
أخرى بالرجوع عن إحدى الوصيتين لا بعينها قال الشافعي رضي الله عنه يقسم
الثلث بينهما قال الأصحاب سببه رد شهادة الرجوع لأنها مجملة وقال القفال
تقبل شهادة الرجوع لأن المشهود عليه والمشهود له معين
وتظهر فائدة الخلاف فيما لو كان شهد كل بينة بالسدس فإن رددنا شهادة
الرجوع المجملة أعطينا كل واحد سدسا كاملا وإن قبلنا الشهادة وزعنا سدسا
واحدا عليهما
وقد تم الكلام في الدعاوى فلنذكر دعوى النسب
= كتاب دعوى النسب وإلحاق القائف=
والنظر في  أركان الإلحاق وهي ثلاثة المستلحق والملحق والإلحاق

- Root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Drawing lots; casting of arrows for division of shares when rights conflict.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A procedural mechanism for resolving competing claims when equal evidence exists, reflecting divine allocation of shares.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal in the sense of physical lots; metaphorical when applied to legal presumption of priority.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause Nesting (Taʿlīq al-Sharṭ) — The protasis "إذا قامت بينة" governs multiple coordinated apodoses, requiring careful tracking of legal hypotheticals.

I say: The fourth branch concerns disputes arising in bequests and manumission.

It contains several questions.

**The First Question:** If evidence establishes that a man manumitted a slave during his death-illness, that slave being one-third of his estate, and another evidence establishes [manumission of] another slave, then the analogical principle is that it is as if he manumitted both simultaneously, and lots are cast between them. However, al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly ruled that half of each slave is manumitted. This ruling must be interpreted as applying to a case where casting lots is not applicable — namely, where the manumission of one preceded the other, for in that case there is no casting of lots. But if one manumission preceded the other yet the order of priority is obscure, there are two opinions: whether it is like simultaneous manumission or like sequential manumission. If we say that lots are not cast, then the conflict of the two evidences is interpreted upon this scenario, and we say: the predominant likelihood is that he manumitted them sequentially, but the matter is obscure, so no lots are cast, and [the estate] is divided between them.

**The Second Question:** The case is the same, but one of the two slaves is one-sixth of the estate. Wherever lots are cast, if the lot falls upon the lesser-valued slave, he is manumitted in full, and half of the more-valuable slave is manumitted to complete the third. If the lot falls upon the more-valuable slave, he alone suffices, for he constitutes the full third. And wherever we adopt the opinion of division, there are two aspects concerning its modality:

- **The First Aspect:** One-third of each slave is manumitted, because the more-valuable slave competes with twice the claim of the lesser-valued slave — just as if one bequeathed all his property to Zayd and one-third of his property to ʿAmr, and the heirs ratified the bequests, the property would be divided between them in fourths, for Zayd competes with three times the claim of ʿAmr.

- **The Second Aspect** — and this is the doctrine of Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him): Three-quarters of the more-valuable slave is manumitted and half of the lesser-valued slave. For the more-valuable slave argues: "If I was manumitted first, then all of me is free; if I was manumitted later, then half of me is free." Thus half is uncontested — there is no dispute concerning it. The dispute concerns only the other half, which is the amount of one-sixth, shared between me and him, so it is divided between them. This reasoning should also be extended to the question of bequests, such that Zayd says: "Two-thirds is uncontested for me; the competition concerns only the third, so it is divided between us." Thus Zayd receives five-sixths and ʿAmr receives one-sixth — and this is the doctrine of Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him).

**The Third Question:** Two unrelated witnesses testified that he bequeathed the manumission of his slave Ghānim, who is one-third of the estate. Two heirs testified that he revoked that and bequeathed [the manumission of] Sālim, who is also one-third. By the testimony of the two heirs, the manumission of Sālim and the revocation of Ghānim's [bequest] are established — for there is no accusation of bias against them in changing the locus of manumission, and no consideration is given to the change of clientage (walāʾ), for a just person is not accused of such a matter. However, if Sālim is one-sixth of the estate, then [the heirs] are accused of bias in diminishing [the freed portion] by one-sixth, so their testimony is rejected to the extent of that one-sixth. When testimony is rejected in part, is it rejected entirely? There are two opinions:

- If we say it is rejected entirely, then both slaves are manumitted: the first by the [original] testimony, since the testimony of revocation is rejected, and the second by the heirs' acknowledgment. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) explicitly ruled their manumission.

- If we say it is not rejected for the remainder, then [the heirs] testified to the revocation of all of Ghānim's [manumission], yet they are accused of bias concerning half of him — since no substitute was established for them — but they are not accused concerning the other half. Thus half of Ghānim is manumitted along with all of Sālim, because half of Ghānim is one-sixth and all of Sālim is one-sixth, and the third suffices for both. It is as if he bequeathed the manumission of half of Ghānim and all of Sālim.

It is also possible to say: revocation is indivisible, so the testimony of revocation of Ghānim's manumission is void, while the testimony of manumission for Ghānim remains. The heirs' testimony is like that of unrelated witnesses — as if both manumissions are established, so lots are cast between them. If the lot falls upon Ghānim, he alone is manumitted; if it falls upon Sālim, he is manumitted along with half of Ghānim to complete the third.

**The Fourth Question:** One evidence testified that he bequeathed one-third to Zayd, another testified [the same] for ʿAmr, and a third testified to the revocation of one of the two bequests without specifying which. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the third is divided between them. The companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: the reason is the rejection of the revocation testimony because it is ambiguous (mujmalah). Al-Qaffāl said: the revocation testimony is accepted, because the one against whom it is testified and the one for whom it is testified are both determinate.

The utility of this disagreement appears in a case where each evidence testified to one-sixth: if we reject the ambiguous revocation testimony, we give each one a full sixth; if we accept the testimony, we distribute a single sixth between them.

The discourse on claims (daʿāwā) is now complete. Let us now mention the claim of lineage (nasab).

= The Book of Claims of Lineage and the Attestation of the Qāʾif =

The consideration concerns the pillars of attestation, which are three: the one who claims lineage (al-mustalḥiq), the one whose lineage is claimed (al-mulḥaq), and the act of attestation (al-ilḥāq).

### | الركن الأول المستلحق

ويصح استلحاق كل حر ذكر يمكن ثبوت النسب منه بنكاح أو وطء محترم فهذه
ثلاثة قيود
الأول الحرية وفي استلحاق العبد والمعتق ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها أنه يصح فلا فرق بين الحر والعبد حتى لو تداعيا جميعا عرض على
القائف وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يقدم الحر على العبد والمسلم على الكافر
وعندنا لا فرق
والثاني لا يلحقهما نسب إلا في نكاح أو وطء بشبهة لأنهما بصدد الولاء
فليس لهما قطع الولاء بمجرد الدعوى
والثالث أن العبد لا ولاء عليه فيلحقه من يستلحقه أما المعتق فالولاء
عليه حاصل فلا تصح دعواه وهذا الخلاف جار لو كان المستلحق عبدا أو معتقا
لأجل الولاء
القيد الثاني الذكورة وفي استلحاق المرأة ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها الصحة كالرجل
والثاني لا لأن الولادة يمكن إثباتها بالشهادة بخلاف جانب الأب
والثالث أنها إن كانت خلية من الزوج لحقها وإن كانت ذات زوج فلا إذ لا
يمكن الإلحاق بها دون الزوج ولا يمكن الإلحاق بالزوج مع إنكاره
القيد الثالث الإمكان وذلك بحقيقة الوطء أو بعقد النكاح مع مع إمكان
الوطء وقد ذكرناه وإنما يمكن النسب من شخصين بأن يجتمعا على وطئها في طهر
واحد إما بالشبهة أو بملك اليمين فإن وطىء الثاني بعد تخلل حيضة فالولد
للثاني إلا أن يكون الأول زوجا فلا ينقطع الإمكان فيه بالحيض لأنه لا يعتبر
في حقه وجود الوطء بل يكفي فراش النكاح مع إمكان الوطء وهذا موجود في الطهر
الثاني وأما ملك اليمين فلا يثبت فراشا والنكاح الفاسد يلحق بالنكاح الصحيح
أو بملك اليمين فيه وجهان ولا خلاف أن فراش النكاح الصحيح ينقطع بفراش آخر
ناسخ له حتى يلحق الولد بالثاني وإن أمكن من حيث الزمان أن يكون منهما

### | الركن الثاني الملحق

وهو كل مدلجي مجرب أهل للشهادة فهذه ثلاثة قيود
الأول المدلجي والصحيح الإختصاص بهم إذ رجعت إليهم الصحابة مع كثرة
الأكياس فيهم ومنهم من قال هذه صنعة تتعلم فمن تعلم جاز  اعتماد قوله
وأما المجرب فنعنى به أن من كان مدلجيا أو ادعى علم القافة لم يقبل قوله
حتى يجرب ثلاثا بأن يرى صبيا بين نسوة ليس فيهن أمه فإن لم يلحق أحضرت نسوة
أخرى ليس فيهن أمه فإن ألحق علمنا أنه بصير فنعرض عليه وإنما يرى النسوة
لأن ولادتهن نعلمها تحقيقا فلا يتعين عدد في التجربة بل المقصود ظهور
بصيرته
وأما كونه أهلا للشهادة فلا بد منه وفيه وجه بعيد أنه لا تشترط الذكورة
والحرية وكأنه إخبار والصحيح أنه لا يشترط العدد وكأن القائف حاكم

### | الركن الثالث في الإلحاق ومحل العرض على القائف

إنما يعرض على القائف صغير تداعاه شخصان كل واحد لو انفرد بالدعوة للحقه
ولا ترجيح لأحدهما على الآخر وخرج على هذه القيود مسائل أربع
الأولى أن إثبات النسب من أبوين غير ممكن عند الشافعي رضي الله عنه فلذلك
لزم العرض على القائف ومستند الشافعي رضي الله عنه حديث مجزز المدلجي وهو
معروف وأبو حنيفة رحمه الله يقول يلحق بهما جميعا ولا نظر إلى قول القائف
ثم عندنا يعتمد قول القائف في مولود صغير أو بالغ ساكت أما البالغ
المجهول إذا استلحقه واحد فوافقه فلا يقبل قول القائف على خلافه لأن الحق
لا يعدوها ولو أنكره البالغ وألحقه القائف لم يصر قوله حجة عليه
الثانية صبي في يد إنسان وهو مستلحقه فاستلحقه غيره لم يعرض على القائف
بعد تقدم صاحب اليد ويده كفراش النكاح والمولود على فراش النكاح إذا ادعاه
من يدعي وطء شبهة لم يلحقه وإن وافقه الزوجان على الوطء بالشبهة لأن حق
الولد يرعى فيه بل إن أقام بينة على الوطء بالشبهة عرض على القائف
الثالثة صبي استحلقه رجل ذو زوجة وهي تنكر ولادته أو استلحقته امرأة ذات
زوج والزوج ينكر ولادتها فليلحق بالرجل المستلحق وفي المرأتين ثلاثة أوجه
أحدهما أنه يلحق زوجة المستلحق وإن أنكرت
والثاني أنه يلحق بالمدعية ويقدر أنها ولدت من المدعي بوطء شبهة
والثالث أنه يعرض في حقهما على القائف
الرابعة إن  لم نجد القائف أو وجدناه وتحي رفإذا بلغ أمرناه بالإنتساب فإن
لم ينتسب حبسانه حتى ينتسب فإذا انتسب إلى أحدهما لحقه وكان اختياره كإلحاق
القائف ولم يقبل رجوعه كما لا يقبل رجوع القائف ودعواه الغلط
والصحيح أن المميز لا يخير بخلاف الحضانة فإن أمر النسب مخطر

### | فروع أربعة

الأول وطىء رجلان في طهر واحد وحبلت وادعى أحدهما وسكت الآخر
فقولان
أحدهما يعرف على القائف
والثاني أنه يلحق بالمدعي
الثاني لو ألقت سقطا يعرض على القائف ولو انفصل حيا ومات يعرض ما لم
يتغير
الثالث نفقة الولد قبل إلحاق القائف عليهما ثم إذا ألحق بأحدهما رجع على
الآخر بما أنفق ولو أوصي له قبله كل واحد منهما حتى يحصل الملك له
الرابع من استلحق صبيا مجهولا فبلغ وانتفى عنه ففيه قولان كالقولين فيمن
حكم بإسلامه تبعا فبلغ وأعرب عن نفسه بالكفر
= كتاب العتق =
ولا يخفى أن العتق قربة ويشهد لنفوذه الكتاب والسنة والإجماع والنظر في
أركانه وخواصه وفروعه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ل-ح-ق (la-ḥa-qa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To join, attach, or annex; the core sense is the binding of one thing to another such that it becomes inseparable in legal effect.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In juristic theology, it denotes the legal attachment of a child's lineage (nasab) to a father, a status that carries inheritance, guardianship, and maintenance obligations.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for physical joining, but here metaphorically (majāz) for a legal construction that establishes paternity through evidentiary means, not biological certainty.
- Root: ق-ي-ف (qā-ya-fa)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Following tracks or traces; the physiognomist (qā'if) reads bodily resemblances as traces of lineage.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A specialized form of testimony (shahādah) based on empirical observation of inherited traits, treated as a valid legal indicator in disputed paternity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for tracking footprints; metaphorical for discerning lineage through physical similarity, a recognized customary practice (ʿurf) in the prophetic era.
- Root: ف-ر-ش (fa-rā-shā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A bed or spread; in law, the marital bed (firāsh) as the locus of presumed paternity.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The legal construct of the marriage bed that establishes a presumption of lineage, overriding mere temporal possibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for bedding; metaphorical for the marital bond that legitimizes sexual access and thus anchors paternity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Restriction (al-Taqyīd bi-al-Sharṭ) — The three qualifiers (ḥurriyyah, dhukūrah, imkān) function as nested conditions that sequentially narrow the scope of the legal act, each parsed as a restrictive clause governing the subject of istiḥāq.
chapters.translation:
I say: The first pillar is the one who seeks to attach lineage (al-mustalḥiq).

It is valid for every free male whose lineage can possibly be established through marriage (nikāḥ) or a protected act of intercourse (waṭ' muḥtaram). These are three restrictions:

The first restriction is freedom (al-ḥurriyyah). Regarding the acknowledgment of lineage by a slave or a freed slave (al-muʿtaq), there are three views:

One view: It is valid, and there is no difference between the free man and the slave. Even if both claim the child simultaneously, the child is presented to the physiognomist (al-qā'if). Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) said: The free man is given precedence over the slave, and the Muslim over the unbeliever. But in our school, there is no difference.

The second view: Lineage is not attached to them except through marriage or intercourse under a semblance of right (shubhah), because they are subject to the bond of clientage (walā'). They cannot sever that clientage merely by a claim.

The third view: The slave has no clientage upon him, so whoever seeks to attach lineage to him may do so. But the freed slave has clientage established upon him, so his claim is not valid. This disagreement applies whether the one seeking attachment is a slave or a freed slave, on account of clientage.

The second restriction is masculinity (al-dhukūrah). Regarding a woman's acknowledgment of lineage, there are three views:

One view: It is valid, just as for a man.

The second view: It is not valid, because birth can be established through testimony (shahādah), unlike the paternal side.

The third view: If she is free of a husband, lineage attaches to her; but if she has a husband, it does not, since attachment cannot be made to her without the husband, nor can it be made to the husband if he denies it.

The third restriction is possibility (al-imkān). This is established either by actual intercourse or by a marriage contract with the possibility of intercourse, as we have mentioned. Lineage can only be possible from two persons if they both have intercourse with her in a single period of purity (ṭuhr). This may occur either through a semblance of right or through ownership of the right hand (milk al-yamīn). If the second man has intercourse after a menstruation has intervened, the child belongs to the second, unless the first is a husband. For the husband, possibility is not severed by menstruation, because actual intercourse is not required in his case; rather, the marriage bed (firāsh al-nikāḥ) suffices along with the possibility of intercourse, and this exists in the second period of purity. As for ownership of the right hand, it does not establish a marriage bed. Regarding whether a corrupt marriage (nikāḥ fāsid) is annexed to a valid marriage or to ownership of the right hand, there are two views. There is no disagreement that the bed of a valid marriage is severed by another bed that supersedes it, so that the child is attached to the second, even if temporal possibility allows that it could be from either.

The second pillar is the one to whom lineage is attached (al-mulḥaq).

This is any trained physiognomist (mudlijī) who is experienced (mujarrab) and qualified for testimony (ahl al-shahādah). These are three restrictions:

The first restriction is being a trained physiognomist (al-mudlijī). The correct view is that this is specific to them, for the Companions referred to them despite the abundance of intelligent men among them. Some said: This is a craft that can be learned, so whoever learns it, reliance on his statement is permissible.

As for being experienced (al-mujarrab), we mean that if a man is a trained physiognomist or claims knowledge of physiognomy (qāfah), his statement is not accepted until he is tested three times. He is shown a boy among women who do not include his mother. If he does not attach him, other women are brought who do not include his mother. If he attaches him, we know he is perceptive, and we present the case to him. The women are shown because we know their births with certainty. No specific number is required for the testing; rather, the goal is the manifestation of his perceptiveness.

As for being qualified for testimony, it is indispensable. There is a remote view that masculinity and freedom are not required, as if it were mere reporting (khabar). The correct view is that numerical count (of witnesses) is not required, as if the physiognomist were an arbiter (ḥākim).

The third pillar concerns the act of attachment and the place of presentation to the physiognomist.

Only a young child is presented to the physiognomist when two persons claim him, each of whom, if alone in the claim, would have lineage attached to him, and neither has precedence over the other. Four issues arise from these restrictions:

The first issue: Establishing lineage from two fathers is impossible according to al-Shāfiʿī (may God be pleased with him), so presentation to the physiognomist becomes necessary. The basis for al-Shāfiʿī is the well-known ḥadīth of Mujazziz al-Mudlijī. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) says: Lineage is attached to both, and no consideration is given to the physiognomist's statement. Then, in our school, the physiognomist's statement is relied upon for a young child or a silent adult. As for an unknown adult, if one person seeks to attach him and he agrees, the physiognomist's statement contrary to that is not accepted, because the right does not go beyond the two of them. If the adult denies it and the physiognomist attaches him, his statement does not become a proof against him.

The second issue: A boy in the custody of a man who has sought to attach him, and then another seeks to attach him — he is not presented to the physiognomist after the precedence of the one in possession. His possession is like a marriage bed. A child born on a marriage bed, if someone claims him claiming intercourse under a semblance of right, lineage is not attached to him, even if the spouses agree on the intercourse under semblance, because the child's right is observed therein. Rather, if he brings proof (bayyinah) of intercourse under semblance, he is presented to the physiognomist.

The third issue: A boy whom a man with a wife seeks to attach, while she denies his birth; or a woman with a husband seeks to attach a girl, while the husband denies her birth. The child is attached to the man who seeks attachment. Regarding the two women, there are three views:

One view: The child is attached to the wife of the one seeking attachment, even if she denies it.

The second view: It is attached to the claimant woman, and it is presumed that she gave birth from the claimant man through intercourse under semblance.

The third view: The case is presented to the physiognomist regarding the two of them.

The fourth issue: If we do not find a physiognomist, or we find him and he is confused (taḥayyara), then when the child reaches maturity, we order him to choose his lineage (intisāb). If he does not choose, we imprison him until he chooses. When he chooses one of the two, lineage is attached to him, and his choice is like the physiognomist's attachment. His retraction is not accepted, just as the physiognomist's retraction is not accepted, nor his claim of error. The correct view is that a discerning child (mumayyiz) is not given the choice, unlike the case of custody (ḥaḍānah), for the matter of lineage is perilous.

Four subsidiary branches:

The first: Two men have intercourse in a single period of purity, and she becomes pregnant. One claims the child and the other remains silent. There are two opinions:

One: The case is referred to the physiognomist.

The second: Lineage is attached to the claimant.

The second: If she miscarries a fetus (siqṭ), it is presented to the physiognomist. If it emerges alive and then dies, it is presented as long as it has not changed.

The third: The child's maintenance (nafaqah) before the physiognomist's attachment is upon both of them. Then, when lineage is attached to one, he recovers from the other what he spent. If each of them bequeaths to him before that, ownership is established for him.

The fourth: Whoever seeks to attach an unknown boy, and the boy reaches maturity and disavows him — there are two opinions, like the two opinions regarding one whose Islam is decreed by following (tabaʿan), then he reaches maturity and expresses unbelief.

= The Book of Manumission (Kitāb al-ʿItq) =

It is no secret that manumission is an act of devotion (qurbah). Its validity is attested by the Book, the Sunnah, and consensus (ijmāʿ). The inquiry concerns its pillars (arkān), its specific properties (khaṣā'iṣ), and its subsidiary branches (furūʿ).

chapters.arabic_text:
### | أما أركانه فثلاثة

الأول المعتق وهو كل مكلف لا حجر عليه بفلس وسفه
الثاني المعتق وهو كل إنسان مملوك لم يتعلق بعينه وثيقة وحق لازم فإن ف
إعتاق المرهون خلافا وإعتاق الطير والبهيمة لاغ على الأصح
الثالث الصيغة وصريحه التحرير والإعتاق وفك الرقبة ورد في القرآن مرة ففي
كونه صريحا وجهان كالمفاداة في الخلع
وأما الكناية فكل ما يحتمل كقوله أنت طالق ولا سلطان لي عليك وحبلك على
غاربك ونظائره

### | فروع أربعة

الأول لو قال لعبده يا مولاي ونوى عتق ولو قال يا سيدي ويا كذبانو للأمة
ونوى لم ينفذ لأنه ينبىء عن التردد وتدبير المنزل دون العتق ويحتمل أن
يقال ينفذ
الثاني أن يقول يا حرة فتعتق إلا أن يكون اسمها حرة وكذلك إذا كان اسم
الغلام آزاذروي وإن كان اسمها قبل الرق حرة فبدل اسمها فقال السيد يا حرة
ثم قال قصدت نداءها باسمها القديم لم يقبل في الظاهر لأن هذا الإسم الآن لا
يليق بها فظاهر اللفظ صريح ولو كان  اسمها القديم فاطمة فغير باسم من أسماء
الإمام فناداها وقال يا فاطمة ونوى العتق لم ينفذ لأن اللفظ لا يشعر به
الثالث لو قال يا آزاذمرد ثم قال أردت وصفه بالجود لم يقبل في الظاهر لأن
اللفظ صريح إلا أن يكون معه قرينه كما لو قال لزوجته أنت طالق وهو يحل
الوثاق عنها وفي قبول نيته في حل الوثاق خلاف
الرابع إذا قال لعبد الغير أعتقتك فإن كان في معرض الإنشاء لغا وإن كان
في معرض الإقرار كان مؤاخذا به إن ملكه يوما من الدهر
واعلم أن العتاق والطلاق يتقاربان وقد فصلنا حكم الألفاظ والتعليقات في
الطلاق فلا نعيده بل نقتصر على ذكر خواص العتق

### | النظر الثاني في خواص العتق

وهي خمسة
السراية والحصول بالقرابة والإمتناع من المريض فيما جاوز الثلث والقرعة
والولاء
الخاصية الأولى السراية قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم من أعتق شركا
له في عبد وله مال قوم عليه الباقي ففهم من هذا أن الشرع متشوف إلى تكميل
العتق فلذلك نقول لو أعتق نصف عبد عتق الجميع بل لو أعتق يده أو عضوا آخر
عتق الجميع وذلك بطريق السراية أو بطريق التعبير بالبعض عن الكل فيه خلاف
ذكرناه في الطلاق وتظهر فائدته في الإضافة إلى العضو المقطوع ولا تثبت
السراية من شخص إلى شخص فإن أعتق الجنين لم تعتق الأم
خلافا للأستاذ أبي إسحاق رحمه الله ولو أعتق الأم عتق الجنين تبعا كما
يتبع في البيع ولو كان الحمل مملوكا للغير فلا يسري وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه
الله يسري
أما العتق فإنما يسري إلى ملك الشريك بشروط أربعة
أحدها أن يكون المعتق موسرا ونعني به أن يكون له من المال قدر قيمة نصيب
الشريك ويعتبر فيه كل ما يباع في الدين فلا يترك له إلا دست ثوب يليق به
ويباع فيه داره وعبده الذي يحتاج إلى خدمته وإن كان لا يباع في الكفارة لأن
هذا دين والمريض ليس موسرا إلا بمقدار الثلث ولو أوصى بعتق بعض  عبد عند
موته لم يسر لأن الميت معسر وقد انتقل ماله إلى الوارث إلا أن يستثني
بالوصية فلو قال أعتقوا نصفه عتقا ساريا أعتقنا النصف ولم يسر لأنه أوصى
بمحال إلا أن يوصي بشراء النصيب الثاني وإعتاقه

### | فرعان
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿ-t-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be free from bondage," "to be released," or "to become ancient/noble." The root denotes liberation from servitude, both physical and metaphorical.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological-juridical terms, it signifies the legal removal of the bond of slavery (riqq) from a human being, restoring full moral and legal agency (taklīf).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to the physical act of freeing a slave; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to spiritual liberation from sin or ignorance, though in legal context only the literal applies.
- Root: س-ر-ي (s-r-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To travel by night," but derivatively "to spread," "to permeate," or "to extend" from one thing to another.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal theory, it denotes the transitive effect of a legal act—here, the automatic extension of manumission from a portion to the whole slave.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning is nocturnal travel; metaphorical usage in jurisprudence indicates the "flow" of a ruling's effect across related subjects.
- Root: ك-ن-ي (k-n-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: "To address by a teknonym" or "to use an indirect expression"; the noun kināyah means an allusive or indirect speech act.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal hermeneutics, it refers to utterances that are not explicit (ṣarīḥ) but require intention (niyyah) or contextual evidence (qarīnah) to determine their operative meaning.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Distinguishes between ṣarīḥ (unequivocal, literal) and kināyah (ambiguous, requiring interpretation)—a crucial rhetorical-legal dichotomy.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taʿlīq and Niyyah (Conditionality and Intent) — In Arabic syntax, the operative force of an utterance (ṣīghah) depends on its grammatical form (e.g., declarative vs. performative) and the speaker's intent, which may be inferred from syntactic context (maqām) or explicit qualification (taʿlīq).
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that the pillars of manumission (arkān al-ʿitq) are three.

The first pillar is the manumitter (al-muʿtiq), who is every legally responsible person (mukallaf) upon whom there is no legal restriction (ḥajr) due to bankruptcy (iflās) or prodigality (safah).

The second pillar is the manumitted slave (al-muʿtaq), who is every human being who is owned as property (mamlūk) and to whose specific person (bi-ʿaynihi) no security document (wathīqah) or binding right (ḥaqq lāzim) is attached. For if one manumits a pledged slave (al-marhūn), there is a divergence of opinion (khilāf) [regarding its validity]; and the manumission of a bird or a beast is void (lāgh) according to the more correct opinion (al-aṣaḥḥ).

The third pillar is the formula (al-ṣīghah). Its explicit wording (ṣarīḥuhu) is: "liberation" (al-taḥrīr), "manumission" (al-iʿtāq), and "release of the neck" (fakk al-raqabah). Since [the term "fakk al-raqabah"] occurs in the Qurʾān once, there are two views (wajhān) concerning whether it is explicit (ṣarīḥ)—analogous to the term "ransoming" (al-mufādāh) in the context of khulʿ (divorce by redemption).

As for the allusive expression (al-kināyah), it is every utterance that admits of [multiple] possibilities, such as one's saying to his slave: "You are free" (anta ṭāliq), or "I have no authority over you" (lā sulṭāna lī ʿalayka), or "Your rope is on your own neck" (ḥabluka ʿalā ghāribika), and similar expressions.

### Four Subsidiary Issues (Furūʿ Arbaʿah)

The first subsidiary issue: If a man says to his slave, "O my master" (yā mawlāya), intending thereby manumission, [it is valid]. But if he says, "O my lord" (yā sayyidī), or "O my liar" (yā kadhdhāb) to a female slave, intending manumission, it does not take effect—because such an utterance suggests hesitation (taraddud) and household management (tadbīr al-manzil) rather than manumission. Yet it may be said [in another view] that it does take effect.

The second subsidiary issue: If he says to his slave-girl, "O free woman" (yā ḥurrah), she becomes free—unless her [actual] name happens to be Ḥurrah. Likewise, if the male slave's name is Āzādhrawī [i.e., "free-born" in Persian], [the same ruling applies]. And if her name before enslavement was Ḥurrah, and her master changed her name, then said, "O Ḥurrah," and afterward claimed, "I intended to call her by her former name," his claim is not accepted in the external forum (fī al-ẓāhir)—because this name now is not fitting for her, so the apparent wording (ẓāhir al-lafẓ) is explicit [in meaning manumission]. But if her former name was Fāṭimah, and he changed it to one of the names of the Imams, then called her, saying, "O Fāṭimah," intending manumission, it does not take effect—because the wording does not indicate it (lā yashʿuru bihi).

The third subsidiary issue: If he says, "O Āzādhmard" [i.e., "O free man" in Persian], then claims, "I intended to describe him as generous (al-jūd)," his claim is not accepted in the external forum—because the wording is explicit [in meaning manumission]. This is unless there is a contextual indicator (qarīnah) accompanying it, as when a man says to his wife, "You are divorced" (anti ṭāliq) while he is actually untying the bonds (ḥall al-withāq) from her; and there is a divergence of opinion (khilāf) concerning the acceptance of his intention [to mean untying bonds rather than divorce].

The fourth subsidiary issue: If he says to another person's slave, "I have manumitted you" (aʿtaqtuka), then if this is uttered in the context of initiating a legal act (fī maʿraḍ al-inshāʾ), it is void (lāgh). But if it is uttered in the context of acknowledgment (fī maʿraḍ al-iqrār), he is held accountable for it (muʾākhadh bihi) if he ever comes to own that slave at any point in time (yawman min al-dahr).

Know that manumission (al-ʿitāq) and divorce (al-ṭalāq) are closely related (yataqārabān). We have already detailed the rulings concerning verbal formulas (alfāẓ) and conditional suspensions (taʿlīqāt) in the chapter on divorce, so we shall not repeat that here. Rather, we shall confine ourselves to mentioning the special characteristics (khaṣāʾiṣ) of manumission.

### The Second Consideration: The Special Characteristics of Manumission

These are five: (1) the transitive effect (al-sarāyah), (2) the attainment [of freedom] through kinship (al-ḥuṣūl bil-qarābah), (3) the restriction [of validity] from a sick person (al-imtināʿ min al-marīḍ) regarding what exceeds one-third [of his estate], (4) the lot (al-qurʿah), and (5) the clientage (al-walāʾ).

The first special characteristic is the transitive effect (al-sarāyah). The Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, said: {«مَنْ أَعْتَقَ شِرْكًا لَهُ فِي عَبْدٍ وَلَهُ مَالٌ قُوِّمَ عَلَيْهِ الْبَاقِي»} — "Whoever manumits his share in a slave, and he has wealth, the remaining [share] is valued against him." From this it is understood that the Sacred Law (al-sharʿ) is desirous (mutashawwif) of completing manumission. Therefore, we say: If a man manumits half of a slave, the whole slave becomes free. Indeed, even if he manumits his hand (yadahu) or another limb (ʿuḍw), the whole slave becomes free—whether this occurs by way of transitive effect (sarāyah) or by way of expressing the part to denote the whole (taʿbīr bil-baʿḍ ʿan al-kull) is a point of divergence (khilāf) we have mentioned in the chapter on divorce. Its practical benefit (fāʾidah) appears in relation to a severed limb (al-ʿuḍw al-maqṭūʿ). The transitive effect does not extend from one person to another: if one manumits a fetus (al-janīn), the mother does not become free—contrary to the view of the Master Abū Isḥāq, may Allah have mercy on him. But if one manumits the mother, the fetus becomes free as a dependent (tabaʿan), just as it follows [the mother] in sale (al-bayʿ). And if the pregnancy (al-ḥaml) is owned by another person, the transitive effect does not apply; Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it does apply.

As for manumission, its transitive effect extends to the share of the partner (sharīk) only under four conditions:

The first condition is that the manumitter be wealthy (mūsir). By this we mean that he possesses wealth equivalent to the value of the partner's share. In assessing this, everything that can be sold to satisfy a debt (mā yubāʿ fī al-dayn) is taken into account, so that nothing is left for him except a garment (dast thawb) befitting him. His house and his slave whom he needs for personal service are sold [to pay this], even though such items would not be sold for the expiatory offering (al-kafārah)—because this is a debt [owed to the partner]. And a sick person (al-marīḍ) is not considered wealthy except up to one-third [of his estate]. If a dying person bequeaths the manumission of part of a slave, the transitive effect does not apply—because the deceased is insolvent (muʿsir) and his wealth has transferred to his heirs, unless he makes an exception through the bequest. Thus, if he says, "Manumit half of him with a transitive manumission" (aʿtiqū niṣfahu ʿitqan sāriyan), we manumit the half, but it does not extend [to the rest]—because he bequeathed something impossible (muḥāl), unless he also bequeaths the purchase of the second share and its manumission.

### Two Subsidiary Issues
