chapters.arabic_text:
الأول لو كان له مال وعليه مثله دين فهل يحلق بالمعسر فيه خلاف كما في
الزكاة لأن السراية حق الله تعالى كالزكاة
الثاني لو كان معسرا ببعض قيمة النصيب فيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه يسري بذلك القدر
والثاني أنه لا يسري إذ لا بد من تبعيض الرق والشريك يتضرر بتبعيض ملكه
كما يتضرر المشتري بتبعيض المبيع عليه في الشفعة
الشرط الثاني أن يتوجه العتق على نصيب نفسه أو على الجميع حتى يتناول
نصيبه فلو قال أعتقت نصيب شريكي لغا قوله ولو قال أعتقت النصف من هذا العبد
فهو محتمل لكل واحد من الجانبين ولكنه لا يخصص بجانب شريكه وهل يخصص بجانبه
أم يقال هو نصف شائع في الجانبين فيه وجهان ولا تظهر ها هنا فائدته لأنه
إذا تناول شيئا من ملكه سرى إلى جميع ملكه ويسري أيضا إلى شريكه إلا أن
يكون معسرا لكن تظهر فائدته في قوله بعت هذا النصف أو في إقراره بنصف
الضيعة المشتركة لثالث ففي وجه يخرج جميع النصف من يده وفي وجه يخرج شطر
النصف من يده وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله ينزل البيع عن نصف الخاص والإقرار
يشيع لأن الإنسان قد يخبر عما في يد الغير ولا يبيع مال الغير وهذا متجه
فليجعل وجها في مذهبنا
الشرط الثالث أن يعتق باختياره فلو ورث نصف قريبه فعتق عليه لم يسر لأن
التقويم تغريم يليق بالتلف
الشرط الرابع أن لا يتعلق بمحل السراية حق لازم فإن تعلق كما لو كان
مرهونا أو مدبرا أو مكاتبا أو مستولدة ففي السراية إلى جميع ذلك خلاف
وبعضها أولى بأن
لا يسري من بعض وذلك بحسب تأكد الحقوق
ثم عتق الموسر متى يسري فيه ثلاثة أقوال
أحدها أنه في الحال حتى لا يتبعض  الرق ما أمكن
والثاني أنه إذا أدى القيمة حتى لا يزول ملك الشريك إلا ببدل يملكه فإن
ذلك أهم من السراية
والثالث أنه موقوف فإذا أدى تبين السراية من وقت العتق وإن تعذر استمر
الر نظرا إلى المعنيين جميعا
ثم ينبني على الأقوال مسائل
الأولى في سراية استيلاد أحد الشريكين الأقوال الثلاثة بالترتيب وأولى
بأن لا يتعجل لأنه علقة عتاقه لا حقيقة عتاقه وقيل أولى بأن يتعجل لأنه فعل
وهو أقوى من القول ثم إذا سريناه لكونه موسرا فعليه نصف المهر ونصف قيمة
الجارية ونصف قيمة الولد إلا إذا فرعنا على أن الملك ينتقل قبيل العلوق
فتسقط قيمة الولد وإن كان معسرا فلا يسري ولو استولدها الثاني أيضا وهو
معسر فهي مستولدتهما فإن أعتق أحدهما نصيبه وهو موسر ففي السراية وجهان
أظهرهما أنه لا يسري لأن السراية بتقدير نقل الملك والمستولدة لا تقبل
النقل ولكن لا يبعد أن يقبل مثل هذا النقل القهري المفضي إلى العتق وكذلك
لو أعتق الكافر نصيبه من عبد مسلم ففي السراية وجهان إذ في ضمنها نقل الملك
ولكن قهرا
المسألة الثانية عبد بين ثلاثة لأحدهم ثلثه ولآخر سدسه
وللآخر نصفه فأعتق اثنان نصيبهما معا وسرى فقيمة محل السراية توزع على
عدد رءوسهما أو على قدر ملكيهما فيه قولان كما في الشفعة وقيل يقطع هاهنا
بالتوزيع على عدد الرءوس لأنه إهلاك فيشبه الجراحات وهو ضعيف لأن الجراحة
لا يتقدر أثرها بقدر غورها حتى يقال بأن أربع جراحات أثر كل واحدة ربع
السراية وها هنا السبب مقدر تحقيقا
المسألة الثالثة إذا حكمنا بتأخير السراية فالقيمة بأي يوم تعتبر فيه
ثلاثة أوجه
أحدها يوم الإعتاق إذ هو سبب الزوال
والثاني بيوم الأداء إذ عنده فوات الملك
والثالث يجب أقصى القيمة بين الإعتاق والأداء وهو الأصح كما يجب أقصى
القيمة بين الجراحة والموت
فرع إذا اختلفا في قدر قيمة العبد وقد مات وتعذر معرفته فالقول قول
الغارم لأن الأصل براءة ذمته وفيه قول آخر ضعيف أن القول قول الطالب  إذ
يبعد أن ينقل ملكه بقول غيره أما إذا ادعى الغارم نقصان القيمة بسبب نقيصة
طارئة فالأصل عدم النقص والأصل براءة الذمة فيخرج على قولي تقابل الأصلين
وليس معنى تقابل الأصلين استحالة الترجيح بل يطلب الترجيح من مدرك آخر سوى
استصحاب الأصول فإن تعذر فليس إلا التوقف أما تخير المفتي بين متناقضين فلا
وجه له
المسألة الرابعة في الطوارىء قبل أداء القيمة على قول التوقف كموت المعتق
أو العبد أو بيع الشريك أو عتقه أو وطئه أو إعسار المعتق أما موت المعتق
فيوجب القيمة في التركة لأنه مستحق عليه الإعتاق وأما موت العبد هل يسقط
القيمة فيه وجهان
أحدهما نعم لخروجه من قبول العتق
والثاني لا لأنه سبق استحقاق العتق على الموت والقيمة وجبت به
أما بيع الشريك فالصحيح أنه لا ينفذ فإنه يبطل استحقاق العتق وأما إعتاقه
ففيه وجهان
أحدهما لا ينفذ لأن الأول استحق إعتاقه من نفسه
والثاني أنه يصح لأن الملك قائم والمقصود أصل العتق
وأما وطؤه فيوجب نصف المهر لنصفها الحر والظاهر أنه لا يجب للنصف الثاني
لأن ملكه باق وفيه وجه أنه يجب للشريك الأول فإن الملك مستحق الإنقلاب إليه
وأما إعسار المعتق فالصحيح أنه يرفع الحجر عن الشريك في التصرف لأنا أخرنا
العتق لأجل حقه فلا يمكن تعطيل ملكه بغير بدل نعم لو كان معسرا أولا فطرآن
اليسار لا يؤثر في السراية
المسألة الخامسة إذا قال أحد الشريكين لصاحبه إذا أعتقت أنت نصيبك فنصيبي
أيضا حر فإذا أعتق المقول له ذلك وكان موسرا ورأينا تعجيل السراية عتق
العبد كله عليه لأنه اجتمع على النصف تعليق وسراية والسراية أولى لكونها
قهرية تابعة لعتق النصف الآخر الذي لا يقبل الدفع وأما التعليق فلفظ يقبل
الدفع وإن فرعنا على التأخير فيعتق النصف الآخر بالتعليق كما لو أنشأالعتق
معه أو بعده إلا إذا فرعنا على أن عتقه لا ينفذ لاستحقاق
السراية فحينئذ يندفع التعليق باستحقاق السراية كما يندفع بنفس السراية
أما إذا كان معسرا فتلغو السراية وينفذ التعليق
ولو قال فنصيبي حر قبله وكانا معسرين عتق كل نصيب على صاحبه وإن كانا
موسرين فهذا من الدور إذ لو عتق قبل مباشرته بحكم التعليق لسرى وامتنعت
المباشرة بعده وانعدمت الصفة التي عليها التعليق فتنعدم السراية فهذا عند
ابن الحداد يقتضي الحجر على المالك في إعتاق نصيب نفسه
المسألة السادسة إذا قال أحدهما لصاحبه قد أعتقت نصيبك وأنت موسر فأنكر
عتق نصيب المدعي مجانا مؤاخذة له بقوله وذلك ظاهر ولكن على قول تعجيل
السراية ثم له أن يحلفه فلو نكل فحلف المدعي أخذ قيمة نصيبه ولم يحكم بعتق
نصيب المدعى عليه بيمينه المردودة لأن دعواه إنما قبلت لأجل قيمة نصيبه
وإلا فدعوى الإنسان على غيره أنه أعتق ملك نفسه غير مسموع بل إنما تسمع
الشهادة على سبيل الحسبة
ولو ادعى كل واحد من الشريكين على الآخر أنه أعتق نصيب نفسه فإن كانا
معسرين بقي العبد رقيقا وإن كانا موسرين عتق العبد وولاؤه موقوف إذ لا
يدعيه أحدهما لنفسه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: س-ر-ي (s-r-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To travel by night; to flow, spread, or permeate gradually through a thing until it encompasses it wholly.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Technical legal term for the automatic extension of a legal effect (e.g., manumission) from one portion of property to the entirety, by virtue of the slave's indivisible humanity.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used here in its ḥaqīqah (literal) sense of "flowing over" — a necessary legal consequence, not a metaphorical extension.
- Root: ق-و-م (q-w-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To stand upright; to assess the value or worth of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, taqwīm = the monetary valuation imposed as a compensatory obligation (ghurm) upon the wealthy co-owner who manumits his share.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The shift from physical standing (ḥaqīqah) to "standing in for value" (majāz mursal) — the assessed price stands in place of the enslaved person's worth.
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿ-t-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To become free, noble, or ancient; the opposite of slavery (riqq).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The theological act of releasing a human from the bondage of ownership, mirroring God's freeing of the soul from servitude to passion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal act of emancipation; the term is never metaphorical when applied to a slave.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clauses (al-Sharṭ wa al-Jawāb) — The particle "law" (if) introduces a hypothetical protasis whose apodosis is suspended upon its fulfillment; the legal rulings here hinge on precise parsing of such conditionals, especially in nested constructions (e.g., "if you free your share, my share is free").
chapters.translation:
I say: The first [issue]: If a man possesses wealth and owes a debt equal to it, does he rank with the insolvent (muʿsir) [regarding the non-propagation of manumission]? There is a divergence of opinion, just as in the case of alms-tax (zakāh), because the right of propagation (sarāyah) is a right of God Most High, like the zakāh.

The second [issue]: If he is insolvent with respect to only part of the value of the share, there are two views:
One of them: that it propagates to that extent.
The second: that it does not propagate, since partial division of the slave's status (tabʿīḍ al-riqq) is unavoidable, and the partner is harmed by the division of his ownership just as the purchaser is harmed by the division of the sold item against him in the case of pre-emption (shufʿah).

The second condition: That the manumission be directed at his own share or at the whole [slave], such that it encompasses his share. Thus, if he says, "I have freed my partner's share," his statement is void. And if he says, "I have freed half of this slave," it is ambiguous, applicable to either side. But it is not restricted to the partner's side. As to whether it is restricted to his own side, or whether it is said to be an undivided half pertaining to both sides — there are two views. Yet its practical benefit does not appear here, because if it encompasses anything of his own property, it propagates to all his property, and it also propagates to his partner — unless he is insolvent. But its benefit appears in his saying, "I have sold this half," or in his acknowledgment (iqrār) of half of a jointly-owned estate (ḍayʿah) to a third party. On one view, the entire half leaves his possession; on another view, only a portion of the half leaves his possession. Abū Ḥanīfah (may God have mercy on him) said: The sale is interpreted as applying to the specific half, while the acknowledgment applies to the undivided share, because a person may report about what is in another's hand, but he does not sell another's property. This is sound, so let it be made a view in our school.

The third condition: That he manumit by his own choice. Thus, if he inherits half of his relative [slave] and the manumission takes effect upon him [by operation of law], it does not propagate, because the valuation (taqwīm) is a compensatory exaction (ghurm) befitting destruction [of property].

The fourth condition: That no entrenched right (ḥaqq lāzim) be attached to the locus of propagation. If such a right is attached — as when the slave is pledged as collateral (marhūn), or is a mudabbar (whose manumission is deferred to the master's death), or a mukātab (who has contracted his freedom for payment), or a umm walad (a slave-mother of her master's child) — then there is a divergence regarding propagation to all such cases. Some of these are more deserving of non-propagation than others, according to the strength of the rights involved.

Then: When does the manumission of a wealthy co-owner propagate? There are three statements:
One: That it propagates immediately, so that the slave's status is not divided as long as possible.
The second: That it propagates when he pays the value, so that the partner's ownership does not cease except in exchange for a substitute (badal) that he owns — for this is more important than propagation.
The third: That it is suspended (mawqūf); if he pays, it becomes clear that propagation occurred from the moment of manumission, and if payment becomes impossible, the enslavement (riqq) continues — considering both meanings together.

Then, upon these statements are built several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the propagation of istīlād (making a slave-woman an umm walad) by one of two co-owners, the three statements apply in order. It is more fitting that it not be hastened, because it is a suspended cause of freedom (ʿalaqah ʿitāqih), not the actual freedom itself. And it was said: It is more fitting that it be hastened, because it is an act (fiʿl), which is stronger than a mere statement. Then, if we make it propagate because he is wealthy, he owes half the dowry (mahr), half the value of the slave-woman, and half the value of the child — unless we adopt the view that ownership transfers just before conception, in which case the child's value drops. If he is insolvent, it does not propagate. If the second co-owner also makes her an umm walad while insolvent, she becomes the umm walad of both. If one of them frees his share while wealthy, there are two views on propagation; the more apparent is that it does not propagate, because propagation entails the transfer of ownership, and an umm walad does not admit transfer. But it is not far-fetched that she admits this kind of forcible transfer that leads to freedom. Likewise, if a disbeliever frees his share of a Muslim slave, there are two views on propagation, since it entails transfer of ownership, but forcibly.

The second issue: A slave is shared among three: one owns a third, another a sixth, and another half. Two of them free their shares simultaneously, and propagation occurs. Is the value of the locus of propagation distributed according to the number of their heads or according to the extent of their ownership? There are two statements, as in pre-emption. And it was said: Here one should definitively distribute by number of heads, because it is an act of destruction (ihlāk), resembling wounds. But this is weak, because the effect of a wound is not proportionate to its depth, such that one could say four wounds each produce a quarter of the effect; whereas here the cause is precisely quantified.

The third issue: If we rule on delaying propagation, by which day is the value assessed? There are three aspects:
One: The day of manumission, since it is the cause of the loss [of the partner's share].
The second: The day of payment, since it is when the loss of ownership occurs.
The third: The maximum value between manumission and payment must be paid — and this is the most correct (al-aṣaḥḥ), just as the maximum value between wounding and death must be paid.

Branch: If they dispute the amount of the slave's value after he has died and it is impossible to ascertain it, the statement of the guarantor (ghārim) is accepted, because the default principle is the innocence of his liability (barāʾat al-dhimmah). There is another weak statement that the claimant's statement is accepted, since it is unlikely that his ownership is transferred by another's mere assertion. But if the guarantor claims a decrease in value due to a supervening defect, the default principle is the absence of the defect, and the default principle is the innocence of liability — so this is resolved according to the two statements on the conflict of default principles (taʿāruḍ al-aṣlayn). The meaning of "conflict of default principles" is not the impossibility of preferring one, but rather that preference is sought from another source besides the mere continuation of the default state (istisḥāb al-uṣūl). If that is impossible, nothing remains but suspension (tawaqquf). As for the muftī choosing arbitrarily between two contradictory [rulings], there is no basis for that.

The fourth issue: Regarding supervening events (ṭawāriʾ) before payment of the value, on the statement of suspension — such as the death of the manumitter, the death of the slave, the partner's sale, his manumission, his sexual intercourse [with the slave-woman], or the manumitter's insolvency. As for the death of the manumitter, it obliges the value from his estate, because manumission was incumbent upon him. As for the death of the slave — does it drop the value? There are two views:
One: Yes, because he has left the capacity for manumission.
The second: No, because the entitlement to manumission preceded death, and the value was obligated by it.

As for the partner's sale [of his share]: The correct view is that it does not execute, for it nullifies the entitlement to manumission. As for his manumission [of his own share]: There are two views:
One: It does not execute, because the first [co-owner] had already become entitled to manumit him from himself.
The second: It is valid, because ownership remains, and the objective is the very fact of manumission.

As for his sexual intercourse [with the slave-woman]: It obliges half the dowry for her free half. The apparent view is that nothing is owed for the second half, because his ownership of it remains. There is a view that it is owed to the first partner, because ownership is entitled to be transferred to him.

As for the manumitter's insolvency: The correct view is that it lifts the restriction (ḥajr) from the partner regarding disposition, because we delayed the manumission for the sake of his right, and his property cannot be rendered inert without a substitute. Yes, if he was insolvent at first, then wealth supervenes, that does not affect propagation.

The fifth issue: If one of two co-owners says to his companion: "If you free your share, then my share is also free" — then when the addressed one frees [his share] while wealthy, and we adopt the view of immediate propagation, the entire slave becomes free upon him, because both a conditional suspension (taʿlīq) and propagation converge upon the half. Propagation takes precedence, because it is forcible, following the manumission of the other half which cannot be repelled. As for the conditional suspension, it is a verbal formula that can be repelled. If we adopt the view of delay, then the other half becomes free by the conditional suspension, just as if he had initiated manumission with it or after it — unless we adopt the view that his manumission does not execute due to the entitlement of propagation; in that case, the conditional suspension is repelled by the entitlement of propagation, just as it is repelled by propagation itself. If he is insolvent, propagation is nullified and the conditional suspension executes.

If he says, "My share is free before it" — and both are insolvent — each share becomes free upon its owner. If both are wealthy, this involves circularity (dawr): for if [the second's share] became free before his direct act by virtue of the conditional suspension, it would propagate, and his subsequent direct act would be prevented, and the condition upon which the suspension was built would cease to exist — thus propagation would cease. This, according to Ibn al-Ḥaddād, entails placing a restriction (ḥajr) upon the owner regarding manumitting his own share.

The sixth issue: If one of them says to his companion: "I have freed your share while you are wealthy," and the other denies it — the share of the claimant is freed gratuitously, as an imposition upon him for his own statement. This is apparent, but [only] on the view of immediate propagation. Then he may administer an oath to him. If he refuses and the claimant swears, he takes the value of his share, but the share of the defendant is not ruled free by the returned oath, because his claim was only accepted for the sake of the value of his share. Otherwise, a person's claim against another that he freed his own property is not heard; rather, testimony is only heard by way of supererogation (ḥisbah).

If each of the two co-owners claims against the other that he freed his own share: if both are insolvent, the slave remains enslaved; if both are wealthy, the slave is freed and his walāʾ (patronage) is suspended, since neither claims it for himself.

chapters.title_en: The Second Property: Emancipation by Kinship
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الخاصية الثانية العتق بالقرابة

وكل من دخل في ملكه أحد أبعاضه عتق عليه إن كان من أهل التبرع فهذه ثلاثة
قيود
الأول قولنا دخل في ملكه وقد تناولنا بهذا الإرث والهبة والشراء وكل ملك
قهرا كان أو اختيارا لأن هذا العتق صلة فلا يستدعي الإختبار والسراية غرامة
فلا تحصل إلا بعد الإختيار
الثاني الأبعاض وقد تناولنا به جميع الفروع والأصول وهو كل من يستحق
النفقة وأخرجنا الإخوة وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يعتق كل ذي رحم محرم
الثالثة أهلية التبرع ويخرج عليه الطفل والمريض والمحجور
أما الطفل ليس لوليه أن يشتري له قريبه الذي يعتق عليه ولو وهب له لم يجز
قبوله حيث تجب نفقته بأن يكون الموهوب غير كسوب والصبي موسر وحيث لا تجب
النفقة في
الحال يجوز القبول وإن كان يتوقع في المآل فلا ينظر إليه ثم إذا قبل عتق
عليه ولو وهب منه نصف قريبه وتوقع من قبوله السراية والغرامة فلا يقبله
الولي وفيه وجه أنه يقبل ولا يسري
أما المريض فلو اشترى قريبه عتق من ثلثه فإن لم يف به فلا يعتق وإن ملكه
بإرث أو هبة فيعتق من الثلث أو رأس المال فيه وجهان
أحدهما من الثلث كما لو اتهب عبدا وأنشأ عتقه
والثاني من رأس المال لأنه عتق بغير اختياره ولم يبذل في مقابلته شيئا
ولو اشتراه بألف وهو يساوي ألفين فقدر المحاباة يخرج على أحد الوجهين
والباقي يحسب من الثلث
أما المحجور بسبب الدين مريضا كان أو مفسلا فيعتق عليه قريبه الذي ورثه
أو اتهبه وإن قلنا إنه يحسب من رأس المال أما إذا اشترى ففي وجه يبطل
الشراء وفي وجه يملك ولا يعتق

### | فرع

إذا قهر الحربي حربيا آخر ملكه فلو قهر أباه فهل يملكه حتى يصح بيعه قال
أبو زيد يملكه لأنه وإن كان يعتق قهرا فقهر العتق ملك والقهر دائم وقال ابن
الحداد لا يملك لأن القرابة دافعة وهي دائمة مع القهر
قاعدة مركبة من عتق القرابة والسراية وهي أن الموسر إذا اشترى نصف قريبه
عتق وسرى وكذا لو اتهب ولو ورث عتق ولم يسر لأنه لا اختيار
واعلم أن اختيار وكيله ونائبه شرعا كاختياره حتى لو أوصى له ببعض أبيه
فمات قبل القبول وورثه أخوه فقبل بنيابته عتق كله على الميت إن كان في
الثلث وفاء لأن قبوله كقبول الميت فكأن الميت ملكه في الحياة
ولو أوصى له بنصف ابن أخيه فمات قبل القبول وورثه أخوه وقبل فهل يسر على
القابل فإنه ابنه فيه وجهان ووجه منع السراية أن قبوله يحصل الملك للميت
أولا ثم ينتقل إليه قهرا
ويجري الوجهان في كل ملك يحصل غير مقصود في نفسه كما لو باع بعض من يعتق
على وارثه بثوب ثم رد الوارث الثوب بعيب رجع إليه بعض قريبه ضمنا لرد العوض
وكذلك إذا عجز مكاتبه وكان في يده بعض قريبه ولو عجز المكاتب نفسه فرجع بعض
قريب السيد إليه لم يسر قطعا

### | الخاصية الثالثة امتناع العتق بالمرض إذا لم يف الثلث به

فلو  أعتق عبدا لا مال له غيره عتق ثلثه ورق ثلثاه للورقة فإن ظهر عليه
دين مستغرق بيع كله في الدين ولو مات العبد قبل موت السيد قال القفال مات
وثلثه حر وثلثاه رقيق وقيل إنه مات حرا لأن الإرقاق إنما يكون حيث يكون
للورثة فيه فائدة وقيل يموت كله رقيقا لأن الثلث إنما يعتق إذا حصل للوارث
ثلثاه وتظهر فائدة هذا فيما لو وهب عبدا وأقبضه ومات ثم مات السيد فيظهر
أثر الخلاف في مؤنة التجهيز وأنها على من أما لو قبله المتهب فهو كالباقي
حتى يغرم قيمة الزائد على الثلث

### | فرع

لو أعتق ثلاثة أعبد لا مال له غيرهم ومات واحد قبل موت السيد قال الأصحاب
يدخل الميت في القرعة فإن خرجت له رق الآخران وإن خرج على أحد الحيين عتق
ثلثاه فقط وهذا إنما يصح على اختيار القفال فأما من جعل الميت قبل السيد
كالمعدوم
فلا ينقدح عنده إدخاله في القرعة أما إذا مات أحدهم بعد موت السيد ولكن
قبل امتداد يد الوارث وقبل القرعة فيدخل في القرعة فإن خرج عليه رق الآخران
وإن خرج على أحد الباقيين عتق ثلثاه ولم يحتسب ما لم يدخل في يد الوارث
عليه وإن كان دخل في يده ولكن مات قبل القرعة ففيه وجهان
أحدهما أنه يحسب عليه حتى لو خرجت على واحد من الحيين عتق بكماله
والثاني لا لأنه كان محجورا عن التصرف قبل القرعة فأي فائدة لليد
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿ-t-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be free" or "to become liberated," denoting the removal of servitude and the restoration of full legal agency.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, it signifies the release from the bondage of ownership, a pious act (qurbah) that establishes the slave's personhood before God and the community.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the legal act of manumission; metaphorically (majāz) it can denote spiritual liberation from sin, but here it is strictly juridical.
- Root: ق-ر-ب (q-r-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity in lineage or blood relation; the root conveys closeness, whether physical, temporal, or genealogical.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Denotes the specific category of relatives (aqārib) who are entitled to maintenance (nafaqah) and whose enslavement is prohibited due to the inherent dignity of kinship.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for blood ties; metaphorical for spiritual nearness to God, but here confined to consanguinity.
- Root: س-ر-ي (s-r-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To travel by night, but in legal usage, it means "to spread" or "to extend" (sarayān), as in the effect of emancipation extending from one part to the whole.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In jurisprudence, it refers to the automatic extension of a legal effect (e.g., freedom) to all shares of a jointly owned slave when one co-owner frees his portion.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for nocturnal journey; metaphorical for the transitive propagation of a legal ruling, a technical majāz in fiqh.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-sharṭ wa al-istithnāʾ) — The text uses "if" (law) and "except" (illā) to delineate precise legal conditions, requiring careful parsing of protasis and apodosis to determine when emancipation is valid or void.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second property is emancipation by kinship. Whoever comes into his possession one of his own body-parts [i.e., a blood relative], it is emancipated upon him, provided he is among those qualified for voluntary donation (ahl al-tabarruʿ). Thus, there are three restrictions.

The first is our statement "comes into his possession." By this we have included inheritance, gift, and purchase, and every form of ownership, whether by compulsion or by choice, because this emancipation is a bond of connection (ṣilah) and thus does not require choice. However, the extension (sarāyah) is a financial liability (gharāmah), so it is not effected except after choice.

The second is "body-parts." By this we have included all branches (furūʿ) and roots (uṣūl), namely, every relative entitled to maintenance. We have excluded siblings. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: Every blood relative within the prohibited degrees (dhū raḥim muḥrim) is emancipated.

The third is qualification for voluntary donation. Excluded by this are the minor, the sick person, and the legally interdicted (maḥjūr).

As for the minor: It is not permissible for his guardian to purchase for him a relative whose emancipation would be incumbent upon him. And if such a relative were gifted to him, it is not permissible to accept it where maintenance is obligatory—namely, when the gifted person is not a wage-earner and the minor is wealthy. But where maintenance is not obligatory at the present moment, acceptance is permissible, even if it is anticipated in the future; that future prospect is not considered. Then, if he accepts, the relative is emancipated upon him. And if half of his relative were gifted to him, and the guardian anticipates from acceptance both the extension (sarāyah) and the financial liability (gharāmah), he does not accept. There is a view that he accepts and the extension does not occur.

As for the sick person: If he purchases his relative, the latter is emancipated from his one-third (thalath). If the one-third does not suffice, then he is not emancipated. If he acquires him by inheritance or gift, then he is emancipated from the one-third or from the entire capital (raʾs al-māl)—there are two views. One is from the one-third, just as if he had been gifted a slave and then initiated his emancipation. The second is from the entire capital, because he was emancipated without his choice and he did not expend anything in exchange for him. And if he purchased him for one thousand while he is worth two thousand, the amount of favoritism (muḥābāh) is adjudicated according to one of the two views, and the remainder is counted from the one-third.

As for the one interdicted due to debt, whether sick or insolvent (mufassal): His relative whom he inherited or was gifted is emancipated upon him, even if we say it is counted from the capital. But if he purchased him, there is a view that the purchase is void, and a view that he owns him but he is not emancipated.

### | Branch

If a warrior (ḥarbī) subjugates another warrior and takes possession of him, then if he subjugates his own father—does he own him such that his sale is valid? Abū Zayd said: He owns him, because even though he is emancipated by compulsion, the compulsion of emancipation is ownership, and the compulsion is perpetual. Ibn al-Ḥaddād said: He does not own him, because the kinship is repulsive (dāfiʿah) and it is perpetual along with the compulsion.

A composite rule combining emancipation by kinship and extension (sarāyah): A wealthy person who purchases half of his relative—the half is emancipated and the extension applies. Likewise, if he is gifted it. But if he inherits it, it is emancipated without extension, because there is no choice.

Know that the choice of his agent (wakīl) and his legal deputy is like his own choice. Thus, if someone bequeaths to him a portion of his father, and the legatee dies before acceptance, and his brother inherits it and accepts on his behalf, the whole father is emancipated upon the deceased, provided the one-third suffices—because his acceptance is like the acceptance of the deceased, as if the deceased owned him during his lifetime.

And if someone bequeaths to him half of his nephew, and he dies before acceptance, and his brother inherits it and accepts—does the extension apply upon the acceptor, since he is his son? There are two views. The view preventing extension is that the acceptance first effects ownership for the deceased, then it transfers to him by compulsion.

These two views apply to every ownership acquired without being intended in itself, as when someone sells a relative of his heir for a garment, then the heir returns the garment due to a defect—a portion of his relative reverts to him incidentally due to the return of the consideration. Likewise, if his mukātib (slave under contract of manumission) becomes insolvent while holding in his hand a portion of the master's relative. And if the mukātib himself becomes insolvent, and a portion of the master's relative reverts to him, the extension does not apply—definitively.

### | The Third Property: The Prohibition of Emancipation During Illness When the One-Third Does Not Suffice

If a sick person emancipates a slave, having no other property, one-third of the slave is free and two-thirds remain enslaved for the heirs. If a comprehensive debt appears against him, the whole slave is sold for the debt. If the slave dies before the master's death, al-Qaffāl said: He dies with one-third free and two-thirds enslaved. It was said: He dies entirely free, because enslavement only occurs where the heirs have a benefit. And it was said: He dies entirely enslaved, because the one-third is only emancipated when the heirs obtain the two-thirds. The utility of this difference appears in the following case: If someone gifts a slave and delivers him, then the donee dies, then the donor dies—the effect of the disagreement appears in the expenses of shrouding and burial (muʾnat al-tajhīz) and upon whom they fall. But if the donee had accepted before the donor's death, he is like the rest, such that he must pay the value exceeding the one-third.

### | Branch

If a sick person emancipates three slaves, having no property other than them, and one dies before the master's death, the authoritative scholars (aṣḥāb) said: The deceased enters the lottery (qurʿah). If the lot falls upon him, the other two remain enslaved. If it falls upon one of the living, only two-thirds of him are emancipated. This is only valid according to al-Qaffāl's choice. As for the one who treats the one who died before the master as non-existent, he cannot accept his inclusion in the lottery. But if one of them dies after the master's death, yet before the heir's hand extends and before the lottery, he enters the lottery. If the lot falls upon him, the other two remain enslaved. If it falls upon one of the remaining two, two-thirds of him are emancipated, and the deceased is not counted—as long as he had not entered the heir's hand. But if he had entered his hand and died before the lottery, there are two views. One: He is counted against him, such that if the lot falls upon one of the living, he is emancipated in full. The second: He is not counted, because he was interdicted from disposition before the lottery—so what benefit is there in the hand?

chapters.title_en: The Fourth Property: The Lot (Qurʿah) — Its Locus and Modality
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الخاصية الرابعة القرعة

والنظر في محلها وكيفيتها
أما محلها فإن أعتق عبيدا معا لا يفي ثلثه بهم فقد أعتق رجل ستة أعبد لا
مال له غيرهم فجزأهم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ثلاثة أجزاء وأقرع بينهم
وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله لا قرعة ويزع عليهم فيعتق من كل واحد ثلثه وهو
القياس ولكن تشوف الشرع إلى تكميل العتق فوجب اتباع الخبر والمذهب أن
القرعة جارية فيما لو أوصى بعتقهم وفيما لو قال الثلث من كل واحد منكم حر
وفيه وجه أن الخبر  إنما ورد في تنجيز العتق على الجميع فلا تلحق به الوصية
ولا صريح التجزئة بل يجري على القياس
أما إذا أعتق على ترتيب فلا خلاف أن السابق يقدم ولا قرعة وأما الوصية
فلا ينظر فيها إلى التقدم والتأخر لأن الموت جامع لوقت العتق وهو واحد نعم
لو دبر عبدا وأوصى بعتق آخر فالمدبر يتصل عتقه بالموت والوصية تقف على
الإنشاء بعده ففيه وجهان
أحدهما تقديم المدبر
والثاني التسوية لأن استحقاق الموصى به يقارب عتق المدبر
فرع في الدور وكيفية الإخراج من الثلث فإذا أعتق ثلاثه أعبد قيمة كل واحد
مائة ولا مال له غيرهم ولكن اكتسب واحد مائة قبل الموت فيقرع بينهم فإن خرج
على المكتسب فلا إشكال وقد عتق وفاز بالكسب ورق الآخران ولو خرج على غيره
عتق ولم يقنع به لأنه يبقى للورثة عبدان ومائة أخرى هي الكسب فيقرع مرة
أخرى بين العبدين الآخرين فإن خرج على غير المكتسب فيعتق منه ثلثه وبه يتم
ثلث أربعمائة إذ مهما رق المكتسب صار المال أربعمائة وإن خرج على المكتسب
وقع الدور لأن كل جزء يعتق منه فيستتبع جزءا من الكسب في مقابلته وينقص
مبلغ الميراث به إذ ما يتبع الجزء يخرج من حساب الميراث فسبيله الجبر
والمقابلة فطريق عمله أن نقول عتق من المكتسب شيء وتبعه مثله لأن الكسب مثل
قيمته ولو كان اكتسب مائتين لقلنا تبعه مثلاه ولو كان اكتسب خمسين لقلنا
تبعه مثل نصفه فإن كان الكسب مائة وتبعه مثله بقي في يد الورثة ثلاثمائة
إلا شيئين إذ أعتقنا شيئا وتبعه مثله وهي تعدل مثلي ما أعتقنا فيكن مائتين
وشيئين أعتقنا مائة وشيئا ففي أيديهم ثلثان إلا شيئين تعدل مائتين وشيئين
فتجبر الثلاث مائة بشيئين فيصير في أيديهم ثلاثمائة تعدل مائتين وأربعة
أشياء فالمائتان بالمائتين قصاص تبقى مائة في مقابلة أربعة أشياء فيكون كل
شيء ربع المائة فقد ظهر لنا أن الذي أعتقنا كان ربع العبد وهو قدر خمس
وعشرين وتبعه من الكسب مثله فتصير خمسين ويبقى في  يد الورثة من بقية الكسب
والعبدين قدر مائتين وخمسين وهو ضعف ما أعتقناه فإنا أعتقنا مائة وخمسا
وعشرين وذلك ما أردنا أن نبين ومهما زادت قيمة عبد فهو ككسبه ولو كانت
جارية فحملت فالحمل كالكسب
الطرف الثاني في كيفية القرعة وكيفية التجزئة أما كيفية القرعة فقد
ذكرناها في كتاب القسمة ويتخير بين أن يكتب اسم العبيد أو يكتب الرق
والحرية ولعل الأسهل أن يكتب اسم الحرية في رقعة والرق في رقعتين وتدرج في
بنادق متساوية وتسلم إلى صبي حتى يعطي كل بعد بندقة وهذا يقطع النزاع في
البداية باسم من تخرج عليه
ولو اتفقوا على أنه إن طار غراب فغانم حر مثلا وإن وضع صبي يده على واحد
فهو حر فذلك لا أثر له بل لا بد من القرعة كما ورد الشرع نعم لا يتعين
الكاغد في الرقعة لكن يجوز بالخشب وغيره وقد أقرع رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم في المغانم مرة بالنوى ومرة بالبعر
أما كيفية التجزئة فإن أعتق ثلاثة أعبد أو ستة وهم متساوو القيمة فيسهل
تجزئتهم بثلاثة أجزاء أما إذا خالفت القيمة العدد فإن أمكن التجزئة إلى
ثلاثة أجزاء بالقيمة فيفعل ولا يبالي بتفاوت العدد حتى لو كانوا أربعة
وقيمة اثنين مائة وقيمة كل واحد من الآخرين مائة جعل الإثنين جزءا واحدا
فإا خرجت لهما القرعة عتقا أما إذا لم يمكن ذلك بأن كانوا ثمانية أعبد مثلا
ولا تنقسم إلى ثلاثة أجزاء إذا تساوت قيمتهم ففيه قولان
أحدهما أنه يجزأ بحيث يقرب من التثليث فيجعل ثلاثة وثلاثة واثنين فإن خرج
على الثلاثة قرعة الحرية لم يعتق جميعهم بل تعاد القرعة بينهم بسهم رق
وسهمي عتق فمن خرج له سهم الرق رق ثلثه وعتق ثلثاه
والثاني أنه يجب التثليث بل يجوز تجزئتهم مثلا أربعة أجزاء سهم عتق
وثلاثة أسهم رق فأي عبدين خرج لهما القرعة بالحرية عتقا ثم تعاد بين الستة
فيجزءون بثلاثة أجزاء ويضرب بينهم سهم عتق وسهما رق فأي عبدين خرج لهما سهم
العتق انحصر  فيهما ثم تعاد بينهما فمن خرج له عتق ثلثاه مع الآخرين والصحيح
أن هذا في الإستحباب وقال الصيدلاني الخلاف في الإستحقاق
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ر-ع (q-r-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: The core meaning is "to cast lots" or "to draw lots" — derived from the notion of striking/pecking (as a bird pecks), indicating a random selection mechanism that severs dispute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological context, the lot is a divinely ordained method of allocation (takhṣīṣ) when claims are equal and indeterminate — it is not a source of entitlement per se but a revealer (muẓhir) of divine decree.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to the physical act of casting marked objects; metaphorical (majāz) extension applies to any fair random selection sanctioned by revelation, even if the physical medium varies.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Ellipsis (al-sharṭ bi-ḥadhf al-jawāb) — In sentences like "if the lot falls upon the earning slave, no problem arises," the apodosis is implied by context, requiring the translator to supply the full conditional structure for clarity.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fourth property is the lot (qurʿah). Consideration is given to its locus (maḥall) and its modality (kayfiyyah).

As for its locus: If a man emancipates slaves jointly, and one-third of his estate does not suffice for all of them — for example, a man emancipated six slaves, having no property other than them — the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) divided them into three portions and cast lots among them. Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him) said: There is no lot; rather, the emancipation is apportioned pro rata, so one-third of each slave is emancipated. This is the analogical reasoning (qiyās). However, the Sacred Law aspired to the completion of emancipation (takmīl al-ʿitq), so following the report (khabar) became obligatory. The established doctrine (madhhab) is that the lot applies in cases of bequest (waṣiyyah) for their emancipation, and in cases where one says: "One-third of each of you is free." There is another view that the report was only transmitted concerning the immediate execution (tanjīz) of emancipation upon all of them, so the bequest and explicit apportionment are not annexed to it; rather, they proceed by analogy.

When emancipation is ordered sequentially, there is no disagreement that the prior one takes precedence and no lot is required. As for bequest, priority and posteriority are not considered therein, because death unifies the time of emancipation, which is a single moment. However, if a man made a tadbīr (contract of emancipation upon death) for one slave and bequeathed the emancipation of another, the mudabbar's emancipation is connected to death, while the bequest awaits its inception (inshāʾ) after death. There are two views on this:
One: The mudabbar is given precedence.
Two: They are treated equally, because the entitlement of the bequeathed one approximates the emancipation of the mudabbar.

A branch on the circularity (dawr) and the method of extraction from the third: If a man emancipates three slaves, each valued at one hundred, having no property other than them, but one of them acquired one hundred before death — then lots are cast among them. If the lot falls upon the earning slave, there is no difficulty: he is emancipated and gains his acquisition, while the other two remain enslaved. If it falls upon another, he is emancipated, but this does not suffice, because two slaves and the one hundred of acquisition remain for the heirs. Lots are cast again between the other two slaves. If it falls upon the non-earning one, one-third of him is emancipated, and thereby one-third of four hundred is completed — for whenever the earning slave remains enslaved, the estate becomes four hundred. If it falls upon the earning slave, circularity occurs, because every portion emancipated from him entails a corresponding portion of the acquisition, and the inheritance amount diminishes thereby — for what follows the portion exits from the inheritance account. Its remedy is algebra and balancing (al-jabr wa-al-muqābalah). The method of its operation is to say: A thing (shayʾ) is emancipated from the earning slave, and its like follows it, because the acquisition equals his value. Had he acquired two hundred, we would say its double follows it; had he acquired fifty, we would say half its like follows it. If the acquisition is one hundred and its like follows it, there remains in the heirs' hands three hundred minus two things — for we emancipated a thing and its like followed it, which equals double what we emancipated. So we have emancipated one hundred and a thing, and in their hands is two-thirds minus two things, equaling two hundred and two things. We balance the three hundred by two things, so in their hands becomes three hundred, equaling two hundred and four things. The two hundred cancels against the two hundred, leaving one hundred against four things, so each thing is one-quarter of one hundred. It has thus become clear to us that what we emancipated was one-quarter of the slave, which is twenty-five, and its like from the acquisition follows it, totaling fifty. There remains in the heirs' hands, from the rest of the acquisition and the two slaves, two hundred and fifty — which is double what we emancipated, for we emancipated one hundred and twenty-five. This is what we intended to clarify. Whenever a slave's value increases, it is like his acquisition; and if a female slave becomes pregnant, the pregnancy is like the acquisition.

The second part: On the modality of the lot and the modality of apportionment. As for the modality of the lot, we have already mentioned it in the Book of Division (qismah). One may choose between writing the names of the slaves or writing "enslavement" (riqq) and "freedom" (ḥurriyyah). Perhaps the easiest is to write "freedom" on one slip and "enslavement" on two slips, roll them into equal-sized balls, and hand them to a child who gives one ball to each — this severs dispute at the outset by the name upon which it falls. If they agreed that "if a crow flies, then Ghānim is free," or "if a child places his hand upon one, he is free," this has no effect; rather, the lot is indispensable, as the Sacred Law has prescribed. However, paper is not mandated for the slip; wood or other materials are permissible. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) cast lots in the spoils (maghānim) once with date-stones and once with camel dung.

As for the modality of apportionment: If one emancipates three or six slaves of equal value, their division into three portions is easy. When value diverges from number, if division into three portions by value is possible, it is done, with no regard to disparity in number — so if there are four slaves, two valued at one hundred and each of the other two at one hundred, the two are made one portion; if the lot falls upon them, both are emancipated. If this is not possible — for example, eight slaves of equal value, which cannot be divided into three equal portions — there are two views:
One: They are divided approximately into thirds, making three, three, and two. If the lot of freedom falls upon the three, not all of them are emancipated; rather, lots are recast among them with one slip of enslavement and two slips of freedom. Whoever draws the enslavement slip — one-third of him remains enslaved and two-thirds are emancipated.
Two: Exact tripartition is not required; rather, they may be divided into four portions — one slip of freedom and three of enslavement. Whichever two slaves draw the freedom slip are emancipated. Then lots are recast among the six, dividing them into three portions, with one freedom slip and two enslavement slips struck among them. Whichever two draw the freedom slip are confined to them, then lots are recast between them; whoever draws it, two-thirds of him is emancipated along with the others. The correct view is that this is recommended (istiḥbāb), while al-Ṣaydalānī held that the disagreement concerns entitlement (istiḥqāq).

chapters.title_en: Section 598 — Branches on Manumission Against Debts and Miscellaneous Sub-Issues
chapters.arabic_text:
### | فرع

إذا كان على الميت دين مستغرق بطل العتق وإن لم يستغرق فالباقي بعد الدين
كأنه كل المال فينفذ العتق بقدر ثلث الباقي وإذا لم يملك إلا عبيدا أعتقهم
فيقرع أولا سهم دين وسهم تركة حتى يتعين بعضهم للدين فيصرف أولا إلى الدين
ثم يقرع للعتق والورثة في
الباقين لأنه ربما يموت من تعين للدين قبل أن يصرف إليه
ولا يجوز أن يكتب رقعة للعتق وأخرى للدين وأخرى للورثة دفعة واحدة لأنه
ربما سبق رقعة العتق ولا يمكن تنفيذه قبل قضاء الدين وفيه وجه أنه يجوز
ثم إذا خرج أولا سهم العتق وقفنا في التنفيذ إلى أن يقضى الدين ثم كيفية
القرعة على الصحيح أن ينظر فإن كان الدين ربع التركة مثلا قسمنا العبيد
أربعة أجزاء وإن كان ثلاثة قسمناهم ثلاثة أجزاء فإذا خرج قرعة الدين لقسم
صرفناه إلى الدين
ثم إذا دفعنا بعض العتق فظهر للميت دين أعدنا القرعة بقدر ما اتسعت
التركة ولا يخفى وجهه

### | النظر الثالث في فروع متفرقة

الأولى إذا أبهم العتق بين جاريتين ثم وطىء إحداهما هل يكون ذلك تعيينا
للملك فيها فيه وجهان ذكرناهما في الطلاق وفي الإستمتاع باللمس والقبلة
وجهان مرتبان وأولى بأن لا يكون تعيينا وفي الإستخدام وجهان مرتبان ويبعد
يجعله تعيينا وبقية أحكام الإبهام ذكرناها في الطلاق
الثاني إذا قال لجاريته أول ولد تلدينه فهو حر فولدت ميتا ثم حيا لم يعتق
الحي وانحلت اليمين بالميت خلافا لأبي حنيفة رحمه الله
الثالث لو قال لعبده أنت ابني ثبت نسبه وعتق إلا أن يكون أكبر سنا منه
فيلغو لأنه ذكر محالا وقال أبو حنيفة رحمه الله يعتق وإن لم يثبت النسب ولو
كان مشهور النسب من غيره لم يثبت النسب وفي العتق وجهان لأن ما صرح به
ممتنع شرعا لا حسا بخلاف من هو أكبر منه
الرابع إذا أعتق الوارث عبدا  من التركة قبل قضاء دين الميت أو باعه فذلك
ينبني على أن تعلق حق الغرم بالتركة كتعلق أرش الجناية أو كتعلق المرتهن أو
يمنع أصل ملك الوارث وفيه ثلاثة أوجه ولعل الأصح أنه إن كان معسرا لم ينفذ
تصرفه وإن كان موسرا فيكون تصرفه كتصرف الراهن
الخامس لو قال إذا أعتقت غانما فسالم حر ثم أعتق غانما وهو مريض وكل واحد
ثلث ماله لم يقرع بينهما بل يعتق غانم لأنه ربما تخرج القرعة على سالم
فيعتق من غير وجود الصفة وهو وجود عتق غانم وفيه وجه أنه يقرع وهو غلط
السادس إذا قال أحد الشريكين إن كان هذا الطائر غرابا فنصيبي حر وقال
الآخر إن لم يكن غرابا فنصيبي حر واستبهم فإن كانا موسرين نفذ عتق العبد إذ
أحدهما حانث وليس لأحدهما أن يطالب الآخر بقيمة السراية وإن كانا معسرين رق
العبد إذ كل واحد يشك في عتق نصيب نفسه والأصل بقاء الملك
فإن اشترى أحدهما نصيب الآخر حكم بعتق نصف العبد إذ تيقن أن في يده نصف
حر وكذا لو اشترى ثالث العبد حكم عليه بحرية نصفه وليس له الرد عليهما ولا
على أحدهما لأن كل واحد يزعم أن نصيبه رقيق وفيه وجه أنه يرد إذا كان جاهلا
وهو فاسد لأن العتق قد نفذ عليه فكيف ينقض
السابع وقف بين يديه غانم وسالم فقال أحدكما حر ثم غاب سالم ووقف ميسر
بجنب غانم فقال أحدكما حر ثم مات قبل البيان وقلنا الوارث لا يقوم مقامه في
التعيين فيقرع بين غانم وسالم فإن خرج على سالم عتق وأقرع بين غانم وميسر
ويعتق من خرج أما إذا خرج أولا على غانم فهل تعاد بينه وبين ميسر فيه وجهان
قال الماسرجسي تعاد لانه أبهم مرتين فيقرع مرتين وقال الأستاذ أبو إسحاق لا
تعاد لأن القرعة كتعيين المالك أو بيانه لما نواه
ولو قال المالك أردت بالإبهامين غانما فقط أو عين غانما عن الإبهامين
لانقطعت المطالبة عنه فينزل الأمر بعد موته على الأول  ويقنع بعتق غانم
الثامن إذا كان له عبدان فقال أعتقت أحدكما على ألف وقبل كل واحد ومات
قبل البيان أقرع بينهما فمن خرج له عتق ولزمه قيمة رقبته لفساد العوض
بالإبهام وفيه وجه أن المسمى أيضا يحتمل الإبهام تبعا للعتق فيلزم الألف
التاسع جارية مشتركة زوجاها من ابن أحد الشريكين فولدت عتق نصفها على أحد
الشريكين لأنه جد المولود ولا يسري عليه لأنه عتق بغير اختياره ولا يجعل
بالإذن في التزويج مختارا وقد تخلل بعد الوطء والعلوق باختيار غيره وقيل
سببه أن الولد ينعقد حرا وإنما يسري العتق الطارىء دون الحرية الأصلية وقد
قيل إنه ينعقد رقيقا ثم يعتق كما لو اشترى قريبه ملكه ثم عتق عليه وعندي
أنه لا يملك بل يندفع الملك بموجب العتق ويكون الإندفاع في معنى الإنقطاع
وكذلك الولد يندفع رقه ولهذا غور ذكرناه في تحصين المآخذ في مسألة شريك
الأب
العاشر المغرور بنكاح الأمة يغرم قيمة الولد للسيد فلو غر بجارية أبيه
ففي لزوم قيمة الولد وجهان
أحدهما أنه لا يجب لأنه يعتق بسبب الجدودة وإن لم يكن ظن المغرور فإنه لو
زوجها من ابنه كان ولده حرا
والثاني أنه يغرم لأن الأب لم يرض بتعرض ولد جاريته للعتق بنكاح ابنه فلا
يفوت عليه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ق-ض-ي (qaḍā)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To settle, fulfill, discharge an obligation; to execute a judgment.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The act of completing what is due, whether by payment (adāʾ) or by legal decree (ḥukm); here, the priority of debt-settlement over testamentary manumission.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) in financial contexts — actual payment; metaphorical (majāz) in legal rulings — judicial determination.
- Root: ق-ر-ع (qurʿah)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: A lot, an arrow used in casting lots; the act of drawing lots.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): A procedural device for resolving ambiguity (ibhām) when rights are indeterminate, akin to divine determination in disputed claims.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — the physical lot; metaphorical — the legal allocation of rights by chance where equity demands.
- Root: ع-ت-ق (ʿitq)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Freedom, liberation from slavery; root denotes purity and release.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Legal manumission, a contract of emancipation that transfers the slave to full legal personhood; restricted by third-party rights (debts, heirs).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal — physical release; metaphorical — legal freedom, often qualified by financial encumbrances.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Syntax (al-sharṭ wa-l-istithnāʾ) — The phrase "if the debt is not exhaustive" (wa-in lam yastaghriq) introduces a conditional clause whose apodosis is governed by the prior ruling; the exceptive "except after the debt" (illā baʿda al-dayn) restricts the operative scope of the estate.
chapters.translation:
### | Branch

If the deceased is burdened by a debt that exhausts the entire estate, the manumission is void. If the debt does not exhaust it, then what remains after the debt is treated as if it were the entire estate, and manumission takes effect to the extent of one-third of the remainder. If he owns nothing but slaves and manumits them, one first casts lots between the share of the debt and the share of the estate, until some of them are designated for the debt. These are then applied first to the debt. Thereafter, lots are cast for manumission and for the heirs among the remaining slaves, because it is possible that the one designated for the debt might die before the debt is paid from him. It is not permissible to write one lot for manumission, another for the debt, and another for the heirs all at once, because the lot for manumission might come out first, and it cannot be executed before the debt is settled. There is one view (wajh) that this is permissible. Then, if the lot for manumission comes out first, we suspend execution until the debt is paid. As for the manner of casting lots, the correct view (al-ṣaḥīḥ) is this: one looks — if the debt is, for example, one-fourth of the estate, we divide the slaves into four parts; if it is one-third, we divide them into three parts. When the lot for the debt falls upon a particular portion, we apply it to the debt. Then, if after we have paid some of the manumission, a debt of the deceased becomes apparent, we repeat the casting of lots to the extent that the estate has expanded (i.e., the newly discovered debt reduces the available remainder). The rationale for this is not hidden.

### | Third Consideration: Miscellaneous Sub-Issues

**First:** If a man ambiguously manumits one of two slave-girls, then has intercourse with one of them — is this a specification (taʿyīn) of her ownership (i.e., that she is the one manumitted)? There are two views (wajhān), which we mentioned in the Book of Divorce (al-ṭalāq). Regarding enjoyment by touch and kissing, there are two ranked views, and it is more apt that this not constitute specification. Regarding employing her in service, there are two ranked views, and it is far-fetched to make it a specification. The remaining rulings on ambiguity (ibhām) we have mentioned in the Book of Divorce.

**Second:** If a man says to his slave-girl, "Any child you give birth to is free," and she gives birth to a stillborn child, then a living one — the living child is not manumitted, and the oath is dissolved by the stillbirth. This contradicts Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him.

**Third:** If a man says to his slave, "You are my son," his lineage is established and he is manumitted — unless the slave is older than him in age, in which case it is void, because he has mentioned something impossible. Abū Ḥanīfah, may God have mercy on him, said: He is manumitted even if lineage is not established. If the slave's lineage is well-known to belong to someone else, lineage is not established, and regarding manumission there are two views, because what he explicitly stated is legally impossible (mumtaniʿ sharʿan), not physically impossible — unlike the case of one who is older than him.

**Fourth:** If an heir manumits a slave from the estate before the deceased's debt is settled, or sells him, this hinges on whether the creditors' right over the estate is like the attachment of the indemnity for injury (arsh al-jināyah), or like the attachment of a pledgee's right (al-murtahin), or whether it prevents the heir's very ownership. There are three views (awjuh). Perhaps the most correct is: if the heir is insolvent (muʿsir), his disposition does not take effect; if he is solvent (mūsir), his disposition is like that of a pledgor (al-rāhin).

**Fifth:** If a man says, "If I manumit Ghānim, then Sālim is free," and then he manumits Ghānim while he is terminally ill, and each one is one-third of his wealth — we do not cast lots between them. Rather, Ghānim is manumitted, because the lot might fall upon Sālim, and he would be manumitted without the existence of the condition (which is the manumission of Ghānim). There is one view that lots are cast, but this is erroneous.

**Sixth:** If one of two co-owners says, "If this bird is a crow, then my share is free," and the other says, "If it is not a crow, then my share is free," and the matter remains ambiguous — if both are solvent, the slave is manumitted, because one of them has certainly broken his oath, and neither may demand from the other the value of the manumission's spread (sirāyah). If both are insolvent, the slave remains enslaved, because each one doubts the manumission of his own share, and the default principle is the continuation of ownership. If one of them purchases the other's share, the half of the slave is judged to be free, because it is certain that in his possession there is a half that is free. Likewise, if a third party purchases the slave, he is judged to have half of him free, and he has no right to return him to both or to either one, because each claims that his share is enslaved. There is one view that he may return him if he was ignorant, but this is corrupt, because manumission has already taken effect upon him — how could it be annulled?

**Seventh:** Ghānim and Sālim were placed before him, and he said, "One of you two is free." Then Sālim disappeared, and a destitute person (maysar) was placed beside Ghānim, and he said, "One of you two is free." Then he died before clarification. We hold that the heir does not stand in his place for specification (taʿyīn). So lots are cast between Ghānim and Sālim. If the lot falls upon Sālim, he is manumitted, and lots are cast between Ghānim and Maysar, and the one upon whom it falls is manumitted. But if the lot first falls upon Ghānim, is a second lot cast between him and Maysar? There are two views. Al-Māsarjisī said: It is repeated, because he expressed ambiguity twice, so lots are cast twice. Al-Ustādh Abū Isḥāq said: It is not repeated, because the lot is like the specification of the owner or his clarification of what he intended. If the owner had said, "By both ambiguities I intended only Ghānim," or he specified Ghānim for both ambiguities, then the claim against him would be cut off, and the matter after his death would rest upon the first (intention), and one would be satisfied with the manumission of Ghānim.

**Eighth:** If a man has two slaves and says, "I have manumitted one of you for a thousand (dirhams)," and each one accepts, and he dies before clarification — lots are cast between them. The one upon whom the lot falls is manumitted, and he is liable for the value of his person (qīmat raqabah), because the consideration is corrupted by the ambiguity. There is one view that the named sum (al-musammā) also admits of ambiguity, following the manumission, so the thousand is obligatory.

**Ninth:** A jointly-owned slave-girl is married by one co-owner to his son, and she gives birth. Half of her is manumitted upon the co-owner (the father), because he is the grandfather of the newborn. But this manumission does not spread (lā yasrī) to the other half, because it occurred without his choice, and he is not deemed to have chosen it by authorizing the marriage. Moreover, the intercourse and conception occurred by the choice of another. It is said that the cause is that the child is conceived free, and only a supervening manumission spreads, not original freedom. It is also said that the child is conceived enslaved, then manumitted — just as if a man purchases his kinsman, he owns him, then he is manumitted upon him. In my view, he does not own him at all; rather, ownership is repelled by the exigency of manumission, and this repulsion is in the sense of cessation. Likewise, the child's enslavement is repelled. This is a subtle point (ghawr) which we mentioned in Taḥṣīn al-Maʾākhidh regarding the case of the father's co-owner.

**Tenth:** The one deceived (al-maghrūr) by a marriage to a slave-girl must pay the value of the child to the master. If he was deceived regarding his father's slave-girl, there are two views on whether the child's value is obligatory:
- One view: It is not obligatory, because the child is manumitted by virtue of grandfatherhood (judūdah), even if the deceived one did not intend this. For if the father had married her to his son, the child would have been free.
- The second view: He must pay, because the father did not consent to his slave-girl's child being subjected to manumission through his son's marriage, so the value is not lost upon him.

chapters.title_en: The Fifth Attribute: Patronage (Walāʾ) — Its Cause, Ruling, and Branches
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الخاصية الخامسة الولاء

والنظر في سببه وحكمه وفروعه
الأول في السبب وسببه زوال الملك بالحرية فكل من زال ملكه عن رقيق
بالحرية فهو مولاه سواء نجز أو علق أو دبر أو كاتب فتمت الكتابة أو استولد
فمات أو أعتق العبد بعوض أو اشترى قريبه فعتق عليه أو ورثه فعتق عليه قرها
أو سرى عتقه إلى نصيب شركه وسواء اتفق الدين عند العتق أو اختلف
ولو باع عبده من نفسه فالظاهر أيضا أن الولاء له وفيه وجه أن لا ولاء له
في هذه الصورة أصلا
وأما حقيقة الولاء فهو لحمة كلحمة النسب كما قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم فلذلك نقول لو شرط في العتق نفي الولاء أو شرطه لغيره أو  شرطه لبيت
المال لغا شرطه وهذا لأن المعتق كالأب فإنه سبب في وجود العبد إذ كان العبد
مفقودا لنفسه موجودا لسيده فقد أوجده
لنفسه بالعتق ولذلك قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لن يجزي ولد والده
حتى يجده مملوكا فيشتريه فيعتقه لأنه إذا أعتقه فقد كافأه على الأبوة إذ
صار سببا لوجوده الحكمي كما كان الأب سببا لوجوده الحسي ولهذا قال بعض
الأصحاب تحرم الصدقة على موالي بني هاشم وإذا أوصى لبني فلان دخل فيهم
مواليهم ولهذا نقلو لا يثبت الولاء بالمخالفة والموالاة خلافا لأبي حنيفة
رحمه الله لأن الولاء ثمرة الإنعام بالإيجاد الحكمي فلا يحصل بالمعاقدة
ولذلك نقول يسترسل ولاء المعتق على أولاد العتيق وأحفاده وعلى معتق العتيق
ومعتق معتقه وإن سفلوا وقد حصل لك من هذا أن الشخص قد يثبت الولاء عليه
لمعتقه أو لمعتق أصوله من أب وأم وجد وجدة أو لمعتق معتقه ويسترسل الولاء
على سائر أحفاد العتيق إلا في ثلاثة مواضع
الأول أن يكون فيهم من مسه الرق فالولاء عليه لمباشر العتق ولعصابته ولا
ينجر إلى معتق الأصول أصلا
الثاني أن يكون فيهم من أبوه حر أصلي ما مس الرق أباه فلا ولاء على ولده
كما لا ولاء عليه وهو مذهب مالك رحمه الله ومنهم من قال يثبت الولاء نظرا
إلى جانب الأم فإنها في محل الولاء وهو ضعيف لأن جانب الأب مقدم في باب
الولاء كما سيأتي في الجد وفيه وجه أن أباه إن كان عربيا يعلم نسبه وأن لا
رق في نسبه فلا ولاء عليه وإن حكم بحريته بظاهر الحال كالتركي والخوزي
والنبطي فيثبت الولاء عليه وهذا مذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله
الثالث أن تكون أمه حرة أصلية وإنما المعتق أبوه فالظاهر ها هنا ثبوت
الولاء نظرا إلى جانب الأب وفيه وجه أنه لا يثبت فعلى هذا لا يثبت الولاء
بالسراية من الأصل إلا على ولد ليس في أصوله حر أصلي
هذه قاعدة الولاء والنظر بعده في التقديم والتأخير والأصل فيه أن  من مسه
الرق
فالولاء عليه لمباشر العتق لا لمعتق أبيه ومعتق أمه فإن لم يمسه الرق بأن
يولد حرا من رقيقين في صورة الغرور أو من معتقين فالولاء عليه لموالي الأب
وهو مقدم على موالي الأم فإن كان الأب رقيقا بعد لا ولاء عليه فالولاء
لموالي الأم إلى أن يعتق الأب فينجر من موالي الأم إلى موالي الأب إلى أن
يتعذر جره إلى موالي الأب بأن يشتري هو أب نفسه فيعتق عليه إذ هو مولى أب
نفسه فلا يمكن إثبات الولاء على نفسه ويبقى الولاء لموالي الأم وقال ابن
سريج ينجر الولاء إليه ويسقط ويصير كشخص لا ولاء عليه أصلا

### | فرعان

أحدهما لو كان الأب رقيقا فأعتق أب الأب ففي انجرار الولاء إليه وجهان
أحدهما لا لأن الأب رقيق فيلزم أن ينجر من موالي الجد إلى موالي الأب إذا
أعتق والمنجر ينبغي أن يستقر ولا ينجر ثانيا
والثاني وهو الأصح أنه ينجر إليه ثم ينجر إلى الأب وليس يشترط استقرار
المنجر
ولو أن مولودا ما مسه الرق وهو من أبوين ما مسهما الرق لكن لكل واحد من
أبويه أبوان رقيقان إلا أم أمه فإنها معتقة فالولاء فيه تبع لولاء أمه
وولاء أمه تبع لولاء أمها فإن أعتق أب أمه انجر الولاء إلى موالي أب الأم
فإن أعتقت أم الأب انجر الولاء إلى موالي أم أمه فإن أعتق أبو أبيه انجر
إلى موالي أب أبيه واستقر فيه
فإن فرضنا الأب رقيقا تصور أن ينجر إلى معتق الأب من معتق الجد أيضا
والمقصود أن أب الأم أولى بالاستتباع من أم الأم وأم الأب أولى من أب الأم
وأب الأب أولى من أم الأب والأب أولى من أب الأب فيقع الإنجرار بحسبه إلى
أن يستقر على ما لا يوجد أولى منه
الفرع الثاني لو أعتق أمة حاملا عتق الجنين وولاء الجنين لموالي الأم لا
لموالي أبيه لأنه عتق بالمباشرة فالمباشرة أولى لمباشرته لا لأنه مولى أمه
وهذا إذا علم أن الجنين كان موجودا  يوم الإعتاق بأن يؤتى به لأقل من ستة
اشهر فإن كان لأقل من أربع سنين بحيث يفترشها الزوج ففيه قولان ذكرنا
نظيرهما في مواضع من حيث إن إثبات النسب يدل على تقدير وجوده وقت العتق
ولكن يجوز أن يكتفي في النسب بالإحتمال ولا يكتفي في الولاية

- Root: و-ل-ي (W-L-Y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is proximity and adjacency (qurb); walāʾ denotes the bond of clientage established through manumission, a relationship of inheritance and mutual support.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, walāʾ is a juristic filiation (nasab ḥukmī) created by the act of freeing a slave, transferring the right of inheritance from the freed person to the manumitter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Used literally (ḥaqīqah) for the legal bond of patronage; metaphorically (majāz) for alliance or friendship, but in this juristic context it is a fixed technical reality.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional and Exceptive Constructions (al-Sharṭ wa al-Istithnāʾ) — The text employs intricate conditional clauses (e.g., "if he is freed... then...") and exceptions ("except in three places") requiring precise parsing to track the logical flow of legal causation.
chapters.translation:
I say: The fifth attribute is patronage (walāʾ). Our inquiry concerns its cause, its ruling, and its branches.

**The First: On Its Cause.** Its cause is the removal of ownership through freedom. Thus, whoever's ownership over a slave is removed by the slave's freedom is his patron (mawlā), whether that freedom was immediate, conditional, through tadbīr (deferred manumission after the master's death), through kitābah (manumission by contract) that was completed, through istīlād (the master's death after begetting a child on his slave-woman), through the slave's redemption of himself for a compensation, through the master purchasing his own relative who then becomes free by his ownership, through inheriting a relative who then becomes free by his ownership, or through the master's act of freeing a share of a jointly-owned slave, whereby the freedom extends (sarā) to the other partner's share. It is equal whether the religion of the parties agreed at the time of manumission or differed. If he sold his slave to himself, the apparent ruling is that patronage belongs to him; yet there is a legal opinion (wajh) that no patronage exists in this scenario at all.

**As for the Reality of Patronage:** It is a bond of flesh (luḥmah) akin to the bond of lineage, as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said. Therefore, we declare: if one stipulates in the manumission the negation of patronage, or stipulates it for another, or stipulates it for the public treasury, his stipulation is void. This is because the manumitter is like a father, for he is a cause of the slave's existence — since the slave was non-existent for himself but existent for his master — and he has brought him into existence for himself through manumission. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A son cannot repay his father unless he finds him as a slave, buys him, and frees him." For when he frees him, he has requited him for his fatherhood, since he became a cause of his juristic existence (wujūd ḥukmī) just as the father was a cause of his sensory existence (wujūd ḥissī). Hence, some of our companions (al-aṣḥāb) said: charity (ṣadaqah) is forbidden to the clients (mawālī) of the Banū Hāshim. And when one bequeaths to "the Banū so-and-so," their clients are included therein. For this reason, they transmitted that patronage is not established through a contract of alliance (mukhālafah) or mutual clientage (muwālāh), contrary to Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him), because patronage is the fruit of beneficence through juristic creation, so it cannot be obtained by a mere contractual agreement.

Therefore, we say: the patronage of the manumitter extends (yastarsil) to the children of the freed person, his grandchildren, and to the manumitter of the freed person, and the manumitter of his manumitter, however far down they descend. From this, you have learned that a person may have patronage established over him for his own manumitter, or for the manumitter of his ancestors — father, mother, grandfather, or grandmother — or for the manumitter of his manumitter. And patronage extends over all the descendants of the freed person, except in three situations:

**The First:** That among them there is one whom slavery has touched (massahu al-riqq). Patronage over him belongs to the one who directly manumitted him and to his ʿaṣabah (agnatic heirs), and it does not transfer at all to the manumitter of his ancestors.

**The Second:** That among them there is one whose father is a free-born person (ḥurr aṣlī) whom slavery never touched his father. Then there is no patronage over his son, just as there is no patronage over him. This is the doctrine of Mālik (may Allah have mercy on him). Among them is one who said: patronage is established, considering the mother's side, for she is in the locus of patronage. But this is weak, because the father's side takes precedence in matters of patronage, as will come in the discussion of the grandfather. There is also a legal opinion (wajh) that if his father was an Arab whose lineage is known and there is no slavery in his ancestry, then no patronage is over him. But if his freedom is established only by outward appearance (ẓāhir al-ḥāl), like a Turk, a Khūzī, or a Nabatean, then patronage is established over him. This is the doctrine of Abū Ḥanīfah (may Allah have mercy on him).

**The Third:** That his mother is a free-born person, and only his father is the freed one. The apparent ruling here is the establishment of patronage, considering the father's side. There is a legal opinion (wajh) that it is not established. Thus, on this basis, patronage is not established through the extension (sarāyah) from the origin except over a child in whose ancestry there is no free-born person at all.

This is the foundational rule of patronage. After this, our inquiry concerns precedence and postponement. The principle therein is: whoever is touched by slavery, patronage over him belongs to the one who directly manumitted him, not to the manumitter of his father or the manumitter of his mother. If slavery did not touch him — i.e., he was born free from two slaves in the case of deception (ghurūr), or from two freed persons — then patronage over him belongs to the clients of the father, and they take precedence over the clients of the mother. If the father is still a slave, there is no patronage over him, so patronage belongs to the clients of the mother until the father is freed, whereupon it transfers from the clients of the mother to the clients of the father — until its transfer to the clients of the father becomes impossible, such as when the son purchases his own father and the father becomes free by his ownership, for he is the patron of his own father, and it is impossible to establish patronage over oneself. In that case, patronage remains with the clients of the mother. Ibn Surayj said: it transfers to him and then falls away, and he becomes like a person over whom there is no patronage at all.

### Two Subsidiary Branches

**The First:** If the father was a slave, and then the father's father was freed, there are two legal opinions (wajhān) regarding whether patronage transfers to him. One: it does not, because the father is a slave, so it would necessitate that it transfers from the clients of the grandfather to the clients of the father when he is freed — but the transferred thing should settle and not transfer a second time. The second — and this is the more correct (al-aṣaḥḥ) — is that it transfers to him, then transfers to the father, and it is not a condition that the transferred thing settles.

If a newborn was never touched by slavery, and his two parents were never touched by slavery, but each of his two parents has two parents who are slaves — except his maternal grandmother, who is a freed woman — then his patronage follows the patronage of his mother, and his mother's patronage follows the patronage of her mother. If the mother's father is freed, patronage transfers to the clients of the mother's father. If the father's mother is freed, patronage transfers to the clients of the father's mother. If the father's father is freed, patronage transfers to the clients of the father's father and settles there.

If we suppose the father is a slave, it is conceivable that it transfers to the manumitter of the father from the manumitter of the grandfather as well. The point is that the mother's father is more entitled to be followed than the mother's mother; the father's mother is more entitled than the mother's father; the father's father is more entitled than the father's mother; and the father is more entitled than the father's father. Thus, the transfer occurs accordingly until it settles upon one above whom no one more entitled exists.

**The Second Branch:** If a man freed a pregnant slave-woman, the fetus is freed as well, and the patronage of the fetus belongs to the clients of the mother, not to the clients of his father — because he was freed by direct manumission (mubāsharah), and direct action takes precedence for its doer, not because he is the client of his mother. This applies when it is known that the fetus existed on the day of manumission — i.e., she gives birth less than six months after the manumission. If she gives birth after less than four years, such that the husband could have had intercourse with her, then there are two rulings (qawlān), the likes of which we have mentioned in other places: the establishment of lineage (nasab) indicates the presumption of his existence at the time of manumission, but it is permissible that probability suffices for lineage while it does not suffice for patronage.

chapters.title_en: The Second Investigation on the Rulings of Patronage (Walāʾ)

### | النظر الثاني في أحكام الولاء

وهي ثلاثة ولاية التزويج وتحمل العقل والوراثة لأن الولاء يفيد العصوبة
وهذه نتائج العصوبة وقد ذكرناها في مواضع ولكن ننبه الآن في الميراث على
أمور
الأول أن المعتق إذا مات ولم يخلف إلا أب المعتق وأمه فلا شيء للأم ولو
خلف ابن المعتق وبنته فلا شيء للبنت ولو خلف أب المعتق وابنه فلا شيء للأب
لأن الأب ليس عصبة مع الإبن والميراث لعصبة المعتق ولا يعصب الأخ أخته في
باب الولاء وعلى الجملة فالولاء يورث به ولا يورث في نفسه وإنما يرث به
العصبات فيقد رموت المعتق بدل موت العتيق يوم موت العتيق وكل من يأخذ
ميراثه بعصوبته فيأخذ ميراث عتيقه ولا يستثنى عن هذا إلا الجد والإخوة فإن
فيهم قولين
أحدهما أن أخ المعتق يقدم على جده لقوة البنوة في العصوبة
والثاني أنهم يتقاسمون كما في ميراث النسب لكن لا معادة بالأخ للأب مع
الجد بل يقدم عليه الأخ للأب ولا يعاد عليه الأخ للأب وهذا مذهب زيد وفيه
وجه أن الأخ للأب يساوي الأخ للأب والأم لأنه لا أثر للأمومة في الولاء
الثاني أن المرأة لا يتصور أن ترث بالولاء إلا إذا باشرت العتق فهي
كالرجل في المباشرة حيث ثبت لها الولاء على عتيقها وعلى أولاد عتيقها وعلى
عتيق عتيقها
الثالث لو خلف رجل ابنين وولاء مولى فالولاء لهما فإن مات أحدهما عن ابن
ثم مات العتيق فميراثه لابن المعتق وليس لابن الإبن شيء لأنه لو قدر موت
المعتق في ذلك الوقت ما ورثه ابن الإبن فلا يرث عتيقه وهو معنى قولهم
الولاء لأقعد ولد المعتق أي الأقرب
الرابع أن النسبة قد تتركب من النسب والعتق فيلتبس  أمره التقديم والتأخير
فقد يثبت الولاء لأب معتق الأب ولمعتق أب المعتق وينبغي أن يقدم معتق الميت
ثم عصبات معتقه ثم معتق معتقه
ولو قيل لك معتق أب وأب معتق فأيهما أولى فهذه أغلوطة فإن الميت له معتق
فولاؤه ولمعتقه وعصبات معتقه فلا يكون لمعتق أبيه وأمه حق فيه فإن ولاء
المباشرة لا ينجر وإنما ينجر ولاء السراية إلى الأولاء فإذن من له أب معتق
فالولاء عليه كان بالمباشرة لمعتقه أو لعصبات معتقه أو لمعتق معتقه إذا كان
له معتق وليس لمعتق أبيه ولاء أصلا فكيف يقابل بأب المعتق وكذلك قد يظن أنه
معتق أب المعتق أولى من معتق معتق المعتق لأنه يدلي بالولاية حيث توسط الأب
وهو غلط لما ذكرناه من أن للميت معتقا فولاؤه بالمباشرة فلا حق فيه لمن
يدلي بإعتاق أبيه

### | فروع مشكلة
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ل-ي (W-L-Y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is proximity, closeness, and assuming authority over another's affairs; walāʾ denotes the bond of clientage established through manumission.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In legal-theological terms, walāʾ is a fictive kinship tie (ṣilat al-riqq al-munqaṭiʿ) that transfers inheritance rights and agnatic solidarity (ʿuṣūbah) from the freed slave to the manumitter.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage refers to actual proximity; metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to legal patronage, where the freed slave's lineage is "attached" to the patron's family.
- Root: ع-ص-ب (ʿ-S-B)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root denotes binding tightly; ʿaṣabah refers to male agnates who inherit through their own personhood (bi-nafsihi) and absorb residual shares.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In inheritance law, ʿuṣūbah is the principle of agnatic succession that excludes females and non-agnates from residual inheritance.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal meaning is "binding" (as in a bundle); metaphorical usage in law denotes the "binding" of inheritance rights to the nearest male relative.
- Sībawayh Rule: Conditional Clause with Implied Protasis (al-sharṭ bi-ḥadhf al-jawāb) — In "لو قدر موت المعتق في ذلك الوقت ما ورثه ابن الإبن", the protasis (law qaddira) is followed by an apodosis (mā warithahu) that is semantically complete, requiring the reader to supply the implied consequence for the legal ruling.
chapters.translation:
I say: The second investigation concerns the rulings of patronage (walāʾ). These are three: the authority of marriage (wilāyat al-tazwīj), the bearing of blood-wit (ḥaml al-ʿaql), and inheritance (irth). This is because patronage confers agnatic solidarity (ʿuṣūbah), and these are the consequences of agnatic solidarity. We have already mentioned these in their proper places, but now we shall draw attention to several matters concerning inheritance.

The first: If the manumitter (al-muʿtiq) dies leaving only the father of the manumitter and his mother, then the mother receives nothing. If he leaves the son of the manumitter and his daughter, then the daughter receives nothing. If he leaves the father of the manumitter and his son, then the father receives nothing — because the father is not an agnate (ʿaṣabah) alongside the son. The inheritance goes to the agnates of the manumitter. The brother does not act as an agnate for his sister in the domain of patronage. In sum, patronage is inherited through (yūrathu bihi) but is not itself inherited (lā yūrathu fī nafsihi). Only agnates inherit through it. Thus, one should imagine the death of the manumitter as a substitute for the death of the freed slave (al-ʿatīq) on the day of the freed slave's death. Everyone who takes his inheritance through his own agnatic bond takes the inheritance of his freed slave. No exception is made to this except for the grandfather and the brothers, concerning whom there are two opinions (qawlān):

One of them: The brother of the manumitter is given precedence over his grandfather, due to the strength of sonship (al-bunūwah) in agnatic solidarity.

The second: They divide the inheritance between them, as in the case of inheritance by lineage (irth al-nasab). However, there is no equalization (muʿādāh) of the brother by the father with the grandfather. Rather, the brother by the father is given precedence over the grandfather, and the grandfather is not made equal to the brother by the father. This is the school of Zayd. There is also a view (wajh) that the brother by the father equals the brother by the father and mother, because motherhood has no effect in patronage.

The second: A woman cannot be conceived of inheriting through patronage except if she herself performed the manumission. She is like a man in direct performance (mubāsharah), where patronage is established for her over her freed slave, over the children of her freed slave, and over the freed slave of her freed slave.

The third: If a man leaves two sons and the patronage of a freed slave, then the patronage belongs to both of them. If one of them dies leaving a son, and then the freed slave dies, his inheritance goes to the son of the manumitter, and the son of the son receives nothing. This is because if one imagined the death of the manumitter at that time, the son of the son would not inherit from him, so he does not inherit from his freed slave. This is the meaning of their statement: "Patronage belongs to the nearest (aqʿad) descendant of the manumitter," i.e., the closest.

The fourth: Lineage may be compounded from both kinship (nasab) and manumission (ʿitq), such that the matter of precedence and postponement becomes confused. Thus, patronage may be established for the father of the manumitter's manumitter, and for the manumitter of the manumitter's father. The correct order is: the manumitter of the deceased should be given precedence, then the agnates of his manumitter, then the manumitter of his manumitter.

If it is said to you: "A man has a manumitted father (muʿtiq ab) and a father who is a manumitter (ab muʿtiq) — which of the two is more deserving?" This is a trick question (aghlūṭah). For the deceased has a manumitter, so his patronage belongs to him, and to the agnates of his manumitter, and to the manumitter of his manumitter. Thus, the manumitter of his father and his mother have no right in it. This is because the patronage of direct performance (walāʾ al-mubāsharah) does not transfer (lā yanjur), whereas the patronage of propagation (walāʾ al-sirāyah) transfers to the first patrons (al-awlāʾ). Therefore, whoever has a manumitted father — the patronage over him belongs, through direct performance, to his manumitter, or to the agnates of his manumitter, or to the manumitter of his manumitter, if he has a manumitter. The manumitter of his father has no patronage at all — so how can he be compared to the manumitter of the deceased? Likewise, one might suppose that the manumitter of the manumitter's father is more deserving than the manumitter of the manumitter's manumitter, because he claims through patronage where the father is an intermediary. This is an error, for the reason we mentioned: the deceased has a manumitter, so his patronage belongs to him through direct performance, and no one who claims through the manumission of his father has any right in it.

### Problematic Branches (Furūʿ Mushkilah)
